question: A 5-year-old boy presents with a 4-day history of unilateral painful vesicular rash on his right flank in the T9 dermatome distribution. He had chickenpox at age 2. Per NICE CKS, what is the diagnosis and management?

options.A: Bullous impetigo — flucloxacillin
options.B: Shingles (herpes zoster) — reactivation of latent varicella-zoster virus; uncommon in children but can occur after primary varicella, especially if first infection was in infancy; oral aciclovir 20 mg/kg four times daily for 5 days for immunocompetent children if presenting within 72 hours of rash onset; analgesia; assess for safeguarding/immunocompromise as a trigger
options.C: Contact dermatitis — topical hydrocortisone
options.D: Scabies — permethrin 5%
options.E: Eczema herpeticum — IV aciclovir

explanation.correct: Shingles in children is uncommon but recognised, especially when primary varicella occurred in infancy. The unilateral dermatomal vesicular rash that does not cross the midline is diagnostic. Treatment with oral aciclovir within 72 hours reduces severity and post-herpetic neuralgia risk. Children with shingles should be assessed for underlying immunosuppression if there are atypical features (multi-dermatomal, disseminated, recurrent). Post-herpetic neuralgia is rare in children but does occur.
explanation.A: Incorrect — Bullous impetigo causes flaccid bullae filled with cloudy fluid, typically on the face/limbs, not dermatomal vesicles.
explanation.B: CORRECT — Shingles: unilateral dermatomal vesicular rash. Oral aciclovir if within 72 hours per NICE CKS.
explanation.C: Incorrect — Contact dermatitis has a distribution matching the contactant — not dermatomal vesicles.
explanation.D: Incorrect — Scabies causes burrows and intensely itchy papules, classically in web spaces and wrists.
explanation.E: Incorrect — Eczema herpeticum is HSV superinfection of eczema-affected skin, presenting with widespread punched-out lesions, not dermatomal vesicles.

reference: NICE CKS — Shingles. https://cks.nice.org.uk/topics/shingles/

question: A 5-year-old child with shingles attends nursery. The parents ask when he can return. Per UKHSA guidance, what is the correct advice on exclusion from school/nursery?

options.A: Exclude for 21 days from rash onset
options.B: Child should stay off nursery until the lesions are crusted over (typically 5-7 days from onset); if all lesions can be securely covered with clothing or dressings, attendance may be possible; advise avoidance of contact with pregnant women without varicella immunity, neonates and immunocompromised individuals until lesions have crusted
options.C: No exclusion required — shingles is not contagious
options.D: Exclude until the rash completely heals (2-3 weeks)
options.E: Exclude only if antiviral therapy is being given

explanation.correct: Per UKHSA (PHE) Health protection in schools and other childcare facilities guidance, children with shingles can return to school/nursery once lesions have crusted, OR if all lesions can be covered. Shingles is contagious through direct contact with vesicle fluid (can cause primary varicella in non-immune contacts, NOT shingles). Key exclusion until crusted: from pregnant women (varicella in pregnancy risks congenital varicella syndrome and severe maternal pneumonitis), neonates (severe disease risk), and immunocompromised individuals.
explanation.A: Incorrect — 21 days is the incubation period for varicella — not a school exclusion duration for shingles.
explanation.B: CORRECT — Off until lesions crusted (or covered); avoid pregnant women, neonates, immunocompromised per UKHSA.
explanation.C: Incorrect — Shingles vesicle fluid contains live virus and can transmit primary varicella to non-immune contacts.
explanation.D: Incorrect — Full healing may take weeks; exclusion only required until lesions crust.
explanation.E: Incorrect — Exclusion is based on infectivity (lesion stage), not on whether antivirals are prescribed.

reference: UKHSA — Health protection in schools and other childcare facilities. https://www.gov.uk/government/publications/health-protection-in-schools-and-other-childcare-facilities

question: A 6-year-old boy with no significant past history presents with his third episode of shingles in 18 months, each in a different dermatome. Per NICE CKS, what is the most important next step?

options.A: Reassure — multiple shingles episodes are common in children
options.B: Investigate for underlying immunosuppression — recurrent shingles (especially multi-dermatomal or frequent episodes) in a child warrants urgent investigation for an underlying immunodeficiency or haematological malignancy (HIV, leukaemia, lymphoma, primary immunodeficiency); arrange FBC, blood film, HIV test, immunoglobulins; paediatric referral
options.C: Start prophylactic aciclovir indefinitely
options.D: Increase frequency of varicella vaccination
options.E: Recommend avoidance of school until further notice

explanation.correct: Recurrent shingles in childhood is uncommon and is a red flag for underlying immunosuppression. Per NICE CKS, investigate for: HIV infection, haematological malignancy (especially leukaemia and lymphoma — both well recognised to present with VZV reactivation), primary immunodeficiency. Baseline investigations: FBC and blood film (looking for blasts, cytopenia, lymphocytosis), HIV test, immunoglobulins, urgent paediatric referral. A single episode of shingles in a healthy child can occur normally, but recurrence demands investigation. Frequent or atypical shingles is also recognised as a presenting feature of childhood leukaemia.
explanation.A: Incorrect — Recurrent shingles in children is NOT common and requires investigation.
explanation.B: CORRECT — Recurrent paediatric shingles: investigate immunosuppression/malignancy. FBC, HIV, immunoglobulins, paediatric referral per NICE CKS.
explanation.C: Incorrect — Long-term prophylactic aciclovir does not address the underlying cause.
explanation.D: Incorrect — Varicella vaccination is not a treatment for established VZV reactivation.
explanation.E: Incorrect — School avoidance is only required for active vesicular lesions until they crust.

reference: NICE CKS — Shingles. NICE NG12 — Suspected cancer. https://cks.nice.org.uk/topics/shingles/

question: A 6-year-old girl presents with bright red cheeks ('slapped cheek' appearance) and mild lacy rash on her arms. She has been mildly unwell with low-grade fever for 2 days. Per NICE CKS, what is the diagnosis and what is the most concerning maternal exposure scenario?

options.A: Measles — measure measles IgM
options.B: Erythema infectiosum (slapped cheek, parvovirus B19); maternal exposure in pregnancy (especially before 20 weeks) carries risk of fetal hydrops, fetal anaemia, and miscarriage from parvovirus B19 crossing the placenta and infecting fetal erythroid precursors; pregnant contacts must have urgent maternal serology (parvovirus B19 IgM and IgG) and obstetric referral if non-immune
options.C: Rubella — measure rubella IgM
options.D: Scarlet fever — penicillin V
options.E: Roseola — supportive care

explanation.correct: Erythema infectiosum (fifth disease, slapped cheek syndrome): caused by parvovirus B19. Classic presentation in school-age children: bright red 'slapped cheek' appearance, then lacy reticular rash on trunk and limbs. Often follows a prodrome of mild systemic symptoms. By the time the rash appears the child is no longer infectious (transmission occurs in the prodromal phase). Maternal exposure during pregnancy is the most clinically significant concern: parvovirus B19 infects fetal erythroid precursors causing severe fetal anaemia, hydrops fetalis (3-9% risk before 20 weeks), and increased miscarriage risk. Pregnant contacts: check IgM and IgG; if non-immune and recently exposed, refer to obstetrics for fetal monitoring (serial USS for hydrops, MCA Doppler).
explanation.A: Incorrect — Measles causes a generalised maculopapular rash with Koplik spots and severe systemic illness, not a slapped cheek appearance.
explanation.B: CORRECT — Slapped cheek (parvovirus B19): maternal exposure carries risk of fetal hydrops/anaemia. Serology + obstetric referral if non-immune.
explanation.C: Incorrect — Rubella causes fine pink maculopapular rash with lymphadenopathy; appearance is different and rare due to MMR.
explanation.D: Incorrect — Scarlet fever causes sandpaper rash, strawberry tongue and pharyngitis, not isolated slapped cheek.
explanation.E: Incorrect — Roseola (HHV-6) causes high fever in infants followed by rash after fever resolves, not slapped cheek.

reference: NICE CKS — Parvovirus B19 infection. RCOG — Parvovirus in pregnancy. https://cks.nice.org.uk/topics/parvovirus-b19-infection/

question: A 4-year-old child has facial rash typical of slapped cheek syndrome. Per UKHSA guidance, when is this child infectious and what is the school exclusion advice?

options.A: Infectious throughout the illness — exclude for 14 days
options.B: The child is infectious DURING the prodromal phase (mild flu-like symptoms before the rash); by the time the slapped cheek rash appears, the child is NO LONGER infectious; no school exclusion is required once rash is visible — child may attend school
options.C: Exclude until rash fully resolves (3 weeks)
options.D: Exclude for 5 days from rash onset
options.E: Infectious only after rash appears

explanation.correct: Per UKHSA and NICE CKS, parvovirus B19 is transmitted via respiratory droplets during the prodromal phase (before the rash appears). Once the characteristic slapped cheek rash develops, the child is no longer contagious because circulating virus has been cleared by host antibodies (the rash itself is immune-complex mediated). Therefore: NO school exclusion is required once the rash is visible. This is unlike most other childhood exanthems. Important counselling for contacts: pregnant women, immunocompromised individuals and those with chronic haemolytic anaemias (sickle cell, thalassaemia) who may already have been exposed before the rash should be advised to seek medical assessment, as transmission may have occurred during the prodromal phase.
explanation.A: Incorrect — Patients are NOT infectious during the rash phase.
explanation.B: CORRECT — Infectious in prodrome only; no school exclusion required once rash visible per UKHSA.
explanation.C: Incorrect — No exclusion required at all once rash is visible.
explanation.D: Incorrect — No exclusion required from rash onset.
explanation.E: Incorrect — The opposite is true — patients are infectious BEFORE rash, not after.

reference: UKHSA — Health protection in schools. NICE CKS — Parvovirus B19. https://cks.nice.org.uk/topics/parvovirus-b19-infection/

question: A 28-year-old pregnant woman at 14 weeks gestation is exposed to her nephew who has confirmed slapped cheek syndrome. Per RCOG and UKHSA guidance, what is the management?

options.A: Reassure — parvovirus has no effect on pregnancy
options.B: Urgent maternal serology: parvovirus B19 IgM and IgG; if IgG positive and IgM negative — immune, reassure; if IgM positive (acute infection) or IgG/IgM negative and recent exposure — refer to fetal medicine for serial USS surveillance for fetal hydrops and middle cerebral artery (MCA) Doppler peak systolic velocity monitoring for fetal anaemia; intrauterine transfusion may be needed for severe fetal anaemia
options.C: Give VZIG immediately
options.D: Terminate the pregnancy
options.E: Vaccinate against parvovirus

explanation.correct: Per RCOG and UKHSA guidance on parvovirus B19 in pregnancy: maternal infection before 20 weeks carries highest risk of fetal hydrops, severe fetal anaemia and miscarriage (overall ~9% risk of fetal loss in first 20 weeks). Approach: (1) Maternal serology — IgM (acute), IgG (immunity); (2) If immune (IgG positive, IgM negative): reassure, no further action; (3) If non-immune or acute infection: refer to fetal medicine; serial ultrasound surveillance (every 1-2 weeks for 12 weeks looking for hydrops); MCA Doppler peak systolic velocity is the best non-invasive marker of fetal anaemia; if severe anaemia detected — intrauterine transfusion via umbilical vein. Most fetuses recover fully if monitored and treated appropriately. There is no parvovirus B19 vaccine. VZIG is for varicella, not parvovirus.
explanation.A: Incorrect — Parvovirus B19 causes significant fetal complications when maternal infection occurs before 20 weeks.
explanation.B: CORRECT — Urgent IgM/IgG; if non-immune, fetal medicine referral for hydrops surveillance + MCA Doppler per RCOG.
explanation.C: Incorrect — VZIG is for varicella zoster, not parvovirus.
explanation.D: Incorrect — Termination is not indicated based on exposure alone; many fetuses recover with monitoring/treatment.
explanation.E: Incorrect — There is no parvovirus B19 vaccine.

reference: RCOG — Parvovirus B19 in pregnancy. UKHSA. https://www.rcog.org.uk/guidance/browse-all-guidance/green-top-guidelines/

question: A 30-week pregnant woman attends her GP after spending 2 hours indoors with her 4-year-old niece who has confirmed chickenpox. Her own varicella immunity status is unknown. Per RCOG guidance, what is the immediate management?

options.A: Reassure — chickenpox is harmless in pregnancy
options.B: Urgent maternal varicella serology (IgG) the same day; if IgG positive — immune, reassure; if IgG negative — varicella zoster immunoglobulin (VZIG) within 10 days of exposure (ideally within 96 hours); if she subsequently develops chickenpox: oral aciclovir 800mg five times daily if >20 weeks and presenting within 24 hours of rash onset; admit if severe disease or respiratory symptoms
options.C: Give oral aciclovir prophylactically without checking serology
options.D: Vaccinate with varicella vaccine immediately
options.E: Repeat serology in 3 weeks

explanation.correct: Per RCOG Green-top Guideline 13 (Chickenpox in pregnancy) and UKHSA guidance: significant contact + non-immune mother = risk of maternal varicella (with risks of varicella pneumonitis, hepatitis, encephalitis, severe disease) AND fetal complications (congenital varicella syndrome if <28 weeks). Immediate action: check maternal varicella IgG; if non-immune, give VZIG within 10 days of exposure (most effective within 96 hours but recent UK guidance allows up to 10 days). If maternal infection develops: oral aciclovir if >20 weeks and within 24 hours of rash; admission if respiratory symptoms, dense rash, immunocompromise, smoker, late pregnancy. Varicella vaccine is live attenuated and contraindicated in pregnancy.
explanation.A: Incorrect — Chickenpox in pregnancy carries significant maternal (pneumonitis) and fetal (CVS) risks.
explanation.B: CORRECT — Same-day IgG; VZIG if non-immune (within 10 days); aciclovir if disease develops per RCOG GTG 13.
explanation.C: Incorrect — Pre-exposure serology determines whether VZIG (not aciclovir) is needed.
explanation.D: Incorrect — Varicella vaccine is live attenuated and contraindicated in pregnancy.
explanation.E: Incorrect — Serology should be checked immediately, not in 3 weeks; delays preclude effective VZIG.

reference: RCOG Green-top Guideline 13 — Chickenpox in pregnancy. https://www.rcog.org.uk/guidance/browse-all-guidance/green-top-guidelines/chickenpox-in-pregnancy-green-top-guideline-no-13/

question: A pregnant woman at 8 weeks gestation develops chickenpox after contact with an infected child. What is the risk of fetal congenital varicella syndrome (CVS) and what management is needed?

options.A: Risk of CVS is 50%; offer termination
options.B: Risk of CVS is approximately 0.5-1% if maternal infection occurs in the first 12 weeks, rising to 2% between 13-20 weeks, then negligible after 28 weeks; offer oral aciclovir if presenting within 24 hours of rash and >20 weeks (under 20 weeks, weigh risks/benefits); refer to fetal medicine for detailed anomaly scan at 16-20 weeks looking for CVS features (limb hypoplasia, skin scarring, microcephaly, cataracts)
options.C: Risk is negligible at any gestation
options.D: Risk is highest at 28-36 weeks gestation
options.E: Risk is only relevant if mother has shingles

explanation.correct: Per RCOG GTG 13: congenital varicella syndrome (CVS) risk varies significantly with gestation at maternal infection. <12 weeks: 0.5-1% risk; 13-20 weeks: 2% risk; >20 weeks: very low risk of CVS but neonatal varicella becomes risk near term/post-natal. CVS features: skin scarring (cicatrices) in dermatomal distribution, limb hypoplasia, neurological abnormalities (microcephaly, cortical atrophy), ocular abnormalities (cataracts, chorioretinitis). Management of established maternal varicella: oral aciclovir 800mg 5x/day if presenting within 24 hours of rash and >20 weeks; under 20 weeks, weigh risks/benefits (aciclovir is category B); fetal medicine referral for detailed anomaly scan at 16-20 weeks. Severe maternal disease — admit for IV aciclovir.
explanation.A: Incorrect — CVS risk is 0.5-2% (gestation-dependent), not 50%. Termination is not routinely offered.
explanation.B: CORRECT — CVS risk ~0.5-1% <12w, 2% 13-20w. Aciclovir if appropriate + fetal medicine referral + anomaly scan per RCOG.
explanation.C: Incorrect — Risk is real (0.5-2%) in the first 20 weeks.
explanation.D: Incorrect — CVS risk decreases after 20 weeks; neonatal varicella becomes the risk near term.
explanation.E: Incorrect — Maternal chickenpox (primary), not shingles, causes CVS.

reference: RCOG Green-top Guideline 13. https://www.rcog.org.uk/guidance/browse-all-guidance/green-top-guidelines/

question: A 36-week pregnant woman develops chickenpox 2 days before delivery. What is the main neonatal concern and management?

options.A: No risk — chickenpox at this gestation is harmless to the baby
options.B: Neonatal varicella infection (severe, can be fatal — mortality up to 20-30% if mother develops rash 7 days before to 7 days after delivery, as transplacental antibodies have not formed); give VZIG to neonate at birth; consider IV aciclovir if neonate develops chickenpox; delay delivery by at least 7 days from maternal rash if possible to allow maternal antibody transfer
options.C: Risk only relates to congenital varicella syndrome
options.D: Treat mother with antibiotics for prophylaxis
options.E: Isolation of mother postnatally for 28 days

explanation.correct: Per RCOG GTG 13: maternal chickenpox in the perinatal period (rash 7 days before to 7 days after delivery) is highest risk to the neonate. In this window, the fetus is exposed to virus but maternal antibodies have not yet formed/crossed the placenta. Neonatal varicella in this period can be severe (haemorrhagic chickenpox, pneumonitis, encephalitis) with mortality 20-30% historically — now lower with antiviral therapy. Management: (1) Delay delivery by 7 days from onset of maternal rash if possible (to allow IgG transfer to fetus); (2) Give VZIG to the neonate at birth; (3) IV aciclovir if neonate develops chickenpox. Mother and baby may need isolation; usual postnatal care otherwise.
explanation.A: Incorrect — Perinatal chickenpox carries highest risk of severe neonatal disease.
explanation.B: CORRECT — Perinatal varicella (within 7d either side): neonatal VZIG + IV aciclovir if disease develops + delay delivery if possible per RCOG.
explanation.C: Incorrect — CVS is the risk in <20 weeks; perinatal infection causes neonatal varicella, not CVS.
explanation.D: Incorrect — Antibiotics have no role in viral chickenpox.
explanation.E: Incorrect — 28-day isolation is not the standard practice; isolation duration is based on infectivity.

reference: RCOG Green-top Guideline 13. https://www.rcog.org.uk/guidance/browse-all-guidance/green-top-guidelines/

question: A 4-year-old child has had 4 days of watery diarrhoea, now becoming bloody. He has been at a petting farm a week ago. He is pale, has reduced urine output, and on examination has petechiae. Bloods show Hb 78 g/L, platelets 35 × 10⁹/L, creatinine 240 µmol/L. Per NICE CKS, what is the diagnosis?

options.A: Inflammatory bowel disease — colonoscopy
options.B: Haemolytic uraemic syndrome (HUS) — classically triggered by Shiga toxin-producing E. coli (STEC, particularly O157, often acquired from undercooked meat or farm animal contact); triad: microangiopathic haemolytic anaemia (low Hb, schistocytes), thrombocytopenia, acute kidney injury; emergency paediatric admission; supportive care (IV fluids, transfusions, dialysis if needed); AVOID antibiotics (may worsen toxin release) and avoid anti-motility agents
options.C: Salmonella gastroenteritis — ciprofloxacin
options.D: Rotavirus gastroenteritis — supportive care only
options.E: Crohn's disease — start prednisolone

explanation.correct: Haemolytic uraemic syndrome (HUS) — typical/diarrhoea-associated (D+ HUS): caused by Shiga toxin-producing E. coli (most commonly O157:H7) in 90% of paediatric cases. Sources: undercooked beef/burgers, unpasteurised milk, contaminated water, farm/petting zoo animals (faecal-oral transmission). Clinical triad: microangiopathic haemolytic anaemia (intravascular destruction of RBCs by fibrin strands in glomerular capillaries; schistocytes on blood film, raised LDH, low haptoglobin), thrombocytopenia, AKI. Pre-HUS prodrome: bloody diarrhoea typically 3-10 days before HUS develops. Management: emergency paediatric admission, supportive care (IV fluids, RBC/platelet transfusions, dialysis if AKI progresses), monitor for complications (seizures, hypertension). Antibiotics for STEC are CONTRAINDICATED — may increase Shiga toxin release and worsen HUS risk. Anti-motility agents also avoided.
explanation.A: Incorrect — IBD doesn't present with this acute triad of MAHA + thrombocytopenia + AKI following bloody diarrhoea.
explanation.B: CORRECT — HUS: STEC O157 post-farm exposure. Triad of MAHA + thrombocytopenia + AKI. Supportive care, NO antibiotics per NICE CKS.
explanation.C: Incorrect — Antibiotics may exacerbate STEC-HUS (cause increased toxin release).
explanation.D: Incorrect — Rotavirus causes watery diarrhoea without bloody stools, AKI or thrombocytopenia.
explanation.E: Incorrect — Crohn's does not present with acute MAHA and AKI.

reference: NICE CKS — Gastroenteritis. RCPCH HUS guidelines. https://cks.nice.org.uk/topics/gastroenteritis/

question: A 3-year-old has 5 days of watery diarrhoea, now mucoid and bloody. He is well-hydrated and feeding. Per NICE CKS, what is the most appropriate investigation?

options.A: Stool culture and sensitivity (including Shiga toxin-producing E. coli testing) — bloody diarrhoea in children requires stool sampling for bacterial pathogens (Campylobacter, Salmonella, Shigella, E. coli including STEC); rotavirus is unlikely to cause bloody diarrhoea; advise strict hygiene, exclusion from nursery until 48 hours after symptoms resolve, watch for signs of HUS (paleness, reduced urine, bruising)
options.B: Upper GI endoscopy
options.C: Empirical antibiotics without investigation
options.D: No investigation — all childhood diarrhoea is self-limiting
options.E: Faecal calprotectin

explanation.correct: Per NICE CKS (Gastroenteritis in children), bloody diarrhoea suggests invasive bacterial cause and requires stool sample for: bacterial culture (Campylobacter, Salmonella, Shigella), E. coli (including specific request for STEC if HUS risk), parasites if suspected (Cryptosporidium, Giardia). Investigation important to identify outbreak organisms (notifiable diseases) and inform contact tracing. School/nursery exclusion: until 48 hours after last episode of diarrhoea or vomiting; longer for STEC (until 2 negative stool samples 48 hours apart for certain risk groups). Antibiotics generally NOT given empirically — they may worsen STEC (HUS risk) and most paediatric bacterial gastroenteritis is self-limiting. Monitor for HUS warning signs.
explanation.A: CORRECT — Bloody diarrhoea: stool culture + STEC testing per NICE CKS; exclude from nursery 48 hours; monitor HUS signs.
explanation.B: Incorrect — Endoscopy is not first-line for acute bloody diarrhoea in a child.
explanation.C: Incorrect — Empirical antibiotics may worsen STEC (HUS risk) and are not first-line.
explanation.D: Incorrect — Bloody diarrhoea warrants investigation to identify bacterial pathogens and HUS risk.
explanation.E: Incorrect — Faecal calprotectin is for chronic inflammatory bowel disease assessment, not acute infective diarrhoea.

reference: NICE CKS — Gastroenteritis. https://cks.nice.org.uk/topics/gastroenteritis/

question: A GP confirms STEC O157 infection in a 5-year-old. Per UKHSA, what is the public health responsibility?

options.A: No action needed — STEC is not a notifiable disease
options.B: STEC O157 is a notifiable disease — the GP must notify the UKHSA (formerly PHE) Health Protection Team without delay; the laboratory will also report; contact tracing for high-risk contacts (other young children, food handlers) and household members; affected child excluded from nursery/school until 2 negative stool samples 48 hours apart (or 14 days clear of symptoms in lower-risk groups)
options.C: Notify only if the child is admitted to hospital
options.D: Notify the GMC
options.E: Inform only the parents — no further public health action

explanation.correct: Per the Health Protection (Notification) Regulations 2010 and UKHSA guidance, certain infectious diseases are statutorily notifiable to the local Health Protection Team. Notifiable diseases include: STEC/VTEC infection, food poisoning, infectious bloody diarrhoea, typhoid, paratyphoid, salmonella, listeriosis, cholera, dysentery, hepatitis A/B/C/E, mumps, measles, rubella, meningitis, meningococcal disease, scarlet fever, tuberculosis, whooping cough, yellow fever and others. GP must notify regardless of laboratory confirmation. UKHSA arranges contact tracing, outbreak investigation, and risk assessment for vulnerable contacts (other young children, food handlers, healthcare workers, residents of care homes). STEC O157 exclusion from school: 2 negative stool samples 48 hours apart for risk groups (under-5s, food handlers, healthcare workers).
explanation.A: Incorrect — STEC O157 is a statutorily notifiable disease.
explanation.B: CORRECT — Notify UKHSA without delay per Health Protection Regulations 2010; school exclusion until 2 negative stools.
explanation.C: Incorrect — Notification is required regardless of hospital admission.
explanation.D: Incorrect — GMC is not the public health body. UKHSA is the correct body.
explanation.E: Incorrect — Parents alone is insufficient; public health investigation is required to prevent outbreaks.

reference: UKHSA — Notifiable diseases. Health Protection (Notification) Regulations 2010. https://www.gov.uk/government/collections/notifications-of-infectious-diseases-noids

question: A 6-year-old boy presents with palpable purpuric rash on his buttocks and back of his legs, abdominal pain, and arthralgia of his ankles. Urine dipstick shows 2+ blood and 1+ protein. Per NICE CKS, what is the diagnosis and most important investigation?

options.A: Idiopathic thrombocytopenic purpura — FBC
options.B: Henoch-Schönlein purpura (IgA vasculitis) — classic tetrad: palpable purpura on extensor surfaces/buttocks (typically lower limbs), abdominal pain (GI vasculitis ± intussusception), arthralgia (knees/ankles), renal involvement (haematuria/proteinuria); most important investigation is URINE DIPSTICK and BP at presentation and weekly for at least 6 months — to detect HSP nephritis (the long-term concern); FBC normal/raised platelets (rules out ITP)
options.C: Meningococcal septicaemia — urgent IV ceftriaxone
options.D: Acute leukaemia — bone marrow biopsy
options.E: Eczema — topical hydrocortisone

explanation.correct: Henoch-Schönlein purpura (HSP), now termed IgA vasculitis: most common vasculitis in children, peak age 4-7 years. Often follows upper respiratory tract infection or streptococcal infection. Classic tetrad: (1) Palpable non-blanching purpura (extensor surfaces, buttocks, lower limbs — gravity-dependent); (2) Arthralgia (knees, ankles); (3) Abdominal pain (GI vasculitis, intussusception, GI bleeding); (4) Renal involvement (haematuria, proteinuria — IgA nephropathy). Most important monitoring: URINE DIPSTICK and BP weekly for first 6 months (HSP nephritis can be silent and is the main long-term morbidity — small risk of progression to chronic kidney disease). FBC: normal platelets distinguishes from ITP. Most cases self-resolve over weeks; analgesia (paracetamol — NSAIDs may worsen renal/GI) for symptom control; refer to paediatrics if significant renal involvement.
explanation.A: Incorrect — ITP causes non-palpable petechial rash with thrombocytopenia (low platelets); HSP has normal platelets.
explanation.B: CORRECT — HSP/IgA vasculitis: purpura + arthralgia + abdo pain + nephritis. Urine dipstick + BP weekly x 6 months per NICE CKS.
explanation.C: Incorrect — Meningococcal septicaemia presents with systemic toxicity, fever, non-blanching rash anywhere; this child is well with localised purpura.
explanation.D: Incorrect — Leukaemia would have abnormal FBC (anaemia, abnormal WCC, low platelets) and constitutional symptoms.
explanation.E: Incorrect — Eczema is not purpuric.

reference: NICE CKS — Henoch-Schönlein purpura. https://cks.nice.org.uk/topics/henoch-schonlein-purpura/

question: A child with confirmed HSP develops severe abdominal pain, vomiting and bloody stools. Per NICE CKS, what is the immediate concern?

options.A: Coeliac disease — coeliac serology
options.B: Intussusception — HSP is the most common cause of secondary intussusception in children; bowel wall vasculitis and haematoma act as a lead point; presents with severe colicky abdominal pain, vomiting, redcurrant jelly stools; urgent admission for ultrasound (target/donut sign) and air enema reduction; surgical intervention if reduction fails or perforation
options.C: Acute appendicitis — wait and review
options.D: Gastroenteritis — oral rehydration
options.E: Constipation — laxatives

explanation.correct: Intussusception in HSP: HSP is the most common cause of secondary intussusception in children (most are idiopathic in infancy). Mechanism: bowel wall vasculitis with submucosal haematoma forms a lead point that telescopes into adjacent bowel. Presentation: severe colicky abdominal pain, drawing up legs, vomiting (may become bilious), bloody/redcurrant jelly stools. The classic triad (pain, vomiting, bloody stools) is present in only a minority. Diagnosis: abdominal USS (target/donut sign — pathognomonic), exclude with concerning HSP presentations. Treatment: air or contrast enema reduction (~80% success); surgical reduction if enema fails or signs of perforation/necrosis. HSP intussusception is typically ileo-ileal rather than ileo-colic (unlike idiopathic infant intussusception) — enema may be less successful.
explanation.A: Incorrect — Coeliac doesn't present acutely with this picture.
explanation.B: CORRECT — HSP-associated intussusception: severe abdo pain + bloody stools = USS + air enema. Most common cause of secondary intussusception in children per NICE CKS.
explanation.C: Incorrect — 'Wait and review' for severe abdominal pain with bloody stools risks bowel necrosis.
explanation.D: Incorrect — Gastroenteritis does not cause severe colicky pain or redcurrant jelly stools.
explanation.E: Incorrect — Constipation does not cause bloody stools or severe vomiting.

reference: NICE CKS — Henoch-Schönlein purpura. https://cks.nice.org.uk/topics/henoch-schonlein-purpura/

question: A 5-year-old has had HSP 8 weeks ago and made a full recovery. His mother asks about long-term follow-up. Per NICE CKS, what monitoring should continue?

options.A: No follow-up needed once acute episode resolves
options.B: Urine dipstick and blood pressure measurements weekly for the first month, then monthly for 3-6 months (some guidance to 12 months); HSP nephritis can develop weeks to months after the acute episode and can be silent; if proteinuria, persistent haematuria or hypertension develops — paediatric nephrology referral
options.C: Annual blood tests for life
options.D: Daily BP at home for 5 years
options.E: Lifelong corticosteroid prophylaxis

explanation.correct: Per NICE CKS, the long-term concern in HSP is HSP nephritis: develops in approximately 30-50% of children with HSP, usually within 4-6 weeks but can present months later. Most have mild disease (microscopic haematuria) that resolves spontaneously, but a small percentage progress to chronic kidney disease. Monitoring schedule: weekly urine dipstick and BP for first month, then less frequently (monthly) for 6-12 months. Refer to paediatric nephrology for: significant proteinuria (urine PCR >50 mg/mmol or ACR >70 mg/mmol), nephritic syndrome (haematuria + hypertension + oedema + renal impairment), nephrotic syndrome, persistent haematuria, hypertension. Long-term follow-up beyond 12 months is not routine for those with normal monitoring throughout.
explanation.A: Incorrect — HSP nephritis can develop weeks to months later and may be silent; routine monitoring is essential.
explanation.B: CORRECT — Weekly urine dipstick + BP for 1 month, then monthly for 6-12 months per NICE CKS.
explanation.C: Incorrect — Annual blood tests for life are not routinely needed if monitoring is normal during the surveillance period.
explanation.D: Incorrect — Daily home BP for 5 years is excessive and not evidence-based.
explanation.E: Incorrect — Lifelong steroids are not given for resolved HSP.

reference: NICE CKS — Henoch-Schönlein purpura. https://cks.nice.org.uk/topics/henoch-schonlein-purpura/

question: A 6-year-old boy is brought in with 3 hours of central abdominal pain, anorexia, and nausea. He has no vomiting yet. There is no fever, no diarrhoea, no urinary symptoms. He is settled and walking. Per NICE NG143, what is the appropriate management?

options.A: Urgent paediatric surgical referral
options.B: Safety-net advice and active observation at home — early appendicitis cannot be excluded but at this stage with no localising signs and the child remaining well, watchful waiting with clear safety-netting is appropriate; advise parents to return urgently if: pain localises to right iliac fossa, fever develops, persistent vomiting, child becomes unwell or pain worsens; review within 12-24 hours or sooner if any red flags
options.C: Prescribe ibuprofen and review in 1 week
options.D: Admit for IV antibiotics
options.E: Stool sample and outpatient gastroenterology referral

explanation.correct: Per NICE NG143 (Appendicitis) and NICE CKS, the assessment of abdominal pain in children requires careful clinical judgement. Early appendicitis often presents with non-specific central/periumbilical pain that later migrates to right iliac fossa (4-12 hours typically). At 3 hours with no localising signs, normal vital signs and the child remaining well: active observation with clear safety-netting is appropriate. Advice to parents: return urgently if pain localises to RIF, persistent vomiting, fever, lethargy, refusal to eat/drink, worsening pain. Review within 12-24 hours. Inappropriate admission/surgery for non-specific pain is also harmful. Red flags requiring immediate referral: peritonism, severe systemic illness, persistent vomiting with dehydration, bilious vomiting, evidence of bowel obstruction.
explanation.A: Incorrect — At 3 hours with no localising signs and a well child, urgent referral is premature and may be inappropriate.
explanation.B: CORRECT — Active observation + clear safety-netting; review within 12-24 hours; return if RIF pain, fever, vomiting per NICE NG143.
explanation.C: Incorrect — A 1-week review is too long; appendicitis can progress to perforation within 24-48 hours.
explanation.D: Incorrect — No indication for IV antibiotics at this stage; would mask evolving picture.
explanation.E: Incorrect — Stool sample is not first-line for this presentation; no diarrhoea or infective features.

reference: NICE NG143 — Suspected appendicitis. NICE CKS — Abdominal pain in children. https://www.nice.org.uk/guidance/ng143

question: A 7-year-old returns 18 hours later with localised right iliac fossa pain, fever 38.5°C and rebound tenderness. His pulse is 120 bpm. Per NICE NG143, what is the next step?

options.A: Continue oral fluids and review in 6 hours
options.B: Urgent (same day) surgical referral — clinical picture of appendicitis with peritoneal signs (rebound) requires immediate paediatric surgical assessment; do not wait for imaging; analgesia, IV access, NBM, IV fluids; appendectomy is the treatment
options.C: Prescribe oral antibiotics and observe at home
options.D: Routine abdominal X-ray as first investigation
options.E: Arrange outpatient CT abdomen

explanation.correct: Per NICE NG143, suspected appendicitis with localised right iliac fossa pain, fever and peritoneal signs (rebound, guarding) requires same-day surgical assessment. Don't delay for imaging — clinical assessment by a surgeon is the first step. Management: analgesia, NBM, IV access, IV fluids, surgical review. Diagnostic imaging (USS or CT) may be used to support diagnosis especially in atypical presentations or female adolescents (to exclude gynaecological causes), but should not delay surgical assessment in clearly clinically suggestive cases. Treatment: appendectomy (laparoscopic or open). Antibiotic therapy alone has been studied as an alternative in selected adult cases but is not routine in paediatric practice in the UK.
explanation.A: Incorrect — Delay risks perforation, peritonitis, sepsis; immediate surgical assessment required.
explanation.B: CORRECT — Immediate surgical referral for clinical appendicitis with peritoneal signs per NICE NG143.
explanation.C: Incorrect — Oral antibiotics + home observation is unsafe for an unwell child with peritoneal signs.
explanation.D: Incorrect — Abdominal X-ray has poor sensitivity for appendicitis and should not delay surgical assessment.
explanation.E: Incorrect — CT is not first-line in children due to radiation concerns; surgical assessment first.

reference: NICE NG143 — Suspected appendicitis. https://www.nice.org.uk/guidance/ng143

question: A 5-year-old has had abdominal pain on and off for 3 months. She has missed school 4 times. There is no weight loss, normal stools, normal growth, no nocturnal pain. Examination is unremarkable. Per NICE CKS, what is the most likely diagnosis?

options.A: Crohn's disease — urgent colonoscopy
options.B: Functional/recurrent abdominal pain of childhood — diagnosis after excluding red flags (no weight loss, no nocturnal pain, normal growth, normal examination, no anaemia); management: reassurance, normal diet and activity, school attendance encouraged, address psychosocial factors (stress, family dynamics), avoid over-investigation; refer to paediatrics only if red flags or severe impact on function
options.C: Appendicitis — surgical referral
options.D: Coeliac disease — coeliac serology only
options.E: Pyelonephritis — urine culture

explanation.correct: Per NICE CKS, functional abdominal pain (recurrent abdominal pain of childhood) is common in school-age children (peak 4-12 years), occurring in ~10-15% of children. Diagnostic features: chronic/recurrent abdominal pain ≥2 months, often periumbilical, episodic, between episodes the child is well, normal growth, normal examination, no red flags. Red flags requiring investigation/referral: weight loss, poor growth, nocturnal pain that wakes child, persistent vomiting, blood in stool, diarrhoea, persistent right-sided or back pain, family history of IBD, anaemia. Management: reassurance after exclusion of red flags, normal diet (no restriction), encourage school attendance, address psychosocial factors (stress, anxiety, family issues), avoid over-investigation which reinforces illness behaviour. Consider CBT/psychological support if persistent.
explanation.A: Incorrect — Crohn's would typically have weight loss, diarrhoea, nocturnal symptoms, growth failure.
explanation.B: CORRECT — Functional abdominal pain of childhood: reassurance, normal activity, school attendance per NICE CKS.
explanation.C: Incorrect — Appendicitis is acute, not recurrent over 3 months.
explanation.D: Incorrect — Coeliac is reasonable to exclude but the description without other features suggests functional pain.
explanation.E: Incorrect — Pyelonephritis is acute with fever and urinary symptoms.

reference: NICE CKS — Recurrent abdominal pain in children. https://cks.nice.org.uk/topics/recurrent-abdominal-pain-in-children/

question: A 32-year-old woman of Afro-Caribbean descent presents with dry cough, fatigue, and a rash showing tender red nodules on her shins (erythema nodosum). CXR shows bilateral hilar lymphadenopathy. Per NICE CKS, what is the likely diagnosis and additional investigations?

options.A: Tuberculosis — sputum AFB
options.B: Sarcoidosis — multisystem granulomatous disease most common in young adults of African descent; classic triad of bilateral hilar lymphadenopathy, erythema nodosum, and arthralgia is called LÖFGREN SYNDROME (good prognosis variant); investigations: serum ACE (raised), calcium (hypercalcaemia from granulomatous 1-alpha-hydroxylase activity), full lung function, urinalysis (renal involvement), ECG (cardiac involvement), eye assessment (uveitis); refer to respiratory or rheumatology
options.C: Lymphoma — urgent biopsy
options.D: Pulmonary embolism — CTPA
options.E: Lupus — ANA and dsDNA

explanation.correct: Sarcoidosis: multisystem non-caseating granulomatous disease of unknown aetiology. Most common in 20-40 year olds; higher prevalence in people of African descent. Classic Löfgren syndrome: bilateral hilar lymphadenopathy + erythema nodosum + arthralgia (often ankles) ± fever — represents acute self-limiting presentation with excellent prognosis (resolves spontaneously in 80-90%). Per NICE CKS, investigation: serum ACE (raised in ~60% — not specific or sensitive), serum calcium (hypercalcaemia in 10-30% — granulomatous macrophages produce 1-alpha-hydroxylase converting 25(OH)D to 1,25(OH)2D), CXR (Stage I = BHL only, Stage II = BHL + infiltrates, Stage III = infiltrates only, Stage IV = fibrosis), full lung function (restrictive, reduced TLCO), urinalysis (renal involvement, hypercalciuria), ECG (cardiac sarcoidosis — heart block, arrhythmia), eye exam (anterior uveitis). Tissue biopsy (transbronchial, lymph node, EBUS) confirms granulomas. Treatment: often self-limiting; corticosteroids if symptomatic organ involvement or progression.
explanation.A: Incorrect — TB causes unilateral upper lobe disease typically; bilateral symmetrical hilar lymphadenopathy with erythema nodosum is classic sarcoid (Löfgren).
explanation.B: CORRECT — Löfgren syndrome / sarcoidosis: BHL + erythema nodosum + arthralgia. Serum ACE/Ca, eye/cardiac assessment per NICE CKS.
explanation.C: Incorrect — Lymphoma typically asymmetric, with systemic B symptoms; not erythema nodosum or BHL with these features.
explanation.D: Incorrect — PE doesn't cause BHL or erythema nodosum.
explanation.E: Incorrect — Lupus can cause similar features but BHL + erythema nodosum is the classic Löfgren tetrad.

reference: NICE CKS — Sarcoidosis. BTS sarcoidosis guidelines. https://cks.nice.org.uk/topics/sarcoidosis/

question: A patient with confirmed pulmonary sarcoidosis is found to have hypercalcaemia and a serum calcium of 3.0 mmol/L. He is asymptomatic. Per BTS sarcoidosis guidelines, what is the underlying mechanism and management?

options.A: Hyperparathyroidism — refer for parathyroidectomy
options.B: Granulomatous macrophages express 1-alpha-hydroxylase converting 25-hydroxyvitamin D to active 1,25-dihydroxyvitamin D outside the normal renal regulation, causing hypercalcaemia and hypercalciuria; management: avoid sunlight exposure (reduces vitamin D synthesis), avoid vitamin D and calcium supplementation, ensure adequate hydration; corticosteroids effective if persistent or symptomatic hypercalcaemia
options.C: Bone metastases — bone scan
options.D: Lithium toxicity — measure serum lithium
options.E: Dehydration — IV fluids only

explanation.correct: Hypercalcaemia in sarcoidosis: occurs in 10-30% of patients. Mechanism: extrarenal production of 1,25-dihydroxyvitamin D (calcitriol) by granulomatous macrophages, which express 1-alpha-hydroxylase enzyme outside normal regulatory pathways (normally this enzyme is renal and tightly regulated by PTH). This causes: increased gut calcium absorption, increased bone resorption, hypercalcaemia and hypercalciuria. Renal complications: nephrocalcinosis, nephrolithiasis, renal impairment. Management per BTS: avoid sun exposure (reduces UV-induced vitamin D synthesis), avoid vitamin D/calcium supplementation, maintain hydration; corticosteroids (prednisolone) are highly effective by suppressing granulomatous 1-alpha-hydroxylase activity. PTH is suppressed (not elevated). Distinct from hyperparathyroidism (where PTH is high).
explanation.A: Incorrect — Hyperparathyroidism causes hypercalcaemia with HIGH PTH; sarcoidosis hypercalcaemia has SUPPRESSED PTH.
explanation.B: CORRECT — Granulomatous 1-alpha-hydroxylase activity. Avoid sun + vitamin D + supplements; steroids if persistent per BTS.
explanation.C: Incorrect — Bone metastases is not the mechanism; the cause is granulomatous vitamin D production.
explanation.D: Incorrect — Lithium toxicity causes a separate clinical syndrome.
explanation.E: Incorrect — IV fluids alone do not address the underlying granulomatous vitamin D production.

reference: BTS — Sarcoidosis clinical guidelines. https://www.brit-thoracic.org.uk/quality-improvement/clinical-statements/

question: A patient newly diagnosed with sarcoidosis (BHL only, no other organ involvement, asymptomatic) asks about treatment. Per BTS, what is the management?

options.A: Lifelong prednisolone 30 mg
options.B: Most asymptomatic Stage I sarcoidosis (BHL alone, no other organ involvement, normal lung function) resolves spontaneously within 1-3 years and does NOT require corticosteroid treatment; monitor with CXR and pulmonary function tests every 6 months; treat only if symptomatic, progressive, or major organ involvement (cardiac, neurological, ocular, severe hypercalcaemia, advanced pulmonary disease)
options.C: Cyclophosphamide chemotherapy
options.D: Methotrexate for life
options.E: Pulmonary lobectomy

explanation.correct: Per BTS sarcoidosis guidelines, treatment depends on stage, symptoms and organ involvement: Stage I (BHL only): spontaneous resolution in ~80% within 1-3 years; no treatment needed if asymptomatic; surveillance with CXR and PFTs every 6 months. Stage II (BHL + infiltrates): 50% resolve spontaneously; treat if symptomatic. Stage III (infiltrates only): 30% resolve; treat if symptomatic or progressive. Stage IV (fibrosis): irreversible; treatment may slow progression. Indications for corticosteroid treatment (prednisolone 20-40 mg, tapering): persistent symptoms affecting QoL, progressive pulmonary disease (declining FVC/TLCO), major organ involvement (cardiac, neurological, ocular, renal, severe hypercalcaemia), persistent skin/joint disease. Methotrexate is second-line for steroid-sparing or refractory disease.
explanation.A: Incorrect — Most asymptomatic stage I disease resolves spontaneously without treatment.
explanation.B: CORRECT — Asymptomatic stage I sarcoidosis: monitoring only; treatment if symptomatic, progressive or major organ involvement per BTS.
explanation.C: Incorrect — Cyclophosphamide is not standard treatment for sarcoidosis.
explanation.D: Incorrect — Methotrexate is second-line in steroid-resistant or steroid-dependent cases; not first-line for stage I.
explanation.E: Incorrect — Surgery has no role in sarcoidosis treatment.

reference: BTS — Sarcoidosis. https://www.brit-thoracic.org.uk/quality-improvement/clinical-statements/

question: A 65-year-old woman has been on ramipril for 6 weeks for hypertension. She presents with extensive rash on both arms and swollen lower limbs, particularly around the lips. The rash is non-itchy. Per BNF and NICE CKS, what is the diagnosis?

options.A: Atopic eczema — topical steroids
options.B: ACE inhibitor-induced angioedema — ACE inhibitors block bradykinin breakdown leading to bradykinin accumulation and angioedema; can occur weeks to YEARS after starting ACEI; non-allergic, non-itchy; commonly affects lips, tongue, face, throat — risk of airway compromise; STOP ACE inhibitor immediately; switch to ARB only after delay (ARBs have lower but not zero risk); avoid all ACEI lifelong; document allergy/intolerance
options.C: Contact dermatitis — patch testing
options.D: Urticaria — antihistamines
options.E: Cellulitis — oral flucloxacillin

explanation.correct: ACE inhibitor-induced angioedema: a well-recognised non-allergic angioedema affecting 0.1-0.7% of ACEI users. Higher risk in: Afro-Caribbean patients (5x higher), older patients, smokers, those with previous angioedema. Mechanism: ACE normally degrades bradykinin; ACEI inhibition causes bradykinin accumulation → increased vascular permeability → angioedema. Distinguishing features: non-pruritic (unlike allergic), no urticaria, non-IgE mediated, can occur weeks to YEARS after starting ACEI (median 6 months but can be immediate or delayed). Sites: face, lips, tongue, oropharynx, larynx (potentially fatal airway compromise), GI tract. Management per BNF: STOP ACE inhibitor immediately; supportive care; antihistamines/steroids less effective than in allergic angioedema; consider icatibant (bradykinin receptor antagonist) for severe cases; avoid all ACEI in future. ARBs have lower risk (no bradykinin effect) but cross-reactivity occurs in ~10% — wait at least 4 weeks before introducing ARB and monitor closely.
explanation.A: Incorrect — Atopic eczema is itchy and chronic; not associated with new ACEI use and lip/limb swelling.
explanation.B: CORRECT — ACEI-induced angioedema: stop ramipril immediately; avoid all ACEI; document; ARB only with caution per BNF.
explanation.C: Incorrect — Contact dermatitis is itchy and follows allergen exposure pattern.
explanation.D: Incorrect — Urticaria is itchy with characteristic wheals; this is angioedema (deeper tissue swelling).
explanation.E: Incorrect — Cellulitis is localised, hot, painful and infective; not the bilateral pattern here.

reference: BNF — Ramipril. NICE CKS — Angioedema. MHRA Drug Safety Update — ACEI angioedema. https://bnf.nice.org.uk/drug/ramipril.html

question: A patient with ACEI-induced angioedema presents acutely with tongue and lip swelling and difficulty swallowing. What is the immediate management?

options.A: Oral antihistamines and observation
options.B: Emergency 999 admission — assess airway (tongue/oropharyngeal swelling can rapidly progress to airway obstruction and death); high-flow oxygen, IV access, IM adrenaline 0.5mg if signs of airway compromise (controversial as the mechanism is bradykinin not histamine, but used due to airway threat); IV chlorphenamine 10mg + IV hydrocortisone 200mg (less effective than in allergic, but routinely given); icatibant (bradykinin B2 receptor antagonist) if available; ICU/anaesthetic support for airway management
options.C: Topical hydrocortisone cream
options.D: Reassurance — angioedema is self-limiting
options.E: Oral prednisolone tablets and review in 3 days

explanation.correct: ACEI-induced angioedema affecting the airway (tongue, oropharynx, larynx) is a medical emergency due to risk of airway obstruction. Management approach: (1) Emergency 999 admission; (2) Airway assessment — if any signs of stridor, voice change or significant tongue swelling, urgent anaesthetic/ENT involvement for potential intubation/surgical airway; (3) High-flow oxygen, IV access; (4) IM adrenaline (0.3-0.5mg) — given despite the bradykinin mechanism due to airway threat, by anaphylaxis algorithm; (5) Antihistamines and corticosteroids — given routinely though less effective than in allergic angioedema; (6) Icatibant (bradykinin B2 receptor antagonist) — increasingly used in hospital for severe cases, NICE supports its use; (7) ICU admission for observation. Mortality from ACEI angioedema is up to 1-2% mostly from airway compromise. Document and avoid all ACEI lifelong.
explanation.A: Incorrect — Oral medication and observation is inadequate for airway-threatening angioedema.
explanation.B: CORRECT — Emergency admission; airway management; adrenaline if airway threat; antihistamines/steroids/icatibant per NICE CKS.
explanation.C: Incorrect — Topical treatment has no role in systemic angioedema.
explanation.D: Incorrect — Airway-threatening angioedema can be rapidly fatal.
explanation.E: Incorrect — Oral medication and outpatient review is unsafe for tongue/oropharyngeal swelling.

reference: NICE CKS — Angioedema. Resuscitation Council UK — Anaphylaxis. https://cks.nice.org.uk/topics/angio-oedema-anaphylaxis/

question: A patient had ACEI-induced angioedema 6 months ago. Her BP is uncontrolled and an alternative antihypertensive is needed. Per NICE NG136, what should be prescribed?

options.A: Lisinopril — different ACEI is safe
options.B: Calcium channel blocker (amlodipine) — first-line alternative after ACEI angioedema; ARBs have lower angioedema risk than ACEI but cross-reactivity occurs in 5-10% — use only if other classes unsuitable, with caution and monitoring; lifelong avoidance of all ACEI; document drug allergy/intolerance clearly in records
options.C: Different ACE inhibitor — only the original is contraindicated
options.D: Aldosterone antagonist — first-line
options.E: Beta-blocker — first-line

explanation.correct: Per NICE NG136 (Hypertension), after ACEI-induced angioedema: all ACE inhibitors are contraindicated lifelong (class effect — switching to another ACEI doesn't help). Switch to: calcium channel blocker (amlodipine) — first-line alternative as no bradykinin effect, well-tolerated. ARBs (losartan, candesartan, valsartan): theoretically lower risk (no bradykinin effect) but cross-reactivity (recurrent angioedema) occurs in 5-10% of ACEI angioedema patients — use with caution, prefer to avoid in first 6-12 months, monitor carefully if used. Thiazide diuretics, beta-blockers and alpha-blockers can also be used. The patient should be counselled and the angioedema clearly documented as an ACE inhibitor allergy/intolerance to prevent re-prescription.
explanation.A: Incorrect — All ACE inhibitors are contraindicated as a class.
explanation.B: CORRECT — CCB (amlodipine) first-line alternative; ARBs with caution due to cross-reactivity per NICE NG136.
explanation.C: Incorrect — All ACE inhibitors carry the same risk; this is a class effect.
explanation.D: Incorrect — Aldosterone antagonist is not first-line for hypertension.
explanation.E: Incorrect — Beta-blocker is not first-line for hypertension per NICE NG136.

reference: NICE NG136 — Hypertension in adults. https://www.nice.org.uk/guidance/ng136

question: A study reports the relative risk (RR) of myocardial infarction in patients on a new drug as 0.65 (95% CI 0.52 to 0.81). How should this be interpreted?

options.A: Patients on the new drug have 65% higher risk of MI
options.B: The new drug reduces relative risk of MI by 35% (1 − 0.65 = 0.35); since the 95% confidence interval (0.52 to 0.81) does not include 1.0, the result is statistically significant at p<0.05; this represents a clinically meaningful reduction in MI risk
options.C: 65% of patients on the drug had MI
options.D: There is no effect — RR less than 1 means no benefit
options.E: The drug increases MI risk by 65%

explanation.correct: Relative risk (RR) interpretation: RR = risk in treatment group / risk in control group. RR < 1: treatment reduces risk (beneficial). RR > 1: treatment increases risk. RR = 1: no difference. RR 0.65 means the treatment group has 65% of the control group's risk — a 35% relative risk reduction (RRR = 1 − RR = 0.35 = 35%). Confidence interval: if 95% CI excludes 1.0, the result is statistically significant. CI 0.52 to 0.81 excludes 1.0 → statistically significant. Always interpret RR alongside absolute risk reduction (ARR) and NNT — a 35% RRR might be a large or small ARR depending on baseline risk. RR is most meaningful when baseline risk is known.
explanation.A: Incorrect — RR 0.65 means 35% LOWER risk, not 65% higher.
explanation.B: CORRECT — RR 0.65 = 35% relative risk reduction. CI 0.52-0.81 excludes 1 = statistically significant.
explanation.C: Incorrect — RR is not the percentage of patients with an outcome.
explanation.D: Incorrect — RR less than 1 means beneficial effect (risk reduction).
explanation.E: Incorrect — RR 0.65 represents a 35% reduction, not 65% increase.

reference: BMJ Statistics Notes — Relative risk and odds ratio. https://www.bmj.com/about-bmj/resources-readers/publications/statistics-square-one

question: A box-and-whisker plot shows the distribution of blood pressure readings. The box extends from 120 to 140, the line within the box is at 130, and the whiskers extend from 105 to 160. What does the line within the box represent?

options.A: The mean blood pressure
options.B: The median blood pressure (50th percentile) — the line inside the box always represents the median; the box represents the interquartile range (IQR = 25th to 75th percentile); whiskers extend to the minimum and maximum values (or 1.5× IQR, with outliers shown as dots); box-and-whisker plots are robust to skewed distributions and visually represent spread without assuming normality
options.C: The mode
options.D: The standard deviation
options.E: The range

explanation.correct: Box-and-whisker plot anatomy: Line in the centre of the box = MEDIAN (50th percentile); Lower edge of box = 25th percentile (Q1, first quartile); Upper edge of box = 75th percentile (Q3, third quartile); Box length = INTERQUARTILE RANGE (IQR = Q3 − Q1); Whiskers extend to the smallest and largest values within 1.5 × IQR of the quartiles (or to minimum/maximum if no outlier definition is used); Outliers beyond whiskers shown as individual points. Box plots are particularly useful for: visualising spread and skew in non-normal distributions; comparing groups; identifying outliers. They do NOT show mean or SD.
explanation.A: Incorrect — Mean is not displayed on a box plot. Median is the central line.
explanation.B: CORRECT — Median (50th percentile) is the line in the box. Box = IQR per standard EBM convention.
explanation.C: Incorrect — Mode is not displayed on a box plot.
explanation.D: Incorrect — SD is not represented on a box plot.
explanation.E: Incorrect — Range is the full spread (min to max) but is not the line in the box.

reference: BMJ Statistics Notes — Box-and-whisker plot. https://www.bmj.com/about-bmj/resources-readers/publications/statistics-square-one

question: A forest plot from a meta-analysis shows the pooled risk ratio of antibiotic prophylaxis for surgical site infection as 0.45 (95% CI 0.37 to 0.55). The diamond is on the LEFT of the line of no effect. The I² statistic is 8%. How should this be interpreted?

options.A: Insufficient evidence — heterogeneity is too high
options.B: Antibiotic prophylaxis significantly reduces surgical site infections (RR 0.45 = 55% relative risk reduction; 95% CI 0.37-0.55 excludes 1.0 = statistically significant; diamond on the left of line of no effect = favours treatment); I² of 8% indicates LOW heterogeneity between studies — the results are consistent across studies, strengthening confidence in the pooled estimate
options.C: Strong evidence but high heterogeneity makes pooling unreliable
options.D: No effect — wide confidence interval
options.E: The diamond on the left means antibiotic prophylaxis is harmful

explanation.correct: Forest plot interpretation: Diamond = pooled effect estimate (centre) and 95% CI (width). Position relative to the line of no effect (RR=1.0): Left of line = favours treatment (lower risk); Right of line = favours control (higher risk); Crosses the line = not statistically significant. Heterogeneity measured by I² statistic: I² 0-25% = low heterogeneity (studies consistent); I² 25-50% = moderate; I² 50-75% = substantial; I² >75% = considerable. I² 8% indicates very low heterogeneity → high confidence in pooled estimate. Combined with statistical significance (CI excludes 1.0) and large effect size (55% RRR), this is robust evidence supporting the intervention. Sometimes random-effects model used if heterogeneity high; fixed-effects appropriate when I² low.
explanation.A: Incorrect — I² of 8% represents LOW heterogeneity, not high.
explanation.B: CORRECT — RR 0.45 = 55% RRR; CI excludes 1 = significant; I² 8% = low heterogeneity, strong evidence.
explanation.C: Incorrect — Heterogeneity is LOW (I² 8%) which strengthens pooling reliability.
explanation.D: Incorrect — CI 0.37-0.55 is narrow and excludes 1 = significant effect.
explanation.E: Incorrect — Left of line of no effect favours TREATMENT (lower risk), not harm.

reference: Cochrane Handbook — Forest plots and heterogeneity. https://training.cochrane.org/handbook

question: A 45-year-old man has been on prednisolone 20mg daily for 3 years for inflammatory arthritis. He develops persistent right hip pain that is worse on weight-bearing. X-ray is normal. Per NICE CKS and BMJ guidance, what is the most likely diagnosis and next investigation?

options.A: Osteoarthritis — analgesia and physiotherapy
options.B: Avascular necrosis (AVN) of the femoral head — long-term high-dose corticosteroids are the most common non-traumatic cause; presents with insidious onset hip/groin pain worsening with weight-bearing; early X-rays are often NORMAL; MRI is the investigation of choice (highly sensitive, shows marrow oedema and crescent sign before X-ray changes); refer to orthopaedics; early intervention (core decompression) may preserve the joint
options.C: Septic arthritis — joint aspiration
options.D: Hip osteoporosis — DEXA scan
options.E: Greater trochanteric bursitis — local corticosteroid injection

explanation.correct: Avascular necrosis (AVN) / osteonecrosis of the femoral head: death of bone tissue due to interrupted blood supply. Risk factors: long-term corticosteroids (most common non-traumatic cause), alcohol excess, trauma, sickle cell disease, SLE, pregnancy, decompression sickness (caisson disease), HIV (high-dose protease inhibitors). Presentation: insidious groin/hip/thigh pain, worse on weight-bearing, progressively limiting movement. Early X-rays are NORMAL (changes take 3-6 months to develop): later findings include subchondral lucency (crescent sign), then bone collapse. MRI is the investigation of choice (very sensitive even in early disease — shows marrow oedema, crescent sign, double-line sign). Management: orthopaedic referral; non-weight-bearing/walking aids; core decompression surgery may preserve the joint in early disease (Stage I-II); femoral head collapse usually requires total hip replacement.
explanation.A: Incorrect — OA causes pain on movement but usually has X-ray changes (joint space narrowing, osteophytes); steroid use raises AVN suspicion.
explanation.B: CORRECT — AVN femoral head from long-term steroids. Normal X-ray with persistent hip pain → MRI per NICE/orthopaedic guidance.
explanation.C: Incorrect — Septic arthritis presents acutely with fever, hot joint and severely limited movement.
explanation.D: Incorrect — Osteoporosis doesn't cause hip pain unless there's a fracture; DEXA assesses BMD not AVN.
explanation.E: Incorrect — Trochanteric bursitis causes lateral hip pain reproducible by palpation, not groin pain on weight-bearing.

reference: NICE CKS — Hip pain. BMJ — Avascular necrosis. https://cks.nice.org.uk/topics/hip-pain/

question: A 55-year-old man on prednisolone 15 mg for 8 months for polymyalgia rheumatica has a sudden new onset of severe hip pain after minor exertion. He cannot weight-bear. Per NICE NG187, what is most likely?

options.A: Osteoporotic fragility fracture of the hip — confirmed on X-ray; long-term oral corticosteroid use (≥7.5mg prednisolone for ≥3 months) causes glucocorticoid-induced osteoporosis (GIOP) with significant fracture risk; immediate orthopaedic admission for fracture management; secondary prevention: ensure bisphosphonate (alendronate first-line), calcium and vitamin D, falls assessment
options.B: Hip osteoarthritis — physiotherapy
options.C: Trochanteric bursitis — local steroid injection
options.D: Sciatic radiculopathy — MRI lumbar spine
options.E: Septic arthritis — joint aspiration

explanation.correct: Glucocorticoid-induced osteoporosis (GIOP): long-term corticosteroid use causes rapid bone loss especially in the first 6 months and continued throughout therapy. Fracture risk increases at doses ≥2.5 mg prednisolone/day, becoming significant at ≥7.5 mg/day. Mechanism: reduced osteoblast function, increased osteoclast activity, reduced gut calcium absorption, increased renal calcium loss, suppression of sex hormones. Per NICE NG187 and Royal Osteoporosis Society: any patient starting prednisolone ≥7.5 mg/day for ≥3 months should be assessed for fracture risk (FRAX) and considered for bone protection. Standard regimen: bisphosphonate (alendronate 70mg weekly), calcium 1000mg + vitamin D 800-1000 IU daily, weight-bearing exercise. Sudden severe hip pain after minor exertion = fragility fracture until proven otherwise; X-ray to confirm, immediate orthopaedic referral.
explanation.A: CORRECT — Steroid-induced osteoporosis with fragility hip fracture from minor trauma. Immediate orthopaedic referral per NICE NG187.
explanation.B: Incorrect — OA is gradual; sudden inability to weight-bear suggests fracture.
explanation.C: Incorrect — Trochanteric bursitis doesn't prevent weight-bearing entirely.
explanation.D: Incorrect — Radiculopathy causes radiating leg pain, not isolated hip pain preventing weight-bearing.
explanation.E: Incorrect — Septic arthritis has fever, joint swelling, and movement limitation but not after minor exertion in this pattern.

reference: NICE NG187 — Osteoporosis. Royal Osteoporosis Society — GIOP. https://www.nice.org.uk/guidance/ng187

question: A patient on long-term prednisolone has both osteoporosis and avascular necrosis as potential causes of hip pain. Which feature most distinguishes them?

options.A: AVN causes acute severe pain; osteoporosis causes pain only with fracture
options.B: AVN typically presents with INSIDIOUS chronic groin/hip pain worsening with weight-bearing, NO trauma, normal early X-rays; osteoporosis itself is painless — pain occurs only when there is a FRACTURE (often after minor trauma); fragility fracture shows on X-ray immediately; AVN may require MRI for early diagnosis
options.C: Both present identically and cannot be distinguished
options.D: AVN affects only knees; osteoporosis affects only spine
options.E: AVN is reversed by stopping steroids; osteoporosis is not

explanation.correct: Distinguishing AVN and osteoporotic fracture in steroid users: AVN of femoral head: insidious onset, often weeks/months of progressive groin/hip/thigh pain, worse on weight-bearing, no clear trauma; early X-rays normal (changes lag 3-6 months); MRI essential for early diagnosis. Osteoporotic hip fracture: usually sudden onset after minor trauma (sometimes none), severe pain, inability to weight-bear; X-ray shows fracture clearly; bone mineral density (DEXA) shows osteoporosis (T-score ≤ -2.5). Both can occur in the same patient on long-term steroids — high index of suspicion. AVN occurs in 5-25% of patients on long-term high-dose corticosteroids. Management: AVN treated with orthopaedic referral, possible core decompression early or hip replacement later; osteoporotic fracture treated with surgical fixation/replacement plus bone protection medications.
explanation.A: Incorrect — AVN is typically gradual onset, not acute; osteoporotic fractures may be sudden after minor trauma.
explanation.B: CORRECT — AVN: insidious pain, normal early X-ray, MRI diagnostic. Fracture: acute pain after trauma, X-ray diagnostic. Both can coexist in steroid users.
explanation.C: Incorrect — They can usually be distinguished by history (acute vs insidious) and X-ray (fracture visible vs normal early AVN).
explanation.D: Incorrect — AVN classically affects femoral head but can affect other sites; osteoporotic fractures occur in vertebrae, hip, wrist.
explanation.E: Incorrect — AVN is generally irreversible once established.

reference: NICE CKS — Hip pain. NICE NG187. https://cks.nice.org.uk/topics/hip-pain/

question: A 7-year-old girl presents with 3 weeks of bilateral hip and knee pain, a non-blanching purpuric rash on her knees and shins, lethargy and pallor. She has lost weight. Per NICE NG12 and NICE CKS, what is the diagnosis and immediate action?

options.A: Henoch-Schönlein purpura — urine dipstick and observation
options.B: Acute leukaemia — same-day FBC and urgent paediatric assessment; combination of bone pain (marrow infiltration), purpura (thrombocytopenia), pallor (anaemia) and constitutional symptoms (weight loss, fatigue) is highly suggestive of acute leukaemia (ALL most common in this age group); diagnosis confirmed by FBC showing cytopenia/blasts + bone marrow biopsy; refer URGENTLY same day per NICE NG12
options.C: Juvenile idiopathic arthritis — rheumatology referral
options.D: Growing pains — reassurance
options.E: Septic arthritis — joint aspiration

explanation.correct: Acute lymphoblastic leukaemia (ALL): most common childhood malignancy, peak age 2-5 years. Per NICE NG12 and NICE CKS, red flags suggesting leukaemia in children include: pallor (anaemia), bruising/purpura (thrombocytopenia), recurrent infections (neutropenia), persistent bone or joint pain (marrow infiltration), unexplained fever, lymphadenopathy, hepatosplenomegaly, weight loss, fatigue. Bone pain (especially night pain or affecting walking) is an important and often-overlooked presenting symptom — marrow infiltration causes bone/joint pain often mistaken for JIA, growing pains or musculoskeletal causes. This child has multiple red flags. Action: SAME-DAY FBC and immediate referral to paediatrics (often referred as 'urgent' to paediatric oncology — same day if available). Do not delay for outpatient assessment. Confirmation: FBC (cytopenia, blasts), peripheral blood film, bone marrow aspirate + trephine biopsy with immunophenotyping. Treatment: chemotherapy (UKALL protocol); cure rate >85% in childhood ALL.
explanation.A: Incorrect — HSP doesn't cause weight loss, profound pallor or constitutional symptoms.
explanation.B: CORRECT — Acute leukaemia red flags: bone pain + purpura + pallor + weight loss. Same-day FBC + urgent paediatric referral per NICE NG12.
explanation.C: Incorrect — JIA doesn't cause purpura or pallor; outpatient rheumatology referral would miss leukaemia.
explanation.D: Incorrect — Growing pains never cause purpura, pallor, weight loss or lethargy.
explanation.E: Incorrect — Septic arthritis is monoarticular with fever, not bilateral with these systemic features.

reference: NICE NG12 — Suspected cancer. NICE CKS — Acute leukaemia. https://www.nice.org.uk/guidance/ng12

question: A 5-year-old presents with limb pain at night for 4 months. He plays normally during the day. Examination is normal. FBC and ESR are normal. Per NICE CKS, what is the likely diagnosis?

options.A: Acute leukaemia — repeat FBC
options.B: Growing pains (benign idiopathic limb pain of childhood) — typical features: bilateral limb pain (lower limbs more common), usually in the evening or waking child at night, NO daytime symptoms, child plays and functions normally, no joint swelling, normal examination, normal investigations; common (10-20% of children); peaks 3-12 years; reassurance, massage, paracetamol/ibuprofen, warm baths; resolves spontaneously
options.C: Septic arthritis — orthopaedic referral
options.D: Juvenile idiopathic arthritis — rheumatology referral
options.E: Henoch-Schönlein purpura — urine dipstick

explanation.correct: Growing pains (benign nocturnal limb pain): common cause of recurrent limb pain in school-age children, affecting 10-20%. Classic features per NICE CKS: bilateral (not unilateral — red flag for malignancy), lower limbs (thighs, calves, behind knees), evening/night-time pain, child wakes crying but can usually be soothed, NO daytime symptoms, NO functional limitation (plays normally next day), normal examination, normal growth, normal investigations. Diagnosis is one of EXCLUSION — important to exclude red flags suggesting leukaemia/malignancy/JIA: unilateral pain, joint swelling, morning stiffness, limp, weight loss, fever, fatigue, pallor, bruising, lymphadenopathy. Management: reassurance, simple analgesia (paracetamol/ibuprofen), massage, warm baths; resolves spontaneously over months to years.
explanation.A: Incorrect — Leukaemia red flags absent; normal FBC and well child with normal examination.
explanation.B: CORRECT — Growing pains: bilateral nocturnal limb pain, well in day, normal exam/investigations. Reassurance per NICE CKS.
explanation.C: Incorrect — Septic arthritis is acute with hot swollen joint and fever.
explanation.D: Incorrect — JIA has joint swelling, morning stiffness and functional impact.
explanation.E: Incorrect — HSP has purpuric rash, abdominal pain, and renal involvement.

reference: NICE CKS — Limb pain in children. https://cks.nice.org.uk/topics/limb-pain-in-children/

question: Which feature in a child with limb pain should prompt URGENT investigation for serious pathology rather than reassurance about growing pains?

options.A: Bilateral lower limb pain at night
options.B: Persistent unilateral pain, joint swelling, daytime limp, weight loss, fever, persistent night-waking with severe pain, pain affecting upper limbs predominantly, abnormal examination (swelling, warmth, restricted movement), pallor, bruising, or systemic symptoms — any of these is a red flag and warrants urgent investigation (FBC, ESR, X-ray) and paediatric referral
options.C: Pain that wakes the child but settles with cuddles
options.D: Resolves by morning with normal play
options.E: Pain only after vigorous exercise

explanation.correct: Red flags in childhood limb pain warranting urgent investigation per NICE CKS: Unilateral pain (growing pains are characteristically bilateral); Joint involvement (swelling, redness, warmth) — JIA, septic arthritis, leukaemia; Daytime limp or refusal to weight-bear — significant pathology; Weight loss, fever, fatigue — malignancy, infection, inflammatory disease; Severe night pain that is unrelieved or wakes child repeatedly — leukaemia, malignancy; Upper limb pain (less common in growing pains, more concerning); Abnormal examination findings (warmth, swelling, restriction); Pallor, bruising, lymphadenopathy — leukaemia; Family history of serious musculoskeletal/autoimmune conditions. Initial investigations: FBC + blood film, ESR, CRP, U&Es, LFTs, X-ray of affected area. Referral: same-day if leukaemia suspected; urgent paediatric/rheumatology if JIA suspected.
explanation.A: Incorrect — Bilateral lower limb night pain with normal day function is CLASSIC growing pains, not a red flag.
explanation.B: CORRECT — Red flags requiring urgent investigation per NICE CKS.
explanation.C: Incorrect — Soothable pain at night with cuddles is classic growing pains.
explanation.D: Incorrect — Resolution by morning with normal play supports growing pains.
explanation.E: Incorrect — Pain after vigorous exercise alone is usually musculoskeletal and benign.

reference: NICE CKS — Limb pain in children. NICE NG12 — Suspected cancer. https://cks.nice.org.uk/topics/limb-pain-in-children/

question: A 72-year-old man has isolated Paget's disease of the bone affecting his right tibia. He has bone pain. His ALP is elevated at 380 U/L. Per NICE CKS, what is the first-line treatment?

options.A: Calcium and vitamin D supplementation only
options.B: Oral bisphosphonate (alendronate or risedronate) — first-line for symptomatic Paget's disease; reduces bone turnover, relieves pain, can normalise ALP; IV zoledronic acid is highly effective alternative (often single dose); monitor with serial ALP measurements; refer to endocrinology/metabolic bone specialist if complex, multifocal, or ALP very high
options.C: Methotrexate weekly
options.D: Prednisolone for life
options.E: Surgical excision of the tibia

explanation.correct: Paget's disease of bone: disorder of accelerated bone remodelling, with disorganised osteoblast and osteoclast activity producing abnormal bone that is enlarged, less compact, more vascular and prone to fracture/deformity. Often asymptomatic and found incidentally (raised ALP). Symptomatic Paget's may cause: bone pain (most common), bony deformity (bowing of long bones, skull thickening), pathological fracture, osteoarthritis of adjacent joints, neurological complications (nerve compression, hearing loss if skull affected), high-output cardiac failure (rare), osteosarcoma (rare). Per NICE CKS: First-line treatment of SYMPTOMATIC Paget's = bisphosphonates (oral alendronate, risedronate or IV zoledronic acid). IV zoledronic acid 5mg single dose is often preferred — high efficacy, sustained ALP normalisation. Monitor: ALP every 3-6 months. Indications for treatment: bone pain, complications, asymptomatic disease in weight-bearing bones or at risk of complications. Calcium/vitamin D supplementation alongside bisphosphonates.
explanation.A: Incorrect — Supplementation alone does not treat Paget's; bisphosphonates are needed to reduce bone turnover.
explanation.B: CORRECT — Bisphosphonates (oral or IV zoledronic acid) first-line for symptomatic Paget's per NICE CKS.
explanation.C: Incorrect — Methotrexate has no role in Paget's disease.
explanation.D: Incorrect — Steroids are not used in Paget's; they accelerate bone loss.
explanation.E: Incorrect — Surgery is reserved for specific complications (severe deformity, fracture); not first-line.

reference: NICE CKS — Paget's disease of bone. https://cks.nice.org.uk/topics/pagets-disease-of-bone/

question: A 68-year-old man with Paget's disease of the femur develops new severe pain in his thigh, weight loss, and a hard lump felt over the femur. ALP has further risen from 400 to 850 U/L. What is the most concerning diagnosis?

options.A: Osteomalacia — measure vitamin D
options.B: Osteosarcoma (Paget's sarcoma) — rare but recognised malignant complication of Paget's disease (<1% of cases but accounts for ~50% of adult osteosarcomas); presents with new severe bone pain, soft tissue mass, rapidly rising ALP, weight loss; urgent referral for X-ray, MRI, bone biopsy; very poor prognosis with 5-year survival <10%
options.C: Worsening of Paget's — increase bisphosphonate dose
options.D: Cellulitis — oral flucloxacillin
options.E: Greater trochanteric bursitis — local steroid injection

explanation.correct: Paget's sarcoma (osteosarcoma arising in pagetic bone): rare but devastating complication of Paget's disease, occurring in <1% of cases but accounts for ~50% of adult osteosarcomas. Risk increases with extensive polyostotic Paget's, long duration. Red flags: new severe pain in pagetic bone, weight loss, palpable mass, disproportionately rising ALP. Urgent investigations: plain X-ray (lytic destruction, soft tissue mass), MRI (extent), bone biopsy for histology. Prognosis is very poor (5-year survival <10% even with aggressive treatment). Other malignant complications: chondrosarcoma, fibrosarcoma, giant cell tumour. Investigate any new significant symptoms in Paget's patient, especially with worsening biochemistry.
explanation.A: Incorrect — Osteomalacia doesn't present with rapid pain progression and palpable mass.
