explanation.B: CORRECT — Paget's sarcoma: new severe pain + mass + rising ALP + weight loss. Urgent investigation per NICE.
explanation.C: Incorrect — Increasing bisphosphonate without investigating new significant symptoms is unsafe — could miss malignant transformation.
explanation.D: Incorrect — Cellulitis is acute infection with erythema, warmth, fever; not consistent with this picture.
explanation.E: Incorrect — Bursitis doesn't cause systemic symptoms or rising ALP.

reference: NICE CKS — Paget's disease. NICE NG12 — Suspected cancer. https://cks.nice.org.uk/topics/pagets-disease-of-bone/

question: A routine blood test in an asymptomatic 65-year-old shows isolated ALP elevation at 320 U/L. He feels well. LFTs otherwise normal, calcium normal. Per NICE CKS, what is the next step?

options.A: Repeat in 1 year — likely transient elevation
options.B: Investigate the cause of isolated raised ALP — ALP can be of bone or liver origin; isoenzymes or ALP/GGT ratio can differentiate (raised GGT with raised ALP = liver; isolated raised ALP with normal GGT = bone); investigations for bone source: ALP isoenzymes, X-ray pelvis/long bones for Paget's, bone-specific markers; for asymptomatic Paget's affecting non-weight-bearing bones — monitoring may be sufficient; treatment indicated if symptomatic or affecting bones at risk
options.C: Refer to oncology
options.D: Start bisphosphonate empirically
options.E: No action needed — isolated ALP rise is always benign

explanation.correct: Isolated raised ALP requires investigation as ALP can be from bone or liver: ALP/GGT ratio is useful — raised GGT alongside ALP suggests hepatic origin (liver disease, biliary obstruction); normal GGT with raised ALP suggests bone origin. Bone-origin ALP causes: Paget's disease (most common cause of raised bone ALP in elderly), metastatic bone disease (especially prostate cancer in men, breast in women), recent fracture, hyperparathyroidism, osteomalacia, osteomyelitis. Investigation: ALP isoenzymes (specific bone vs liver fractions), calcium, phosphate, vitamin D, PTH, X-ray of affected/likely affected areas (pelvis common Paget's site), urinary calcium. For confirmed Paget's: management depends on symptoms and bones affected: Asymptomatic + non-weight-bearing bones (e.g., skull base only, distal radius) — monitor; Symptomatic, weight-bearing bones, near joints, or at-risk locations — treat with bisphosphonate.
explanation.A: Incorrect — Persistent ALP elevation requires investigation, not just repeat testing.
explanation.B: CORRECT — Differentiate bone vs liver origin; X-ray and ALP isoenzymes per NICE CKS for isolated raised ALP.
explanation.C: Incorrect — Oncology referral isn't routinely first-line; investigate cause first.
explanation.D: Incorrect — Empirical treatment without diagnosis is inappropriate.
explanation.E: Incorrect — Isolated ALP elevation has important differential diagnosis including malignancy.

reference: NICE CKS — Paget's disease. NICE CKS — Abnormal liver function tests. https://cks.nice.org.uk/topics/pagets-disease-of-bone/

question: A 28-year-old man has incidentally found bilirubin of 38 µmol/L (predominantly unconjugated) on routine bloods. He is well, with normal LFTs otherwise, normal FBC, no haemolysis, and no medication history. Per NICE CKS, what is the most likely diagnosis?

options.A: Gilbert's syndrome — autosomal recessive (or autosomal dominant with incomplete penetrance) deficiency of UDP-glucuronosyltransferase (UGT1A1) reducing bilirubin conjugation; isolated unconjugated hyperbilirubinaemia (usually <70 µmol/L), normal LFTs, no haemolysis, jaundice precipitated by fasting, illness, dehydration, exercise; benign condition needing no treatment; reassurance only
options.B: Hepatitis C — hepatitis C antibody
options.C: Haemolytic anaemia — reticulocyte count
options.D: Primary biliary cholangitis — anti-mitochondrial antibody
options.E: Wilson's disease — caeruloplasmin

explanation.correct: Gilbert's syndrome: most common inherited cause of unconjugated hyperbilirubinaemia, affecting 5-10% of population. Mode of inheritance: autosomal recessive (most common) or autosomal dominant with reduced penetrance — reduced activity of UDP-glucuronosyltransferase 1A1 (UGT1A1) enzyme that conjugates bilirubin. Features: isolated mild unconjugated hyperbilirubinaemia (usually <70 µmol/L); normal AST/ALT/ALP/GGT; normal FBC, reticulocytes (no haemolysis); jaundice intermittent — precipitated by fasting, illness, dehydration, vigorous exercise; otherwise asymptomatic. Per NICE CKS: diagnosis often clinical with characteristic features; no specific test required; genetic testing rarely needed. Management: no treatment required; reassurance. Important: certain drugs metabolised by UGT1A1 (irinotecan, atazanavir, indinavir) require caution in Gilbert's patients.
explanation.A: CORRECT — Gilbert's syndrome: isolated unconjugated hyperbilirubinaemia, otherwise normal, benign. Reassurance only per NICE CKS.
explanation.B: Incorrect — Hepatitis C causes mixed conjugated/unconjugated pattern with raised transaminases.
explanation.C: Incorrect — Haemolysis would show low Hb, raised reticulocytes, raised LDH; this patient has normal FBC and no features of haemolysis.
explanation.D: Incorrect — PBC affects middle-aged women with raised ALP and pruritis; pattern is cholestatic.
explanation.E: Incorrect — Wilson's would have mixed/conjugated picture with neurological features and Kayser-Fleischer rings.

reference: NICE CKS — Gilbert's syndrome. https://cks.nice.org.uk/topics/jaundice/

question: A 25-year-old man with known Gilbert's syndrome is started on irinotecan chemotherapy. Per BNF, what is the concern?

options.A: No concern — Gilbert's syndrome is benign
options.B: Patients with Gilbert's syndrome have reduced UGT1A1 activity which is needed to metabolise SN-38 (the active metabolite of irinotecan); reduced metabolism causes increased SN-38 levels and significantly increased risk of severe neutropenia, diarrhoea and toxicity; dose reduction or alternative chemotherapy may be required; UGT1A1 genotyping is sometimes used to guide irinotecan dosing
options.C: Increased efficacy of irinotecan
options.D: Gilbert's worsens during chemotherapy
options.E: Reduced bilirubin during chemotherapy

explanation.correct: UGT1A1 polymorphisms in Gilbert's syndrome have important pharmacogenomic implications. UGT1A1 conjugates not only bilirubin but also SN-38 (active metabolite of irinotecan, a topoisomerase I inhibitor used in colorectal cancer). Patients with reduced UGT1A1 activity have: increased SN-38 levels and exposure; significantly increased risk of irinotecan toxicity — severe diarrhoea, neutropenia, sepsis. UGT1A1 genotyping (particularly UGT1A1*28 allele) is sometimes performed before irinotecan to guide dose reduction. Other drugs with UGT1A1 metabolism where Gilbert's may be relevant: atazanavir, indinavir (HIV protease inhibitors — increased indirect hyperbilirubinaemia), tranilast, raltegravir. BNF flags Gilbert's syndrome as a consideration in irinotecan and atazanavir prescribing.
explanation.A: Incorrect — Gilbert's has clinically significant pharmacogenomic implications for certain drugs.
explanation.B: CORRECT — Reduced UGT1A1 → reduced SN-38 metabolism → severe toxicity. Dose reduction or genotyping per BNF.
explanation.C: Incorrect — Increased SN-38 leads to toxicity, not therapeutic benefit.
explanation.D: Incorrect — Gilbert's doesn't worsen during chemotherapy; the issue is drug metabolism.
explanation.E: Incorrect — Bilirubin may rise (not fall) due to competition with irinotecan metabolites.

reference: BNF — Irinotecan. https://bnf.nice.org.uk/drug/irinotecan.html

question: A patient is investigated for jaundice. Bilirubin is 60 µmol/L, predominantly conjugated; LFTs normal; haemolysis screen negative; liver USS normal. What is the most likely diagnosis?

options.A: Gilbert's syndrome
options.B: Dubin-Johnson syndrome — autosomal recessive inherited disorder caused by mutations in MRP2/ABCC2 gene encoding a canalicular transporter; results in isolated conjugated hyperbilirubinaemia (defect in bilirubin excretion into bile after conjugation); benign condition; characteristic black liver pigmentation on biopsy (lipofuscin); diagnosis often clinical after excluding other causes; no specific treatment needed
options.C: Crigler-Najjar syndrome
options.D: Acute hepatitis A
options.E: Choledocholithiasis

explanation.correct: Dubin-Johnson syndrome: rare autosomal recessive condition caused by mutations in the MRP2/ABCC2 gene encoding a canalicular conjugated bilirubin transporter. Defect in EXCRETION of conjugated bilirubin from hepatocytes into bile — bilirubin is normally conjugated but cannot be transported out. Features: isolated CONJUGATED hyperbilirubinaemia (40-150 µmol/L); normal LFTs (no liver damage); no haemolysis; liver biopsy shows characteristic black pigmentation (lipofuscin deposition in lysosomes). Benign condition with normal life expectancy. Distinguish from: Gilbert's (UNCONJUGATED hyperbilirubinaemia from reduced conjugation); Crigler-Najjar (more severe UGT1A1 deficiency causing severe unconjugated hyperbilirubinaemia from birth — Type 1 fatal in infancy without phototherapy/transplantation); Rotor syndrome (similar to Dubin-Johnson but no liver pigmentation). Compare bilirubin pattern: unconjugated raised → Gilbert's, haemolysis, Crigler-Najjar; conjugated raised → Dubin-Johnson, Rotor, biliary obstruction, hepatocellular disease.
explanation.A: Incorrect — Gilbert's causes UNCONJUGATED hyperbilirubinaemia; this is conjugated.
explanation.B: CORRECT — Dubin-Johnson: isolated conjugated hyperbilirubinaemia, normal LFTs, benign, MRP2/ABCC2 mutation.
explanation.C: Incorrect — Crigler-Najjar causes severe UNCONJUGATED hyperbilirubinaemia (Gilbert's variant), not conjugated.
explanation.D: Incorrect — Hepatitis A causes raised transaminases and clinical illness; LFTs would not be normal.
explanation.E: Incorrect — Choledocholithiasis would cause raised ALP/GGT and dilated biliary tree on USS.

reference: BMJ Best Practice — Hyperbilirubinaemia. https://bestpractice.bmj.com/topics/en-gb/3000038

question: A 45-year-old man with resistant hypertension on three antihypertensives is found to have a serum potassium of 2.9 mmol/L and sodium 144 mmol/L. Per NICE NG136, what is the most likely diagnosis?

options.A: Cushing's syndrome — 24-hour urinary cortisol
options.B: Primary aldosteronism (Conn's syndrome) — autonomous aldosterone secretion (adrenal adenoma or bilateral adrenal hyperplasia); causes hypertension, hypokalaemia (often), metabolic alkalosis, mildly elevated sodium; screening test: aldosterone:renin ratio (ARR) — raised aldosterone with suppressed renin; confirmation: saline suppression test; localisation: adrenal CT, adrenal vein sampling; treatment: aldosterone antagonist (spironolactone, eplerenone) or surgical adrenalectomy for adenoma
options.C: Phaeochromocytoma — urinary metanephrines
options.D: Renal artery stenosis — renal artery USS
options.E: Essential hypertension — no further investigation

explanation.correct: Primary aldosteronism (Conn's syndrome): one of the most common causes of secondary/resistant hypertension (5-10% of hypertensive patients overall, up to 20% of resistant hypertension). Two main pathological subtypes: aldosterone-producing adenoma (Conn's adenoma, 30%) — unilateral, surgically curable; bilateral adrenal hyperplasia (60%) — treated medically. Clinical features: hypertension (often resistant), hypokalaemia (often but not always — can have normal K+), metabolic alkalosis, mildly elevated sodium. Per NICE NG136 and Endocrine Society guidelines: screening with aldosterone:renin ratio (ARR) — primary aldosteronism shows raised aldosterone with suppressed renin. Patient should withdraw interfering medications (spironolactone, eplerenone, beta-blockers, diuretics) for accurate testing — usually need to switch to doxazosin and verapamil. Confirmation: saline suppression test (failure to suppress aldosterone). Localisation: CT adrenals; adrenal vein sampling (gold standard for determining unilateral vs bilateral source). Treatment: unilateral adenoma → laparoscopic adrenalectomy; bilateral hyperplasia → aldosterone antagonist (spironolactone or eplerenone).
explanation.A: Incorrect — Cushing's typically has truncal obesity, striae, raised cortisol; hypokalaemia less typical unless severe ectopic ACTH.
explanation.B: CORRECT — Primary aldosteronism: resistant HTN + hypokalaemia. Screen with ARR per NICE NG136 / Endocrine Society.
explanation.C: Incorrect — Phaeochromocytoma causes paroxysmal HTN with palpitations, sweating, headache; less hypokalaemia.
explanation.D: Incorrect — Renal artery stenosis would have raised renin (not suppressed); important to differentiate.
explanation.E: Incorrect — Hypokalaemia with hypertension requires investigation for secondary cause.

reference: NICE NG136 — Hypertension. Endocrine Society — Primary Aldosteronism Guideline. https://www.nice.org.uk/guidance/ng136

question: A patient with confirmed primary aldosteronism has bilateral adrenal hyperplasia on imaging. Per Endocrine Society guidelines, what is the preferred medical management?

options.A: Surgical bilateral adrenalectomy
options.B: Spironolactone (aldosterone receptor antagonist) — first-line medical treatment for bilateral adrenal hyperplasia (and for patients with unilateral adenoma who decline surgery or are not surgical candidates); start 25-50mg daily, titrate to BP and potassium response; common adverse effects: gynaecomastia (men), menstrual irregularity (women), erectile dysfunction; eplerenone is more selective alternative with fewer hormonal side effects but more expensive; monitor BP, potassium, renal function
options.C: ACE inhibitor monotherapy
options.D: Beta-blocker monotherapy
options.E: Lifelong oral corticosteroids

explanation.correct: Per Endocrine Society guidelines on primary aldosteronism, medical treatment is preferred for bilateral adrenal hyperplasia (bilateral disease cannot be cured surgically without complete adrenalectomy and lifelong adrenal insufficiency). Spironolactone: first-line aldosterone receptor antagonist. Starting dose 12.5-25mg daily, titrated to 100-400mg daily based on BP and potassium response. Side effects: gynaecomastia (up to 10%), menstrual irregularity, erectile dysfunction (because spironolactone also blocks androgen receptors — non-selective). Eplerenone: more selective mineralocorticoid receptor antagonist with fewer hormonal side effects; preferred if spironolactone causes gynaecomastia. Other agents: amiloride (epithelial sodium channel blocker, less effective than spironolactone). Monitor: BP, potassium (risk of hyperkalaemia), creatinine. Bilateral adrenalectomy is rarely performed due to subsequent adrenal insufficiency requiring lifelong replacement.
explanation.A: Incorrect — Bilateral adrenalectomy causes adrenal insufficiency requiring lifelong steroids — not preferred.
explanation.B: CORRECT — Spironolactone first-line for bilateral adrenal hyperplasia; eplerenone if side effects per Endocrine Society.
explanation.C: Incorrect — ACE inhibitors are less specific and effective for primary aldosteronism.
explanation.D: Incorrect — Beta-blockers have minimal effect on aldosterone-driven HTN.
explanation.E: Incorrect — Oral corticosteroids treat adrenal insufficiency or autoimmune disease, not Conn's syndrome.

reference: Endocrine Society — Primary Aldosteronism Clinical Practice Guideline. https://academic.oup.com/jcem/article/101/5/1889/2804729

question: Before screening for primary aldosteronism with the aldosterone:renin ratio, which medications must usually be withheld for accurate results?

options.A: Paracetamol and aspirin
options.B: Spironolactone, eplerenone, amiloride (mineralocorticoid antagonists/K-sparing diuretics) — withhold for at least 4-6 weeks; also avoid beta-blockers (suppress renin, falsely raising ARR), ACE inhibitors/ARBs (lower aldosterone), and diuretics (alter potassium); convert antihypertensives to non-interfering agents: doxazosin (alpha-blocker), verapamil/diltiazem (non-dihydropyridine CCB), hydralazine; correct hypokalaemia before testing
options.C: All medications can be continued
options.D: Only PPIs need to be stopped
options.E: Only statins need to be stopped

explanation.correct: Accurate ARR (aldosterone:renin ratio) testing requires withdrawal of interfering medications: Mineralocorticoid receptor antagonists (spironolactone, eplerenone): suppress aldosterone and elevate renin — false negative; withhold for 4-6 weeks. Potassium-sparing diuretics (amiloride): similar effect. Beta-blockers: suppress renin — false POSITIVE; ideally stop 2 weeks before testing. ACE inhibitors/ARBs: reduce aldosterone — may cause false negative; stop 2 weeks before. Diuretics: alter potassium and volume status. Non-interfering agents to use as substitutes: doxazosin (alpha-blocker), verapamil/diltiazem (non-dihydropyridine CCB), hydralazine. Correct hypokalaemia before testing as low K+ can artificially suppress aldosterone (falsely lowering ARR). Patient ideally upright/seated for at least 2 hours before sampling. Maintain normal salt intake. Repeat sampling if ARR borderline.
explanation.A: Incorrect — Paracetamol and aspirin don't interfere with ARR.
explanation.B: CORRECT — Withhold spironolactone, eplerenone for 4-6 weeks; consider others; substitute with non-interfering agents per Endocrine Society.
explanation.C: Incorrect — Several medications significantly affect ARR results and require withdrawal/substitution.
explanation.D: Incorrect — PPIs don't affect ARR.
explanation.E: Incorrect — Statins don't affect ARR.

reference: Endocrine Society — Primary Aldosteronism Guidelines. https://academic.oup.com/jcem/article/101/5/1889/2804729

question: A 78-year-old woman presents with thoracic back pain and a clear thoracic kyphosis on examination. She has lost 6 cm in height over 5 years. Per NICE NG187, what is the most likely diagnosis and key investigation?

options.A: Multiple myeloma — urgent serum electrophoresis
options.B: Osteoporotic vertebral fractures with secondary kyphosis — height loss >4 cm + thoracic kyphosis is highly suggestive of vertebral compression fractures; investigate with thoracolumbar spine X-rays (lateral views; vertebral fractures often asymptomatic but cumulative); DEXA scan to confirm osteoporosis; calculate FRAX 10-year fracture risk; treat with bisphosphonate (alendronate first-line), calcium and vitamin D; investigate for secondary causes if young/atypical (DEXA T-score, vitamin D, calcium, TFTs, myeloma screen)
options.C: Ankylosing spondylitis — HLA-B27
options.D: Cervical spondylosis — MRI cervical spine
options.E: Mechanical back pain — physiotherapy and reassurance

explanation.correct: Osteoporotic vertebral fractures: often asymptomatic (only 30% are clinically recognised); cause progressive height loss, thoracic kyphosis ('dowager's hump'), chronic back pain, reduced exercise tolerance, restrictive lung disease in severe cases. Per NICE NG187, risk factors: postmenopausal woman, age >70, family history of hip fracture, low BMI, glucocorticoid use, smoking, excess alcohol, conditions (rheumatoid arthritis, malabsorption, hyperthyroidism, hypogonadism). Investigation: thoracolumbar spine X-rays (lateral views — vertebral fracture assessment shows wedge, biconcave or crush fractures); DEXA scan (lumbar spine and hip, T-score ≤ -2.5 = osteoporosis); FRAX score for 10-year fracture risk; biochemistry (calcium, phosphate, ALP, vitamin D, TFTs, myeloma screen if atypical, U&Es). Treatment per NICE: bisphosphonate (alendronate 70mg weekly is first-line), calcium 1000mg + vitamin D 800-1000 IU daily, weight-bearing exercise, falls prevention. Vertebral fracture is a strong indicator of future fracture risk and should not be missed.
explanation.A: Incorrect — Myeloma can cause vertebral fractures but the typical presentation (postmenopausal woman, gradual height loss/kyphosis) is osteoporosis; myeloma screen if atypical features (anaemia, renal impairment, hypercalcaemia).
explanation.B: CORRECT — Osteoporotic vertebral fractures: height loss + kyphosis. X-ray + DEXA + bisphosphonate per NICE NG187.
explanation.C: Incorrect — Ankylosing spondylitis is inflammatory back pain in young men, not progressive kyphosis in elderly women.
explanation.D: Incorrect — Cervical spondylosis would cause neck pain and radiculopathy, not thoracic kyphosis.
explanation.E: Incorrect — Height loss and kyphosis warrant investigation, not just reassurance.

reference: NICE NG187 — Osteoporosis. NICE CKS — Osteoporosis. https://www.nice.org.uk/guidance/ng187

question: An 80-year-old woman with osteoporosis is unable to tolerate oral alendronate due to oesophagitis. Per NICE NG187, what is the next treatment option?

options.A: No alternative available — accept fracture risk
options.B: Switch to alternative bone protection: IV zoledronic acid (5mg infusion annually — bisphosphonate avoiding oesophageal issues), subcutaneous denosumab (60mg every 6 months — RANKL inhibitor), or risedronate (alternative oral bisphosphonate with fewer GI side effects); choice depends on patient preference and clinical context
options.C: Increase oral alendronate dose
options.D: Add prednisolone for bone protection
options.E: Stop all treatment

explanation.correct: Per NICE NG187 and NICE TA464, alternatives to oral alendronate when not tolerated: IV zoledronic acid: 5mg infusion annually — bypasses GI tract entirely, very effective; flu-like reaction common after first infusion (give paracetamol); contraindicated if eGFR <35 ml/min. Denosumab: 60mg subcutaneous injection every 6 months — RANKL inhibitor (different mechanism, prevents osteoclast formation); NICE TA464 approved for postmenopausal women with low BMD who cannot tolerate other treatments; important: must NOT be stopped without alternative therapy (rebound vertebral fractures within months of discontinuation). Other oral options: risedronate (35mg weekly — less GI irritation than alendronate; same administration rules — upright for 30 minutes), ibandronate (monthly oral or 3-monthly IV). Strontium ranelate withdrawn from UK due to cardiovascular concerns. Other agents for severe osteoporosis: teriparatide (PTH analogue, daily SC injection), romosozumab (NICE TA791).
explanation.A: Incorrect — Many effective alternatives are available.
explanation.B: CORRECT — IV zoledronic acid, denosumab, or risedronate per NICE NG187 / TA464.
explanation.C: Incorrect — Increasing dose worsens oesophageal irritation.
explanation.D: Incorrect — Prednisolone worsens osteoporosis significantly.
explanation.E: Incorrect — Untreated osteoporosis has high fracture risk; switch to alternative.

reference: NICE NG187. NICE TA464 — Denosumab. https://www.nice.org.uk/guidance/ng187

question: A 75-year-old woman on denosumab for 4 years for osteoporosis stops it without alternative therapy. 8 months later she presents with multiple new vertebral fractures. What is the explanation?

options.A: Coincidental — vertebral fractures common in this age group
options.B: Rebound bone loss / multiple vertebral fractures (MVF) after denosumab discontinuation — when denosumab is stopped, suppressed osteoclast activity rebounds with rapid loss of bone density and high fracture risk within 6-12 months; per MHRA Drug Safety Update, denosumab must NEVER be stopped without immediately transitioning to another bone protection agent (usually a bisphosphonate); current guidance recommends giving zoledronic acid or oral bisphosphonate for at least 12 months after stopping denosumab
options.C: Calcium toxicity from supplementation
options.D: Magnesium deficiency
options.E: Side effect of denosumab still active

explanation.correct: Rebound bone loss and multiple vertebral fractures after denosumab discontinuation: a well-recognised, serious complication highlighted by MHRA Drug Safety Updates and NICE. Mechanism: denosumab is a RANKL inhibitor that completely suppresses osteoclast activity (deeper suppression than bisphosphonates); when stopped, there is rapid rebound activation of osteoclasts, leading to rapid bone resorption and microarchitectural deterioration. Multiple vertebral fractures often occur within 6-12 months of stopping. Risk factors: longer duration of treatment, previous vertebral fracture, advanced age. Per MHRA/NICE: denosumab must NEVER be stopped without transitioning to alternative bone protection — usually IV zoledronic acid or oral bisphosphonate continued for at least 12 months. If denosumab is delayed (planned or missed dose), give within a few weeks; consider alternative if extended interruption. This concept is high-yield for AKT exams.
explanation.A: Incorrect — Multiple vertebral fractures within 8 months of stopping denosumab is the recognised rebound phenomenon.
explanation.B: CORRECT — Rebound MVF post-denosumab. Never stop without bisphosphonate cover per MHRA Drug Safety Update.
explanation.C: Incorrect — Calcium toxicity causes hypercalcaemia symptoms, not vertebral fractures.
explanation.D: Incorrect — Magnesium deficiency causes neuromuscular symptoms, not vertebral fractures.
explanation.E: Incorrect — Denosumab's effects rapidly reverse after stopping; this is rebound bone loss not side effect.

reference: MHRA Drug Safety Update — Denosumab rebound. https://www.gov.uk/drug-safety-update

question: A 3-year-old boy is brought with 10 days of pallor, petechiae, fatigue and frequent bruising. He has been more lethargic. On examination there is hepatosplenomegaly. Per NICE NG12, what is the most likely diagnosis and immediate action?

options.A: Iron deficiency anaemia — start ferrous sulphate
options.B: Acute leukaemia (most likely ALL) — same-day FBC + immediate paediatric referral; triad of pallor (anaemia), petechiae/bruising (thrombocytopenia), recurrent infections/lethargy + hepatosplenomegaly is highly suggestive of acute leukaemia; FBC will show cytopenia and likely blasts; bone marrow biopsy with immunophenotyping confirms diagnosis; treatment with chemotherapy via paediatric oncology
options.C: Henoch-Schönlein purpura — urine dipstick and observation
options.D: Idiopathic thrombocytopenic purpura — observation
options.E: Aplastic anaemia — non-urgent haematology referral

explanation.correct: Acute lymphoblastic leukaemia (ALL): most common childhood cancer, peak age 2-5 years. Per NICE NG12 and NICE CKS, red flags suggesting leukaemia: pallor (anaemia), petechiae/bruising/bleeding (thrombocytopenia), recurrent infections (neutropenia), bone pain, weight loss, fatigue, hepatosplenomegaly, lymphadenopathy. Combination of features = same-day referral. SAME-DAY FBC and IMMEDIATE paediatric referral required. Bone marrow biopsy with immunophenotyping, cytogenetics confirms diagnosis. UK paediatric ALL: cure rate >85% with modern chemotherapy (UKALL protocol). Treatment phases: induction (achieves remission), consolidation, maintenance over ~2-3 years. Risk stratification based on age, WBC at presentation, cytogenetics, MRD response.
explanation.A: Incorrect — Iron deficiency anaemia doesn't cause petechiae, bruising or hepatosplenomegaly.
explanation.B: CORRECT — ALL: pallor + petechiae + hepatosplenomegaly + lethargy. Same-day FBC and urgent paediatric referral per NICE NG12.
explanation.C: Incorrect — HSP has palpable purpura (not petechiae), abdominal pain, arthralgia, normal FBC.
explanation.D: Incorrect — ITP has isolated thrombocytopenia without anaemia, hepatosplenomegaly or other red flags.
explanation.E: Incorrect — Aplastic anaemia is rare; presentation with pallor, petechiae and hepatosplenomegaly is more suggestive of leukaemia, and either way requires SAME-DAY (not non-urgent) referral.

reference: NICE NG12 — Suspected cancer. NICE CKS — Acute leukaemia. https://www.nice.org.uk/guidance/ng12

question: An 8-year-old with newly diagnosed ALL is undergoing induction chemotherapy. She presents to A&E with fever 38.5°C and feels unwell. Her last chemotherapy was 7 days ago. Per BTOG/UKHSA febrile neutropenia guidance, what is the immediate action?

options.A: Oral paracetamol and review in 24 hours
options.B: Emergency admission, urgent FBC, blood cultures, and empirical IV broad-spectrum antibiotics (piperacillin-tazobactam or meropenem) within 1 hour of presentation — febrile neutropenia (temperature ≥38°C with absolute neutrophil count <0.5 × 10⁹/L, or anticipated to fall below) is a medical emergency due to risk of sepsis and rapid deterioration; do NOT wait for confirmation of neutropenia — treat empirically; chemotherapy nadir typically 7-14 days post-treatment
options.C: Oral antibiotics and review at GP
options.D: Antipyretics only — common in chemotherapy patients
options.E: Wait for FBC results before action

explanation.correct: Febrile neutropenia: medical emergency in oncology patients. Definition: temperature ≥38.0°C (or two readings ≥37.5°C in an hour) with neutrophil count <0.5 × 10⁹/L or expected to fall to <0.5. Chemotherapy nadir typically 7-14 days post-cycle (this patient's last chemo was 7 days ago — high risk). Per NICE CG151 (Neutropenic sepsis) and NCEPOD: immediate management algorithm (within 1 hour — 'door to needle' time): (1) Recognise — do not assume infection requires confirmed neutropenia first; (2) Resuscitation as needed (oxygen, IV fluids); (3) Cultures: blood cultures (peripheral and central line if present), MSU, sputum, swabs of suspected sites; (4) Empirical IV broad-spectrum antibiotics within 1 hour: piperacillin-tazobactam 4.5g IV first-line (per Trust protocol; alternative meropenem); (5) Admit to oncology unit. Mortality of untreated neutropenic sepsis: up to 20-30%. All chemotherapy patients should carry a 'neutropenic sepsis card' advising emergency presentation if any fever or signs of infection.
explanation.A: Incorrect — Delay risks fatal sepsis.
explanation.B: CORRECT — Febrile neutropenia: emergency admission + IV antibiotics within 1 hour per NICE CG151. Do not wait for FBC confirmation.
explanation.C: Incorrect — Oral antibiotics insufficient for potential neutropenic sepsis.
explanation.D: Incorrect — Antipyretics mask the fever and delay treatment of life-threatening sepsis.
explanation.E: Incorrect — Treatment is started empirically — do not wait for FBC results.

reference: NICE CG151 — Neutropenic sepsis. https://www.nice.org.uk/guidance/cg151

question: A child in remission from ALL is due routine vaccinations. Per the Green Book, what is the advice on live vaccines during and after chemotherapy?

options.A: All vaccines can be given normally throughout treatment
options.B: Live vaccines (MMR, BCG, varicella, oral polio, yellow fever) are CONTRAINDICATED during chemotherapy and for at least 6 months after completion (some guidance up to 12 months); inactivated vaccines (DTaP, IPV, Hib, MenC, MenB, pneumococcal, HPV, influenza) can usually be given but immune response may be reduced — revaccination after treatment completion often recommended; specialist advice from paediatric oncology team needed
options.C: Live vaccines preferred during chemotherapy for stronger response
options.D: All vaccines must be stopped permanently after chemotherapy
options.E: Only oral polio vaccine is allowed during chemotherapy

explanation.correct: Per the Green Book (UK Immunisation against infectious disease) Chapter 6 (Contraindications and special considerations) and Chapter 7 (Immunisation of individuals with underlying medical conditions): live vaccines (containing attenuated organisms — MMR, BCG, varicella, oral polio (no longer used in UK), yellow fever, rotavirus, herpes zoster) are CONTRAINDICATED in immunosuppressed patients due to risk of disseminated disease from the vaccine organism. During chemotherapy and for at least 6 months after completion (longer for stem cell transplantation), live vaccines are avoided. Inactivated vaccines: not contraindicated but immune response may be reduced; revaccination/booster after treatment may be recommended. Specialist advice from paediatric oncology recommended for individualised guidance. Household contacts should be up to date with vaccinations (including live vaccines like MMR, varicella) to protect the immunosuppressed patient through herd immunity — household contacts can receive live vaccines safely except for oral polio (rarely used). Annual influenza vaccine recommended for the patient and household contacts.
explanation.A: Incorrect — Live vaccines are specifically contraindicated during chemotherapy.
explanation.B: CORRECT — Live vaccines contraindicated during chemo and 6 months after per Green Book; inactivated can be given.
explanation.C: Incorrect — Live vaccines risk causing disease in immunocompromised patients.
explanation.D: Incorrect — Vaccines can resume after a suitable interval post-treatment.
explanation.E: Incorrect — Oral polio is also a live vaccine and is contraindicated.

reference: Green Book — Immunisation against infectious disease. https://www.gov.uk/government/collections/immunisation-against-infectious-disease-the-green-book

question: A 68-year-old man with severe COPD on triple therapy (ICS/LABA/LAMA) continues to have 4 exacerbations per year. His blood eosinophils are 0.15 × 10⁹/L. He is a non-smoker. Per NICE NG115, what is the next appropriate treatment step?

options.A: Add roflumilast — first-line for all frequent exacerbators
options.B: Prophylactic azithromycin — for patients with ≥3 exacerbations/year on optimised inhaled therapy; pre-treatment checks required: ECG (QTc), audiometry, sputum culture for NTM, LFTs; dose 250mg three times weekly; reduces exacerbation frequency by ~37%
options.C: Long-term oral prednisolone maintenance
options.D: Stop ICS immediately — low eosinophils means no benefit
options.E: Increase ICS dose

explanation.correct: Per NICE NG115, prophylactic azithromycin is recommended for patients with COPD and frequent exacerbations (typically ≥3/year) despite optimised inhaled triple therapy, who are non-smokers. It reduces COPD exacerbations by approximately 37% (Albert et al, NEJM 2011 — the ALBERT trial). Pre-treatment mandatory checks: ECG (QTc >450ms is a contraindication due to arrhythmia risk), audiometry (ototoxicity risk), sputum culture and chest imaging to exclude NTM infection (azithromycin monotherapy selects for macrolide-resistant NTM), LFTs. Review at 6 months for ongoing benefit. Roflumilast is specifically for chronic bronchitis phenotype (productive cough ≥3 months/year for ≥2 consecutive years) with FEV1 <50% and frequent exacerbations — not blanket use.
explanation.A: Incorrect — Roflumilast is specifically for the chronic bronchitis phenotype with FEV1 <50%; not first-line add-on therapy for all frequent exacerbators.
explanation.B: CORRECT — Azithromycin prophylaxis per NICE NG115 for ≥3 exacerbations/year on optimised inhaled therapy, non-smoker. Pre-treatment ECG, audiometry, NTM exclusion required.
explanation.C: Incorrect — Long-term oral prednisolone maintenance is not recommended in COPD — causes significant harm (osteoporosis, diabetes, Cushingoid features) without sustained benefit.
explanation.D: Incorrect — ICS withdrawal is considered for low eosinophils (<0.1) with recurrent pneumonia — not the immediate next step for a frequent exacerbator on triple therapy.
explanation.E: Incorrect — Increasing ICS dose has minimal additional efficacy and increases pneumonia risk further.

reference: NICE NG115 — COPD in over 16s: diagnosis and management. https://www.nice.org.uk/guidance/ng115

question: Before starting prophylactic azithromycin for COPD, a GP checks the patient's ECG. The QTc is 460ms. Per NICE NG115 and BNF, what is the correct action?

options.A: Start azithromycin at half dose
options.B: Do not start azithromycin — QTc >450ms is a contraindication due to risk of life-threatening arrhythmia (torsades de pointes); review other QT-prolonging medications; consider alternative strategies for exacerbation prevention (roflumilast if chronic bronchitis phenotype, mucolytics, pulmonary rehabilitation optimisation, vaccination); cardiology input if QTc needs formal assessment
options.C: Start azithromycin and repeat ECG in 4 weeks
options.D: Switch to clarithromycin instead — no QT effect
options.E: QTc 460ms is normal — proceed with azithromycin

explanation.correct: Per NICE NG115 and BNF, QTc prolongation is a key contraindication to prophylactic azithromycin in COPD. Azithromycin is a macrolide antibiotic that inhibits cardiac hERG (IKr) potassium channels → QTc prolongation → risk of torsades de pointes (polymorphic ventricular tachycardia) which can be fatal. Contraindications per NICE NG115: QTc >450ms in males or >470ms in females (thresholds vary slightly between guidelines — generally >450ms warrants caution). Additional QT risk factors: concurrent QT-prolonging drugs (amiodarone, domperidone, antipsychotics, certain antibiotics), hypokalaemia, hypomagnesaemia, bradycardia, history of cardiac arrhythmia. Clarithromycin also prolongs QTc — not an alternative. If azithromycin contraindicated: review if roflumilast appropriate, mucolytics (carbocisteine), optimise vaccination, pulmonary rehabilitation.
explanation.A: Incorrect — There is no evidence that half-dose azithromycin is safer for QTc; contraindication remains.
explanation.B: CORRECT — QTc >450ms: do not start azithromycin per NICE NG115. Consider alternatives.
explanation.C: Incorrect — Starting then repeating ECG risks arrhythmia in the interim.
explanation.D: Incorrect — Clarithromycin also prolongs QTc and carries the same risk — not an alternative.
explanation.E: Incorrect — QTc 460ms is prolonged (normal <440ms in men). This is a specific contraindication.

reference: NICE NG115 — COPD. BNF — Azithromycin. https://bnf.nice.org.uk/drug/azithromycin.html

question: A 70-year-old woman with COPD on ICS/LABA/LAMA has been prescribed prophylactic azithromycin for 8 months. Routine audiometry reveals 20dB hearing loss in the right ear. Per BNF, what is the appropriate action?

options.A: Continue azithromycin — hearing loss is unrelated
options.B: Stop azithromycin — sensorineural hearing loss (ototoxicity) is a recognised adverse effect of azithromycin; this is dose-dependent but can be irreversible; stopping promptly may prevent further progression; document and report via Yellow Card; reassess COPD management strategy
options.C: Reduce azithromycin dose to 250mg once weekly
options.D: Add hearing aids and continue azithromycin
options.E: Switch to erythromycin — no ototoxicity risk

explanation.correct: Per BNF, macrolide antibiotics (azithromycin, clarithromycin, erythromycin) can cause ototoxicity — sensorineural hearing loss and tinnitus. Risk: cumulative dose-dependent; may be irreversible if not detected early. This is why NICE NG115 mandates baseline audiometry before starting prophylactic azithromycin and regular monitoring (every 6-12 months). New hearing loss in a patient on azithromycin must be attributed to the drug until proven otherwise. Action: stop azithromycin promptly; audiological follow-up; assess whether hearing loss stabilises or resolves after stopping; report via MHRA Yellow Card (important as azithromycin ototoxicity in COPD prophylaxis setting needs pharmacovigilance). Erythromycin also carries ototoxicity risk — not a safe alternative.
explanation.A: Incorrect — New sensorineural hearing loss on azithromycin is likely azithromycin-induced ototoxicity until excluded.
explanation.B: CORRECT — Stop azithromycin due to ototoxicity per BNF; Yellow Card report; audiological follow-up.
explanation.C: Incorrect — Reducing dose doesn't reverse established ototoxicity; stopping is required.
explanation.D: Incorrect — Continuing risks further irreversible hearing loss.
explanation.E: Incorrect — Erythromycin also causes ototoxicity — not a safer alternative.

reference: BNF — Azithromycin adverse effects. NICE NG115. https://bnf.nice.org.uk/drug/azithromycin.html

question: A 7-year-old boy presents with a 3-day sore throat, fever and white exudate visible on both tonsils. He has no cough. Per NICE NG84, what clinical scoring tool helps determine antibiotic prescribing and what is the first-line antibiotic?

options.A: No scoring tool needed — all children with tonsillitis need antibiotics
options.B: FeverPAIN or Centor score guides antibiotic use; FeverPAIN score ≥4 (Fever in 24h, Purulence, Attended rapidly ≤3 days, severely Inflamed tonsils, No cough/coryza) = likely bacterial; first-line: phenoxymethylpenicillin (penicillin V) 250mg four times daily for 5-10 days; avoid amoxicillin (causes rash in EBV/glandular fever which can mimic tonsillitis)
options.C: Amoxicillin 500mg three times daily — first-line for all tonsillitis
options.D: Co-amoxiclav 312.5mg three times daily for 7 days
options.E: No antibiotics — all childhood tonsillitis is viral

explanation.correct: Per NICE NG84 (Sore throat: antimicrobial prescribing), clinical scoring tools guide antibiotic decisions in sore throat/tonsillitis. FeverPAIN score: Fever in preceding 24 hours (1 point), Purulence — exudate on tonsils (1 point), Attended rapidly — ≤3 days from onset (1 point), severely Inflamed tonsils (1 point), No cough or coryza (1 point). Score 0-1: very likely viral — no antibiotics. Score 2-3: uncertain — consider delayed antibiotic prescription. Score 4-5: likely bacterial — immediate antibiotic appropriate. Centor criteria: tonsillar exudate, tender anterior cervical lymphadenopathy, absence of cough, fever — each 1 point; score ≥3 suggests bacterial. First-line antibiotic: phenoxymethylpenicillin (penicillin V) 250mg (under 5 years), 500mg (5-17 years), QDS for 5-10 days. AVOID amoxicillin/ampicillin — causes florid maculopapular rash in EBV (glandular fever) which is in the differential; if rash occurs with amoxicillin, arrange monospot/EBV serology.
explanation.A: Incorrect — Most sore throats/tonsillitis are viral; antibiotics are indicated only when clinical scoring suggests bacterial cause.
explanation.B: CORRECT — FeverPAIN/Centor score; penicillin V first-line; avoid amoxicillin per NICE NG84.
explanation.C: Incorrect — Amoxicillin should be avoided in tonsillitis as it causes rash in EBV.
explanation.D: Incorrect — Co-amoxiclav is not first-line for uncomplicated tonsillitis.
explanation.E: Incorrect — ~30% of tonsillitis is bacterial (Group A Streptococcus) and benefits from antibiotics.

reference: NICE NG84 — Sore throat (acute): antimicrobial prescribing. https://www.nice.org.uk/guidance/ng84

question: A 10-year-old treated with amoxicillin for presumed tonsillitis develops a widespread maculopapular rash 48 hours after starting treatment. What does this indicate and what should be done?

options.A: Penicillin allergy — document and avoid all penicillins lifelong
options.B: Likely Epstein-Barr virus (EBV) infection — amoxicillin/ampicillin causes a florid, non-allergic maculopapular rash in approximately 90% of patients with concurrent EBV/glandular fever; arrange Paul-Bunnell (monospot) test and EBV IgM/IgG serology; stop amoxicillin; this is NOT a true penicillin allergy — document clearly; most patients can safely receive penicillin in future
options.C: Stevens-Johnson syndrome — urgent dermatology referral
options.D: Drug reaction — prescribe oral antihistamines and continue amoxicillin
options.E: Measles — viral exanthem

explanation.correct: Amoxicillin rash in EBV: amoxicillin and ampicillin cause a characteristic widespread erythematous maculopapular rash in ~90% of patients with concurrent Epstein-Barr virus (EBV/infectious mononucleosis) infection. The mechanism is immune-complex mediated — not IgE-mediated Type 1 hypersensitivity (i.e., not a true penicillin allergy). Clinical context: child with tonsillitis treated with amoxicillin, rash appears 1-3 days after starting treatment. Investigation: Paul-Bunnell/monospot test (heterophile antibodies), EBV IgM (acute infection). Correct documentation: 'amoxicillin rash in context of EBV — NOT penicillin allergy' — this is critical; incorrectly labelling as penicillin allergy leads to lifelong inappropriate avoidance of penicillin. This is why NICE NG84 specifically warns AGAINST prescribing amoxicillin for sore throat — use penicillin V instead. If genuine uncertainty about allergy: refer to allergy clinic for challenge testing.
explanation.A: Incorrect — This is NOT a true penicillin allergy — it is an EBV-amoxicillin drug interaction; documenting as penicillin allergy has serious long-term consequences.
explanation.B: CORRECT — EBV-amoxicillin rash: monospot test; stop amoxicillin; NOT penicillin allergy per NICE NG84.
explanation.C: Incorrect — Stevens-Johnson syndrome is much more severe (mucosal involvement, skin detachment) and uncommon.
explanation.D: Incorrect — Continuing amoxicillin with EBV extends unnecessary treatment of what is now confirmed viral.
explanation.E: Incorrect — Measles rash starts at head/neck and descends; preceded by prodrome and Koplik spots.

reference: NICE NG84 — Sore throat. NICE CKS — Infectious mononucleosis. https://www.nice.org.uk/guidance/ng84

question: A 16-year-old presents with 7 days of severe sore throat, marked fatigue, posterior cervical lymphadenopathy and hepatosplenomegaly. Monospot is positive. Per NICE CKS, what sport restriction applies and why?

options.A: No restrictions — glandular fever is mild
options.B: Avoid contact sports and vigorous physical activity for at least 3-4 weeks from symptom onset due to risk of splenic rupture — glandular fever causes splenomegaly (palpable in ~50%); an enlarged spleen is fragile and can rupture with minor trauma (even a cough or bump); splenic rupture is a rare but potentially fatal emergency; sport can usually resume after 4 weeks if splenomegaly has resolved clinically
options.C: Sports restriction for 6 months
options.D: Restriction only for the first 48 hours of illness
options.E: No sport restriction — only driving is affected

explanation.correct: Infectious mononucleosis (EBV glandular fever): per NICE CKS, splenomegaly occurs in approximately 50% of patients, usually peaking in the second week. The enlarged spleen is at risk of traumatic rupture (even from non-direct trauma such as sudden exertion, Valsalva, or minor contact). Splenic rupture occurs in <0.5% of EBV patients but is life-threatening (internal haemorrhage). Management: avoid contact sports, vigorous exercise and activities with abdominal impact for at least 3-4 weeks from onset (4 weeks is often quoted; some guidelines recommend up to 8 weeks for high-contact sports). Return to sport: when symptoms resolved and splenomegaly has clinically resolved (USS if uncertainty). General management of EBV/glandular fever: supportive — rest, adequate hydration, paracetamol/ibuprofen for pain and fever; avoid amoxicillin; avoid corticosteroids routinely (only for airway compromise, severe thrombocytopenia, haemolytic anaemia). Fatigue often persists for weeks to months.
explanation.A: Incorrect — Glandular fever causes splenomegaly with significant rupture risk; sports restriction is essential.
explanation.B: CORRECT — No contact sports for 3-4 weeks (splenic rupture risk) per NICE CKS.
explanation.C: Incorrect — 6 months is excessive; 3-4 weeks is standard guidance.
explanation.D: Incorrect — Restriction for 48 hours is inadequate; splenomegaly persists for weeks.
explanation.E: Incorrect — Driving restriction applies to specific medical conditions; sport restriction is the relevant advice here.

reference: NICE CKS — Infectious mononucleosis. https://cks.nice.org.uk/topics/infectious-mononucleosis/

question: A 32-year-old man is worried about a red, smooth irregular patch on his tongue that has been there for 3 months and changes shape slightly each week. He is a non-smoker and drinks minimal alcohol. Per NICE CKS, what is the most likely diagnosis and management?

options.A: Leukoplakia — urgent 2WW biopsy
options.B: Geographic tongue (benign migratory glossitis) — benign condition causing irregular smooth erythematous patches with whitish margins that characteristically migrate in pattern over days to weeks; no malignant potential; no treatment required; reassure the patient; review only if symptomatic or features change to suggest leukoplakia/erythroplakia
options.C: Oral candidiasis — nystatin suspension
options.D: Oral lichen planus — topical steroids
options.E: Aphthous ulceration — topical corticosteroids

explanation.correct: Geographic tongue (benign migratory glossitis): benign inflammatory condition of the tongue dorsum affecting ~1-3% of the population. Pathognomonic features: well-demarcated smooth erythematous patches (atrophic papillae) with raised whitish borders that MIGRATE in pattern over days to weeks — the changing pattern is diagnostic. Usually asymptomatic; some patients report mild sensitivity to spicy or acidic foods. No malignant potential. Per NICE CKS: no investigation or treatment needed for asymptomatic cases — reassurance is the key intervention. If symptomatic: avoid triggers (spicy/acidic foods), topical benzydamine, rarely topical corticosteroid for severe cases. Key distinction from serious conditions: unlike leukoplakia (white non-scraped patch, potentially premalignant) or erythroplakia (red patch, high malignant risk), geographic tongue MOVES in pattern and is clearly benign.
explanation.A: Incorrect — Geographic tongue is benign; leukoplakia is a static white patch with malignant potential (requires biopsy).
explanation.B: CORRECT — Geographic tongue: reassure, no treatment needed per NICE CKS.
explanation.C: Incorrect — Oral candidiasis causes white plaques that can be scraped off (pseudomembranous) or diffuse redness (erythematous); doesn't migrate in pattern.
explanation.D: Incorrect — Oral lichen planus causes Wickham striae (white lacy pattern) or erosive changes; doesn't migrate.
explanation.E: Incorrect — Aphthous ulcers are painful discrete ulcers with a yellow base and red halo; not migrating patches.

reference: NICE CKS — Oral ulceration and general oral health. https://cks.nice.org.uk/

question: A 55-year-old male smoker presents with a white non-scraped patch on the lateral border of his tongue that has been present for 2 months and is not painful. Per NICE CKS and NICE NG12, what is the appropriate management?

options.A: Reassure — benign finding in smokers
options.B: Urgent 2WW oral surgery/maxillofacial referral — oral leukoplakia (white patch not scraped off, not attributable to any known cause) is a potentially premalignant lesion; risk of malignant transformation is ~1-3%/year overall, higher on ventrolateral tongue; risk factors: smoking, alcohol, HPV; requires biopsy for histological grading (dysplasia); management: smoking cessation, alcohol reduction, regular surveillance; biopsy if any change in appearance or symptoms
options.C: Prescribe nystatin — likely oral candidiasis
options.D: Review in 12 months — no urgent action
options.E: Geographic tongue — reassure

explanation.correct: Oral leukoplakia: white patch or plaque on the oral mucosa that cannot be rubbed off and cannot be characterised as any other known lesion. Classified as a potentially premalignant oral disorder (PPOD). Per NICE NG12, any unexplained oral mucosal patch (leukoplakia, erythroplakia, red and white lesions) requires urgent 2WW referral for specialist assessment and biopsy. Risk of malignant transformation: leukoplakia overall 1-3%/year; erythroplakia (red patch) up to 40%; mixed red/white patches (erythroleukoplakia) ~7-18%. High-risk sites: ventrolateral tongue, floor of mouth, soft palate. Risk factors: tobacco (smoking, chewing), betel nut, alcohol, HPV-16. Management: stop smoking and alcohol; biopsy under specialist care; surveillance every 6-12 months; dysplastic lesions: excision/laser ablation. Geographic tongue (benign migratory glossitis) is clearly distinct — migrating pattern, different appearance, clearly benign.
explanation.A: Incorrect — Leukoplakia in a smoker requires urgent referral, not reassurance.
explanation.B: CORRECT — Urgent 2WW referral for oral leukoplakia per NICE NG12.
explanation.C: Incorrect — Candidiasis can mimic leukoplakia but candida plaques can be scraped off; this lesion cannot — requires biopsy.
explanation.D: Incorrect — A 12-month review delay is unacceptable for a potentially premalignant lesion.
explanation.E: Incorrect — Geographic tongue migrates; leukoplakia is static and histologically distinct.

reference: NICE NG12 — Suspected cancer: recognition and referral. https://www.nice.org.uk/guidance/ng12

question: A 40-year-old woman presents with painful recurrent oral ulcers affecting the buccal mucosa, lasting 7-14 days and recurring monthly. She has no other symptoms. Per NICE CKS, what is the most likely diagnosis and management?

options.A: Oral cancer — urgent biopsy
options.B: Recurrent aphthous stomatitis (RAS/aphthous ulcers) — most common cause of recurrent oral ulceration; well-demarcated painful ulcers with yellow/grey base and erythematous halo; three types (minor, major, herpetiform); minor aphthae (most common: <10mm, heal within 10-14 days without scarring); management: topical corticosteroid (betamethasone mouthwash or triamcinolone paste), chlorhexidine mouthwash; exclude underlying cause (haematinic deficiency — FBC, B12, folate, ferritin; coeliac disease — tTG IgA; Crohn's; Behçet's if other systemic features); advise avoidance of SLS-containing toothpaste
options.C: Herpes simplex — oral aciclovir
options.D: Geographic tongue — no treatment
options.E: Oral lichen planus — prednisolone

explanation.correct: Recurrent aphthous stomatitis (RAS): most common oral mucosal condition, affecting ~20% of the population. Three clinical types: Minor (80%): ulcers <10mm, heal without scarring in 10-14 days; Major (10%): ulcers >10mm, heal over weeks, may scar; Herpetiform (10%): multiple tiny (1-3mm) ulcers that can coalesce. Per NICE CKS: exclude underlying causes in recurrent/severe aphthae: haematinic deficiency (iron — ferritin, B12, folate — FBC/blood film), coeliac disease (tTG IgA — associated in 5% of RAS), IBD, HIV, Behçet's disease (if genital ulcers or uveitis also present). Management: topical steroids (betamethasone 500mcg dissolved in water as mouthwash, or triamcinolone paste), chlorhexidine gluconate 0.2% mouthwash (antiplaque, mildly helpful), avoid SLS (sodium lauryl sulphate) in toothpaste — may worsen ulcers. Systemic treatment for severe refractory cases: colchicine, thalidomide (specialists only).
explanation.A: Incorrect — Oral cancer causes a non-healing ulcer, typically on lateral tongue or floor of mouth, firm indurated edge; not recurrent aphthous ulcers.
explanation.B: CORRECT — RAS: topical steroids, exclude haematinic deficiency and coeliac per NICE CKS.
explanation.C: Incorrect — Herpes simplex (primary) causes acute stomatitis with gingival involvement; recurrent herpes labialis is on the lip not buccal mucosa.
explanation.D: Incorrect — Geographic tongue is a painless migrating patch, not ulcers.
explanation.E: Incorrect — Oral lichen planus causes white striae or erosive lesions, typically bilateral, not discrete aphthous ulcers.

reference: NICE CKS — Mouth ulcers. https://cks.nice.org.uk/topics/mouth-ulcers/

question: A 62-year-old man with COPD is started on inhaled fluticasone/salmeterol. Six weeks later he presents with productive cough, fever and new consolidation on CXR. His COPD has been stable. Per MHRA drug safety guidance and NICE NG115, what is the complication?

options.A: COPD exacerbation — increase bronchodilators
options.B: Inhaled corticosteroid (ICS)-associated pneumonia — ICS use in COPD significantly increases the risk of pneumonia compared to bronchodilator therapy alone (unlike in asthma); MHRA Drug Safety Update highlights this risk; consider ICS withdrawal especially if blood eosinophils <0.1 × 10⁹/L; switch to LABA/LAMA dual bronchodilation if recurrent pneumonia
options.C: COPD exacerbation from viral infection — oseltamivir
options.D: Drug reaction to salmeterol
options.E: Pleural effusion — USS guided aspiration

explanation.correct: Per MHRA Drug Safety Update and NICE NG115, inhaled corticosteroids (ICS) in COPD patients increase the risk of pneumonia by approximately 1.5-2× compared to those not on ICS. This is unlike asthma where ICS clearly benefit without this pneumonia risk. Key evidence: TORCH trial (fluticasone/salmeterol vs placebo) showed significantly higher pneumonia rates with ICS. MHRA issued a safety update requiring patients to be informed of this risk. Clinical implication: ICS should only be used in COPD when appropriate (eosinophil-guided — higher eosinophils suggest more anti-inflammatory benefit, less pneumonia risk); recurrent pneumonia on ICS → consider withdrawal; blood eosinophil count <0.1 × 10⁹/L → ICS less likely to benefit and higher pneumonia risk → consider LABA/LAMA without ICS. Per NICE NG115, blood eosinophil count guides ICS use in COPD.
explanation.A: Incorrect — New fever, productive cough and consolidation represent pneumonia, not simply an exacerbation requiring bronchodilator adjustment.
explanation.B: CORRECT — ICS-associated pneumonia in COPD; MHRA safety update; consider ICS withdrawal per NICE NG115.
explanation.C: Incorrect — Oseltamivir is for influenza; bacterial pneumonia requires antibiotics.
explanation.D: Incorrect — Salmeterol (LABA) doesn't typically cause pneumonia.
explanation.E: Incorrect — Consolidation (not effusion) is the finding; USS-guided aspiration is for pleural effusion.

reference: MHRA Drug Safety Update — ICS and COPD pneumonia. NICE NG115. https://www.gov.uk/drug-safety-update

question: A GP reviews a COPD patient on triple therapy (fluticasone/salmeterol/tiotropium). Blood eosinophils are 0.06 × 10⁹/L and she has had 2 pneumonias in 12 months. Per NICE NG115, what is the recommended management of her ICS?

options.A: Increase ICS dose — more anti-inflammatory cover needed
options.B: Consider withdrawing ICS component — blood eosinophils <0.1 × 10⁹/L indicate minimal ICS benefit in preventing exacerbations; combined with 2 ICS-associated pneumonias, the risk-benefit ratio strongly favours ICS withdrawal; switch to LABA/LAMA dual bronchodilation; taper ICS gradually (do not stop abruptly — exacerbation risk); monitor closely for increased exacerbation frequency after withdrawal
options.C: Add a second ICS for synergistic effect
options.D: Switch ICS from fluticasone to budesonide and continue
options.E: Continue current therapy — eosinophil count is irrelevant

explanation.correct: Per NICE NG115, blood eosinophil count guides ICS use in COPD: Eosinophils ≥0.3 × 10⁹/L: high likelihood of benefit from ICS; Eosinophils 0.1-0.3 × 10⁹/L: uncertain benefit — clinical judgement; Eosinophils <0.1 × 10⁹/L: ICS unlikely to benefit (low exacerbation prevention) AND higher pneumonia risk. With <0.1 eosinophils AND recurrent ICS-associated pneumonia: ICS withdrawal is strongly indicated. Withdrawal method: taper gradually over weeks (do not abruptly stop — risk of adrenal insufficiency with high-dose ICS and risk of exacerbation if patient relies on ICS). Maintain LABA/LAMA (dual bronchodilation). Monitor: spirometry, exacerbation frequency, symptoms after withdrawal. Evidence for withdrawal: WISDOM trial showed non-inferiority of ICS withdrawal vs continuation in selected COPD patients when LABA/LAMA maintained.
explanation.A: Incorrect — Increasing ICS in a patient with low eosinophils and recurrent ICS pneumonias increases harm without benefit.
explanation.B: CORRECT — ICS withdrawal: eosinophils <0.1 + recurrent pneumonia = withdraw ICS; maintain LABA/LAMA per NICE NG115.
explanation.C: Incorrect — Dual ICS has no evidence base and would increase harm.
explanation.D: Incorrect — All ICS carry pneumonia risk in COPD; switching ICS type doesn't solve the problem.
explanation.E: Incorrect — Eosinophil count is a key biomarker for ICS decision-making per NICE NG115.

reference: NICE NG115 — COPD. https://www.nice.org.uk/guidance/ng115

question: A patient using a budesonide/formoterol inhaler for COPD asks how to reduce the risk of developing oral candidiasis. Per BNF and NICE, what advice should be given?

options.A: Stop using the ICS inhaler immediately
options.B: Rinse mouth with water and spit after each inhalation; use a spacer device with pressurised metered-dose inhalers (pMDI) to reduce oropharyngeal drug deposition; these measures significantly reduce incidence of oral candidiasis
options.C: Prescribe prophylactic oral fluconazole daily
options.D: Switch to a non-steroid inhaler
options.E: Gargle with antiseptic mouthwash before use

explanation.correct: Per BNF and NICE guidance, inhaled corticosteroid (ICS) use causes local immunosuppression of oropharyngeal mucosa leading to oral candidiasis (Candida albicans overgrowth). Prevention: (1) Rinse mouth with water and spit thoroughly after every ICS inhalation — removes residual steroid from oral mucosa; (2) Use a spacer device with pMDIs — reduces oropharyngeal deposition of large steroid particles, improving lung delivery and reducing local side effects; (3) Dry powder inhalers (DPIs) generally have lower oropharyngeal deposition than pMDIs without spacers. Treatment of established oral candidiasis: topical nystatin suspension first-line; systemic fluconazole 150mg single dose if topical fails. Prophylactic daily fluconazole is not routinely recommended. Dysphonia (hoarse voice) is another common local side effect of ICS, also reduced by rinsing.
explanation.A: Incorrect — ICS should not be stopped; preventive measures are effective.
explanation.B: CORRECT — Rinse and spit after each ICS use; spacer with pMDI per BNF/NICE.
explanation.C: Incorrect — Daily prophylactic fluconazole is not routinely recommended; simple measures (rinsing) are effective.
explanation.D: Incorrect — Some ICS use is indicated; switch to different device type may help but not stopping ICS.
explanation.E: Incorrect — Antiseptic mouthwash before (not after) use has no evidence; rinsing AFTER is the correct approach.

reference: BNF — Inhaled corticosteroids: side effects. NICE NG115. https://bnf.nice.org.uk/

question: A 58-year-old man presents with 2 weeks of fever, night sweats, weight loss, and a new pan-systolic murmur. He had a dental procedure 6 weeks ago. He uses IV drugs occasionally. Per NICE CG64, what is the most likely diagnosis and immediate investigation?

options.A: Viral myocarditis — troponin and echocardiogram
options.B: Infective endocarditis (IE) — diagnosis based on Duke criteria; immediate blood cultures (3 sets from different sites before antibiotics), urgent echocardiogram (transthoracic ± transoesophageal), FBC, CRP, ESR; empirical IV antibiotics after cultures; Duke major criteria: positive blood cultures, echocardiographic findings (vegetation, abscess); Duke minor criteria: fever >38°C, risk factor (IV drug use, valvular disease, recent dental procedure), embolic phenomena, vascular phenomena
options.C: Pneumonia — CXR and sputum culture
options.D: Rheumatic fever — throat swab and ASO titre
options.E: Tuberculosis — sputum AFB and Mantoux

explanation.correct: Infective endocarditis (IE): infection of cardiac endothelium (usually heart valves). Per NICE CG64 and ESC guidelines, Duke criteria guide diagnosis: Definite: 2 major OR 1 major + 3 minor OR 5 minor criteria. Major criteria: (1) Positive blood cultures — typical organism (Streptococcus viridans, Staphylococcus aureus, HACEK group, Enterococcus), OR persistently positive cultures, OR single positive Coxiella; (2) Echocardiographic evidence — vegetation, abscess, dehiscence of prosthetic valve. Minor criteria: predisposing cardiac condition or IV drug use; fever >38°C; vascular phenomena (emboli, Janeway lesions, intracranial haemorrhage); immunological phenomena (Osler nodes, Roth spots, positive rheumatoid factor, glomerulonephritis); microbiological — positive cultures not meeting major criteria. Management: empirical IV antibiotics after 3 blood cultures — amoxicillin + flucloxacillin + gentamicin (or vancomycin if penicillin-allergic or MRSA risk); duration 4-6 weeks; surgery if: haemodynamic compromise, large vegetation, abscess, persistent infection.
explanation.A: Incorrect — Myocarditis causes chest pain and cardiac failure without fever and new murmur in this context.
explanation.B: CORRECT — IE: blood cultures × 3 before antibiotics + urgent echo + IV antibiotics per NICE CG64.
explanation.C: Incorrect — Pneumonia doesn't cause new cardiac murmur or weeks of night sweats.
explanation.D: Incorrect — Rheumatic fever follows streptococcal pharyngitis in children/young adults — typically; this patient is older and has IE risk factors.
explanation.E: Incorrect — TB causes chronic systemic illness but doesn't cause new cardiac murmur in this way.

reference: NICE CG64 — Prophylaxis against infective endocarditis. ESC Guidelines on IE 2023. https://www.nice.org.uk/guidance/cg64

question: A patient with confirmed Streptococcus viridans infective endocarditis asks why the dentist didn't give antibiotic prophylaxis before the procedure. Per NICE CG64, is antibiotic prophylaxis before dental procedures currently recommended for at-risk patients?

options.A: Yes — all patients with valvular heart disease should receive amoxicillin before dental procedures
options.B: No — NICE CG64 (2008) advises AGAINST routine antibiotic prophylaxis for dental procedures in patients at risk of IE; evidence showed prophylaxis was not effective in preventing IE and overuse increased antibiotic resistance; emphasis is instead on maintaining good oral hygiene, regular dental review, and patient education about IE symptoms
options.C: Prophylaxis only needed for prosthetic valves
options.D: Prophylaxis with amoxicillin 3g is given 1 hour before dental procedures
options.E: NICE recommends prophylaxis for all invasive procedures including dental

explanation.correct: Per NICE CG64 (2008, reviewed 2016 and 2023 — guidance maintained): antibiotic prophylaxis before dental procedures is NOT recommended routinely for patients at risk of IE in England and Wales. This is a controversial but evidence-based recommendation: the previous practice of giving antibiotics before dental procedures lacked robust evidence of efficacy; bacteraemia from routine daily activities (chewing, tooth brushing) may be more significant than procedural bacteraemia; overuse of prophylactic antibiotics increases resistance and anaphylaxis risk. NICE CG64 recommends: explain to at-risk patients why prophylaxis is not recommended; emphasise importance of maintaining good oral hygiene (brushing twice daily, regular dental review) — the most effective prevention; advice on IE symptoms (fever, new murmur, embolic events) — early presentation. Note: European (ESC) and American (AHA/ACC) guidelines still recommend prophylaxis in high-risk groups (prosthetic valves, previous IE) — NICE differs from international guidance; this is a high-yield AKT distinction.
explanation.A: Incorrect — NICE CG64 specifically does NOT recommend routine prophylaxis for dental procedures.
explanation.B: CORRECT — NICE CG64: no routine prophylaxis; emphasise oral hygiene and IE symptom awareness.
explanation.C: Incorrect — Even for prosthetic valves, NICE does not recommend dental prophylaxis (unlike ESC/AHA).
explanation.D: Incorrect — This was the pre-NICE CG64 practice — it is no longer recommended.
explanation.E: Incorrect — NICE CG64 specifically states prophylaxis is NOT recommended for dental/other procedures.

reference: NICE CG64 — Prophylaxis against infective endocarditis. https://www.nice.org.uk/guidance/cg64

question: A patient with IE develops sudden left-sided weakness and visual disturbance during treatment. CXR shows new pleural effusion. Per ESC IE guidelines, what complication is this?

options.A: Side effect of IV antibiotics
options.B: Systemic embolisation — vegetation fragments from the infected valve embolise to distant sites; cerebral emboli (stroke/TIA), splenic infarcts, renal infarcts, septic pulmonary emboli (right-sided IE), retinal emboli (Roth spots); this is an indication for considering surgery (embolisation on therapy, large mobile vegetation >10mm); neurology consultation and imaging urgently
options.C: Heart failure from valve destruction — reduce IV fluids
options.D: Drug fever from antibiotics
options.E: Pericarditis — add aspirin

explanation.correct: Systemic embolisation is the most common extracardiac complication of IE, occurring in 20-50% of cases. Right-sided IE (typical in IV drug users) embolises to the lungs → septic pulmonary emboli → cavitating lung lesions, pleural effusion, empyema. Left-sided IE embolises to systemic circulation → cerebral emboli (stroke/TIA — most feared; 20% of IE patients), splenic/renal infarcts (abdominal pain), retinal emboli (Roth spots — white-centred haemorrhages on fundoscopy), peripheral emboli (Janeway lesions on palms/soles — painless; Osler nodes on fingers — painful, immune complex-mediated). Per ESC IE guidelines, indications for urgent surgery include: large mobile vegetation (>10mm) with embolisation, severe valve regurgitation causing haemodynamic compromise, perivalvular abscess, persistent infection. Embolisation despite antibiotic therapy with large vegetation is a surgical indication.
explanation.A: Incorrect — IV antibiotic side effects don't cause focal neurological deficit or pleural effusion.
explanation.B: CORRECT — Systemic embolisation: cerebral emboli (stroke), septic pulmonary emboli (effusion). Consider surgery per ESC.
explanation.C: Incorrect — Valve destruction causes heart failure with pulmonary oedema, not focal neurology.
explanation.D: Incorrect — Drug fever is generalised; doesn't cause focal deficit or pleural effusion.
explanation.E: Incorrect — Pericarditis in IE suggests perivalvular abscess extension, not embolisation.

reference: ESC Guidelines on Infective Endocarditis 2023. https://www.escardio.org/Guidelines/Clinical-Practice-Guidelines/

question: A 28-year-old woman with known epilepsy is on sodium valproate 1000mg daily and waiting to see neurology. She has been seizure-free for 3 months. She attends the GP and mentions she has been feeling unwell with some increased seizure activity. Per NICE CG137 and MHRA guidance, what is the correct management while awaiting the neurology appointment?

options.A: Stop valproate immediately
options.B: Continue current medication unchanged and advise the patient not to stop or change valproate without specialist input — abrupt changes to anti-epileptic therapy outside specialist guidance risk status epilepticus (a life-threatening emergency); ensure neurology appointment is expedited; if seizure breakthrough is occurring, document clearly and escalate urgency; per MHRA, valproate should not be started or changed in women of childbearing potential without specialist review and valproate pregnancy prevention programme compliance
options.C: Double the valproate dose immediately
options.D: Switch to levetiracetam without specialist input
options.E: Start carbamazepine in addition to valproate

explanation.correct: Per NICE CG137 (Epilepsies: diagnosis and management) and MHRA valproate safety guidance, changes to antiepileptic drug (AED) therapy should only be made under specialist supervision. For a patient awaiting neurology review: (1) Do NOT stop or change AED — abrupt cessation of valproate can precipitate status epilepticus (a medical emergency with mortality up to 20%); (2) Continue current medication; (3) Document breakthrough seizure activity and escalate urgency of neurology referral accordingly; (4) MHRA valproate Pregnancy Prevention Programme (PPP): valproate is teratogenic — if this is a woman of childbearing potential, ensure she is enrolled in the PPP, using effective contraception, and has had the MHRA toolkit discussed. The GP should not alter AED regimens without specialist input — this is a NICE CG137 principle. If there are signs of status epilepticus: emergency admission.
explanation.A: Incorrect — Abrupt valproate cessation risks life-threatening status epilepticus.
explanation.B: CORRECT — Continue valproate unchanged; expedite neurology; no GP-initiated dose changes per NICE CG137.
explanation.C: Incorrect — Doubling dose without specialist guidance risks toxicity.
explanation.D: Incorrect — Switching AEDs without specialist supervision is dangerous and inappropriate.
explanation.E: Incorrect — Adding carbamazepine without specialist input has unpredictable pharmacokinetic interactions.

reference: NICE CG137 — Epilepsies: diagnosis and management. MHRA — Valproate PPP. https://www.nice.org.uk/guidance/cg137

question: A 32-year-old woman with epilepsy on sodium valproate attends for a routine review. Per MHRA 2023 Pregnancy Prevention Programme requirements, what must the GP do at this consultation?

options.A: No specific action needed — epilepsy management is the neurologist's responsibility only
options.B: Ensure the patient is enrolled in the MHRA Valproate Pregnancy Prevention Programme (PPP): (1) Annual review of ongoing need for valproate; (2) Confirm she understands the teratogenic risks (10-11% major malformations, 30-40% neurodevelopmental disorders); (3) Confirm she is using highly effective contraception; (4) Confirm annual specialist review has occurred; (5) Sign the risk acknowledgement form with the patient; (6) Prescribe maximum 30-day supply; document in notes
options.C: Stop valproate and switch to safer alternative immediately
options.D: Test pregnancy status and if negative continue without further action
options.E: No specific women's health consideration for epilepsy medications

explanation.correct: Per MHRA 2023 Valproate Pregnancy Prevention Programme (PPP): valproate (Epilim, Depakote) is absolutely contraindicated in women of childbearing potential UNLESS the conditions of the PPP are met. GP responsibilities in the PPP: (1) Annual review of valproate indication — is it still needed? Are safer alternatives appropriate? (Neurology must lead on this if epilepsy); (2) Ensure patient enrolled in PPP — has received MHRA patient information pack; (3) Confirm highly effective contraception is in place (implant, IUS, combined pill — ideally LARC); (4) Confirm annual specialist review has occurred (neurologist for epilepsy); (5) Patient signs the 'Risk Acknowledgement Form' at each prescription; (6) Prescribe maximum 30-day supply (not repeatable without review); (7) Document all discussions. These obligations apply to GPs prescribing or co-signing valproate prescriptions. Failure to comply with PPP is a regulatory and professional responsibility concern.
explanation.A: Incorrect — GPs share responsibility for PPP compliance at every consultation involving valproate.
explanation.B: CORRECT — Annual PPP review: contraception confirmed, risks discussed, form signed, 30-day supply per MHRA 2023.
explanation.C: Incorrect — GP should not unilaterally stop valproate; epilepsy AED changes require neurologist input.
explanation.D: Incorrect — Pregnancy testing alone is insufficient — ongoing contraception and risk documentation required.
explanation.E: Incorrect — Valproate in women of childbearing age has specific mandatory MHRA obligations.

reference: MHRA — Valproate Pregnancy Prevention Programme 2023. https://www.gov.uk/drug-safety-update

question: A 26-year-old woman with juvenile myoclonic epilepsy on valproate 1000mg daily is planning a pregnancy. She asks about switching. Per NICE CG137 and MHRA, what are the issues with switching in JME specifically?

options.A: All AEDs are equally effective for JME — switch to any alternative
options.B: Juvenile myoclonic epilepsy (JME) is particularly challenging — valproate is the most effective AED for JME (broad-spectrum; covers myoclonus, absence, generalised tonic-clonic seizures); lamotrigine can worsen myoclonic jerks in JME; levetiracetam is an alternative but has lower efficacy; any switch MUST be neurologist-led — risk of seizure relapse (including status epilepticus) during transition; pre-conception planning should start months before attempting pregnancy
options.C: Switch to carbamazepine — safest in pregnancy
options.D: All women with JME should stop all AEDs before pregnancy
options.E: Valproate is safe in the first trimester only

explanation.correct: Per NICE CG137 and MHRA, pre-conception epilepsy management in women on valproate is complex. JME-specific issues: valproate is the most effective AED for JME — efficacy ~85-90%; Lamotrigine: can WORSEN myoclonic seizures in JME — a critical and often missed point; levetiracetam: effective for some JME patients but overall lower efficacy than valproate; perampanel: emerging evidence for JME. Pre-conception advice: ideally start neurological review 6-12 months before planned pregnancy; specialist review to assess: is valproate still essential? Could slow cross-tapering to levetiracetam/topiramate work?; start folic acid 5mg daily 3 months before conception; never stop valproate abruptly — status epilepticus risk (particularly dangerous in pregnancy). The dilemma: untreated/uncontrolled seizures in pregnancy also harm the fetus. MHRA: if valproate continued in pregnancy (after all alternatives tried and failed), document explicit informed consent and ensure fetal medicine surveillance.
explanation.A: Incorrect — AEDs are NOT interchangeable for JME; lamotrigine can worsen myoclonus in JME.
explanation.B: CORRECT — JME: valproate most effective; lamotrigine can worsen JME; neurologist-led switch only; pre-conception planning per NICE/MHRA.
explanation.C: Incorrect — Carbamazepine is a narrow-spectrum AED for focal epilepsy; can worsen generalised epilepsies like JME.
explanation.D: Incorrect — Stopping AEDs without specialist advice risks status epilepticus and is dangerous in pregnancy.
explanation.E: Incorrect — Valproate causes teratogenic effects throughout pregnancy — there is no 'safe' trimester.

reference: NICE CG137 — Epilepsies. MHRA Valproate PPP. https://www.nice.org.uk/guidance/cg137

question: An 8-year-old boy on trimethoprim prophylaxis for recurrent UTIs has a routine dipstick showing leucocytes 2+ and nitrites positive. He is asymptomatic. Per NICE NG224, what is the correct management?

options.A: Asymptomatic bacteriuria in children on prophylaxis requires no treatment — treat only if symptomatic
options.B: Send MSU for culture and sensitivity — asymptomatic positive dipstick in a child on prophylaxis suggests a breakthrough infection despite trimethoprim; culture identifies the organism and sensitivity pattern; if culture confirms significant bacteriuria (>10⁵ CFU/ml), treat with a different antibiotic (not trimethoprim which may have prophylaxis-selected resistance); reassess the prophylaxis regimen
options.C: Increase trimethoprim dose immediately
options.D: Asymptomatic bacteriuria in children should always be treated — start co-amoxiclav
options.E: Repeat dipstick in 2 weeks

explanation.correct: Per NICE NG224 (Urinary tract infections in under 16s), prophylactic antibiotics in children aim to prevent symptomatic UTIs. A positive dipstick (nitrites + leucocytes) in an asymptomatic child on prophylaxis: asymptomatic bacteriuria (ASB) — debated whether to treat in children on prophylaxis; however a breakthrough infection despite prophylaxis needs investigation.
