Key steps: (1) Send MSU for culture — confirm organism and sensitivity; check if resistant to trimethoprim (commonly develops on trimethoprim prophylaxis); (2) If symptomatic UTI: treat with appropriate antibiotic per sensitivities (not trimethoprim if resistant); (3) If truly asymptomatic bacteriuria with no symptoms: NICE NG224 generally advises not treating ASB; however, in a child on prophylaxis this suggests prophylaxis may be failing — review need for prophylaxis, renal tract anatomy USS; (4) Antibiotic choice: nitrofurantoin or cefalexin per sensitivities. Note: routine dipstick monitoring in asymptomatic children on prophylaxis is not recommended by NICE — dipstick only if symptomatic.
explanation.A: Incorrect — While ASB is generally not treated, a breakthrough on prophylaxis warrants culture to check for resistance and assess prophylaxis efficacy.
explanation.B: CORRECT — MSU for culture in child on prophylaxis with positive dipstick; identify resistance pattern; review prophylaxis per NICE NG224.
explanation.C: Incorrect — Without culture, increasing trimethoprim risks treating a resistant organism.
explanation.D: Incorrect — Asymptomatic bacteriuria in children is NOT routinely treated per NICE NG224.
explanation.E: Incorrect — A positive dipstick in a child on prophylaxis warrants culture, not a 2-week delay.

reference: NICE NG224 — Urinary tract infections in under 16s. https://www.nice.org.uk/guidance/ng224

question: A 6-year-old girl has had her third UTI in 6 months. Urine cultures show E. coli sensitive to trimethoprim and nitrofurantoin each time. Per NICE NG224, what should be considered after recurrent UTIs?

options.A: No further action — recurrent UTIs are normal in girls
options.B: Investigate for urinary tract abnormality: renal USS (first-line imaging); consider voiding cystourethrogram (VCUG/MCUG) if upper UTI with abnormal USS or recurrent UTIs; consider antibiotic prophylaxis (trimethoprim 2mg/kg at night or nitrofurantoin 1mg/kg at night); review bladder and bowel habits (constipation and bladder dysfunction are common underlying causes); refer to paediatric urology/nephrology if recurrent UTIs or abnormal imaging
options.C: Prescribe long-term co-amoxiclav for 2 years
options.D: Only treat when symptomatic — no prophylaxis needed
options.E: Immediate cystoscopy under general anaesthetic

explanation.correct: Per NICE NG224, recurrent UTIs in children (particularly girls) require investigation and consideration of prophylaxis. Renal USS: indicated for all children after second UTI (lower threshold for infants and atypical presentations). MCUG/VCUG: indicated in specific circumstances (abnormal USS, recurrent upper UTIs, pyelonephritis in young children, suspicion of vesicoureteric reflux). Antibiotic prophylaxis: consider after recurrent UTIs (generally ≥2-3 episodes) — trimethoprim 2mg/kg daily at night (preferred; once daily, low dose) or nitrofurantoin 1mg/kg daily (caution in renal impairment). Importantly, address modifiable risk factors: constipation (common cause of bladder dysfunction and urinary stasis → recurrent UTI); double voiding; good fluid intake; hygiene. Refer to paediatric nephrology/urology for VUR management (surveillance, prophylaxis, surgical intervention for high-grade VUR). Per NICE NG224 updated 2023: review the decision for prophylaxis at 6-12 months.
explanation.A: Incorrect — Three UTIs in 6 months is NOT normal and requires investigation for underlying anatomy/dysfunction.
explanation.B: CORRECT — Renal USS; consider MCUG; antibiotic prophylaxis; address constipation/bladder dysfunction per NICE NG224.
explanation.C: Incorrect — Co-amoxiclav is not the recommended prophylaxis antibiotic; trimethoprim or nitrofurantoin are first-line.
explanation.D: Incorrect — Prophylaxis after recurrent UTIs is appropriate and supported by NICE NG224.
explanation.E: Incorrect — Cystoscopy under GA is not first-line investigation for recurrent UTIs in children.

reference: NICE NG224 — Urinary tract infections in under 16s. https://www.nice.org.uk/guidance/ng224

question: A 5-year-old child on trimethoprim prophylaxis develops a high fever, rigors, vomiting and loin pain. Urine culture shows trimethoprim-resistant E. coli. Per NICE NG224, what is the immediate management?

options.A: Double the trimethoprim dose and review in 24 hours
options.B: Hospital admission — pyelonephritis (upper UTI) in a child who has failed prophylaxis with trimethoprim-resistant organism; IV antibiotics (co-amoxiclav or ceftriaxone per local protocol, based on sensitivities); IV fluids; renal USS; review prophylaxis regimen after treatment; consider renal tract imaging
options.C: Nitrofurantoin — appropriate for upper UTI
options.D: Oral cefalexin and outpatient review in 48 hours
options.E: No treatment needed — children clear UTIs without antibiotics

explanation.correct: Per NICE NG224, upper UTI (pyelonephritis) in children with systemic features (high fever, rigors, vomiting, loin pain) requires: (1) Hospital admission if: under 3 months, seriously ill, unable to take oral antibiotics, clinical pyelonephritis; (2) IV antibiotics after urine culture — co-amoxiclav or ceftriaxone per local guidelines, adjusted by sensitivity results; (3) IV fluids if dehydrated; (4) Renal USS — performed within 6 hours if not responding to treatment, or within 24 hours if responding; (5) Review and change prophylaxis: trimethoprim prophylaxis has failed; switch to nitrofurantoin prophylaxis or consider cefalexin pending sensitivity review; (6) Paediatric nephrology referral. Critical point: nitrofurantoin is NOT appropriate for upper UTI (pyelonephritis) — it does not achieve therapeutic tissue concentrations in the kidney; it is only suitable for lower UTI.
explanation.A: Incorrect — Trimethoprim-resistant organism with upper UTI symptoms requires hospital admission, not increased trimethoprim.
explanation.B: CORRECT — Hospital admission + IV antibiotics + renal USS for pyelonephritis with resistant organism per NICE NG224.
explanation.C: Incorrect — Nitrofurantoin is CONTRAINDICATED for upper UTI/pyelonephritis — inadequate renal tissue concentration.
explanation.D: Incorrect — Outpatient management is insufficient for pyelonephritis with systemic features and prophylaxis failure.
explanation.E: Incorrect — Untreated pyelonephritis causes renal scarring, sepsis and potential kidney failure.

reference: NICE NG224 — Urinary tract infections in under 16s. https://www.nice.org.uk/guidance/ng224

question: A 78-year-old woman with a urethral catheter develops fever 38.8°C, rigors, loin pain and confusion. Her eGFR is 58 ml/min. Per NICE NG111 and NICE NG195, which antibiotic is correct for catheter-associated upper UTI at this eGFR?

options.A: Nitrofurantoin 100mg modified-release twice daily
options.B: Co-amoxiclav 625mg three times daily orally (or IV if unable to swallow) — first-line for catheter-associated upper UTI; covers common pathogens (E. coli, Enterococcus); nitrofurantoin is CONTRAINDICATED for upper UTI (pyelonephritis) regardless of eGFR — it does not achieve adequate renal tissue concentrations; change catheter at start of treatment; treat for 7-14 days
options.C: Nitrofurantoin 50mg four times daily — still safe at eGFR 58
options.D: Trimethoprim 200mg twice daily
options.E: No antibiotic — treat with catheter change only

explanation.correct: Per NICE NG111 (UTI in adults) and NICE NG195 (UTI antimicrobial prescribing): catheter-associated UTI (CAUTI) with upper tract features (fever, rigors, loin pain, confusion) = upper UTI/urosepsis — requires broad-spectrum oral or IV antibiotic therapy. NITROFURANTOIN: specifically contraindicated for upper UTI/pyelonephritis because it does not achieve adequate tissue concentrations in the renal parenchyma — only appropriate for uncomplicated lower UTI; ALSO contraindicated if eGFR <30 ml/min (inadequate urinary concentrations). At eGFR 58: nitrofurantoin could be used for lower UTI but is STILL contraindicated for upper UTI regardless of eGFR. First-line for catheter-associated upper UTI: co-amoxiclav 625mg TDS orally or IV; alternative if penicillin allergic: ciprofloxacin 500mg BD (but check local resistance). Also: change the catheter at the start of treatment (biofilm on catheter harbours pathogens resistant to antibiotics); blood cultures if systemically unwell; treat 7-14 days.
explanation.A: Incorrect — Nitrofurantoin CONTRAINDICATED for upper UTI — inadequate renal tissue concentration.
explanation.B: CORRECT — Co-amoxiclav for catheter-associated upper UTI; nitrofurantoin contraindicated for pyelonephritis per NICE NG111/NG195.
explanation.C: Incorrect — Any nitrofurantoin dose is contraindicated for upper UTI regardless of eGFR.
explanation.D: Incorrect — Trimethoprim 3 days is for uncomplicated lower UTI; not appropriate for upper UTI or CAUTI with systemic features.
explanation.E: Incorrect — Catheter change alone is insufficient for symptomatic upper UTI.

reference: NICE NG111 — UTI in adults. NICE NG195 — UTI antimicrobial prescribing. https://www.nice.org.uk/guidance/ng111

question: A 75-year-old woman with an indwelling urinary catheter has routine dipstick showing leucocytes 3+ and nitrites positive. She feels completely well with no fever, no pain, no confusion. Per NICE NG111, what is the correct management?

options.A: Treat with trimethoprim 200mg twice daily for 7 days
options.B: Do not treat — asymptomatic bacteriuria (ASB) in catheterised patients should NOT be treated with antibiotics; treatment increases antibiotic resistance and side effects without clinical benefit; management: ensure good catheter care (aseptic technique, closed drainage system, adequate hydration); change catheter only if symptomatic UTI, catheter blocked, or at scheduled replacement time
options.C: Send urine culture and treat when results available
options.D: Change catheter and start antibiotics prophylactically
options.E: Increase fluid intake only

explanation.correct: Per NICE NG111, asymptomatic bacteriuria (ASB) in catheterised patients should NOT be treated with antibiotics. This is one of the most important antimicrobial stewardship principles in elderly care. Rationale: catheterised patients almost always have bacteriuria (80-100% of long-term catheterised patients have bacteriuria within 30 days — this is colonisation, not infection); treatment of ASB in catheterised patients does not prevent progression to symptomatic UTI, does not reduce morbidity, but DOES: increase antibiotic resistance, C. difficile risk, adverse drug effects. Symptoms that indicate treatment IS needed: fever, new loin pain, new confusion/delirium (in context of UTI rather than other cause), haematuria (new onset), systemically unwell, malodorous urine alone is NOT sufficient. Per NICE: do not use dipstick to screen catheterised patients for UTI routinely — diagnose UTI on clinical symptoms, not dipstick alone.
explanation.A: Incorrect — Treating asymptomatic bacteriuria in catheterised patients increases resistance without benefit.
explanation.B: CORRECT — ASB in catheterised patients: no treatment per NICE NG111; treat only if symptomatic.
explanation.C: Incorrect — Sending culture and treating when results available still treats ASB unnecessarily.
explanation.D: Incorrect — Prophylactic catheter change + antibiotics is not indicated for asymptomatic bacteriuria.
explanation.E: Incorrect — While good hydration is beneficial, the main point is NO ANTIBIOTICS for asymptomatic bacteriuria.

reference: NICE NG111 — Urinary tract infections in adults. https://www.nice.org.uk/guidance/ng111

question: A 70-year-old woman with catheter-associated UTI is being treated. Urine culture shows ESBL-producing E. coli. Per NICE NG111 and antimicrobial stewardship principles, what does ESBL mean and what is the treatment implication?

options.A: ESBL organisms are always sensitive to penicillin
options.B: Extended-spectrum beta-lactamase (ESBL) producing E. coli: produces enzymes that destroy most beta-lactam antibiotics (penicillins, cephalosporins, aztreonam); render most oral antibiotics ineffective; treatment: ertapenem (IV, carbapenem) or IV meropenem are typically required; pivmecillinam or fosfomycin may be active depending on sensitivities; microbiology advice essential; infection control measures (side room, contact precautions); report to UKHSA as notifiable
options.C: ESBL bacteria are untreatable — arrange palliative care
options.D: Increase co-amoxiclav dose — adequate for ESBL
options.E: Nitrofurantoin covers ESBL organisms reliably

explanation.correct: Extended-spectrum beta-lactamase (ESBL) producing bacteria (most commonly E. coli and Klebsiella): a significant and growing public health problem. ESBLs break down most penicillins and cephalosporins rendering them ineffective. Treatment: carbapenems (meropenem, ertapenem) are typically required for serious systemic ESBL infections — this requires IV administration; pivmecillinam (oral) and fosfomycin may retain activity for lower UTIs pending sensitivity testing. Per NICE NG111 and PHE/UKHSA guidance: always act on microbiology sensitivity report; contact microbiology for advice; infection control: isolate patient (single room), contact precautions (gloves, apron), notify ward/facility. ESBL infections are associated with: community-acquired (travel to high-prevalence areas — Indian subcontinent), healthcare settings, prior antibiotics. Not UKHSA notifiable per se, but ESBL bacteraemia is enhanced surveillance. Microbiological advice is essential for treatment decisions.
explanation.A: Incorrect — ESBL organisms are specifically resistant to most penicillins.
explanation.B: CORRECT — ESBL: resistant to most beta-lactams; carbapenems typically needed for serious infection; microbiology advice essential.
explanation.C: Incorrect — ESBL infections are treatable — carbapenems are effective.
explanation.D: Incorrect — Co-amoxiclav is a beta-lactam and is destroyed by ESBL enzymes.
explanation.E: Incorrect — Nitrofurantoin may or may not be active; should only be used if sensitivity confirms it, and not for upper UTI.

reference: NICE NG111 — UTI in adults. UKHSA — ESBL guidance. https://www.nice.org.uk/guidance/ng111

question: A 78-year-old woman with AF is prescribed rivaroxaban 20mg daily. Her creatinine is 148 µmol/L. Per BNF and NICE, why must creatinine clearance (not eGFR) be calculated for rivaroxaban dosing?

options.A: eGFR is always preferred for all drug dosing
options.B: Rivaroxaban is renally cleared and its dose must be adjusted based on creatinine clearance (CrCl) calculated using the Cockcroft-Gault equation — eGFR (as reported routinely by labs) is normalised to 1.73m² body surface area, making it less reliable for drug dosing in elderly patients with low muscle mass; Cockcroft-Gault CrCl calculation: (140 − age) × weight (kg) × [1.04 female / 1.23 male] / serum creatinine (µmol/L); rivaroxaban dose reduction: CrCl 15-49 ml/min → 15mg daily (AF indication); CrCl <15 → avoid
options.C: CrCl and eGFR are identical — either can be used
options.D: Rivaroxaban dose is fixed regardless of renal function
options.E: Only dialysis patients need dose adjustment for rivaroxaban

explanation.correct: Per BNF and MHRA guidance, certain drugs require Cockcroft-Gault creatinine clearance (CrCl) calculation for dosing rather than the lab-reported eGFR. Key drugs requiring Cockcroft-Gault CrCl: rivaroxaban, apixaban, edoxaban, dabigatran (all DOACs), metformin, digoxin, lithium, aminoglycosides. Why CrCl differs from eGFR in elderly: eGFR (MDRD/CKD-EPI equations) is normalised to 1.73m² body surface area — in elderly patients with low muscle mass, serum creatinine may be deceptively low (little muscle to produce creatinine), making eGFR appear higher than actual function; Cockcroft-Gault incorporates age and weight, providing a better estimate of actual renal drug clearance. Rivaroxaban AF dosing: CrCl ≥50 ml/min → 20mg daily (with evening meal); CrCl 15-49 ml/min → 15mg daily (with evening meal); CrCl <15 ml/min → avoid. Calculate CrCl before prescribing and at each review in elderly patients.
explanation.A: Incorrect — For drug dosing, Cockcroft-Gault CrCl is preferred over lab-reported eGFR for certain drugs including DOACs.
explanation.B: CORRECT — Cockcroft-Gault CrCl needed for rivaroxaban dosing; elderly low muscle mass makes eGFR unreliable per BNF.
explanation.C: Incorrect — CrCl and eGFR differ especially in elderly patients with low muscle mass.
explanation.D: Incorrect — Rivaroxaban dose must be reduced when CrCl 15-49 ml/min.
explanation.E: Incorrect — Dose adjustment is required at CrCl <50 ml/min, not just dialysis.

reference: BNF — Rivaroxaban dosing. NICE NG196 — AF. https://bnf.nice.org.uk/drug/rivaroxaban.html

question: A 82-year-old woman weighing 52kg has a serum creatinine of 120 µmol/L. Her lab-reported eGFR is 42 ml/min/1.73m². Per the Cockcroft-Gault equation, what is her creatinine clearance and how does this affect rivaroxaban prescribing?

options.A: CrCl = eGFR = 42 ml/min — prescribe rivaroxaban 15mg daily
options.B: CrCl = (140−82) × 52 × 1.04 / 120 = 58×52×1.04/120 = 26.3 ml/min — this is substantially LOWER than the eGFR of 42; at CrCl 26.3 ml/min (15-49 range) → rivaroxaban 15mg daily with evening meal is appropriate; this case demonstrates why Cockcroft-Gault is used for drug dosing in elderly women with low muscle mass — eGFR overestimates real clearance
options.C: CrCl cannot be calculated without urine sample
options.D: At eGFR 42 → rivaroxaban 20mg daily is correct
options.E: CrCl is only relevant for gentamicin dosing

explanation.correct: Cockcroft-Gault calculation: CrCl (ml/min) = [(140 − age) × weight (kg)] × [1.04 for females, 1.23 for males] / serum creatinine (µmol/L). For this patient: CrCl = (140−82) × 52 × 1.04 / 120 = 58 × 52 × 1.04 / 120 = 3133.5 / 120 = 26.1 ml/min. Compared to lab-reported eGFR of 42 ml/min — this is a meaningful difference of ~16 ml/min. The discrepancy is explained by the patient's low weight and advanced age (low muscle mass → low creatinine production → creatinine appears deceptively 'normal' relative to actual GFR). At CrCl 26 ml/min: rivaroxaban 15mg daily with evening meal is appropriate (CrCl 15-49 range). If prescribing rivaroxaban 20mg based on eGFR 42, this patient would be overdosed, increasing bleeding risk. This calculation is a common AKT exam question type.
explanation.A: Incorrect — CrCl 26 ml/min ≠ eGFR 42 ml/min; the correct Cockcroft-Gault calculation gives a much lower value.
explanation.B: CORRECT — CrCl ~26 ml/min by Cockcroft-Gault (not 42); rivaroxaban 15mg daily per BNF.
explanation.C: Incorrect — Cockcroft-Gault uses serum creatinine, not urine collection.
explanation.D: Incorrect — Using eGFR 42 for dosing here is incorrect and would lead to overdosing.
explanation.E: Incorrect — Cockcroft-Gault is required for multiple drugs including all DOACs.

reference: BNF — Rivaroxaban. Cockcroft DW, Gault MH. https://bnf.nice.org.uk/drug/rivaroxaban.html

question: Which of the following medications does NOT require Cockcroft-Gault creatinine clearance calculation for dose adjustment, instead using the standard eGFR?

options.A: Dabigatran
options.B: Digoxin
options.C: Metformin — NICE NG28 advises dose review using eGFR thresholds (stop if eGFR <30, reduce if eGFR 30-45) making eGFR appropriate for metformin decision-making; unlike DOACs, metformin dosing guidance is based on eGFR thresholds in UK guidelines
options.D: Lithium
options.E: Rivaroxaban

explanation.correct: This is a nuanced pharmacology question. Most renally-cleared drugs use Cockcroft-Gault CrCl for dose adjustment. However, NICE NG28 guidelines for metformin dose adjustment in type 2 diabetes use eGFR thresholds specifically: eGFR ≥45: standard metformin; eGFR 30-44: continue with caution, consider dose reduction; eGFR <30: STOP metformin. The SPC for metformin uses CrCl (Cockcroft-Gault) but UK NICE guidance uses eGFR for practical prescribing decisions — this is a UK-specific guidance point. Drugs requiring Cockcroft-Gault CrCl: all DOACs (rivaroxaban, apixaban, edoxaban, dabigatran), digoxin, lithium, gentamicin, vancomycin. Drugs where eGFR guides UK clinical practice: metformin (NICE NG28), most antihypertensives, ramipril dose guidance (Renal Drug Handbook). Always check the specific guideline for the drug in question.
explanation.A: Incorrect — Dabigatran requires Cockcroft-Gault CrCl for dosing (avoid if CrCl <30).
explanation.B: Incorrect — Digoxin requires Cockcroft-Gault CrCl for dose adjustment in renal impairment.
explanation.C: CORRECT — Metformin dosing in UK practice uses eGFR thresholds per NICE NG28 (though SPC uses CrCl).
explanation.D: Incorrect — Lithium levels must be monitored closely with renal function; Cockcroft-Gault relevant.
explanation.E: Incorrect — Rivaroxaban requires Cockcroft-Gault CrCl for dosing decisions.

reference: NICE NG28 — Type 2 diabetes. BNF — Metformin. https://www.nice.org.uk/guidance/ng28

question: A 52-year-old man presents with 6 months of erectile dysfunction (ED). He has no obvious psychological cause. Per NICE CKS, what are the three initial blood investigations recommended?

options.A: PSA, FSH and LH
options.B: TSH (thyroid function), HbA1c (diabetes — most common organic cause of ED), fasting lipids (dyslipidaemia and cardiovascular risk); these three investigations screen for the most common reversible causes of organic ED; also check testosterone if low libido, testosterone deficiency suspected
options.C: Testosterone, FSH, LH
options.D: Full blood count, ESR, CRP
options.E: Prolactin, FSH, LH

explanation.correct: Per NICE CKS (Erectile dysfunction), initial investigations for organic ED include screening for common underlying causes: (1) HbA1c or fasting glucose — diabetes mellitus is the most common organic cause of ED (affects 50-75% of diabetic men through neuropathy, vasculopathy, hormonal effects); (2) Fasting lipid profile — dyslipidaemia is a major vascular risk factor and ED is often a sentinel marker of cardiovascular disease (the 'canary in the coalmine' — ED may precede cardiac events by 2-5 years); (3) TSH — hypothyroidism and hyperthyroidism both cause ED; (4) Testosterone (fasting morning) — hypogonadism causes reduced libido and ED; (5) BP, BMI, cardiovascular risk assessment. The recall point specifically states TSH, HbA1c and lipids — these match NICE CKS guidance for initial first-line investigations in organic ED.
explanation.A: Incorrect — PSA screening is separate; FSH/LH alone without testosterone is incomplete.
explanation.B: CORRECT — TSH, HbA1c and fasting lipids: initial investigations for organic ED per NICE CKS.
explanation.C: Incorrect — Testosterone/FSH/LH are relevant if hypogonadism suspected but not the initial first-line three.
explanation.D: Incorrect — FBC, ESR, CRP are inflammatory markers not the primary ED investigations.
explanation.E: Incorrect — Prolactin is checked if prolactinoma suspected (low testosterone, galactorrhoea, visual field defect) — not initial first-line.

reference: NICE CKS — Erectile dysfunction. https://cks.nice.org.uk/topics/erectile-dysfunction/

question: A 55-year-old man with well-controlled hypertension on amlodipine has erectile dysfunction. He is otherwise well, BP 130/80, HbA1c normal, lipids normal, testosterone normal. Per NICE NG17 (PDE5 inhibitors) and NICE NG143, what is the first-line treatment?

options.A: Intracavernosal alprostadil injection — first-line treatment
options.B: Phosphodiesterase-5 (PDE5) inhibitor — sildenafil (Viagra), tadalafil, vardenafil or avanafil; all are similarly effective (~60-80% response rate); tadalafil 5mg daily is often preferred (longer duration allows more spontaneous activity); also address lifestyle (weight loss, smoking cessation, alcohol reduction, exercise); consider whether antihypertensive is contributing (beta-blockers and thiazides increase ED risk; amlodipine is relatively neutral)
options.C: Testosterone replacement therapy
options.D: Refer to urology immediately
options.E: Vacuum erection device — first-line before any pharmacotherapy

explanation.correct: Per NICE CKS and NICE NG17 (Treatment of erectile dysfunction, 2013), PDE5 inhibitors are first-line pharmacological treatment for ED: Sildenafil 50mg (Viagra) on demand ~30-60min before intercourse; Tadalafil 10-20mg on demand or 5mg daily (preferred for regular sexual activity); Vardenafil and avanafil — alternatives. PDE5 inhibitors: inhibit phosphodiesterase type 5 → increased cGMP → smooth muscle relaxation → cavernosal blood flow → erection (require sexual stimulation to work). Contraindications: concurrent nitrates (absolute — risk of severe hypotension), recent MI/stroke (<6 months), unstable angina. Note: sildenafil is available OTC (pharmacy) since 2018. Lifestyle: weight loss, smoking cessation, alcohol reduction, exercise all improve ED. Antihypertensive consideration: amlodipine (CCB) is relatively neutral for ED; beta-blockers and thiazides increase ED risk — consider switching if relevant. Testosterone: only if documented deficiency.
explanation.A: Incorrect — Intracavernosal alprostadil is second-line after PDE5 inhibitor failure.
explanation.B: CORRECT — PDE5 inhibitor (sildenafil, tadalafil) first-line per NICE CKS.
explanation.C: Incorrect — Testosterone replacement only if documented testosterone deficiency with symptoms.
explanation.D: Incorrect — Urology referral for failed medical treatment or suspected organic pathology — not first-line.
explanation.E: Incorrect — Vacuum erection devices are alternative/adjunct, not routinely first-line before pharmacotherapy.

reference: NICE CKS — Erectile dysfunction. NICE NG17. https://cks.nice.org.uk/topics/erectile-dysfunction/

question: A 60-year-old man with angina on isosorbide mononitrate asks for sildenafil for ED. Per BNF, why is this combination absolutely contraindicated?

options.A: Risk of priapism increases
options.B: PDE5 inhibitors and nitrates cause potentially fatal hypotension — both lower blood pressure via different but additive mechanisms; nitrates release NO → cGMP → vasodilation; PDE5 inhibitors prevent cGMP breakdown → potentiate nitrate-induced vasodilation; the combination causes severe, potentially life-threatening hypotension; PDE5 inhibitors are absolutely contraindicated with any nitrate (long or short-acting); alternative ED treatment: alprostadil, vacuum device; discuss cardiological status before any ED treatment
options.C: Sildenafil reduces angina benefit of nitrates
options.D: Risk of tachycardia and arrhythmia
options.E: Nitrates reduce PDE5 inhibitor efficacy

explanation.correct: PDE5 inhibitor + nitrate = absolute contraindication (one of the most dangerous drug interactions in primary care). Mechanism: Nitrates (ISMN, GTN, ISDN): donate nitric oxide → activates guanylyl cyclase → increased cGMP → vascular smooth muscle relaxation → vasodilation. PDE5 inhibitors (sildenafil, tadalafil, vardenafil): inhibit PDE5 enzyme that degrades cGMP → potentiate nitrate-mediated vasodilation → additive BP reduction → potentially fatal hypotension with cardiovascular collapse. Clinical significance: even a single GTN spray given to a man who has taken sildenafil in the past 24 hours (48 hours for tadalafil) can cause severe hypotension. Per BNF: contraindicated with all nitrates — including long-acting nitrates (ISMN), short-acting (GTN spray/sublingual), nitrate patches, IV nitrates. Management of this patient: cannot prescribe PDE5 inhibitor while on nitrates; alternatives for ED: alprostadil (intraurethral MUSE or intracavernosal Caverject), vacuum erection device; discuss cardiovascular risk of sexual activity with cardiologist; consider whether nitrate can be stopped (unlikely in active angina).
explanation.A: Incorrect — Priapism is a side effect of PDE5 inhibitors but is not the primary concern here; hypotension is.
explanation.B: CORRECT — Fatal hypotension from additive nitric oxide/cGMP potentiation. Absolute contraindication per BNF.
explanation.C: Incorrect — Sildenafil doesn't reduce nitrate efficacy; it dramatically potentiates it.
explanation.D: Incorrect — The primary risk is hypotension, not tachyarrhythmia.
explanation.E: Incorrect — Nitrates don't reduce PDE5 inhibitor efficacy — the opposite (potentiation) occurs.

reference: BNF — Sildenafil drug interactions. https://bnf.nice.org.uk/drug/sildenafil.html

question: A 35-year-old contact lens wearer presents with 3 days of severe right eye pain, photophobia, tearing and blurred vision. He wears extended-wear lenses and sometimes showers with them in. Slit lamp shows a corneal ulcer with surrounding oedema. Per NICE CKS, what pathogen must be urgently excluded?

options.A: Herpes simplex virus — dendritic ulcer
options.B: Acanthamoeba keratitis — a parasitic corneal infection associated almost exclusively with contact lens wear; risk factors: wearing lenses in water (shower, swimming, hot tub), poor lens hygiene, tap water contact; causes severe, disproportionate pain (out of proportion to signs), photophobia, pseudodendrites; staining shows ring infiltrate; urgent ophthalmology referral essential; treatment: prolonged topical PHMB (polyhexamethylene biguanide) + propamidine; can cause blindness if untreated
options.C: Bacterial keratitis — topical ofloxacin
options.D: Fungal keratitis — topical natamycin
options.E: Allergic keratoconjunctivitis — topical antihistamine

explanation.correct: Acanthamoeba keratitis: a rare but sight-threatening infection caused by Acanthamoeba (a free-living amoeba found in water, soil and air). Almost exclusively associated with contact lens wear (>90% of cases in developed countries). Key risk factors: water contact while wearing lenses (showering, swimming, using tap water to rinse cases/lenses), poor hygiene, extended/overnight wear. Clinical features: severe, disproportionate ocular pain (often the most prominent feature), photophobia, lacrimation, blurred vision, conjunctival injection; ring-shaped stromal infiltrate is pathognomonic on slit lamp. Diagnosis: corneal scrape for culture (specific media required — notify lab), confocal microscopy. Treatment per ophthalmology: prolonged (6-12 months) topical PHMB ± propamidine (Brolene) ± dibromopropamidine; early diagnosis dramatically improves prognosis. All contact lens wearers should be counselled: never wear lenses in water (shower, pool, sea), always use proprietary lens solution, replace cases frequently.
explanation.A: Incorrect — HSV keratitis causes a dendritic ulcer (confirmed by fluorescein) not a ring infiltrate; no contact lens association.
explanation.B: CORRECT — Acanthamoeba: contact lens + water exposure + severe pain + ring infiltrate. Urgent ophthalmology + PHMB per NICE CKS.
explanation.C: Incorrect — Bacterial keratitis also occurs with contact lenses but is more common; however the severe disproportionate pain and water exposure history make Acanthamoeba the priority exclusion.
explanation.D: Incorrect — Fungal keratitis typically follows trauma with plant material; not contact lens-associated.
explanation.E: Incorrect — Allergic keratoconjunctivitis is bilateral, itchy, without ulcer.

reference: NICE CKS — Red eye. https://cks.nice.org.uk/topics/red-eye/

question: A GP counsels a contact lens wearer following an eye infection scare. Per NICE CKS and College of Optometrists guidance, which specific activity most increases the risk of Acanthamoeba keratitis and must be strictly avoided?

options.A: Using eye drops while wearing lenses
options.B: Wearing contact lenses in any water — showers, swimming pools, hot tubs, rivers, sea; Acanthamoeba is ubiquitous in water sources including treated tap water; even brief water contact with lenses creates a film allowing amoeba to adhere; lens users should always remove lenses before water contact and use only proprietary contact lens solution
options.C: Using daily disposable lenses
options.D: Wearing lenses for 8 hours per day
options.E: Using lubricating eye drops

explanation.correct: Per NICE CKS and College of Optometrists guidance, the single most important preventable risk factor for Acanthamoeba keratitis is contact with water while wearing contact lenses. Acanthamoeba is found in tap water, river water, sea water, swimming pools and hot tubs — even treated/chlorinated water. Prevention: (1) Remove lenses before any water contact — showering, bathing, swimming, hot tub, water sports; (2) Never rinse lenses or cases with tap water — use only proprietary contact lens solution; (3) Never top up lens solution — empty, rinse and refill case with fresh solution; (4) Replace cases monthly; (5) Wash and thoroughly dry hands before handling lenses; (6) Replace extended wear lenses as scheduled; (7) Do not sleep in lenses unless specifically designed and prescribed for extended wear; (8) Remove lenses if eye becomes red, uncomfortable or painful — do not 'push through' with an irritated eye.
explanation.A: Incorrect — Using lubricating drops while wearing lenses is common practice and not particularly risky.
explanation.B: CORRECT — Water contact while wearing lenses is the primary risk for Acanthamoeba per NICE CKS.
explanation.C: Incorrect — Daily disposables have LOWER infection risk (fresh lens daily, no case needed).
explanation.D: Incorrect — 8 hours per day is within recommended wearing time for most lenses.
explanation.E: Incorrect — Lubricating drops are safe and recommended for comfort.

reference: NICE CKS — Red eye. College of Optometrists — Contact lens hygiene. https://cks.nice.org.uk/topics/red-eye/

question: A GP sees a contact lens wearer with a painful red eye. He is unsure whether to treat in primary care or refer. Per NICE CKS, which features of a red eye in a contact lens wearer mandate SAME-DAY urgent ophthalmology referral?

options.A: Mild redness with bilateral symptoms
options.B: Reduced visual acuity, severe pain, corneal opacity or infiltrate visible, photophobia, unilateral eye involvement in a contact lens wearer — these features suggest microbial keratitis (bacterial, Acanthamoeba or fungal) requiring urgent ophthalmology; contact lens wearers with red eye should be referred more readily than the general population as they have higher risk of serious keratitis
options.C: Discharge only — conjunctivitis doesn't need urgent referral
options.D: Bilateral redness with watering — allergic conjunctivitis
options.E: Redness that resolves when lenses removed

explanation.correct: Per NICE CKS (Red eye), urgent same-day ophthalmology referral is indicated for: reduced visual acuity (always urgent), severe eye pain (beyond mild discomfort), corneal opacity or infiltrate, photophobia, ciliary flush (circumcorneal redness suggesting intraocular inflammation), contact lens wear with any significant symptoms. Contact lens wearers specifically: any painful red eye in a contact lens wearer should have a low threshold for urgent referral — bacterial keratitis, Acanthamoeba and fungal keratitis all present similarly and all require urgent specialist assessment; delay risks corneal scarring and blindness. Primary care management of red eye appropriate only for: mild follicular conjunctivitis, allergic conjunctivitis (bilateral, itchy), episcleritis (mild, red, no pain), sub-conjunctival haemorrhage (no pain, no visual loss). A contact lens wearer with red eye should: remove lenses immediately, do not re-insert until assessed by specialist.
explanation.A: Incorrect — Mild bilateral redness suggests allergic/viral conjunctivitis; less urgent.
explanation.B: CORRECT — Reduced acuity, severe pain, corneal opacity, photophobia in lens wearer: same-day urgent ophthalmology per NICE CKS.
explanation.C: Incorrect — Purulent discharge with mild symptoms can be managed in primary care, but corneal symptoms cannot.
explanation.D: Incorrect — Bilateral redness with watering and itch = allergic conjunctivitis; manageable in primary care.
explanation.E: Incorrect — Redness resolving on lens removal suggests lens intolerance/overwear — not urgent but requires lens review.

reference: NICE CKS — Red eye. https://cks.nice.org.uk/topics/red-eye/

question: A 65-year-old woman was given timolol (beta-blocker) eye drops for suspected glaucoma by an optometrist. 2 hours later she has severe unilateral eye pain, headache, nausea, vomiting, halos around lights and markedly reduced vision. IOP is 62 mmHg. Per NICE CKS, what is the diagnosis?

options.A: Allergic reaction to timolol — topical antihistamine
options.B: Acute angle-closure glaucoma (AACG) — timolol (a beta-blocker eye drop) causes pupillary dilation in susceptible individuals with narrow iridocorneal angles; this blocks aqueous drainage → acute IOP rise; classic features: severe unilateral eye pain, headache, nausea/vomiting, reduced vision, coloured halos around lights, fixed mid-dilated pupil, hazy cornea, shallow anterior chamber; medical emergency — same-day ophthalmology admission; treatment: IV acetazolamide 500mg, topical pilocarpine (constrict pupil to open angle), topical timolol, betamethasone; definitive: laser peripheral iridotomy (creates alternative aqueous drainage route)
options.C: Hypertensive emergency — check BP
options.D: Migraine with aura — sumtatriptan
options.E: Retinal detachment — urgent surgical repair

explanation.correct: Acute angle-closure glaucoma (AACG): ophthalmic emergency caused by rapid IOP rise from blocked aqueous humour outflow. In susceptible individuals (anatomically shallow anterior chambers — typically hypermetropic elderly women), mydriasis (pupil dilation) causes the peripheral iris to bow forward, mechanically obstructing the trabecular meshwork. Precipitants of pupil dilation in susceptible patients: anticholinergic medications (e.g., tropicamide, ipratropium, tricyclics, antihistamines), topical beta-blockers (timolol) — paradoxically can dilate pupils in some patients, emotional stress, low light conditions. Classic features: sudden severe unilateral headache/eye pain, halos around lights (corneal oedema), nausea/vomiting, markedly reduced vision, fixed semi-dilated (mid-dilated) pupil, hazy/steamy cornea, raised IOP (>30 mmHg; often 50-70+). Management: same-day emergency admission to ophthalmology; IV acetazolamide 500mg (reduces aqueous production); topical pilocarpine 2-4% (miosis → opens angle), topical timolol, supine position (facilitates drainage); definitive: laser peripheral iridotomy. IOP >21 mmHg is raised; IOP 62 mmHg is critical.
explanation.A: Incorrect — Allergic reaction doesn't cause acute IOP rise, halos, mid-dilated fixed pupil or this severity of eye pain.
explanation.B: CORRECT — Acute angle-closure glaucoma: timolol-precipitated in susceptible patient. Emergency IV acetazolamide + pilocarpine + ophthalmology admission per NICE CKS.
explanation.C: Incorrect — Hypertensive emergency doesn't cause eye pain, halos and raised IOP.
explanation.D: Incorrect — Migraine can cause visual aura but not raised IOP or unilateral eye pain of this nature.
explanation.E: Incorrect — Retinal detachment causes painless visual loss (curtain effect); not severe eye pain or halos.

reference: NICE CKS — Glaucoma. https://cks.nice.org.uk/topics/glaucoma/

question: A GP is asked which common medication classes should be avoided or used with caution in patients with a history of narrow-angle glaucoma. Per BNF and NICE CKS, which is correct?

options.A: Beta-blockers — always contraindicated
options.B: Anticholinergic drugs and adrenergic agonists — cause mydriasis (pupil dilation), which in susceptible narrow-angle patients can precipitate acute angle-closure; examples: tricyclic antidepressants, antihistamines (first-generation), antipsychotics, ipratropium, tropicamide, sympathomimetics; these can be used with caution in open-angle glaucoma (POAG) but should be avoided in acute angle-closure or suspected narrow angles unless ophthalmologically reviewed
options.C: All antidepressants are safe in glaucoma
options.D: NSAIDs are the main drugs to avoid
options.E: Corticosteroids must be avoided in all types of glaucoma

explanation.correct: Per BNF and NICE CKS, medications that cause mydriasis (pupil dilation) are the main concern in narrow-angle (acute angle-closure) glaucoma: (1) Anticholinergics: tricyclic antidepressants (amitriptyline, dosulepin), antihistamines (chlorphenamine, promethazine), antipsychotics (especially older agents), atropine, ipratropium, scopolamine, over-the-counter cold remedies; (2) Sympathomimetics/adrenergics: systemic or topical decongestants (pseudoephedrine, phenylephrine), adrenaline. Open-angle glaucoma (POAG — the most common type): most medications are safe as angle is not blocked mechanically. BNF: if a drug states 'caution/avoid in glaucoma' — this typically refers to angle-closure/narrow-angle glaucoma, not POAG. Many patients carry a card stating their glaucoma type — important to know which type before prescribing. Corticosteroids can raise IOP and worsen glaucoma (both types) with long-term use — but avoidance in ALL glaucoma is overstated.
explanation.A: Incorrect — Beta-blockers (systemic) are not primarily contraindicated in glaucoma; topical timolol is actually used to TREAT open-angle glaucoma.
explanation.B: CORRECT — Anticholinergics and sympathomimetics cause mydriasis → precipitate angle-closure in susceptible patients per BNF.
explanation.C: Incorrect — Tricyclics (anticholinergic) are specifically cautioned in narrow-angle glaucoma.
explanation.D: Incorrect — NSAIDs are not specifically problematic for glaucoma.
explanation.E: Incorrect — Corticosteroids raise IOP with long-term use but 'all glaucoma' avoidance is too broad.

reference: BNF — Anticholinergics and glaucoma. NICE CKS — Glaucoma. https://bnf.nice.org.uk/

question: A 70-year-old man has been diagnosed with primary open-angle glaucoma (POAG) at his optometrist. Per NICE NG81, what is the first-line treatment?

options.A: Laser peripheral iridotomy
options.B: Prostaglandin analogue eye drops (latanoprost 0.005% once nightly) — first-line for newly diagnosed POAG with IOP ≥24 mmHg; reduces IOP by increasing uveoscleral outflow; very effective (lowers IOP by 25-35%); side effects: iris pigmentation (irreversible), eyelash lengthening, periorbital fat atrophy; beta-blocker eye drops (timolol) are second-line alternative (caution in asthma, bradycardia, heart block)
options.C: Topical timolol first-line for all glaucoma
options.D: Trabeculectomy surgery immediately
options.E: Systemic acetazolamide long-term

explanation.correct: Per NICE NG81 (Glaucoma: diagnosis and management), primary open-angle glaucoma (POAG) — the most common form of glaucoma (chronic, painless, gradual visual field loss, optic disc cupping, raised IOP usually): First-line topical treatment: prostaglandin analogue (PGA) — latanoprost 0.005% one drop at night; bimatoprost or travoprost are alternatives. PGAs reduce IOP by increasing uveoscleral aqueous outflow. Evidence: most effective single agent for IOP reduction, once-daily dosing improves adherence. Second-line: topical beta-blocker (timolol 0.25-0.5% BD) — contraindicated in: asthma, severe COPD, bradycardia, heart block; may cause systemic effects (absorbed into circulation via nasolacrimal duct — press inner canthus after instillation). Other agents: carbonic anhydrase inhibitors (dorzolamide), alpha-2 agonists (brimonidine). Laser trabeculoplasty (SLT): increasingly used as first-line alternative to drops. Surgery (trabeculectomy): for advanced disease or medical failure. Target IOP: individualised based on baseline IOP and optic nerve status.
explanation.A: Incorrect — Laser peripheral iridotomy is for angle-closure glaucoma (AACG) — not POAG.
explanation.B: CORRECT — Prostaglandin analogue (latanoprost) first-line for POAG per NICE NG81.
explanation.C: Incorrect — Timolol is second-line per NICE NG81; prostaglandin analogue is first-line.
explanation.D: Incorrect — Surgery (trabeculectomy) is for advanced or medically refractory POAG.
explanation.E: Incorrect — Systemic acetazolamide is for acute angle-closure emergency — not long-term POAG management.

reference: NICE NG81 — Glaucoma: diagnosis and management. https://www.nice.org.uk/guidance/ng81

question: A 55-year-old woman presents with a 4-month history of bilateral small joint pain, morning stiffness lasting over 1 hour, and functional limitation. She has no tophi. Rheumatoid factor is negative and anti-CCP antibody is also negative. Per NICE NG100, what is the most appropriate next management step?

options.A: Diagnose gout — start allopurinol
options.B: Urgent rheumatology referral — rheumatoid arthritis can be seronegative (RF and anti-CCP both negative in ~20% of RA patients); the clinical picture (bilateral small joint arthritis, prolonged morning stiffness, functional limitation for >4 weeks) meets criteria for urgent referral per NICE NG100; early DMARD therapy (methotrexate) improves outcomes and prevents joint damage; do not delay referral based on negative serology
options.C: Reassure — seronegative means not RA
options.D: Start prednisolone and review in 3 months
options.E: Request MRI before referral

explanation.correct: Per NICE NG100 (Rheumatoid arthritis in adults: management), urgent rheumatology referral is indicated for suspected RA. Seronegative RA: approximately 20-30% of RA patients are seronegative (RF negative and anti-CCP negative) — seronegative RA is still RA with the same outcomes and treatment needs. NICE NG100 criteria for urgent referral: small joint involvement + morning stiffness >30 minutes + functional limitation ± joint swelling — refer without delay. Per ACR/EULAR 2010 classification criteria for RA: joint involvement pattern + serology + acute-phase reactants + symptom duration are all weighted — a seronegative patient with multiple involved joints can still meet criteria. Benefits of early DMARD treatment (within 3-6 months of symptom onset): significantly better long-term joint outcomes; methotrexate (first-line DMARD) is most effective started early. GP role: initiate analgesia (NSAIDs), baseline investigations (FBC, ESR/CRP, RF, anti-CCP, X-ray hands/feet), refer urgently.
explanation.A: Incorrect — Gout typically causes acute monoarthritis or oligoarthritis with tophi; bilateral symmetrical small joints with prolonged morning stiffness suggests RA.
explanation.B: CORRECT — Seronegative RA (20-30%): urgent rheumatology referral per NICE NG100; seronegative doesn't exclude RA.
explanation.C: Incorrect — Seronegative does not exclude RA — 20-30% of RA is seronegative.
explanation.D: Incorrect — Starting prednisolone as primary treatment without specialist input and diagnosis is inappropriate.
explanation.E: Incorrect — MRI is useful in specialist assessment but should not delay urgent referral.

reference: NICE NG100 — Rheumatoid arthritis in adults. https://www.nice.org.uk/guidance/ng100

question: A GP receives a referral template for a 48-year-old man with suspected RA. Per NICE NG100, which baseline investigations should the GP arrange BEFORE or ALONGSIDE the rheumatology referral?

options.A: None — rheumatology will arrange all investigations
options.B: FBC, ESR, CRP, rheumatoid factor (RF), anti-CCP antibodies, U&Es, LFTs, urate (to exclude gout), X-ray hands and feet (anteroposterior views — baseline for joint damage surveillance); these enable rheumatology to assess disease activity and commence DMARD therapy without additional delay at the specialist appointment
options.C: Only RF and anti-CCP — nothing else
options.D: MRI hands — most specific for RA
options.E: Bone scan — excludes malignancy first

explanation.correct: Per NICE NG100 and BSR referral guidance, GPs should arrange baseline investigations before or alongside the urgent rheumatology referral for suspected RA. This allows: (1) Rheumatologist to review results at first appointment — reducing delays to starting DMARD therapy; (2) Establishes baseline before potentially hepatotoxic/myelosuppressive DMARD therapy. Recommended baseline: FBC (baseline before methotrexate — monitor for cytopaenias), ESR and CRP (disease activity markers), RF and anti-CCP (serology — both can be negative in 20-30%), U&Es and LFTs (baseline for DMARD safety monitoring), urate (exclude gout as differential), X-rays of hands and feet (AP views — baseline for erosive damage; may be normal early in disease). Optional: glucose (methotrexate caution in diabetes), hepatitis B/C serology (methotrexate immunosuppression reactivation risk). These investigations help the rheumatologist discuss diagnosis, start DMARDs and counsel on disease activity at the first appointment.
explanation.A: Incorrect — GPs can and should arrange baseline investigations to avoid delays at specialist appointment.
explanation.B: CORRECT — FBC, ESR, CRP, RF, anti-CCP, U&Es, LFTs, urate, X-ray hands/feet baseline per NICE NG100.
explanation.C: Incorrect — Serology alone is insufficient; baseline bloods for DMARD safety monitoring are needed.
explanation.D: Incorrect — MRI is not the standard first-line baseline investigation for RA referral.
explanation.E: Incorrect — Bone scan is not routinely needed and would delay appropriate management.

reference: NICE NG100 — Rheumatoid arthritis. https://www.nice.org.uk/guidance/ng100

question: A patient with established RA attends the GP with an acute monoarthritis affecting only the right knee — red, hot, swollen, exquisitely tender. Her RA has been well-controlled on methotrexate. Per NICE CKS and BSR, what must be excluded immediately?

options.A: RA flare — increase methotrexate
options.B: Septic arthritis — must be excluded in any acute hot monoarthritis in an immunosuppressed patient (methotrexate); joint aspiration (synovial fluid — WBC >50,000 suggests septic; Gram stain and culture) and blood cultures before antibiotics; admit for IV antibiotics (flucloxacillin or ceftriaxone); do NOT delay for imaging; septic arthritis in an RA patient can occur at any joint and can destroy a joint within days if untreated
options.C: Crystal arthropathy (gout/pseudogout) — start colchicine
options.D: Deep vein thrombosis — Doppler USS
options.E: Haemarthrosis — check APTT and PT

explanation.correct: Acute hot monoarthritis in a patient with RA on immunosuppressive therapy (methotrexate): septic arthritis must be actively excluded before assuming RA flare or crystal arthropathy. Septic arthritis is more common in patients with: RA (compromised joints + immunosuppression), prosthetic joints, diabetes, IV drug use, skin breakdown. Per NICE CKS and BSR: any acute hot joint → joint aspiration — the most important diagnostic procedure; synovial fluid analysis: appearance (turbid/purulent in septic), WBC >50,000 cells/mm³ with >75% neutrophils suggests septic; Gram stain (positive in ~50-60%); culture. Blood cultures before antibiotics. Treatment: emergency IV antibiotics — empirical flucloxacillin (if Staphylococcus suspected) or ceftriaxone (if gonococcal/Gram-negative suspected); wash-out/lavage of joint; treat underlying RA flare only after septic arthritis excluded. Untreated septic arthritis destroys cartilage within 24-48 hours → permanent disability.
explanation.A: Incorrect — Increasing methotrexate for a potentially septic joint could be fatal. Septic arthritis must be excluded first.
explanation.B: CORRECT — Septic arthritis exclusion priority: joint aspiration + blood cultures + IV antibiotics per NICE CKS.
explanation.C: Incorrect — Crystal arthritis is possible (common with RA) but septic arthritis must be excluded — joint aspiration will distinguish.
explanation.D: Incorrect — DVT causes leg swelling/pain but not joint hotness/redness of this nature.
explanation.E: Incorrect — Haemarthrosis is possible but less likely without anticoagulation or coagulopathy history.

reference: NICE CKS — Hot swollen joint. BSR — Septic arthritis. https://cks.nice.org.uk/topics/hot-swollen-joint-in-adults/

question: A 35-year-old man presents with excessive thirst, polyuria (4-6 litres/day), nocturia and dilute urine. He was recently involved in a road traffic accident with a head injury. Serum sodium is 148 mmol/L, plasma osmolality 305 mOsm/kg, urine osmolality 80 mOsm/kg. Per NICE CKS and endocrine guidelines, what is the diagnosis?

options.A: Type 1 diabetes mellitus — HbA1c
options.B: Diabetes insipidus (DI) — characterised by hypotonic polyuria from deficiency of ADH (central DI — post-head injury, most likely here: hypothalamic or pituitary stalk damage) or ADH resistance (nephrogenic DI); distinguishing features: high serum Na+ and osmolality, very low urine osmolality (<300 mOsm/kg despite dehydration); confirms DI rather than primary polydipsia; investigate with water deprivation test ± desmopressin challenge to differentiate central vs nephrogenic
options.C: Psychogenic polydipsia — reassure
options.D: Cushing's syndrome — dexamethasone suppression test
options.E: SIADH — fluid restriction

explanation.correct: Diabetes insipidus (DI): deficiency of or resistance to antidiuretic hormone (ADH/vasopressin). Central DI: insufficient ADH production (hypothalamus) or release (pituitary): causes — head trauma (pituitary stalk injury), neurosurgery, craniopharyngioma, sarcoidosis, TB, Langerhans cell histiocytosis, idiopathic. Nephrogenic DI: normal ADH but collecting duct is unresponsive: causes — lithium (most common drug cause), hypercalcaemia, hypokalaemia, chronic kidney disease, hereditary. Biochemical features: high serum sodium (hypernatraemia), high plasma osmolality, paradoxically low urine osmolality (<300, often <100 mOsm/kg). Compare with primary polydipsia: LOW plasma sodium, LOW plasma osmolality (overdrinking dilutes plasma). Water deprivation test (Hickey-Hare or modified): withhold fluids → monitor plasma/urine osmolality; desmopressin (ADH analogue) injection: if urine osmolality increases >50% → central DI (ADH responsive); if no/little response → nephrogenic DI. Treatment: central DI → intranasal/oral desmopressin; nephrogenic DI → treat cause, thiazide diuretics (paradoxically reduce urine output), low-sodium diet.
explanation.A: Incorrect — DM causes elevated plasma glucose with glucosuria; urine osmolality would be HIGH (concentrated with glucose) not low.
explanation.B: CORRECT — Post-traumatic central DI: high Na+, high plasma osmolality, low urine osmolality. Water deprivation test + desmopressin challenge per NICE CKS.
explanation.C: Incorrect — Primary polydipsia causes LOW plasma osmolality (diluted by overdrinking); here it is HIGH.
explanation.D: Incorrect — Cushing's causes different features; this is DI post-head trauma.
explanation.E: Incorrect — SIADH causes LOW sodium from ADH excess — the opposite of DI.

reference: NICE CKS — Diabetes insipidus. https://cks.nice.org.uk/topics/diabetes-insipidus/

question: A 35-year-old man presents with swelling of his penis. On examination the foreskin cannot be retracted. Per NICE CKS, what is the most appropriate management?

options.A: Forcible retraction under anaesthesia
options.B: Assess whether this is physiological or pathological phimosis. In adults, pathological phimosis (scarring, balanitis xerotica obliterans) requires treatment. First-line: topical betamethasone 0.05% cream applied twice daily for 4-8 weeks achieves retractability in 70-80%. If topical treatment fails: surgical referral for preputioplasty or circumcision
options.C: Emergency circumcision
options.D: No treatment — phimosis always resolves spontaneously in adults
options.E: Dilatation with probes under local anaesthesia

explanation.correct: Per NICE CKS, pathological phimosis in adults (unlike physiological phimosis in children) requires treatment. The foreskin becomes scarred and non-retractile, often due to balanitis xerotica obliterans (BXO — a chronic inflammatory condition). First-line: topical corticosteroid (betamethasone 0.05-0.1% twice daily for 4-8 weeks); 70-80% success rate with medical therapy. If fails or BXO confirmed: surgical options include preputioplasty (widens foreskin while preserving it) or circumcision. Forcible retraction is contraindicated as it causes tearing and worsening scarring.
explanation.A: Incorrect — Forcible retraction causes tearing and worsens scarring.
explanation.B: CORRECT — Topical betamethasone first-line for pathological phimosis in adults per NICE CKS.
explanation.C: Incorrect — Emergency circumcision is for paraphimosis (foreskin trapped behind glans) not phimosis.
explanation.D: Incorrect — Pathological phimosis in adults does not resolve spontaneously.
explanation.E: Incorrect — Dilation is not recommended as initial management.

reference: NICE CKS — Phimosis. https://cks.nice.org.uk/topics/phimosis/

question: A 40-year-old man has a non-retractile foreskin with a white plaque at the tip. Biopsy confirms balanitis xerotica obliterans (BXO). Per guidelines, what is the definitive treatment and long-term concern?

options.A: Oral fluconazole — treat as candidiasis
options.B: Circumcision is the definitive treatment for BXO (topical steroids have limited efficacy once fibrosis is established). Long-term concern: BXO is a chronic inflammatory condition associated with penile intraepithelial neoplasia (PIN) and squamous cell carcinoma of the penis in a small proportion of patients — long-term follow-up recommended
options.C: Oral antibiotics — treat as infection
options.D: Intralesional corticosteroid injections
options.E: Reassure — BXO has no long-term sequelae

explanation.correct: Balanitis xerotica obliterans (BXO, also known as lichen sclerosus of the penis): chronic progressive inflammatory dermatosis causing white, fibrotic plaques on the glans and foreskin. Pathognomonic white plaque with loss of normal architecture. Treatment: topical steroids for early disease; circumcision is definitive when established. Long-term association with squamous cell carcinoma of the penis — BXO is a recognised premalignant condition in approximately 5-10% of cases, particularly in uncircumcised patients. Post-circumcision surveillance of the glans is recommended. BNF and urology guidelines recommend regular review.
explanation.A: Incorrect — BXO is not a fungal infection; antifungals have no role.
explanation.B: CORRECT — Circumcision definitive for BXO. Long-term risk of SCC of penis requires surveillance.
explanation.C: Incorrect — BXO is inflammatory/fibrotic, not bacterial.
explanation.D: Incorrect — Intralesional injections are not standard management.
explanation.E: Incorrect — BXO has an association with penile SCC requiring follow-up.

reference: EAU — Guidelines on Penile Cancer. NICE CKS — Balanitis. https://cks.nice.org.uk/topics/balanitis/

question: A 45-year-old man presents with sudden-onset pain and an inability to retract his foreskin after it became trapped behind the glans. Per NICE CKS, what is the diagnosis and immediate management?

options.A: Phimosis — topical betamethasone
options.B: Paraphimosis — a urological emergency where the retracted foreskin becomes trapped proximal to the glans, causing constriction and oedema; immediate reduction required: ice/compression to reduce oedema then manual reduction of foreskin; if fails: surgical dorsal slit or circumcision; refer urgently to urology
options.C: Balanitis — topical clotrimazole
options.D: Penile fracture — immediate surgery
options.E: Reassure — will resolve spontaneously

explanation.correct: Paraphimosis: a urological emergency distinct from phimosis. Occurs when the foreskin, once retracted, cannot be returned to its normal position over the glans — the constricting ring of foreskin causes venous and lymphatic obstruction, progressive oedema, and if untreated, arterial compromise and gangrene of the glans. Common after catheterisation if foreskin is not replaced. Immediate management: compression (manual squeezing for 2-5 minutes) to reduce oedema, then manual reduction pushing the glans back through the foreskin ring; topical anaesthetic or ice may help; if fails — dorsal slit or emergency circumcision under local/general anaesthesia. Urgent urology referral always required.
explanation.A: Incorrect — Phimosis is inability to retract the foreskin from its normal position; paraphimosis is the trapped retracted state.
explanation.B: CORRECT — Paraphimosis: emergency. Compression + manual reduction; surgical if fails per NICE CKS urology guidance.
explanation.C: Incorrect — Balanitis is inflammation of the glans; not a trapped foreskin emergency.
explanation.D: Incorrect — Penile fracture occurs with intercourse-related trauma causing a cracking sound and rapid detumescence.
explanation.E: Incorrect — Paraphimosis is a time-sensitive emergency — arterial compromise can cause gangrene within hours.

reference: NICE CKS — Paraphimosis. https://cks.nice.org.uk/topics/phimosis/

question: A 35-year-old employee has been off work due to back pain for 2 weeks. They ask their employer about Statutory Sick Pay (SSP). Per HMRC guidance, who qualifies for SSP?

options.A: Only full-time permanent employees
options.B: SSP is payable to employees (not self-employed) who: earn at least £123 per week (Lower Earnings Limit 2024/25); have been ill for at least 4 consecutive days including non-working days (qualifying days); are under State Pension age. SSP is paid at £116.75 per week (2024/25) for up to 28 weeks. Self-employed, those earning below the LEL, and agency workers may not qualify
options.C: All UK workers including self-employed
options.D: Only those who have been employed for more than 1 year
options.E: Only NHS employees

explanation.correct: Per HMRC SSP rules (2024/25): SSP qualifications — employee (not self-employed or contractors); earnings ≥£123/week (Lower Earnings Limit); ill for ≥4 consecutive days (Period of Incapacity for Work — PIW, includes weekends/non-working days); under State Pension age. Waiting days: first 3 days of sickness are not paid (waiting days); SSP starts from day 4. Rate: £116.75/week (April 2024). Duration: up to 28 weeks. Employer must pay SSP; HMRC no longer reimburses employers (ended 2014). After 28 weeks: Employment and Support Allowance (ESA) may be available. GP role: issue fit note (MED3) from day 8 of absence (first 7 days: self-certification). SSP1 form given to employee when SSP ends.
explanation.A: Incorrect — Part-time, fixed-term and agency workers can also qualify if they meet the earnings and employment criteria.
explanation.B: CORRECT — SSP: employed, earning ≥£123/week, ill ≥4 consecutive days, under State Pension age per HMRC.
explanation.C: Incorrect — Self-employed individuals do NOT qualify for SSP.
explanation.D: Incorrect — No minimum length of employment is required for SSP — it applies from day 1 of employment.
explanation.E: Incorrect — SSP applies to all qualifying private and public sector employees.

reference: HMRC — Statutory Sick Pay. https://www.gov.uk/statutory-sick-pay

question: A 42-year-old man with terminal cancer has been off work for 30 weeks on SSP. His employer asks what happens next. Per HMRC guidance, what is the process when SSP ends?

options.A: SSP continues indefinitely for terminal illness
options.B: When SSP ends (after 28 weeks maximum): employer must issue SSP1 form within 7 days informing the employee that SSP is ending; employee can then apply for Employment and Support Allowance (ESA) or Universal Credit. For terminal illness specifically, the Special Rules for Terminal Illness (SRTI) pathway allows fast-track benefit processing with DS1500/SR1 form (completed by GP or specialist) — usually processed within days without a face-to-face assessment
options.C: Employer must continue paying SSP for up to 2 years
options.D: Employee must return to work regardless
options.E: Employee is automatically transferred to Universal Credit

explanation.correct: SSP maximum duration is 28 weeks. When ending: SSP1 form issued by employer within 7 days; employee can claim Employment and Support Allowance (ESA) or Universal Credit. For terminal illness: Special Rules for Terminal Illness (SRTI) — previously the DS1500 form (now SR1 form) allows fast-track processing. Patients with terminal illness (defined as life expectancy ≤12 months) can receive benefits quickly without waiting period and without work capability assessment. The SR1 form is completed by a registered medical professional (GP, hospital clinician). The patient does not need to see the form. Benefits payable under SRTI: ESA/PIP/ADP/Universal Credit. GPs should know about the SR1 form for their terminal patients.
explanation.A: Incorrect — SSP has a strict maximum of 28 weeks.
explanation.B: CORRECT — SSP1 form at end; ESA/UC next; terminal illness fast-tracked with SR1 form per HMRC/DWP.
explanation.C: Incorrect — SSP is employer-funded for maximum 28 weeks only.
explanation.D: Incorrect — An employee with terminal illness cannot be forced to return to work.
explanation.E: Incorrect — Automatic transfer doesn't happen; employee must apply for UC/ESA.

reference: HMRC — SSP. DWP — Special Rules for Terminal Illness. https://www.gov.uk/statutory-sick-pay

question: A self-employed electrician is off work with a work-related injury for 6 weeks. He asks his GP about SSP. What is the correct advice and what benefits might he qualify for?

options.A: He qualifies for SSP — all workers qualify
options.B: Self-employed individuals do NOT qualify for SSP (which is an employer-paid benefit for employees). Alternative benefits for self-employed: Employment and Support Allowance (ESA) — contributory ESA if sufficient National Insurance contributions; Universal Credit — if income below threshold; if work-related injury: Industrial Injuries Disablement Benefit (IIDB) may be available. Advise claiming relevant DWP benefits and ensure fit note is issued from day 8
options.C: Self-employed can claim SSP from HMRC directly
options.D: He qualifies for SSP at reduced rate
options.E: No benefits are available for self-employed

explanation.correct: SSP is an employer-funded benefit paid to EMPLOYEES — self-employed individuals have no employer to pay SSP. The self-employed must use alternative benefits: Contributory ESA (New-Style ESA): requires 2+ years of Class 1 or Class 2 NI contributions in the past 2-3 years; Universal Credit: means-tested income support if income drops below threshold; Industrial Injuries Disablement Benefit (IIDB): for prescribed industrial diseases or accidents at work (relevant for work-related injury); Personal Independence Payment (PIP): for longer-term disability. GPs should issue fit notes (MED3) from day 8 of absence for benefit claim evidence. Self-employed patient should be signposted to Citizens Advice or DWP for benefit entitlement assessment.
explanation.A: Incorrect — SSP is specifically for employees, not self-employed.
explanation.B: CORRECT — Self-employed cannot claim SSP. Alternatives: ESA, Universal Credit, IIDB per DWP guidance.
explanation.C: Incorrect — HMRC does not pay SSP directly to self-employed individuals.
explanation.D: Incorrect — There is no reduced-rate SSP for self-employed.
explanation.E: Incorrect — Several benefits may be available through DWP for self-employed individuals.

reference: DWP — Benefits for self-employed. HMRC — SSP. https://www.gov.uk/employment-support-allowance

question: A GP is asked to complete a DS1500 form for a 58-year-old patient with metastatic lung cancer. Per DWP guidance, what has replaced the DS1500 form and who can complete it?

options.A: DS1500 is still in current use — nothing has changed
options.B: The DS1500 form was replaced by the SR1 form (Special Rules for Terminal Illness) from April 2022. The SR1 form can be completed by any registered medical professional including GPs, hospital doctors, specialist nurses, or other registered healthcare professionals. It certifies that the patient has a progressive disease and death can reasonably be expected within 12 months. The patient does not need to be aware a form has been submitted
options.C: Only hospital consultants can complete the SR1 form
options.D: The form has been abolished — patients self-certify
options.E: Only palliative care specialists complete the SR1 form

explanation.correct: The DS1500 (Special Rules for Terminal Illness) was replaced by the SR1 form from April 2022 in England, Scotland and Wales. Key changes: SR1 can be completed by a wider range of healthcare professionals (GPs, hospital clinicians, specialist nurses, other registered healthcare professionals — not just doctors); criterion changed from 'reasonably expected to die within 6 months' to 'progressive disease and death reasonably expected within 12 months' (wider eligibility); application process simplified. Purpose: allows people with terminal illness to access certain DWP benefits (ESA, PIP, UC, ADP in Scotland) quickly without capability assessment and with higher payment rates. The patient does not need to be informed that a form has been submitted (doctor judges appropriateness). GPs should be familiar with the SR1 form for their terminal patients.
explanation.A: Incorrect — DS1500 was replaced by SR1 from April 2022.
explanation.B: CORRECT — SR1 form from April 2022, completed by any registered healthcare professional, 12-month prognosis criterion per DWP.
explanation.C: Incorrect — SR1 can be completed by GPs and other healthcare professionals.
explanation.D: Incorrect — The special rules form still exists and is important for benefit access.
explanation.E: Incorrect — Any registered healthcare professional can complete it, not only palliative care specialists.

reference: DWP — SR1 form Special Rules for Terminal Illness. https://www.gov.uk/government/publications/dwp-factual-medical-reports-guidance-for-healthcare-professionals

question: A GP completes an SR1 form for a patient with terminal cancer without telling the patient. The patient later asks about SR1 forms. Per DWP guidance and GMC confidentiality principles, is the GP's approach correct?

options.A: The GP should always get the patient's explicit consent before completing an SR1
options.B: The SR1 form process specifically allows healthcare professionals to submit the form without the patient's knowledge, if the clinician judges that disclosure would cause harm (e.g. severe distress in a patient unaware of their prognosis). This is a recognised exception to the general consent principle — the process is designed this way. However, good practice includes discussing the process sensitively with patients if possible
options.C: Completing the form without consent is illegal
options.D: The form must always be shown to the patient before submission
options.E: SR1 can only be submitted if the patient requests it

explanation.correct: The SR1/DS1500 special rules process is unique in that it is specifically designed to allow submission without the patient's knowledge if the clinician judges this to be in their interest (e.g., patient is unaware of their terminal prognosis or disclosure might cause severe harm). This is an exceptional allowance compared to standard GMC consent principles. DWP guidance explicitly states: the form can be submitted on behalf of the patient without their knowledge. Good practice: where appropriate, discuss sensitively with patient that certain benefits are available and that a form has been or may be completed; where the patient does not know their prognosis, clinician uses their judgement. The completed form goes to DWP to support benefit claims.
explanation.A: Incorrect — Unlike most medical documents, explicit consent is not always required for SR1 submission.
explanation.B: CORRECT — SR1 can be submitted without patient knowledge per DWP special rules guidance — unique exception.
explanation.C: Incorrect — The process is legal and specifically designed to allow this.
explanation.D: Incorrect — Patient does not need to see the form.
explanation.E: Incorrect — The SR1 can be completed at the clinician's initiative.

reference: DWP — SR1 guidance for healthcare professionals. https://www.gov.uk/government/publications/dwp-factual-medical-reports-guidance-for-healthcare-professionals

question: A 65-year-old patient with inoperable pancreatic cancer is applying for Personal Independence Payment (PIP). Her GP is asked to complete the SR1 form. What does the SR1 form certify?

options.A: That the patient is unable to work
options.B: That the patient has a progressive disease and death can reasonably be expected within 12 months — this allows fast-track access to benefits under the Special Rules for Terminal Illness (SRTI) without face-to-face assessment and usually within days of application
options.C: That the patient requires full-time nursing care
options.D: That the patient qualifies for a blue badge parking permit
options.E: That the patient has a terminal diagnosis confirmed by biopsy

explanation.correct: The SR1 form certifies that the patient has a progressive disease and their death can reasonably be expected within 12 months. This is the SRTI (Special Rules for Terminal Illness) criterion. Benefits accessed via SR1 fast-track: PIP (higher rate daily living component, no mobility assessment required), ESA (support group from day 1), Universal Credit, ADP (Scotland). The form does not require biopsy confirmation — it is based on clinical prognosis. Once submitted: benefit decision usually made within 24-72 hours without further assessment. The form can be submitted by any registered healthcare professional and without the patient's knowledge if appropriate. GPs are well placed to identify patients who may benefit from this fast-track pathway.
explanation.A: Incorrect — SR1 certifies prognosis, not specifically inability to work.
explanation.B: CORRECT — SR1: progressive disease with death expected within 12 months = fast-track SRTI benefits per DWP.
explanation.C: Incorrect — SR1 is not a nursing care certification.
explanation.D: Incorrect — Blue badge is a separate application through local authority.
explanation.E: Incorrect — Biopsy confirmation is not required — clinical prognosis is sufficient.

reference: DWP — SR1 Special Rules for Terminal Illness. https://www.gov.uk/government/publications/dwp-factual-medical-reports-guidance-for-healthcare-professionals

question: A GP practice asks about the annual influenza vaccination programme. Per PHE Green Book and NHS guidance, which patient groups are eligible for free NHS influenza vaccine?

options.A: Only patients aged 65 and over
options.B: Eligible groups include: all aged 65+; aged 6 months–64 years with chronic conditions (respiratory disease including asthma, heart disease, CKD, liver disease, neurological conditions, diabetes, immunosuppression, asplenia); pregnant women; all children aged 2–17 years (live attenuated nasal spray); frontline healthcare workers; carers of immunocompromised; residents of care homes
options.C: Only immunocompromised patients
options.D: All adults but no children
options.E: Only healthcare workers and care home residents

explanation.correct: Per PHE Green Book Chapter 19 and NHS influenza programme, annual flu vaccine is offered free to: All aged 65+; Pregnant women (any trimester); Those aged 6 months–64 with chronic disease (respiratory, cardiac, renal, hepatic, neurological, diabetes, immunosuppression including HIV, asplenia/hyposplenia); Morbid obesity (BMI ≥40); Carers of immunocompromised/older/disabled people; Frontline health and social care workers; All children aged 2–17 years (live attenuated influenza vaccine LAIV nasal spray preferred if no contraindication — e.g. severe asthma, aspirin use, immunocompromised). Children aged 6 months–2 years with clinical risk groups receive inactivated vaccine. LAIV is contraindicated in immunosuppressed patients and those on aspirin/salicylates.
explanation.A: Incorrect — Eligibility extends to many groups under 65.
explanation.B: CORRECT — Multiple eligible groups including clinical risk groups, pregnant, children 2-17, carers, HCWs per PHE Green Book.
explanation.C: Incorrect — Many non-immunocompromised groups are eligible.
explanation.D: Incorrect — Children aged 2-17 are a key eligible group.
explanation.E: Incorrect — Many other groups are eligible beyond HCWs and care home residents.

reference: PHE Green Book — Chapter 19 Influenza. https://www.gov.uk/government/collections/immunisation-against-infectious-disease-the-green-book

question: A 4-year-old healthy child is brought for her annual flu vaccine. Per PHE Green Book, which vaccine should be given and what are the contraindications?

options.A: Inactivated intramuscular influenza vaccine
options.B: Live attenuated influenza vaccine (LAIV) nasal spray — preferred route for all healthy children aged 2–17 years; intranasal, painless, better immune response; contraindications to LAIV: currently wheezing or severe/uncontrolled asthma, receiving aspirin/salicylate therapy (Reye's syndrome risk), immunosuppression (patient or household contact), pregnancy (not applicable to child but relevant), CSF leak, cochlear implant
options.C: High-dose inactivated vaccine
options.D: No vaccine — only over-65s need annual flu vaccine
options.E: Oral live vaccine

explanation.correct: Per PHE Green Book Chapter 19: children aged 2-17 years should receive live attenuated influenza vaccine (LAIV — Fluenz Tetra) as a nasal spray, preferred over intramuscular inactivated vaccine due to: better immune response (intranasal mimics natural infection, stimulates mucosal immunity), easier administration (no needle), possible herd protection benefit. Dose: 0.1ml per nostril (0.2ml total). Contraindications to LAIV: severe egg allergy (contains egg protein — but low egg-content preparations safe in most egg-allergic); wheezing in the past 72 hours or active asthma attack; severe/unstable asthma; aspirin or salicylate therapy (risk of Reye's syndrome from live attenuated influenza); immunosuppression of patient or close household contact; pregnancy (not relevant for child). If LAIV contraindicated: use inactivated injectable influenza vaccine. This child is healthy with no contraindications — LAIV appropriate.
explanation.A: Incorrect — Inactivated IM vaccine is used only when LAIV is contraindicated.
explanation.B: CORRECT — LAIV nasal spray preferred for healthy children 2-17 per PHE Green Book; contraindications include severe asthma, aspirin use, immunosuppression.
explanation.C: Incorrect — High-dose inactivated vaccine is for adults ≥65 years.
explanation.D: Incorrect — Children 2-17 are a key group in the NHS flu programme.
explanation.E: Incorrect — There is no oral flu vaccine.

reference: PHE Green Book — Chapter 19 Influenza. https://www.gov.uk/government/collections/immunisation-against-infectious-disease-the-green-book

question: A pregnant woman at 24 weeks asks if she should have the flu vaccine. Per PHE and NICE guidance, what is the recommendation and timing?

options.A: Avoid flu vaccine in pregnancy — all vaccines are contraindicated
options.B: Inactivated influenza vaccine is strongly recommended in ALL pregnant women at ANY stage of pregnancy (1st, 2nd or 3rd trimester) — pregnancy increases risk of severe influenza complications; reduces maternal, fetal and neonatal morbidity; maternal antibody transfer provides some protection to newborns in first months of life. Administer inactivated vaccine (NOT LAIV which is live attenuated). Free on NHS. Ideally offered from September onwards in the annual programme
options.C: Only safe in the third trimester
options.D: Only required if the woman has underlying conditions
options.E: LAIV nasal spray is preferred in pregnancy
