explanation.correct: Per PHE Green Book and NICE, inactivated influenza vaccine is recommended and safe for all pregnant women at any stage of pregnancy. Rationale: pregnancy reduces respiratory reserve and immunity; influenza in pregnancy causes increased risk of hospitalisation, premature delivery and perinatal death; maternal vaccination reduces these risks and provides passive immunity to the neonate (antibody transfer) for first few months of life. Key points: inactivated (killed) vaccine only — LAIV (live attenuated) is contraindicated in pregnancy; given in any trimester without safety concerns; ideally offered from September annually; free on NHS as pregnant women are priority group. Evidence: large safety studies confirm no increased risk of adverse pregnancy outcomes from inactivated flu vaccine. Also recommend pertussis (Tdap) at 16-32 weeks and COVID boosters in pregnancy.
explanation.A: Incorrect — Inactivated vaccines (including flu) are safe and recommended in pregnancy.
explanation.B: CORRECT — Inactivated influenza vaccine strongly recommended in all pregnant women at any trimester. LAIV contraindicated per PHE Green Book.
explanation.C: Incorrect — Safe in all trimesters — no need to wait.
explanation.D: Incorrect — ALL pregnant women are an eligible priority group regardless of underlying conditions.
explanation.E: Incorrect — LAIV is a live attenuated vaccine and is contraindicated in pregnancy.

reference: PHE Green Book — Chapter 19 Influenza. https://www.gov.uk/government/collections/immunisation-against-infectious-disease-the-green-book

question: A newly appointed locum GP doctor is found to have insufficient MMR immunity (MMR IgG serology: rubella IgG negative, measles IgG equivocal). Per PHE Green Book and NHS occupational health guidance, what should be done?

options.A: No action needed — MMR is only for children
options.B: The doctor should receive two doses of MMR vaccine (separated by at least 1 month) to achieve adequate immunity. Healthcare workers require documented protection against measles, mumps and rubella as they can transmit to vulnerable patients. Per PHE Green Book: non-immune healthcare workers should be offered and should accept MMR (unless contraindicated — pregnancy, immunosuppression). Ensure occupational health records are updated
options.C: Test all patients the doctor has seen for measles exposure
options.D: MMR is contraindicated in adults
options.E: One dose of measles-only vaccine is sufficient

explanation.correct: Per PHE Green Book Chapter 21 (Measles), Chapter 23 (MMR) and NHS occupational health guidance: healthcare workers who are not immune to measles, mumps and/or rubella should receive MMR vaccine (two doses, ≥1 month apart). Rationale: MMR is a live attenuated vaccine providing long-lasting immunity; healthcare workers are at risk of exposure and risk transmitting to vulnerable patients (immunocompromised, pregnant women, infants too young to vaccinate). Serology interpretation: if measles IgG equivocal or rubella IgG negative → non-immune → vaccinate. Contraindications to MMR: pregnancy (defer until after delivery), severe immunosuppression (HIV with CD4 <200, chemotherapy, high-dose steroids). Post-vaccination: evidence of immunity on serology before returning to clinical areas where vulnerable patients are seen. This is both an occupational health and patient safety requirement.
explanation.A: Incorrect — MMR is recommended for non-immune adults including healthcare workers.
explanation.B: CORRECT — Two doses of MMR ≥1 month apart for non-immune healthcare worker per PHE Green Book.
explanation.C: Incorrect — Retrospective patient testing is not required unless the doctor has active measles (not the case here).
explanation.D: Incorrect — MMR is safe and recommended for non-immune adults.
explanation.E: Incorrect — MMR covers measles, mumps and rubella simultaneously; single antigen vaccines are not routinely available in UK.

reference: PHE Green Book — Chapter 21 Measles. Chapter 23 MMR. https://www.gov.uk/government/collections/immunisation-against-infectious-disease-the-green-book

question: A 28-year-old female GP trainee (ST2) has insufficient rubella immunity. She is planning to become pregnant in 6 months. Per PHE guidance, what is the advice?

options.A: Delay MMR until after pregnancy
options.B: Administer MMR now (live vaccine). Advise to avoid pregnancy for at least 1 month after MMR (JCVI recommendation). If she becomes pregnant sooner than planned: the theoretical risk from MMR in early pregnancy has NOT resulted in observed congenital rubella syndrome from inadvertent vaccination in pregnancy — reassure if inadvertent exposure, but termination is not recommended solely on this basis. She needs rubella immunity before pregnancy to protect fetus
options.C: MMR is contraindicated in women of childbearing age
options.D: Use rubella IgG immunoglobulin instead
options.E: Recheck rubella serology — one test is unreliable

explanation.correct: Per PHE Green Book and JCVI guidance: women of childbearing age who are rubella non-immune should receive MMR vaccine and advised to avoid pregnancy for at least 1 month after vaccination (previous recommendation was 3 months — now shortened to 1 month based on evidence). Rationale: congenital rubella syndrome (CRS) is devastating — 85% risk of fetal abnormality (heart defects, cataracts, deafness, IUGR) if rubella acquired in first trimester. Post-MMR pregnancy avoidance: 1 month minimum. If inadvertent pregnancy within 1 month: theoretical risk from live attenuated vaccine has never been demonstrated to cause CRS in studies — reassure patient; termination is NOT recommended solely on the basis of post-vaccination inadvertent pregnancy. Check serology post-vaccination to confirm seroconversion (some 5% fail to seroconvert to rubella after first dose). Occupational health record must document immunity.
explanation.A: Incorrect — Rubella immunity is needed before pregnancy; delaying until after is too late.
explanation.B: CORRECT — MMR now; avoid pregnancy for 1 month; reassure if inadvertent pregnancy (no documented CRS from vaccine) per PHE.
explanation.C: Incorrect — MMR is recommended for non-immune women of childbearing age specifically to prevent CRS.
explanation.D: Incorrect — Immunoglobulin provides passive, temporary immunity; it does not protect against CRS in a future pregnancy.
explanation.E: Incorrect — A single serology result showing rubella IgG negative is reliable; MMR should be given.

reference: PHE Green Book — Chapter 23 MMR. https://www.gov.uk/government/collections/immunisation-against-infectious-disease-the-green-book

question: A 32-year-old man who grew up abroad has no documentation of MMR vaccination. He has two children aged 4 and 6 who attend primary school. Per PHE guidance, what should be offered?

options.A: No vaccines needed — he is likely immune from natural infection
options.B: Two doses of MMR vaccine (minimum 1 month apart) for this adult with no documented immunity. Adults born after 1970 who have not received two documented doses of MMR and have no confirmed history of measles/mumps/rubella should be vaccinated. No need to check serology first — vaccinating someone already immune is safe. MMR is free on NHS for those who have missed it
options.C: Measles IgG serology first — only vaccinate if negative
options.D: MMR is only given to children under 18
options.E: Single dose sufficient for adults

explanation.correct: Per PHE Green Book Chapter 21-23 and NHS catch-up vaccination guidance: any adult without documented 2-dose MMR vaccination history and no confirmed immunity should receive two doses of MMR (at least 1 month apart) as part of the national catch-up programme. No serology is required before vaccination — vaccinating an already-immune person is safe (no harm from extra dose). Free on NHS. Key clinical context: children in primary school face measles exposure risk; the parent having unvaccinated children and unimmunised himself represents household transmission risk. MMR is safe in immunocompetent adults; contraindications: current pregnancy, severe immunosuppression. Post-vaccination: immunity typically lifelong after 2 doses.
explanation.A: Incorrect — Natural infection rates vary by country of origin; without documentation, vaccination is recommended.
explanation.B: CORRECT — Two doses MMR for undocumented adult. No serology needed first. Free on NHS per PHE catch-up guidance.
explanation.C: Incorrect — While serology is an option, it is not required before vaccination — vaccinating immune individuals is safe.
explanation.D: Incorrect — MMR catch-up programme applies to adults of any age who missed vaccination.
explanation.E: Incorrect — Two doses are required for full protection.

reference: PHE Green Book — Chapter 21-23. NHS catch-up vaccinations. https://www.gov.uk/government/collections/immunisation-against-infectious-disease-the-green-book

question: A 90-year-old man dies in a care home having had pneumonia for 5 days. He had been diagnosed with frailty, vascular dementia and hypertension. He had not been seen by a doctor in the past 2 weeks. Per the Medical Examiner process and NICE/GMC guidance on death certification, what should be entered on the medical certificate of cause of death (MCCD)?

options.A: 1a: Old age
options.B: 1a: Bronchopneumonia. 1b: Vascular dementia. 2: Frailty of old age. Pneumonia (bronchopneumonia) is the immediate cause of death (1a); underlying conditions contributing are vascular dementia (1b — underlying condition leading to 1a) and frailty/old age in Part 2 (contributing but not directly leading to 1a). 'Old age' can legitimately appear on the MCCD when the patient is 80+ and no other more specific cause is identified — but 'old age' alone is not sufficient when a specific terminal condition (pneumonia) is present
options.C: 1a: Natural causes
options.D: 1a: Frailty. 1b: Old age
options.E: Refer to coroner — all deaths in care homes must be referred

explanation.correct: Per GMC guidance on death certification (Writing a medical certificate of cause of death) and Medical Examiner guidance: MCCD structure: Part 1 — sequence leading directly to death (1a: immediate cause; 1b: cause of 1a; 1c: cause of 1b); Part 2 — other significant conditions contributing to death but not in causal sequence. 'Old age' as a term: acceptable on MCCD for patients aged 80+ when no other more specific cause identifiable, per recent ONS/GMC guidance update; however, if a specific terminal condition (bronchopneumonia) is clearly the immediate cause, this should be the primary entry. For this patient: 1a — Bronchopneumonia; 1b — Vascular dementia (pre-existing condition impairing swallow/immune response leading to pneumonia); Part 2 — Frailty of old age. Medical Examiner system: since April 2024, independent Medical Examiners scrutinise all deaths not reported to the coroner; GP must ensure MCCD is completed within 5 days.
explanation.A: Incorrect — 'Old age' alone when a specific terminal cause (bronchopneumonia) is present is insufficient.
explanation.B: CORRECT — 1a Bronchopneumonia, 1b Vascular dementia, Part 2 Frailty of old age per GMC death certification guidance.
explanation.C: Incorrect — 'Natural causes' is not an acceptable entry on the MCCD — a specific diagnosis is required.
explanation.D: Incorrect — Frailty in 1a without the specific terminal cause is insufficient.
explanation.E: Incorrect — Care home deaths do not require automatic coroner referral unless the circumstances meet referral criteria (unexpected death, unknown cause, etc.).

reference: GMC — Completing a death certificate. ONS — Death certification guidance. https://www.gmc-uk.org/ethical-guidance/ethical-guidance-for-doctors/certification-of-death-and-preparation-of-cremation-forms

question: A 90-year-old man dies in hospital. His death is reviewed by the Medical Examiner. The GP had not seen him in the past 14 days. Per the Notification of Deaths Regulations 2019 and GMC guidance, must this death be referred to the coroner?

options.A: Yes — all hospital deaths must be referred to the coroner
options.B: Not necessarily — coroner referral is required only when specific criteria are met: cause of death unknown or uncertain; death due to industrial disease, accident, surgery, drugs, violence, neglect, or suspicious circumstances; patient not seen by a registered medical practitioner in the 28 days before death (if GP is completing MCCD) — however Medical Examiners can now facilitate MCCD completion even without a prior 28-day GP attendance under certain circumstances. The Medical Examiner will assess whether coroner referral is needed
options.C: Yes — not seeing the patient in 14 days always requires coroner referral
options.D: Coroner referral is not required if the death is in hospital
options.E: Coroner referral is only for violent deaths

explanation.correct: Per Notification of Deaths Regulations 2019 and GMC death certification guidance: coroner referral is required when: cause of death is uncertain or unknown; death related to industrial disease, accident, violence, neglect, drugs, surgical procedure, or suspicious circumstances; patient not seen by a registered medical practitioner in 28 days before death (in England and Wales — though Medical Examiners now provide additional flexibility); any death in custody; any neonate death (<28 days old). In this case: hospital death with known cause (pneumonia in context of dementia and frailty) but not seen by GP in 14 days — if a treating hospital doctor can certify cause of death and has seen the patient within 28 days, coroner referral may not be required. Medical Examiner reviews all deaths not referred to the coroner since April 2024. The Medical Examiner will advise if coroner referral is needed.
explanation.A: Incorrect — Not all hospital deaths require coroner referral — specific criteria must be met.
explanation.B: CORRECT — Coroner referral only if specific criteria met per Notification of Deaths Regulations 2019. Medical Examiner assesses need.
explanation.C: Incorrect — The 28-day rule applies to whether a doctor has seen the patient before death, not automatically triggering coroner referral.
explanation.D: Incorrect — Hospital deaths still require coroner referral if the criteria are met.
explanation.E: Incorrect — Many categories beyond violent deaths require referral.

reference: Notification of Deaths Regulations 2019. GMC — Death certification. https://www.legislation.gov.uk/uksi/2019/1112/contents

question: Per the Medical Examiner system introduced across England in April 2024, what is the role of the Medical Examiner?

options.A: Medical Examiners carry out post-mortem examinations
options.B: Medical Examiners are senior doctors who independently scrutinise the circumstances and cause of death for all deaths not referred to the coroner; they ensure accurate cause of death documentation; speak to bereaved families to explain the cause of death and receive any concerns; identify if coroner referral is needed; improve accuracy of death data and identify potentially missed learning
options.C: Medical Examiners replace the coroner
options.D: Medical Examiners are only involved in deaths in police custody
options.E: Medical Examiners prescribe controlled drugs for terminally ill patients

explanation.correct: The Medical Examiner (ME) system became a statutory requirement across England and Wales from April 2024 (following piloting since 2019). Medical Examiners are senior doctors (hospital consultants or GPs with special training) who: independently scrutinise ALL deaths not referred to the coroner; review MCCD for accuracy and completeness; speak to bereaved families (giving them an opportunity to raise concerns); identify cases needing coroner referral; improve death data accuracy; identify learning opportunities. They do NOT conduct post-mortems (pathologists do that under the coroner's direction). ME offices are based in NHS trusts but will cover community deaths too. Medical Examiner Officers (MEO) support the MEs in administration and family communication. This system aims to reduce undetected non-natural deaths and improve death certification quality.
explanation.A: Incorrect — Post-mortems are conducted by pathologists under coroner direction, not Medical Examiners.
explanation.B: CORRECT — Medical Examiners independently scrutinise deaths, ensure accurate MCCD, speak to families, identify coroner referrals per statutory ME system from April 2024.
explanation.C: Incorrect — Medical Examiners work alongside the coroner system; they identify which cases need coroner referral.
explanation.D: Incorrect — Medical Examiners review all community and hospital deaths not referred to the coroner.
explanation.E: Incorrect — Prescribing controlled drugs has no connection to Medical Examiners.

reference: NHS — Medical Examiner system. https://www.england.nhs.uk/patient-safety/patient-safety-improvement-programmes/medical-examiner-system/

question: A 28-year-old woman presents with acute visual loss in her right eye over 24 hours. She describes pain on eye movement and a central visual field defect (scotoma) affecting her right eye. Visual acuity is 6/36 right, 6/6 left. Colour vision is reduced in the right eye. Per NICE CKS, what is the most likely diagnosis and next step?

options.A: Migraine with visual aura — sumatriptan
options.B: Optic neuritis — inflammation of the optic nerve, most commonly demyelinating (associated with multiple sclerosis in 50% of cases); features: acute unilateral visual loss, pain on eye movement (retroorbital), central scotoma, reduced colour vision (red desaturation), relative afferent pupillary defect (RAPD); urgent ophthalmology referral; MRI brain and orbits (multiple periventricular T2 lesions suggest MS); consider IV methylprednisolone to speed recovery (does not improve final visual outcome)
options.C: Acute angle-closure glaucoma — topical pilocarpine
options.D: Retinal detachment — urgent ophthalmology
options.E: Amaurosis fugax — carotid Doppler

explanation.correct: Optic neuritis: inflammation of the optic nerve, most commonly demyelinating in young adults. Clinical features: acute unilateral visual loss (hours to days); retroorbital pain worsening on eye movement (90%); central scotoma (area of visual field loss at fixation); reduced colour vision and contrast sensitivity (red desaturation — patient sees red objects as less vivid); relative afferent pupillary defect (RAPD — swinging flashlight test: affected pupil dilates when light swung from normal to affected eye). Fundoscopy: may be normal (retrobulbar neuritis) or show disc oedema. Investigation: MRI brain and orbits — periventricular white matter lesions (Dawson's fingers) suggest established MS. Treatment: NICE CKS and MS Society guidance — IV methylprednisolone 1g daily for 3 days speeds recovery but does not improve final visual acuity at 6 months. Association with MS: 50% of optic neuritis patients go on to develop MS within 15 years; 25% of MS patients present with optic neuritis.
explanation.A: Incorrect — Migraine aura causes positive visual phenomena (zigzag/scintillating scotoma) that evolve and resolve; it is bilateral cortical phenomena — not unilateral pain on eye movement.
explanation.B: CORRECT — Optic neuritis: acute unilateral visual loss + pain on eye movement + central scotoma + RAPD. MRI for MS. IV methylprednisolone per NICE CKS.
explanation.C: Incorrect — Acute angle-closure glaucoma causes red eye, haloes around lights, raised IOP — not central scotoma or pain on eye movement.
explanation.D: Incorrect — Retinal detachment causes 'curtain' visual field loss without pain on eye movement.
explanation.E: Incorrect — Amaurosis fugax is transient monocular visual loss from retinal TIA — resolves within 30 minutes with no pain on eye movement.

reference: NICE CKS — Optic neuritis. MS Society — Optic neuritis. https://cks.nice.org.uk/topics/multiple-sclerosis/

question: A patient with a right optic nerve lesion has a RAPD (relative afferent pupillary defect). Per neurological examination principles, on the swinging flashlight test, what is observed?

options.A: Both pupils dilate equally when light is shone in either eye
options.B: When light is swung from the normal left eye to the affected right eye, the right pupil DILATES (instead of constricting) due to reduced afferent input from the damaged right optic nerve; this is the RAPD (Marcus Gunn pupil); direct light reflex in affected eye is reduced; consensual reflex from normal eye is intact. RAPD indicates optic nerve or severe retinal disease on that side
options.C: The right pupil is permanently dilated
options.D: Both pupils constrict when light is shone in the right eye
options.E: RAPD only occurs with complete blindness

explanation.correct: Relative afferent pupillary defect (RAPD, Marcus Gunn pupil): tested with swinging flashlight test. Normal: both pupils constrict when light shone in either eye (direct and consensual reflexes). In RAPD (damage to right optic nerve): shining light in the right eye: reduced afferent signal → less pupillary constriction signal reaching Edinger-Westphal nucleus → both pupils dilate compared to when light was in the normal eye; shining light in the left eye: normal afferent signal → both pupils constrict normally. On swinging the light from left to right eye: paradoxical dilation of both pupils as light moves to the affected side. This is the RAPD. RAPD indicates damage to the optic nerve (or severe/asymmetric retinal disease) on the affected side. Causes: optic neuritis, optic nerve compression/trauma, severe retinal detachment, central retinal artery occlusion. Note: RAPD does NOT occur with lens opacity, amblyopia or cortical lesions.
explanation.A: Incorrect — In RAPD, pupils do NOT dilate equally; the response is asymmetric.
explanation.B: CORRECT — RAPD: affected eye dilates when light swung to it (reduced afferent input). Marcus Gunn pupil.
explanation.C: Incorrect — A fixed dilated pupil suggests third nerve palsy or pharmacological dilation — not RAPD.
explanation.D: Incorrect — In RAPD, shining light in the affected eye produces LESS constriction (not more).
explanation.E: Incorrect — RAPD can occur with partial optic nerve damage; complete blindness is not required.

reference: NICE CKS — Optic neuritis. Clinical ophthalmology — RAPD. https://cks.nice.org.uk/topics/multiple-sclerosis/

question: A 30-year-old woman recovers from optic neuritis with near-full visual recovery. Per NICE NG220 and MS Society guidance, what is the key counselling point about her risk of MS?

options.A: She has no risk of MS — optic neuritis is unrelated
options.B: Approximately 50% of patients with isolated optic neuritis will develop MS within 15 years; risk is higher if MRI brain shows white matter lesions (Dawson's fingers in periventricular distribution); she should be referred to neurology for MRI brain and orbital MRI; if MRI shows lesions consistent with MS (McDonald criteria), disease-modifying therapy may be appropriate. Reassure that visual prognosis is generally good even with MS
options.C: She will definitely develop MS
options.D: MS risk only applies if the optic neuritis is bilateral
options.E: MS risk is only relevant after age 50

explanation.correct: Per NICE NG220 (MS in adults) and MS Society UK, the relationship between optic neuritis and MS is well established: 50% of optic neuritis patients develop clinically definite MS within 15 years (Optic Neuritis Treatment Trial — ONTT data); 25% of MS patients present with optic neuritis as their first symptom. MRI brain markedly influences prognosis: normal MRI: 25% risk of MS at 15 years; MRI with ≥1 lesion: 72% risk at 15 years. McDonald criteria 2017: if MRI shows lesions disseminated in space, optic neuritis qualifies as one attack — MS can be diagnosed with one clinical episode if MRI provides evidence of dissemination in space and time. Treatment: if MS diagnosed — disease-modifying therapy (interferon beta, glatiramer acetate, or high-efficacy agents) can reduce relapse rate.
explanation.A: Incorrect — Optic neuritis is a recognised first presentation of MS in 25% of MS cases.
explanation.B: CORRECT — ~50% develop MS within 15 years. Higher risk with abnormal MRI. Neurology referral for McDonald criteria assessment per NICE NG220.
explanation.C: Incorrect — 50% risk, not certainty — half do NOT develop MS.
explanation.D: Incorrect — Bilateral optic neuritis is actually less specific for MS than unilateral (may suggest neuromyelitis optica spectrum disorder — anti-AQP4 antibody positive).
explanation.E: Incorrect — MS risk from optic neuritis is most relevant in young adults 20-40 years.

reference: NICE NG220 — Multiple sclerosis. MS Society UK. https://www.nice.org.uk/guidance/ng220

question: A 55-year-old man presents with horizontal diplopia that is worse when looking to the right. On examination he cannot abduct his right eye. His left eye movements are normal. Per neuroanatomy principles, which cranial nerve is affected and what are the causes?

options.A: Right third nerve palsy — ptosis and down-and-out deviation
options.B: Right sixth nerve (abducens nerve) palsy — the sixth cranial nerve innervates the lateral rectus muscle (abduction); lesion causes failure of right eye abduction (eye deviates medially at rest), horizontal diplopia maximal on right gaze; has the LONGEST intracranial course of any CN — vulnerable to raised intracranial pressure; causes: raised ICP (false localising sign), microvascular (diabetes, hypertension — most common in adults), MS, tumour, Wernicke's, trauma, cavernous sinus thrombosis
options.C: Right fourth nerve palsy — vertical diplopia
options.D: Right seventh nerve palsy — facial droop
options.E: Right third nerve palsy — mydriasis and ptosis

explanation.correct: Sixth nerve (abducens nerve) palsy: CN VI innervates the ipsilateral lateral rectus (LR) muscle responsible for abduction. Lesion of CN VI: failure of ipsilateral abduction; eye deviates medially (esotropia at rest); horizontal diplopia (two images side by side) maximal on ipsilateral horizontal gaze. The sixth nerve has the LONGEST intracranial course of any cranial nerve — makes it particularly vulnerable to raised intracranial pressure (CN VI can be stretched across the petrous bone when the brain stem is displaced downward — called a 'false localising sign' as VI palsy doesn't localise precisely to VI nucleus). Common causes per NICE: Microvascular (diabetes, hypertension, atherosclerosis — most common in adults, typically resolves in 3 months); Raised intracranial pressure (brain tumour, idiopathic intracranial hypertension); Wernicke's encephalopathy (thiamine deficiency); MS plaque; Trauma; Cavernous sinus thrombosis; Meningitis. All new CN VI palsies require urgent ophthalmology/neurology assessment to exclude serious cause.
explanation.A: Incorrect — Third nerve palsy causes: ptosis (levator palpebrae), down-and-out deviation (only SO and LR intact), ± mydriasis (posterior communicating artery aneurysm — surgical 3rd nerve palsy).
explanation.B: CORRECT — Right 6th nerve palsy: failure abduction right eye. Long intracranial course; microvascular is most common adult cause; can be false localising sign of raised ICP.
explanation.C: Incorrect — Fourth nerve palsy causes vertical/torsional diplopia with superior oblique failure.
explanation.D: Incorrect — Seventh nerve palsy causes facial muscle weakness, not ocular movement abnormality.
explanation.E: Incorrect — Third nerve palsy has ptosis, mydriasis and down-and-out deviation.

reference: NICE CKS — Diplopia. Neurology — Cranial nerve palsies. https://cks.nice.org.uk/topics/diplopia/

question: A 65-year-old diabetic man develops sudden-onset right sixth nerve palsy with horizontal diplopia. He has no other neurological symptoms. Per NICE CKS, what is the immediate investigation and expected prognosis?

options.A: Urgent carotid Doppler — suspect carotid disease
options.B: Urgent MRI brain (same day or next day) to exclude structural cause (tumour, aneurysm, MS, cavernous sinus); if MRI normal in a diabetic patient, microvascular infarction is the most likely cause — typically resolves spontaneously within 3 months; manage diabetes; monitor; if persists beyond 3 months or new symptoms develop — re-investigate
options.C: Reassure — all 6th nerve palsies in diabetics are benign
options.D: CT head only — MRI not needed
options.E: No imaging — monitor for 6 months before investigating

explanation.correct: Per NICE CKS and RCOphth guidance on cranial nerve palsies: ALL new cranial nerve palsies require urgent assessment. In a diabetic patient, microvascular sixth nerve palsy is most likely but structural causes (tumour, aneurysm, raised ICP) must be excluded. Urgent MRI brain (ideally with contrast): excludes tumour, metastasis, demyelination, cavernous sinus lesion, raised ICP. If MRI normal + typical microvascular risk factors (diabetes, hypertension, age >50): microvascular CN6 palsy diagnosed — typically resolves spontaneously within 3 months. Management: optimise diabetes control; review BP; reassure; arrange prism glasses to reduce diplopia if needed; follow-up at 3 months — if not resolved, re-investigate. Red flags requiring immediate imaging: bilateral 6th nerve palsy, additional cranial nerve involvement, any signs of raised ICP (headache, papilloedema), young patient without vascular risk factors.
explanation.A: Incorrect — Carotid Doppler investigates TIA/amaurosis fugax — not the first-line for CN VI palsy.
explanation.B: CORRECT — Urgent MRI to exclude structural cause. If normal and diabetic — microvascular; resolves in 3 months per NICE CKS.
explanation.C: Incorrect — Even in diabetics, structural causes must be excluded before attributing to microvascular disease.
explanation.D: Incorrect — MRI is superior to CT for cranial nerve pathology; CT alone is insufficient.
explanation.E: Incorrect — Monitoring for 6 months before imaging risks missing a serious structural cause.

reference: NICE CKS — Diplopia. RCOphth — Management of cranial nerve palsies. https://cks.nice.org.uk/topics/diplopia/

question: A 30-year-old woman with recurrent severe headaches and visual obscurations (brief visual blurring on postural change) is found on examination to have bilateral papilloedema and an abducens nerve palsy. BMI is 38. Per NICE CKS, what is the most likely diagnosis?

options.A: Migraine — sumatriptan
options.B: Idiopathic intracranial hypertension (IIH, pseudotumour cerebri) — raised intracranial pressure without a structural lesion; classic in obese young women; features: headache, visual obscurations, pulsatile tinnitus, papilloedema, CN VI palsy (false localising sign from raised ICP); diagnosis: MRI normal, LP shows raised opening pressure (>25 cmH2O); treatment: weight loss (most effective), acetazolamide, repeat LP, optic nerve sheath fenestration if visual loss threatens
options.C: Subarachnoid haemorrhage — CT head
options.D: Temporal arteritis — ESR and prednisolone
options.E: Meningitis — LP immediately

explanation.correct: Idiopathic intracranial hypertension (IIH): raised ICP with normal brain imaging and normal CSF composition. Classic demographic: obese young women (BMI >30 in 90%). Presentation: positional headaches (worse lying/bending forward), visual obscurations (brief bilateral visual blurring on posture change — warning sign of threatened visual loss), pulsatile tinnitus (whooshing in ears synchronous with pulse), CN VI palsy (false localising sign — stretched sixth nerve from raised ICP). Diagnosis: MRI brain (normal parenchyma, may show 'empty sella', flattened posterior globes, dilated optic nerve sheaths, transverse venous sinus stenosis); LP opening pressure >25 cmH2O with normal CSF composition. Treatment: weight loss (primary treatment — 10% weight loss can lead to remission); acetazolamide (carbonic anhydrase inhibitor, reduces CSF production); CSF drainage procedures (serial LP, lumboperitoneal shunt); optic nerve sheath fenestration for imminent visual loss.
explanation.A: Incorrect — Migraine doesn't cause papilloedema or CN VI palsy.
explanation.B: CORRECT — IIH: obese young woman + headaches + papilloedema + CN VI palsy + visual obscurations. MRI then LP per NICE CKS.
explanation.C: Incorrect — SAH causes sudden thunderclap headache; papilloedema and CN VI in a young obese woman without thunderclap onset points to IIH.
explanation.D: Incorrect — Temporal arteritis affects older patients with raised inflammatory markers and jaw claudication.
explanation.E: Incorrect — Meningitis is the correct management if bacterial meningitis suspected, but this patient's chronic history with obesity suggests IIH.

reference: NICE CKS — Idiopathic intracranial hypertension. https://cks.nice.org.uk/topics/idiopathic-intracranial-hypertension/

question: A GP performs a cover-uncover test on a 5-year-old girl with suspected strabismus. When the left eye is covered, the right eye is observed to move inward to take up fixation. What does this indicate?

options.A: Normal eye movements
options.B: The right eye has a manifest divergent squint (exotropia) — when the left eye was covered, the right eye had to move INWARD (adduct) to fix on the target, indicating it was previously deviated outward; the cover-uncover test reveals MANIFEST squint (tropia, not phoria); this eye requires urgent orthoptic assessment and management to prevent amblyopia
options.C: The left eye has a convergent squint
options.D: The child has a latent squint (phoria) — no intervention needed
options.E: This is a normal finding in children under 5

explanation.correct: Cover-uncover test: used to detect manifest squint (tropia). Method: ask child to fixate on a target; cover one eye; observe the uncovered eye. If the UNCOVERED eye moves when the other is covered: MANIFEST squint (tropia) present — the uncovered eye was not previously fixating; the direction of movement indicates the direction of squint: moves INWARD (nasally) = was deviated OUTWARD = exotropia; moves OUTWARD (temporally) = was deviated INWARD = esotropia (convergent squint — more common in children). In this case: right eye moves inward when left covered → right eye was diverged = manifest right exotropia. Alternating cover test (cover-uncover alternating): detects latent squint (phoria) — movement when cover is alternated indicates phoria, normally suppressed by binocular vision. Management of manifest squint in children: urgent orthoptic referral; amblyopia (lazy eye) prevention with patching; spectacle correction; surgery if needed.
explanation.A: Incorrect — Normal eyes do not move when the other is covered in the cover-uncover test.
explanation.B: CORRECT — Right eye moves inward when left covered = manifest right exotropia (divergent squint). Urgent orthoptic referral per NICE CKS.
explanation.C: Incorrect — Left eye convergent squint would show the LEFT eye moving outward when RIGHT eye covered.
explanation.D: Incorrect — A phoria (latent squint) is detected on the alternating cover test, not the cover-uncover test.
explanation.E: Incorrect — Eye movement on cover-uncover testing is always abnormal; it indicates manifest squint.

reference: NICE CKS — Squint. https://cks.nice.org.uk/topics/squint/

question: A parent brings their 3-year-old son for a routine developmental check. During eye examination the GP performs a cover test and notices the right eye turns inward when the left eye is covered (right convergent squint). What is the primary concern and management?

options.A: Refer at age 7 — amblyopia can be treated up to that age
options.B: Urgent orthoptic referral — convergent squint (esotropia) in children risks amblyopia (lazy eye) if the deviating eye is suppressed; younger age of treatment = better visual outcome; treatment: spectacle correction if refractive error is present (accommodative esotropia often corrects fully with spectacles), patching of the dominant eye to force use of the amblyopic eye, surgery if residual squint; optimal treatment window is before age 7-8 when visual cortex is still plastic
options.C: Reassure — most childhood squints resolve spontaneously by age 5
options.D: Refer to the GP ophthalmologist — routine appointment within 6 months
options.E: Topical atropine to the dominant eye — first-line

explanation.correct: Per NICE CKS, convergent squint (esotropia) in childhood requires early treatment to prevent amblyopia. Amblyopia: reduction in vision in one eye (the deviating eye) due to abnormal visual cortical development during the critical period (birth to approximately 7-8 years) — when visual cortex is neuroplastic. If the deviating eye is continuously suppressed, cortical connections for that eye fail to develop normally → permanent visual impairment. Management priorities: (1) Orthoptic assessment — refraction under cycloplegia; (2) Spectacle correction — many esotropias (accommodative) fully or partially correct with hyperopic glasses; (3) Patching (occlusion therapy) — cover dominant eye 2-6 hours/day to force use of amblyopic eye; (4) Surgery — if significant angle remains after spectacle correction. Critical period: before age 7-8, reversal of amblyopia is possible; after this age, amblyopia becomes fixed. Referral should be urgent — not delayed.
explanation.A: Incorrect — Referral should be urgent (weeks), not delayed until age 7.
explanation.B: CORRECT — Urgent orthoptic referral for convergent squint; amblyopia treatment before age 7-8 critical window per NICE CKS.
explanation.C: Incorrect — Squint does NOT resolve spontaneously — all squints in children need assessment.
explanation.D: Incorrect — 6-month wait is unacceptably long; amblyopia risk is real and treatment urgency is high.
explanation.E: Incorrect — Topical atropine (penalisation) is a second-line patching alternative — not first-line.

reference: NICE CKS — Squint. https://cks.nice.org.uk/topics/squint/

question: An 18-month-old child presents with a new inward-turning left eye. On ophthalmoscopy the GP notices absence of the normal red reflex on the left side (leukocoria — white pupil reflex). Per NICE NG12, what is the most urgent diagnosis to exclude?

options.A: Cataract — routine ophthalmology referral
options.B: Retinoblastoma — the most common primary intraocular malignancy of childhood; leukocoria (white pupil reflex replacing normal red reflex) is the most common presenting sign (60%); squint is the second most common; urgent 2WW oncology/ophthalmology referral; fundoscopy under anaesthesia; treatment: chemotherapy, intravitreal/intra-arterial chemotherapy, enucleation for advanced disease; survival >95% in UK with early treatment
options.C: Retinal detachment — arrange USS
options.D: Amblyopia — patching
options.E: Anisometropia — spectacle correction

explanation.correct: Retinoblastoma: the most important cause of leukocoria in children under 5. A white/yellowish pupil reflex (leukocoria) instead of the normal red reflex requires SAME-DAY urgent ophthalmology referral per NICE NG12 (Suspected cancer: recognition and referral). Retinoblastoma epidemiology: 40-45 cases/year in UK; 60% unilateral, 40% bilateral (bilateral = hereditary form); median age of diagnosis 18 months. Presentation: leukocoria (white reflex on photographs — important sign parents may notice in flash photography), squint (from visual impairment), visual loss, red painful eye (advanced disease). Diagnosis: fundoscopy under general anaesthesia by experienced ophthalmologist; orbital USS, MRI. Treatment: depends on stage — local therapy (laser, cryotherapy), chemotherapy (carboplatin, vincristine, etoposide), intravitreal chemotherapy, enucleation for advanced cases. Prognosis: survival >95% in UK. Genetic counselling essential — RB1 gene mutation identified; screen siblings and offspring.
explanation.A: Incorrect — Congenital cataract also causes absent red reflex but should be referred urgently (SAME DAY) — not routine. Retinoblastoma must be excluded first.
explanation.B: CORRECT — Leukocoria + squint in an infant = retinoblastoma until proven otherwise. Same-day urgent 2WW ophthalmology per NICE NG12.
explanation.C: Incorrect — Retinal detachment is rare in this age group; retinoblastoma is the priority diagnosis.
explanation.D: Incorrect — Amblyopia does not cause leukocoria.
explanation.E: Incorrect — Anisometropia does not cause absent red reflex.

reference: NICE NG12 — Suspected cancer. CLSG — Retinoblastoma UK. https://www.nice.org.uk/guidance/ng12

question: A 55-year-old woman on methotrexate 15mg weekly for rheumatoid arthritis develops increasing breathlessness, dry cough and dyspnoea. She is not on any new medications. Her chest X-ray shows bilateral interstitial infiltrates. Per BNF and NICE guidance, which adverse effect has occurred?

options.A: Community-acquired pneumonia — prescribe amoxicillin
options.B: Methotrexate-induced pneumonitis (MTX lung toxicity) — an idiosyncratic hypersensitivity reaction causing interstitial pneumonitis; features: dry cough, progressive dyspnoea, fever, bilateral interstitial infiltrates on CXR, reduced TLCO; can occur at any dose or time; STOP methotrexate immediately; give systemic corticosteroids; refer to respiratory/rheumatology; lung function monitoring (TLCO) at baseline and during treatment
options.C: Heart failure — start furosemide
options.D: Pulmonary embolism — CTPA
options.E: Pleural effusion — pleural aspiration

explanation.correct: Methotrexate pneumonitis: an idiosyncratic hypersensitivity reaction (not dose-dependent — can occur at low doses after variable duration). Estimated incidence 1-5% of RA patients on MTX. Features: dry cough, progressive breathlessness, fever; CXR bilateral interstitial infiltrates; reduced TLCO on spirometry; peripheral blood eosinophilia in some. Differential: infection (PCP, bacterial), NSIP/UIP from RA itself. Management: STOP methotrexate immediately — do NOT restart; high-resolution CT chest (ground-glass opacification); BAL to exclude infection; systemic corticosteroids (prednisolone 0.5-1 mg/kg). Prognosis: generally good recovery with MTX withdrawal and steroids; mortality <2%. Baseline TLCO should be measured before starting MTX and monitored. MTX must NOT be restarted after pneumonitis. Alternative DMARDs: leflunomide, hydroxychloroquine, sulfasalazine.
explanation.A: Incorrect — Although pneumonia must be excluded (CXR and sputum culture), the clinical pattern in a patient on MTX strongly suggests MTX pneumonitis.
explanation.B: CORRECT — MTX pneumonitis: stop methotrexate immediately + corticosteroids + respiratory referral per BNF.
explanation.C: Incorrect — Heart failure causes wet lungs and peripheral oedema — not bilateral interstitial infiltrates with dry cough.
explanation.D: Incorrect — PE causes acute onset breathlessness; bilateral infiltrates are not typical of PE.
explanation.E: Incorrect — Pleural effusion would be unilateral or bilateral fluid (not infiltrates) and without the dry cough pattern.

reference: BNF — Methotrexate adverse effects. BSR methotrexate guidelines. https://bnf.nice.org.uk/drug/methotrexate.html

question: A patient on methotrexate and trimethoprim for a UTI develops pancytopenia and severe mucositis. Per BNF, what pharmacological interaction caused this?

options.A: Methotrexate causes additive infection risk with trimethoprim
options.B: Both trimethoprim and methotrexate inhibit dihydrofolate reductase (DHFR) — dual DHFR inhibition causes profound folate deficiency even with folic acid supplementation; this leads to bone marrow suppression (pancytopenia) and mucositis; trimethoprim is contraindicated with methotrexate; alternative antibiotics for UTI in this patient: nitrofurantoin or cefalexin
options.C: Trimethoprim increases methotrexate absorption
options.D: The interaction is only relevant with high-dose methotrexate
options.E: Folic acid supplementation fully prevents this interaction

explanation.correct: The methotrexate-trimethoprim interaction is a critical, potentially fatal pharmacodynamic drug interaction. Both drugs inhibit DHFR (dihydrofolate reductase): methotrexate (primary mechanism for its anti-inflammatory and anti-neoplastic effects); trimethoprim (mechanism for its antibacterial effect — inhibits bacterial DHFR, but also inhibits human DHFR). Dual inhibition causes: severe folate deficiency → failure of DNA synthesis → bone marrow suppression (pancytopenia — potentially fatal), severe mucositis, hepatotoxicity. This interaction applies to LOW-DOSE weekly methotrexate (as used in RA/psoriasis) — not only high-dose oncology. Per BNF: trimethoprim and co-trimoxazole are CONTRAINDICATED with methotrexate. Safe alternatives for UTI: nitrofurantoin (eGFR ≥45 ml/min), cefalexin, amoxicillin (if susceptible). Folic acid supplementation reduces but does NOT fully prevent this interaction.
explanation.A: Incorrect — The mechanism is pharmacodynamic DHFR inhibition, not infection risk.
explanation.B: CORRECT — Dual DHFR inhibition → pancytopenia and mucositis. Trimethoprim contraindicated with MTX per BNF.
explanation.C: Incorrect — Trimethoprim affects DHFR enzymatic activity, not methotrexate absorption.
explanation.D: Incorrect — This interaction applies to low-dose weekly MTX used in inflammatory conditions.
explanation.E: Incorrect — Folic acid partially protects against some MTX side effects but cannot overcome dual DHFR inhibition from combined use.

reference: BNF — Methotrexate interactions. Trimethoprim. https://bnf.nice.org.uk/interaction/methotrexate.html

question: A patient on methotrexate for psoriasis needs a routine NSAID for back pain. Per BNF, what is the concern and what advice should be given?

options.A: No interaction — NSAIDs and methotrexate are commonly co-prescribed without concern
options.B: NSAIDs can increase methotrexate toxicity by reducing renal clearance of methotrexate (prostaglandin-mediated renal blood flow reduction); short courses at standard doses are generally used with caution; avoid high-dose or prolonged NSAIDs; monitor renal function; paracetamol is a safer alternative for analgesia; avoid in patients with pre-existing renal impairment
options.C: NSAIDs prevent methotrexate working effectively
options.D: NSAIDs must never be used with any dose of methotrexate
options.E: COX-2 inhibitors are safe as they have no interaction with methotrexate

explanation.correct: Per BNF, NSAIDs and methotrexate have a clinically important interaction. NSAIDs inhibit prostaglandin synthesis (COX inhibition) → reduced renal afferent arteriolar dilation → reduced renal blood flow and GFR → reduced renal clearance of methotrexate → accumulation of methotrexate → toxicity (bone marrow suppression, mucositis, hepatotoxicity, nephrotoxicity). This risk is dose-dependent and additive with renal impairment. Management: avoid regular/high-dose NSAIDs with methotrexate; short-term low-dose use may be acceptable with appropriate monitoring and patient education; paracetamol is preferable; monitor FBC, LFTs and creatinine if NSAIDs are unavoidable; patient should know to report symptoms of methotrexate toxicity (mouth ulcers, unusual bruising, breathlessness, fever). COX-2 inhibitors have the same mechanism (renal prostaglandin inhibition) and same interaction.
explanation.A: Incorrect — The NSAID-methotrexate interaction is clinically significant and documented in the BNF.
explanation.B: CORRECT — NSAIDs reduce MTX renal clearance → toxicity risk. Use cautiously; paracetamol preferred; avoid in renal impairment per BNF.
explanation.C: Incorrect — NSAIDs increase methotrexate toxicity, not reduce efficacy.
explanation.D: Incorrect — Short-term low-dose NSAIDs may be used with caution; absolute prohibition is overly strict.
explanation.E: Incorrect — COX-2 inhibitors have the same renal prostaglandin inhibition mechanism as traditional NSAIDs.

reference: BNF — Methotrexate interactions. https://bnf.nice.org.uk/interaction/methotrexate.html

question: A GP performs a ring block (digital nerve block) on a big toe using 5ml of 2% lidocaine for an ingrowing toenail procedure. Shortly after injection, the patient develops perioral tingling, confusion, twitching and then a short generalised seizure. Per AAGBI guidelines, what is the diagnosis and treatment?

options.A: Vasovagal syncope — supine position and wait
options.B: Local anaesthetic systemic toxicity (LAST) — caused by inadvertent intravascular injection or absorbed excess lidocaine; CNS toxicity precedes cardiac; features: metallic taste, perioral tingling → confusion/agitation → convulsions → cardiovascular collapse; treatment per AAGBI: 20% Intralipid IV (1.5 ml/kg bolus then infusion as lipid sink); call for help; ABC resuscitation; treat seizures with benzodiazepine; CPR if cardiac arrest
options.C: Allergic reaction — adrenaline IM
options.D: Stroke — CT head
options.E: Epileptic seizure — buccal midazolam

explanation.correct: Local anaesthetic systemic toxicity (LAST): rare but potentially fatal complication of LA injection. Lidocaine is a sodium channel blocker — systemic toxicity causes progressive CNS and cardiac effects: CNS (early): metallic taste, perioral tingling/numbness, tinnitus, confusion, agitation; CNS (late): convulsions, coma; Cardiac: prolonged PR, wide QRS, ventricular arrhythmias, cardiovascular collapse. AAGBI LAST guidelines: stop LA injection; call for help; ABC; supplemental O2; IV access; seizure control (benzodiazepine preferred over thiopental/propofol); INTRALIPID 20% (specific antidote — 'lipid sink' mechanism) 1.5 ml/kg bolus IV over 1 min, then 0.25 ml/kg/min infusion; repeat bolus if cardiovascular instability; maximum 12 ml/kg; CPR if cardiac arrest; continue Intralipid through arrest. Ring blocks: typically safer as digital arteries are small but intravascular injection still possible. Adrenaline in ring blocks: can cause digital ischaemia/gangrene — modern evidence suggests it is safer than previously thought in standard concentrations, but high concentrations remain avoidable.
explanation.A: Incorrect — Vasovagal syncope causes brief LOC without seizure or metallic taste preceding it.
explanation.B: CORRECT — LAST: CNS toxicity → seizure. Intralipid 20% specific antidote + ABC per AAGBI.
explanation.C: Incorrect — Allergic reaction to true amide local anaesthetics (like lidocaine) is extremely rare; this is systemic toxicity, not allergy.
explanation.D: Incorrect — Stroke doesn't explain the perioral tingling and progression from LA injection.
explanation.E: Incorrect — Although midazolam treats the seizure, Intralipid is the specific antidote that must be given.

reference: AAGBI — Management of Severe Local Anaesthetic Toxicity. https://www.aagbi.org/

question: A GP is about to perform an ingrowing toenail procedure. Per BNF, what is the maximum safe dose of lidocaine for infiltration and why does adding adrenaline increase this limit?

options.A: Maximum 100mg regardless of whether adrenaline is added
options.B: Lidocaine without adrenaline: maximum 3 mg/kg (up to 200 mg). Lidocaine with adrenaline: maximum 7 mg/kg (up to 500 mg). Adrenaline causes local vasoconstriction, reducing systemic absorption of lidocaine — allowing a higher total dose to be used safely. Adrenaline also prolongs anaesthetic duration by reducing washout
options.C: No dose limit — lidocaine is always safe
options.D: Maximum 50mg in all circumstances
options.E: Bupivacaine has no dose limit unlike lidocaine

explanation.correct: Per BNF: Lidocaine without adrenaline: maximum dose 3 mg/kg, up to 200 mg total (example: 70 kg patient = 210 mg → limit to 200 mg). Lidocaine with adrenaline (epinephrine): maximum 7 mg/kg, up to 500 mg. Mechanism: adrenaline causes local vasoconstriction at injection site → reduces systemic absorption of LA into bloodstream → peak plasma lidocaine concentration is lower → safer to give higher total dose. Additional benefit: prolongs duration of anaesthesia (less LA washed away), reduces bleeding at site, improves surgical field. Cautions for adrenaline in LA: traditional concern about digital blocks (toe, finger) — adrenaline may cause digital ischaemia by vasoconstricting digital arteries. Modern evidence (RCTs) shows low-concentration adrenaline (1:100,000-1:200,000) in digital blocks is safe in most patients; still avoid in patients with peripheral vascular disease, Raynaud's, sickle cell. Bupivacaine: maximum 2 mg/kg (without adrenaline) — more cardiotoxic than lidocaine.
explanation.A: Incorrect — Adding adrenaline significantly increases the safe maximum dose.
explanation.B: CORRECT — Lidocaine: 3 mg/kg without adrenaline; 7 mg/kg with adrenaline. Adrenaline reduces systemic absorption per BNF.
explanation.C: Incorrect — Local anaesthetic toxicity is dose-dependent; dose limits are critical for safety.
explanation.D: Incorrect — 50 mg is not the correct limit for standard adult patients.
explanation.E: Incorrect — Bupivacaine has its own dose limits (2 mg/kg); and it is more cardiotoxic than lidocaine.

reference: BNF — Lidocaine. Local anaesthetic doses. https://bnf.nice.org.uk/drug/lidocaine-hydrochloride.html

question: A GP is about to perform an ingrowing toenail procedure for a patient who has a known allergy to lidocaine. Per BNF, what is an appropriate alternative local anaesthetic?

options.A: No alternative exists — cancel the procedure
options.B: Prilocaine — an amide local anaesthetic with a different molecular structure to lidocaine but in the same class; if true allergy to amides is confirmed, use an ESTER local anaesthetic (procaine, chloroprocaine) which has a different chemical class and does not cross-react with amides. True allergy to amide LAs is very rare — most reactions are vasovagal or toxic; allergy testing/referral recommended before assuming class allergy
options.C: Use higher dose lidocaine — small amounts are safe even in allergy
options.D: Bupivacaine is always safe in lidocaine allergy
options.E: General anaesthesia is the only alternative

explanation.correct: Local anaesthetics are divided into two main classes: Amides: lidocaine, prilocaine, bupivacaine, ropivacaine, mepivacaine, levobupivacaine. These share a similar molecular structure and can cross-react (allergy to one amide may predict allergy to others in the class). Esters: procaine, tetracaine (amethocaine), benzocaine, chloroprocaine. Amides and esters do NOT cross-react. True allergy to amide LAs is actually very rare (<1% of adverse reactions to LAs). Most 'reactions' are: vasovagal, systemic toxicity from overdose/intravascular injection, or adrenaline effects. If true allergy confirmed: switch class (ester LA). Recommended approach for a patient reporting LA allergy: careful history (what was the reaction?); referral for allergy testing if unclear; if confirmed allergy — use ester class. In practice, prilocaine, mepivacaine or bupivacaine are sometimes used as alternatives within amide class if reaction was mild/uncharacteristic, but with caution.
explanation.A: Incorrect — Alternative local anaesthetics from the ester class are available.
explanation.B: CORRECT — Ester LAs (procaine, chloroprocaine) if true amide allergy confirmed; allergy to one amide may cross-react with other amides per BNF.
explanation.C: Incorrect — Using an allergen (lidocaine) even in small amounts in a confirmed allergy risks anaphylaxis.
explanation.D: Incorrect — Bupivacaine is also an amide and will likely cross-react.
explanation.E: Incorrect — Alternative LAs are available; GA is disproportionate for a minor procedure.

reference: BNF — Local anaesthetics. https://bnf.nice.org.uk/drug/lidocaine-hydrochloride.html

question: A 62-year-old man with type 2 diabetes has an annual review. His urine ACR is 5.8 mg/mmol on two separate samples. His BP is 134/82 mmHg. He is not on any antihypertensive therapy. Per NICE NG28, what should be added?

options.A: Amlodipine — calcium channel blockers are first-line for all diabetic patients
options.B: ACE inhibitor (e.g. ramipril) or ARB (e.g. losartan) — first-line for diabetic nephropathy with microalbuminuria (ACR 3-30 mg/mmol) regardless of blood pressure; provides specific renoprotection by reducing intraglomerular pressure and slowing CKD progression in diabetics; monitor eGFR, creatinine and potassium 2 weeks after starting
options.C: No treatment needed — ACR 5.8 mg/mmol is normal
options.D: Diuretic only — BP is too high
options.E: Dual ACE inhibitor and ARB combination

explanation.correct: Per NICE NG28 (Type 2 diabetes in adults) and NICE NG203 (CKD), microalbuminuria (ACR 3-30 mg/mmol — also called A2 category per NICE NG203 staging) in a diabetic patient warrants: ACE inhibitor or ARB therapy REGARDLESS of blood pressure — started for renoprotection not just BP lowering. Mechanism: ACE inhibitors and ARBs reduce efferent arteriolar tone → decrease intraglomerular pressure → reduce albuminuria and slow CKD progression. Target BP in diabetics with CKD: <130/80 mmHg. Monitor: eGFR, creatinine (accept up to 30% rise — greater than this suggests renal artery stenosis) and potassium 1-2 weeks after starting. Continue if stable. ACE+ARB dual blockade is NOT recommended (ONTARGET trial — increased adverse events). If eGFR ≥45: consider SGLT2 inhibitor (dapagliflozin) for additional CKD protection per NICE NG203.
explanation.A: Incorrect — Amlodipine lowers BP but has no specific renoprotective effect in diabetics — ACE/ARB is first-line.
explanation.B: CORRECT — ACE inhibitor first-line for diabetic nephropathy with microalbuminuria (A2) regardless of BP per NICE NG28.
explanation.C: Incorrect — ACR 5.8 mg/mmol is in the A2 (microalbuminuria) range (3-30 mg/mmol) and requires action.
explanation.D: Incorrect — Diuretics alone do not provide specific renoprotection in diabetes.
explanation.E: Incorrect — ACE+ARB dual blockade is contraindicated per ONTARGET trial evidence.

reference: NICE NG28 — Type 2 diabetes. NICE NG203 — CKD. https://www.nice.org.uk/guidance/ng28

question: A 68-year-old man has both benign prostatic hyperplasia (BPH) causing lower urinary tract symptoms and hypertension requiring treatment. Per NICE NG136 and NICE NG123 on LUTS in men, which antihypertensive would treat both conditions?

options.A: Bendroflumethiazide — first-line for both
options.B: Doxazosin (or another alpha-1 blocker) — alpha-1 adrenergic receptor blockers cause: systemic arterial vasodilation (antihypertensive effect) AND relaxation of prostate and bladder neck smooth muscle (reduces bladder outlet obstruction and improves urine flow); doxazosin is licensed for both BPH and hypertension
options.C: Bisoprolol — beta-blockers treat both BPH and hypertension
options.D: Spironolactone — treats both conditions
options.E: Tamsulosin — treats hypertension and BPH

explanation.correct: Alpha-1 blockers (alpha-1 adrenergic receptor antagonists): doxazosin, prazosin, terazosin — licensed for both hypertension and BPH. Mechanism: alpha-1 receptors present in: vascular smooth muscle (blockade → vasodilation → BP reduction) AND prostate stroma and bladder neck (blockade → smooth muscle relaxation → reduced bladder outlet resistance → improved urine flow). Per NICE NG136 and NICE NG123: doxazosin is a useful dual-use agent in men with both hypertension and BPH. Practical consideration: postural hypotension is a significant side effect of alpha-1 blockers — advise patient to rise slowly; start at low dose and titrate. Tamsulosin and alfuzosin are more uro-selective alpha-1A/D blockers — less systemic BP lowering → less antihypertensive effect → preferred for BPH alone without hypertension. Prazosin (mentioned in the recall) is an older alpha-1 blocker — less used now due to twice/three times daily dosing versus once daily doxazosin.
explanation.A: Incorrect — Bendroflumethiazide has no beneficial effect on BPH.
explanation.B: CORRECT — Doxazosin (alpha-1 blocker) treats both hypertension and BPH per NICE NG136 and NG123.
explanation.C: Incorrect — Beta-blockers have no beneficial effect on BPH symptoms.
explanation.D: Incorrect — Spironolactone treats heart failure, ascites and hyperaldosteronism — not BPH.
explanation.E: Incorrect — Tamsulosin is uro-selective and has minimal antihypertensive effect — not first-line for hypertension.

reference: NICE NG136 — Hypertension in adults. NICE NG123 — LUTS in men. https://www.nice.org.uk/guidance/ng136

question: A 9-year-old child weighing 32 kg presents to the GP with anaphylaxis following a bee sting. Per NICE CG134 and BNF, what is the correct dose of adrenaline for intramuscular injection?

options.A: 0.5 ml of 1:1000 (500 mcg) — adult dose
options.B: 0.3 ml of 1:1000 IM (300 mcg) — for children aged 6-12 years; inject into the anterolateral thigh; use adrenaline 1:1000 (1 mg/ml) formulation; can repeat after 5 minutes if no improvement; this equates to approximately the EpiPen dose (0.3 mg) for children ≥25 kg
options.C: 0.15 ml of 1:1000 (150 mcg) — for children under 6
options.D: 0.1 ml of 1:10,000 IV — intravenous only

explanation.correct: Per NICE CG134 (Anaphylaxis) and BNF paediatric adrenaline doses for anaphylaxis: Adults and children >12 years: 0.5 mg IM (0.5 ml of 1:1000). Children 6-12 years: 0.3 mg IM (0.3 ml of 1:1000). Children <6 years: 0.15 mg IM (0.15 ml of 1:1000). This child is 9 years old = 0.3 ml of 1:1000 IM (300 mcg). Inject into the anterolateral middle third of the thigh (lateral aspect — faster absorption than deltoid). The 1:1000 formulation = 1 mg/ml. Repeat after 5 minutes if no improvement. Note: EpiPen (0.3 mg) = 6-12 years or 25+ kg; EpiPen Jr (0.15 mg) = under 6 or 15-25 kg. Concentration used: ALWAYS 1:1000 for IM use. Do NOT use IV adrenaline in anaphylaxis unless in cardiac arrest (specialist setting). Documentation and referral to allergy specialist post-anaphylaxis for adrenaline auto-injector prescription.
explanation.A: Incorrect — 0.5 ml is the adult dose; a 9-year-old receives 0.3 ml.
explanation.B: CORRECT — 0.3 ml of 1:1000 IM for 6-12 year olds per NICE CG134/BNF.
explanation.C: Incorrect — 0.15 ml is for children under 6 years of age.
explanation.D: Incorrect — IV adrenaline 1:10,000 is for cardiac arrest only — not for acute anaphylaxis management.
explanation.E: Incorrect — 1 ml (1000 mcg) would be a massive overdose.

reference: NICE CG134 — Anaphylaxis. BNF — Adrenaline doses. https://www.nice.org.uk/guidance/cg134

question: A 62-year-old man is being considered for prostate cancer screening. His GP checks his PSA. Per NICE NG131 and BNF, which medication commonly used in BPH significantly reduces PSA levels?

options.A: Tamsulosin — reduces PSA by 50%
options.B: Finasteride (5-alpha reductase inhibitor) — reduces PSA levels by approximately 50% after 6 months of use; this MUST be accounted for when interpreting PSA results (multiply the PSA value by 2 to get the estimated 'true' PSA in patients on finasteride); failure to account for this reduction may lead to missed prostate cancer diagnosis; dutasteride has a similar effect
options.C: Doxazosin — reduces PSA
options.D: Sildenafil — reduces PSA
options.E: Oxybutynin — reduces PSA

explanation.correct: 5-alpha reductase inhibitors (5-ARIs) — finasteride (for BPH) and dutasteride: inhibit conversion of testosterone to dihydrotestosterone (DHT); DHT drives prostatic epithelial cell growth and PSA production; blocking DHT reduces prostate volume and PSA production. Effect on PSA: PSA reduces by approximately 50% after 6 months on finasteride. Clinical importance for cancer screening: if a man on finasteride has a PSA measured, the result must be doubled to estimate his 'true' PSA level (e.g., if PSA = 2.5 ng/mL on finasteride → estimated true PSA = 5.0 ng/mL, above the threshold for referral); failure to adjust leads to underdetection of prostate cancer. Per NICE NG131 (Prostate cancer) and PSA testing guidelines: always check if patient is on finasteride/dutasteride before interpreting PSA. Tamsulosin and doxazosin (alpha-blockers) do NOT affect PSA levels.
explanation.A: Incorrect — Tamsulosin (alpha-1 blocker) does NOT affect PSA.
explanation.B: CORRECT — Finasteride reduces PSA by ~50%; multiply result by 2 for true PSA per NICE NG131.
explanation.C: Incorrect — Doxazosin (alpha-1 blocker) does not affect PSA.
explanation.D: Incorrect — Sildenafil (PDE5 inhibitor for erectile dysfunction/BPH) does not affect PSA.
explanation.E: Incorrect — Oxybutynin (anticholinergic for OAB) does not affect PSA.

reference: NICE NG131 — Prostate cancer. BNF — Finasteride. https://www.nice.org.uk/guidance/ng131

question: A 28-year-old woman who is currently breastfeeding her 4-month-old baby requests emergency contraception after unprotected intercourse. Per FSRH guidance, which oral emergency contraceptive should NOT be used in breastfeeding women and why?

options.A: Levonorgestrel — contraindicated in breastfeeding
options.B: Ulipristal acetate (ellaOne) — FSRH advises against use in breastfeeding: ulipristal is a progesterone receptor modulator that is excreted in breast milk; potential effects on the breastfed infant are unknown; recommendation is to avoid or if used, to express and discard breast milk for 7 days after taking ulipristal
options.C: Copper IUD — contraindicated in breastfeeding
options.D: All emergency contraceptives are contraindicated in breastfeeding
options.E: No emergency contraception is contraindicated in breastfeeding

explanation.correct: Per FSRH Emergency Contraception guidelines, the key distinction in breastfeeding: Levonorgestrel 1.5mg (Levonelle): small amounts excreted in breast milk; FSRH advises it can be used in breastfeeding — express and discard milk for 8 hours if concerned, or take immediately after a feed; generally considered compatible with breastfeeding. Ulipristal acetate (ellaOne 30mg): FSRH advises AGAINST use in breastfeeding women — ulipristal excreted in breast milk; unknown effects on breastfed infant; if taken, express and discard all milk for 7 days; this effectively means breastfeeding must cease for 7 days making it impractical. Copper IUD: most effective EC (>99% effective at any time up to 5 days); no hormonal effect; safe in breastfeeding — preferred option for a breastfeeding woman needing EC. Summary: if oral EC needed → levonorgestrel preferred; best option in breastfeeding → copper IUD.
explanation.A: Incorrect — Levonorgestrel is considered compatible with breastfeeding (discard milk for 8 hours if concerned) per FSRH.
explanation.B: CORRECT — Ulipristal should be avoided in breastfeeding; if used, discard milk for 7 days per FSRH.
explanation.C: Incorrect — Copper IUD is safe and preferred in breastfeeding women requiring EC.
explanation.D: Incorrect — Levonorgestrel and copper IUD are appropriate options in breastfeeding.
explanation.E: Incorrect — Ulipristal is specifically advised against in breastfeeding.

reference: FSRH — Emergency Contraception guideline. https://www.fsrh.org/standards-and-guidance/

question: A 22-year-old woman on the progesterone-only pill (POP, desogestrel 75 mcg) needs emergency contraception. She had UPSI 48 hours ago. Per FSRH guidance, what specific interaction must be considered if ulipristal is used?

options.A: No interaction — ulipristal and POP can be taken simultaneously
options.B: Ulipristal and progestogen-containing contraceptives mutually reduce each other's efficacy — ulipristal is a progesterone receptor modulator (PRM); concurrent progestogen use may reduce ulipristal's EC efficacy. FSRH recommends: STOP the POP before taking ulipristal; do NOT restart POP for 5 days after ulipristal (use additional contraception — condoms — during this period AND for 9 days after restarting the POP)
options.C: Stop POP permanently after ulipristal
options.D: No need to stop POP — interaction is theoretical only
options.E: Take double dose of ulipristal to overcome the interaction

explanation.correct: Per FSRH EC guideline, ulipristal acetate (UPA) interacts with progestogen-containing methods: UPA is a selective progesterone receptor modulator (SPRM) — exerts its EC effect by delaying/inhibiting ovulation through progesterone receptor occupancy. Concurrent progesterone (from POP, COCP, implant, Mirena IUS) can COMPETE with UPA at the progesterone receptor → reduces UPA efficacy. FSRH recommendation: stop POP before taking UPA; do not restart POP for 5 days after UPA (the window when UPA is active); use condoms for 5 days after UPA AND for a further 9 days after restarting the POP. Note for COCP and POP combined interaction: similar rules apply — 5-day gap before restarting hormonal contraception. If levonorgestrel is used instead: no clinically significant interaction with progestogen-only methods — restart POP immediately after.
explanation.A: Incorrect — Concurrent progestogen significantly reduces ulipristal's EC efficacy.
explanation.B: CORRECT — Stop POP; do not restart for 5 days post-UPA; use condoms 5 days post-UPA + 9 days after restarting POP per FSRH.
explanation.C: Incorrect — POP can be restarted after 5 days.
explanation.D: Incorrect — The interaction is clinically significant and affects EC efficacy.
explanation.E: Incorrect — Increasing ulipristal dose is not recommended and does not overcome progestogen receptor competition.

reference: FSRH — Emergency Contraception guideline. https://www.fsrh.org/standards-and-guidance/

question: A 19-year-old woman requests emergency contraception. She weighs 90 kg (BMI 33). She had UPSI 36 hours ago. Per FSRH guidance, which oral emergency contraceptive is preferred for women with higher BMI and why?

options.A: Levonorgestrel — equally effective regardless of weight
options.B: Ulipristal acetate (ellaOne) — evidence suggests levonorgestrel EC has reduced efficacy in women with higher BMI (>70 kg or BMI >26 may reduce efficacy; BMI >30 significantly reduces efficacy); ulipristal maintains better efficacy across the weight range. FSRH guidance: consider ulipristal or copper IUD as preferred options for women >70 kg or BMI >26; copper IUD remains the most effective option at any weight
options.C: Double-dose levonorgestrel for higher BMI
options.D: No oral EC is effective in women with BMI >30 — copper IUD only
options.E: Weight has no effect on emergency contraceptive efficacy

explanation.correct: Per FSRH EC guideline, the effect of BMI on oral EC: Levonorgestrel: pharmacokinetic studies show significantly reduced peak plasma concentrations and AUC in heavier women → reduced efficacy. FSRH advises: women >70 kg or BMI >26 should be offered ulipristal or copper IUD in preference to levonorgestrel. Ulipristal: pharmacokinetics less affected by weight; maintains better efficacy in higher BMI women compared to levonorgestrel. Copper IUD: most effective EC option at ANY weight (>99% effective); not affected by BMI. FSRH guidance (2017, updated 2023): offer ulipristal or Cu-IUD as preferred options for BMI >26 or weight >70 kg; if levonorgestrel is the only option available, it should still be offered (some benefit). Double-dose levonorgestrel is NOT recommended by FSRH (insufficient evidence; increases side effects).
explanation.A: Incorrect — Levonorgestrel efficacy is reduced in women with higher BMI.
explanation.B: CORRECT — Ulipristal preferred over levonorgestrel for BMI >26 or weight >70 kg per FSRH guidance.
explanation.C: Incorrect — FSRH does not recommend double-dose levonorgestrel; evidence is insufficient.
explanation.D: Incorrect — Ulipristal is also effective in higher BMI women; copper IUD is optimal but not the only option.
explanation.E: Incorrect — Weight significantly affects levonorgestrel efficacy.

reference: FSRH — Emergency Contraception guideline. https://www.fsrh.org/standards-and-guidance/

question: A 32-year-old woman had unprotected sexual intercourse on holiday 4 days ago (96 hours). She presents requesting emergency contraception. Per FSRH guidance, what is the most effective option at this time point?

options.A: Levonorgestrel 1.5 mg — effective up to 5 days
options.B: Copper intrauterine device (Cu-IUD) — the most effective method of emergency contraception at any time point (>99% effective); effective up to 5 days (120 hours) after unprotected sexual intercourse; also provides long-term ongoing contraception; can be inserted up to day 19 of a regular 28-day cycle (5 days after earliest expected ovulation); insertion may be uncomfortable — pre-procedure counselling and analgesia recommended
options.C: Ulipristal 30 mg — only oral option at 96 hours
options.D: No emergency contraception is effective at 96 hours
options.E: Combined OCP — Yuzpe method

explanation.correct: At 96 hours (4 days) post-UPSI, the options per FSRH EC guideline: Levonorgestrel 1.5 mg: licensed only up to 72 hours (3 days) — OUTSIDE its licensed window at 96 hours. Ulipristal acetate 30 mg: licensed up to 120 hours (5 days) — is an option at 96 hours as an oral alternative. Copper IUD: most effective option at 96 hours AND up to 5 days (120 hours) post-UPSI; >99% effective; also effective up to day 19 of a regular cycle; suitable for ongoing contraception; no oral option is as effective. At 96 hours: preferred options are Cu-IUD (most effective) or ulipristal (licensed oral option). Cu-IUD is the recommended MOST EFFECTIVE choice at this time point. Post-insertion: advise pregnancy test if no period within 4 weeks.
explanation.A: Incorrect — Levonorgestrel is licensed only up to 72 hours — 96 hours is outside its licensed window.
explanation.B: CORRECT — Cu-IUD most effective EC at any time point up to 5 days. >99% effective per FSRH.
explanation.C: Incorrect — Ulipristal IS an option at 96 hours but is less effective than Cu-IUD.
explanation.D: Incorrect — Both Cu-IUD and ulipristal are effective at 96 hours.
explanation.E: Incorrect — Yuzpe method (COCP for EC) is outdated, less effective, and has more side effects.

reference: FSRH — Emergency Contraception guideline. https://www.fsrh.org/standards-and-guidance/

question: A woman requesting a copper IUD for emergency contraception asks about the procedure. Per FSRH guidance, what key point about IUD insertion timing determines whether it can be used as EC?

options.A: Can only be inserted in the first 3 days after UPSI
options.B: The Cu-IUD can be inserted up to 5 days (120 hours) after the first episode of unprotected sexual intercourse OR up to day 19 of a regular 28-day cycle (which is 5 days after earliest likely ovulation day 14 — allowing for up to 5 days of sperm survival). This ensures the IUD acts before implantation in all cases. If cycle length or last period is uncertain, clinical judgement and pregnancy testing are required
options.C: Can only be inserted before ovulation
options.D: Timing doesn't matter — Cu-IUD is effective at any point in the cycle
options.E: Must be inserted within 24 hours of UPSI for maximum efficacy

explanation.correct: Per FSRH, the Cu-IUD as EC can be inserted: up to 5 days (120 hours) after the first episode of UPSI in a cycle; OR up to day 19 of a regular 28-day cycle (calculated as day 14 [earliest ovulation] + 5 days [maximum sperm survival] = up to day 19). Mechanism: copper is spermicidal and prevents fertilisation; also may prevent implantation by altering the endometrial environment. Efficacy >99% at any time point up to 5 days. Practical considerations: exclude ongoing pregnancy before insertion (urine pregnancy test); exclude STIs (STI screening before or at time of insertion; antibiotic prophylaxis per local protocol); pre-insertion analgesia (NSAID 1 hour before); inform about insertion discomfort; post-insertion: ongoing contraception for as long as desired (Cu-IUD lasts 5-10 years depending on type). Screen for Chlamydia before or at time of insertion.
explanation.A: Incorrect — Cu-IUD can be inserted up to 5 days after UPSI, not just 3 days.
explanation.B: CORRECT — Cu-IUD effective up to 5 days post-UPSI OR day 19 of regular cycle per FSRH.
explanation.C: Incorrect — Cu-IUD can be inserted after ovulation — it prevents implantation as well as fertilisation.
explanation.D: Incorrect — Timing IS important — beyond day 19 of a regular cycle, there is risk of interfering with an established implantation (not an EC use).
explanation.E: Incorrect — No need to insert within 24 hours; up to 5 days or day 19.

reference: FSRH — Emergency Contraception guideline. https://www.fsrh.org/standards-and-guidance/

question: A 25-year-old woman had Cu-IUD inserted for EC 3 weeks ago. She would like to continue it for long-term contraception. She has no periods yet post-insertion. Per FSRH guidance, what should be done?

options.A: Remove the IUD — it should not be kept long-term
options.B: Perform a urine pregnancy test — if negative: the Cu-IUD can be retained for ongoing contraception (lasts 5-10 years); if positive: urgent referral for assessment (ectopic pregnancy must be excluded — IUD in situ increases relative risk of ectopic if pregnancy occurs); discuss ongoing contraception plans
options.C: Advise that IUD never works as long-term contraception
options.D: No action needed — skip the pregnancy test
options.E: Immediately start a hormonal contraceptive alongside the IUD

explanation.correct: Per FSRH EC guideline and FSRH IUD guideline: after Cu-IUD insertion for EC, if no period within 4 weeks: perform urine pregnancy test. If pregnancy test NEGATIVE: Cu-IUD can remain in situ for long-term contraception — depending on the type and age at insertion, modern Cu-IUDs provide contraception for 5-10 years (e.g. T380A: 10 years; Nova-T380: 5 years; Flexi-T300: 5 years). If pregnancy test POSITIVE: must exclude ectopic pregnancy urgently (IUD in situ — risk of ectopic pregnancy is higher than in the general population if pregnancy occurs on IUD); referral to EPAU. Post-EC Cu-IUD retention: an important counselling point at the time of insertion that the IUD can be used as ongoing contraception rather than just one-off EC — this is cost-effective and avoids future unintended pregnancies.
explanation.A: Incorrect — Cu-IUD can and should be offered as ongoing contraception after EC use.
explanation.B: CORRECT — Pregnancy test at 4 weeks; if negative, IUD remains for ongoing contraception per FSRH.
explanation.C: Incorrect — Cu-IUD is highly effective long-term contraception (5-10 years).
explanation.D: Incorrect — A pregnancy test is mandatory at 4 weeks if no period.
explanation.E: Incorrect — No need for additional hormonal contraceptive alongside Cu-IUD — dual contraception is unnecessary and Cu-IUD alone is highly effective.

reference: FSRH — Emergency Contraception and IUD guidelines. https://www.fsrh.org/standards-and-guidance/

question: A 14-year-old boy of Mediterranean origin has routine bloods showing: Hb 105 g/L, MCV 65 fl (low), MCH 20 pg (low), ferritin 45 mcg/L (normal). Per BSH guidelines, what is the most likely diagnosis?

options.A: Iron deficiency anaemia — start ferrous sulphate
options.B: Beta-thalassaemia trait (beta-thalassaemia minor) — microcytic anaemia with NORMAL ferritin (distinguishes from iron deficiency where ferritin would be low); in iron deficiency, ferritin is low; thalassaemia trait shows: low MCV, low MCH, low/normal Hb, normal ferritin, raised HbA2 (>3.5%) on Hb electrophoresis; confirm with haemoglobin electrophoresis and HPLC; genetic counselling and partner screening essential if planning a family
options.C: Sickle cell trait — no treatment needed
options.D: Vitamin B12 deficiency — macrocytic anaemia
options.E: Lead poisoning — blood lead level
