explanation.correct: Distinguishing iron deficiency from thalassaemia trait in microcytic anaemia: Iron deficiency: low MCV, low MCH, LOW ferritin (<15 mcg/L), normal HbA2; responds to iron treatment. Thalassaemia trait (alpha or beta): low MCV, low MCH, NORMAL/high ferritin, raised HbA2 (>3.5%) in beta-thalassaemia trait; does NOT respond to iron (iron stores are normal). Key discriminating test: SERUM FERRITIN (normal = not iron deficiency); confirmation: Hb electrophoresis/HPLC showing raised HbA2 (beta-thalassaemia trait) or normal HbA2 with family history (alpha-thalassaemia trait — diagnosis requires alpha gene deletion analysis). Per BSH guidelines: do NOT give iron supplementation if ferritin is normal (iron overload risk). Clinical significance: thalassaemia trait is generally asymptomatic; risk is in offspring if BOTH parents have trait → risk of thalassaemia major (or sickle-thalassaemia). Genetic counselling mandatory. Haemoglobinopathy questionnaire in antenatal care screens for this.
explanation.A: Incorrect — Ferritin is NORMAL — iron deficiency is not the diagnosis. Do not give iron.
explanation.B: CORRECT — Thalassaemia trait: microcytic anaemia + normal ferritin + Mediterranean origin. Hb electrophoresis for HbA2 per BSH.
explanation.C: Incorrect — Sickle cell trait does not cause microcytic anaemia; Hb and indices are usually normal.
explanation.D: Incorrect — B12/folate deficiency causes MACROCYTIC (large MCV) anaemia, not microcytic.
explanation.E: Incorrect — Lead poisoning in a 14-year-old without specific exposure is unlikely and would have other features.

reference: BSH — Guidelines for the laboratory diagnosis of haemoglobinopathies. https://b-s-h.org.uk/guidelines/

question: Both parents of an unborn child are found to have beta-thalassaemia trait on antenatal screening. Per NICE CG6 and NHS Sickle Cell and Thalassaemia Screening Programme guidance, what is the risk to their child and what should be offered?

options.A: 25% chance of beta-thalassaemia major — offer prenatal diagnosis (chorionic villus sampling at 11-14 weeks or amniocentesis at 15-18 weeks) to determine fetal genotype; if beta-thalassaemia major confirmed, parents can be counselled about the implications and offered the option of termination of pregnancy
options.B: No risk — thalassaemia trait in both parents does not affect the child
options.C: 100% chance of severe thalassaemia — no need to test
options.D: 50% chance of thalassaemia trait only — reassure
options.E: Test the child after birth — no prenatal options available

explanation.correct: Per NICE CG6 and NHS Sickle Cell and Thalassaemia Screening Programme: If both parents have beta-thalassaemia trait: each pregnancy has: 25% chance of beta-thalassaemia major (inherits abnormal beta gene from BOTH parents — requires lifelong blood transfusions, iron chelation, possible SCT); 50% chance of beta-thalassaemia trait (like parents — clinically mild); 25% chance of normal genotype. Parents should be referred for specialist genetic counselling (haematologist/clinical geneticist). Prenatal diagnosis options: Chorionic villus sampling (CVS) at 11-14 weeks — fetal DNA from placental tissue; Amniocentesis at 15-18 weeks — amniotic fluid fetal cells. Both tests carry approximately 0.5-1% risk of miscarriage. Preimplantation genetic testing (PGT): IVF with testing of embryos before implantation — avoids need for termination. If thalassaemia major confirmed: full counselling including natural history, treatments, quality of life — parents make informed choice.
explanation.A: CORRECT — 25% risk of thalassaemia major. CVS or amniocentesis offered for prenatal diagnosis per NICE CG6.
explanation.B: Incorrect — Both parents with trait gives 25% risk of major, 50% trait, 25% normal.
explanation.C: Incorrect — The risk of major is 25%, not 100%.
explanation.D: Incorrect — 50% trait is correct, but there is also 25% major risk — which is the critical concern.
explanation.E: Incorrect — Prenatal diagnosis via CVS or amniocentesis is available and widely offered.

reference: NICE CG6 — Sickle cell disease management. NHS Sickle Cell and Thalassaemia Screening Programme. https://www.gov.uk/government/collections/sickle-cell-and-thalassaemia-screening-programme-evidence-maps

question: A GP practice is reviewing its haemoglobinopathy screening protocol. Per NHS Sickle Cell and Thalassaemia Screening Programme, what mode of inheritance describes thalassaemia?

options.A: X-linked recessive — only males affected
options.B: Autosomal recessive — both parents must be carriers for a child to be affected; thalassaemia affects males and females equally; alpha-thalassaemia: alpha globin gene deletions (chromosome 16); beta-thalassaemia: point mutations in beta globin gene (chromosome 11); heterozygote = trait (carrier); homozygous = major (severe disease)
options.C: Autosomal dominant — one parent is sufficient
options.D: X-linked dominant
options.E: Mitochondrial inheritance

explanation.correct: Thalassaemia inheritance: AUTOSOMAL RECESSIVE. Alpha-thalassaemia: caused by deletions of alpha globin genes on chromosome 16 (2 alpha genes per chromosome, 4 total); 1 deletion = silent carrier; 2 deletions = alpha trait (mild anaemia); 3 deletions = HbH disease (moderate); 4 deletions = Hb Barts (hydrops fetalis — usually fatal in utero). Beta-thalassaemia: caused by point mutations (>200 variants) in beta globin gene on chromosome 11; heterozygous = beta-thalassaemia trait (mild microcytic anaemia, raised HbA2); homozygous or compound heterozygous = beta-thalassaemia major (severe transfusion-dependent haemolytic anaemia). Both alpha and beta thalassaemia are autosomal recessive — affects males and females equally; BOTH parents must be carriers (trait) for a child to be at risk of major disease. Note: the question in the recall document states 'X-linked recessive' which is INCORRECT — this appears to be a deliberate distractor in the AKT exam; the correct answer is autosomal recessive.
explanation.A: Incorrect — Thalassaemia is NOT X-linked. Both males and females can be carriers and affected. This is a common AKT trap.
explanation.B: CORRECT — Thalassaemia is autosomal recessive. Both parents must carry a mutation for major disease in a child.
explanation.C: Incorrect — Autosomal dominant means one abnormal copy causes disease (e.g. familial hypercholesterolaemia) — not the case for thalassaemia.
explanation.D: Incorrect — X-linked dominant is rare and not relevant to thalassaemia.
explanation.E: Incorrect — Mitochondrial inheritance is matrilineal and not relevant to thalassaemia.

reference: NHS Sickle Cell and Thalassaemia Screening Programme. BSH — Haemoglobinopathies. https://b-s-h.org.uk/guidelines/

question: A GP reviews a patient who has developed Clostridium difficile (C. diff) diarrhoea after a course of antibiotics. Per NICE NG190 and PHE, which classes of antibiotic are most commonly associated with C. diff infection?

options.A: Penicillin V and erythromycin
options.B: Broad-spectrum cephalosporins (especially 2nd and 3rd generation), clindamycin, and fluoroquinolones (ciprofloxacin, levofloxacin) have the highest risk of precipitating C. diff infection by disrupting the normal gut microbiome; co-amoxiclav is also associated; narrow-spectrum agents (phenoxymethylpenicillin, amoxicillin) have lower risk
options.C: Trimethoprim and nitrofurantoin
options.D: Metronidazole itself causes C. diff
options.E: All antibiotics carry equal C. diff risk

explanation.correct: Per NICE NG190 (Clostridioides difficile infection) and PHE guidance, certain antibiotics carry higher C. diff risk: HIGH RISK: Broad-spectrum cephalosporins (especially 2nd/3rd generation — cephalexin lower risk than cefuroxime/ceftriaxone); Clindamycin (historically highest risk); Fluoroquinolones (ciprofloxacin, levofloxacin — major driver of recent outbreaks); Co-amoxiclav (co-prescribed frequently). LOWER RISK: Narrow-spectrum penicillins (phenoxymethylpenicillin, amoxicillin alone); Macrolides (azithromycin, clarithromycin); Metronidazole (used to TREAT C. diff); Nitrofurantoin; Trimethoprim. NICE NG190: prescribe shortest course needed; use narrow-spectrum when possible to reduce C. diff risk. PHE: hospitals and care settings have specific antimicrobial stewardship programmes targeting high-risk agents. C. diff testing: if ≥3 loose stools in 24 hours not attributable to another cause in patient who received antibiotics in the past 12 weeks — request stool for C. diff toxin and GDH.
explanation.A: Incorrect — Penicillin V and erythromycin are relatively lower risk.
explanation.B: CORRECT — Broad-spectrum cephalosporins, clindamycin, fluoroquinolones highest C. diff risk per NICE NG190.
explanation.C: Incorrect — Trimethoprim and nitrofurantoin are lower-risk antibiotics for C. diff.
explanation.D: Incorrect — Metronidazole is actually a first-line TREATMENT for mild C. diff — it does not cause it.
explanation.E: Incorrect — C. diff risk varies significantly by antibiotic class.

reference: NICE NG190 — Clostridioides difficile infection. https://www.nice.org.uk/guidance/ng190

question: A 72-year-old care home resident develops profuse watery diarrhoea, crampy abdominal pain and low-grade fever after a course of ciprofloxacin. C. diff toxin is confirmed. Per NICE NG190, what is the first-line treatment for a first episode of non-severe C. diff?

options.A: IV metronidazole
options.B: Oral vancomycin 125 mg four times daily for 10 days — per NICE NG190 (updated 2021), oral vancomycin is now first-line for all C. diff infections (replacing oral metronidazole as first-line); fidaxomicin 200 mg twice daily for 10 days is an alternative (fewer recurrences, reserved when vancomycin not suitable or in high-risk recurrence settings)
options.C: Oral metronidazole 400 mg three times daily
options.D: IV vancomycin — oral vancomycin not absorbed
options.E: No treatment — C. diff resolves with stopping the causative antibiotic alone

explanation.correct: Per NICE NG190 (Clostridioides difficile infection, updated 2021): First-line treatment ALL severity: oral vancomycin 125 mg QDS for 10 days — replaced oral metronidazole as first-line (evidence shows superior cure rates and fewer recurrences). Second-line/alternative: fidaxomicin 200 mg BD for 10 days — approved as alternative; evidence suggests fewer recurrences (important in high-risk recurrence patients); slightly more expensive. Severe/life-threatening C. diff: oral/nasogastric/rectal vancomycin ± IV metronidazole; consider early surgical review; consider bezlotoxumab (antibody against C. diff toxin) in high recurrence-risk patients. Stop the causative antibiotic if possible. Infection control measures: hand hygiene (soap and water — alcohol gel ineffective against C. diff spores), side-room isolation, contact precautions, dedicated commodes. Note: IV vancomycin is NOT effective for C. diff GI infection (insufficient gut luminal concentration from systemic route — must use ORAL vancomycin).
explanation.A: Incorrect — IV metronidazole is used as an ADDITION in severe life-threatening disease — not first-line for non-severe.
explanation.B: CORRECT — Oral vancomycin 125 mg QDS for 10 days is now first-line for all C. diff per NICE NG190 (2021 update).
explanation.C: Incorrect — Oral metronidazole was first-line until NICE NG190 2021 update changed this to oral vancomycin.
explanation.D: Incorrect — IV vancomycin is NOT effective for C. diff (poor luminal concentration).
explanation.E: Incorrect — Stopping causative antibiotic alone is insufficient — antibiotic treatment for C. diff is required.

reference: NICE NG190 — Clostridioides difficile infection. https://www.nice.org.uk/guidance/ng190

question: A care home nurse asks about hand hygiene measures for C. diff infection control. Per PHE guidance, what is the key difference between C. diff and other healthcare-associated infections regarding hand decontamination?

options.A: Alcohol hand gel is the most effective for C. diff
options.B: Alcohol-based hand gel is INEFFECTIVE against C. difficile spores — C. diff forms environmentally resistant spores that are NOT killed by alcohol; soap and water is MANDATORY for hand hygiene in C. diff settings; alcohol gel alone is insufficient; additionally: sporicidal cleaning agents (chlorine-based products) required for environmental decontamination of rooms, surfaces and equipment
options.C: No hand hygiene change is needed — standard precautions sufficient
options.D: Gloves alone are sufficient — no hand washing needed
options.E: Bleach hand gel should be used instead of soap and water

explanation.correct: Clostridium difficile spores: C. diff produces spores that are: resistant to alcohol (alcohol-based handrub fails to inactivate spores); environmentally persistent (can survive on surfaces for months); only destroyed by physical removal (soap and water washing — mechanical removal of spores from hands) or chlorine-based sporicidal agents (e.g. sodium hypochlorite for environmental cleaning). Per PHE C. diff infection prevention and control guidance: Mandatory soap and water hand washing (NOT alcohol gel) when caring for patients with suspected or confirmed C. diff; Contact precautions: gloves and apron; Side room isolation; Sporicidal environmental cleaning; Dedicated equipment (thermometers, blood pressure cuffs). Alcohol hand gel may SUPPLEMENT soap and water hand washing but cannot replace it for C. diff.
explanation.A: Incorrect — Alcohol gel does NOT kill C. diff spores — soap and water is mandatory.
explanation.B: CORRECT — C. diff spores not killed by alcohol; soap and water mandatory; sporicidal cleaning for environment per PHE.
explanation.C: Incorrect — Standard precautions (alcohol gel) are insufficient for C. diff.
explanation.D: Incorrect — Gloves reduce hand contamination but soap and water hand washing is still essential on removal.
explanation.E: Incorrect — There is no bleach hand gel product; soap and water is the recommended hand hygiene measure.

reference: PHE — Clostridium difficile infection: guidance. NICE NG190. https://www.nice.org.uk/guidance/ng190

question: A 22-year-old heterosexual man presents with urethral discharge and dysuria. Per BASHH guidelines, what is the most appropriate first-line investigation for chlamydia diagnosis?

options.A: Urethral swab only
options.B: First-catch urine (FCU) sample — in men, NAAT (nucleic acid amplification test) on first-catch urine is the investigation of choice for chlamydia and gonorrhoea; first-catch urine means the first 20-30 ml of urine passed (not midstream); higher sensitivity than urethral swab for chlamydia in males; additionally, a urethral swab should be taken if gonorrhoea is suspected
options.C: Midstream urine culture
options.D: Blood serology for chlamydia antibodies
options.E: Seminal fluid analysis

explanation.correct: Per BASHH guidelines on chlamydia and gonorrhoea testing in men: NAAT (nucleic acid amplification test) on FIRST-CATCH URINE (FCU) is first-line for detecting Chlamydia trachomatis in heterosexual men. First-catch urine = first 20-30 ml voided (not midstream) — this contains the highest concentration of urethral cells shed into urine. Higher sensitivity than urethral swab for chlamydia in males. For gonorrhoea: urethral swab (for culture and sensitivity to guide antibiotic treatment) AND NAAT on FCU. For MSM: additional rectal swab and pharyngeal swab. Serology has no role in acute chlamydia diagnosis — antibodies develop too slowly and may indicate past infection. NAAT is significantly more sensitive than culture (90%+ sensitivity for NAAT vs 70-80% culture).
explanation.A: Incorrect — Urethral swab alone is less sensitive than FCU NAAT for chlamydia.
explanation.B: CORRECT — First-catch urine NAAT is first-line for chlamydia diagnosis in heterosexual men per BASHH.
explanation.C: Incorrect — Midstream urine culture is for bacterial UTI — not appropriate for chlamydia/gonorrhoea.
explanation.D: Incorrect — Serology (antibodies) takes weeks to develop and cannot diagnose acute infection.
explanation.E: Incorrect — Seminal fluid analysis is for fertility assessment — not STI diagnosis.

reference: BASHH — UK National Guideline for the Management of Chlamydia trachomatis. https://www.bashh.org/guidelines

question: A 25-year-old heterosexual man is confirmed to have chlamydia from a first-catch urine NAAT. He has had two sexual partners in the past 3 months. Per BASHH, what partner notification advice should be given?

options.A: Only notify partners if they develop symptoms
options.B: All sexual partners in the past 6 months (or the most recent partner if the last contact was more than 6 months ago) should be notified, tested and offered treatment. The patient can be given a patient notification letter/card to inform partners themselves (patient referral), or the GUM clinic/practice can contact partners directly with the patient's consent (provider referral). Contact tracing prevents onward transmission and reinfection
options.C: Only notify partners with whom unprotected intercourse occurred
options.D: Partner notification is voluntary and not recommended
options.E: Only the most recent partner needs notification

explanation.correct: Per BASHH chlamydia guidelines and PHE guidance on partner notification (contact tracing): Standard look-back period for chlamydia: all sexual partners in the past 6 months (or most recent partner if last contact >6 months ago). Partner notification methods: Patient referral: patient informs partners themselves; may be given a notification letter/card; provider referral: health advisor contacts partners directly with patient's explicit consent (more effective but resource-intensive); conditional referral: patient agrees to notify within an agreed time, failing which the clinic notifies. Why partner notification matters: chlamydia is usually asymptomatic in both sexes (especially women); untreated → PID, ectopic pregnancy, tubal factor infertility; chlamydia is a notifiable disease in Scotland (not in England and Wales, but PHE monitors through national surveillance). Both the index case and notified partners should be tested AND treated (test-and-treat reduces reinfection).
explanation.A: Incorrect — Chlamydia is often asymptomatic; waiting for symptoms means delayed diagnosis and complications.
explanation.B: CORRECT — All partners in past 6 months; patient or provider referral; test and treat per BASHH.
explanation.C: Incorrect — All partners (regardless of condom use — condoms reduce but don't eliminate chlamydia transmission) in the look-back period.
explanation.D: Incorrect — Partner notification is a core public health function and strongly recommended.
explanation.E: Incorrect — All partners in 6-month window should be notified, not just the most recent.

reference: BASHH — Chlamydia trachomatis guideline. https://www.bashh.org/guidelines

question: A 26-year-old man is diagnosed with rectal chlamydia from a rectal NAAT (MSM). Per BASHH guidelines, how does the treatment differ from urogenital chlamydia?

options.A: Same treatment — doxycycline 100mg BD for 7 days
options.B: Rectal chlamydia treatment: doxycycline 100 mg twice daily for 7 days is first-line (same as urogenital); AVOID azithromycin 1g single dose for rectal chlamydia (significantly lower cure rates for rectal infection compared to urogenital — azithromycin is no longer recommended for rectal chlamydia per updated BASHH guidelines). Test of cure at 3-4 weeks post-treatment is RECOMMENDED for rectal chlamydia (unlike urogenital where TOC is not routine)
options.C: Azithromycin 1g single dose — preferred for rectal infection
options.D: Ciprofloxacin 500mg BD for 7 days
options.E: No treatment needed — rectal chlamydia is self-limiting

explanation.correct: Per updated BASHH chlamydia guidelines, important distinction between urogenital and rectal chlamydia treatment: Urogenital chlamydia: doxycycline 100mg BD for 7 days (preferred) OR azithromycin 1g single dose (alternative). Rectal chlamydia: doxycycline 100mg BD for 7 days ONLY — do NOT use azithromycin; studies show significantly lower cure rates for rectal chlamydia with azithromycin compared to doxycycline (azithromycin cure rate ~60-80% for rectal vs >95% for doxycycline). BASHH now specifically recommends doxycycline over azithromycin for rectal chlamydia. Test of cure: NOT routinely recommended for urogenital chlamydia (after doxycycline); IS recommended for rectal chlamydia at 3-4 weeks post-treatment. Additional considerations: MSM patients should be offered full STI screen (rectal gonorrhoea, pharyngeal gonorrhoea, HIV, syphilis, hepatitis B/C) at the same visit.
explanation.A: Incorrect — This is correct for urogenital chlamydia, but the key point for rectal is that AZITHROMYCIN must be avoided.
explanation.B: CORRECT — Doxycycline 7 days for rectal chlamydia; avoid azithromycin; TOC at 3-4 weeks per BASHH.
explanation.C: Incorrect — Azithromycin has significantly lower cure rates for rectal chlamydia and is NOT recommended.
explanation.D: Incorrect — Ciprofloxacin is not used for chlamydia.
explanation.E: Incorrect — Chlamydia requires treatment; untreated rectal chlamydia can cause proctitis and ongoing transmission.

reference: BASHH — Chlamydia trachomatis UK Guideline. https://www.bashh.org/guidelines

question: A hospital loses the clinical notes for a patient (Mr Jones) who was previously treated there and is now under the GP's care. The GP needs the information to continue treatment. Per the Caldicott Principles and NHS Records Management Code of Practice, what should the GP do?

options.A: Start fresh without any hospital records
options.B: Contact the hospital to request re-creation of the summary records; the hospital has a duty to maintain adequate clinical records and recreate what is available from other sources (electronic records, letters, imaging reports, pharmacy records); if records are irretrievable, document clearly in GP records the known clinical information; ensure the patient's summary care record (SCR) is up to date; request discharge summaries and letters from the hospital electronic systems; document the fact that original notes have been lost
options.C: Refer the patient back to hospital to start fresh
options.D: Ask the patient to recall their own medical history — no other action needed
options.E: No action — the GP can manage without hospital records

explanation.correct: Per the NHS Records Management Code of Practice (2021) and Caldicott Principles: Healthcare organisations have a legal and professional duty to maintain patient records. If records are lost: the hospital must investigate and attempt to recover records from: electronic patient record systems (most hospitals now have EPR — letters, results, imaging remain accessible even if paper notes lost); pharmacy records; clinic letters already sent (accessible from NHS spine/shared care record systems); imaging PACS (picture archiving and communication systems). The GP should: formally request the hospital to provide all available clinical information from electronic sources; document in GP records what is known and that original notes were lost; update the Summary Care Record to ensure medication/allergy information is current; consider requesting key clinical records from other treating specialists; involve the Caldicott Guardian if significant information governance breach. The loss of patient records may require a significant event analysis at the hospital and reporting to CQC if there is a systematic pattern.
explanation.A: Incorrect — Starting fresh without attempting record recovery could compromise patient safety.
explanation.B: CORRECT — Contact hospital to recreate records from electronic sources; document known information; update SCR per NHS Records Management Code.
explanation.C: Incorrect — Referring back without attempting record recovery wastes resources and delays care.
explanation.D: Incorrect — Patient recall is unreliable; systematic record recovery is required.
explanation.E: Incorrect — Lost records represent a patient safety risk; action is required.

reference: NHS Records Management Code of Practice 2021. Caldicott Principles. https://www.nhsx.nhs.uk/information-governance/guidance/records-management-code/

question: A counsellor working for the GP practice submits a Freedom of Information Act request asking for information about the number of patient complaints received by the practice in the past year. Per the Freedom of Information Act 2000 and GMC confidentiality guidance, what should the practice do?

options.A: Refuse all FOI requests — health data is always exempt
options.B: Respond to the FOI request within 20 working days: the FOI Act 2000 allows any person to request information held by public authorities (including GP practices as NHS contractors). Practice must respond within 20 working days. Information about NUMBER of complaints is likely disclosable as aggregate data does not identify individual patients. However, details identifying patients are exempt under the Data Protection Act 2018/UK GDPR (personal data exemption). Aggregate statistical data (e.g. number of complaints per year) is generally disclosable
options.C: Share all complaint details including patient names
options.D: Only respond if the counsellor is a registered healthcare professional
options.E: FOI requests can be ignored if inconvenient

explanation.correct: Freedom of Information Act 2000 (FOIA): applies to public authorities including NHS bodies and GP practices as NHS contractors. Any person (the counsellor's professional status is irrelevant) can request information. Requirements: respond within 20 working days; can refuse only if information falls within an exemption. Key exemptions relevant here: Personal data (s.40 FOIA / UK GDPR): information identifying individuals is exempt — detailed complaint records identifying patients cannot be disclosed; Qualified exemptions (e.g. commercial interest): may apply if sensitive business information. Aggregate statistics (number of complaints without patient identification): likely disclosable. Practice should: provide aggregate data (number of complaints received); withhold any patient-identifying information under data protection exemption; provide a refusal notice explaining any exemptions applied; signpost the requester to the Information Commissioner's Office (ICO) if unhappy with response. Note: GP practices are also subject to Subject Access Requests (SARs) under UK GDPR — different from FOI.
explanation.A: Incorrect — Not all health-related information is exempt; aggregate statistics are generally disclosable.
explanation.B: CORRECT — Respond within 20 working days; aggregate complaint numbers likely disclosable; patient-identifying details exempt under UK GDPR per FOIA 2000.
explanation.C: Incorrect — Patient names and identifying complaint details are exempt under UK GDPR.
explanation.D: Incorrect — FOI applies to anyone — professional status of requester is irrelevant.
explanation.E: Incorrect — Failure to respond to FOIA within 20 working days is a breach of the Act and reportable to ICO.

reference: Freedom of Information Act 2000. ICO — Guide to FOI. https://ico.org.uk/for-organisations/guide-to-freedom-of-information/

question: An 11-year-old boy has been diagnosed with Osgood-Schlatter disease. His parents ask what to expect. Per NICE CKS, what is the prognosis?

options.A: Requires surgery in most cases
options.B: Osgood-Schlatter disease is a self-limiting traction apophysitis that resolves spontaneously when skeletal maturity is reached (growth plate fuses) — typically by age 16-18 years in males; in the majority of cases (90%+) there are no long-term sequelae; a small proportion have persistent pain from a bony ossicle at the tibial tuberosity; activity modification, ice, analgesia and physiotherapy during symptomatic period; reassure parents
options.C: Leads to permanent disability in adolescents
options.D: Requires corticosteroid injection to prevent progression
options.E: Causes long-term degenerative knee disease

explanation.correct: Osgood-Schlatter disease (OSD): traction apophysitis of the tibial tuberosity growth plate, occurring during adolescent growth spurts (ages 10-15 in boys, 8-13 in girls). The quadriceps pull via the patellar tendon causes microavulsions at the immature tibial tuberosity apophysis. Prognosis per NICE CKS: self-limiting in >90% of cases — resolves when the tibial apophysis fuses at skeletal maturity (approximately 16-18 years males, 14-16 years females). Residual symptoms in adulthood: minority (5-10%) have persistent tenderness over the tibial tuberosity due to a persistent ossicle (small bone fragment at the apophysis); these rarely require surgery (excision of ossicle). Long-term OA or disability is NOT expected. Management during symptomatic period: relative rest, ice, NSAIDs/paracetamol, quadriceps stretching, physiotherapy; sport modification (reduce running/jumping during flares); rarely requires cast immobilisation.
explanation.A: Incorrect — Surgery is rarely needed (<5%) and only for persistent ossicle in adults — not the typical outcome.
explanation.B: CORRECT — OSD is self-limiting, resolves at skeletal maturity. Reassure parents per NICE CKS.
explanation.C: Incorrect — OSD does not lead to permanent disability in the vast majority.
explanation.D: Incorrect — Corticosteroid injection is NOT used in OSD and may weaken the patellar tendon.
explanation.E: Incorrect — OSD does not cause long-term degenerative knee disease in most patients.

reference: NICE CKS — Osgood-Schlatter disease. https://cks.nice.org.uk/topics/osgood-schlatter-disease/

question: A 48-year-old man presents with episodic severe hypertension, pounding headache, profuse sweating, and palpitations. These episodes last 15-20 minutes. His BP during an episode is 220/130 mmHg. Per NICE CKS, what is the most likely diagnosis and appropriate investigation?

options.A: Essential hypertension — start amlodipine
options.B: Phaeochromocytoma — catecholamine-secreting tumour of the adrenal medulla; classic triad: episodic headache, sweating, palpitations; paroxysmal hypertension; investigation: 24-hour urinary catecholamines and metanephrines (or plasma free metanephrines — more sensitive); localisation with CT/MRI adrenals; treat with alpha blockade (phenoxybenzamine) FIRST then beta-blocker; surgical excision
options.C: Migraine — sumatriptan
options.D: Panic disorder — SSRI
options.E: Carcinoid syndrome — urinary 5-HIAA

explanation.correct: Phaeochromocytoma (pheo): catecholamine-secreting neuroendocrine tumour, most often in adrenal medulla (90%), rarely extra-adrenal (paraganglioma). The classic triad of paroxysmal headache, diaphoresis and palpitations with episodic hypertension is highly specific (>90% PPV). Mnemonic: 5 P's — Pressure (hypertension), Perspiration, Palpitations, Pain (headache), Pallor (or flushing). Episodes may be triggered by: exercise, positional change, anaesthesia, certain medications (beta-blockers, metoclopramide, tricyclics). Investigation per NICE CKS: First-line biochemistry: 24-hour urinary metanephrines (metanephrine and normetanephrine — most sensitive) OR plasma free metanephrines. Imaging: CT/MRI of abdomen/pelvis for adrenal localisation. MIBG scan if CT/MRI inconclusive. Management: pre-operatively: alpha-1 blocker (phenoxybenzamine) 2-3 weeks before surgery (CRITICAL: never give beta-blocker first — causes unopposed alpha stimulation and hypertensive crisis); then add beta-blocker; surgical laparoscopic adrenalectomy.
explanation.A: Incorrect — Essential hypertension doesn't cause episodic paroxysmal symptoms with this classic triad.
explanation.B: CORRECT — Phaeochromocytoma: episodic headache/sweating/palpitations/BP. 24-hour urinary metanephrines. Alpha blockade first per NICE CKS.
explanation.C: Incorrect — Migraine causes unilateral headache without episodic extreme BP elevations.
explanation.D: Incorrect — Panic disorder can mimic but doesn't cause BP 220/130 mmHg consistently.
explanation.E: Incorrect — Carcinoid causes flushing, diarrhoea and wheeze but episodic paroxysmal BP elevation is more specific for pheo.

reference: NICE CKS — Phaeochromocytoma. https://cks.nice.org.uk/topics/phaeochromocytoma/

question: A 70-year-old man has a well-demarcated red velvety plaque on his left lower leg that has been present and slowly enlarging for 2 years. It is not raised, does not bleed and doesn't change shape. Per NICE NG12 and NICE CKS, what is the most likely diagnosis?

options.A: Psoriasis — topical betamethasone
options.B: Bowen's disease (squamous cell carcinoma in situ) — a form of intraepidermal SCC; presents as a slowly enlarging, well-demarcated, erythematous, slightly scaly or crusted plaque; stable for months/years; risk factors: sun exposure, HPV, immunosuppression, previous radiation; management: urgent 2WW dermatology referral if suspected (differential includes SCC, BCC, melanoma — all require biopsy); treatment: topical 5-fluorouracil, imiquimod, photodynamic therapy, cryotherapy or excision
options.C: Discoid eczema — topical hydrocortisone
options.D: Lichen planus — topical corticosteroid
options.E: Pigmented basal cell carcinoma — urgent dermatology

explanation.correct: Bowen's disease (SCC in situ): intraepidermal squamous cell carcinoma that has not yet invaded the dermis. Per NICE NG12 and NICE CKS: clinical features — well-demarcated, slowly enlarging erythematous plaque, often scaly or warty surface, stable for long periods, may be solitary or multiple; common sites: sun-exposed areas (lower limbs, dorsum of hands, face) and covered areas if HPV-related. If left untreated: approximately 3-5% progress to invasive SCC. Urgenr 2WW referral per NICE NG12 for any non-healing/persistent red plaque in elderly patient to exclude SCC, BCC, melanoma. Biopsy confirms diagnosis. Treatment: depends on size/location — topical 5-fluorouracil (5-FU) cream, imiquimod cream, photodynamic therapy (PDT), cryotherapy, or surgical excision. Bowen's should not be treated as eczema (steroid alone will worsen by potentially masking and delaying diagnosis).
explanation.A: Incorrect — Psoriasis causes well-demarcated silver-scaled plaques typically on extensor surfaces, scalp, nails; responds to topical steroids.
explanation.B: CORRECT — Bowen's disease (SCC in situ): stable red plaque, elderly, lower limb. 2WW dermatology per NICE NG12.
explanation.C: Incorrect — Discoid eczema has circular weeping lesions that fluctuate and respond to topical steroids.
explanation.D: Incorrect — Lichen planus has violaceous flat-topped polygonal papules with Wickham striae — not stable red plaque.
explanation.E: Incorrect — Pigmented BCC has rolled pearly edges and pigmentation — not a flat red stable plaque.

reference: NICE NG12 — Suspected cancer. NICE CKS — Bowen's disease. https://cks.nice.org.uk/topics/bowens-disease/

question: A GP practice is seeing families from a South Asian community for haemoglobinopathy screening. A parent asks about the mode of inheritance of thalassaemia. Per NHS Sickle Cell and Thalassaemia Screening Programme, what is the correct answer?

options.A: X-linked recessive — only affects males
options.B: Autosomal recessive — both males and females can be affected; both parents must be carriers (trait) for a child to have a 25% risk of the full condition (major); thalassaemia affects people of all genders equally; alpha-thalassaemia gene on chromosome 16, beta-thalassaemia gene on chromosome 11
options.C: Autosomal dominant — one parent is sufficient to cause disease
options.D: Mitochondrial — passed from mother only
options.E: X-linked dominant

explanation.correct: This is a direct recall point from the AKT paper — the question states 'mode of transmission of thalassaemia... X-linked recessive' — this appears to be WRONG in the recall (likely a distractor in the actual exam). The correct answer is AUTOSOMAL RECESSIVE, not X-linked recessive. Thalassaemia: alpha-thalassaemia (chromosome 16 deletions) and beta-thalassaemia (chromosome 11 mutations) — both autosomal recessive; both males and females can carry the trait or be affected by major disease equally. X-linked recessive disorders (e.g. haemophilia A/B, G6PD deficiency, Duchenne muscular dystrophy) predominantly affect males because they have only one X chromosome (XY) — females with one affected X chromosome are usually carriers. Thalassaemia does NOT follow this pattern. AKT exam trap: the recall document lists 'X-linked recessive' as the answer — this is likely the WRONG answer to avoid, meaning the correct answer is autosomal recessive.
explanation.A: Incorrect — X-linked recessive is incorrect for thalassaemia — this is a common exam trap. Both males and females are equally affected.
explanation.B: CORRECT — Thalassaemia is AUTOSOMAL RECESSIVE. Affects males and females equally. Not X-linked per NHS Screening Programme.
explanation.C: Incorrect — Autosomal dominant means one copy causes disease; thalassaemia requires two copies.
explanation.D: Incorrect — Mitochondrial inheritance is purely maternal; thalassaemia is nuclear chromosomal.
explanation.E: Incorrect — X-linked dominant is rare and not relevant to thalassaemia.

reference: NHS Sickle Cell and Thalassaemia Screening Programme. BSH Guidelines. https://b-s-h.org.uk/guidelines/

question: A 42-year-old man has a total cholesterol of 9.2 mmol/L and LDL of 6.8 mmol/L. He has xanthomata on his Achilles tendons and a father who died of MI at 48. Per NICE CG71, what is the most likely diagnosis and what mode of inheritance does it follow?

options.A: Polygenic hypercholesterolaemia — no genetic testing needed
options.B: Familial hypercholesterolaemia (FH) — autosomal dominant condition most commonly caused by mutations in LDLR (LDL receptor), APOB, or PCSK9 genes; very high LDL from birth; heterozygous FH (1 in 250 population); tendon xanthomata are PATHOGNOMONIC; premature CVD; NICE CG71: cascade screening of first-degree relatives; statin therapy from childhood; PCSK9 inhibitors (evolocumab, alirocumab) for statin-insufficient patients
options.C: Secondary hypercholesterolaemia — check TSH
options.D: Type IIa hyperlipoproteinaemia — no genetic basis
options.E: Autosomal recessive hypercholesterolaemia — very rare

explanation.correct: Familial hypercholesterolaemia (FH): most common serious genetic lipid disorder. Inheritance: AUTOSOMAL DOMINANT (one abnormal gene copy causes disease); heterozygous FH: 1 in 250 (most common); homozygous FH: 1 in 250,000 (severe — total cholesterol >13 mmol/L, CVD in childhood). Clinical features: markedly elevated total cholesterol and LDL from birth; tendon xanthomata (Achilles, extensor tendons of hands — PATHOGNOMONIC for FH); xanthelasma (non-specific); corneal arcus before age 45 (significant); premature atherosclerotic CVD (men <55 years, women <60 years). Diagnosis per NICE CG71: Simon Broome Register criteria or Dutch Lipid Score. Management: high-intensity statin (atorvastatin 80mg) — lifelong; ezetimibe add-on; PCSK9 inhibitors (evolocumab, alirocumab — NICE TA394) for those with established CVD or at high risk who remain above LDL targets on maximal therapy; cascade genetic/clinical screening of first-degree relatives.
explanation.A: Incorrect — Polygenic hypercholesterolaemia causes milder elevation; tendon xanthomata and premature family CVD point to FH.
explanation.B: CORRECT — FH: autosomal dominant. Tendon xanthomata + very high LDL + family history premature CVD. Cascade screening per NICE CG71.
explanation.C: Incorrect — Secondary causes (hypothyroidism, nephrotic syndrome) should be excluded, but tendon xanthomata are specifically associated with FH.
explanation.D: Incorrect — FH is a specific genetic disorder — it does have a genetic basis.
explanation.E: Incorrect — Autosomal recessive FH (due to LDLRAP1 mutations) is extremely rare; heterozygous FH (autosomal dominant) is the common form.

reference: NICE CG71 — Familial hypercholesterolaemia. https://www.nice.org.uk/guidance/cg71

question: A 62-year-old man wakes up with sudden complete hearing loss in his right ear. He has no pain, no vertigo, no preceding illness. Audiometry confirms profound right-sided sensorineural hearing loss with normal left. Per NICE CKS and NICE NG98, what is the diagnosis and urgent management?

options.A: Earwax — syringe and review
options.B: Sudden sensorineural hearing loss (SSHL) — acute onset unilateral SNHL (>30 dB loss across 3 consecutive frequencies within 72 hours); urgent SAME-DAY ENT referral (NICE NG98 and NICE CKS); treatment: high-dose oral corticosteroids (prednisolone 1 mg/kg up to 60 mg daily for 7-14 days) started as early as possible — maximise recovery; audiological reassessment at 1 month; investigate for underlying cause (acoustic neuroma — MRI IAMs)
options.C: Reassure — sudden hearing loss always resolves spontaneously
options.D: Prescribe decongestants — likely Eustachian tube dysfunction
options.E: Refer routinely to ENT in 6 weeks

explanation.correct: Sudden sensorineural hearing loss (SSHL): defined as ≥30 dB loss across 3 consecutive audiometric frequencies within 72 hours in one ear. True SSHL is a medical emergency. Incidence: 5-20 per 100,000 per year. Causes: idiopathic (>90%); viral (measles, mumps, VZV, CMV); vascular (labyrinthine artery occlusion); autoimmune; Meniere's; acoustic neuroma. Per NICE NG98 and NICE CKS: SAME-DAY ENT referral (emergency); high-dose oral corticosteroids started ASAP (prednisolone 1 mg/kg/day for 7-14 days); intratympanic steroids may be offered as salvage therapy if oral steroids fail. Without treatment: approximately 65% spontaneous partial recovery; with early steroid treatment: improved recovery rates. Full recovery uncommon in profound loss. MRI IAMs to exclude acoustic neuroma (vestibular schwannoma). Early treatment is critical — prognosis worsens with delay.
explanation.A: Incorrect — Earwax causes conductive, not sensorineural, hearing loss — audiometry confirms SNHL.
explanation.B: CORRECT — SSHL: same-day ENT referral + oral prednisolone immediately per NICE NG98/CKS.
explanation.C: Incorrect — Spontaneous partial recovery occurs in ~65% but treatment improves outcomes — urgent referral mandatory.
explanation.D: Incorrect — Eustachian tube dysfunction causes conductive loss; this is audiometry-confirmed SNHL.
explanation.E: Incorrect — Routine 6-week referral is unacceptably delayed for SSHL — prognosis worsens significantly with delay.

reference: NICE NG98 — Hearing loss in adults. NICE CKS — Sudden sensorineural hearing loss. https://www.nice.org.uk/guidance/ng98

question: A GP performs tuning fork tests on a patient with hearing loss in the left ear. Rinne test: left ear — bone conduction louder than air conduction (BC>AC). Weber test lateralises to the left. What is the diagnosis?

options.A: Left sensorineural hearing loss
options.B: Left conductive hearing loss — negative Rinne (BC>AC) on the LEFT ear indicates conductive hearing loss on that side; Weber lateralises to the AFFECTED ear (left) in conductive loss because bone-conducted sound is better perceived in the ear with impaired air conduction pathway; causes: wax impaction, otitis media with effusion, tympanic membrane perforation, otosclerosis
options.C: Right sensorineural hearing loss
options.D: Bilateral sensorineural hearing loss
options.E: Normal hearing

explanation.correct: Tuning fork test interpretation (512 Hz): Rinne test: Air conduction (AC) compared to Bone conduction (BC) at same ear. Normal: AC>BC (positive Rinne). Conductive loss: BC>AC (negative Rinne) — air conduction is reduced but bone bypasses the conductive pathway. Sensorineural loss: AC>BC (positive Rinne but reduced hearing overall). Weber test: Sound placed on vertex — should not lateralise in normal hearing. Lateralises to AFFECTED ear in conductive loss (bone vibrations are perceived better in the ear where AC is blocked — the masking effect of ambient noise is removed). Lateralises to BETTER ear in sensorineural loss (the cochlea/nerve with less damage perceives sound better). This patient: Negative Rinne LEFT (BC>AC) = left conductive loss; Weber to LEFT = conductive loss left side. Confirmed: LEFT CONDUCTIVE HEARING LOSS. Causes: otosclerosis (common cause in young adults — progressive conductive loss, negative Rinne, no evidence of infection), otitis media with effusion, wax, perforated TM, ossicular chain disruption.
explanation.A: Incorrect — Left SNHL would show: positive Rinne (AC>BC) left and Weber lateralising to RIGHT (better ear).
explanation.B: CORRECT — Negative Rinne left (BC>AC) + Weber to left = LEFT CONDUCTIVE HEARING LOSS.
explanation.C: Incorrect — Right SNHL would show positive Rinne both ears, Weber lateralising RIGHT.
explanation.D: Incorrect — Bilateral SNHL shows positive Rinne bilaterally, Weber not lateralising.
explanation.E: Incorrect — BC>AC (negative Rinne) is always abnormal on the side tested.

reference: NICE NG98 — Hearing loss in adults. https://www.nice.org.uk/guidance/ng98

question: A 39-year-old woman presents with hot flushes, night sweats, irregular periods and mood changes. FSH is measured twice and is >40 IU/L on both occasions. She has no uterus (previous hysterectomy). Per NICE NG23, what is the appropriate HRT?

options.A: Combined HRT (oestrogen + progestogen) — required for all women
options.B: Oestrogen-only HRT — women who have had a hysterectomy do NOT have a uterus and therefore do NOT need progestogen (progestogen is only required to protect the endometrium from oestrogen-induced hyperplasia/cancer); oestrogen-only HRT is therefore appropriate and preferred (lower risk of breast cancer and VTE than combined HRT)
options.C: No HRT — FSH alone confirms premature ovarian insufficiency requiring observation only
options.D: Progesterone-only HRT — most appropriate
options.E: SSRI only — not appropriate for FSH >40 in a 39-year-old

explanation.correct: Per NICE NG23 (Menopause), HRT selection depends on uterine status: Women WITH intact uterus: COMBINED HRT (oestrogen + progestogen) required — progestogen protects endometrium from unopposed oestrogen stimulation (which would cause endometrial hyperplasia and endometrial carcinoma). Women WITHOUT uterus (hysterectomy): OESTROGEN-ONLY HRT — no progestogen needed; lower risk of breast cancer and VTE compared to combined HRT. This 39-year-old: FSH >40 IU/L on two occasions = premature ovarian insufficiency (POI) diagnosis (before age 40); previous hysterectomy = no uterus → oestrogen-only HRT. Additional point: for POI at age 39, HRT should be continued until average age of menopause (51) at minimum to prevent long-term complications (cardiovascular, osteoporosis, cognitive effects of oestrogen deficiency). NICE NG23 strongly recommends HRT for POI.
explanation.A: Incorrect — Combined (oestrogen + progestogen) HRT is only needed when the uterus is intact.
explanation.B: CORRECT — Post-hysterectomy + POI (FSH >40): oestrogen-only HRT per NICE NG23.
explanation.C: Incorrect — POI at 39 with severe symptoms requires HRT — NICE NG23 strongly recommends treatment.
explanation.D: Incorrect — Progesterone-only HRT does not address oestrogen deficiency symptoms or long-term risks of POI.
explanation.E: Incorrect — SSRIs may help vasomotor symptoms but do not address the oestrogen deficiency; HRT is appropriate for POI.

reference: NICE NG23 — Menopause. https://www.nice.org.uk/guidance/ng23

question: A 14-year-old boy who plays football 5 times a week presents with anterior knee pain specifically at the tibial tuberosity. He has a tender bony lump just below his right kneecap. The pain started 3 months ago and is worse after activity. Per NICE CKS, what is the diagnosis and management?

options.A: Patellofemoral pain syndrome — quadriceps strengthening
options.B: Osgood-Schlatter disease — traction apophysitis of the tibial tuberosity occurring during adolescent growth spurts; the patellar tendon pulls on the developing tibial apophysis causing inflammation; management is conservative: relative rest from pain-provoking activities, ice, analgesia (paracetamol/ibuprofen), quadriceps and hamstring stretching; condition is self-limiting and resolves at skeletal maturity (~16-18 years)
options.C: Anterior cruciate ligament tear — MRI knee
options.D: Septic arthritis — joint aspiration
options.E: Patella fracture — X-ray and orthopaedic referral

explanation.correct: Osgood-Schlatter disease: the most common cause of knee pain in active adolescents (peak 10-15 years, more common in boys). During rapid growth spurts the patellar tendon repeatedly pulls on the immature tibial tuberosity apophysis causing microavulsion and inflammation. Key features: localised tenderness and swelling at the tibial tuberosity (not at the joint line); worsened by running, jumping, kneeling; relieved by rest. X-ray may show fragmentation of tibial tuberosity (not always needed for diagnosis). Per NICE CKS: conservative management — relative rest (reduce but don't stop activity), ice, NSAIDs/paracetamol, quadriceps and hamstring stretching programme. The condition is benign and self-limiting — most resolve completely when the growth plate fuses (~age 16-18). A small residual bony prominence may persist but is painless. Surgical intervention needed in <1%.
explanation.A: Incorrect — Patellofemoral pain causes peripatellar aching, not isolated tibial tuberosity tenderness with bony prominence.
explanation.B: CORRECT — Osgood-Schlatter: tibial tuberosity tenderness in active adolescent. Conservative + self-limiting per NICE CKS.
explanation.C: Incorrect — ACL tear presents with acute injury, swelling and positive Lachman/anterior drawer test.
explanation.D: Incorrect — Septic arthritis causes fever, hot joint effusion and severely limited movement.
explanation.E: Incorrect — Patella fracture is traumatic and acute; not a gradual onset activity-related condition.

reference: NICE CKS — Osgood-Schlatter disease. https://cks.nice.org.uk/topics/osgood-schlatter-disease/

question: A parent of a 13-year-old with Osgood-Schlatter disease asks whether her son should stop all sport entirely. Per NICE CKS, what advice should be given?

options.A: Complete sports ban until age 18
options.B: Complete sports restriction is not required or recommended; advise relative rest — continue modified activity as pain allows, reducing high-impact activities (jumping, sprinting) during flares; sport can resume when pain is tolerable; the condition resolves with skeletal maturity and most athletes return to full activity without long-term sequelae; stretching exercises and ice after activity help manage symptoms
options.C: Immediate surgical referral
options.D: Cast immobilisation for 6 weeks
options.E: Steroid injection into the tibial tuberosity

explanation.correct: Per NICE CKS, complete activity restriction is not required for Osgood-Schlatter disease and is generally counterproductive. Recommended approach: relative rest — modify activity rather than stop completely; reduce high-impact loading during flares; ice after sport; NSAIDs/paracetamol for pain; quadriceps and hamstring flexibility programme; return to normal activity levels when pain is tolerable. The condition is self-limiting and the vast majority of children continue to participate in sport, albeit with modifications during symptomatic periods. Prognosis: excellent — resolves when growth plate fuses at skeletal maturity. Only a small residual painless prominence may remain. Steroid injections are specifically avoided (risk of subcutaneous atrophy and patellar tendon weakening). Surgical intervention (excision of ossicle) reserved for rare persistent adult cases.
explanation.A: Incorrect — Complete sports ban is unnecessary and counterproductive.
explanation.B: CORRECT — Relative rest + modified activity + stretching. Complete restriction not needed per NICE CKS.
explanation.C: Incorrect — Surgical referral is rarely needed and not for first presentation.
explanation.D: Incorrect — Immobilisation is not recommended and delays recovery.
explanation.E: Incorrect — Steroid injection at the tibial tuberosity is specifically avoided due to risks of tendon weakening and skin atrophy.

reference: NICE CKS — Osgood-Schlatter disease. https://cks.nice.org.uk/topics/osgood-schlatter-disease/

question: A 25-year-old man with previous Osgood-Schlatter disease as a teenager still has a painful prominent bony lump at his tibial tuberosity. He cannot kneel without severe pain. X-ray shows a separate ossicle at the tuberosity. Per NICE CKS, what treatment is appropriate?

options.A: Reassure — always resolves with age
options.B: Surgical excision of the ossicle — in adults with persistent symptomatic ossicle causing kneeling pain or functional limitation after conservative measures have failed, surgical excision can be considered; this is performed via a small incision and has good outcomes; conservative measures should be tried first: physiotherapy, modification of activities, NSAIDs, knee padding for kneeling
options.C: Steroid injection immediately
options.D: Amputation of the lower limb
options.E: Joint replacement

explanation.correct: In a small minority of patients with Osgood-Schlatter disease, an unfused ossicle persists into adulthood causing ongoing pain, particularly with kneeling activities. The painful ossicle sits within the patellar tendon at the tibial tuberosity. Management in adults: (1) Conservative first: activity modification, knee padding for kneeling, NSAIDs, physiotherapy to strengthen surrounding musculature; (2) If conservative measures fail and symptoms significantly impair function: surgical excision of the ossicle — performed via a small anterior approach, with removal of the bony fragment and repair of the patellar tendon insertion; outcomes are generally excellent; return to full activity within 3-6 months. This is not common — most Osgood-Schlatter fully resolves in adolescence. However, the adult persistent form is a recognised clinical entity that benefits from surgical intervention when conservative management has failed.
explanation.A: Incorrect — While most resolve in adolescence, adult persistent ossicles may require surgical treatment.
explanation.B: CORRECT — Adult persistent Osgood-Schlatter with ossicle: surgery after failed conservative per NICE CKS.
explanation.C: Incorrect — Steroid injection at tibial tuberosity is avoided due to tendon weakening risk.
explanation.D: Incorrect — Amputation is not appropriate.
explanation.E: Incorrect — Joint replacement is for degenerative joint disease, not ossicle.

reference: NICE CKS — Osgood-Schlatter disease. https://cks.nice.org.uk/topics/osgood-schlatter-disease/

question: A 55-year-old man works night shifts and rarely goes outdoors. He presents with diffuse bone pain, proximal muscle weakness, waddling gait and difficulty climbing stairs. Blood tests show calcium 2.05 mmol/L (low-normal), phosphate 0.62 mmol/L (low) and ALP 390 U/L (raised). Per NICE CKS, what is the next investigation?

options.A: Bone marrow biopsy
options.B: Serum 25-hydroxyvitamin D (25(OH)D) — the pattern of low-normal calcium, low phosphate and raised ALP with diffuse bone pain and proximal myopathy in a patient with limited sun exposure is classic osteomalacia (adult vitamin D deficiency); 25(OH)D is the correct confirmatory test; treatment: loading dose vitamin D3 (colecalciferol 300,000 IU in divided doses) followed by maintenance supplementation; exclude underlying malabsorption
options.C: MRI spine
options.D: Bone density DEXA scan
options.E: Serum PTH only

explanation.correct: Osteomalacia: inadequate mineralisation of osteoid matrix in adults, caused by vitamin D deficiency. Risk factors: limited sun exposure (night workers, housebound, covered clothing), malabsorption (coeliac, Crohn's, bariatric surgery), chronic liver disease, CKD, certain anticonvulsants. Biochemical pattern: low or low-normal calcium, low phosphate (renal phosphate wasting), markedly raised ALP (osteoblastic activity), raised PTH (secondary hyperparathyroidism), low 25(OH)D. Per NICE CKS, the confirmatory test is serum 25-hydroxyvitamin D: deficiency <25 nmol/L, insufficiency 25-50 nmol/L. X-ray may show Looser zones (pseudofractures). Treatment: loading dose colecalciferol 300,000 IU total (split over weeks) then maintenance; investigate and treat underlying cause; calcium supplementation if dietary intake inadequate.
explanation.A: Incorrect — Bone marrow biopsy is for haematological malignancy, not osteomalacia.
explanation.B: CORRECT — Serum 25(OH)D confirms vitamin D deficiency causing osteomalacia per NICE CKS.
explanation.C: Incorrect — MRI spine is for neurological symptoms or malignancy, not the first investigation for this pattern.
explanation.D: Incorrect — DEXA measures bone mineral density (osteoporosis), not osteomalacia specifically.
explanation.E: Incorrect — PTH is raised secondarily but doesn't confirm the diagnosis; 25(OH)D is the specific test.

reference: NICE CKS — Vitamin D deficiency in adults. https://cks.nice.org.uk/topics/vitamin-d-deficiency-in-adults/

question: A 70-year-old housebound woman is found to have vitamin D deficiency (25(OH)D 14 nmol/L). She has no symptoms. Per NICE CKS, what treatment is recommended?

options.A: Dietary advice only — eat more oily fish
options.B: Loading dose colecalciferol (vitamin D3) 300,000 IU given in divided doses over 6-10 weeks, followed by maintenance supplementation (800-1000 IU daily); calcium supplementation if dietary intake inadequate (<700mg/day); review 25(OH)D level after 3 months of loading to confirm adequacy
options.C: Active vitamin D (alfacalcidol) 1mcg daily — first choice for all deficiency
options.D: No treatment — asymptomatic deficiency requires no action
options.E: IV vitamin D infusion weekly

explanation.correct: Per NICE CKS (Vitamin D deficiency in adults), treatment of vitamin D deficiency: Loading phase (to rapidly correct deficiency): colecalciferol (vitamin D3) — total loading dose 300,000 IU given as divided doses (e.g., 50,000 IU weekly for 6 weeks, or 25,000 IU fortnightly — varies by formulation). Maintenance phase: colecalciferol 800-2000 IU daily (NICE recommends at least 800 IU daily for bone health in at-risk groups). Calcium: supplement if dietary intake <700mg/day (1000mg elemental calcium daily). Alfacalcidol/calcitriol (active vitamin D): reserved for patients with impaired hydroxylation (CKD, hypoparathyroidism) — not first-line for nutritional deficiency. Follow-up: recheck 25(OH)D 3 months after loading to confirm treatment adequacy; aim for >50 nmol/L (some guidelines aim >75 nmol/L).
explanation.A: Incorrect — Dietary advice alone is insufficient for established deficiency (25(OH)D 14 nmol/L).
explanation.B: CORRECT — Loading colecalciferol 300,000 IU then maintenance per NICE CKS.
explanation.C: Incorrect — Alfacalcidol is for CKD/hypoparathyroidism, not nutritional deficiency.
explanation.D: Incorrect — Asymptomatic deficiency still causes bone loss, muscle weakness and fracture risk — treatment required.
explanation.E: Incorrect — IV vitamin D is not standard treatment for nutritional deficiency.

reference: NICE CKS — Vitamin D deficiency in adults. https://cks.nice.org.uk/topics/vitamin-d-deficiency-in-adults/

question: A patient with confirmed osteomalacia has a 25(OH)D of 8 nmol/L. Despite loading dose vitamin D, calcium remains low at 1.95 mmol/L after 3 months. What should be investigated?

options.A: Repeat loading dose and recheck in another 3 months
options.B: Investigate for malabsorption — persistent hypocalcaemia despite loading dose suggests impaired vitamin D absorption; check coeliac serology (anti-TTG IgA + total IgA), consider endoscopy/duodenal biopsy; exclude other causes: renal failure (impaired 1-alpha-hydroxylation — check eGFR), primary hypoparathyroidism (low PTH), pseudohypoparathyroidism, severe liver disease; if malabsorption confirmed may need higher doses or parenteral vitamin D
options.C: Add fluoride supplementation
options.D: Switch to alfacalcidol only
options.E: Discharge — treatment failure is expected

explanation.correct: Failure to correct osteomalacia/hypocalcaemia despite adequate loading dose suggests impaired vitamin D absorption or metabolism. Key causes to investigate: Malabsorption: coeliac disease (most common UK cause of malabsorption causing vitamin D deficiency — check anti-tTG IgA + total IgA; if coeliac confirmed, vitamin D deficiency will recur without treating underlying coeliac); Crohn's disease; short bowel syndrome; biliary disease (fat-soluble vitamin absorption); Renal failure: impaired conversion of 25(OH)D to active 1,25(OH)2D — treat with alfacalcidol or calcitriol; Liver disease: impaired 25-hydroxylation; Hypoparathyroidism: low PTH causing hypocalcaemia — check PTH; Anticonvulsants (phenytoin, carbamazepine — accelerate vitamin D catabolism); Tumour-induced osteomalacia (rare — caused by FGF-23 secreting mesenchymal tumours). Per NICE CKS: investigate underlying cause in all confirmed osteomalacia cases, not just treat symptomatically.
explanation.A: Incorrect — Repeating loading dose without investigating the cause delays treatment of potentially serious underlying pathology.
explanation.B: CORRECT — Persistent hypocalcaemia despite loading = investigate malabsorption (coeliac serology), renal function, liver function per NICE CKS.
explanation.C: Incorrect — Fluoride is not relevant to osteomalacia treatment.
explanation.D: Incorrect — Alfacalcidol is appropriate for renal failure but switching without diagnosis is not the correct approach.
explanation.E: Incorrect — Treatment failure always requires investigation of underlying cause.

reference: NICE CKS — Vitamin D deficiency. Coeliac UK. https://cks.nice.org.uk/topics/vitamin-d-deficiency-in-adults/

question: Per the UK National Screening Committee (UK NSC) and NICE, which of the following conditions is NOT included in the UK newborn bloodspot (heel prick) screening programme?

options.A: PKU (phenylketonuria)
options.B: Biliary atresia — biliary atresia is NOT screened for in the UK newborn bloodspot programme; it is diagnosed clinically when neonatal jaundice persists beyond 2 weeks; GPs and health visitors must check stool colour using the 'baby check' stool colour chart at the 6-week review and refer urgently if pale/white stools are noted alongside jaundice
options.C: Congenital hypothyroidism
options.D: Sickle cell disease
options.E: Cystic fibrosis

explanation.correct: The UK Newborn Bloodspot Screening Programme (heel prick at 5 days old) screens for 9 conditions: PKU (phenylketonuria), congenital hypothyroidism, sickle cell disease, cystic fibrosis, MCADD (medium-chain acyl-CoA dehydrogenase deficiency), maple syrup urine disease (MSUD), isovaleric acidaemia (IVA), glutaric aciduria type 1 (GA1), homocystinuria (HCU). Biliary atresia is NOT included in the bloodspot programme because there is no suitable biochemical bloodspot marker for it. Instead, detection relies on: health visitor assessment at 6-8 weeks (jaundice + pale stools + dark urine); 'baby check' stool colour chart issued to all parents; GP review at 6-8 weeks. Per NICE CG98: any jaundiced baby at 14 days (2 weeks) must have split bilirubin measured; if pale/white stools + jaundice → urgent referral for biliary atresia exclusion as Kasai portoenterostomy must be performed before 60-70 days for best outcome.
explanation.A: Incorrect — PKU IS included in the UK newborn bloodspot programme.
explanation.B: CORRECT — Biliary atresia is NOT screened for by bloodspot; detection is clinical (stool colour card + jaundice assessment at 6-8 weeks) per UK NSC.
explanation.C: Incorrect — Congenital hypothyroidism IS included.
explanation.D: Incorrect — Sickle cell disease IS included.
explanation.E: Incorrect — Cystic fibrosis IS included.

reference: UK NSC — Newborn bloodspot screening. NICE CG98. https://www.gov.uk/guidance/newborn-blood-spot-screening-programme-overview

question: A health visitor notices a 6-week-old baby still has jaundice. The mother shows her the stool colour card and the stools are pale yellow/cream. Per NICE CG98, what must happen?

options.A: Reassure — jaundice at 6 weeks is always physiological
options.B: Same-day urgent referral to paediatrics to exclude biliary atresia — jaundice persisting beyond 2 weeks with pale/acholic stools is a red flag requiring urgent investigation; Kasai portoenterostomy must be performed before 60-70 days of life for best outcome; delay leads to progressive liver cirrhosis
options.C: Recheck at 8 weeks if still jaundiced
options.D: Start phototherapy at home
options.E: Check maternal blood group for haemolytic disease

explanation.correct: Per NICE CG98 (Neonatal jaundice): jaundice persisting beyond 14 days (2 weeks) in a term baby or 21 days in a preterm baby requires investigation. Pale/acholic stools alongside jaundice is a cardinal sign of biliary atresia (obstructed bile flow — no bile reaching intestine). Management: SAME-DAY urgent paediatric referral. The stool colour chart (Baby Check card) is issued to all parents in the UK to identify pale stools. Pale stools + persistent jaundice + dark urine = biliary atresia until proven otherwise. The Kasai portoenterostomy (hepatoportoenterostomy) is the surgical treatment — success rate drops dramatically after 60-70 days. Investigation pathway: split bilirubin (conjugated fraction >20% = pathological), liver ultrasound, hepatobiliary scintigraphy (HIDA scan), liver biopsy. No delay is acceptable.
explanation.A: Incorrect — Physiological jaundice resolves by 2 weeks. Persistent jaundice + pale stools at 6 weeks is a surgical emergency.
explanation.B: CORRECT — Same-day urgent paediatric referral for biliary atresia exclusion. Kasai before 60-70 days per NICE CG98.
explanation.C: Incorrect — Waiting until 8 weeks risks missing the optimal surgical window.
explanation.D: Incorrect — Phototherapy is for unconjugated hyperbilirubinaemia; conjugated jaundice has a different cause.
explanation.E: Incorrect — Haemolytic disease causes unconjugated jaundice in the first days; this is persistent conjugated jaundice.

reference: NICE CG98 — Neonatal jaundice. https://www.nice.org.uk/guidance/cg98

question: The UK NSC evaluates conditions for screening. Which criteria must be met for a condition to be included in a national screening programme?

options.A: Condition must be common and treatable
options.B: Wilson and Jungner criteria (1968) updated by UK NSC: the condition must be an important health problem with known natural history; it must have a recognisable latent or early symptomatic stage; there must be a suitable screening test with acceptable sensitivity, specificity and safety; an accepted treatment must be available; facilities for diagnosis and treatment must be available; the cost of case-finding must be economically balanced relative to benefits; the screening programme must be continuous and reviewed
options.C: Only conditions affecting newborns can be screened
options.D: Screening is automatically offered if a treatment exists
options.E: Any GP can recommend adding a new screening programme

explanation.correct: The Wilson and Jungner criteria (WHO 1968) remain the foundation of screening programme evaluation. Key principles: (1) The condition should be an important public health problem; (2) Natural history of the condition should be well understood; (3) There should be an early/latent stage detectable before symptomatic presentation; (4) A suitable screening test exists — sensitive (few false negatives), specific (few false positives), safe, acceptable to the population; (5) An effective treatment is available and agreed upon; (6) Facilities for follow-up and treatment must be available; (7) The screening test must be acceptable to patients; (8) Cost-effectiveness: the benefit must justify the cost and harms (including false positives causing anxiety/harm). The UK NSC applies these criteria and additionally evaluates harms from screening (overdiagnosis, anxiety, harm from investigation of false positives). Biliary atresia fails because there is no suitable bloodspot marker — it is detected clinically via the stool colour card programme instead.
explanation.A: Incorrect — Common and treatable alone is insufficient; natural history, test suitability, cost-effectiveness and harm all matter.
explanation.B: CORRECT — Wilson and Jungner criteria updated by UK NSC: disease, test, treatment and system requirements all must be met.
explanation.C: Incorrect — Screening programmes exist for adults (cervical, bowel, breast, abdominal aortic aneurysm, diabetic eye).
explanation.D: Incorrect — Treatment availability is necessary but not sufficient; test performance, harms and cost-effectiveness must all be acceptable.
explanation.E: Incorrect — The UK NSC is the body that evaluates and recommends additions to national screening programmes.

reference: UK NSC — Criteria for appraising the viability of a screening programme. https://www.gov.uk/government/publications/evidence-review-criteria-national-screening-programmes

question: A 6-week-old baby has had a positive newborn bloodspot result for PKU. Per NICE and PKU guidelines, what is the immediate management?

options.A: Reassure — PKU is harmless if diagnosed early
options.B: Urgent referral to a metabolic diseases centre; initiate a phenylalanine-restricted diet (low phenylalanine formula) immediately; PKU (phenylketonuria) causes accumulation of phenylalanine due to deficiency of phenylalanine hydroxylase (PAH), causing irreversible intellectual disability and seizures if untreated; early dietary treatment prevents neurological damage entirely
options.C: Start enzyme replacement therapy
options.D: Repeat bloodspot test at 3 months
options.E: No treatment needed until child is symptomatic

explanation.correct: Phenylketonuria (PKU): autosomal recessive condition (PAH gene) causing phenylalanine hydroxylase deficiency — phenylalanine cannot be converted to tyrosine and accumulates. Consequences if untreated: severe intellectual disability, microcephaly, epilepsy, behavioural problems, mousy body odour (from phenylacetic acid). Newborn screening detects PKU before any symptoms develop. Per NICE and NHS specialist guidelines: urgent referral to metabolic team (within days of positive result); start low-phenylalanine diet immediately (special formula replacing natural protein); lifelong dietary management with very low phenylalanine intake; regular monitoring of phenylalanine levels. If diet started within first weeks of life, intellectual development is entirely normal. Additional treatments: sapropterin dihydrochloride (synthetic BH4 cofactor) for BH4-responsive PKU (~25-30% of cases — reduces phenylalanine levels); pegvaliase (PAL enzyme, for adults with poorly controlled PKU). Maternal PKU: women with PKU must have strict phenylalanine control before and during pregnancy to prevent maternal PKU syndrome (fetal microcephaly, intellectual disability).
explanation.A: Incorrect — PKU is NOT harmless — untreated it causes irreversible intellectual disability. Early treatment prevents all complications.
explanation.B: CORRECT — Urgent metabolic referral + immediate low-phenylalanine diet per NHS/NICE. Prevents all neurological damage.
explanation.C: Incorrect — Enzyme replacement therapy is not standard first-line treatment for PKU.
explanation.D: Incorrect — Waiting 3 months while phenylalanine accumulates causes irreversible brain damage.
explanation.E: Incorrect — Treatment must start before symptoms to prevent neurological damage.

reference: NHS — PKU screening and treatment. NICE CKS — Phenylketonuria. https://www.nhs.uk/conditions/phenylketonuria/

question: A 7-year-old child with PKU is brought because his mother reports he has a peculiar smell and is becoming more difficult to manage behaviourally. He has had all routine immunisations. Per PKU guidelines, what is most likely happening?

options.A: The child has developed an allergy to vaccines
options.B: Dietary non-compliance — the mousy/musty odour is caused by phenylacetic acid (a phenylpyruvate metabolite) excreted in urine and sweat when phenylalanine levels are high; behavioural problems are an early sign of neurotoxicity from elevated phenylalanine; urgent re-assessment of phenylalanine levels, dietary review and re-engagement with the metabolic team is required
options.C: Normal development — the smell is coincidental
options.D: Coeliac disease complication
options.E: Vaccine injury

explanation.correct: In children with PKU who develop elevated phenylalanine levels (due to dietary non-compliance, illness or inadequate monitoring), characteristic signs include: mousy or musty body odour (from phenylacetic acid, a metabolite of phenylpyruvate produced when the phenylalanine hydroxylase pathway is overwhelmed); behavioural problems, irritability, poor concentration (early neurotoxic effects of elevated phenylalanine); if prolonged elevated levels: cognitive decline, eczema-like rash, pale skin/hair (phenylalanine competes with tyrosine for melanin synthesis). The immunisation history is a red herring — children with PKU receive normal immunisation schedules; the smell and behaviour change are metabolic, not vaccine-related. Action: urgent phenylalanine blood level check, dietary assessment, re-engagement with specialist metabolic clinic, reinforce dietary adherence.
explanation.A: Incorrect — Vaccines are not associated with the clinical picture described.
explanation.B: CORRECT — Elevated phenylalanine (dietary non-compliance): mousy odour + behaviour change. Urgent metabolic review.
explanation.C: Incorrect — Mousy odour in PKU is a specific metabolic sign, not coincidental.
explanation.D: Incorrect — Coeliac disease does not cause mousy odour.
explanation.E: Incorrect — The timing and nature of symptoms are metabolic, not vaccine-related.

reference: British Inherited Metabolic Disease Group (BIMDG) — PKU management. https://www.bimdg.org.uk/

question: A woman with known PKU plans to become pregnant. Per NICE and BIMDG guidelines, what is the most important pre-conception intervention?

options.A: Stop the low-phenylalanine diet in pregnancy — safe to eat normally
options.B: Achieve strict pre-conceptual phenylalanine control (ideally <360 µmol/L) before conception and maintain throughout pregnancy; maternal PKU syndrome (microcephaly, intellectual disability, congenital heart disease) affects the fetus from elevated maternal phenylalanine even though the fetus may not have PKU itself (heterozygous); refer to metabolic team for pre-conception counselling and intensified dietary management
options.C: Only low phenylalanine diet from 20 weeks onwards
options.D: Phenylalanine is harmless to the fetus — maternal PKU has no fetal implications
options.E: Terminate the pregnancy — PKU precludes safe pregnancy

explanation.correct: Maternal PKU syndrome is one of the most important aspects of PKU management. Even when the fetus is NOT homozygous for PKU (just a carrier), elevated maternal phenylalanine in the intrauterine environment causes: fetal microcephaly, severe intellectual disability, congenital heart defects (especially ventricular septal defects and tetralogy of Fallot), intrauterine growth restriction, facial dysmorphology. This is because phenylalanine crosses the placenta and accumulates in fetal tissues at even higher concentrations than maternal levels. Per BIMDG and NICE: women with PKU must achieve phenylalanine <360 µmol/L BEFORE conception and maintain this throughout pregnancy with intensive dietary management and monitoring. Pre-conception counselling is essential. If phenylalanine is controlled pre-conception and maintained through pregnancy, normal fetal outcomes can be expected. This requires close specialist metabolic team involvement throughout.
explanation.A: Incorrect — Stopping the diet in pregnancy causes maternal PKU syndrome — one of the most preventable causes of intellectual disability.
explanation.B: CORRECT — Pre-conception phenylalanine control <360 µmol/L before conception and throughout pregnancy prevents maternal PKU syndrome per BIMDG.
explanation.C: Incorrect — Brain development begins at conception — waiting until 20 weeks is far too late.
explanation.D: Incorrect — Elevated maternal phenylalanine is highly neurotoxic to the fetus regardless of fetal genotype.
explanation.E: Incorrect — Pregnancy with PKU can have excellent outcomes with good metabolic control; termination is not indicated.

reference: BIMDG — PKU and pregnancy. https://www.bimdg.org.uk/

question: A 28-year-old woman at her first antenatal booking appointment has a urine dipstick showing 2+ leucocytes and 3+ nitrites. She has no urinary symptoms. Per NICE NG121 and PHE, what is the recommended action?

options.A: Reassure — asymptomatic bacteriuria in pregnancy does not need treatment
options.B: Send midstream urine (MSU) for culture and sensitivity; if confirmed asymptomatic bacteriuria (≥10⁵ colony-forming units per mL of a single organism) — treat with appropriate antibiotic per culture sensitivities; asymptomatic bacteriuria in pregnancy significantly increases risk of ascending infection (pyelonephritis), preterm labour and low birth weight if untreated; treatment reduces these risks
options.C: Start empirical antibiotics without culture
options.D: Repeat dipstick in 4 weeks
options.E: Catheter specimen of urine only

explanation.correct: Asymptomatic bacteriuria in pregnancy: present in 2-5% of pregnant women; unlike in non-pregnant adults (where it is not treated), asymptomatic bacteriuria in pregnancy IS treated because untreated cases have a 20-40% risk of progressing to pyelonephritis (which can cause preterm labour, sepsis, low birth weight). Per NICE NG121 (Antenatal care) and PHE guidance: screen all pregnant women at first antenatal visit with MSU culture; treat confirmed bacteriuria (≥10⁵ CFU/mL on culture) based on sensitivities; usual agents: cefalexin, nitrofurantoin (avoid near term — neonatal haemolysis risk), trimethoprim (avoid first trimester — folate antagonist), amoxicillin if sensitive. Treatment duration: 7 days. Repeat MSU 7 days after treatment to confirm clearance. Test of cure MSU is important in pregnancy. Universal MSU screening at booking is a standard of antenatal care.
explanation.A: Incorrect — Asymptomatic bacteriuria in pregnancy IS treated unlike in non-pregnant adults — 20-40% risk of pyelonephritis if untreated.
explanation.B: CORRECT — MSU culture; treat confirmed bacteriuria per culture per NICE NG121.
explanation.C: Incorrect — Culture first ensures correct antibiotic choice and avoids treating contamination.
explanation.D: Incorrect — Repeat dipstick delays diagnosis and treatment of a condition with significant fetal risk.
explanation.E: Incorrect — Catheter specimen not needed for routine asymptomatic bacteriuria screening.

reference: NICE NG121 — Antenatal care. https://www.nice.org.uk/guidance/ng121

question: A 30-week pregnant woman is prescribed nitrofurantoin for confirmed asymptomatic bacteriuria. Her GP queries the timing. Per BNF and NICE NG121, is nitrofurantoin safe throughout pregnancy?

options.A: Safe throughout all trimesters
