options.B: Nitrofurantoin is safe in the first and second trimesters but should be avoided at term (≥36 weeks) due to risk of neonatal haemolytic anaemia — nitrofurantoin can cause haemolysis in G6PD-deficient neonates and may cause haemolysis in term newborns as their red cells are more susceptible; at 30 weeks it can still be used — document the risk discussion; alternative: cefalexin
options.C: Nitrofurantoin is completely contraindicated in pregnancy
options.D: Nitrofurantoin is only safe in the third trimester
options.E: Nitrofurantoin dose must be halved in pregnancy

explanation.correct: Per BNF and NICE NG121, nitrofurantoin prescribing in pregnancy: First and second trimester: can be used for UTI/asymptomatic bacteriuria; standard dose (50-100mg QDS or 100mg MR BD for 7 days); Third trimester (near term, ≥36 weeks): AVOID — risk of neonatal haemolytic anaemia (nitrofurantoin can cause haemolysis particularly in G6PD-deficient neonates whose hepatic enzyme maturation is incomplete near term). At 30 weeks: use with caution; benefit likely outweighs risk; document discussion; alternatives include cefalexin (safe throughout pregnancy) or amoxicillin (if susceptibility confirmed). Trimethoprim: avoid in first trimester (folate antagonist — neural tube defect risk); avoid in third trimester (antifolate); can be used in second trimester. Penicillins (amoxicillin, cefalexin): safest options throughout pregnancy if organism sensitive.
explanation.A: Incorrect — Nitrofurantoin should be avoided at term (≥36 weeks) due to neonatal haemolysis risk.
explanation.B: CORRECT — Safe in first/second trimester, avoid at term (≥36 weeks). At 30 weeks can use with caution per BNF.
explanation.C: Incorrect — Not completely contraindicated — safe in first and second trimesters.
explanation.D: Incorrect — The opposite is true — third trimester (term) should be avoided.
explanation.E: Incorrect — Dose is not halved in pregnancy.

reference: BNF — Nitrofurantoin in pregnancy. NICE NG121. https://bnf.nice.org.uk/drug/nitrofurantoin.html

question: A pregnant woman is diagnosed with a UTI. She is penicillin allergic (mild rash only). Per NICE NG195 and BNF, what is the preferred antibiotic?

options.A: Ciprofloxacin — safe in all penicillin-allergic pregnant women
options.B: Nitrofurantoin (if <36 weeks) or cefalexin (cephalosporin — cross-reactivity with penicillin is low, ~1-2%, and mild prior reaction does not preclude cephalosporins); ciprofloxacin and other fluoroquinolones are contraindicated in pregnancy (arthropathy in animal models, avoid); trimethoprim safe in second trimester only; erythromycin is an alternative if no other option suitable
options.C: Co-amoxiclav — safe despite penicillin allergy
options.D: Tetracycline — safe throughout pregnancy
options.E: Metronidazole — covers UTI in pregnancy

explanation.correct: Per BNF, NICE NG195 (UTI antimicrobial prescribing) and NICE NG121: Antibiotics safe in pregnancy for UTI (if penicillin allergy): Nitrofurantoin: safe first/second trimester (avoid ≥36 weeks); Cefalexin (cephalosporin): safe throughout pregnancy — cross-reactivity with penicillin is only 1-2% and a mild rash as the prior penicillin reaction does not preclude cefalexin; use with informed caution; Trimethoprim: safe in second trimester only (avoid first — folate antagonism; avoid third — antifolate); Erythromycin: can be used if other options not suitable. Avoid in pregnancy: Fluoroquinolones (ciprofloxacin, levofloxacin) — arthropathy risk, avoid in pregnancy and breastfeeding; Tetracyclines — fetal dental discolouration, bone effects (avoid after first trimester); Co-amoxiclav — contains amoxicillin (penicillin) so contraindicated in true penicillin allergy; Metronidazole has activity against anaerobes and protozoa, not standard UTI treatment.
explanation.A: Incorrect — Fluoroquinolones (ciprofloxacin) are contraindicated in pregnancy due to arthropathy risk.
explanation.B: CORRECT — Nitrofurantoin (<36w) or cefalexin (low cross-reactivity with penicillin, safe throughout) per BNF/NICE NG195.
explanation.C: Incorrect — Co-amoxiclav contains penicillin (amoxicillin); contraindicated in penicillin allergy.
explanation.D: Incorrect — Tetracyclines cause fetal tooth discolouration and bone/cartilage effects — avoid after first trimester.
explanation.E: Incorrect — Metronidazole does not cover typical UTI pathogens (E. coli, Klebsiella).

reference: NICE NG195 — UTI antimicrobial prescribing. BNF — Antibiotics in pregnancy. https://www.nice.org.uk/guidance/ng195

question: A 92-year-old man is brought by his daughter. He has poor personal hygiene, bilateral coarse resting tremor, pedal oedema, confusion, and falls. She mentions he drinks 'a few cans daily'. His pulse is irregular. Per NICE CG115 and NICE CKS, what is the most likely unifying diagnosis?

options.A: Parkinson's disease — start levodopa
options.B: Chronic alcohol excess causing: alcoholic cardiomyopathy (atrial fibrillation, cardiac failure causing pedal oedema), alcohol-related tremor (coarse, postural/resting), cognitive impairment (frontal lobe atrophy, Wernicke-Korsakoff risk), poor self-care and falls; alcohol AUDIT screening; CAGE questionnaire; safe alcohol withdrawal protocol; social care assessment and safeguarding
options.C: Normal ageing — no treatment needed
options.D: Hypothyroidism — check TFTs
options.E: Essential tremor — propranolol

explanation.correct: Chronic alcohol excess in the elderly: frequently underdiagnosed and presents with multiple system involvement. Manifestations: CNS — tremor (coarse, worse with withdrawal), cognitive impairment, cerebellar ataxia, falls, peripheral neuropathy; Cardiovascular — alcoholic cardiomyopathy, dilated cardiomyopathy, atrial fibrillation, heart failure (pedal oedema); Liver — hepatitis, cirrhosis; Nutritional — thiamine deficiency (Wernicke-Korsakoff), B12 deficiency; Immune suppression — recurrent infections; Social — self-neglect. Per NICE CG115 (Alcohol-use disorders: harmful drinking and alcohol dependence), AUDIT-C screening tool should be used; brief interventions effective in primary care; if dependent, medically supervised withdrawal using chlordiazepoxide/diazepam Symptom-Triggered or fixed-schedule regimen; vitamin B (thiamine — Pabrinex) supplementation to prevent Wernicke's encephalopathy; safeguarding assessment for self-neglect; carer support. The irregular pulse (AF) + oedema + tremor + cognitive decline + self-neglect in an elderly alcohol user is a classic combination.
explanation.A: Incorrect — Parkinson's tremor is resting, unilateral at onset, with bradykinesia; doesn't explain AF and oedema.
explanation.B: CORRECT — Chronic alcohol excess: multiple system effects. AUDIT + withdrawal + thiamine + safeguarding per NICE CG115.
explanation.C: Incorrect — This clinical picture is NOT normal ageing — it requires active assessment and treatment.
explanation.D: Incorrect — Hypothyroidism causes slow tremor, bradycardia, not AF and this combination.
explanation.E: Incorrect — Essential tremor is bilateral postural/kinetic but doesn't explain AF, oedema, cognitive decline and self-neglect.

reference: NICE CG115 — Alcohol-use disorders. https://www.nice.org.uk/guidance/cg115

question: The 92-year-old is found to be dependent on alcohol. He is to be assisted with withdrawal. Per NICE CG100 and BNF, what is the most important preventive medication alongside alcohol withdrawal?

options.A: Vitamin C only
options.B: High-dose parenteral thiamine (IV/IM Pabrinex — B1) BEFORE and during withdrawal — thiamine deficiency is universal in alcohol-dependent patients; glucose infusion in a thiamine-depleted patient precipitates Wernicke's encephalopathy (ophthalmoplegia, ataxia, confusion) which can progress to Korsakoff's syndrome (irreversible anterograde amnesia); all alcohol-dependent patients undergoing withdrawal must receive high-dose parenteral thiamine; DO NOT give IV glucose without thiamine first
options.C: Folic acid only
options.D: Vitamin D only
options.E: Iron supplementation

explanation.correct: Per NICE CG100 (Alcohol-use disorders: physical complications) and BNF: Wernicke's encephalopathy (WE) prevention is mandatory during alcohol withdrawal. Mechanism: alcohol prevents thiamine absorption, storage and utilisation; thiamine is essential for glucose metabolism in the CNS; acute glucose loading (IV dextrose) in a thiamine-deficient patient overwhelms what little thiamine remains, precipitating acute WE. Classic triad of WE: ophthalmoplegias, cerebellar ataxia, confusion — only ~10% have all three. Treatment and prevention: Pabrinex (IV thiamine — B complex including B1, B2, B3, B6, C) — high-dose parenteral thiamine is given prophylactically to all at-risk patients; dose: 1-2 pairs Pabrinex IM/IV twice daily for 5 days in those at risk, or daily for those with suspected acute WE; oral thiamine inadequate in severe deficiency due to impaired gut absorption. The rule: thiamine BEFORE glucose in any alcohol-dependent patient receiving IV glucose.
explanation.A: Incorrect — Vitamin C is in Pabrinex but the most important component is thiamine (B1).
explanation.B: CORRECT — Parenteral thiamine (Pabrinex) before glucose to prevent Wernicke's encephalopathy per NICE CG100/BNF.
explanation.C: Incorrect — Folic acid is important for megaloblastic anaemia but not the immediate priority.
explanation.D: Incorrect — Vitamin D deficiency is common in alcoholics but not the emergency here.
explanation.E: Incorrect — Iron supplementation is not the immediate priority.

reference: NICE CG100 — Alcohol-use disorders: physical complications. BNF — Pabrinex. https://www.nice.org.uk/guidance/cg100

question: The AUDIT-C questionnaire is used to screen for alcohol problems. A 50-year-old man scores 9 on the full AUDIT. Per NICE CG115, what level of problem does this indicate and what intervention is appropriate?

options.A: Low risk — no action needed
options.B: AUDIT score 8-15 indicates hazardous or harmful drinking; brief intervention (BI) is recommended — 5-15 minutes discussing alcohol use, risks, advice to reduce consumption; extended BI or referral to alcohol specialist if score 16+ or signs of dependence (CAGE positive, morning drinking, withdrawal symptoms); AUDIT score 0-7 = lower risk, 8-15 = hazardous/harmful, 16-19 = harmful/possibly dependent, 20+ = high likely dependence
options.C: Immediate alcohol detoxification in hospital
options.D: Prescribe naltrexone immediately
options.E: Refer to police — alcohol is illegal above a threshold

explanation.correct: Per NICE CG115 (Alcohol-use disorders: prevention) and PHE guidance, the AUDIT (Alcohol Use Disorders Identification Test) scoring: 0-7: lower-risk drinking; simple advice if in clinical context. 8-15: hazardous/harmful drinking; BRIEF INTERVENTION (BI) recommended — 5-15 minute structured conversation covering current drinking habits, risks, advice on reducing intake, motivational interviewing elements. 16-19: harmful drinking; EXTENDED BI (multiple sessions) or referral to alcohol services. 20+: likely alcohol dependence; specialist referral; structured alcohol treatment programme. AUDIT-C is a shortened 3-question version of AUDIT; CAGE is a 4-question tool for dependence. Brief interventions in primary care are cost-effective and evidence-based — NNT approximately 8 for reducing alcohol intake to safe levels. Most alcohol-related GP consultations represent an opportunity for brief intervention.
explanation.A: Incorrect — AUDIT 9 indicates hazardous/harmful drinking requiring brief intervention.
explanation.B: CORRECT — AUDIT 8-15: brief intervention per NICE CG115. 5-15 minutes discussing risks and reduction.
explanation.C: Incorrect — Detoxification is for dependent drinkers (AUDIT 16+, or with dependence features); not AUDIT 9.
explanation.D: Incorrect — Naltrexone is for relapse prevention in treated alcohol dependence, not for hazardous drinking.
explanation.E: Incorrect — Alcohol consumption is legal; police involvement is not appropriate.

reference: NICE CG115 — Alcohol-use disorders: prevention. https://www.nice.org.uk/guidance/cg115

question: A 68-year-old man has had bilateral hand tremors for 20 years. The tremors are present when he holds his hands outstretched (postural) and when he uses them (kinetic/action), but absent at rest. He drinks alcohol occasionally which relieves the tremors. There are no other neurological signs. Per NICE CKS, what is the diagnosis and first-line treatment?

options.A: Parkinson's disease — levodopa
options.B: Essential tremor — the most common movement disorder; bilateral postural and kinetic tremor, typically hands (may also affect head/voice); absent at rest; classically improved by alcohol; long history (20 years) and absence of other neurological signs; first-line treatment: propranolol 40-120mg daily (or other beta-blocker); second-line: primidone; refer to neurology if diagnostic uncertainty or treatment-refractory
options.C: Cerebellar tremor — MRI brain
options.D: Drug-induced tremor — review medications
options.E: Physiological tremor — caffeine reduction only

explanation.correct: Essential tremor (ET): most common movement disorder, affects approximately 4-5% of the population over 65. Key features: bilateral (hands, may affect head giving 'yes-yes' or 'no-no' movements, voice); postural and kinetic tremor (present during activity and sustained posture — NOT at rest); typically absent during complete rest; classically improved by small amounts of alcohol (not a recommended treatment but a characteristic historical feature); frequency 6-12 Hz; often positive family history (~50%); long-standing stable course with gradual progression. Per NICE CKS: first-line pharmacological treatment: propranolol (non-selective beta-blocker) 40-120mg daily — effective in ~50-60% of patients; alternative: primidone 50-750mg daily; if refractory: neurology referral for DBS (deep brain stimulation), focused ultrasound (newer option). Distinguished from Parkinson's: ET has no bradykinesia, no rigidity, no postural instability, bilateral onset, action tremor not resting tremor.
explanation.A: Incorrect — Parkinson's has resting tremor (not action), unilateral onset, bradykinesia and rigidity.
explanation.B: CORRECT — Essential tremor: bilateral action/postural tremor improved by alcohol. Propranolol first-line per NICE CKS.
explanation.C: Incorrect — Cerebellar tremor is intention tremor (worsens approaching target), with other cerebellar signs (dysmetria, nystagmus).
explanation.D: Incorrect — 20-year stable tremor without recent medication change makes drug-induced tremor unlikely.
explanation.E: Incorrect — Physiological tremor is fine, normal, affects all people under stress/anxiety/caffeine — not the degree described.

reference: NICE CKS — Essential tremor. https://cks.nice.org.uk/topics/essential-tremor/

question: A 65-year-old woman with essential tremor has not responded to propranolol and cannot tolerate primidone. Per NICE CKS and NICE guidance, what are the options?

options.A: No further treatment available
options.B: Second-line options include: atenolol (cardioselective beta-blocker — useful if pulmonary disease precludes propranolol), gabapentin, topiramate; if significantly disabling tremor refractory to medications: neurology referral for deep brain stimulation (DBS) of thalamic nucleus (VIM — ventral intermediate nucleus) — highly effective; newer: focused ultrasound thalamotomy; botulinum toxin injections for hand or head tremor can reduce amplitude
options.C: Increase propranolol to 480mg daily
options.D: Start levodopa immediately
options.E: Refer to psychiatry

explanation.correct: Per NICE CKS (Essential tremor), management of treatment-refractory essential tremor: Second-line medications: atenolol (alternative beta-blocker, cardioselective — useful if respiratory disease contraindicates propranolol), topiramate (anticonvulsant with some evidence for ET), gabapentin, nadolol, sotalol. Referral to neurology if: diagnostic uncertainty, significant functional impairment from medication-refractory tremor. Surgical/interventional options for disabling medication-refractory ET: Deep brain stimulation (DBS) of the thalamic VIM nucleus — most established surgical treatment; highly effective, immediate improvement; requires neurostimulator implantation; Magnetic resonance-guided focused ultrasound (MRgFUS) thalamotomy — NICE IPG611 recommends with specialist oversight; unilateral, non-invasive, less suitable for bilateral tremor; Stereotactic radiosurgery (gamma knife); Botulinum toxin type A injections — useful for head tremor and writing tremor. Propranolol dose should not exceed 320mg/day (standard maximum) — increasing to 480mg is not recommended.
explanation.A: Incorrect — Multiple second-line and interventional options exist.
explanation.B: CORRECT — Second-line: atenolol/gabapentin/topiramate; DBS or focused ultrasound for refractory per NICE CKS.
explanation.C: Incorrect — Exceeding standard maximum propranolol dose is not recommended.
explanation.D: Incorrect — Levodopa is for Parkinson's disease, not essential tremor.
explanation.E: Incorrect — Essential tremor is a movement disorder — neurological not psychiatric management.

reference: NICE CKS — Essential tremor. NICE IPG611 — Focused ultrasound. https://cks.nice.org.uk/topics/essential-tremor/

question: A patient presents asking whether their essential tremor will progress to Parkinson's disease. Per NICE CKS and published evidence, what is the association?

options.A: Essential tremor invariably leads to Parkinson's disease
options.B: There is a small but statistically increased risk — epidemiological studies suggest individuals with essential tremor have approximately 2-4 times the population risk of developing Parkinson's disease; however, the vast majority of ET patients do NOT develop Parkinson's and the conditions are clinically and pathologically distinct; essential tremor is not a precursor to Parkinson's in most cases; reassurance with explanation of the distinct mechanisms is appropriate
options.C: Essential tremor completely protects against Parkinson's disease
options.D: All essential tremor converts to Parkinson's by age 80
options.E: There is no association between essential tremor and Parkinson's disease

explanation.correct: The relationship between ET and Parkinson's disease is complex and still debated. Epidemiological data suggests a modest increased risk — ET patients have approximately 2-4 times the baseline population risk of subsequently developing Parkinson's disease. Potential explanations: (1) Diagnostic misclassification — some 'ET' cases may be early tremor-dominant Parkinson's (ET-PD overlap); (2) Shared underlying pathophysiology in a subset; (3) Both diseases involve cerebellar-thalamic-cortical circuit dysfunction. However: the vast majority of ET patients (>95%) do NOT develop Parkinson's disease; ET and Parkinson's have different tremor characteristics (resting vs action), different pathology, and different treatments; the increased risk does not alter management of ET; patients should be reassured but informed that clinical features that suggest Parkinson's (bradykinesia, rigidity, unilateral resting tremor) should prompt reassessment. DaTSCAN (dopamine transporter scan) can differentiate ET (normal) from Parkinson's (reduced DAT uptake) if clinically uncertain.
explanation.A: Incorrect — The vast majority of ET patients do NOT develop Parkinson's disease.
explanation.B: CORRECT — Small increased risk (~2-4x) but most ET patients do not progress to Parkinson's. Distinct conditions per NICE CKS.
explanation.C: Incorrect — ET does not protect against Parkinson's.
explanation.D: Incorrect — Not all or even most ET patients develop Parkinson's.
explanation.E: Incorrect — There is a modest epidemiological association, though causation is not established.

reference: NICE CKS — Essential tremor. NICE NG71 — Parkinson's disease. https://cks.nice.org.uk/topics/essential-tremor/

question: A 70-year-old woman is examined. She has a tremor of her right hand that occurs when she is threading a needle (fine motor activity). When resting the hand on her lap, the tremor is absent. She also has mild cogwheeling rigidity of her right wrist. Per NICE NG71, what is the most likely diagnosis?

options.A: Essential tremor — propranolol
options.B: Parkinson's disease — the resting tremor (pill-rolling, disappearing during purposeful activity) is the classic presentation; HOWEVER, Parkinson's tremor can also occur during activity in some patients; cogwheeling rigidity + unilateral onset + tremor during precision fine motor work (threading) with resting component = Parkinson's disease; refer to Parkinson's specialist per NICE NG71; do NOT start treatment without specialist confirmation
options.C: Cerebellar tremor — MRI brain
options.D: Drug-induced tremor — review medications
options.E: Physiological tremor — reassure

explanation.correct: Parkinson's disease tremor: classically a resting tremor (4-6 Hz, 'pill-rolling' — thumb over index finger), typically present at rest and suppressed during purposeful movement. However, in practice, Parkinson's tremor can also re-emerge during fine motor tasks (threading, writing) — this is called 're-emergent tremor' and is characteristic of PD. The additional feature of cogwheeling rigidity (jerky resistance to passive movement around a joint, from superimposed tremor on lead-pipe rigidity) is a cardinal sign of Parkinson's disease. Per NICE NG71: diagnosis is clinical (UK Parkinson's Disease Society Brain Bank Criteria); refer to specialist (neurologist or geriatrician with expertise); do NOT start levodopa/dopamine agonist in primary care without specialist assessment; DaTSCAN may be used to differentiate if diagnostic uncertainty. Asymmetric/unilateral onset is characteristic of PD (ET is bilateral from the start).
explanation.A: Incorrect — Essential tremor is bilateral, action/postural, no cogwheeling; propranolol not appropriate if PD suspected.
explanation.B: CORRECT — Parkinson's disease: re-emergent tremor + cogwheeling + unilateral onset. Specialist referral per NICE NG71.
explanation.C: Incorrect — Cerebellar tremor is intention tremor (worsening as limb approaches target), with other cerebellar signs.
explanation.D: Incorrect — Drug-induced parkinsonism is possible (antipsychotics, metoclopramide) but cogwheeling + this age + tremor pattern suggests idiopathic PD.
explanation.E: Incorrect — Physiological tremor is fine and bilateral; does not cause cogwheeling.

reference: NICE NG71 — Parkinson's disease in adults. https://www.nice.org.uk/guidance/ng71

question: A 68-year-old man with Parkinson's disease (diagnosed 3 years ago, now on levodopa 250mg three times daily) notices that his medications wear off between doses (motor fluctuations). He has increasing 'off' periods. Per NICE NG71, what adjustment strategy can be used?

options.A: Double the levodopa dose only
options.B: Strategies for motor fluctuations per NICE NG71: reduce the interval between levodopa doses (more frequent smaller doses); add a COMT inhibitor (entacapone — inhibits peripheral levodopa metabolism, extending its effect); add a MAO-B inhibitor (rasagiline, selegiline — extends dopamine effect); add a dopamine agonist (pramipexole, ropinirole); consider modified-release levodopa; refer to Parkinson's disease nurse/specialist for optimisation; consider apomorphine (subcutaneous) for severe fluctuations
options.C: Stop levodopa immediately and switch to amantadine
options.D: Start haloperidol for tremor control
options.E: Reduce levodopa — symptoms suggest toxicity

explanation.correct: Motor fluctuations in Parkinson's disease: wearing-off phenomenon (predictable return of symptoms before next dose) is increasingly common with long-term levodopa use (occurs in ~50% of patients after 5 years). Mechanism: reduced striatal dopamine storage capacity over time leads to shorter duration of response to each levodopa dose. Per NICE NG71: Management strategies: (1) Reduce dose intervals (e.g., from TDS to QDS or more frequent); (2) Add entacapone (COMT inhibitor — available as combined Stalevo formulation with levodopa/carbidopa): blocks peripheral COMT enzyme that breaks down levodopa; (3) Add rasagiline/selegiline (MAO-B inhibitor): inhibits central dopamine breakdown; (4) Add dopamine agonist (pramipexole, ropinirole, rotigotine patch); (5) Modified-release levodopa for overnight off periods; (6) Severe cases: apomorphine SC injections or infusion (dopamine agonist, bypasses gut absorption), duodopa infusion (levodopa/carbidopa directly into intestine). Specialist PD nurse and neurologist involvement essential.
explanation.A: Incorrect — Simply doubling the dose may increase dyskinesias without addressing the timing issue.
explanation.B: CORRECT — Multiple strategies for wearing-off: reduce intervals, add entacapone/rasagiline/dopamine agonist per NICE NG71.
explanation.C: Incorrect — Stopping levodopa abruptly risks neuroleptic malignant syndrome-like syndrome in PD.
explanation.D: Incorrect — Haloperidol (antipsychotic) blocks dopamine receptors and severely worsens Parkinson's disease.
explanation.E: Incorrect — Reducing levodopa worsens motor function.

reference: NICE NG71 — Parkinson's disease in adults. https://www.nice.org.uk/guidance/ng71

question: A 74-year-old woman is admitted to hospital with a hip fracture. She has Parkinson's disease. The surgical team asks about her levodopa medication. Per NICE NG71 and NHS medicines optimisation guidelines, what is the critical prescribing instruction?

options.A: Levodopa can be withheld for 24-48 hours post-operatively without any significant risk
options.B: Parkinson's disease medications must NEVER be withheld without specialist advice — missed doses cause rapid deterioration including severe rigidity, inability to swallow, respiratory failure, and neuroleptic malignant syndrome (NMS)-like syndrome (hyperthermia, extreme rigidity, autonomic instability); PDNS (Parkinson's Disease Nurse Specialist) must be contacted immediately; administer medications at the EXACT prescribed times; if unable to swallow: use rotigotine patch or nasogastric/PEG levodopa; document 'critical medicine — must not be omitted'
options.C: Replace levodopa with haloperidol whilst nil by mouth
options.D: Levodopa should be halved post-operatively
options.E: Levodopa can safely be stopped and restarted after 3 days

explanation.correct: Parkinson's disease medications are 'critical medicines' — missing even one dose can cause serious deterioration. Per NICE NG71 and Parkinson's UK 'Get It On Time' campaign: PD medications must be given at prescribed times (NOT just 'with drug round'); late or missed doses risk: severe rigidity, reduced mobility, aspiration pneumonia (from swallowing difficulty), unable to cooperate with physiotherapy, NMS-like syndrome (hyperthermia, extreme muscle rigidity, consciousness impairment, autonomic instability). If patient cannot swallow: rotigotine patch (dopamine agonist available as transdermal patch — can replace oral dopaminergic drugs); nasogastric tube levodopa; dispersible co-careldopa/co-beneldopa via NG/PEG. Haloperidol is absolutely contraindicated in Parkinson's disease — blocks dopamine receptors causing severe worsening. PDNS should be contacted pre-operatively when possible. 'Parkinson's medications — do not delay or omit' must be documented clearly.
explanation.A: Incorrect — Even 1-2 missed doses can cause serious rapid deterioration in PD.
explanation.B: CORRECT — Critical medicines: never omit. PDNS contact. Rotigotine patch or NG if unable to swallow per NICE NG71.
explanation.C: Incorrect — Haloperidol is absolutely contraindicated in Parkinson's disease.
explanation.D: Incorrect — Halving dose post-operatively risks severe motor deterioration.
explanation.E: Incorrect — Three days without PD medication is extremely dangerous and potentially fatal.

reference: NICE NG71 — Parkinson's disease. Parkinson's UK — Get It On Time. https://www.nice.org.uk/guidance/ng71

question: A 35-year-old man presents with a 3-month history of scrotal swelling. On examination the right scrotum has a soft, non-tender fluid-filled swelling. Transillumination is positive. He is otherwise well. Per NICE CKS, what is the diagnosis and management?

options.A: Testicular cancer — urgent 2WW referral
options.B: Hydrocele — benign fluid collection within the tunica vaginalis; primary (idiopathic) hydrocele: transilluminates brilliantly, testis palpable separately, soft, non-tender; in adults, conservative management if asymptomatic; surgical correction (hydrocelectomy or aspiration/sclerotherapy) if symptomatic; always USS if testis cannot be clearly separated from swelling to exclude underlying testicular pathology
options.C: Epididymo-orchitis — doxycycline
options.D: Inguinal hernia — surgical repair
options.E: Varicocele — reassure

explanation.correct: Hydrocele: collection of serous fluid in the potential space between the visceral and parietal layers of the tunica vaginalis. Primary (idiopathic): unknown cause in adults; Secondary: associated with epididymo-orchitis, trauma, testicular tumour, TB — must be excluded. Clinical assessment: transillumination (brilliant transillumination = fluid; poor transillumination = blood or pus); testis palpable separately; soft, non-tender; can get above the swelling (unlike inguinal hernia). Per NICE CKS: if testis clearly palpable and transillumination positive — manage conservatively if asymptomatic; USS should be arranged to exclude underlying pathology if: testis not clearly palpable, non-transilluminating component, any doubt; secondary hydroceles (associated with orchitis) require treatment of the underlying cause; primary hydroceles: surgery if symptomatic (hydrocelectomy), aspiration/sclerotherapy (less durable).
explanation.A: Incorrect — Clear transillumination + testis palpable separately = benign hydrocele. 2WW not needed for this presentation.
explanation.B: CORRECT — Primary hydrocele: positive transillumination, conservative if asymptomatic; USS if testis not palpable per NICE CKS.
explanation.C: Incorrect — Epididymo-orchitis is painful, tender, with fever and urinary symptoms.
explanation.D: Incorrect — Inguinal hernia: cannot get above the swelling; bowel sounds may be heard; does not transilluminate.
explanation.E: Incorrect — Varicocele feels like a 'bag of worms', does not transilluminate, worse when standing.

reference: NICE CKS — Scrotal pain and swelling. https://cks.nice.org.uk/topics/scrotal-pain-and-swelling/

question: A 40-year-old man has a right-sided scrotal swelling that does NOT transilluminate. The testis cannot be felt separately from the mass. There is no pain or fever. Per NICE NG12, what is the urgent concern and management?

options.A: Reassure — large hydroceles do not transilluminate
options.B: Urgent 2WW urology referral and scrotal ultrasound — non-transilluminable scrotal mass where testis cannot be felt separately must be considered testicular cancer until USS proves otherwise; NICE NG12 mandates same-day or very urgent referral; testicular cancer is the most common solid tumour in men aged 20-45; USS is the investigation of choice (sensitivity >95%); do NOT attempt aspiration of undiagnosed scrotal mass
options.C: Course of antibiotics and review in 6 weeks
options.D: Reassure and arrange USS in 6 weeks
options.E: MRI scrotum as first investigation

explanation.correct: Per NICE NG12 (Suspected cancer: recognition and referral): any unexplained non-transilluminable scrotal mass in an adult should be referred urgently (2WW) to urology. Testicular cancer is the most common solid tumour in men aged 20-45 (peak 25-35 years). Types: germ cell tumours account for ~95% (seminoma 50%, non-seminoma 45%); non-germ cell (Leydig cell, Sertoli cell tumours). Clinical features: painless (most common — 75%), unilateral testicular swelling or mass, sensation of heaviness; occasionally painful. USS: first investigation; sensitivity >95% for testicular tumours; characteristics — heterogeneous hypoechoic mass. Tumour markers: AFP (alpha-fetoprotein — raised in non-seminoma), beta-hCG (raised in 50% non-seminoma, 10-15% pure seminoma), LDH (prognosis). Management: surgical orchidectomy via inguinal approach (not scrotal — to prevent inguinal lymph node seeding). Prognosis: excellent overall (95% 5-year survival); stage I localised seminoma: >99% cure rate.
explanation.A: Incorrect — Large hydroceles can occasionally be less brilliantly transilluminable but a NON-transilluminable mass where the testis is not separately palpable requires urgent investigation.
explanation.B: CORRECT — Non-transilluminable mass, testis not palpable: urgent 2WW + USS per NICE NG12. Testicular cancer until excluded.
explanation.C: Incorrect — Antibiotics without USS delays diagnosis of potentially curable cancer.
explanation.D: Incorrect — 6-week delay for a possible testicular cancer is unacceptable.
explanation.E: Incorrect — USS is the first investigation of choice for scrotal masses; MRI is used for staging after diagnosis.

reference: NICE NG12 — Suspected cancer. https://www.nice.org.uk/guidance/ng12

question: A 3-year-old boy has a right-sided hydrocele noted at birth. It fluctuates in size — larger in the evening, smaller in the morning. Per NICE CKS, what is the significance of this and management?

options.A: Surgical repair urgently — all hydroceles need immediate intervention
options.B: Communicating hydrocele — fluctuating size indicates a patent processus vaginalis connecting peritoneal cavity to the tunica vaginalis; fluid accumulates during the day (activity/gravity) and reduces when lying down overnight; most resolve spontaneously by age 1-2; if persistent beyond age 2-3, surgical ligation of the patent processus vaginalis (herniotomy) is recommended as there is risk of herniation; conservative management with observation to age 2 is appropriate if diagnosed in infancy
options.C: Reassure — all paediatric hydroceles are permanent
options.D: Aspirate the hydrocele at this appointment
options.E: Refer to paediatric oncology

explanation.correct: Communicating hydrocele in children: caused by a patent processus vaginalis (failure of obliteration of the peritoneal diverticulum that descends with the testis during development). Fluid flows freely between peritoneal cavity and tunica vaginalis. Clinical clue: fluctuating size — larger in the day (upright, active) as peritoneal fluid accumulates, smaller or absent in the morning after overnight recumbency (fluid redistributes back to peritoneum). Distinguishes from non-communicating (simple) hydrocele which has constant size. Important distinction from inguinal hernia: communicating hydrocele contains only fluid (transilluminates); inguinal hernia contains bowel/omentum (does not transilluminate, bowel sounds, cannot always reduce). Management: most communicating hydroceles resolve spontaneously by age 1-2; if still present beyond age 2-3: surgical ligation of patent processus vaginalis (herniotomy) via groin incision — prevents later inguinal hernia; aspiration is not appropriate (fluid re-accumulates from peritoneum).
explanation.A: Incorrect — Urgent surgery is not needed; conservative observation is appropriate in infancy.
explanation.B: CORRECT — Communicating hydrocele: fluctuates with posture/activity. Watch until 2-3 years; surgery if persistent per NICE CKS.
explanation.C: Incorrect — Most paediatric communicating hydroceles resolve spontaneously.
explanation.D: Incorrect — Aspiration is ineffective for communicating hydrocele (fluid returns from peritoneum).
explanation.E: Incorrect — Paediatric communicating hydrocele is a benign anatomical variation, not a malignancy concern.

reference: NICE CKS — Scrotal pain and swelling. https://cks.nice.org.uk/topics/scrotal-pain-and-swelling/

question: A 5-year-old girl is noted at school to have reduced hearing bilaterally. Audiometry confirms bilateral conductive hearing loss of 30 dB. Tympanometry shows bilateral type B (flat) curves. She has no pain, no fever and no discharge. She has had this for 10 weeks. Per NICE CG60, what is the management?

options.A: Prescribe oral antibiotics for 14 days
options.B: Watchful waiting for a further 5 weeks (total 13 weeks from symptom onset) — otitis media with effusion (OME/glue ear) is common in children; most resolve spontaneously by 3 months; antibiotic, antihistamine, decongestant use is NOT recommended; if bilateral persisting OME beyond 13 weeks with hearing loss affecting development, quality of life or learning: refer ENT for possible grommet insertion (ventilation tubes) ± hearing aids
options.C: Immediately refer for grommet insertion
options.D: Start nasal corticosteroid spray for 3 months
options.E: Hearing aids only — grommets are never used in children

explanation.correct: Otitis media with effusion (OME, glue ear): the most common cause of acquired conductive hearing loss in children, affecting approximately 80% of children at some point. Fluid in the middle ear space (no acute inflammation). Tympanometry type B curve = flat, no pressure peak = fluid in middle ear. Per NICE CG60: watchful waiting for 3 months (13 weeks from symptom onset or referral — whichever is later); most (50%) resolve spontaneously within 3 months, 90% within 12 months; NOT recommended: antibiotics, antihistamines, decongestants, nasal steroids; autoinflation (Otovent balloon device) has some evidence and can be tried. If bilateral OME persisting beyond 13 weeks with: significant bilateral hearing loss (>25 dB) affecting speech, language or learning development, quality of life: refer ENT; grommets (ventilation tubes) improve hearing and QoL; hearing aids are an alternative, especially in children unsuitable for surgery. Children with Down syndrome, cleft palate: refer earlier.
explanation.A: Incorrect — Antibiotics are not recommended for OME — it is not an infective acute otitis media.
explanation.B: CORRECT — Watchful waiting to 13 weeks total. If persisting: ENT referral for grommets per NICE CG60.
explanation.C: Incorrect — 10 weeks is before the 13-week threshold; watchful waiting appropriate at this stage.
explanation.D: Incorrect — Nasal steroids are not recommended for OME per NICE CG60.
explanation.E: Incorrect — Grommets ARE used in children with persistent OME and are recommended by NICE CG60 in appropriate cases.

reference: NICE CG60 — Surgical management of otitis media with effusion in children. https://www.nice.org.uk/guidance/cg60

question: A 4-year-old with Down syndrome is found to have bilateral OME with moderate hearing loss at his developmental assessment. Per NICE CG60, does the standard 3-month watchful waiting period apply?

options.A: Yes — Down syndrome children should wait the same 3 months
options.B: No — children with Down syndrome, cleft palate or other developmental disorders associated with hearing impairment should be referred earlier than the standard 13-week threshold; hearing loss has disproportionate impact on speech, language and cognitive development in children with these conditions; prompt ENT referral, hearing assessment, and consideration of grommets or hearing aids is recommended
options.C: Down syndrome children never benefit from grommets
options.D: Wait 2 years before ENT referral
options.E: Cochlear implants are first-line for OME in Down syndrome

explanation.correct: Per NICE CG60, certain groups of children warrant earlier referral than the standard 13-week watchful waiting period: Children with conditions where hearing loss has particularly significant developmental impact — Down syndrome (trisomy 21), cleft palate (very high rates of OME — ~50% persist beyond 12 months), other developmental disorders, learning disabilities; Children already experiencing significant speech/language delay; Children with unilateral significant hearing loss in the context of OME. Rationale: in children with Down syndrome, hearing loss compounds existing developmental challenges (cognitive development, speech, communication, social integration); early intervention with grommets or hearing aids is clinically beneficial. Additionally: OME is extremely common in Down syndrome (due to hypotonia affecting Eustachian tube function and structural differences). Early ENT referral, regular audiology review and active management are standard care.
explanation.A: Incorrect — Standard watchful waiting does not apply to Down syndrome children with OME.
explanation.B: CORRECT — Earlier ENT referral for Down syndrome + OME per NICE CG60 due to disproportionate developmental impact.
explanation.C: Incorrect — Grommets are beneficial for Down syndrome children with persistent OME and hearing loss.
explanation.D: Incorrect — A 2-year wait is inappropriate given the developmental impact of hearing loss.
explanation.E: Incorrect — Cochlear implants are for sensorineural hearing loss; OME causes conductive loss managed with grommets/hearing aids.

reference: NICE CG60 — Surgical management of OME in children. https://www.nice.org.uk/guidance/cg60

question: A child has persistent bilateral OME with bilateral hearing loss of 35 dB at 6 months. He is 8 years old with speech delay. Per NICE CG60, what is the most appropriate intervention?

options.A: Continue watchful waiting for another 6 months
options.B: Grommet insertion (bilateral myringotomy and ventilation tube insertion) — indicated for bilateral OME with significant hearing loss (>25-30 dB) persisting beyond 13 weeks, especially with speech delay or quality of life impact; grommets restore hearing immediately, improving speech and language outcomes; extruded spontaneously in most children within 6-12 months; adenoidectomy may be added if recurrent OME
options.C: Refer to special educational needs only
options.D: Aspiration of middle ear fluid under LA
options.E: Permanent hearing aids instead of grommets

explanation.correct: Per NICE CG60, indications for grommet insertion: bilateral OME persisting >3 months (13 weeks) with bilateral hearing loss ≥25-30 dB that is affecting development, quality of life, behaviour, speech and language, or educational performance. This child has: 6 months of bilateral OME (well beyond 13-week threshold), 35 dB hearing loss (significant), speech delay (functional impact) — all criteria clearly met for surgical intervention. Grommet (ventilation tube) procedure: bilateral myringotomy (small incision in tympanic membrane) + insertion of small plastic ventilation tube; performed under general anaesthetic; restores hearing immediately; tube extrudes spontaneously in 6-12 months (short-term) or longer-duration tubes (T-tubes) for recurrent cases; adenoidectomy added if recurrent OME post-grommets. Hearing aids: alternative when surgery declined or contraindicated; also recommended alongside grommets if hearing loss persists after tube extrusion. NICE evidence: grommets provide hearing improvement equivalent to hearing aids in the short term; both improve quality of life and language outcomes.
explanation.A: Incorrect — Further watchful waiting is inappropriate at 6 months with functional impairment — threshold is 13 weeks.
explanation.B: CORRECT — Grommets indicated: bilateral OME >13 weeks + >25 dB hearing loss + speech delay per NICE CG60.
explanation.C: Incorrect — Educational support alone does not address the hearing impairment.
explanation.D: Incorrect — Aspiration without tube insertion is not the standard procedure.
explanation.E: Incorrect — Hearing aids are an alternative/complementary option but grommets are first-line surgical intervention for appropriate cases.

reference: NICE CG60 — Surgical management of OME in children. https://www.nice.org.uk/guidance/cg60

question: A 22-year-old female runner with BMI 18.2 and weight 50 kg presents with 8 months of absent periods. She trains twice daily. Per NICE CKS, what is the diagnosis and management?

options.A: PCOS — clomifene for ovulation induction
options.B: Hypothalamic amenorrhoea — suppression of the hypothalamic-pituitary-ovarian axis from excessive exercise, low body weight and caloric restriction (the female athlete triad: low energy availability, menstrual dysfunction, low bone density); management: reduce exercise intensity and frequency, increase caloric intake, target weight gain to restore ovulation; psychological assessment and support (underlying eating disorder in some patients); DEXA scan to assess bone density if >6 months amenorrhoea
options.C: Premature ovarian insufficiency — FSH level
options.D: Thyroid disease — TFTs
options.E: Start COCP to restore periods

explanation.correct: Hypothalamic amenorrhoea (HA): functional suppression of the hypothalamic-pituitary-ovarian (HPO) axis due to energy deficiency, psychological stress, or excessive exercise — or a combination. Energy deficiency: insufficient caloric intake relative to energy expenditure → reduced GnRH pulsatility → reduced FSH/LH → anovulation. Classic scenario: female athlete + low BMI + high exercise load + caloric restriction. The Female Athlete Triad: (1) Low energy availability (with or without disordered eating); (2) Menstrual dysfunction (hypothalamic amenorrhoea); (3) Low bone mineral density (increased fracture risk). Per NICE CKS: investigations to exclude other causes (FSH, LH, prolactin, TFTs, pregnancy test, testosterone); FSH/LH typically low-normal (not elevated as in POI); DEXA scan if amenorrhoea >6 months; Management: reduce exercise volume, increase caloric intake, nutritional rehabilitation, psychological support (CBT for disordered eating if present), calcium/vitamin D if low BMD. Do NOT use COCP as a substitute for energy restoration — it masks the problem without treating the underlying cause and does not protect bone adequately.
explanation.A: Incorrect — PCOS has features of hyperandrogenism, polycystic ovaries, irregular periods from anovulation; not appropriate here.
explanation.B: CORRECT — Hypothalamic amenorrhoea: female athlete triad. Reduce exercise + increase calories + DEXA + psychological assessment per NICE CKS.
explanation.C: Incorrect — Premature ovarian insufficiency has elevated FSH (>25 IU/L on 2 occasions 4 weeks apart).
explanation.D: Incorrect — TFTs should be checked to exclude thyroid disease but the clinical context makes hypothalamic amenorrhoea most likely.
explanation.E: Incorrect — COCP induces withdrawal bleed but doesn't restore HPO axis function or protect bone density adequately.

reference: NICE CKS — Amenorrhoea. https://cks.nice.org.uk/topics/amenorrhoea/

question: A 24-year-old athlete with hypothalamic amenorrhoea is found to have reduced bone mineral density (T-score −2.1 at lumbar spine). She is reluctant to reduce training. Per NICE and IOC consensus, which pharmacological bone protection is most appropriate in this scenario?

options.A: Bisphosphonate (alendronate) — first-line for all low BMD
options.B: Bisphosphonates are NOT first-line in young premenopausal women with hypothalamic amenorrhoea — evidence is limited; potential teratogenicity concerns if pregnancy occurs; preferred approach: restore energy availability and body weight (weight restoration is the most effective intervention for bone recovery); if persistent after 12 months: combined oestrogen/progesterone (COCP or transdermal oestrogen + cyclic progesterone) can improve bone density; the underlying cause must be addressed; refer to endocrinology if not improving
options.C: Denosumab — first-line for athletes
options.D: No bone protection available in young women
options.E: Calcitonin nasal spray

explanation.correct: Bone protection in hypothalamic amenorrhoea/female athlete triad: unlike postmenopausal osteoporosis, management in young women requires specific considerations. Per NICE NG187, IOC consensus on the female athlete triad, and endocrine society guidance: First priority: treat the underlying cause — restore energy availability, weight gain, reduce exercise load. This is the most effective intervention and can lead to significant bone recovery; Bisphosphonates: NOT recommended as first-line in premenopausal women with HA — potential teratogenicity (persist in bone for years, may affect fetal skeletal development in future pregnancy), limited evidence of efficacy in HA specifically, residual accumulation concerns; Oestrogen/progesterone: COCP or transdermal oestrogen (preferred in HA) + cyclic progesterone after 12 months of persistent amenorrhoea not responding to lifestyle changes — may help preserve/improve bone density; Calcium and vitamin D: supplementation if intake inadequate; DEXA: monitoring annually if amenorrhoea persists.
explanation.A: Incorrect — Bisphosphonates are not first-line in premenopausal women with HA due to teratogenicity concerns and limited evidence.
explanation.B: CORRECT — Energy restoration primary intervention. Bisphosphonates not first-line. Oestrogen after 12 months if persisting per IOC/NICE.
explanation.C: Incorrect — Denosumab has the same concerns in premenopausal women.
explanation.D: Incorrect — Oestrogen/progesterone and lifestyle restoration are available and effective.
explanation.E: Incorrect — Calcitonin is not standard management in this context.

reference: NICE NG187. IOC Consensus Statement on the Female Athlete Triad. https://www.nice.org.uk/guidance/ng187

question: A 21-year-old woman presents with secondary amenorrhoea for 5 months. BMI is 17.8, she has recently started gymnastics training 2 hours daily. Per NICE CKS, what is the most important initial investigation to exclude?

options.A: Prolactin level
options.B: Pregnancy test — pregnancy is the most common cause of secondary amenorrhoea and must ALWAYS be excluded first before any other investigations; after pregnancy excluded: FSH, LH, prolactin, TFTs, testosterone, weight and BMI assessment
options.C: DEXA scan immediately
options.D: MRI brain
options.E: Coeliac serology

explanation.correct: Per NICE CKS (Amenorrhoea), the first investigation in any woman with secondary amenorrhoea is a PREGNANCY TEST — this must be excluded before any other investigations as pregnancy is the most common cause. Only after pregnancy is excluded should other investigations be performed: FSH and LH (pituitary gonadotrophin levels — low in hypothalamic amenorrhoea, high in premature ovarian insufficiency); prolactin (elevated in hyperprolactinaemia from prolactinoma or drug-induced); TFTs (hypothyroidism causes menstrual disturbance); testosterone (elevated in PCOS or androgen-excess states); assessment of weight, BMI, exercise history (hypothalamic amenorrhoea). Investigations for systemic causes: coeliac (malabsorption causing hypothalamic amenorrhoea), chronic illness. DEXA and MRI are later investigations if appropriate. Failing to exclude pregnancy before starting investigations can lead to inappropriate tests and delayed diagnosis.
explanation.A: Incorrect — Prolactin is important but pregnancy must be excluded first.
explanation.B: CORRECT — Pregnancy test FIRST before any other investigation for secondary amenorrhoea per NICE CKS.
explanation.C: Incorrect — DEXA is appropriate later if HA confirmed and persists >6 months.
explanation.D: Incorrect — MRI brain (pituitary) is indicated if prolactin is elevated.
explanation.E: Incorrect — Coeliac serology is not the most important initial investigation.

reference: NICE CKS — Amenorrhoea. https://cks.nice.org.uk/topics/amenorrhoea/

question: A 35-year-old woman delivered 8 months ago following a complicated postpartum haemorrhage requiring blood transfusion. She has not menstruated since delivery and is unable to breastfeed despite attempts. She has persistent fatigue, cold intolerance, and reduced libido. Per NICE CKS, what is the most likely diagnosis?

options.A: Physiological lactational amenorrhoea — normal after delivery
options.B: Sheehan's syndrome (postpartum hypopituitarism) — pituitary necrosis caused by peripartum haemorrhage and shock; the pituitary gland enlarges in pregnancy and is vulnerable to ischaemia; presents with failure to lactate (prolactin deficiency — earliest sign), absent menses, fatigue, cold intolerance (hypothyroidism), reduced libido (hypogonadism), adrenal insufficiency; investigations: pituitary hormone profile (FSH, LH, TSH, FT4, prolactin, cortisol, IGF-1, GH); MRI pituitary (empty sella); treatment: hormone replacement for each deficient axis
options.C: Postpartum depression — antidepressant
options.D: Iron deficiency anaemia — ferrous sulphate
options.E: Type 2 diabetes — HbA1c

explanation.correct: Sheehan's syndrome (postpartum pituitary necrosis): caused by severe obstetric haemorrhage causing pituitary ischaemia. The anterior pituitary gland doubles in size during pregnancy (lactotroph hyperplasia) but blood supply does not increase proportionally — making it vulnerable to ischaemic necrosis during peripartum hypotension. Features: (1) Failure to lactate — prolactin deficiency (first sign, immediate postpartum); (2) Secondary amenorrhoea — gonadotrophin deficiency (FSH/LH); (3) Hypothyroidism symptoms (cold intolerance, fatigue, weight gain) — TSH deficiency; (4) Adrenal insufficiency (fatigue, hypotension) — ACTH deficiency; (5) Growth hormone deficiency (lethargy, metabolic changes); (6) Diabetes insipidus (posterior pituitary — rare in Sheehan's, unlike other pituitary causes). Investigations: MRI shows empty sella; pituitary hormone profile. Treatment: lifelong hormone replacement (hydrocortisone, levothyroxine, oestrogen/progestogen, GH). Sheehan's is the most common cause of hypopituitarism in developing countries and still seen in the UK.
explanation.A: Incorrect — Lactational amenorrhoea requires successful breastfeeding; inability to lactate is the key feature of Sheehan's.
explanation.B: CORRECT — Sheehan's syndrome: PPH + inability to lactate + amenorrhoea + panhypopituitary features. MRI pituitary + hormone profile per NICE CKS.
explanation.C: Incorrect — Postpartum depression doesn't explain the inability to lactate or cold intolerance.
explanation.D: Incorrect — Iron deficiency explains fatigue but not the inability to lactate or amenorrhoea.
explanation.E: Incorrect — Diabetes doesn't explain this combination of symptoms.

reference: NICE CKS — Hypopituitarism. Pituitary Foundation. https://cks.nice.org.uk/topics/hypopituitarism/

question: A woman diagnosed with Sheehan's syndrome undergoes a pituitary hormone profile. Which hormone deficiency is most immediately life-threatening if not replaced?

options.A: Growth hormone
options.B: Cortisol (ACTH deficiency causing secondary adrenal insufficiency) — adrenocortical failure from ACTH deficiency causes: fatigue, hypotension, hypoglycaemia, hyponatraemia, inability to mount a stress response (risk of adrenal crisis); without cortisol replacement, patients can die from adrenal crisis during intercurrent illness or surgery; hydrocortisone replacement is the most immediately life-threatening deficiency to treat; also need steroid sick-day rules education
options.C: Prolactin — most important for reproduction
options.D: Growth hormone
options.E: Testosterone

explanation.correct: In panhypopituitarism (Sheehan's or other causes), the order of urgency for hormone replacement: (1) Cortisol (hydrocortisone for secondary adrenal insufficiency) — MOST URGENT: adrenal crisis (hypotension, hypoglycaemia, hyponatraemia, collapse) can be fatal; stress response is completely absent; must be replaced before thyroid hormone (giving T4 without cortisol can precipitate adrenal crisis by increasing cortisol metabolism); (2) Thyroid hormone (levothyroxine) — second priority; given AFTER cortisol replacement is established; (3) Sex hormones (oestrogen/testosterone) — quality of life, bone density; (4) Growth hormone — metabolic benefits, quality of life; not first priority; (5) Prolactin — replacement not available or required (no clinical syndrome from prolactin deficiency except failure to lactate). Key principle: in any panhypopituitary patient, always replace cortisol BEFORE thyroid hormone.
explanation.A: Incorrect — Growth hormone deficiency causes metabolic effects and impaired QoL but is not immediately life-threatening.
explanation.B: CORRECT — Cortisol deficiency (secondary adrenal insufficiency) is the most life-threatening; must be replaced first before thyroid hormone.
explanation.C: Incorrect — Prolactin deficiency causes failure to lactate — not immediately life-threatening.
explanation.D: Incorrect — GH is the same as A — metabolic effects, not immediately fatal.
explanation.E: Incorrect — Testosterone/oestrogen affect fertility and bone density but are not immediately life-threatening.

reference: NICE CKS — Hypopituitarism. Society for Endocrinology — Hypopituitarism guidelines. https://cks.nice.org.uk/topics/hypopituitarism/

question: A 32-year-old woman had a PPH 2 years ago. She has been unable to conceive since. FSH is 3.2 IU/L (low), LH 1.8 IU/L (low), oestradiol low. Prolactin is undetectable. Per NICE CKS, what does this biochemical pattern suggest?

options.A: Premature ovarian insufficiency — FSH should be high
options.B: Hypopituitarism with secondary hypogonadism — low FSH and LH with low oestradiol (secondary hypogonadism) and undetectable prolactin; in a woman with previous PPH this is highly consistent with Sheehan's syndrome (secondary hypogonadism due to loss of gonadotrophins, not primary ovarian failure); in premature ovarian insufficiency FSH would be very HIGH (>25 IU/L) because ovaries are failing to respond and fail to suppress FSH
options.C: PCOS — testosterone level
options.D: Anorexia nervosa — eating disorder assessment
options.E: Normal results — retest in 6 months

explanation.correct: Distinguishing primary (ovarian) from secondary (hypothalamic/pituitary) hypogonadism is critical: Primary hypogonadism (premature ovarian insufficiency): ovaries failing → low oestradiol → high FSH and LH (pituitary tries to compensate by increasing stimulation); gonadotrophins elevated. Secondary hypogonadism (hypopituitarism/hypothalamic amenorrhoea): pituitary/hypothalamus failing → low FSH and LH → low oestradiol; gonadotrophins low/normal. This patient: low FSH, low LH, low oestradiol + undetectable prolactin (consistent with pituitary destruction as in Sheehan's). The undetectable prolactin is a key clue — in most causes of amenorrhoea, prolactin is normal or elevated, never undetectable. Undetectable prolactin + low gonadotrophins after PPH = Sheehan's syndrome until proven otherwise. Further investigation: full pituitary profile (ACTH/cortisol, TSH, GH/IGF-1), MRI pituitary (empty sella), referral to endocrinology.
explanation.A: Incorrect — POI has HIGH FSH; this has LOW FSH = secondary not primary.
explanation.B: CORRECT — Low FSH, LH + low oestradiol + undetectable prolactin after PPH = hypopituitarism (Sheehan's). Secondary not primary hypogonadism per NICE CKS.
explanation.C: Incorrect — PCOS typically has normal/mildly elevated LH with normal/low FSH (elevated LH:FSH ratio), elevated testosterone, polycystic ovaries.
explanation.D: Incorrect — Anorexia causes hypothalamic suppression with low-normal FSH/LH; undetectable prolactin after PPH specifically suggests Sheehan's.
explanation.E: Incorrect — These results are clearly abnormal and require urgent endocrinology referral.

reference: NICE CKS — Hypopituitarism. https://cks.nice.org.uk/topics/hypopituitarism/

question: A 52-year-old man is found to have a blood pressure of 148/92 mmHg at a routine NHS Health Check. He has no symptoms and no evidence of target organ damage. His 10-year cardiovascular risk (QRISK3) is 8%. Per NICE NG136, what is the appropriate management?

options.A: Start antihypertensive medication immediately
options.B: Stage 1 hypertension (clinic BP 140-159/90-99 mmHg, ABPM/HBPM daytime average 135-149/85-94 mmHg) WITHOUT target organ damage, established CVD or diabetes AND QRISK3 <10%: lifestyle advice only; no antihypertensive medication at this stage; review in 12 months; lifestyle interventions: weight reduction, low-salt diet (<6g/day), regular aerobic exercise, reduce alcohol, stop smoking, DASH diet
options.C: Start atenolol 50mg daily
options.D: Admit to hospital for BP monitoring
options.E: Recheck in 5 years only

explanation.correct: Per NICE NG136 (Hypertension in adults: diagnosis and management): diagnosis: confirm with ABPM or HBPM (24-hour ambulatory or home monitoring) before treatment. Clinic BP ≥140/90 → confirm with ABPM/HBPM. Treatment thresholds: Stage 1 HTN (clinic 140-159/90-99, ABPM daytime average 135-149/85-94): offer drug treatment if age <80 + target organ damage OR established CVD OR renal disease OR diabetes OR 10-year CV risk ≥10%; if none of these → lifestyle advice only with 12-month review. Stage 2 HTN (clinic ≥160/100 mmHg): offer drug treatment regardless of CV risk. This patient: Stage 1 HTN, no organ damage, no CVD, no diabetes, QRISK3 8% (<10%) → lifestyle advice only, no medication. Lifestyle interventions reduce BP by 5-15 mmHg.
explanation.A: Incorrect — NICE NG136 does not recommend medication for Stage 1 HTN with QRISK <10% and no target organ damage.
explanation.B: CORRECT — Stage 1 HTN + QRISK3 <10% + no organ damage: lifestyle advice only, review 12 months per NICE NG136.
explanation.C: Incorrect — Beta-blockers are not first-line for hypertension; no medication indicated at this stage.
explanation.D: Incorrect — Admission is not required for Stage 1 HTN without hypertensive emergency.
explanation.E: Incorrect — Review in 12 months is appropriate; 5 years is too long to wait.

reference: NICE NG136 — Hypertension in adults. https://www.nice.org.uk/guidance/ng136

question: A 58-year-old African-Caribbean woman has confirmed Stage 2 hypertension (ABPM daytime average 155/98 mmHg). She has no comorbidities, no target organ damage and no diabetes. Per NICE NG136, what is the first-line antihypertensive?

options.A: ACE inhibitor (ramipril) — first-line for all patients
options.B: Calcium channel blocker (amlodipine) — NICE NG136 recommends CCB or thiazide-like diuretic as first-line for African or Caribbean family origin patients (regardless of age) as ACE inhibitors and ARBs are less effective in this population due to lower circulating renin levels; CCB (amlodipine) is preferred first-line; if CCB not tolerated: thiazide-like diuretic (indapamide or chlortalidone)
options.C: Beta-blocker (atenolol) — first-line for all ethnicities
options.D: Spironolactone — first-line for resistant hypertension
options.E: ACE inhibitor + beta-blocker combination immediately

explanation.correct: Per NICE NG136, antihypertensive drug selection is stratified by age and ethnicity: Step 1 treatment: Under 55, not of African/Caribbean family origin: ACE inhibitor (or ARB if ACE intolerant) — first-line; 55 or over OR of African/Caribbean family origin at any age: CCB (amlodipine) first-line; if CCB not tolerated: thiazide-like diuretic (indapamide preferred, chlortalidone alternative). Rationale for ethnicity-specific guidance: Black African/Caribbean patients typically have a low-renin form of hypertension where the renin-angiotensin system plays a lesser role — hence ACE inhibitors/ARBs are less effective as monotherapy in this population. CCBs work well across all renin levels. If Step 1 inadequate: Step 2 = ACE inhibitor (or ARB) + CCB. Step 3 = ACE inhibitor (or ARB) + CCB + thiazide-like diuretic. Step 4 (resistant, check for Conn's) = add spironolactone/doxazosin.
explanation.A: Incorrect — ACE inhibitor is first-line for younger (<55) non-African/Caribbean patients; not this patient.
explanation.B: CORRECT — African/Caribbean family origin: CCB (amlodipine) first-line per NICE NG136.
explanation.C: Incorrect — Beta-blockers are not first-line for hypertension per NICE NG136.
explanation.D: Incorrect — Spironolactone is used at Step 4 for resistant hypertension.
explanation.E: Incorrect — Combination is not first-line; monotherapy is the initial approach.

reference: NICE NG136 — Hypertension in adults. https://www.nice.org.uk/guidance/ng136

question: A 62-year-old man is on amlodipine + ramipril for hypertension but BP remains 158/96 mmHg. Per NICE NG136 Step 3, what should be added?

options.A: Beta-blocker (bisoprolol)
options.B: Thiazide-like diuretic (indapamide or chlortalidone) — NICE NG136 Step 3 = ACE inhibitor/ARB + CCB + thiazide-like diuretic; adds a third antihypertensive agent with different mechanism; chlortalidone or indapamide preferred over bendroflumethiazide (better evidence for cardiovascular outcomes); if still uncontrolled at Step 4: check adherence and 24-hour ABPM; add spironolactone (25-50mg) if K+ <4.5 mmol/L, or doxazosin/bisoprolol if K+ ≥4.5
options.C: Add a second ACE inhibitor
options.D: Start lithium
options.E: Add another CCB (nifedipine)

explanation.correct: Per NICE NG136 management algorithm: Step 1: ACE inhibitor/ARB OR CCB OR thiazide-like diuretic (based on age/ethnicity). Step 2: ACE inhibitor/ARB + CCB. Step 3: ACE inhibitor/ARB + CCB + thiazide-like diuretic. Preferred thiazide-like diuretics: indapamide or chlortalidone (evidence from ACCOMPLISH, ALLHAT trials for cardiovascular outcomes); NOT bendroflumethiazide (less evidence). This patient is already on ACE inhibitor (ramipril) + CCB (amlodipine) = Step 2; next is Step 3 = add thiazide-like diuretic. Step 4 (resistant hypertension — BP still elevated on 3 agents): (1) Confirm adherence; (2) Consider ABPM to confirm true resistance; (3) If K+ <4.5 mmol/L: add spironolactone 25mg (investigates for Conn's syndrome and treats aldosterone-driven HTN); If K+ ≥4.5: add alpha-blocker (doxazosin) or beta-blocker (bisoprolol). NICE NG136 is one of the most frequently tested topics in the AKT.
explanation.A: Incorrect — Beta-blocker is Step 4, not Step 3.
explanation.B: CORRECT — Step 3 = add thiazide-like diuretic (indapamide/chlortalidone) per NICE NG136.
explanation.C: Incorrect — You cannot add a second ACE inhibitor — dual renin-angiotensin blockade is contraindicated.
explanation.D: Incorrect — Lithium is a mood stabiliser, not an antihypertensive.
explanation.E: Incorrect — Two CCBs simultaneously is not recommended.

reference: NICE NG136 — Hypertension in adults. https://www.nice.org.uk/guidance/ng136

question: A 68-year-old man has a stamping high-stepping gait bilaterally. Romberg's test is positive (unsteady with eyes closed). He has loss of vibration sense and proprioception in both feet with normal muscle power. Per neurological principles, which pathway is affected?

options.A: Pyramidal (corticospinal) tract — upper motor neurone
options.B: Dorsal columns (posterior columns) — carry vibration sense, proprioception and discriminative touch; loss causes sensory ataxia (stamping gait, Romberg positive — patient depends on vision for balance); positive Romberg confirms dorsal column lesion (vision compensates when eyes open but balance fails when eyes closed); causes: vitamin B12 deficiency (subacute combined degeneration), tabes dorsalis (neurosyphilis), MS, Friedreich's ataxia, compressive myelopathy
options.C: Cerebellar pathways — intention tremor, dysdiadochokinesia
options.D: Spinothalamic tract — pain and temperature
options.E: Lower motor neurone — weakness and wasting

explanation.correct: Dorsal column (posterior column) anatomy and function: carry IPSILATERAL fibres for: vibration (128 Hz tuning fork), proprioception (joint position sense), discriminative touch (2-point discrimination), pressure sensation. Ascend ipsilaterally in the posterior cord to the nucleus gracilis/cuneatus in the medulla, then cross (decussate) and ascend as medial lemniscus to thalamus. Dorsal column lesion causes sensory ataxia: loss of proprioceptive feedback leads to unsteady gait compensated by visual input; characteristic stamping gait (patient over-strides to generate visual/proprioceptive feedback); Romberg POSITIVE (unsteady with eyes closed — visual compensation removed). Romberg test: positive = sensory ataxia (dorsal column or sensory neuropathy); negative = cerebellar ataxia. Cervical cord dorsal column lesion: Lhermitte's sign (electric shock sensation down spine on neck flexion — pathognomonic of MS or B12 deficiency). Key causes of posterior column disease: vitamin B12 deficiency (subacute combined degeneration — also affects lateral corticospinal tracts), neurosyphilis (tabes dorsalis), MS, Friedreich's ataxia, compressive myelopathy (e.g. cervical spondylosis).
explanation.A: Incorrect — Pyramidal/UMN tract lesion causes spasticity, hyperreflexia, extensor plantar response — not sensory loss or Romberg positive.
explanation.B: CORRECT — Dorsal columns: vibration + proprioception loss + stamping gait + positive Romberg = sensory ataxia.
explanation.C: Incorrect — Cerebellar ataxia causes intention tremor, dysdiadochokinesia, nystagmus; Romberg is negative (base remains wide with eyes open).
explanation.D: Incorrect — Spinothalamic carries pain and temperature; lesion causes contralateral dissociated sensory loss.
explanation.E: Incorrect — LMN lesion causes wasting, fasciculations, flaccid weakness — not sensory ataxia.

reference: NICE CKS — Vitamin B12 deficiency. Neurological examination resources. https://cks.nice.org.uk/topics/vitamin-b12-deficiency/

question: A 65-year-old man has bilateral dorsal column signs. Blood tests show B12 84 pmol/L (low), MCV 108 fL, Hb 9.2 g/L. He is a strict vegan. Per NICE CKS and BNF, what is the cause and treatment?

options.A: Folate deficiency — folic acid 5mg
options.B: Vitamin B12 deficiency causing subacute combined degeneration of the cord (SACD) — B12 deficiency from dietary insufficiency (strict veganism — B12 found only in animal products); treatment: IM hydroxocobalamin 1mg on alternate days for 2 weeks (loading), then 1mg every 3 months for life; oral B12 (cyanocobalamin) can be used for dietary deficiency if absorption is intact; also give folic acid 5mg daily; neurological signs may partially but not fully reverse; check for folate deficiency co-exists
options.C: Pernicious anaemia — intrinsic factor antibody, treat with oral B12
options.D: Iron deficiency — ferrous sulphate
options.E: No treatment needed — B12 levels are not clinically significant

explanation.correct: Subacute combined degeneration of the cord (SACD): demyelination of posterior AND lateral columns of spinal cord from B12 deficiency. Posterior column: vibration/proprioception loss, sensory ataxia, Romberg positive. Lateral column (corticospinal tracts): UMN signs (spasticity, extensor plantar responses). Peripheral neuropathy also common. May also have: megaloblastic anaemia (macrocytosis), glossitis, cognitive impairment, optic atrophy. Per NICE CKS: Dietary B12 deficiency (veganism): oral cyanocobalamin (1mg daily) is appropriate as absorption pathway is intact. Neurological involvement: IM hydroxocobalamin loading doses (1mg alternate days × 2 weeks minimum, some guidelines continue more intensively if neurological features persist) then 1mg every 3 months (or every 2 months if neurological involvement). Important: give folic acid as well (co-deficiency common); do NOT give folic acid alone in B12 deficiency — may precipitate/worsen neurological complications. Neurological recovery: variable; often partial; good prognosis if treated early.
explanation.A: Incorrect — Folate deficiency causes macrocytic anaemia but NOT dorsal column/SACD neurological features.
explanation.B: CORRECT — Dietary B12 deficiency causing SACD. IM hydroxocobalamin loading + 3-monthly maintenance per NICE CKS.
explanation.C: Incorrect — Pernicious anaemia (intrinsic factor deficiency) has the same SACD features but requires IM B12 (absorption impaired); the clinical context here is dietary deficiency from veganism.
explanation.D: Incorrect — Iron deficiency causes microcytic anaemia; B12 deficiency causes macrocytic anaemia with neurological features.
explanation.E: Incorrect — B12 84 pmol/L is clearly low and causing SACD — urgent treatment required.

reference: NICE CKS — Vitamin B12 deficiency. BNF — Hydroxocobalamin. https://cks.nice.org.uk/topics/vitamin-b12-deficiency/

question: A neurologist asks the GP to start B12 injections for a patient with confirmed pernicious anaemia (positive intrinsic factor antibody). Per BNF and NICE CKS, what is the correct treatment regimen?

options.A: Oral cyanocobalamin 1mg daily indefinitely
options.B: IM hydroxocobalamin: loading — 1mg three times per week for 2 weeks (if no neurological involvement); 1mg on alternate days for 2-3 weeks (if neurological involvement, for as long as improvement occurs); maintenance: 1mg every 3 months for life (every 2 months if neurological involvement persisting); do NOT use oral B12 for pernicious anaemia (intrinsic factor absent — impaired absorption)
options.C: IM hydroxocobalamin 1mg monthly for 3 months then stop
options.D: Folic acid 5mg daily only
options.E: No treatment necessary if asymptomatic

explanation.correct: Per BNF and NICE CKS, pernicious anaemia treatment with IM hydroxocobalamin: Pernicious anaemia = lack of intrinsic factor (autoimmune gastric parietal cell or intrinsic factor antibodies) → impaired ileal B12 absorption. Oral B12 is NOT effective (absorption pathway destroyed). IM hydroxocobalamin is the only treatment: WITHOUT neurological involvement: 1mg IM three times weekly for 2 weeks loading, then 1mg every 3 months maintenance for life. WITH neurological involvement: 1mg IM on alternate days for 2-3 weeks (or longer as long as continued improvement), then 1mg every 2 months for life (more frequent maintenance to maximise neurological recovery). Always check folate and give folic acid if deficient. Coeliac disease and other causes of malabsorption also require IM injections. Dietary deficiency (veganism, strict vegetarianism) with intact absorption: oral cyanocobalamin 1-50mg daily or IM hydroxocobalamin.
explanation.A: Incorrect — Oral B12 is not effective for pernicious anaemia (absorption is impaired due to absent intrinsic factor).
explanation.B: CORRECT — IM hydroxocobalamin loading then 3-monthly maintenance (2-monthly if neurological) per BNF/NICE CKS.
explanation.C: Incorrect — B12 injections are lifelong in pernicious anaemia — stopping causes recurrence.
explanation.D: Incorrect — Folic acid alone can worsen neurological B12 deficiency and does not replace B12.
explanation.E: Incorrect — Pernicious anaemia requires lifelong B12 replacement to prevent haematological and neurological complications.

reference: BNF — Hydroxocobalamin. NICE CKS — Pernicious anaemia. https://bnf.nice.org.uk/drug/hydroxocobalamin.html

question: A 35-year-old woman on olanzapine 15mg daily for schizophrenia reports her periods have become irregular over the past 6 months — cycles now every 45-60 days with reduced flow. Per NICE NG10 and BNF, what is the most likely cause?

options.A: Premature ovarian insufficiency — FSH level urgently
options.B: Hyperprolactinaemia induced by olanzapine — olanzapine blocks dopamine D2 receptors in the tuberoinfundibular pathway; dopamine normally inhibits prolactin release from the anterior pituitary; D2 blockade removes this inhibition causing hyperprolactinaemia; clinical effects: menstrual irregularity/amenorrhoea, galactorrhoea, sexual dysfunction, reduced bone density; measure serum prolactin; if significantly elevated: consider switching to a prolactin-sparing antipsychotic (aripiprazole, quetiapine) with psychiatry input
options.C: PCOS — ultrasound pelvis
options.D: Thyroid disease — TFTs
options.E: Normal side effect — no action needed

explanation.correct: Antipsychotic-induced hyperprolactinaemia: antipsychotics that block dopamine D2 receptors in the tuberoinfundibular pathway reduce dopaminergic inhibition of prolactin secretion → elevated prolactin. Prolactin levels by antipsychotic: High prolactin-elevating: risperidone (highest), haloperidol, amisulpride, olanzapine (moderate), chlorpromazine. Prolactin-sparing (low effect): aripiprazole (partial D2 agonist), quetiapine, clozapine. Clinical consequences of hyperprolactinaemia: menstrual disturbance (oligomenorrhoea, amenorrhoea), galactorrhoea, sexual dysfunction (decreased libido, anorgasmia), decreased bone mineral density (increased fracture risk), gynaecomastia (men). Per NICE NG10 and Maudsley Guidelines: measure prolactin in all antipsychotic patients with menstrual symptoms; if symptomatic hyperprolactinaemia — consider switching to prolactin-sparing agent (aripiprazole, quetiapine) after discussion with psychiatrist; aripiprazole can be added as an adjunct to reduce prolactin without changing main antipsychotic. Exclude other causes (pregnancy, hypothyroidism, pituitary tumour).
explanation.A: Incorrect — POI would have elevated FSH; olanzapine history makes hyperprolactinaemia more likely.
explanation.B: CORRECT — Olanzapine-induced hyperprolactinaemia: D2 blockade → raised prolactin → menstrual irregularity. Measure prolactin; consider switch to prolactin-sparing agent per NICE NG10.
explanation.C: Incorrect — PCOS features include hyperandrogenism, weight gain, polycystic ovaries; olanzapine history is the key clue.
explanation.D: Incorrect — TFTs should be checked as part of the workup but olanzapine is the most likely cause.
explanation.E: Incorrect — Hyperprolactinaemia is a clinically significant adverse effect with long-term consequences (bone loss) requiring management.

reference: NICE NG10 — Psychosis and schizophrenia. Maudsley Prescribing Guidelines. https://www.nice.org.uk/guidance/ng10

question: A 40-year-old woman on haloperidol has a prolactin of 1,850 mIU/L (normal <530 mIU/L). Per Maudsley and NICE NG10, what is the management approach?

options.A: Stop haloperidol immediately
options.B: If drug-induced hyperprolactinaemia is confirmed (prolactin raised, correlating with antipsychotic introduction): if symptomatic and clinically appropriate — consider switching to a prolactin-sparing antipsychotic (aripiprazole, quetiapine) after psychiatric input; if switching is not possible — aripiprazole 5-15mg can be added as an adjunct (partial D2 agonist reduces prolactin by competing with haloperidol without full antagonism); DEXA if >6 months hyperprolactinaemia; ensure MRI pituitary excluded prolactinoma if prolactin >5000 mIU/L or no antipsychotic explanation
options.C: Immediately start cabergoline
options.D: No action needed — prolactin elevation is expected with haloperidol
options.E: Measure prolactin-releasing hormone

explanation.correct: Per Maudsley Prescribing Guidelines in Psychiatry and NICE NG10, management of antipsychotic-induced hyperprolactinaemia: First: confirm drug causation (prolactin elevated in context of antipsychotic use, especially high-prolactin agent like haloperidol/risperidone/amisulpride). Exclude: pregnancy, hypothyroidism (TFTs), prolactinoma (MRI if prolactin very high >5000 mIU/L or not proportionate to drug, or no antipsychotic explanation). If drug-induced: Symptomatic, switch possible (psychiatric stability allows): switch to prolactin-sparing antipsychotic (aripiprazole or quetiapine) with psychiatry input. Switch not possible: add aripiprazole 5-15mg (partial D2 agonist — competes at D2 receptor, reduces haloperidol-induced D2 blockade in tuberoinfundibular pathway, lowers prolactin without affecting antipsychotic efficacy in mesolimbic pathway). Monitor bone density: DEXA if prolactin elevated >6 months. Cabergoline (dopamine agonist): used in prolactinoma but may worsen psychosis in schizophrenia patients — not first-line.
