explanation.B: CORRECT — Treat with sensitivity-guided cefalexin; review and refer for specialist reassessment of prophylaxis per NICE NG224.
explanation.C: Incorrect — IV antibiotics are reserved for children who cannot tolerate oral medication or are systemically unwell/septic.
explanation.D: Incorrect — Cefalexin is sensitive — this child CAN be treated with an oral antibiotic.
explanation.E: Incorrect — The immediate priority is treating the acute infection with appropriate antibiotics; prophylaxis changes should follow specialist review.

reference: NICE NG224 — Urinary tract infection in under 16s. https://www.nice.org.uk/guidance/ng224

question: A 2-year-old girl presents with her third UTI in 6 months. She has been treated successfully each time. Her renal USS was normal. Per NICE NG224, what is the indication for considering prophylactic antibiotics in this child?

options.A: All children under 3 with any UTI should automatically receive 2 years of prophylaxis
options.B: Prophylactic antibiotics are recommended for children with recurrent UTIs (typically 3 or more per year, or 2 or more in 6 months in some guidance) when the benefit of preventing recurrent infections and their complications (renal scarring, pyelonephritis) outweighs the risk of antibiotic resistance and side effects; trimethoprim or nitrofurantoin at low dose nightly are the usual agents
options.C: Prophylaxis is never given to children under 5 — natural immunity will develop
options.D: Prophylaxis is only indicated if vesicoureteric reflux (VUR) is confirmed on MCUG
options.E: A single UTI in a girl under 2 is sufficient indication for lifelong prophylaxis

explanation.correct: Per NICE NG224 (UTI in under 16s): antibiotic prophylaxis is considered for children with recurrent UTIs — typically when there have been 2 or more symptomatic UTIs in a 6-month period, or 3 or more per year, particularly in younger children where the risk of renal scarring from repeated pyelonephritis is significant. Agents: trimethoprim (once nightly at a quarter of the therapeutic dose) or nitrofurantoin (if eGFR adequate) are standard. Duration: generally reviewed every 6-12 months. Imaging: NICE NG224 recommends renal USS after first UTI in all children under 6 months, and after recurrent UTIs in older children; DMSA scan 4-6 months after acute pyelonephritis in children under 3 to detect renal scarring. VUR (detected on MCUG) may influence prophylaxis decisions but is not a prerequisite for starting prophylaxis.
explanation.A: Incorrect — Automatic prophylaxis for all children under 3 with any UTI is not the NICE guidance; prophylaxis is based on frequency of recurrence.
explanation.B: CORRECT — Recurrent UTIs (2+ in 6 months or 3+ per year) are the typical indication for prophylaxis per NICE NG224; trimethoprim or nitrofurantoin nightly.
explanation.C: Incorrect — Prophylaxis IS used in children under 5 when indicated — recurrent UTIs in young children carry the highest risk of renal scarring.
explanation.D: Incorrect — Prophylaxis is not exclusively for confirmed VUR; recurrent infection frequency alone is an indication regardless of MCUG findings.
explanation.E: Incorrect — A single UTI in a girl under 2 does not automatically warrant prophylaxis — the pattern of recurrence drives the decision.

reference: NICE NG224 — Urinary tract infection in under 16s. https://www.nice.org.uk/guidance/ng224

question: A 42-year-old woman with a confirmed phaeochromocytoma is scheduled for laparoscopic adrenalectomy in 3 weeks. Per endocrinology and anaesthetic guidelines, what pre-operative preparation is essential?

options.A: No pre-operative medication is needed — general anaesthesia is safe
options.B: Alpha-blockade pre-operatively for 10-14 days before surgery (phenoxybenzamine is first-line non-competitive alpha blocker; alternatively doxazosin) — prevents hypertensive crisis during induction and tumour manipulation; followed by beta-blockade (only AFTER adequate alpha-blockade to prevent unopposed alpha-stimulation causing severe hypertension); adequate hydration to expand contracted plasma volume; patient should be volume loaded with high-sodium diet
options.C: Beta-blocker only — controls catecholamine excess
options.D: Emergency surgery without any pre-operative preparation — delay increases risk
options.E: Corticosteroid pre-loading only — adrenal surgery always risks Addisonian crisis

explanation.correct: Pre-operative preparation for phaeochromocytoma resection is critical to prevent life-threatening intraoperative hypertensive crises. Per Endocrine Society and anaesthetic guidelines: Step 1 — Alpha-adrenoceptor blockade: phenoxybenzamine (non-competitive alpha-1 and alpha-2 blocker — drug of choice for pre-op prep; irreversible so provides stable blockade): start 10-14 days before surgery; titrate to target BP <130/80 mmHg; OR competitive alpha-1 blocker (doxazosin, prazosin) as alternative. Step 2 — Beta-blockade: ONLY after at least 3-7 days of adequate alpha-blockade; NEVER start beta-blocker first — unopposed alpha-stimulation (from catecholamine surge with beta-blocked vasodilation) can cause severe vasoconstriction and hypertensive crisis; use for tachycardia or arrhythmia control. Step 3 — Volume expansion: high-salt diet and increased fluid intake (catecholamine-secreting tumours cause plasma volume contraction due to vasoconstriction); prevents severe hypotension after tumour resection.
explanation.A: Incorrect — Unblocked phaeochromocytoma during surgery can cause fatal hypertensive crises, arrhythmias and cardiovascular collapse — alpha-blockade is mandatory.
explanation.B: CORRECT — Alpha-blockade first (phenoxybenzamine 10-14 days pre-op), then beta-blockade only after; volume expansion per endocrine/anaesthetic guidelines.
explanation.C: Incorrect — Beta-blocker ALONE in phaeochromocytoma is DANGEROUS — removes beta-vasodilatory tone leaving unopposed alpha-mediated vasoconstriction → severe hypertension.
explanation.D: Incorrect — Elective adrenalectomy for phaeochromocytoma should always have pre-operative blockade; emergency surgery without prep is reserved for life-threatening haemorrhage.
explanation.E: Incorrect — Corticosteroid cover is appropriate for adrenal insufficiency risk if BOTH adrenals are being removed — not the primary preparation for phaeochromocytoma.

reference: Endocrine Society Clinical Practice Guideline — Pheochromocytoma. https://www.endocrine.org/clinical-practice-guidelines

question: A 54-year-old man presents with episodic severe headaches, sweating attacks and palpitations, each lasting 20-30 minutes and occurring 2-3 times per week. His BP during an attack is 210/118 mmHg, returning to normal between episodes. He is not on any antihypertensive. Per NICE CKS, what investigation is most specific for the suspected diagnosis?

options.A: 24-hour ambulatory BP monitoring — to document white coat hypertension
options.B: 24-hour urinary fractionated metanephrines (or plasma free metanephrines) — the most sensitive and specific test for phaeochromocytoma; metanephrines are stable metabolites of catecholamines; 24-hour urine metanephrines have sensitivity >95% and specificity >85%
options.C: Random serum adrenaline during an attack
options.D: Urinary vanillylmandelic acid (VMA) — first-line investigation
options.E: CT abdomen to look for adrenal mass — imaging is the first-line investigation

explanation.correct: Phaeochromocytoma: a catecholamine-secreting tumour of the adrenal medulla (90%) or extra-adrenal paraganglioma (10%). Classic triad: episodic headache, sweating, palpitations with hypertensive crises. Per NICE CKS and Endocrine Society guidelines: first-line biochemical investigation is 24-hour urinary fractionated metanephrines (normetanephrine + metanephrine) or plasma free metanephrines (metanephrine + normetanephrine). Why metanephrines not catecholamines: catecholamines are secreted episodically (may miss the peak); metanephrines are continuously produced from catecholamine metabolism and are more stable — higher sensitivity. Urinary VMA was historically used but is less sensitive and specific than metanephrines (now largely superseded). After biochemical confirmation: imaging (CT/MRI abdomen + pelvis) to localise the tumour. Then functional imaging (MIBG scan or Gallium DOTATATE PET-CT) if CT/MRI inconclusive.
explanation.A: Incorrect — Ambulatory BP monitoring assesses hypertension patterns but does not diagnose phaeochromocytoma biochemically.
explanation.B: CORRECT — 24-hour urinary fractionated metanephrines (or plasma free metanephrines) is the most sensitive/specific first-line test for phaeochromocytoma per NICE CKS.
explanation.C: Incorrect — Random catecholamine levels are highly variable due to episodic secretion and stress effects — unreliable for diagnosis.
explanation.D: Incorrect — Urinary VMA has been largely superseded by metanephrines, which are more sensitive and specific.
explanation.E: Incorrect — Imaging is done AFTER biochemical confirmation of catecholamine excess — imaging first risks missing biochemically active small tumours and false positive incidentalomas.

reference: NICE CKS — Phaeochromocytoma. https://cks.nice.org.uk/topics/phaeochromocytoma/

question: A 58-year-old man presents with a 3 cm well-demarcated erythematous scaly plaque on his lower leg for 8 months. Biopsy confirms Bowen's disease (SCC in situ). He also has 3 smaller lesions (0.8 cm each). Per NICE CKS, which treatment modality is most appropriate for multiple small Bowen's disease lesions?

options.A: Surgical excision of all four lesions simultaneously
options.B: Topical 5-fluorouracil 5% cream (Efudix) or topical imiquimod 5% — suitable for small (<2 cm), multiple, or superficial Bowen's lesions where surgery would be impractical; 5-FU: applied BD for 3-4 weeks, produces inflammatory response and lesion regression; imiquimod 5%: applied 3-5 times per week for 16 weeks (off-label); both achieve 80-90% cure rates for suitable lesions; cryotherapy also suitable for small accessible lesions
options.C: Mohs surgery for each lesion
options.D: Watch and wait — Bowen's disease always regresses spontaneously
options.E: Oral acitretin — systemic retinoid for multiple Bowen's lesions

explanation.correct: Per NICE CKS and BAD guidelines for Bowen's disease: treatment selection depends on lesion size, number, site and patient factors. For multiple small (<2 cm) lesions: topical therapies are practical and effective. 5-fluorouracil 5% cream (5-FU/Efudix): antimetabolite inhibiting thymidylate synthase → prevents DNA synthesis in rapidly dividing dysplastic cells; applied BD for 3-4 weeks; expected response: erythema, erosion, crusting (inflammatory reaction — this is the therapeutic effect); cure rates 80-90% for Bowen's. Topical imiquimod 5% (Aldara): immune response modifier (TLR-7 agonist); off-label for Bowen's; applied 3-5×/week for up to 16 weeks; similar cure rates. Cryotherapy: suitable for small (<1-2 cm), accessible lesions with good vascular supply. PDT: preferred for large (>2 cm) or lower leg lesions (poor healing). For this patient: topical treatment is practical for 3 small lesions; the large 3 cm lesion (poor healing on lower leg) should be considered for PDT.
explanation.A: Incorrect — Multiple surgical excisions simultaneously would be impractical for 4 lesions and carry high morbidity on the lower leg with poor healing.
explanation.B: CORRECT — Topical 5-FU or imiquimod for small multiple Bowen's lesions per NICE CKS/BAD; PDT for the large lower-leg lesion.
explanation.C: Incorrect — Mohs surgery is for high-risk invasive SCC in cosmetically sensitive areas — not for multiple SCC in situ (Bowen's) on the lower leg.
explanation.D: Incorrect — Bowen's disease carries a 3-5% risk of progression to invasive SCC and requires active treatment; it does not reliably regress.
explanation.E: Incorrect — Oral acitretin (systemic retinoid) is used for field treatment in extensive actinic keratoses or in immunosuppressed patients — not standard first-line for multiple Bowen's lesions.

reference: NICE CKS — Bowen's disease. BAD guidelines. https://cks.nice.org.uk/topics/bowens-disease/

question: A 68-year-old man is referred with a well-demarcated solitary erythematous scaly plaque on his lower leg, confirmed as Bowen's disease on biopsy. The lesion measures 3.5 cm diameter. Per NICE CKS and BAD guidelines, what is the most appropriate treatment for a large Bowen's disease lesion?

options.A: Watch and wait — Bowen's disease never becomes invasive
options.B: Photodynamic therapy (PDT) — the preferred treatment for large (>2 cm) Bowen's disease lesions particularly on the lower leg where healing is poor; a photosensitising agent (methyl aminolaevulinate — MAL) is applied, followed by activation with red light; effective with good cosmetic outcome and suitable for large, multiple or awkwardly sited lesions
options.C: Wide local excision with 1 cm margins — as for invasive SCC
options.D: Mohs micrographic surgery — required for all Bowen's disease
options.E: Topical hydrocortisone cream for 8 weeks — reduces the dysplasia

explanation.correct: Per NICE CKS and British Association of Dermatology (BAD) guidelines for Bowen's disease: treatment choice depends on size, site, number of lesions, and patient factors. Options: cryotherapy (suitable for small, <1-2 cm, accessible lesions); topical 5-fluorouracil 5% cream (self-applied for 4-6 weeks); topical imiquimod 5% (off-label); photodynamic therapy (PDT): preferred for LARGE (>2 cm), MULTIPLE, or lower-leg lesions. Why lower leg is special: poor vascularity and healing make surgery and cryotherapy more problematic on the lower leg. PDT: methyl aminolaevulinate (MAL) applied under occlusion for 3 hours, then red light activation; 2 treatment sessions 1 week apart; cure rates 80-95% for Bowen's disease; good cosmetic outcome. Excision: appropriate for smaller lesions in surgically accessible sites; 3-4 mm margins for SCC in situ.
explanation.A: Incorrect — Bowen's disease carries a 3-5% risk of progression to invasive SCC and should be treated.
explanation.B: CORRECT — PDT is preferred for large (>2 cm) Bowen's disease, particularly on lower leg per NICE CKS/BAD guidelines.
explanation.C: Incorrect — Wide excision with 1 cm margins is used for invasive SCC, not for SCC in situ (Bowen's). Narrower margins (3-4 mm) are used if excising Bowen's.
explanation.D: Incorrect — Mohs surgery is reserved for invasive high-risk SCC in cosmetically sensitive areas — not routinely for Bowen's disease.
explanation.E: Incorrect — Topical corticosteroids have no role in treating Bowen's disease dysplasia.

reference: NICE CKS — Bowen's disease. BAD guidelines. https://cks.nice.org.uk/topics/bowens-disease/

question: A 32-year-old Afro-Caribbean man presents with a painful crisis affecting his back and legs. He is known to have sickle cell disease. His Hb is 68 g/L (baseline 82 g/L). Per NICE NG143 (sickle cell disease) and British Society for Haematology guidelines, what is the acute management?

options.A: Discharge with oral analgesia — sickle cell pain crises always resolve without treatment
options.B: IV morphine or equivalent opioid within 30 minutes of arrival; paracetamol and NSAID (if renal function adequate) as adjuncts; IV fluids; oxygen only if SpO2 <95%; regular pain reassessment (NRS scale); early specialist haematology involvement; assess for complications (acute chest syndrome, stroke, aplastic crisis)
options.C: Immediate blood transfusion — always the first-line treatment
options.D: Hydroxycarbamide IV for acute crisis
options.E: Wait for pain to peak before giving opioids — early opioids worsen crisis

explanation.correct: Per NICE NG143 (Sickle cell disease) and BSH guidelines: acute vaso-occlusive crisis management: Analgesia: strong opioid (morphine IV/SC or equivalent) within 30 minutes of hospital arrival (not to wait for assessment completion); do NOT delay analgesia; patient-controlled analgesia (PCA) is effective; paracetamol regularly as adjunct; NSAID (ibuprofen) if no contraindication (renal function, peptic ulcer disease); Fluids: IV hydration (dehydration worsens sickling); Oxygen: only if SpO2 <95% — routine oxygen is NOT indicated in normoxic patients; Temperature monitoring (fever may indicate infection — sickle cell patients are functionally asplenic); Precipitants: identify and treat (infection, dehydration, cold exposure); Complications to assess for: acute chest syndrome (new chest infiltrate + fever/hypoxia — most common cause of sickle cell death — manage with exchange transfusion, antibiotics, oxygen, HDU); stroke (exchange transfusion); aplastic crisis (B19 parvovirus — treat with transfusion). Hydroxycarbamide: long-term prevention of crises — NOT for acute crisis treatment.
explanation.A: Incorrect — Sickle cell crises cause severe pain and tissue ischaemia requiring active management; discharge without adequate analgesia and hydration is unsafe.
explanation.B: CORRECT — IV opioid within 30 minutes + paracetamol/NSAID + IV fluids; O2 only if SpO2 <95%; assess for complications per NICE NG143/BSH.
explanation.C: Incorrect — Blood transfusion is NOT routine for all sickle cell crises; it is specifically indicated for: aplastic crisis, acute chest syndrome, acute stroke, symptomatic severe anaemia.
explanation.D: Incorrect — Hydroxycarbamide (hydroxyurea) is used for long-term prevention of crises (increases HbF production); it has no role in acute crisis treatment.
explanation.E: Incorrect — Early opioid analgesia within 30 minutes of arrival is the standard of care per NICE NG143; delaying analgesia is contrary to guidance.

reference: NICE NG143 — Sickle cell disease. BSH guidelines. https://www.nice.org.uk/guidance/ng143

question: A couple attend pre-conception counselling. Both are confirmed carriers of beta-thalassaemia trait (heterozygous). Per genetics and NHS screening guidance, what is their risk of having an affected child and what options are available?

options.A: 25% risk of an affected child (thalassaemia major); 50% carrier; 25% unaffected — autosomal recessive inheritance; options include preimplantation genetic diagnosis (PGD) via IVF, prenatal diagnosis (chorionic villus sampling at 11-14 weeks or amniocentesis at 15-20 weeks) with termination if affected; or continuing pregnancy with awareness
options.B: 50% risk — one parent always passes on the affected gene
options.C: No risk — carriers of beta-thalassaemia trait are immune from having affected children
options.D: 100% risk — both carriers will always produce affected offspring
options.E: The risk is only significant if both parents are of Mediterranean or Southeast Asian origin

explanation.correct: Beta-thalassaemia: autosomal recessive condition (chromosome 11 — HBB gene). Two carrier parents (Bb × Bb): 25% chance of thalassaemia major (BB — severely affected, requires lifelong transfusions); 50% carriers (Bb — thalassaemia trait, mild/no symptoms); 25% completely unaffected (bb). Per NHS Sickle Cell and Thalassaemia Screening Programme and RCOG guidelines: couples where both are carriers should be referred to a specialist haemoglobinopathy counsellor. Options: preimplantation genetic diagnosis (PGD) via IVF — embryos screened before implantation; prenatal diagnosis — chorionic villus sampling (CVS at 11-14 weeks) or amniocentesis (15-20 weeks) with fetal genotyping; if affected fetus: couple may choose termination or continuation. Thalassaemia major: without treatment, severe haemolytic anaemia causing death in infancy; with treatment: regular blood transfusions + iron chelation (desferrioxamine) + possible bone marrow transplantation (curative).
explanation.A: CORRECT — 25% thalassaemia major risk; 50% carrier; 25% unaffected. PGD and prenatal diagnosis available per NHS screening/RCOG guidance.
explanation.B: Incorrect — 50% risk applies to autosomal dominant inheritance, not autosomal recessive.
explanation.C: Incorrect — Two carriers of autosomal recessive conditions have a 25% chance of an affected child per pregnancy.
explanation.D: Incorrect — 100% risk would require both parents to be homozygous affected — carriers are heterozygous.
explanation.E: Incorrect — The 25% risk applies regardless of ethnicity; while thalassaemia is more prevalent in Mediterranean, Middle Eastern, South Asian and Southeast Asian populations, the genetics apply universally.

reference: NHS — Sickle Cell and Thalassaemia Screening. RCOG guidelines. https://www.nhs.uk/conditions/thalassaemia/

question: A 45-year-old man is found incidentally to have a total cholesterol of 9.8 mmol/L, LDL 7.2 mmol/L, and HDL 1.3 mmol/L. His father had a myocardial infarction at age 42 and his brother has a cholesterol of 8.9 mmol/L. Per NICE CG71 and Simon Broome criteria, what is the most likely diagnosis and initial management?

options.A: Secondary hyperlipidaemia — check TFTs, LFTs, renal function, and HbA1c first
options.B: Familial hypercholesterolaemia (FH) — autosomal dominant mutation in LDL receptor gene (LDLR), apolipoprotein B (APOB) or PCSK9; Simon Broome criteria: definite FH if LDL >4.9 mmol/L plus tendon xanthomata OR DNA evidence of mutation; probable FH if LDL >4.9 mmol/L plus family history of premature CVD or elevated cholesterol; refer to lipid clinic; high-intensity statin (rosuvastatin 40mg); cascade screening of first-degree relatives
options.C: Dietary modification only for 6 months before starting medication
options.D: Start low-intensity statin and recheck in 12 months
options.E: No treatment required — cholesterol of 9.8 mmol/L is within normal limits for his age

explanation.correct: Familial hypercholesterolaemia (FH): autosomal DOMINANT (not recessive) condition caused by mutations in LDL receptor (LDLR — most common, 85%), apolipoprotein B (APOB — 5%), or PCSK9 gene (~1%) — leading to markedly elevated LDL cholesterol from birth. Simon Broome criteria for adults: DEFINITE FH: LDL >4.9 mmol/L (TC >7.5 mmol/L) AND tendon xanthomata in patient or first/second degree relative, OR DNA-confirmed mutation. PROBABLE FH: LDL >4.9 mmol/L AND family history of premature MI (<50 in 1st degree relative, <60 in 2nd degree) OR family history of raised cholesterol. This patient: LDL 7.2 mmol/L + father with MI at 42 + brother with elevated cholesterol = PROBABLE/DEFINITE FH. Per NICE CG71: refer to lipid clinic; high-intensity statin (atorvastatin 80mg or rosuvastatin 40mg); target LDL reduction ≥50%; cascade screening for first-degree relatives; consider ezetimibe or PCSK9 inhibitor if statin insufficient.
explanation.A: Incorrect — Secondary causes should be excluded, but this family history and LDL level strongly point to FH — investigation and treatment should proceed simultaneously.
explanation.B: CORRECT — Probable/definite FH: refer lipid clinic, high-intensity statin, cascade screen first-degree relatives per NICE CG71.
explanation.C: Incorrect — FH requires urgent statin therapy; dietary modification alone is insufficient for genetic LDL receptor dysfunction.
explanation.D: Incorrect — Low-intensity statin is inadequate for FH — high-intensity statin (atorvastatin 80mg or rosuvastatin 40mg) is required per NICE CG71.
explanation.E: Incorrect — LDL of 7.2 mmol/L is markedly elevated and with this family history represents very high cardiovascular risk requiring urgent treatment.

reference: NICE CG71 — Identification and management of familial hypercholesterolaemia. https://www.nice.org.uk/guidance/cg71

question: A 38-year-old woman with confirmed familial hypercholesterolaemia is on atorvastatin 80mg. Her LDL remains at 5.1 mmol/L (target <2.6 mmol/L per NICE CG71). She has no other cardiovascular risk factors. Per NICE CG71 and TA394, what is the next step?

options.A: Increase atorvastatin to 160 mg — double the dose
options.B: Add ezetimibe 10mg daily — first add-on therapy when statin alone is insufficient; inhibits intestinal cholesterol absorption; LDL lowering of approximately 15-20% additional; if still not at target, consider PCSK9 inhibitor (evolocumab or alirocumab) via specialist
options.C: Stop atorvastatin and start rosuvastatin 5 mg to reduce side effects
options.D: Refer for LDL apheresis immediately without trying additional medication
options.E: Accept current LDL — targets are aspirational only and do not require add-on therapy

explanation.correct: Per NICE CG71 (FH) and NICE TA394 (Evolocumab): when maximum tolerated statin dose is insufficient to achieve LDL targets in FH, the stepwise approach is: Step 1 — Maximum tolerated statin (atorvastatin 80mg or rosuvastatin 40mg); Step 2 — Add ezetimibe 10mg (first-line add-on; inhibits Niemann-Pick C1-Like 1 protein in the small intestinal brush border; reduces LDL by additional 15-20%); Step 3 — If still not at target with statin + ezetimibe: PCSK9 inhibitors (evolocumab or alirocumab — monoclonal antibodies against PCSK9; can reduce LDL by 50-60%; given SC every 2 weeks or monthly) via specialist lipid clinic. Step 4 — LDL apheresis (extracorporeal LDL removal): for homozygous FH or severe heterozygous FH unresponsive to maximal drug therapy. Atorvastatin maximum licensed dose is 80mg — cannot double to 160mg.
explanation.A: Incorrect — Atorvastatin 80mg is the maximum licensed dose. Exceeding this is not appropriate.
explanation.B: CORRECT — Add ezetimibe 10mg as first add-on to maximum statin per NICE CG71; PCSK9 inhibitor via specialist if still insufficient.
explanation.C: Incorrect — Switching to a lower dose of rosuvastatin would reduce LDL lowering — not appropriate when the goal is to reach target.
explanation.D: Incorrect — LDL apheresis is reserved for homozygous FH or severe heterozygous FH after maximal drug therapy has failed — not the next step here.
explanation.E: Incorrect — NICE CG71 sets a specific LDL target of <2.6 mmol/L (or >50% reduction from baseline) — targets require active pursuit.

reference: NICE CG71 — Familial hypercholesterolaemia. NICE TA394. https://www.nice.org.uk/guidance/cg71

question: A 68-year-old man presents with sudden onset complete right-sided hearing loss over 3 hours. He denies any preceding ear infection, head injury or noise exposure. His right ear drum looks normal. Per NICE CKS and ENT guidelines, what is this and what is the urgency?

options.A: Wax impaction — syringe the ear and review
options.B: Sudden sensorineural hearing loss (SSNHL) — defined as ≥30 dB sensorineural hearing loss across at least 3 consecutive audiometric frequencies within 72 hours; this is an otological emergency; refer same-day (within 24 hours) to ENT/audiovestibular medicine; first-line treatment: oral corticosteroids (prednisolone 1 mg/kg/day up to 60 mg for 7-10 days) within 72 hours of onset maximises recovery; intratympanic steroids if oral steroids contraindicated
options.C: Refer routinely to audiology within 18 weeks
options.D: Reassure — sudden hearing loss in the elderly is always due to presbyacusis and resolves spontaneously
options.E: Start oral antibiotics — sudden hearing loss is caused by otitis media

explanation.correct: Sudden sensorineural hearing loss (SSNHL): definition — ≥30 dB SNHL over ≥3 audiometric frequencies within 72 hours. Idiopathic SSNHL is most common (90%) — cause unknown; theories: viral cochleitis, vascular event, autoimmune. Per NICE CKS and British Association of Otorhinolaryngology (BAO-HNS): SSNHL is an ENT emergency requiring same-day (within 24-48 hours) specialist assessment. Time-critical treatment: oral prednisolone started within 72 hours gives best recovery outcomes (up to 60-65% partial or full recovery vs ~32% spontaneous recovery); prednisolone 1 mg/kg/day (max 60 mg) for 7-14 days; intratympanic steroid injection: for those where oral steroids are contraindicated or as rescue therapy. Investigations (in ENT): pure tone audiogram (confirm and characterise); MRI IAM with gadolinium (after initial treatment — to exclude acoustic neuroma); Bloods: FBC, ESR, autoimmune screen, Lyme serology. Do NOT wait — every hour of delay reduces prognosis.
explanation.A: Incorrect — Wax does not cause sudden complete unilateral SNHL. A normal drum makes conductive loss unlikely — this is SSNHL.
explanation.B: CORRECT — SSNHL: same-day ENT referral; oral prednisolone within 72 hours for best recovery outcomes per NICE CKS/BAO-HNS.
explanation.C: Incorrect — Routine 18-week audiology referral is entirely inappropriate for SSNHL — this is a same-day ENT emergency.
explanation.D: Incorrect — Presbyacusis is gradual bilateral high-frequency loss — sudden complete unilateral SNHL is a red flag emergency requiring urgent treatment.
explanation.E: Incorrect — Otitis media causes conductive hearing loss with an abnormal drum (injection, effusion). Normal drum + sudden SNHL = SSNHL not otitis media.

reference: NICE CKS — Sudden sensorineural hearing loss. BAO-HNS guidelines. https://cks.nice.org.uk/topics/sudden-sensorineural-hearing-loss/

question: A 55-year-old woman presents with a 4-day history of left-sided painful vesicular eruption on the pinna, ear canal and left side of the face with ipsilateral facial weakness (House-Brackmann grade III). She also has vertigo and left-sided hearing loss. Per NICE CKS, what is the diagnosis and management?

options.A: Bell's palsy — oral prednisolone only
options.B: Ramsay Hunt syndrome (herpes zoster oticus) — reactivation of varicella-zoster virus in the geniculate ganglion of the facial nerve (CN VII); triad: ipsilateral facial palsy + otalgia + herpetic vesicles in the ear/pinna; cochleo-vestibular involvement (hearing loss, tinnitus, vertigo) occurs in many cases; treat with oral aciclovir 800 mg 5 times daily for 7 days PLUS prednisolone 60 mg daily for 5 days; outcomes worse than Bell's palsy — early antiviral treatment improves prognosis
options.C: Otitis externa — topical ciprofloxacin ear drops
options.D: Acoustic neuroma — MRI IAM urgently
options.E: Cholesteatoma — refer for tympanoplasty

explanation.correct: Ramsay Hunt syndrome (Herpes Zoster Oticus): VZV reactivation in the geniculate ganglion of the facial nerve within the temporal bone. Classic triad: (1) painful herpetic vesicles on the pinna, external auditory canal, or tympanic membrane; (2) ipsilateral facial nerve palsy (LMN pattern — forehead sparing absent, unlike UMN); (3) otalgia. Cochleo-vestibular features (up to 50%): SNHL, tinnitus, vertigo, nystagmus. Distinguished from Bell's palsy: Bell's palsy = idiopathic LMN facial palsy with NO vesicles; Ramsay Hunt = VZV-associated with vesicles. Prognosis: worse than Bell's palsy — only 50-70% complete recovery vs >85% Bell's. Per NICE CKS: combination antiviral + steroid: aciclovir 800 mg 5 times daily (or valaciclovir 1g TDS) for 7 days PLUS prednisolone 60 mg/day for 5 days (then taper); start within 72 hours of onset for best outcome; eye care (if eye closure incomplete): lubricating drops, nocturnal eye tape.
explanation.A: Incorrect — Bell's palsy has no vesicles and is treated with prednisolone alone; antivirals are not routinely added. Ramsay Hunt has vesicles and REQUIRES antiviral + steroid combination.
explanation.B: CORRECT — Ramsay Hunt: VZV vesicles + facial palsy ± hearing loss/vertigo. Aciclovir + prednisolone for 7 days per NICE CKS.
explanation.C: Incorrect — Otitis externa causes canal inflammation and pain but does not cause facial palsy or hearing loss.
explanation.D: Incorrect — Acoustic neuroma causes gradual unilateral SNHL without the acute vesicular eruption and facial palsy combination.
explanation.E: Incorrect — Cholesteatoma is a destructive squamous epithelium expansion behind the eardrum causing conductive hearing loss without vesicles or acute facial palsy.

reference: NICE CKS — Ramsay Hunt syndrome. https://cks.nice.org.uk/topics/ramsay-hunt-syndrome/

question: A 55-year-old woman presents complaining of difficulty hearing in noisy environments and needing the TV louder. Pure tone audiometry shows a symmetrical sloping high-frequency sensorineural hearing loss bilaterally. She has no tinnitus and no vertigo. Per NICE CKS, what is the most likely diagnosis and management?

options.A: Bilateral acoustic neuromas — urgent MRI IAM bilaterally
options.B: Presbyacusis (age-related sensorineural hearing loss) — the most common cause of hearing loss in older adults; characterised by bilateral symmetrical high-frequency SNHL; managed with hearing aid referral via NHS audiology; no curative treatment; reassurance; safety advice regarding driving and telephone use
options.C: Ménière's disease — betahistine and low-sodium diet
options.D: Bilateral otosclerosis — refer for stapedectomy
options.E: Noise-induced hearing loss — all bilateral SNHL in adults is from noise exposure

explanation.correct: Presbyacusis (age-related hearing loss): the most common cause of hearing loss globally and the most common cause of SNHL in adults over 50. Characterised by: bilateral symmetrical high-frequency SNHL on pure tone audiometry (audiogram shows sloping loss, worse at high frequencies — 4-8 kHz); gradual onset over years; difficulty hearing in background noise (selective impairment of speech discrimination in noise); no vertigo, no tinnitus (though tinnitus can coexist). Cause: cumulative degeneration of cochlear hair cells (particularly basal turn encoding high frequencies) from ageing, noise exposure and genetic factors. Per NICE CKS: refer to NHS audiology for hearing aid fitting (digital hearing aids available free via NHS); no curative treatment; Cochlear implant for severe-profound SNHL not responding to hearing aids. Red flags requiring ENT referral: asymmetrical SNHL (must exclude acoustic neuroma), sudden SNHL, unilateral SNHL.
explanation.A: Incorrect — Bilateral acoustic neuromas are very rare and associated with neurofibromatosis type 2; symmetrical audiogram and no additional features make this very unlikely.
explanation.B: CORRECT — Presbyacusis: bilateral symmetrical high-frequency SNHL in older adult; NHS hearing aids per NICE CKS.
explanation.C: Incorrect — Ménière's disease causes episodic vertigo + fluctuating low-frequency SNHL + tinnitus + aural fullness — not a stable symmetrical high-frequency loss.
explanation.D: Incorrect — Otosclerosis causes CONDUCTIVE hearing loss (abnormal Rinne test — BC>AC) — not sensorineural hearing loss.
explanation.E: Incorrect — Noise-induced hearing loss causes a characteristic 4 kHz notch on audiogram and requires occupational history; presbyacusis is the most common diagnosis for bilateral symmetric high-frequency SNHL in older adults.

reference: NICE CKS — Hearing loss in adults. https://cks.nice.org.uk/topics/hearing-loss-in-adults/

question: A 58-year-old man presents with a 3-month history of progressive unilateral left-sided sensorineural hearing loss with tinnitus. He denies vertigo. Pure tone audiometry shows asymmetric low-frequency SNHL on the left. Per NICE CKS, what is the most important diagnosis to exclude and investigation?

options.A: Presbyacusis — bilateral, so unilateral loss does not fit; no investigation needed
options.B: Acoustic neuroma (vestibular schwannoma) — any unilateral SNHL or unilateral tinnitus should raise suspicion; MRI internal auditory meati (IAM) with gadolinium is the gold standard investigation; urgent ENT referral for assessment and MRI request; acoustic neuromas are benign tumours of CN VIII Schwann cells that can be managed with surveillance, stereotactic radiosurgery or microsurgical excision
options.C: Ménière's disease requires no imaging — diagnose clinically and treat with betahistine
options.D: Bilateral audiometry and hearing aid fitting as first step
options.E: CT temporal bones — preferred over MRI for acoustic neuroma detection

explanation.correct: Per NICE CKS and ENT guidelines: UNILATERAL SNHL or unilateral tinnitus requires exclusion of acoustic neuroma (vestibular schwannoma) — a benign tumour of the Schwann cells of the vestibular division of CN VIII growing in the internal auditory canal and/or cerebellopontine angle. Symptoms: progressive unilateral SNHL (any frequency), unilateral tinnitus, later — vertigo, facial numbness (CN V compression), facial weakness. Investigation: MRI IAM with gadolinium — gold standard; sensitivity >99%; detects tumours as small as 1-2 mm. CT temporal bones detects bony erosion in larger tumours but misses small intracanalicular acoustic neuromas. ENT referral is mandatory for any unexplained asymmetric SNHL. Management: observation (small tumours, elderly) with serial MRI; stereotactic radiosurgery (Gamma Knife); microsurgical excision. Note: Ménière's disease also causes unilateral hearing loss but is episodic with vertigo and fullness — acoustic neuroma must be excluded first.
explanation.A: Incorrect — Unilateral SNHL absolutely requires investigation — acoustic neuroma must be excluded regardless of the patient's age.
explanation.B: CORRECT — Unilateral SNHL: MRI IAM with gadolinium to exclude acoustic neuroma; urgent ENT referral per NICE CKS.
explanation.C: Incorrect — Ménière's disease is a diagnosis of exclusion after acoustic neuroma has been ruled out by MRI.
explanation.D: Incorrect — Hearing aids should not be fitted for unilateral SNHL until acoustic neuroma is excluded.
explanation.E: Incorrect — CT temporal bones can miss small intracanalicular acoustic neuromas; MRI with gadolinium is the gold standard.

reference: NICE CKS — Acoustic neuroma. https://cks.nice.org.uk/topics/acoustic-neuroma/

question: A 37-year-old woman with premature ovarian insufficiency (POI) diagnosed 2 years ago is on HRT (oestradiol patch + micronised progesterone). She asks about bone health monitoring. Per NICE NG23 and RCP guidance, what is recommended?

options.A: No bone health monitoring is needed while on HRT
options.B: DEXA scan at diagnosis for baseline bone mineral density — women with POI are at significantly increased risk of osteoporosis due to prolonged premenopausal oestrogen deficiency; repeat DEXA every 3-5 years or more frequently if risk factors present; HRT (or COCP) is the most important bone-protective intervention; calcium and vitamin D supplementation if dietary intake inadequate; weight-bearing exercise
options.C: DEXA scan only if fracture occurs
options.D: Start bisphosphonate immediately regardless of DEXA result
options.E: Bone protection monitoring is only needed after age 50

explanation.correct: Per NICE NG23 and The Premature Ovarian Insufficiency (POI) guideline (2023 update from RCP/BMS): women with POI have significantly higher lifetime risk of osteoporosis compared with women who experience natural menopause at 51. Reason: extended years of oestrogen deficiency from the age of diagnosis — bone density declines at accelerated rate during this period. DEXA scan: recommended at diagnosis for baseline bone mineral density; repeated every 3-5 years (more frequently if: severe bone loss on previous DEXA, persistent symptoms, poor compliance with HRT, additional risk factors such as systemic steroid use, eating disorder, family history of fracture). HRT/COCP: the most effective bone-protective intervention for POI; bisphosphonates are generally NOT required unless bone density is very low AND HRT is not tolerated (HRT replaces physiological oestrogen — bisphosphonates are added when needed). Calcium (700-1200 mg/day) and vitamin D (800-1000 IU/day) supplementation: if dietary intake insufficient.
explanation.A: Incorrect — Bone monitoring is specifically recommended for POI as accelerated bone loss can occur even while on HRT if compliance is poor or HRT dose insufficient.
explanation.B: CORRECT — DEXA at diagnosis for baseline; every 3-5 years thereafter; HRT is key bone protection; calcium/vitamin D if needed per NICE NG23.
explanation.C: Incorrect — Waiting for a fracture before investigating bone density is reactive rather than preventive — POI warrants proactive monitoring.
explanation.D: Incorrect — Bisphosphonates are not first-line for all POI patients; HRT is the primary bone-protective intervention; bisphosphonates are added if HRT insufficient or not tolerated.
explanation.E: Incorrect — POI occurs before age 40 and bone protection monitoring should start at diagnosis — waiting until 50 misses many years of accelerated bone loss.

reference: NICE NG23 — Menopause. RCP — Premature Ovarian Insufficiency guidelines. https://www.nice.org.uk/guidance/ng23

question: A 39-year-old woman has an FSH of 68 IU/L on two occasions 4 weeks apart with amenorrhoea for 8 months. She has hot flushes and vaginal dryness. Per NICE NG23, what is the diagnosis and what important health consideration must be discussed alongside HRT?

options.A: Polycystic ovary syndrome — clomifene citrate
options.B: Premature ovarian insufficiency (POI) — FSH >25 IU/L on two occasions 4+ weeks apart before age 40; bone health is a critical concern as prolonged oestrogen deficiency causes premature bone loss and increased fracture risk; HRT (or COCP) is strongly recommended until the natural age of menopause (approximately 51) to protect bone density and cardiovascular health; DEXA scan for baseline bone density
options.C: Normal perimenopause — no treatment needed at 39
options.D: Pituitary adenoma secreting excess FSH — MRI pituitary urgently
options.E: HRT should be avoided in POI due to increased cancer risk

explanation.correct: Premature ovarian insufficiency (POI): ovarian function ceases before age 40 (by definition) — affecting approximately 1% of women under 40 and 0.1% under 30. Diagnostic criteria: amenorrhoea >4 months + FSH >25 IU/L on two separate occasions ≥4 weeks apart. Per NICE NG23: HRT or COCP is strongly recommended in POI until the natural age of menopause (~51 years). Rationale: prolonged oestrogen deficiency from a young age causes: accelerated bone loss (osteoporosis, fragility fractures), premature cardiovascular disease, sexual dysfunction, neurological effects (cognitive), psychological impact. DEXA scan at diagnosis for baseline bone mineral density. Fertility: approximately 5% of women with POI may still ovulate spontaneously; oocyte donation is the most effective option for pregnancy. The HRT in POI is REPLACEMENT therapy restoring physiological oestrogen levels — the breast cancer risk concern applies to HRT taken BEYOND the natural menopause age, not to replacement therapy in POI.
explanation.A: Incorrect — PCOS is associated with normal or low FSH with elevated LH and androgens — FSH of 68 IU/L indicates ovarian failure, not PCOS.
explanation.B: CORRECT — POI: FSH >25 on two occasions <40 years. HRT recommended until age ~51 for bone/cardiovascular protection per NICE NG23.
explanation.C: Incorrect — FSH of 68 IU/L at age 39 with 8 months amenorrhoea is diagnostic of POI — this is not normal perimenopause and requires treatment.
explanation.D: Incorrect — Elevated FSH in this context reflects absent negative feedback from failing ovaries — not pituitary overproduction.
explanation.E: Incorrect — HRT in POI is STRONGLY recommended by NICE NG23; the cancer risk profile of HRT in POI is different from HRT taken after natural menopause as it is restoring physiological hormone levels.

reference: NICE NG23 — Menopause. https://www.nice.org.uk/guidance/ng23

question: A 58-year-old man has a resting ECG reported as showing first-degree heart block. His PR interval is 240 ms. He is asymptomatic and his ECG is otherwise normal. Per NICE and ESC guidelines, what is the most appropriate management?

options.A: Urgent cardiology referral and pacemaker implantation
options.B: No specific treatment required — first-degree AV block (PR interval >200 ms) is benign in asymptomatic patients; review medications that may prolong PR interval (beta-blockers, verapamil, diltiazem, digoxin, amiodarone); routine cardiology follow-up if other concerns; no pacing indicated
options.C: Start atropine to shorten the PR interval
options.D: Admit for 24-hour telemetry monitoring
options.E: Stop all current medications immediately

explanation.correct: First-degree AV block: defined as PR interval >200 ms (0.20 seconds) with every P wave conducted to the ventricles (no dropped beats). The PR interval represents conduction time through the AV node. It is NOT a block in the traditional sense — all impulses conduct, just more slowly. Causes: vagal tone (athletes), inferior MI (RCA supplies AV node), medications (beta-blockers, calcium channel blockers, digoxin, amiodarone), myocarditis, electrolyte disturbance (hyperkalaemia), structural heart disease. Per ESC Cardiac Pacing Guidelines: asymptomatic first-degree AV block — no pacing indicated; no specific treatment required. Key review: check medications that slow AV conduction — if iatrogenic and PR interval is very prolonged (>300 ms) with symptoms, dose reduction may be appropriate. Rare exception: very marked first-degree block (PR >300-320 ms) can occasionally cause 'pacemaker syndrome-like' symptoms (from suboptimal AV timing) — specialist review warranted.
explanation.A: Incorrect — Pacemaker implantation is not indicated for asymptomatic first-degree AV block per ESC guidelines.
explanation.B: CORRECT — First-degree AV block in an asymptomatic patient: benign, no treatment required; review PR-prolonging medications per ESC pacing guidelines.
explanation.C: Incorrect — Atropine is a vagolytic used for symptomatic bradycardia/high-degree AV block in acute settings — not appropriate for asymptomatic first-degree block.
explanation.D: Incorrect — Inpatient telemetry is not required for asymptomatic first-degree AV block.
explanation.E: Incorrect — Stopping all medications abruptly is unsafe and disproportionate; specifically review PR-prolonging drugs if clinically relevant.

reference: ESC Guidelines on Cardiac Pacing 2021. https://www.escardio.org/Guidelines

question: A 78-year-old woman attends for a routine ECG. She is asymptomatic. The ECG shows: regular P waves at 72/min, followed by progressively lengthening PR intervals over 3 beats, then a dropped QRS, then the cycle repeats. Per NICE and ESC guidelines, what is this ECG pattern and management?

options.A: Complete heart block — permanent pacemaker immediately
options.B: Mobitz Type I (Wenckebach) second-degree AV block — progressive PR prolongation then a dropped beat; in asymptomatic patients, particularly when associated with inferior MI or vagal tone, this is often benign; monitor, avoid AV-nodal blocking drugs (beta-blockers, digoxin, verapamil, diltiazem), refer to cardiology for assessment
options.C: First-degree heart block — no action required
options.D: Mobitz Type II second-degree AV block — requires urgent pacing
options.E: Atrial flutter with variable block — rate control with digoxin

explanation.correct: Mobitz Type I (Wenckebach) second-degree AV block: progressive PR interval lengthening over consecutive beats until one P wave fails to conduct (dropped QRS), then the cycle resets. Distinguished from Mobitz II (sudden dropped beat without PR prolongation). Wenckebach characteristics: block is typically at the level of the AV node (proximal); associated with: inferior MI (RCA supplies AV node), vagal tone, myocarditis, beta-blocker/calcium channel blocker/digoxin toxicity. Prognosis: generally benign in the absence of structural heart disease or symptoms. Management per ESC Pacing Guidelines: asymptomatic Wenckebach — no pacing required; avoid AV-nodal blocking drugs; cardiology review; treat reversible causes. If symptomatic (dizziness, syncope, pre-syncope) — pacemaker may be indicated. Mobitz II (sudden dropped beats, often wide QRS escape) carries higher risk of progression to complete heart block and is more often a pacing indication.
explanation.A: Incorrect — Complete heart block has AV dissociation (P and QRS completely independent). Wenckebach has a maintained relationship with progressive PR lengthening before the dropped beat.
explanation.B: CORRECT — Mobitz I (Wenckebach): progressive PR prolongation then dropped beat. Benign in asymptomatic patient; avoid AV-nodal drugs; cardiology review per ESC guidelines.
explanation.C: Incorrect — First-degree AV block has a prolonged but constant PR interval with every P wave conducting. There are no dropped beats.
explanation.D: Incorrect — Mobitz Type II shows sudden dropped beats (no preceding PR prolongation) and is a higher-risk finding that more often requires pacing. This is Wenckebach (Type I).
explanation.E: Incorrect — Atrial flutter shows a characteristic sawtooth atrial pattern at ~300/min with variable ventricular response. This ECG has sinus P waves.

reference: ESC Guidelines on Cardiac Pacing 2021. https://www.escardio.org/Guidelines

question: A 65-year-old man presents with two episodes of syncope. His ECG shows: regular P waves with a constant PR interval, then sudden dropped QRS complexes (2:1 pattern — every other P wave blocked). The QRS when present is wide (0.16 seconds) with LBBB morphology. Per ESC guidelines, what is the risk of this ECG and management?

options.A: Mobitz I (Wenckebach) — benign; reassure and discharge
options.B: Mobitz Type II second-degree AV block with LBBB — high risk of progression to complete heart block and sudden cardiac death; the wide QRS indicates block below the AV node (infranodal — His-Purkinje system); syncope with this pattern is an indication for urgent permanent pacemaker implantation; admit same-day for cardiology assessment
options.C: First-degree AV block — no treatment required
options.D: Ventricular tachycardia — synchronised DC cardioversion
options.E: Physiological AV block from athletic training — no treatment

explanation.correct: Mobitz Type II second-degree AV block: sudden dropped beats WITHOUT preceding PR prolongation; PR interval is constant when beats do conduct. The wide QRS (LBBB morphology) indicates the block is at the infranodal level (His-Purkinje system) — below the AV node. This is a high-risk finding: infranodal block can deteriorate without warning into complete heart block and asystole. Risk factors indicating urgent pacing: Mobitz II + wide QRS complex (infranodal) + syncope. Per ESC Cardiac Pacing Guidelines 2021: Mobitz II with symptoms (syncope/pre-syncope) is a Class I indication for permanent pacemaker, particularly when the QRS is wide. Even asymptomatic Mobitz II with wide QRS is often a pacing indication (Class IIa). Same-day hospital admission and cardiology assessment is essential.
explanation.A: Incorrect — Wenckebach (Mobitz I) has progressive PR prolongation before the dropped beat. This ECG shows sudden dropped beats with constant PR (Mobitz II). These are different diagnoses with very different prognoses.
explanation.B: CORRECT — Mobitz II + LBBB + syncope: high risk of progression to complete heart block. Urgent permanent pacemaker per ESC 2021 (Class I indication).
explanation.C: Incorrect — First-degree block has prolonged but constant PR with all P waves conducting. This has dropped beats.
explanation.D: Incorrect — This is a conduction block, not a tachyarrhythmia. Cardioversion is inappropriate.
explanation.E: Incorrect — Athletic AV block is vagally mediated Wenckebach during sleep/rest — not Mobitz II with wide QRS in a symptomatic older adult.

reference: ESC Guidelines on Cardiac Pacing 2021. https://www.escardio.org/Guidelines

question: A 52-year-old man is in the GP waiting room when he collapses. The receptionist finds him unresponsive and not breathing normally. The AED advises 'shock advised'. Per Resuscitation Council UK (RCUK) 2021 guidelines, what is the correct sequence of actions?

options.A: Give adrenaline first, then CPR, then defibrillation
options.B: Deliver one shock immediately; resume CPR immediately for 2 minutes (30:2 ratio) without checking for pulse after each shock; reanalyse rhythm after 2 minutes; continue until ROSC, advanced help arrives or decision to stop; adrenaline 1mg IV after 3rd shock then every 3-5 minutes; amiodarone 300mg IV after 3rd shock if shockable rhythm persists
options.C: Check pulse first; only start CPR if no pulse felt within 10 seconds
options.D: Three stacked shocks before starting CPR
options.E: Analyse rhythm every 30 seconds — pause CPR for analysis

explanation.correct: Per Resuscitation Council UK (RCUK) Adult Advanced Life Support 2021 guidelines for shockable rhythms (VF/pulseless VT): AED/defibrillator advises shock → deliver shock → immediately resume CPR (do NOT check pulse after shock — delays are harmful) → 2 minutes of CPR (30 compressions: 2 breaths ratio, or continuous compressions if advanced airway in situ) → reanalyse rhythm → if still shockable: shock 2 → CPR 2 minutes → shock 3 → CPR 2 minutes. After 3rd shock: adrenaline (epinephrine) 1 mg IV/IO + amiodarone 300 mg IV/IO. Subsequent adrenaline: every 3-5 minutes (alternate cycles). Second amiodarone dose: 150 mg after 5th shock if rhythm remains shockable. Key principle: MINIMISE INTERRUPTIONS to chest compressions — hands-off time must be kept to <5 seconds for each shock; no pulse check after shock; CPR resumes immediately.
explanation.A: Incorrect — Adrenaline is given after the 3rd shock in RCUK 2021 ALS — not before defibrillation.
explanation.B: CORRECT — Shock immediately; resume CPR for 2 minutes; reanalyse; adrenaline after 3rd shock; amiodarone after 3rd shock per RCUK 2021 ALS.
explanation.C: Incorrect — In cardiac arrest, checking for a pulse is unreliable and wastes critical time; the AED 'shock advised' indicates a shockable rhythm — proceed with defibrillation.
explanation.D: Incorrect — Stacked shocks (multiple shocks before CPR) were removed from guidelines; single shock followed immediately by CPR is the current RCUK recommendation.
explanation.E: Incorrect — Rhythm analysis is performed every 2 minutes (at the end of each CPR cycle) — not every 30 seconds. Frequent pauses reduce CPR quality.

reference: Resuscitation Council UK — Adult ALS guidelines 2021. https://www.resus.org.uk/library/2021-resuscitation-guidelines

question: A 62-year-old man presents with an anterior STEMI and is taken for primary PCI. Post-procedure, his ECG shows new ST elevation in leads V1-V4 persisting at 48 hours along with a new pansystolic murmur. Per cardiology guidelines, what complication should be suspected?

options.A: Pericarditis — common after MI, treat with aspirin and colchicine
options.B: Ventricular septal defect (VSD) — a mechanical complication of anterior MI (LAD territory) typically occurring 3-7 days post-STEMI; septal necrosis causes an acute left-to-right shunt; presents with new pansystolic murmur, haemodynamic deterioration and oxygenation step-up from right atrium to pulmonary artery; requires urgent echocardiogram; high mortality without surgical/percutaneous closure
options.C: Acute mitral regurgitation from papillary muscle rupture — inferior MI more commonly causes this
options.D: Right ventricular infarction — treated with IV fluids and avoiding nitrates
options.E: Dressler syndrome — autoimmune pericarditis 2-10 weeks post-MI

explanation.correct: Post-STEMI mechanical complications — rare but life-threatening: (1) Ventricular septal defect (VSD): occurs 3-7 days post-anterior MI (LAD/septal branches); septal wall necrosis → rupture → left-to-right shunt; presentation: new loud pansystolic murmur (louder at left sternal edge), acute haemodynamic deterioration, pulmonary oedema, cardiogenic shock. Diagnosis: bedside echo (step-up in O2 saturation from RA to PA on right heart catheter). Treatment: urgent surgical repair or percutaneous closure; high mortality. (2) Papillary muscle rupture → acute mitral regurgitation: occurs with inferior MI (posterior papillary muscle — RCA territory); softer murmur radiating to axilla; pulmonary oedema. (3) Free wall rupture → haemopericardium, tamponade, death. The pansystolic murmur at 48 hours post-anterior STEMI = VSD until proven otherwise.
explanation.A: Incorrect — Post-MI pericarditis (early) causes pleuritic chest pain and a friction rub — not a new pansystolic murmur with haemodynamic change.
explanation.B: CORRECT — Post-anterior STEMI pansystolic murmur = VSD until proven otherwise. Urgent echo + cardiology/cardiac surgery per guidelines.
explanation.C: Incorrect — Papillary muscle rupture causes acute MR and is more common after inferior MI (posterior papillary muscle from RCA). Anterior STEMI more commonly causes VSD.
explanation.D: Incorrect — RV infarction (inferior/posterior MI) causes elevated JVP, hypotension, clear lungs. Not associated with anterior STEMI + new murmur.
explanation.E: Incorrect — Dressler syndrome occurs 2-10 weeks post-MI and causes pleuritic chest pain with pericardial effusion — not an acute pansystolic murmur at 48 hours.

reference: ESC Guidelines — Management of STEMI. https://www.escardio.org/Guidelines

question: A GP is reviewing the ECG of a 55-year-old man and notices: no P waves, an irregular baseline with fine fibrillatory waves at 350-600/min, and an irregular ventricular response at 90/min with narrow QRS complexes. Per NICE NG196, what is this rhythm and initial management?

options.A: Atrial flutter — refer for DC cardioversion
options.B: Atrial fibrillation (AF) — most common sustained cardiac arrhythmia; requires assessment of: stroke risk (CHA₂DS₂-VASc score for anticoagulation decision), ventricular rate control (target <110 bpm at rest using beta-blocker or calcium channel blocker), and consideration of rhythm control (cardioversion, antiarrhythmic drugs, ablation); exclude reversible causes (thyroid disease, infection)
options.C: Sinus tachycardia — reassure and monitor
options.D: Ventricular fibrillation — emergency defibrillation immediately
options.E: Junctional rhythm — no treatment required

explanation.correct: Atrial fibrillation (AF): no organised P waves (replaced by fine fibrillatory baseline), irregularly irregular ventricular response, narrow QRS (unless aberrant conduction). Affects approximately 1.5 million in the UK — most common sustained arrhythmia. Per NICE NG196: (1) Rate control: first-line in most patients; target resting HR <110 bpm; use beta-blocker (bisoprolol) or rate-limiting CCB (diltiazem, verapamil); digoxin for sedentary patients or as add-on. (2) Stroke prevention: CHA₂DS₂-VASc score ≥1 (men), ≥2 (women) = anticoagulate with DOAC (apixaban, rivaroxaban, edoxaban, dabigatran) or warfarin; assess bleeding risk (ORBIT score). (3) Rhythm control: for symptomatic AF despite rate control, younger patients, recent onset; options: cardioversion, antiarrhythmics (flecainide if no structural disease; amiodarone), AF ablation. (4) Investigate and treat reversible causes: TFTs, FBC, renal function, echocardiogram.
explanation.A: Incorrect — Atrial flutter has a regular sawtooth atrial pattern at ~300/min and usually a regular ventricular rate (150/min in 2:1 block). This ECG is irregularly irregular with fibrillatory baseline — AF.
explanation.B: CORRECT — AF: irregularly irregular, no P waves. NICE NG196: rate control + CHA₂DS₂-VASc-guided anticoagulation + consider rhythm control.
explanation.C: Incorrect — Sinus tachycardia has regular P waves before each QRS with a rate 100-150/min. This has no P waves and is irregular.
explanation.D: Incorrect — VF shows chaotic high-amplitude disorganised activity with no discernible QRS complexes — a cardiac arrest rhythm. This patient has a pulse with organised QRS complexes.
explanation.E: Incorrect — Junctional rhythm has narrow QRS with absent or inverted P waves near the QRS at a rate of 40-60/min. Not the irregular AF pattern described.

reference: NICE NG196 — Atrial fibrillation. https://www.nice.org.uk/guidance/ng196

question: A 45-year-old woman presents with a 3-month history of pain and stiffness in both hands worse in the morning for >1 hour. Examination reveals swelling and tenderness of the MCPs and PIPs bilaterally. RF is positive and anti-CCP is strongly positive. Per NICE NG100, what is the diagnosis and first-line DMARD treatment?

options.A: Osteoarthritis — paracetamol and physiotherapy
options.B: Rheumatoid arthritis — autoimmune synovitis; first-line DMARD is methotrexate (plus folic acid 5 mg weekly to reduce side effects); alternative first-line DMARDs: hydroxychloroquine, sulfasalazine, leflunomide; combination DMARD therapy ('COBRA' protocol) may be used; treat-to-target strategy aiming for DAS28 remission or low disease activity; biologics (anti-TNF, JAK inhibitors) if 2 DMARDs fail per NICE NG100
options.C: Psoriatic arthritis — require skin examination first
options.D: Reactive arthritis — check for preceding infection
options.E: Gout — allopurinol and colchicine immediately

explanation.correct: Rheumatoid arthritis (RA): symmetrical small joint polyarthritis (MCPs, PIPs, wrists), morning stiffness >1 hour, positive RF and anti-CCP antibodies (anti-CCP is more specific than RF: 95% specificity). Per NICE NG100 (Rheumatoid arthritis in adults): refer to rheumatology within 3 weeks of presentation (earlier if very active disease); first-line DMARD: methotrexate (oral or SC, starting 7.5-10 mg weekly, titrate to 25 mg); folic acid 5 mg weekly (taken on a different day) reduces methotrexate side effects (mucositis, hepatotoxicity, nausea); monitoring: FBC, LFTs, U&E fortnightly until stable then every 3 months; combination DMARDs (methotrexate + hydroxychloroquine + sulfasalazine = 'COBRA') used in moderate-severe disease; biologics (anti-TNF: adalimumab, etanercept; JAK inhibitors: baricitinib, upadacitinib) if ≥2 DMARDs fail; DAS28 score used to assess disease activity and guide treatment escalation.
explanation.A: Incorrect — Osteoarthritis predominantly affects DIPs, thumb CMC, knees, hips; morning stiffness <30 minutes; RF/anti-CCP negative.
explanation.B: CORRECT — RA: symmetrical MCP/PIP synovitis + positive anti-CCP/RF. Methotrexate + folic acid first-line DMARD per NICE NG100.
explanation.C: Incorrect — Psoriatic arthritis can be seronegative and cause MCP/PIP involvement but anti-CCP positivity strongly suggests RA over PsA.
explanation.D: Incorrect — Reactive arthritis causes asymmetric, typically lower limb oligoarthritis following infection — not symmetrical bilateral hand polyarthritis with positive anti-CCP.
explanation.E: Incorrect — Gout causes acute monoarthritis (typically first MTP) with elevated uric acid — not symmetrical bilateral polyarthritis with positive anti-CCP.

reference: NICE NG100 — Rheumatoid arthritis. https://www.nice.org.uk/guidance/ng100

question: A 32-year-old man presents with a 6-month history of inflammatory low back pain (worse at night, better with exercise, morning stiffness >45 minutes), bilateral buttock pain and anterior uveitis. His CRP is 28 mg/L. Per NICE NG65, what is the most likely diagnosis and key investigation?

options.A: Lumbar disc prolapse — MRI lumbar spine urgently
options.B: Axial spondyloarthritis (axSpA) / ankylosing spondylitis — characterised by inflammatory back pain, sacroiliitis, HLA-B27 positivity (90% of AS); uveitis is a classic extra-articular feature; HLA-B27 blood test and MRI sacroiliac joints (detects early sacroiliitis before X-ray changes); refer to rheumatology
options.C: Reactive arthritis — check for preceding STI or GI infection
options.D: Fibromyalgia — amitriptyline and pain management programme
options.E: Osteoporotic vertebral fractures — DEXA scan

explanation.correct: Axial spondyloarthritis (axSpA) including ankylosing spondylitis: a seronegative spondyloarthropathy characterised by inflammatory back pain and sacroiliitis. Inflammatory back pain features (per ASAS criteria): onset <40 years, insidious onset, improvement with exercise (not rest), worse at night/morning, responds to NSAIDs. Extra-articular manifestations: anterior uveitis (25-40% — recurrent acute unilateral iritis), psoriasis, inflammatory bowel disease, aortic regurgitation. Per NICE NG65 (Spondyloarthritis): HLA-B27 testing (positive in ~90% of ankylosing spondylitis in white Europeans); MRI sacroiliac joints (detects bone marrow oedema/sacroiliitis before X-ray erosions appear — crucial for early diagnosis); refer to rheumatology. Treatment: regular NSAIDs (first-line); physiotherapy; anti-TNF biologics if inadequate response to 2 NSAIDs (adalimumab, etanercept); IL-17 inhibitors (secukinumab).
explanation.A: Incorrect — Mechanical back pain (disc prolapse) is worse with activity, better at rest, and does not cause morning stiffness >45 minutes or uveitis.
explanation.B: CORRECT — Axial spondyloarthritis: inflammatory back pain + uveitis + raised CRP. HLA-B27 + MRI SIJ per NICE NG65.
explanation.C: Incorrect — Reactive arthritis (formerly Reiter's) presents within weeks of a triggering infection with asymmetric peripheral arthritis and urethritis — not a 6-month history of back pain with uveitis.
explanation.D: Incorrect — Fibromyalgia causes widespread musculoskeletal pain with normal inflammatory markers — CRP 28 mg/L and uveitis argue strongly against fibromyalgia.
explanation.E: Incorrect — Osteoporotic fractures occur in elderly patients with mechanical pain — not a young man with inflammatory back pain, raised CRP and uveitis.

reference: NICE NG65 — Spondyloarthritis. https://www.nice.org.uk/guidance/ng65

question: A 28-year-old man with confirmed ankylosing spondylitis has failed 2 NSAIDs. His BASDAI score is 5.2 (range 0-10). Per NICE TA383 and TA28, what is the next treatment option?

options.A: Oral methotrexate — first DMARD in axial spondyloarthritis
options.B: Anti-TNF biologic therapy (e.g. adalimumab, etanercept, infliximab, certolizumab) — indicated when BASDAI ≥4 after failure of 2 or more NSAIDs; approved by NICE TA383; alternatively IL-17A inhibitor (secukinumab or ixekizumab — NICE TA407) is equally effective and first-line biologic option; exclude TB and hepatitis B before starting
options.C: Oral prednisolone long-term — systemic steroids are the backbone of AS treatment
options.D: Physiotherapy alone is sufficient for BASDAI >4
options.E: Sulfasalazine — effective for axial disease in ankylosing spondylitis

explanation.correct: Per NICE TA383 (TNF-alpha inhibitors for AS) and NICE TA407 (Secukinumab for AS): biologic therapy is indicated when: BASDAI (Bath Ankylosing Spondylitis Disease Activity Index) ≥4 AND inadequate response to ≥2 NSAIDs. Anti-TNF agents: adalimumab, etanercept, infliximab, certolizumab, golimumab. IL-17 inhibitors: secukinumab, ixekizumab. Both classes are NICE-approved as first-line biologic therapy with comparable efficacy. Pre-biologic screening: TB (Mantoux/IGRA), hepatitis B/C, HIV. Important: conventional DMARDs (methotrexate, sulfasalazine) are NOT effective for axial disease in AS — they are only used for associated peripheral arthritis. Systemic corticosteroids are not a long-term treatment for AS. Physiotherapy: important adjunct throughout, but not sufficient alone for active disease (BASDAI ≥4).
explanation.A: Incorrect — Methotrexate and other conventional DMARDs are not effective for axial spondyloarthritis — they do not reduce spinal inflammation or radiographic progression.
explanation.B: CORRECT — BASDAI ≥4 after 2 NSAIDs: anti-TNF or IL-17 inhibitor per NICE TA383/TA407. Pre-screen for TB and hepatitis B.
explanation.C: Incorrect — Systemic corticosteroids are not recommended for long-term management of axial spondyloarthritis due to limited efficacy and significant side effects.
explanation.D: Incorrect — Physiotherapy is an important but insufficient treatment when BASDAI ≥4 with failed NSAIDs — biologic therapy is indicated.
explanation.E: Incorrect — Sulfasalazine has very limited evidence for axial AS; it may be considered for peripheral arthritis only — not for the spinal/sacroiliac disease.

reference: NICE TA383 — TNF-alpha inhibitors for AS. NICE TA407 — Secukinumab for AS. https://www.nice.org.uk/guidance/ta383

question: A 55-year-old man presents with central crushing chest pain for 45 minutes radiating to his left arm. His ECG shows 2 mm ST elevation in leads V1-V4. Per NICE NG185, what is the most time-critical intervention and what are the time targets?

options.A: Give aspirin and discharge with GTN spray — wait to see if symptoms resolve
options.B: Primary percutaneous coronary intervention (PPCI) is the treatment of choice for STEMI if PCI-capable centre can be reached within 120 minutes of first medical contact; aspirin 300 mg + ticagrelor 180 mg (or prasugrel); call 999 immediately; activate the PPCI pathway; door-to-balloon time target: <90 minutes; if PPCI not achievable within 120 minutes: fibrinolysis with alteplase/tenecteplase within 30 minutes of hospital arrival (door-to-needle time <30 min)
options.C: Thrombolysis is always first-line for STEMI regardless of location
options.D: Heparin IV infusion and observe on the ward
options.E: Echocardiogram first to confirm the diagnosis before any treatment

explanation.correct: Per NICE NG185 (Acute coronary syndromes) and ESC STEMI guidelines: STEMI is defined by: symptoms + ST elevation ≥1 mm in ≥2 contiguous limb leads or ≥2 mm in ≥2 contiguous precordial leads (V1-V4 here = anterior STEMI — LAD territory). Treatment algorithm: Primary PCI (PPCI) — gold standard; angioplasty + stent opens the occluded artery mechanically; superior to thrombolysis if achievable within 120 minutes of first medical contact; target: door-to-balloon time <90 minutes. Dual antiplatelet therapy: aspirin 300 mg + ticagrelor 180 mg (PLATO trial) or prasugrel 60 mg loading (TRITON trial) — given before PCI. Anticoagulation: UFH or bivalirudin during PCI. Fibrinolysis — if PCI not achievable within 120 minutes: alteplase or tenecteplase IV; door-to-needle target <30 minutes; if fibrinolysis successful → transfer to PCI centre within 3-24 hours for angiography ('pharmaco-invasive strategy').
explanation.A: Incorrect — GTN and discharge is entirely inappropriate for STEMI. This is a life-threatening emergency requiring immediate reperfusion.
explanation.B: CORRECT — PPCI within 120 minutes of first medical contact; door-to-balloon <90 min; aspirin + ticagrelor; fibrinolysis if PPCI not achievable per NICE NG185.
explanation.C: Incorrect — Thrombolysis is ONLY used when PPCI is not achievable within 120 minutes. PPCI is superior when accessible within this time window.
explanation.D: Incorrect — Heparin infusion alone without reperfusion is inadequate for STEMI management.
explanation.E: Incorrect — Echocardiogram is not required before initiating reperfusion therapy in STEMI — the ECG diagnosis is sufficient to activate the PPCI pathway.

reference: NICE NG185 — Acute coronary syndromes. https://www.nice.org.uk/guidance/ng185

question: A 62-year-old woman is reviewed 6 weeks after an anterior STEMI treated with PPCI. She is now on aspirin, ticagrelor, bisoprolol, ramipril and atorvastatin. Per NICE NG185 and ACS secondary prevention guidelines, how long should dual antiplatelet therapy (DAPT) be continued?

options.A: 1 month — then stop both antiplatelets
options.B: 12 months of dual antiplatelet therapy (aspirin + ticagrelor or prasugrel) post-ACS and PCI is the standard recommendation per NICE NG185 and ESC guidelines; after 12 months: continue aspirin indefinitely; ticagrelor/prasugrel stopped (unless high ischaemic risk outweighs bleeding risk — specialist decision); extended DAPT beyond 12 months considered in selected high ischaemic risk patients
options.C: Aspirin lifelong only — no DAPT is needed after discharge
options.D: DAPT indefinitely — never stop in any patient post-ACS
options.E: Stop all antiplatelets at 6 months if no further chest pain

explanation.correct: Per NICE NG185 and ESC ACS Guidelines: after ACS (STEMI or NSTEMI) treated with PCI and stent implantation: DAPT duration: 12 months — aspirin + ticagrelor 90 mg BD (preferred: PLATO trial) or prasugrel 10 mg OD (TRITON trial; avoid if: prior stroke/TIA, weight <60 kg, age >75 years). Rationale: prevents in-stent thrombosis (particularly drug-eluting stents requiring 12 months DAPT). After 12 months: continue aspirin 75 mg indefinitely; stop ticagrelor/prasugrel. Exceptions: shorter DAPT (1-3 months): high bleeding risk (HBR) patients — e.g. on anticoagulation, prior GI bleed; extended DAPT (>12 months, e.g. ticagrelor 60 mg BD — PEGASUS trial): high ischaemic risk, no bleeding risk; complex multi-vessel disease, recurrent events. All other secondary prevention medications: aspirin indefinitely, beta-blocker for 12 months+ if LVSD, ACE inhibitor (especially if LVSD), high-intensity statin.
explanation.A: Incorrect — 1 month DAPT is insufficient after ACS/PCI and risks in-stent thrombosis. 12 months is the standard recommendation.
explanation.B: CORRECT — 12 months DAPT post-ACS/PCI (aspirin + ticagrelor/prasugrel); then aspirin alone indefinitely per NICE NG185.
explanation.C: Incorrect — Aspirin alone after ACS without DAPT is inferior to 12 months of DAPT for prevention of recurrent MI and stent thrombosis.
explanation.D: Incorrect — Indefinite DAPT increases bleeding risk without proportionate benefit beyond 12 months in standard risk patients; duration should be guided by ischaemic vs bleeding risk balance.
explanation.E: Incorrect — 6 months is insufficient for standard-risk ACS/PCI patients; drug-eluting stents require 12 months DAPT per guidelines.

reference: NICE NG185 — Acute coronary syndromes. ESC ACS guidelines. https://www.nice.org.uk/guidance/ng185

question: A 67-year-old man presents to the GP with central chest tightness on walking uphill for the past 2 months, relieved within 5 minutes of rest. He has no symptoms at rest. His resting ECG is normal. Per NICE NG185 and CG95, what is the most appropriate first investigation?

options.A: Resting ECG only — normal ECG excludes stable angina
options.B: CT coronary angiography (CTCA) — per NICE CG95 update and NG185: CTCA is now first-line investigation for stable chest pain with suspected angina in adults; demonstrates coronary artery anatomy and quantifies stenosis; replaces exercise tolerance testing (ETT) and myocardial perfusion imaging (MPI) as first-line; refer to chest pain clinic via rapid access pathway
options.C: Exercise tolerance test (ETT) on treadmill — first-line for stable angina
options.D: Cardiac MRI — gold standard for all angina investigations
options.E: Coronary artery calcium score only — treat if score >100

explanation.correct: Per NICE CG95 (2016 update) and NICE NG185: stable chest pain investigation in the UK has changed significantly. CTCA is now first-line for adults with suspected stable angina who have not previously been investigated. CTCA: provides anatomical information — degree of coronary artery stenosis (% luminal narrowing); highly sensitive for obstructive CAD; rules out coronary artery disease if negative. Advantages over ETT: ETT has limited sensitivity (~60%) and specificity (~70%); ETT measures functional capacity not anatomy; many patients cannot achieve target HR; CTCA is non-invasive and accurate. If CTCA shows: no coronary artery disease → stable angina excluded; obstructive CAD (>70% stenosis in major vessel) → functional assessment (fractional flow reserve CT, stress perfusion MRI, or MPI) or invasive coronary angiography ± revascularisation; non-obstructive CAD → optimise medical therapy. Chest pain clinic: patients with suspected stable angina should be referred to a rapid access chest pain clinic (RACPC) within 2 weeks.
explanation.A: Incorrect — Normal resting ECG does not exclude stable angina — the ECG is typically normal between episodes; a normal resting ECG has very limited diagnostic value for stable angina.
explanation.B: CORRECT — CTCA is the first-line investigation for stable chest pain with suspected angina per NICE CG95/NG185; replaces ETT as first-line.
explanation.C: Incorrect — Exercise tolerance test is no longer first-line for suspected stable angina per current NICE guidance; CTCA has replaced it.
explanation.D: Incorrect — Cardiac MRI (stress perfusion MRI) is a functional test used when CTCA is inconclusive or contraindicated — not the first-line investigation.
explanation.E: Incorrect — Coronary artery calcium score quantifies calcified plaque burden but does not directly assess luminal stenosis and is not the recommended first-line investigation for symptomatic angina.

reference: NICE CG95 — Chest pain of recent onset. NICE NG185. https://www.nice.org.uk/guidance/cg95

question: A 32-year-old woman has recurrent SVT managed with beta-blockers. She wishes to become pregnant. Per cardiological and obstetric guidance, which drugs are safe for SVT management in pregnancy?

options.A: Amiodarone — safest antiarrhythmic in pregnancy
options.B: Adenosine (for acute termination of SVT) and beta-blockers (metoprolol or atenolol for prophylaxis — with caution) are the most frequently used; adenosine: safe in all trimesters for acute SVT termination; beta-blockers: relatively safe but associated with fetal growth restriction (particularly atenolol); metoprolol preferred; flecainide: relatively safe in pregnancy for SVT without structural heart disease; amiodarone: avoid — causes fetal hypothyroidism, IUGR and neonatal thyroid disease
options.C: Verapamil IV is the safest acute treatment in pregnancy
options.D: No treatment needed — all SVTs are safe in pregnancy
options.E: DC cardioversion is absolutely contraindicated in pregnancy

explanation.correct: SVT management in pregnancy requires careful drug selection due to fetal exposure: Adenosine: safe in all trimesters for acute SVT termination; short half-life (<10 seconds); does not significantly cross the placenta; remains first-line for acute SVT in pregnancy per ESC guidelines. Beta-blockers: metoprolol (beta-1 selective) preferred over atenolol; atenolol associated with fetal growth restriction in first trimester (avoid if possible); beta-blockers are most commonly used for SVT prophylaxis in pregnancy; monitor for neonatal bradycardia and hypoglycaemia. Flecainide: considered relatively safe for SVT prophylaxis in pregnancy without structural heart disease. Verapamil IV: can cause maternal hypotension and fetal bradycardia — used with caution, not first-line. Amiodarone: AVOID — causes fetal hypothyroidism, IUGR, neonatal bradycardia, thyroid abnormalities; only for refractory life-threatening arrhythmias. DC cardioversion: safe in pregnancy when clinically indicated — fetal risk from unsynchronised cardioversion is very low.
explanation.A: Incorrect — Amiodarone should be AVOIDED in pregnancy due to fetal hypothyroidism, IUGR and neonatal thyroid disease.
explanation.B: CORRECT — Adenosine (acute SVT) and metoprolol (prophylaxis) are safe; amiodarone is avoided; DC cardioversion is safe when needed per ESC pregnancy guidelines.
explanation.C: Incorrect — Verapamil IV can cause significant maternal hypotension and fetal bradycardia — adenosine is preferred for acute SVT in pregnancy.
explanation.D: Incorrect — Sustained SVT can compromise maternal cardiac output and fetal perfusion — treatment is required for symptomatic or sustained episodes.
explanation.E: Incorrect — DC cardioversion is safe in pregnancy and is the treatment of choice for haemodynamically unstable arrhythmias that do not respond to medication.

reference: ESC Guidelines — Cardiovascular disease during pregnancy 2018. https://www.escardio.org/Guidelines

question: A 48-year-old woman has palpitations occurring twice weekly, each lasting 5-10 minutes. A 7-day ambulatory ECG captures her symptoms: during palpitations the ECG shows: regular narrow complex tachycardia at 178/min with no visible P waves (or P waves buried within the QRS). Per NICE NG196, what is the most likely arrhythmia?
