options.A: Atrial fibrillation — irregularly irregular narrow complex tachycardia
options.B: AV nodal re-entrant tachycardia (AVNRT) — the most common cause of regular narrow complex tachycardia (SVT) in adults; characterised by a re-entrant circuit within the AV node; P waves are absent or visible just after the QRS (retrograde); abrupt onset/offset; responds to vagal manoeuvres and IV adenosine; definitive treatment: radiofrequency catheter ablation
options.C: Sinus tachycardia — normal physiological response to exercise
options.D: Ventricular tachycardia — broad complex, requires immediate DC cardioversion
options.E: Atrial flutter — sawtooth pattern at 300/min

explanation.correct: AV nodal re-entrant tachycardia (AVNRT): the most common paroxysmal SVT in adults (accounts for ~60% of SVTs). Mechanism: dual AV nodal pathways (fast and slow) create a re-entrant circuit; typically slow-fast AVNRT — conduction down the slow pathway and retrogradely up the fast pathway. ECG: regular narrow complex tachycardia 140-220/min; P waves buried within or just after the QRS (retrograde atrial activation near-simultaneous with ventricular). Symptoms: abrupt onset/offset palpitations (classically described as pounding in the neck), dizziness. Per NICE NG196: acute termination: vagal manoeuvres (Valsalva, carotid sinus massage) → IV adenosine (6mg rapid bolus IV; if no response 12mg; monitor for bronchospasm — withhold in asthmatics). Prevention: beta-blockers, flecainide (if no structural heart disease), verapamil. Definitive: radiofrequency catheter ablation (>95% cure rate).
explanation.A: Incorrect — AF is irregularly irregular with no P waves and a chaotic baseline. This tachycardia is regular.
explanation.B: CORRECT — AVNRT: regular narrow complex SVT at 150-220/min, P waves in/after QRS, abrupt onset/offset. Adenosine for acute termination; ablation for cure per NICE NG196.
explanation.C: Incorrect — Sinus tachycardia has clearly visible P waves before each QRS, gradual onset/offset, and rate rarely exceeds 150/min at rest.
explanation.D: Incorrect — VT is broad complex (QRS >0.12s). This is narrow complex — AVNRT.
explanation.E: Incorrect — Atrial flutter has characteristic sawtooth flutter waves at 300/min with ventricular rate typically 150/min (2:1 block).

reference: NICE NG196 — Atrial fibrillation and arrhythmias. https://www.nice.org.uk/guidance/ng196

question: A 35-year-old man presents to the GP with palpitations. During the episode his ECG shows: regular narrow complex tachycardia at 196/min with a short PR interval of 0.09 seconds and a delta wave visible on the initial upstroke of the QRS on the resting ECG. Per guidelines, what is the diagnosis and important management consideration?

options.A: Sinus tachycardia — no action needed
options.B: Wolff-Parkinson-White (WPW) syndrome — accessory pathway (Bundle of Kent) bypasses the AV node causing ventricular pre-excitation (short PR, delta wave on resting ECG); in AF, the accessory pathway can conduct very rapidly to the ventricles causing ventricular rates >300/min and ventricular fibrillation; AVOID AV-nodal blocking drugs (adenosine, beta-blockers, verapamil, digoxin) if AF develops with WPW — they may accelerate accessory pathway conduction; refer to electrophysiology for catheter ablation (curative)
options.C: Brugada syndrome — avoid sodium channel blockers and arrange ICD
options.D: Long QT syndrome — avoid QT-prolonging drugs
options.E: AVNRT — adenosine is safe and first-line in all narrow complex SVTs

explanation.correct: Wolff-Parkinson-White (WPW) syndrome: congenital accessory conduction pathway (Bundle of Kent) connecting atria to ventricles, bypassing the AV node. Resting ECG: short PR (<0.12s), delta wave (slurred upstroke of QRS due to ventricular pre-excitation), widened QRS. During SVT: usually orthodromic AVRT — narrow complex tachycardia (conduction down AV node, retrograde up accessory pathway). CRITICAL RISK: if AF develops in WPW, the accessory pathway can conduct extremely rapidly to the ventricles (>300/min) → ventricular fibrillation → sudden cardiac death. CONTRAINDICATED in WPW with AF: adenosine, beta-blockers, verapamil, diltiazem, digoxin — these block the AV node but may facilitate rapid conduction via the accessory pathway. Management of WPW with AF: IV flecainide or DC cardioversion. Definitive treatment: electrophysiology study + radiofrequency catheter ablation (>95% cure). Refer ALL WPW patients to electrophysiology.
explanation.A: Incorrect — Short PR + delta wave + SVT is WPW, not sinus tachycardia. This diagnosis carries a risk of sudden cardiac death if unrecognised.
explanation.B: CORRECT — WPW: short PR, delta wave, accessory pathway. Avoid AV-nodal blockers if AF develops (VF risk). Electrophysiology referral for ablation.
explanation.C: Incorrect — Brugada syndrome shows right bundle branch block pattern with ST elevation in V1-V3 — not delta waves and short PR.
explanation.D: Incorrect — Long QT syndrome shows prolonged QT interval — not short PR and delta wave.
explanation.E: Incorrect — Adenosine is specifically CONTRAINDICATED in WPW with AF. It can precipitate rapid accessory pathway conduction and VF. This is a critical prescribing safety point.

reference: ESC Guidelines — SVT management 2019. https://www.escardio.org/Guidelines

question: A 28-year-old man presents with a 4-month history of bloody diarrhoea (6-8 loose stools per day), urgency, mucus and 5 kg weight loss. Colonoscopy confirms continuous mucosal inflammation from the rectum to the splenic flexure. Per NICE NG130, what is the diagnosis and induction treatment for a moderate-severe flare?

options.A: Crohn's disease — azathioprine and prednisolone
options.B: Ulcerative colitis — the continuous mucosal inflammation from the rectum confirms UC (Crohn's is typically patchy/skip lesions); moderate-severe flare (Truelove-Witts criteria: >6 bloody stools/day + systemic features): oral prednisolone 40 mg/day for induction; aminosalicylate (5-ASA: mesalazine) for maintenance; if no response to oral steroids within 72 hours: IV corticosteroids; if IV steroids fail: IV ciclosporin or infliximab as rescue therapy; colectomy if medical rescue fails
options.C: Infectious colitis — stool MC&S only; antibiotics for all cases
options.D: IBS — antispasmodics and dietary modification
options.E: Microscopic colitis — budesonide 9 mg daily

explanation.correct: Ulcerative colitis (UC): continuous mucosal inflammation starting from the rectum (proctitis → left-sided → extensive/pancolitis). Truelove-Witts severity criteria: Mild: <4 bloody stools/day, no systemic features; Moderate: 4-6 bloody stools/day, mild systemic features; Severe: >6 bloody stools/day + at least one of: HR >90, temperature >37.8°C, Hb <105 g/L, ESR >30 mm/hr. This patient: 6-8 bloody stools = moderate-severe. Per NICE NG130 (Ulcerative colitis): Mild-moderate proctitis/left-sided UC: topical (rectal) 5-ASA ± oral 5-ASA. Moderate-severe left-sided/extensive UC: oral prednisolone 40 mg/day (4-8 weeks then taper); continue 5-ASA maintenance; if no improvement at 72 hours on oral steroids: admit for IV hydrocortisone 100 mg QDS; if IV steroids fail at 72 hours: IV ciclosporin or infliximab rescue; subtotal colectomy if rescue fails. Crohn's distinction: patchy transmural inflammation, skip lesions, any part of GI tract, cobblestoning, fistulae.
explanation.A: Incorrect — Continuous inflammation from the rectum is the hallmark of UC, not Crohn's disease (which causes patchy skip lesions). Management also differs.
explanation.B: CORRECT — UC: continuous rectal mucosal inflammation; moderate-severe: oral prednisolone 40mg; 5-ASA maintenance; IV steroids/ciclosporin/infliximab rescue if needed per NICE NG130.
explanation.C: Incorrect — Infectious colitis is a differential (stool cultures should be sent) but 4-month history with confirmed colonoscopic mucosal changes confirms chronic inflammatory bowel disease.
explanation.D: Incorrect — IBS does not cause bloody diarrhoea, weight loss or colonoscopic mucosal changes.
explanation.E: Incorrect — Microscopic colitis causes watery non-bloody diarrhoea with a normal-appearing colonoscopy (diagnosis by biopsy). This patient has bloody diarrhoea and visible mucosal changes.

reference: NICE NG130 — Ulcerative colitis. https://www.nice.org.uk/guidance/ng130

question: A 35-year-old woman with extensive ulcerative colitis has been in remission on mesalazine 2.4g/day for 18 months. She is now planning a pregnancy. Per NICE NG130 and BSG guidance on IBD in pregnancy, what should she be counselled about her medications?

options.A: Stop all UC medications before conception — all drugs are teratogenic
options.B: Continue mesalazine (5-ASA) throughout pregnancy — it is safe for both mother and fetus; active UC during pregnancy carries greater risks (preterm birth, low birthweight, miscarriage) than the medication; methotrexate must be stopped 3-6 months before conception (teratogenic); azathioprine can be continued in pregnancy if essential; biologics (infliximab, adalimumab) are generally continued in pregnancy under specialist supervision
options.C: Switch to sulfasalazine only — all other 5-ASAs are contraindicated in pregnancy
options.D: Mesalazine must be stopped in the third trimester only
options.E: Pregnancy always causes remission in UC — no medication needed

explanation.correct: Per NICE NG130, BSG IBD in pregnancy guidelines, and ECCO guidelines: mesalazine (5-ASA): safe throughout all trimesters of pregnancy and breastfeeding; continue at the current dose; active UC is more dangerous to the fetus than mesalazine. Key drug safety in IBD pregnancy: SAFE to continue: mesalazine, sulfasalazine (+ folic acid 5 mg — sulfasalazine inhibits dihydrofolate reductase), prednisolone (short course for flares), azathioprine (continue if well-controlled on it), biologics (anti-TNF: infliximab, adalimumab — continue under specialist; stop 3rd trimester biologics noted in some guidance — specialist decision due to cord transfer). MUST STOP: methotrexate (stop 3-6 months before conception — teratogenic, causes methotrexate embryopathy: CNS defects, limb abnormalities); thalidomide (teratogenic). General principle: the risks of uncontrolled active IBD during pregnancy (preterm birth, low birth weight, miscarriage, caesarean section) outweigh the risks of most IBD medications.
explanation.A: Incorrect — Stopping all IBD medications risks disease relapse; active UC during pregnancy causes significant maternal and fetal morbidity.
explanation.B: CORRECT — Mesalazine is safe throughout pregnancy; active UC is more dangerous than mesalazine; stop methotrexate pre-conception; azathioprine can be continued per NICE NG130/BSG.
explanation.C: Incorrect — All 5-ASA preparations (mesalazine, balsalazide, olsalazine) are generally safe in pregnancy; there is no requirement to switch specifically to sulfasalazine.
explanation.D: Incorrect — Mesalazine is safe throughout all three trimesters — it should not be stopped in any trimester.
explanation.E: Incorrect — Pregnancy has variable effects on IBD; UC may improve, worsen or remain stable — this is not reliable and medication should not be stopped on the basis that 'pregnancy causes remission'.

reference: NICE NG130 — Ulcerative colitis. BSG IBD in pregnancy guidelines. https://www.nice.org.uk/guidance/ng130

question: A 42-year-old man with longstanding extensive UC (pancolitis for 15 years) attends for a review. Per NICE NG130 and BSG guidelines, what colonoscopic surveillance schedule is recommended to monitor his cancer risk?

options.A: No surveillance is needed — UC does not increase colorectal cancer risk
options.B: Colonoscopic surveillance starting 8-10 years after symptom onset: annually if high risk (primary sclerosing cholangitis, stricture, previous dysplasia, active endoscopic inflammation); every 3 years if low risk (extensive UC in remission, no PSC, no previous dysplasia); every 1-2 years if intermediate risk per BSG guidelines; chromoendoscopy preferred to detect flat dysplasia
options.C: Annual colonoscopy from diagnosis in all UC patients
options.D: Colonoscopy only when symptomatic — routine surveillance is not evidence-based
options.E: CEA blood test every 6 months — equal to colonoscopy for CRC detection in UC

explanation.correct: Ulcerative colitis and colorectal cancer (CRC) risk: extensive UC (beyond the splenic flexure) significantly increases CRC risk — approximately 2% at 10 years, 8% at 20 years, 18% at 30 years. Per BSG IBD surveillance guidelines (2022) and NICE NG130: Surveillance begins 8-10 years after symptom onset (not from diagnosis). Risk stratification: Low risk: extensive UC in remission, no PSC, no previous dysplasia → colonoscopy every 3-4 years. Intermediate risk: mild endoscopic inflammation, post-inflammatory polyps → every 2-3 years. High risk: PSC (annual from PSC diagnosis), stricture, previous low-grade dysplasia, severe/active endoscopic inflammation → every year. Technique: chromoendoscopy (indigo carmine or methylene blue dye spraying) is preferred as it highlights flat dysplasia invisible on white light colonoscopy. Biopsies: targeted biopsies of suspicious areas; systematic random biopsies no longer recommended if chromoendoscopy available.
explanation.A: Incorrect — Extensive longstanding UC significantly increases CRC risk; surveillance colonoscopy is specifically recommended by NICE NG130 and BSG guidelines.
explanation.B: CORRECT — Surveillance from 8-10 years after onset; risk-stratified 1-4 year intervals; chromoendoscopy per NICE NG130/BSG 2022.
explanation.C: Incorrect — Annual colonoscopy from diagnosis would be excessive and impractical for all UC patients; the 8-10 year starting point and risk-stratified intervals are the correct approach.
explanation.D: Incorrect — Surveillance colonoscopy is recommended for extensive UC as dysplasia is often endoscopically invisible — waiting for symptoms misses early detectable dysplasia.
explanation.E: Incorrect — CEA is not validated or recommended for CRC surveillance in UC patients; colonoscopy with chromoendoscopy is the standard.

reference: NICE NG130 — Ulcerative colitis. BSG IBD surveillance guidelines 2022. https://www.nice.org.uk/guidance/ng130

question: A 26-year-old man presents with a 6-month history of right iliac fossa pain, non-bloody diarrhoea, 7 kg weight loss and a perianal fistula. CRP is 88 mg/L. Colonoscopy shows skip lesions, cobblestoning, and transmural inflammation from the terminal ileum. Per NICE NG129, what is the diagnosis and what investigation confirms disease extent?

options.A: Ulcerative colitis — continuous colonic inflammation from the rectum
options.B: Crohn's disease — characterised by transmural, patchy (skip lesion) inflammation that can affect any part of the GI tract from mouth to anus; perianal disease (fistula, abscess) is specific to Crohn's; MRI small bowel (MRI enterography) is the investigation of choice for assessing small bowel extent; capsule endoscopy also used; per NICE NG129: induce remission with corticosteroids or exclusive enteral nutrition (children); azathioprine or mercaptopurine for maintenance; biologics for moderate-severe disease
options.C: Irritable bowel syndrome with perianal Crohn's disease — treat with antispasmodics
options.D: Infective gastroenteritis — prescribe ciprofloxacin
options.E: Intestinal tuberculosis — test for TB before any treatment

explanation.correct: Crohn's disease: transmural, granulomatous inflammation; can affect any part of the GI tract; patchy ('skip') lesions; cobblestone mucosa; deep fissuring ulcers; fistulae (entero-enteric, entero-cutaneous, perianal); extra-intestinal manifestations (arthritis, uveitis, erythema nodosum, pyoderma gangrenosum). Distinguishing from UC: Crohn's — transmural, any segment, perianal disease, granulomas on histology, non-bloody diarrhoea more common; UC — mucosal, continuous from rectum, no perianal fistulae, bloody diarrhoea. Per NICE NG129: MRI enterography (MRI small bowel) is preferred for assessing small bowel disease extent and perianal Crohn's (superior soft tissue resolution, no radiation vs CT). Capsule endoscopy: good sensitivity for small bowel mucosal disease when MRI inconclusive (contraindicated if stricture suspected). Treatment: induction: oral prednisolone or budesonide (ileal/right colonic); EEN (exclusive enteral nutrition) especially in children; maintenance: azathioprine/6-mercaptopurine; biologics (anti-TNF: adalimumab, infliximab; vedolizumab; ustekinumab) for moderate-severe/refractory disease.
explanation.A: Incorrect — UC causes continuous mucosal inflammation from the rectum; patchy skip lesions, perianal fistula and transmural involvement are hallmarks of Crohn's disease.
explanation.B: CORRECT — Crohn's disease: transmural skip lesions, perianal fistula, terminal ileitis; MRI enterography for small bowel assessment per NICE NG129.
explanation.C: Incorrect — IBS does not cause structural abnormalities on colonoscopy, weight loss, elevated CRP or perianal fistula.
explanation.D: Incorrect — Infective gastroenteritis is acute and self-limiting; 6-month history with colonoscopic changes excludes acute infection as the sole diagnosis.
explanation.E: Incorrect — TB should be excluded before starting anti-TNF biologics (IGRA test), but the clinical and colonoscopic picture here is consistent with Crohn's disease — Crohn's treatment should not be indefinitely deferred.

reference: NICE NG129 — Crohn's disease. https://www.nice.org.uk/guidance/ng129

question: A 32-year-old woman with ileocolonic Crohn's disease has failed two immunomodulators (azathioprine, then methotrexate). Her Harvey-Bradshaw Index is 12 (severe disease). Per NICE TA187 and NG129, what is the next treatment?

options.A: Increase azathioprine dose — insufficient dose is the cause of failure
options.B: Anti-TNF biologic therapy (adalimumab or infliximab) — indicated for severe active Crohn's disease that has failed conventional therapy (immunomodulators); per NICE TA187/TA352: adalimumab or infliximab are approved; exclude TB (IGRA/Mantoux) and hepatitis B before starting; after 12 weeks (induction), assess response — continue if significant response; if anti-TNF fails: ustekinumab (NICE TA456) or vedolizumab (NICE TA352)
options.C: Dietary modification alone — avoid trigger foods
options.D: Immediate surgery — Crohn's always requires colectomy after immunomodulator failure
options.E: Long-term oral prednisolone — maintain remission with steroids

explanation.correct: Per NICE TA187 (Adalimumab for Crohn's), NICE TA187 and NG129: Anti-TNF biologics are indicated when: moderate-severe active Crohn's disease (HBI >8 or CDAI >300, or steroid-dependent/refractory disease) AND inadequate response to conventional therapy (corticosteroids + ≥1 immunomodulator). Options: infliximab (IV infusion at 0, 2, 6 weeks then 8-weekly — ACCENT I trial); adalimumab (SC injection at weeks 0, 2, then fortnightly — CLASSIC, CHARM trials). Pre-treatment screening: IGRA/Mantoux (latent TB — anti-TNF reactivates TB); Hepatitis B serology; Hepatitis C; HIV; Varicella immunity. Response assessment at 12 weeks: if significant response → continue; if no response → switch anti-TNF or escalate. If anti-TNF fails: ustekinumab (IL-12/23 inhibitor — NICE TA456 for Crohn's), vedolizumab (gut-selective integrin inhibitor — NICE TA352), risankizumab. Long-term steroids: not appropriate for Crohn's maintenance (bone loss, metabolic side effects, adrenal suppression).
explanation.A: Incorrect — The patient has failed two different immunomodulators — the issue is not underdosing; biologic therapy is the appropriate next step.
explanation.B: CORRECT — Anti-TNF biologic (adalimumab or infliximab) for severe Crohn's after immunomodulator failure; pre-screen for TB and hepatitis B per NICE TA187/NG129.
explanation.C: Incorrect — Dietary modification is an adjunct in Crohn's management (EEN for induction in children; specific carbohydrate diets) but is not sufficient for severe active disease.
explanation.D: Incorrect — Surgery is not automatically the next step after immunomodulator failure; biologic therapy is tried before considering surgery for ileocolonic Crohn's.
explanation.E: Incorrect — Long-term oral prednisolone is not an appropriate maintenance strategy for Crohn's — it does not modify disease course and has significant cumulative side effects.

reference: NICE TA187 — Adalimumab for Crohn's. NICE NG129. https://www.nice.org.uk/guidance/ta187

question: A 29-year-old man with Crohn's disease is about to start adalimumab. The GP needs to ensure pre-biologic screening is complete. Per NICE NG129, BSG guidance and BNF, which combination of pre-treatment tests is required?

options.A: FBC only — adalimumab suppresses bone marrow
options.B: Tuberculosis screening (IGRA or Mantoux test); Hepatitis B serology (HBsAg, anti-HBc, anti-HBs); Hepatitis C antibody; HIV test; Varicella-zoster IgG (chickenpox immunity); FBC; LFTs; and ensure vaccinations are up to date before starting (live vaccines contraindicated once on biologic)
options.C: CT chest to exclude TB — serology tests are unreliable
options.D: No pre-biologic screening required for adalimumab
options.E: Colonoscopy to confirm disease extent before starting adalimumab

explanation.correct: Pre-biologic therapy screening (anti-TNF such as adalimumab, infliximab) per NICE NG129, BSG guidelines and BNF: Latent TB: IGRA (interferon-gamma release assay: QuantiFERON-TB Gold or T-SPOT) preferred; Mantoux (tuberculin skin test) as alternative; if positive: treat latent TB (isoniazid 6 months) before starting anti-TNF. Rationale: anti-TNF blocks TNF-alpha which is essential for granuloma maintenance — reactivates latent TB. Hepatitis B: HBsAg (active infection), anti-HBc (past exposure), anti-HBs (protective immunity); positive HBsAg or anti-HBc: refer hepatology — anti-TNF can reactivate HBV causing fulminant hepatitis. Hepatitis C: screen and treat if positive before starting. HIV: baseline testing. Varicella-zoster IgG: seronegative patients should be vaccinated (live vaccine) BEFORE starting biologic (live vaccines absolutely contraindicated once on anti-TNF). Vaccinations: MMR, pneumococcal, influenza, hepatitis B vaccine if seronegative — all given BEFORE starting biologic. Blood tests: FBC (baseline), LFTs (baseline), renal function.
explanation.A: Incorrect — FBC alone is entirely insufficient pre-biologic screening; IGRA for TB and hepatitis serology are critically important safety checks.
explanation.B: CORRECT — IGRA (TB), hepatitis B serology, hepatitis C, HIV, varicella IgG, FBC, LFTs; vaccinations updated before starting; live vaccines contraindicated once on biologic per NICE NG129/BSG/BNF.
explanation.C: Incorrect — CT chest is not the recommended TB screening test; IGRA is preferred as it detects latent TB that may be CT-invisible.
explanation.D: Incorrect — Pre-biologic screening is mandatory and legally/clinically required before initiating anti-TNF therapy.
explanation.E: Incorrect — Colonoscopy for disease staging may be appropriate but is not a mandatory pre-biologic safety screening requirement; the focus of pre-treatment screening is infection safety.

reference: NICE NG129 — Crohn's disease. BSG pre-biologic screening. BNF — Adalimumab. https://www.nice.org.uk/guidance/ng129

question: A 35-year-old woman with well-controlled asthma on ICS/LABA (fluticasone/salmeterol) attends for a routine review. She reports using her SABA (salbutamol) reliever 4-5 times per week. Per NICE NG80, is her asthma controlled and what should the GP do?

options.A: Asthma is well-controlled — SABA use 4-5 times per week is acceptable
options.B: Asthma is uncontrolled — SABA use >2 days per week indicates uncontrolled asthma; review inhaler technique and adherence first; if technique is good, step up treatment; consider referral to specialist asthma clinic; prescribe no more than 12 SABA inhalers per year (>12/year = marker of poor control and increased mortality risk per MHRA/BTS); assess for potential triggers
options.C: Add oral prednisolone daily — uncontrolled asthma always requires systemic steroids
options.D: Switch to LAMA only — salbutamol should be stopped
options.E: Double the ICS dose is never appropriate — step down instead

explanation.correct: Per NICE NG80 (Asthma), BTS/SIGN guidelines: markers of uncontrolled asthma: SABA use >2 days per week (more than 2 puffs per occasion); nocturnal symptoms; any activity limitation; any need for oral corticosteroids. This patient: SABA 4-5 times per week = uncontrolled asthma on ICS/LABA. Action steps: (1) Verify diagnosis; (2) Review inhaler technique (poor technique causes apparent non-response); (3) Check adherence; (4) Identify and address triggers; (5) If technique/adherence confirmed: step up to next BTS/SIGN step. MHRA/NICE safety guidance: prescribing >12 SABA inhalers per year is a red flag for poor control and is associated with increased risk of severe attacks and asthma death; prescribers should not issue more than 12 per year without review. Consider referral to specialist asthma clinic if uncontrolled despite optimal step-up.
explanation.A: Incorrect — SABA use >2 days per week is a marker of uncontrolled asthma requiring action per NICE NG80/BTS.
explanation.B: CORRECT — Uncontrolled asthma (SABA >2 days/week); review technique/adherence; step up; limit to ≤12 SABA inhalers/year; consider referral per NICE NG80/MHRA guidance.
explanation.C: Incorrect — Long-term daily oral prednisolone is not appropriate for managing uncontrolled asthma at this level — step up ICS/LABA therapy is the correct approach first.
explanation.D: Incorrect — LAMA (tiotropium) is an add-on therapy at BTS Step 4 — not a replacement for SABA. Salbutamol reliever should not be stopped.
explanation.E: Incorrect — Stepping up ICS dose or adding further controller therapy IS appropriate for uncontrolled asthma at this step.

reference: NICE NG80 — Asthma. MHRA — SABA overuse. https://www.nice.org.uk/guidance/ng80

question: A 24-year-old woman with asthma is 22 weeks pregnant and has an acute asthma attack in the GP surgery. Her peak flow is 210 L/min (her personal best is 480 L/min = 44% of best). She is breathless at rest but can speak in sentences. Per BTS/SIGN asthma guidelines and RCOG guidance, what is the severity and acute management?

options.A: Mild attack — give salbutamol 2 puffs via spacer and review in 1 hour
options.B: Moderate to severe acute asthma — peak flow 44% of best indicates a moderate-severe attack; give salbutamol 2.5-5 mg nebuliser and ipratropium 0.5mg nebuliser; oral prednisolone 40-50 mg (or IV hydrocortisone 100 mg); oxygen to maintain SpO2 94-98%; call 999/arrange urgent hospital admission; fetal monitoring is important in severe asthma in pregnancy
options.C: Near-fatal attack — immediate intubation and ventilation in the GP surgery
options.D: Give salbutamol inhaler and monitor at home — prednisolone is contraindicated in pregnancy
options.E: Refer to obstetrics only — respiratory conditions in pregnancy are managed by obstetricians

explanation.correct: Per BTS/SIGN asthma guidelines: acute asthma severity classification: Moderate: PEFR 50-75% best/predicted, SpO2 ≥92%, can talk. Severe: PEFR 33-50% best, SpO2 ≥92%, difficulty talking. Life-threatening: PEFR <33% best, SpO2 <92%, exhaustion, silent chest, cyanosis. This patient: PEFR 44% = severe. Management: salbutamol 2.5-5 mg nebulised (repeat every 20 minutes); ipratropium 0.5 mg nebulised; oral prednisolone 40-50 mg (IV hydrocortisone 100 mg if unable to swallow); oxygen (target SpO2 94-98%); urgent hospital admission. Prednisolone IS safe in pregnancy (benefits outweigh risks) — per RCOG and BTS/SIGN: never withhold prednisolone from a pregnant woman with acute severe asthma. Fetal wellbeing monitoring needed. Magnesium sulphate IV 1.2-2g over 20 min if poor response.
explanation.A: Incorrect — PEFR 44% is not a mild attack — it is severe. Mild attack would be PEFR >75%.
explanation.B: CORRECT — Severe acute asthma: nebulised salbutamol + ipratropium + oral prednisolone + O2 + urgent hospital admission. Prednisolone IS safe in pregnancy per BTS/SIGN/RCOG.
explanation.C: Incorrect — Near-fatal asthma has PEFR <33% with SpO2 <92%, cyanosis, silent chest, exhaustion. This patient can speak in sentences.
explanation.D: Incorrect — Prednisolone is NOT contraindicated in pregnancy for acute severe asthma — withholding it risks maternal and fetal hypoxia.
explanation.E: Incorrect — Acute asthma in pregnancy is a medical emergency managed by the acute medical team with obstetric input, not by obstetrics alone.

reference: BTS/SIGN — Asthma guideline 2019. RCOG — Asthma in pregnancy. https://www.brit-thoracic.org.uk/quality-improvement/guidelines/asthma/

question: A 30-year-old pregnant woman at 28 weeks has her asthma reviewed. She is currently on salbutamol PRN only and has daily symptoms and 3 night wakings per week. Per NICE NG80 and BTS/SIGN, at which treatment step does she sit and what should be added?

options.A: Step 1 — increase salbutamol dose only
options.B: Step 2 — daily symptoms and nocturnal symptoms indicate uncontrolled asthma at Step 1; add an inhaled corticosteroid (ICS — e.g. beclometasone 200-800 mcg daily); ICS is safe throughout pregnancy and is the most important preventer medication; do NOT withhold ICS in pregnancy — uncontrolled asthma carries greater risks to the fetus than ICS
options.C: Step 4 — all pregnant women need high-dose ICS plus LABA
options.D: No medication change — accept suboptimal control during pregnancy
options.E: Step 3 — add LABA before trying ICS first

explanation.correct: Per NICE NG80 and BTS/SIGN asthma management guidelines: BTS/SIGN stepwise approach: Step 1: SABA (salbutamol) PRN only — mild intermittent symptoms. Step 2: Low-dose ICS (e.g. beclometasone 200-400 mcg BDP equivalent daily) — when: symptoms >2/week OR nocturnal symptoms OR SABA use >2 days/week OR any nocturnal symptoms. This patient: daily symptoms + 3 night wakings/week → Step 2 treatment is clearly indicated. ICS safety in pregnancy: well-established safety profile throughout all trimesters; do NOT withhold ICS. Uncontrolled asthma in pregnancy → fetal hypoxia, IUGR, preterm delivery — risks far exceed any theoretical ICS risk. Step 3 (if Step 2 insufficient): add LABA (salmeterol or formoterol) to ICS. Step 4+: specialist review, additional agents.
explanation.A: Incorrect — Simply increasing salbutamol dose does not address the underlying airway inflammation — ICS preventer therapy is required.
explanation.B: CORRECT — Daily symptoms + nocturnal symptoms = Step 2: add ICS. ICS is safe in pregnancy. Greater risk from uncontrolled asthma per NICE NG80/BTS.
explanation.C: Incorrect — Step 4 (high-dose ICS + LABA + other agents) is for uncontrolled asthma despite lower step treatment. This patient is on Step 1 requiring Step 2.
explanation.D: Incorrect — Accepting poor asthma control in pregnancy is dangerous — uncontrolled asthma reduces fetal oxygenation and increases risk of prematurity and IUGR.
explanation.E: Incorrect — LABA should never be used as monotherapy or before ICS. BTS Step 2 is ICS first; LABA added at Step 3 only.

reference: NICE NG80 — Asthma. BTS/SIGN asthma guideline. https://www.nice.org.uk/guidance/ng80

question: A 65-year-old man with known COPD (GOLD stage 3, FEV1 45%) is reviewed. He has had 3 exacerbations requiring antibiotics in the past 12 months. He is on LABA/LAMA. His blood eosinophil count is 320 cells/microlitre. Per NICE NG115 and GOLD 2024, what additional treatment should be considered?

options.A: Start oral prednisolone long-term maintenance
options.B: Add inhaled corticosteroid (ICS) to his existing LABA/LAMA (triple therapy) — per NICE NG115 and GOLD 2024: ICS is recommended as add-on to LABA/LAMA when blood eosinophil count ≥300 cells/microlitre AND ≥2 exacerbations or ≥1 hospitalisation per year; this patient meets criteria (eosinophils 320, 3 exacerbations); triple ICS/LABA/LAMA therapy reduces exacerbation frequency
options.C: No further treatment — LABA/LAMA is maximum COPD therapy
options.D: Roflumilast (PDE4 inhibitor) for all patients with frequent exacerbations
options.E: Oral azithromycin prophylaxis first — eosinophil count is irrelevant

explanation.correct: Per NICE NG115 and GOLD 2024 COPD management: ICS in COPD is NOT used routinely (unlike asthma) due to risk of pneumonia. ICS is specifically indicated as triple therapy (ICS/LABA/LAMA) when: blood eosinophil count ≥300 cells/microlitre AND ≥2 moderate exacerbations or ≥1 hospitalisation in the past year. Why eosinophils matter: higher eosinophil counts predict response to ICS in COPD (eosinophilic inflammation responds to corticosteroids); counts ≥300 = highest benefit; counts 100-300 = intermediate; <100 = unlikely to benefit and higher pneumonia risk. This patient: eosinophils 320 + 3 exacerbations → qualifies for ICS add-on. Alternative for frequent exacerbators: azithromycin 250 mg 3×/week (prophylactic long-term macrolide) — if not already used; roflumilast (NICE TA461): add-on for chronic bronchitic COPD with FEV1 <50% and ≥2 exacerbations despite LABA/LAMA/ICS — Step 4. The choice depends on individual characteristics.
explanation.A: Incorrect — Long-term oral prednisolone for maintenance in COPD is not recommended — causes diabetes, osteoporosis, adrenal suppression without sustained benefit.
explanation.B: CORRECT — Triple therapy (ICS + LABA/LAMA) for blood eosinophils ≥300 + ≥2 exacerbations per year per NICE NG115/GOLD 2024.
explanation.C: Incorrect — ICS as add-on to LABA/LAMA (triple therapy) is an evidence-based next step for this patient profile.
explanation.D: Incorrect — Roflumilast (PDE4 inhibitor) is considered after triple therapy if chronic bronchitis + FEV1 <50% + frequent exacerbations — not before ICS.
explanation.E: Incorrect — Long-term azithromycin is another option for frequent exacerbators but eosinophil count IS relevant for the ICS decision — both can be considered but ICS/triple therapy is the primary next step here.

reference: NICE NG115 — COPD. GOLD 2024. https://www.nice.org.uk/guidance/ng115

question: A 70-year-old man with COPD (FEV1 38% — GOLD stage 3) has a moderate exacerbation with increased breathlessness, purulent sputum and raised CRP. He is managed at home. Per NICE NG115, what constitutes appropriate management?

options.A: Admission to hospital is mandatory for all COPD exacerbations
options.B: Home management with: antibiotic (amoxicillin, doxycycline or clarithromycin for 5 days per NICE NG115); oral prednisolone 30 mg for 5 days; increase SABA frequency; review and step up maintenance inhaler therapy; follow-up within 2 weeks of exacerbation; admission indicated if: severe breathlessness at rest, SpO2 <90%, cyanosis, confusion, inability to cope at home, rapid deterioration
options.C: Antibiotics are not indicated — all COPD exacerbations are viral
options.D: Oral prednisolone for 14 days is standard treatment
options.E: IV aminophylline is first-line for COPD exacerbation at home

explanation.correct: Per NICE NG115 (COPD) and GOLD 2024: moderate COPD exacerbation (increased symptoms not requiring hospitalisation): Antibiotics: indicated when purulent sputum change (green/yellow) is present (indicates bacterial aetiology — Haemophilus influenzae, Streptococcus pneumoniae, Moraxella catarrhalis); oral amoxicillin 500mg TDS, doxycycline 200mg loading then 100mg OD, or clarithromycin 500mg BD for 5 days. Oral prednisolone: 30 mg once daily for 5 days (not longer — 7-14 day courses do not add benefit and increase side effects including osteoporosis with repeated courses). Short-acting bronchodilator: increase SABA frequency (salbutamol) ± SAMA (ipratropium). Follow-up: within 2 weeks of exacerbation onset — review spirometry, inhaler technique, maintenance therapy, offer pulmonary rehabilitation referral. Admission criteria: severe dyspnoea, confusion, SpO2 <90%, cyanosis, rapid worsening, inadequate home support, comorbidities (PE, pneumonia, cardiac failure).
explanation.A: Incorrect — Moderate COPD exacerbations without alarm features can be safely managed at home per NICE NG115.
explanation.B: CORRECT — Home management: antibiotic (5 days) + prednisolone 30mg 5 days + increased SABA; 2-week follow-up; admit if alarm features per NICE NG115.
explanation.C: Incorrect — Purulent sputum change in COPD exacerbation indicates bacterial involvement; antibiotics are indicated when purulence is present per NICE NG115.
explanation.D: Incorrect — 5 days of prednisolone 30 mg is equivalent to longer courses in COPD exacerbations (REDUCE trial) — 14 days has no additional benefit and greater side effects.
explanation.E: Incorrect — IV aminophylline is a hospital inpatient treatment for severe acute COPD exacerbation — it is not used in home management.

reference: NICE NG115 — COPD. https://www.nice.org.uk/guidance/ng115

question: A 68-year-old man with COPD (FEV1 32%) has an acute severe exacerbation requiring admission. Arterial blood gas on air shows: pH 7.28, pCO2 8.9 kPa, pO2 6.4 kPa, HCO3 30 mmol/L. Per NICE NG115 and BTS non-invasive ventilation guidelines, what does this ABG indicate and what is the treatment?

options.A: Type 1 respiratory failure — high-flow oxygen via non-rebreather mask
options.B: Type 2 (hypercapnic) respiratory failure with acute-on-chronic respiratory acidosis (pH 7.28, raised pCO2 8.9, raised HCO3 suggesting chronic CO2 retention, hypoxia) — per NICE NG115: non-invasive ventilation (NIV/BiPAP) is indicated; target SpO2 88-92% with controlled oxygen (not high-flow — risks CO2 retention in hypercapnic patients); NIV: BiPAP settings typically IPAP 14-20 cmH2O, EPAP 4-5 cmH2O; improves ventilation, reduces pCO2, avoids intubation
options.C: Metabolic alkalosis — start sodium bicarbonate
options.D: Normal ABG — no action required
options.E: High-flow oxygen via non-rebreather mask to target SpO2 >98%

explanation.correct: ABG interpretation: pH 7.28 = acidosis; pCO2 8.9 kPa = elevated (normal 4.7-6.0) = respiratory acidosis; pO2 6.4 kPa = hypoxia; HCO3 30 mmol/L = elevated (normal 22-26) = metabolic compensation (chronic CO2 retention → kidneys retain HCO3 to compensate). Conclusion: Type 2 respiratory failure (hypercapnia + hypoxia) with acute-on-chronic respiratory acidosis (partially compensated — pH still low despite elevated HCO3). Indicates acute deterioration on a background of chronic hypercapnia (COPD). Per NICE NG115 and BTS NIV guidelines: NIV/BiPAP is indicated for: pH <7.35 AND pCO2 >6.5 kPa (after controlled oxygen and nebulisers); associated with COPD exacerbation. Controlled oxygen: target SpO2 88-92% in COPD with hypercapnia — high-flow oxygen drives off hypoxic ventilatory drive and worsens CO2 retention; use 24-28% Venturi mask. NIV: IPAP ~14-20 cmH2O, EPAP 4-5 cmH2O; reduces work of breathing, improves alveolar ventilation, reduces intubation rate by ~50%.
explanation.A: Incorrect — Type 1 failure: hypoxia with normal/low pCO2. This has elevated pCO2 = Type 2. High-flow oxygen in Type 2 failure causes CO2 retention.
explanation.B: CORRECT — Type 2 respiratory failure with acute-on-chronic acidosis (pH 7.28, pCO2 8.9): NIV/BiPAP; controlled O2 target SpO2 88-92% per NICE NG115/BTS.
explanation.C: Incorrect — Metabolic alkalosis would show: high pH, high HCO3, normal pCO2. Here pH is low (acidosis) with high pCO2 (respiratory cause).
explanation.D: Incorrect — pH 7.28, pCO2 8.9, pO2 6.4 is critically abnormal — not normal.
explanation.E: Incorrect — High-flow oxygen targeting SpO2 >98% in a hypercapnic COPD patient worsens CO2 retention; target SpO2 88-92% with controlled O2.

reference: NICE NG115 — COPD. BTS Non-invasive ventilation. https://www.nice.org.uk/guidance/ng115

question: A 35-year-old man is found to have a serum calcium of 2.96 mmol/L on two occasions. PTH is 8.2 pmol/L (mildly elevated). He is asymptomatic. Per NICE CKS and NICE NG132, what is the most likely diagnosis and how should it be managed?

options.A: Hypercalcaemia of malignancy — urgent CT chest/abdomen/pelvis
options.B: Primary hyperparathyroidism (PHPT) — autonomous PTH secretion from a parathyroid adenoma (80%), hyperplasia (15%) or carcinoma (<1%) causing hypercalcaemia; in an asymptomatic young patient: confirm with 24-hour urine calcium (to exclude familial hypocalciuric hypercalcaemia — FHH, which has low urine calcium and elevated PTH); refer to endocrinology; parathyroidectomy recommended for patients <50 years with PHPT regardless of symptoms per NICE NG132
options.C: Sarcoidosis — serum ACE and chest X-ray
options.D: Vitamin D toxicity — stop all supplements
options.E: Thiazide diuretic effect — check medication list and stop if applicable

explanation.correct: Primary hyperparathyroidism (PHPT): most common cause of hypercalcaemia in outpatient/primary care setting; elevated (or inappropriately normal) PTH with hypercalcaemia. Causes: solitary parathyroid adenoma (80%), multigland hyperplasia (15%, can be part of MEN1 or MEN2A), parathyroid carcinoma (<1%). Diagnosis: serum calcium elevated + PTH elevated (or inappropriately normal — suppressed PTH expected with high calcium; any detectable PTH with hypercalcaemia suggests parathyroid pathology). Key exclusion: familial hypocalciuric hypercalcaemia (FHH) — autosomal dominant inactivating mutation in CaSR (calcium-sensing receptor); presents identically but benign, no treatment needed; distinguished by 24-hour urine calcium-creatinine clearance ratio <0.01 (low urinary calcium in FHH vs higher in PHPT). Per NICE NG132 (Hyperparathyroidism): parathyroidectomy is recommended for: all patients <50 years (regardless of symptoms); symptomatic PHPT at any age; asymptomatic PHPT with serum calcium ≥2.85 mmol/L, osteoporosis, or CKD.
explanation.A: Incorrect — Malignancy-related hypercalcaemia is associated with SUPPRESSED/low PTH (PTH-independent hypercalcaemia from PTHrP or bone metastases). Elevated PTH with hypercalcaemia points to PHPT.
explanation.B: CORRECT — PHPT: elevated Ca + elevated PTH. Exclude FHH with 24-hour urine calcium. Age <50 → parathyroidectomy recommended per NICE NG132.
explanation.C: Incorrect — Sarcoidosis causes hypercalcaemia via 1-alpha hydroxylase in granulomas (elevated 1,25-dihydroxyvitamin D); PTH is suppressed — not elevated.
explanation.D: Incorrect — Vitamin D toxicity elevates 25-OHD and 1,25-OH2D, suppresses PTH — not elevates it.
explanation.E: Incorrect — Thiazides cause mild hypercalcaemia by enhancing renal calcium reabsorption, with suppressed PTH. Elevated PTH here indicates PHPT.

reference: NICE NG132 — Hyperparathyroidism. https://www.nice.org.uk/guidance/ng132

question: A 55-year-old woman has confirmed primary hyperparathyroidism (serum calcium 2.89 mmol/L, PTH 9.1 pmol/L). She is asymptomatic. DEXA shows T-score -2.6 (osteoporosis). Per NICE NG132, is she a candidate for parathyroidectomy?

options.A: No surgery indicated — she is asymptomatic
options.B: Yes — per NICE NG132 criteria for parathyroidectomy in asymptomatic PHPT: osteoporosis (T-score ≤-2.5 at any site) IS an indication for surgery regardless of symptoms; additional criteria: age <50 years, serum calcium ≥2.85 mmol/L, creatinine clearance <60 mL/min, 24-hour urine calcium >400 mg/day; this patient has osteoporosis → refer to endocrinology/surgery for parathyroidectomy
options.C: Medical management with bisphosphonates only — surgery is too risky
options.D: Cinacalcet is first-line — avoid surgery in all women over 50
options.E: Watchful waiting with annual calcium measurements — no action unless symptomatic

explanation.correct: Per NICE NG132 (Hyperparathyroidism — primary): indications for parathyroidectomy in asymptomatic PHPT: (1) Age <50 years; (2) Serum calcium ≥2.85 mmol/L; (3) Reduced bone mineral density — T-score ≤-2.5 at any site (lumbar spine, hip, distal radius) OR Z-score ≤-2.0; (4) CKD stage 3b or worse (eGFR <45 ml/min/1.73m²); (5) 24-hour urinary calcium >10 mmol/day (>400 mg/day). This patient: T-score -2.6 = osteoporosis → criterion met → parathyroidectomy is recommended. Parathyroidectomy: minimally invasive (focused/targeted approach using sestamibi scan ± USS for pre-operative localisation); cure rate >95%; resolves hypercalcaemia, improves bone density, reduces fracture risk. Cinacalcet: calcimimetic agent (allosteric activator of CaSR — reduces PTH secretion); used when surgery is contraindicated or declined — not first-line over surgery.
explanation.A: Incorrect — Asymptomatic does not mean no surgery is needed; osteoporosis (T-score ≤-2.5) is a specific indication for parathyroidectomy per NICE NG132.
explanation.B: CORRECT — Osteoporosis (T-score -2.6 ≤-2.5) is an indication for parathyroidectomy in asymptomatic PHPT per NICE NG132.
explanation.C: Incorrect — Bisphosphonates can improve bone density in PHPT but do not address the underlying parathyroid pathology; surgery is preferred when criteria are met.
explanation.D: Incorrect — Cinacalcet is used when surgery is not feasible — it is not first-line over surgery for patients meeting surgical criteria.
explanation.E: Incorrect — This patient meets operative criteria (osteoporosis T-score ≤-2.5); watchful waiting is not appropriate in this situation.

reference: NICE NG132 — Hyperparathyroidism (primary). https://www.nice.org.uk/guidance/ng132

question: A 62-year-old woman with known breast cancer presents with severe nausea, vomiting, drowsiness and polyuria. Serum calcium is 3.45 mmol/L. Per NICE CKS and oncology guidelines, what is the immediate management?

options.A: Oral bisphosphonate — start alendronate immediately
options.B: IV fluid resuscitation with 0.9% sodium chloride (saline) — the cornerstone of acute hypercalcaemia management; target urine output 100-150 ml/hour; once rehydrated: IV bisphosphonate (zoledronic acid 4 mg over 15 minutes OR pamidronate 60-90 mg over 2-4 hours) — reduces osteoclast-mediated bone resorption; full effect in 2-4 days; treat underlying malignancy; denosumab if bisphosphonate-refractory; furosemide only if fluid overloaded
options.C: Oral calcium supplements — the body needs calcium to regulate levels
options.D: Calcitonin SC — only treatment needed for hypercalcaemia of malignancy
options.E: Furosemide 80 mg IV — first-line treatment to force calcium excretion

explanation.correct: Hypercalcaemia of malignancy: most common paraneoplastic syndrome; caused by: PTHrP secretion (most common — squamous cell lung, breast, renal cancers), lytic bone metastases (breast, myeloma), 1-alpha hydroxylase activity (lymphomas). Acute management (serum Ca >3.0 mmol/L with symptoms): IV 0.9% saline: 2-4 litres per day (corrects dehydration, promotes calciuric diuresis — calcium follows sodium); target urine output 100-150 ml/hour; furosemide only if patient is fluid overloaded (NOT routine — previously recommended but has fallen out of favour as routine). IV bisphosphonate: zoledronic acid 4 mg IV over 15-30 minutes (most potent; adjust dose for renal function); OR pamidronate 60-90 mg IV over 2-4 hours; onset of full effect 48-72 hours; avoid with eGFR <30 without nephrologist input. Denosumab (RANKL inhibitor) 120 mg SC: if bisphosphonate-refractory or contraindicated due to renal impairment. Calcitonin: fast-acting (hours) but tachyphylaxis develops within 48 hours — used as bridge therapy in severe symptomatic hypercalcaemia.
explanation.A: Incorrect — Oral bisphosphonates are for chronic bone protection in malignancy, not for acute symptomatic hypercalcaemia which requires IV treatment.
explanation.B: CORRECT — IV saline first (2-4L/day + urine output monitoring); then IV zoledronic acid or pamidronate per NICE CKS/oncology guidelines.
explanation.C: Incorrect — Calcium supplements would worsen hypercalcaemia dramatically.
explanation.D: Incorrect — Calcitonin has a fast but short-lived effect (tachyphylaxis within 48 hours); IV saline + bisphosphonate is the primary acute treatment.
explanation.E: Incorrect — Furosemide was historically used but is now reserved only for patients who develop fluid overload during IV saline treatment; routine furosemide is no longer recommended for hypercalcaemia.

reference: NICE CKS — Hypercalcaemia. https://cks.nice.org.uk/topics/hypercalcaemia/

question: A 45-year-old man is found to have hypertension (158/96 mmHg) with hypokalaemia (K+ 2.9 mmol/L) on two occasions despite not taking diuretics. Aldosterone:renin ratio (ARR) is markedly elevated at 1,400 pmol/mU. Per NICE CKS and Endocrine Society guidelines, what is the likely diagnosis and investigation to differentiate the subtypes?

options.A: Conn's syndrome (primary aldosteronism) is excluded — diuretics cause hypokalaemia not hypertension
options.B: Primary aldosteronism (PA) — autonomous aldosterone secretion independent of renin; causes hypertension + hypokalaemia; ARR >750-1000 is highly suggestive; differentiation of unilateral (aldosteronoma/Conn's tumour) vs bilateral hyperplasia requires CT adrenals + adrenal vein sampling (AVS); unilateral adenoma → adrenalectomy (curative); bilateral hyperplasia → lifelong mineralocorticoid antagonist (spironolactone or eplerenone)
options.C: Secondary hyperaldosteronism from renal artery stenosis — renal USS Doppler
options.D: Phaeochromocytoma — urinary metanephrines
options.E: No further investigation — hypertension + hypokalaemia can be treated empirically with spironolactone

explanation.correct: Primary aldosteronism (PA / hyperaldosteronism): autonomous aldosterone secretion → sodium retention + potassium excretion → hypertension + hypokalaemia + suppressed renin. ARR (aldosterone:renin ratio): screening test; elevated in PA; ARR >750-1000 pmol/mU (lab-dependent) is highly suggestive. Confirmation: saline suppression test (IV saline fails to suppress aldosterone) or fludrocortisone suppression test. Subtype differentiation (essential — treatment depends on this): CT adrenal: detects adenomas >1 cm (but misses small adenomas); adrenal vein sampling (AVS): gold standard for lateralisation — measures aldosterone:cortisol ratio from left vs right adrenal vein; lateralised secretion → unilateral adenoma → adrenalectomy (curative in 30-50%); non-lateralised → bilateral hyperplasia → spironolactone (1st line) or eplerenone. Secondary aldosteronism: elevated renin (due to stimulus: renal artery stenosis, cardiac failure, liver cirrhosis) → secondary aldosterone rise; ARR normal/low (renin elevated proportionately).
explanation.A: Incorrect — This patient is NOT on diuretics; hypokalaemia + hypertension in the absence of diuretics is a red flag for primary aldosteronism.
explanation.B: CORRECT — Primary aldosteronism: elevated ARR; CT adrenal + AVS to differentiate unilateral adenoma (surgery) vs bilateral hyperplasia (spironolactone) per Endocrine Society/NICE CKS.
explanation.C: Incorrect — Secondary aldosteronism (from RAS) has elevated renin, not suppressed; ARR would be normal/low. The very high ARR here indicates PRIMARY aldosteronism.
explanation.D: Incorrect — Phaeochromocytoma causes catecholamine excess (episodic hypertension, headache, sweating, palpitations) — not aldosterone-driven hypokalaemia.
explanation.E: Incorrect — Empirical spironolactone without confirming the subtype (unilateral vs bilateral) would deprive the patient of a potentially curative adrenalectomy if an adenoma is present.

reference: Endocrine Society — Primary Aldosteronism Guidelines. NICE CKS. https://www.endocrine.org/clinical-practice-guidelines

question: A 52-year-old woman is found to have a 2.8 cm right adrenal incidentaloma on CT done for another indication. The lesion has a Hounsfield unit (HU) value of 18 on unenhanced CT. Per Endocrine Society and ESE guidelines, what hormonal assessment is mandatory?

options.A: No hormonal assessment needed — all incidentalomas are benign
options.B: All adrenal incidentalomas require screening for: (1) cortisol hypersecretion — 1 mg overnight dexamethasone suppression test (DST: cortisol >50 nmol/L post-dex = autonomous cortisol secretion); (2) phaeochromocytoma — 24-hour urinary fractionated metanephrines or plasma free metanephrines (must exclude BEFORE any adrenal biopsy or surgery); (3) primary aldosteronism — aldosterone:renin ratio if hypertensive or hypokalaemic; HU 18 is indeterminate (lipid-poor lesion — <10 HU = lipid-rich = likely adenoma; >10 HU = less certain)
options.C: Biopsy first to establish the diagnosis — then hormone tests if needed
options.D: Only measure urinary cortisol — other hormones not clinically relevant
options.E: Repeat CT in 10 years — no action unless >4 cm

explanation.correct: Adrenal incidentaloma: adrenal mass ≥1 cm discovered incidentally. Per European Society of Endocrinology (ESE) and Endocrine Society guidelines: mandatory hormonal assessment for ALL adrenal incidentalomas: (1) Pheochromocytoma exclusion — 24-hour urinary fractionated metanephrines or plasma free metanephrines; must be done BEFORE any biopsy or surgery (undetected phaeochromocytoma + surgery = hypertensive crisis); (2) Autonomous cortisol secretion — 1 mg overnight DST (give 1 mg dexamethasone at 23:00, measure serum cortisol at 08:00; cortisol >50 nmol/L = autonomous secretion = 'mild autonomous cortisol secretion' previously called subclinical Cushing's); (3) Primary aldosteronism — ARR if hypertensive or hypokalaemic. CT characteristics: <10 HU unenhanced = lipid-rich adenoma (benign, low risk); >10 HU = lipid-poor (risk of malignancy higher); HU 18 here is indeterminate → further characterisation with washout CT or MRI. Size >4 cm or irregular margins → consider adrenalectomy.
explanation.A: Incorrect — Not all incidentalomas are benign and hormonal assessment is mandated by ESE/Endocrine Society guidelines for all adrenal incidentalomas.
explanation.B: CORRECT — All incidentalomas: 1 mg DST (cortisol secretion), plasma/urine metanephrines (phaeochromocytoma), ARR if hypertensive/hypokalaemic; HU 18 is indeterminate per ESE guidelines.
explanation.C: Incorrect — Biopsy of adrenal lesion without phaeochromocytoma exclusion is dangerous and contraindicated — must exclude phaeochromocytoma first.
explanation.D: Incorrect — Urinary cortisol alone is insufficient — overnight DST is the standard cortisol screening test; phaeochromocytoma exclusion is also mandatory.
explanation.E: Incorrect — Any adrenal incidentaloma requires hormonal assessment at discovery regardless of size.

reference: ESE Guidelines — Adrenal incidentaloma 2023. Endocrine Society. https://www.endocrine.org/clinical-practice-guidelines

question: A 48-year-old man is investigated for a 4.5 cm adrenal mass with Hounsfield units 32 and no washout on delayed CT. His urinary metanephrines and cortisol are normal. His ARR is normal. Per ESE guidelines, what is the management?

options.A: Discharge — all hormone tests are normal so the mass is benign
options.B: Surgical resection (adrenalectomy) — per ESE guidelines: adrenal masses ≥4 cm with lipid-poor appearance (HU >10), no washout (indeterminate on imaging), and/or heterogeneous/irregular features carry sufficient risk of adrenocortical carcinoma (ACC) to warrant resection; ACC is rare but associated with high mortality if not resected early; size ≥4 cm + HU >10 without washout = imaging criteria for surgery
options.C: FNA biopsy — to confirm ACC histologically before surgery
options.D: Repeat CT in 5 years — imaging surveillance is sufficient for all adrenal masses
options.E: MRI adrenal to replace the CT for all management decisions

explanation.correct: Per ESE Adrenal Incidentaloma Guidelines 2023: size and imaging characteristics guide management: <4 cm + HU <10 (lipid-rich) + no hormone excess: low risk adenoma → no surgery; follow-up with repeat imaging in 6-12 months. ≥4 cm OR HU >10 OR heterogeneous/irregular features OR no washout OR growth on follow-up: indeterminate/suspicious → recommend surgical resection if patient is fit. Adrenocortical carcinoma (ACC): rare (1-2 per million), but 25% of adrenal masses >6 cm are ACC; even 4-6 cm range has significant malignancy risk. FNA biopsy: NOT recommended for primary adrenal mass assessment — cannot distinguish adenoma from ACC (cytology unreliable); risk of tumour seeding; used only to confirm metastasis from a known non-adrenal primary. Laparoscopic adrenalectomy: standard for masses <8-10 cm; open adrenalectomy for larger or invasive lesions.
explanation.A: Incorrect — Normal hormones do not exclude ACC — the majority of ACCs are non-functioning. Size ≥4 cm + lipid-poor imaging (HU >10) warrants surgical assessment.
explanation.B: CORRECT — ≥4 cm + HU >10 + no washout = indeterminate imaging → surgical resection recommended per ESE 2023 guidelines.
explanation.C: Incorrect — FNA biopsy of primary adrenal lesions cannot reliably distinguish ACC from adenoma and carries a risk of seeding — not recommended by ESE guidelines.
explanation.D: Incorrect — Imaging surveillance alone is insufficient for this imaging profile (4.5 cm, HU 32, no washout); surgery is recommended.
explanation.E: Incorrect — MRI adrenal is an alternative characterisation tool but would not change the management decision for a 4.5 cm lipid-poor mass — surgery is still indicated.

reference: ESE Guidelines — Management of adrenal incidentaloma 2023. https://www.eje-online.org

question: A 72-year-old man presents with a 6-hour history of sudden onset right arm weakness, right facial droop and expressive dysphasia. His NIHSS is 8. CT head shows no haemorrhage. He arrives at hospital 3.5 hours after symptom onset. Per NICE NG128 (Stroke), what is the time-critical treatment and criteria?

options.A: Aspirin 300 mg immediately — thrombolysis is not available for strokes
options.B: IV alteplase (thrombolysis) — indicated for ischaemic stroke within 4.5 hours of symptom onset; give immediately if: ischaemic stroke confirmed on CT (no haemorrhage), symptom onset <4.5 hours, NIHSS assessed, BP <185/110 mmHg, no contraindications (recent surgery, anticoagulants with INR >1.7, major haemorrhage); door-to-needle target: 60 minutes; consider mechanical thrombectomy for large vessel occlusion (LVO) up to 24 hours if penumbra imaging criteria met
options.C: Warfarin immediately — anticoagulation for ischaemic stroke
options.D: Wait 24 hours before any treatment — thrombolysis is too risky in the first 24 hours
options.E: Aspirin 300 mg daily for 2 weeks — standard treatment for all strokes

explanation.correct: Per NICE NG128 (Stroke and transient ischaemic attack in over 16s): IV alteplase (tPA): licensed for ischaemic stroke within 4.5 hours of symptom onset; assessment: CT head to exclude haemorrhage (absolute contraindication); clinical assessment (NIHSS); BP control if >185/110 mmHg (treat with IV labetalol); contraindications: anticoagulants (warfarin INR >1.7, DOAC within 48 hours), major surgery/trauma <3 months, active bleeding, severe stroke (NIHSS >25), CT showing major early infarct changes (>1/3 MCA territory). Target: door-to-needle time <60 minutes (ideally <45 minutes). Mechanical thrombectomy (MT): for large vessel occlusion (ICA, M1 MCA); can be performed up to 24 hours if advanced penumbra imaging (CT perfusion or DWI/PWI MRI mismatch) shows viable brain; associated with +2 additional independent survivors per 10 treated (HERMES meta-analysis). This patient: 3.5 hours onset, no haemorrhage, NIHSS 8 → IV alteplase NOW + assess for LVO → mechanical thrombectomy if LVO confirmed.
explanation.A: Incorrect — Aspirin is NOT the acute treatment of choice when thrombolysis is indicated; aspirin is used if thrombolysis is not given, and after 24 hours post-thrombolysis.
explanation.B: CORRECT — IV alteplase within 4.5 hours for ischaemic stroke; door-to-needle <60 min; assess for LVO and mechanical thrombectomy per NICE NG128.
explanation.C: Incorrect — Anticoagulation is NOT given acutely for ischaemic stroke (increases haemorrhagic transformation risk); anticoagulation is started for AF-related stroke after 2-14 days per guidelines.
explanation.D: Incorrect — Waiting 24 hours before treatment is opposite to the evidence — the benefit of thrombolysis is time-dependent ('time is brain': ~1.9 million neurons die per minute of ischaemia).
explanation.E: Incorrect — Aspirin 300 mg is given for 14 days in ischaemic stroke where thrombolysis was NOT given; it is not the treatment when thrombolysis is indicated and the patient is within the time window.

reference: NICE NG128 — Stroke. https://www.nice.org.uk/guidance/ng128

question: A 68-year-old man had a TIA 2 days ago (15 minutes of right arm weakness, fully resolved). He has not been seen yet. His ABCD² score is 5. Per NICE NG128, what is the appropriate management timeline?

options.A: Routine neurology appointment within 3 months
options.B: Urgent specialist assessment within 24 hours of symptom onset (or as soon as possible if >24 hours) — per NICE NG128: TIA/suspected TIA should be seen by a specialist within 24 hours of symptom onset; start aspirin 300 mg immediately (unless contraindicated); carotid imaging (duplex USS) if anterior circulation event; brain MRI (DWI); 12-lead ECG + 24-hour cardiac monitoring for AF; consider dual antiplatelet (aspirin + clopidogrel for 21-90 days per POINT/CHANCE trials); statin; antihypertensive
options.C: Admit to stroke unit for thrombolysis — TIA symptoms have resolved so alteplase cannot be given
options.D: No treatment needed — TIA symptoms resolved so no stroke risk
options.E: Start anticoagulation with rivaroxaban immediately for all TIA patients

explanation.correct: Per NICE NG128 (Stroke and TIA): TIA is a neurological emergency — high early stroke risk (up to 10% in first 48 hours, 20% in first month after untreated TIA). NICE recommends: specialist assessment within 24 hours of symptom onset (or as soon as possible if presenting later). ABCD² score (predicts 2-day stroke risk): age ≥60 (1 pt), BP ≥140/90 (1 pt), clinical features: unilateral weakness (2 pts)/speech without weakness (1 pt), duration ≥60 min (2 pts)/10-59 min (1 pt), diabetes (1 pt); score ≥4 = high risk. Immediate treatment on diagnosis: aspirin 300 mg stat + continue 75 mg daily. Dual antiplatelet therapy: aspirin + clopidogrel 75 mg for 21 days to 3 months (POINT and CHANCE trials — reduces recurrent stroke by ~25% vs aspirin alone). Investigations: carotid USS (anterior circulation TIA — carotid stenosis); brain DWI MRI (may show small completed infarct = TIA equivalent); ECG + cardiac monitoring (detect AF). Carotid endarterectomy: if ipsilateral symptomatic stenosis 50-99% per NASCET criteria → within 2 weeks ideally.
explanation.A: Incorrect — Routine 3-month appointment is not appropriate for TIA — the highest stroke risk is within the first 48-72 hours and specialist assessment within 24 hours is required per NICE NG128.
explanation.B: CORRECT — TIA: specialist within 24 hours; aspirin 300mg immediately; dual antiplatelet; carotid USS; DWI MRI; cardiac monitoring per NICE NG128.
explanation.C: Incorrect — Thrombolysis (alteplase) is for acute ischaemic stroke with ongoing deficits — not for resolved TIA.
explanation.D: Incorrect — Resolved TIA symptoms do not mean zero stroke risk — untreated TIA carries up to 10% stroke risk in the first 48 hours; urgent assessment and secondary prevention are essential.
explanation.E: Incorrect — Anticoagulation is used specifically for AF-related cardioembolic TIA/stroke (after confirmation of AF); it is not first-line for all TIA patients.

reference: NICE NG128 — Stroke and TIA. https://www.nice.org.uk/guidance/ng128

question: A 66-year-old woman has had an ischaemic stroke due to AF (non-valvular). She is 10 days post-stroke and medically stable. Her CHA₂DS₂-VASc is 5. Per NICE NG128 and NG196, when and with what should anticoagulation be started?

options.A: Start anticoagulation within 24 hours of stroke — same as TIA management
options.B: Start DOAC anticoagulation at 2-14 days post-ischaemic stroke from AF — the 'rule of halves' timing (2 days for TIA, 3-7 days for minor stroke, 7-14 days for major stroke) aims to reduce haemorrhagic transformation risk while preventing recurrent cardioembolic stroke; DOAC preferred over warfarin (apixaban, rivaroxaban, edoxaban or dabigatran); never restart anticoagulation after haemorrhagic transformation
options.C: Start warfarin immediately — DOACs are contraindicated after stroke
options.D: Never anticoagulate after stroke — risk of haemorrhagic transformation is too high
options.E: Anticoagulation only if INR is <2 at day 1

explanation.correct: Per NICE NG128 and NG196 (AF): after ischaemic stroke due to AF, anticoagulation is essential to prevent recurrent cardioembolic stroke (risk ~12% per year without anticoagulation). Timing: the '1-3-6-12 rule' (adapted per NICE/ESC): TIA: anticoagulate within 24 hours or as soon as AF confirmed; Minor stroke (mild deficit): 3 days; Moderate stroke: 6-7 days; Major stroke/large infarct: 12-14 days. Rationale for delay: haemorrhagic transformation of ischaemic stroke (HT) is a risk — early anticoagulation may convert ischaemic to haemorrhagic infarct; delay balances HT risk vs recurrence risk. DOAC preferred per NICE NG196 and ESC AF guidelines (apixaban, rivaroxaban, edoxaban, dabigatran) — superior to warfarin for AF stroke prevention with lower bleeding risk. Contraindications to anticoagulation: confirmed haemorrhagic transformation; large cardioembolic infarcts with significant haemorrhagic conversion; severe uncontrolled hypertension.
explanation.A: Incorrect — Immediate anticoagulation after major ischaemic stroke from AF risks haemorrhagic transformation; delayed initiation (2-14 days depending on stroke severity) is the correct approach.
explanation.B: CORRECT — Start DOAC at 2-14 days post-stroke (severity-dependent); DOAC preferred over warfarin per NICE NG128/NG196.
explanation.C: Incorrect — DOAC is preferred over warfarin for AF-related stroke prevention per NICE NG196; warfarin is not first-line.
explanation.D: Incorrect — AF-related ischaemic stroke is a strong indication for long-term anticoagulation; the risk of recurrence without anticoagulation significantly outweighs the risk of haemorrhagic transformation with delayed anticoagulation.
explanation.E: Incorrect — INR monitoring at day 1 is not the basis for anticoagulation timing decisions after AF-related stroke; timing is based on stroke severity (TIA/minor/moderate/major).

reference: NICE NG128 — Stroke. NICE NG196 — Atrial fibrillation. https://www.nice.org.uk/guidance/ng128

question: A GP is reviewing the current NHS childhood immunisation schedule. A health visitor asks what vaccines are given at 8 weeks (first set of injections). Per the current NHS schedule, which vaccines are given at 8 weeks?

options.A: MMR and MenB only
options.B: 6-in-1 (DTaP/IPV/Hib/HepB — diphtheria, tetanus, acellular pertussis, inactivated polio, Haemophilus influenzae type b, hepatitis B), rotavirus (oral), MenB (meningococcal B) — three separate vaccines at the 8-week appointment; this is typically the first and most complex vaccination appointment
options.C: BCG and hepatitis B only
options.D: Pneumococcal conjugate vaccine (PCV) only
options.E: 6-in-1 only — MenB is given at 12 weeks

explanation.correct: Per NHS childhood immunisation schedule (England, 2024): At 8 weeks: (1) 6-in-1 injection (Infanrix hexa or equivalent): diphtheria, tetanus, pertussis (whooping cough), polio, Haemophilus influenzae type b (Hib), hepatitis B — covers 6 diseases in one injection; given IM into anterolateral thigh; (2) Rotavirus vaccine (oral drops — Rotarix): protects against rotavirus gastroenteritis; given orally; (3) MenB (meningococcal B vaccine — Bexsero): protects against Neisseria meningitidis serogroup B; given IM. Schedule summary: 8 weeks: 6-in-1 + rotavirus + MenB; 12 weeks: 6-in-1 2nd dose + rotavirus 2nd dose + PCV (pneumococcal); 16 weeks: 6-in-1 3rd dose + MenB 2nd dose; 1 year: Hib/MenC booster + MMR + PCV booster + MenB booster (3rd dose); 12-13 years (Year 8): HPV; 14 years (Year 9): 3-in-1 teenage booster (Td/IPV) + MenACWY.
explanation.A: Incorrect — MMR is given at 1 year (and 3 years 4 months as pre-school booster) — not at 8 weeks. MenB is given at 8 weeks but not alone.
explanation.B: CORRECT — 8 weeks: 6-in-1 (DTaP/IPV/Hib/HepB) + rotavirus (oral) + MenB injection per NHS 2024 schedule.
explanation.C: Incorrect — BCG is given to high-risk neonates (not at 8 weeks routinely). HepB is included within the 6-in-1 vaccine.
explanation.D: Incorrect — PCV (pneumococcal) is given at 12 weeks (not 8 weeks) per the current NHS schedule.
explanation.E: Incorrect — MenB IS given at 8 weeks (along with 6-in-1 and rotavirus) per the NHS 2024 schedule.

reference: NHS — Childhood immunisation schedule 2024. https://www.nhs.uk/vaccinations/nhs-vaccinations-and-when-to-have-them/

question: A mother brings her 12-year-old daughter for her NHS vaccinations. The daughter has received all routine vaccinations to date. Per the NHS childhood immunisation schedule, which vaccine is she due at age 12-13 (school year 8)?

options.A: MMR booster — third dose at age 12
options.B: HPV vaccine (Gardasil 9) — offered to all girls AND boys aged 12-13 in Year 8; protects against HPV types 6, 11, 16, 18, 31, 33, 45, 52, 58; prevents cervical cancer, other anogenital cancers, and genital warts; 2-dose schedule (0 and 6-12 months) if started before age 15; 3-dose schedule if started age 15 or older
options.C: Hepatitis B booster — routine booster at age 12
options.D: Varicella vaccine — offered to all 12-year-olds without prior chickenpox
options.E: BCG vaccine — routine booster at age 12

explanation.correct: Per NHS childhood immunisation schedule (current 2024): at age 12-13 (Year 8): HPV vaccine (Gardasil 9 — 9-valent HPV vaccine protecting against HPV 6, 11, 16, 18, 31, 33, 45, 52, 58). Since September 2019: offered to ALL children (girls AND boys) in Year 8. Why: protects against: HPV 16/18 — cause 70% of cervical cancers; HPV 31/33/45/52/58 — cause additional 20% of cervical cancers; HPV 6/11 — cause 90% of genital warts; other HPV-related cancers (oropharyngeal, anal, vulval, vaginal, penile). Dosing schedule: 2 doses (0 and 6-12 months apart) if first dose given before age 15; 3 doses (0, 1-2, 6 months) if started age 15+. Catch-up to age 25 for those who missed school programme. BCG is no longer routine but offered to high-risk neonates. No routine booster for hepatitis B, MMR (2 doses already given), or varicella (not on NHS routine schedule).
explanation.A: Incorrect — MMR is given at 1 year and 3 years 4 months (pre-school booster). There is no routine MMR booster at age 12.
explanation.B: CORRECT — HPV vaccine (Gardasil 9) is the Year 8 (age 12-13) vaccine for all children on the NHS schedule.
explanation.C: Incorrect — Hepatitis B is given in infancy (8, 12 and 16 weeks); there is no routine booster at age 12 on the NHS schedule.
explanation.D: Incorrect — Varicella vaccine is not on the routine NHS childhood immunisation schedule (offered to high-risk groups and healthcare workers but not universally).
explanation.E: Incorrect — BCG is no longer given routinely at age 13 on the NHS schedule; it is offered to high-risk neonates.

reference: NHS — Childhood immunisation schedule 2024. https://www.nhs.uk/vaccinations/nhs-vaccinations-and-when-to-have-them/

question: A practice nurse asks about the MMR vaccine schedule. A new GP registrar queries whether MMR is contraindicated in egg allergy. Per NICE CKS and PHE immunisation guidelines, what is the correct advice?

options.A: MMR is absolutely contraindicated in all children with any egg allergy
options.B: MMR vaccine is safe to administer in children with egg allergy including severe anaphylaxis to egg — the MMR vaccine is not grown on egg-containing medium; previous recommendations advising against MMR in egg allergy were based on outdated information; MMR should be given in the normal setting with standard 15-minute post-vaccination observation; specialist referral is only needed for anaphylaxis to a PREVIOUS DOSE of MMR itself
options.C: MMR can be given in mild egg allergy only; severe egg allergy requires hospital administration
options.D: A skin prick test with egg protein must be performed before MMR in any child with egg allergy
options.E: Only the measles component carries risk in egg allergy — give measles vaccine separately

explanation.correct: Per PHE/UKHSA 'The Green Book' (Immunisation against Infectious Disease) and NICE CKS: MMR vaccine IS SAFE in children with egg allergy including severe anaphylaxis to egg. Rationale: MMR (Priorix, M-M-RvaxPro) is produced in chick embryo fibroblast cell cultures — NOT in egg white. The residual ovalbumin content is extremely low (nanogram quantities) — insufficient to trigger anaphylaxis. Evidence: multiple large studies confirm MMR is safe in egg-allergic children including those with severe/anaphylactic reactions to egg. Current guidance: administer MMR in the normal community setting (GP surgery/school); observe for 15 minutes post-vaccination as standard; no need for hospital setting; no skin testing required. Exception: specialist referral is required for allergy to a PREVIOUS DOSE of MMR vaccine (not egg allergy) — possible reaction to neomycin or gelatin in the vaccine.
explanation.A: Incorrect — MMR is NOT contraindicated in egg allergy. This is outdated guidance that has been superseded by evidence and current PHE/NICE guidance.
explanation.B: CORRECT — MMR is safe in all egg allergy including severe anaphylaxis. No special precautions needed. Referral only for allergy to previous MMR dose per PHE Green Book.
explanation.C: Incorrect — There is no differentiation between mild and severe egg allergy for MMR administration — MMR is safe in all.
explanation.D: Incorrect — Skin prick testing before MMR is not required or recommended in egg allergy per PHE guidance.
explanation.E: Incorrect — The three components of MMR are formulated together and all are safe in egg allergy. Separate vaccines are not available or recommended.

reference: PHE — The Green Book: Immunisation against Infectious Disease. https://www.gov.uk/government/collections/immunisation-against-infectious-disease-the-green-book

question: A 52-year-old woman presents with a 3-month history of postmenopausal bleeding (PMB). She had her last period at age 50. Per NICE NG12, what is the appropriate management?

options.A: Reassure — PMB is common in the first year after menopause
options.B: Urgent 2-week wait (2WW) referral to gynaecology — PMB (any vaginal bleeding more than 12 months after the last menstrual period) requires urgent specialist assessment to exclude endometrial cancer; investigation: transvaginal ultrasound (TVS) — endometrial thickness >4 mm in postmenopausal woman warrants endometrial sampling (hysteroscopy + biopsy or pipelle biopsy); endometrial cancer is the most common gynaecological malignancy in the UK
options.C: Start progestogen for 3 months — likely hormonal imbalance
options.D: Pelvic USS only — refer only if USS is abnormal
options.E: Repeat cervical smear — cervical cancer is the most likely cause

explanation.correct: Per NICE NG12 (Suspected cancer): postmenopausal bleeding (PMB = any vaginal bleeding occurring ≥12 months after the last period) is a red flag symptom requiring urgent 2-week wait referral to exclude endometrial cancer. Endometrial cancer: most common gynaecological malignancy in the UK; approximately 9,700 new cases/year; 75% present with PMB; 5-year survival >80% if stage I. Causes of PMB: endometrial cancer/atypical hyperplasia, endometrial polyps, endometrial atrophy (most common benign cause), cervical pathology, vulval/vaginal lesions, HRT-related bleeding. Investigation at specialist: transvaginal ultrasound (TVS): endometrial thickness ≤4 mm = low risk (atrophy likely); >4 mm = requires endometrial sampling; hysteroscopy with directed biopsy (gold standard); pipelle endometrial biopsy (outpatient — 85% sensitivity for endometrial cancer). Note: PMB in women taking HRT still requires investigation.
explanation.A: Incorrect — PMB is defined as bleeding ≥12 months after the last period. Any PMB requires urgent investigation — it is never automatically dismissed as normal.
explanation.B: CORRECT — PMB = 2WW referral to gynaecology; TVS ± endometrial biopsy to exclude endometrial cancer per NICE NG12.
explanation.C: Incorrect — Prescribing progestogen without investigation could mask endometrial cancer — this is unsafe.
explanation.D: Incorrect — NICE NG12 recommends direct 2WW referral — delaying with GP-arranged pelvic USS first may cause unacceptable delays in suspected cancer diagnosis.
explanation.E: Incorrect — Cervical cancer is NOT the most likely cause of PMB; endometrial cancer is the primary concern. Cervical smear screens for cervical cancer but is not the appropriate investigation for PMB.

reference: NICE NG12 — Suspected cancer. https://www.nice.org.uk/guidance/ng12

question: A 45-year-old woman presents with a 4-week history of blood-stained nipple discharge from the right breast. She has no palpable lump. Her mammogram is normal. Per NICE NG12, what is the appropriate management?

options.A: Reassure — normal mammogram excludes malignancy
options.B: Urgent 2WW referral to breast clinic — blood-stained nipple discharge in a woman ≥50 should be referred on a suspected cancer pathway; in women under 50, non-blood-stained discharge alone from a single duct is the typical presentation of ductal papilloma; however blood-stained discharge at any age warrants urgent assessment; ductal papilloma is the most common benign cause but ductal carcinoma in situ (DCIS) and malignancy must be excluded
options.C: Prescribe bromocriptine and repeat in 3 months
options.D: No further investigation — ductal papilloma always resolves spontaneously
options.E: Refer routinely (not urgently) to breast clinic within 18 weeks

explanation.correct: Blood-stained nipple discharge: always requires investigation to exclude malignancy. Causes: intraductal papilloma (most common benign cause — benign polyp within the lactiferous duct), ductal carcinoma in situ (DCIS), invasive carcinoma, duct ectasia (usually brown/green discharge). Per NICE NG12 (Suspected cancer): blood-stained nipple discharge in women ≥50 = urgent suspected cancer referral (2WW). In women under 50: urgent referral is still recommended for blood-stained discharge. A normal mammogram does NOT exclude ductal pathology — mammography is relatively insensitive for intraductal lesions. Assessment in breast clinic: clinical examination, breast USS, ductography/galactography, ductoscopy, or surgical microdochectomy (excision of the affected duct — both diagnostic and therapeutic for ductal papilloma). Ductal papilloma: benign; presents with intermittent blood-stained/serous unilateral single-duct discharge; treated by surgical excision.
explanation.A: Incorrect — Normal mammogram does not exclude intraductal pathology or DCIS; blood-stained nipple discharge requires breast clinic assessment regardless.
explanation.B: CORRECT — Blood-stained nipple discharge: urgent breast clinic referral to exclude DCIS and malignancy per NICE NG12. Ductal papilloma is the common benign cause.
explanation.C: Incorrect — Bromocriptine suppresses prolactin and is used for galactorrhoea — not for blood-stained nipple discharge.
explanation.D: Incorrect — Ductal papilloma does not always resolve spontaneously and blood-stained discharge requires exclusion of malignancy; surgical excision is often required.
