explanation.E: Incorrect — Routine 18-week referral is not appropriate for blood-stained nipple discharge — urgent/suspected cancer pathway referral is required per NICE NG12.

reference: NICE NG12 — Suspected cancer: recognition and referral. https://www.nice.org.uk/guidance/ng12

question: A 38-year-old woman presents with clear watery discharge from both nipples when expressed. She is not pregnant or breastfeeding. Her prolactin is 3,200 mIU/L (elevated). She takes no medications. Per NICE CKS, what is the most important diagnosis to exclude and what is the investigation?

options.A: This is physiological — reassure without investigation
options.B: Prolactinoma — a prolactin-secreting pituitary adenoma is the most common pituitary tumour; elevated prolactin in a non-pregnant, non-breastfeeding woman with galactorrhoea requires MRI pituitary with gadolinium; treatment: dopamine agonist (cabergoline preferred over bromocriptine for tolerability) reduces prolactin and tumour size
options.C: Hypothyroidism — check TSH only; TSH stimulates prolactin
options.D: Breast cancer — urgent 2WW mammogram
options.E: Ductal papilloma — refer for microdochectomy

explanation.correct: Hyperprolactinaemia with galactorrhoea: causes — physiological (pregnancy, breastfeeding), drug-induced (dopamine antagonists: antipsychotics, metoclopramide, domperidone, methyldopa), hypothyroidism (TRH stimulates prolactin), prolactinoma, renal failure (reduced clearance), macroprolactinaemia. This patient: no pregnancy, no breastfeeding, no medications → prolactinoma is the most important diagnosis to exclude. Per NICE CKS: MRI pituitary with gadolinium is the investigation of choice for suspected prolactinoma. Also check: TSH (hypothyroidism raises prolactin), renal function, drug history. Prolactinomas: microadenoma (<10 mm) or macroadenoma (≥10 mm — may cause visual field defects from optic chiasm compression). Treatment: cabergoline (dopamine agonist — D2 receptor agonist, suppresses prolactin secretion; very effective at reducing tumour size); bromocriptine (alternative — more side effects). Surgery: reserved for cabergoline-resistant or visual field compromise cases.
explanation.A: Incorrect — Galactorrhoea with elevated prolactin in a non-pregnant, non-breastfeeding woman is not physiological — prolactinoma must be excluded urgently.
explanation.B: CORRECT — Prolactinoma: most likely cause of elevated prolactin + galactorrhoea in non-pregnant woman with no medications. MRI pituitary + cabergoline treatment per NICE CKS.
explanation.C: Incorrect — TSH should be checked but is not the priority investigation; MRI pituitary is more urgent given significantly elevated prolactin without other obvious cause.
explanation.D: Incorrect — Clear bilateral expressed discharge with elevated prolactin is galactorrhoea from hyperprolactinaemia — not blood-stained discharge from malignancy.
explanation.E: Incorrect — Ductal papilloma causes blood-stained or serous unilateral single-duct discharge — not bilateral milky galactorrhoea with elevated prolactin.

reference: NICE CKS — Hyperprolactinaemia. https://cks.nice.org.uk/topics/hyperprolactinaemia/

question: A GP suspects Cushing's syndrome in a 38-year-old woman with truncal obesity, purple striae, proximal myopathy, and easy bruising. Her blood pressure is 152/94 mmHg. Per NICE CKS, which is the recommended first-line screening test?

options.A: Random serum cortisol — elevated cortisol confirms Cushing's
options.B: At least two of the following first-line tests: 24-hour urinary free cortisol (UFC) — two separate 24-hour collections (elevations >3× ULN are highly specific); late-night salivary cortisol (LNSC) — two measurements (cortisol normally low at midnight; elevated LNSC in Cushing's due to loss of diurnal rhythm); 1 mg overnight dexamethasone suppression test (DST) — cortisol >50 nmol/L at 08:00 after 1 mg dexamethasone at 23:00 suggests Cushing's; per NICE CKS: two tests recommended to reduce false positives
options.C: Plasma ACTH level only — elevated ACTH confirms Cushing's disease
options.D: MRI pituitary — imaging confirms Cushing's syndrome
options.E: Serum glucose — hyperglycaemia is diagnostic of Cushing's

explanation.correct: Per NICE CKS and Endocrine Society Clinical Practice Guideline: first-line tests for suspected Cushing's syndrome: (1) 24-hour urinary free cortisol (UFC): measures integrated cortisol secretion; two collections recommended (day-to-day variation); sensitivity ~90%; specificity ~95% at >3× ULN. (2) Late-night salivary cortisol (LNSC): most physiologically meaningful (normal cortisol nadir at midnight abolished in Cushing's); non-invasive; two samples. (3) 1 mg overnight DST: most widely used; sensitivity ~95%; 1 mg dexamethasone given at 23:00, cortisol measured at 08:00; cortisol >50 nmol/L = abnormal (suppression failure = autonomous cortisol). 48-hour low-dose DST: used as confirmatory test. ACTH: measured AFTER confirming hypercortisolism — used to differentiate ACTH-dependent (pituitary/ectopic) from ACTH-independent (adrenal) Cushing's. Random cortisol: not useful — normal physiological diurnal variation makes random results uninterpretable.
explanation.A: Incorrect — Random serum cortisol fluctuates widely with diurnal rhythm and stress; it is not a valid screening test for Cushing's syndrome.
explanation.B: CORRECT — First-line screening: 24-hour UFC (×2), late-night salivary cortisol (×2), OR 1 mg overnight DST; two tests recommended per NICE CKS/Endocrine Society.
explanation.C: Incorrect — Plasma ACTH is used to differentiate ACTH-dependent from ACTH-independent Cushing's AFTER hypercortisolism is confirmed — it is not a first-line screening test.
explanation.D: Incorrect — MRI pituitary is ordered after biochemical confirmation of Cushing's disease (ACTH-dependent) to localise the pituitary adenoma — not as screening.
explanation.E: Incorrect — Hyperglycaemia is a consequence of Cushing's syndrome but is not diagnostic — many other causes exist.

reference: NICE CKS — Cushing's syndrome. Endocrine Society Clinical Practice Guideline. https://cks.nice.org.uk/topics/cushings-syndrome/

question: A 52-year-old man presents with proximal muscle weakness, hypokalaemia (K+ 2.9 mmol/L) and hypertension. His serum cortisol is very high (>3000 nmol/L) and ACTH is elevated at 95 pg/ml. He has no features of classic Cushing's syndrome (no striae, no moon face). Per NICE CKS, what type of Cushing's and what is the most likely cause?

options.A: ACTH-independent Cushing's — adrenal adenoma causing excess cortisol with suppressed ACTH
options.B: Ectopic ACTH syndrome — extremely high cortisol + elevated ACTH + severe hypokalaemia + rapid onset without classic cushingoid features; most commonly from small cell lung cancer, bronchial carcinoid, or thymoma; investigate with CT chest/abdomen/pelvis + high-dose dexamethasone suppression test (ectopic ACTH fails to suppress); refer urgently to endocrinology
options.C: Cushing's disease — pituitary adenoma; classic features always present
options.D: Exogenous steroid use — most common cause of Cushing's overall
options.E: Adrenal carcinoma — surgical resection is first-line

explanation.correct: Ectopic ACTH syndrome: non-pituitary, non-adrenal tumour secreting ACTH independently. Key distinguishing features from Cushing's disease (pituitary): extremely high cortisol (often >2000-3000 nmol/L — much higher than pituitary-driven Cushing's); severe hypokalaemia (ACTH-driven mineralocorticoid excess — aldosterone-independent); rapid onset; often NO classic Cushingoid features (rapid tumour progression means insufficient time to develop typical appearance); weight loss (from the primary tumour). ACTH is elevated (rules out adrenal cause — which suppresses ACTH). Common causes: small cell lung carcinoma (most common malignant cause), bronchial carcinoid, thymic carcinoid, medullary thyroid carcinoma, islet cell tumours. Per NICE CKS: High-dose dexamethasone suppression test — cortisol suppresses in Cushing's disease (pituitary) but NOT in ectopic ACTH or adrenal disease. CT chest/abdomen/pelvis; Gallium DOTATATE PET for carcinoid. Treatment: treat the primary tumour; metyrapone or ketoconazole to control cortisol pending definitive treatment.
explanation.A: Incorrect — ACTH-independent Cushing's (adrenal adenoma) would show LOW/suppressed ACTH (negative feedback from autonomous cortisol). This patient has elevated ACTH.
explanation.B: CORRECT — Ectopic ACTH: very high cortisol + elevated ACTH + severe hypokalaemia + no classic Cushingoid features. CT chest + high-dose dexamethasone test per NICE CKS.
explanation.C: Incorrect — Cushing's disease (pituitary) also has elevated ACTH but typically causes classic Cushingoid features and moderately elevated cortisol; it PARTIALLY suppresses on high-dose dexamethasone. Ectopic ACTH does not suppress.
explanation.D: Incorrect — Exogenous steroids are the most common OVERALL cause but would suppress endogenous ACTH and cortisol — not cause very high ACTH.
explanation.E: Incorrect — Adrenal carcinoma causes ACTH-independent Cushing's with suppressed (low) ACTH, not elevated ACTH.

reference: NICE CKS — Cushing's syndrome. https://cks.nice.org.uk/topics/cushings-syndrome/

question: A 44-year-old woman with confirmed Cushing's disease (pituitary microadenoma on MRI) has morning cortisol of 890 nmol/L and has failed high-dose dexamethasone suppression. Per NICE CKS and endocrinology guidelines, what is the first-line treatment?

options.A: Long-term metyrapone — this is the definitive treatment for Cushing's disease
options.B: Transsphenoidal surgical resection of the pituitary adenoma — first-line treatment for Cushing's disease; remission rates 65-90% in expert centres; if surgery fails or is contraindicated: radiotherapy (pituitary-directed stereotactic radiosurgery) and/or cortisol-lowering drugs (metyrapone, ketoconazole, cabergoline, pasireotide); bilateral adrenalectomy as last resort (causes Nelson's syndrome — ACTH-secreting pituitary tumour enlargement)
options.C: Adrenalectomy — remove both adrenal glands as the primary approach
options.D: Oral prednisolone — reduces ACTH feedback
options.E: Spironolactone — manages the mineralocorticoid effects

explanation.correct: Cushing's disease: pituitary-driven Cushing's syndrome from an ACTH-secreting pituitary adenoma. Per NICE CKS and Endocrine Society guidelines: first-line treatment is transsphenoidal surgical resection — neurosurgeon removes the adenoma via the nasal passage and sphenoid sinus; minimally invasive; remission (cortisol normalisation) in 65-90% in experienced pituitary centres. Remission definition: post-operative cortisol <50 nmol/L. If surgical failure or recurrence: repeat surgery, pituitary radiotherapy (Gamma Knife stereotactic radiosurgery), medical therapy (metyrapone — 11-beta-hydroxylase inhibitor; ketoconazole — steroid synthesis inhibitor; cabergoline — reduces ACTH from some adenomas; pasireotide — somatostatin analogue reducing ACTH), or bilateral adrenalectomy. Nelson's syndrome: after bilateral adrenalectomy, removal of negative feedback causes rapid ACTH-secreting pituitary tumour enlargement — hyperpigmentation + mass effects.
explanation.A: Incorrect — Metyrapone reduces cortisol synthesis and can be used as bridge therapy or second-line, but it is NOT the definitive first-line treatment — surgery is.
explanation.B: CORRECT — Transsphenoidal surgery is first-line for Cushing's disease (pituitary adenoma) per NICE CKS/Endocrine Society.
explanation.C: Incorrect — Bilateral adrenalectomy is a last resort option (causes Nelson's syndrome) — not first-line.
explanation.D: Incorrect — Oral prednisolone would worsen Cushing's syndrome further — it has no role in treating it.
explanation.E: Incorrect — Spironolactone may manage some mineralocorticoid effects symptomatically but does not treat the underlying cause.

reference: NICE CKS — Cushing's syndrome. https://cks.nice.org.uk/topics/cushings-syndrome/

question: A 26-year-old woman presents with a 6-week history of pelvic pain, dyspareunia and deep dyspareunia. Examination reveals uterine tenderness and limited mobility (fixed retroversion). CA-125 is mildly elevated at 68 U/mL. Per NICE NG73, what is the likely diagnosis and management pathway?

options.A: Ovarian cancer — urgent 2WW referral
options.B: Endometriosis — NICE NG73 recommends diagnosing endometriosis clinically based on symptoms (pelvic pain, dysmenorrhoea, deep dyspareunia, cyclical symptoms) and examination; laparoscopy is the definitive diagnostic and therapeutic tool; first-line medical management: combined hormonal contraceptive (COCP) or progestogen (norethisterone or DMPA); GNRH analogue if initial treatment fails; CA-125 mild elevation is non-specific and does not indicate malignancy
options.C: Pelvic inflammatory disease — oral doxycycline and metronidazole
options.D: Uterine fibroids — refer for MRI pelvis
options.E: Ovarian cyst — routine USS

explanation.correct: Endometriosis: ectopic endometrial tissue outside the uterus (most commonly: ovaries — endometrioma 'chocolate cysts', peritoneum, rectovaginal septum, uterosacral ligaments). Symptoms: dysmenorrhoea (cyclical pelvic pain worse during menstruation), deep dyspareunia (pain during intercourse from posterior involvement), chronic pelvic pain, subfertility, cyclical bowel/bladder symptoms. Examination findings: uterine tenderness, fixed retroversion (adhesions), tenderness in posterior fornix (recto-vaginal involvement). Per NICE NG73 (Endometriosis): diagnose based on symptoms + examination; do NOT delay treatment whilst waiting for laparoscopy. CA-125: mildly elevated in endometriosis, PID, pregnancy — not specific for malignancy in this clinical context. First-line medical treatment: COCP (continuous use for 3-6 months); or progestogen (norethisterone 5 mg TDS, or DMPA 150 mg IM every 12 weeks); GnRH analogue (e.g. zoladex/goserelin) as second-line; add-back HRT with GnRH analogues if used >6 months. Laparoscopy: definitive diagnosis + excision of lesions; preferred for severe disease or treatment failure.
explanation.A: Incorrect — CA-125 68 U/mL in a 26-year-old with symptoms strongly suggesting endometriosis is not indicative of ovarian cancer. Mild CA-125 elevation is common in endometriosis.
explanation.B: CORRECT — Endometriosis: NICE NG73; clinical diagnosis; COCP or progestogen first-line; CA-125 mild elevation is non-specific; laparoscopy for definitive diagnosis/treatment.
explanation.C: Incorrect — PID typically presents with acute onset, fever, purulent discharge, and bilateral adnexal tenderness; deep dyspareunia + fixed retroversion + 6-week history points more strongly to endometriosis.
explanation.D: Incorrect — Fibroids cause dysmenorrhoea and menorrhagia but fixed retroversion, deep dyspareunia and pelvic adhesive signs are more characteristic of endometriosis.
explanation.E: Incorrect — Routine USS for an ovarian cyst alone would not explain all the features; clinical diagnosis and treatment per NICE NG73 is appropriate first.

reference: NICE NG73 — Endometriosis. https://www.nice.org.uk/guidance/ng73

question: A 29-year-old woman with endometriosis and infertility for 18 months is reviewed. She has completed 6 months of COCP without significant improvement in pain. She and her partner have normal fertility investigations. Per NICE NG73 and fertility guidelines, what is the next step?

options.A: Continue COCP for another 12 months before any further action
options.B: Refer for laparoscopy — laparoscopic excision/ablation of endometriosis improves fertility outcomes and is the gold standard for both diagnosis and treatment; NICE NG73 recommends referral to a specialist endometriosis service; women with endometriosis-related subfertility should not have gonadotrophin-releasing hormone (GnRH) analogues as these suppress ovulation and are not appropriate when trying to conceive; IVF may be considered for tubal/moderate-severe endometriosis
options.C: Start GnRH analogue immediately to suppress endometriosis — this improves fertility
options.D: Start clomifene citrate for ovulation induction
options.E: Intrauterine insemination (IUI) without laparoscopy first

explanation.correct: Per NICE NG73 (Endometriosis) and NICE NG156 (Fertility problems): endometriosis + infertility: laparoscopy is indicated to: confirm and stage endometriosis (revised ASRM staging: I-IV); treat lesions (excision or ablation of peritoneal/ovarian endometriosis); drain/remove endometriomas; adhesiolysis. Evidence: laparoscopic excision of stage I/II endometriosis improves pregnancy rates (Marcoux NEJM 1997). GNRH analogues for endometriosis pre-IVF: GnRH agonist for 3-6 months before IVF may improve IVF outcomes in severe endometriosis (endometrioma — down-regulation improves environment) — but GnRH analogues ALONE without assisted conception do NOT improve natural fertility (suppress ovulation). COCP/progestogen: manage symptoms but also suppress ovulation — inappropriate while trying to conceive. IVF: indicated for bilateral tubal damage, moderate-severe endometriosis, failed laparoscopic treatment. Clomifene: used for unexplained infertility or anovulation — not for endometriosis-related subfertility specifically.
explanation.A: Incorrect — The COCP has failed to improve symptoms at 6 months AND is suppressing ovulation — it should be stopped if the patient is trying to conceive; laparoscopy is the next step.
explanation.B: CORRECT — Laparoscopy for diagnosis and treatment; refer to specialist endometriosis service per NICE NG73; stop COCP to allow conception; GnRH analogue contraindicated while trying to conceive.
explanation.C: Incorrect — GnRH analogues suppress ovulation — they cannot be used when the goal is pregnancy; they suppress endometriosis but do not improve natural fertility.
explanation.D: Incorrect — Clomifene induces ovulation and is used for anovulatory infertility (e.g. PCOS) — not appropriate for endometriosis-related subfertility where laparoscopy is indicated.
explanation.E: Incorrect — IUI without addressing the underlying endometriosis has poor evidence; laparoscopy first to diagnose and treat is preferred per guidelines.

reference: NICE NG73 — Endometriosis. NICE NG156 — Fertility problems. https://www.nice.org.uk/guidance/ng73

question: A 32-year-old woman is found on USS to have a 6 cm left ovarian endometrioma ('chocolate cyst'). She is not currently trying to conceive. Per NICE NG73, RCOG and ESHRE guidelines, what is the recommended management?

options.A: Immediate IVF — all women with endometrioma should proceed to IVF
options.B: Laparoscopic cystectomy (stripping of the endometrioma) — preferred surgical approach for endometriomas ≥4 cm; excision of the cyst wall rather than drainage/coagulation is recommended (lower recurrence rate, better ovarian reserve preservation in skilled hands); aspiration alone has high recurrence; GnRH analogue for 3 months pre-operatively may reduce vascularity; NICE NG73 recommends referral to specialist endometriosis service
options.C: Simple aspiration and drainage under USS guidance
options.D: Oophorectomy — all endometriomas require removal of the ovary
options.E: Continue COCP for 12 months — endometriomas always regress with hormonal suppression

explanation.correct: Per NICE NG73, RCOG and ESHRE endometriosis guidelines: ovarian endometrioma management (for symptomatic endometrioma or those ≥4 cm): laparoscopic cystectomy (stripping technique): preferred to drainage alone; involves dissection and removal of the cyst wall; recurrence rate ~20% at 5 years (vs >80% recurrence with aspiration alone); CONCERNS with cystectomy: removal of some normal ovarian cortex alongside the cyst wall → reduced ovarian reserve (AMH may decline post-operatively, particularly if bilateral); this is unavoidable but minimised by skilled surgeons. Pre-operative GnRH analogue (3 months): reduces cyst vascularity, may improve surgical field. Aspiration: high recurrence; used only in specific circumstances (e.g. immediately before IVF egg collection). Oophorectomy: reserved for recurrent endometrioma after previous cystectomy, or in women who have completed their family — not first-line in a 32-year-old. COCP: does not significantly reduce established endometrioma size.
explanation.A: Incorrect — IVF is indicated for endometriosis-related infertility — it is not the primary management for an endometrioma in a woman not currently trying to conceive.
explanation.B: CORRECT — Laparoscopic cystectomy (stripping) for endometrioma ≥4 cm; lower recurrence than aspiration; preserve ovarian reserve; specialist endometriosis service per NICE NG73.
explanation.C: Incorrect — Aspiration alone has an extremely high recurrence rate (>80%) and is not recommended as the primary surgical treatment for endometrioma.
explanation.D: Incorrect — Oophorectomy in a 32-year-old for a first endometrioma is disproportionate and would cause premature ovarian insufficiency.
explanation.E: Incorrect — COCP does not significantly reduce the size of established endometriomas; surgical treatment is required for large symptomatic endometriomas.

reference: NICE NG73 — Endometriosis. ESHRE endometriosis guidelines. https://www.nice.org.uk/guidance/ng73

question: A 42-year-old woman presents with heavy menstrual bleeding (HMB) causing iron deficiency anaemia. She passes clots and changes her pad every hour on heavy days. Her uterus is normal on examination. Per NICE NG88, what is the first-line investigation and initial management?

options.A: Immediate hysterectomy — the only cure for HMB
options.B: Transvaginal ultrasound (TVS) to exclude structural causes (fibroids, polyps, adenomyosis); FBC to confirm anaemia; first-line medical treatment options per NICE NG88: levonorgestrel IUS (Mirena — most effective medical treatment, first choice if no contraindication); or combined oral contraceptive pill; or tranexamic acid; or NSAIDs (mefenamic acid); treat iron deficiency anaemia (ferrous sulphate)
options.C: D&C (dilatation and curettage) — diagnostic and therapeutic
options.D: Endometrial ablation is first-line for all HMB
options.E: Hysteroscopy is mandatory before any treatment

explanation.correct: Per NICE NG88 (Heavy menstrual bleeding): assessment: TVS to assess for structural pathology (fibroid, polyp, adenomyosis — these influence management); FBC (confirm iron deficiency anaemia); thyroid function (hypothyroidism can cause HMB); coagulation screen (if HMB from menarche or family history of bleeding disorder — von Willebrand's disease). Medical management (no structural cause identified — 'dysfunctional uterine bleeding'): First choice: LNG-IUS (levonorgestrel intrauterine system — Mirena): releases 20 mcg LNG/day locally → reduces endometrial proliferation → reduces blood loss by ~90%; also provides contraception; lasts 5 years. If LNG-IUS declined: tranexamic acid 1g TDS (days 1-4, antifibrinolytic) OR mefenamic acid 500mg TDS (NSAID — reduces blood loss + dysmenorrhoea) OR COCP. Second-line medical: norethisterone 5mg TDS days 5-26 OR DMPA. Surgical options: endometrial ablation (effective for dysfunctional HMB — NovaSure, ThermaChoice); hysterectomy (definitive — 100% cure, offered if medical treatment fails or declined). D&C is not therapeutic for HMB.
explanation.A: Incorrect — Hysterectomy is a second-line surgical option after failed medical treatment; it is not first-line for HMB without contraindication to medical therapy.
explanation.B: CORRECT — TVS + FBC; LNG-IUS (Mirena) as first-line medical treatment per NICE NG88; treat anaemia.
explanation.C: Incorrect — D&C (dilatation and curettage) is a diagnostic procedure with no lasting therapeutic effect on HMB; it is not standard management.
explanation.D: Incorrect — Endometrial ablation is a second-line surgical option when medical treatment has failed or is declined; it is not first-line for all HMB.
explanation.E: Incorrect — Hysteroscopy may be required if TVS findings are abnormal or suspicious — it is not mandatory before initiating medical treatment for uncomplicated HMB.

reference: NICE NG88 — Heavy menstrual bleeding. https://www.nice.org.uk/guidance/ng88

question: A 38-year-old woman presents with dysmenorrhoea, heavy menstrual bleeding and a uniformly enlarged, soft, tender uterus. TVS shows a bulky uterus with heterogeneous myometrium and poor definition between endometrium and myometrium. Per NICE NG88, what is the likely diagnosis?

options.A: Uterine fibroid (leiomyoma) — solitary intramural mass
options.B: Adenomyosis — heterotopic endometrial glands and stroma within the myometrium; characterised by a uniformly enlarged, globular, soft, tender uterus; TVS features: heterogeneous myometrium, myometrial cysts, asymmetric myometrial thickening, ill-defined junctional zone; symptoms: heavy menstrual bleeding, secondary dysmenorrhoea; management: LNG-IUS first-line; if severe symptoms and family complete: consider GnRH analogue (bridge to surgery) or hysterectomy (curative)
options.C: Endometrial cancer — refer urgently
options.D: Ovarian cyst — TVS confirms diagnosis
options.E: Pelvic inflammatory disease — treat with antibiotics

explanation.correct: Adenomyosis: endometrial glands and stroma invade the myometrium → diffuse uterine enlargement, myometrial hypertrophy, abnormal uterine bleeding, and dysmenorrhoea. Classic presentation: 35-50-year-old woman; dysmenorrhoea + HMB + uniformly enlarged globular 'boggy' uterus. TVS features: heterogeneous myometrium (asymmetric); myometrial cysts (>2-3 mm); asymmetric myometrial thickening; indistinct endometrial-myometrial junctional zone. MRI adeno: gold standard imaging — shows junctional zone thickening >12 mm. Per NICE NG88: medical management: LNG-IUS is first-line for adenomyosis-associated HMB (reduces both bleeding and dysmenorrhoea); also: COCP, progestogen (norethisterone, DMPA), GnRH analogue (short-term, bridge to surgery). Definitive treatment: hysterectomy (only curative option — adenomyosis recurs after conservative procedures). Adenomyosis vs fibroids: fibroids cause asymmetric focal uterine enlargement with discrete hypoechoic masses on TVS; adenomyosis causes diffuse homogeneous enlargement.
explanation.A: Incorrect — Fibroids cause focal asymmetric enlargement with discrete well-defined hypoechoic masses on TVS; adenomyosis causes diffuse heterogeneous enlargement without discrete masses.
explanation.B: CORRECT — Adenomyosis: uniformly enlarged tender uterus + TVS heterogeneous myometrium + ill-defined junctional zone; LNG-IUS first-line per NICE NG88.
explanation.C: Incorrect — Endometrial cancer presents with PMB/abnormal bleeding with endometrial thickening on TVS, not a uniformly enlarged myometrium with heterogeneous appearance.
explanation.D: Incorrect — Ovarian cysts are separate from the uterus and do not cause uterine enlargement on examination.
explanation.E: Incorrect — PID causes acute bilateral adnexal tenderness with fever and discharge — not a uniformly enlarged tender uterus on chronic review.

reference: NICE NG88 — Heavy menstrual bleeding. https://www.nice.org.uk/guidance/ng88

question: A 45-year-old woman has been on the LNG-IUS for 18 months for HMB. She has had amenorrhoea for 6 months and is pleased with this outcome. She now wonders about HRT for perimenopausal symptoms (hot flushes, night sweats). Per NICE NG23 and BMS guidance, what should the GP advise?

options.A: She must remove the LNG-IUS before starting HRT
options.B: The LNG-IUS (Mirena) can be used as the progestogen component of combined HRT — she can add transdermal or oral oestrogen to her existing LNG-IUS; this provides menopausal symptom relief while the LNG-IUS protects the endometrium; LNG-IUS for HRT is licensed for 5 years; she does not need to remove it
options.C: She does not need oestrogen — the LNG-IUS treats all menopausal symptoms
options.D: She cannot use HRT as she has had amenorrhoea for 6 months — she must wait 12 months without periods
options.E: Start progesterone-only HRT — LNG-IUS provides oestrogen

explanation.correct: Per NICE NG23 (Menopause) and British Menopause Society (BMS) guidance: the LNG-IUS (Mirena) is licensed for use as the progestogen component of sequential or continuous combined HRT. In perimenopausal/menopausal women who have a Mirena IUS: the IUS protects the endometrium from oestrogen-induced hyperplasia (replaces oral/patch progestogen); the woman can simply add oestrogen (transdermal oestradiol patch, gel, or oral oestradiol) to address vasomotor symptoms; this is a convenient and well-tolerated form of combined HRT. LNG-IUS for HRT use: licensed for 5 years (same duration as for contraception/HMB); the progestogen component is local to the uterus — systemic progestogen side effects are minimal. Advantages: amenorrhoea maintained (if already achieved); simplified regimen; good endometrial protection. Do NOT need to remove the IUS — it functions as the progestogen component of HRT.
explanation.A: Incorrect — Removal of the LNG-IUS is not required; it can be used as the progestogen component of combined HRT.
explanation.B: CORRECT — LNG-IUS can be the progestogen component of HRT; add oestrogen (patch/gel/oral) for vasomotor symptoms; licensed for 5 years for this purpose per NICE NG23/BMS.
explanation.C: Incorrect — The LNG-IUS releases progestogen locally and does NOT treat vasomotor menopausal symptoms (hot flushes, night sweats) — oestrogen is required for this.
explanation.D: Incorrect — There is no requirement to wait 12 months without periods before starting HRT in a woman who is perimenopausal; symptoms drive the decision.
explanation.E: Incorrect — The LNG-IUS provides progestogen (not oestrogen); starting additional progestogen-only preparation would be double progestogen with no oestrogen — incorrect approach.

reference: NICE NG23 — Menopause. BMS guidelines. https://www.nice.org.uk/guidance/ng23

question: A 34-year-old woman (G2P1) presents at 32 weeks gestation with sudden onset severe constant epigastric pain, headache and visual disturbance. BP is 168/108 mmHg. Urine dipstick shows 3+ protein. Platelets are 78 × 10⁹/L, ALT 290 IU/L and Hb 90 g/L. Per RCOG and NICE NG133, what is the diagnosis and immediate management?

options.A: Pre-eclampsia — oral labetalol and outpatient review
options.B: HELLP syndrome (Haemolysis, Elevated Liver enzymes, Low Platelets) — a severe variant of pre-eclampsia; diagnostic criteria: microangiopathic haemolytic anaemia (Hb low, abnormal blood film), AST/ALT >70 IU/L, platelets <100×10⁹/L; emergency admission to obstetric HDU; IV antihypertensive (labetalol IV); magnesium sulphate for seizure prophylaxis; steroids (betamethasone) for fetal lung maturation; urgent delivery (mode by obstetric assessment); correct coagulopathy; monitor fetal wellbeing
options.C: Normal pregnancy — epigastric pain is reflux
options.D: Appendicitis — surgical referral
options.E: Severe gestational hypertension — blood pressure monitoring at home

explanation.correct: HELLP syndrome: a severe obstetric emergency occurring in the context of pre-eclampsia (some overlap; HELLP can occur without classic hypertension/proteinuria). Diagnostic criteria (Tennessee criteria): Haemolysis: microangiopathic haemolytic anaemia — low Hb, elevated LDH, abnormal peripheral blood smear; Elevated Liver enzymes: AST >70 IU/L (or AST >3× ULN); Low Platelets: <100×10⁹/L. Per RCOG Green-top and NICE NG133: Management: immediate HDU admission; IV labetalol (or IV hydralazine) for BP >160/110 mmHg (target <150/100); IV magnesium sulphate: seizure prophylaxis for severe pre-eclampsia/HELLP (4g loading dose over 5-10 minutes, then 1g/hour infusion); betamethasone 12 mg IM ×2 doses 24 hours apart (fetal lung maturation — gestational age <34 weeks); urgent delivery: mode dependent on obstetric assessment — aim delivery within 24-48 hours in severe HELLP; blood products if platelets <50 before delivery or active bleeding.
explanation.A: Incorrect — Oral labetalol and outpatient review is entirely inappropriate for HELLP syndrome — this is a life-threatening emergency requiring immediate hospitalisation.
explanation.B: CORRECT — HELLP syndrome: haemolysis + elevated liver enzymes + low platelets in pre-eclampsia context. Emergency HDU admission, IV antihypertensive, MgSO4, steroids, urgent delivery per RCOG/NICE NG133.
explanation.C: Incorrect — Severe epigastric pain + hypertension + proteinuria + thrombocytopenia + elevated liver enzymes in pregnancy = HELLP until proven otherwise.
explanation.D: Incorrect — Appendicitis is a differential for right-sided pain in pregnancy but does not explain hypertension, proteinuria, thrombocytopenia and elevated liver enzymes.
explanation.E: Incorrect — Home monitoring is appropriate for gestational hypertension alone; HELLP with these biochemical derangements requires emergency admission.

reference: RCOG Green-top Guideline — Severe pre-eclampsia/eclampsia. NICE NG133. https://www.rcog.org.uk/guidance

question: A 28-year-old woman at 28 weeks gestation has a blood pressure of 144/92 mmHg on two occasions 4 hours apart. Urine dipstick shows 2+ protein. She has no headache or visual disturbance. Per NICE NG133, what is the diagnosis and management?

options.A: Gestational hypertension — no treatment needed below 160/110
options.B: Pre-eclampsia (new hypertension ≥140/90 after 20 weeks + significant proteinuria ≥300 mg/24h or PCR ≥30 mg/mmol) — admit to hospital for assessment; start antihypertensive if BP ≥140/90 (labetalol first-line, alternatives: nifedipine, methyldopa); fetal monitoring; blood tests: FBC, LFTs, U&E, LDH, urate; consider low-dose aspirin from 12 weeks for prevention in future pregnancies; plan for timing and mode of delivery based on severity
options.C: Start immediate delivery — all pre-eclampsia at 28 weeks requires immediate caesarean section
options.D: Oral methyldopa only — no monitoring needed if BP controlled
options.E: Discharge with BP monitoring daily at home — only admit if BP >160/110

explanation.correct: Per NICE NG133 (Hypertension in pregnancy): pre-eclampsia definition: new hypertension (≥140/90 mmHg) developing after 20 weeks gestation PLUS significant proteinuria (urinary protein:creatinine ratio ≥30 mg/mmol, or ≥300 mg in 24-hour urine, or 2+ on dipstick if no quantitative test available). Management: hospital admission for initial assessment (all pre-eclampsia diagnosed de novo); antihypertensive treatment: labetalol oral (1st line), alternatives: nifedipine (modified release), methyldopa; target BP: <135/85 mmHg (systolic <135, diastolic <85); investigations: FBC (thrombocytopenia?), LFTs (AST elevation?), urea, creatinine, urate; LDH (haemolysis?); fetal assessment: CTG, growth scan, umbilical artery Doppler. Delivery timing: 34-36 weeks for stable mild-moderate PE; immediate delivery for severe PE/HELLP or signs of maternal/fetal compromise. Aspirin for prevention: 150 mg aspirin from 12-36 weeks for women with high-risk factors identified on first trimester screening.
explanation.A: Incorrect — Gestational hypertension is hypertension without proteinuria; this patient has proteinuria = pre-eclampsia; monitoring alone without treatment is not appropriate.
explanation.B: CORRECT — Pre-eclampsia: admit; labetalol first-line antihypertensive; blood tests; fetal monitoring; delivery planning per NICE NG133.
explanation.C: Incorrect — Immediate delivery is not required for all pre-eclampsia at 28 weeks; stable mild-moderate PE can be managed conservatively until 34-36 weeks.
explanation.D: Incorrect — Methyldopa is an alternative antihypertensive but monitoring and blood tests are essential for pre-eclampsia management — oral methyldopa alone with no monitoring is unsafe.
explanation.E: Incorrect — Pre-eclampsia at 28 weeks requires hospital admission for assessment, not home monitoring.

reference: NICE NG133 — Hypertension in pregnancy. https://www.nice.org.uk/guidance/ng133

question: A GP is reviewing a woman's pre-pregnancy history. She had severe pre-eclampsia in her first pregnancy at 32 weeks. She is now planning her second pregnancy. Per NICE NG133 and RCOG guidance, what preventive measures are recommended?

options.A: No preventive treatment is available — pre-eclampsia always recurs
options.B: Low-dose aspirin 150 mg daily from 12-16 weeks of pregnancy until 36 weeks (or delivery if earlier) — per NICE NG133 and RCOG: aspirin reduces risk of recurrent pre-eclampsia by approximately 24% (ASPRE trial); also: first trimester combined screening (MAP, uterine artery Doppler, PLGF, PAPP-A) at 11-13 weeks to quantify risk; calcium supplementation (1g/day) if dietary calcium intake low; referral to high-risk obstetric unit for monitoring; serial growth scans from 24 weeks
options.C: Prophylactic corticosteroids from 16 weeks
options.D: Low molecular weight heparin from conception
options.E: Sildenafil — vasodilator proven to prevent pre-eclampsia recurrence

explanation.correct: Per NICE NG133: risk factors for pre-eclampsia warranting low-dose aspirin: previous hypertensive disease in pregnancy; chronic kidney disease; autoimmune conditions (SLE, antiphospholipid syndrome); diabetes; chronic hypertension; AND women with ≥1 moderate risk factor at first trimester screening (nulliparity, BMI >35, family history, multiple pregnancy, age >40, interpregnancy interval >10 years). Low-dose aspirin: 150 mg daily from 12-16 weeks to 36 weeks gestation (stopping at 36 weeks reduces risk of post-partum haemorrhage); mechanism: inhibits thromboxane A2 production → reduces placental vasospasm and improves implantation; ASPRE trial: 150 mg aspirin started at 11-14 weeks in high-risk women reduced pre-eclampsia <37 weeks by 62% and <34 weeks by 82%. First-trimester screening algorithm (Fetal Medicine Foundation model): combines maternal factors, uterine artery Doppler, PLGF, PAPP-A, MAP at 11-13 weeks → identifies high-risk women for aspirin; significantly superior to risk-factor approach alone.
explanation.A: Incorrect — Aspirin significantly reduces recurrence risk of pre-eclampsia when taken from the first trimester per NICE NG133 and ASPRE trial.
explanation.B: CORRECT — Low-dose aspirin 150 mg from 12-16 weeks to 36 weeks; first trimester risk-based screening; calcium supplementation; high-risk obstetric care per NICE NG133.
explanation.C: Incorrect — Prophylactic corticosteroids are used for fetal lung maturation in anticipated preterm delivery — not for pre-eclampsia prevention.
explanation.D: Incorrect — LMWH is used in antiphospholipid syndrome and thrombophilia management in pregnancy, but is not the standard preventive treatment for pre-eclampsia recurrence.
explanation.E: Incorrect — Sildenafil (STRIDER trial) did not improve outcomes in severe early-onset fetal growth restriction and was not found to prevent pre-eclampsia; it is not recommended.

reference: NICE NG133 — Hypertension in pregnancy. RCOG guidance. https://www.nice.org.uk/guidance/ng133

question: A 25-year-old woman at 8 weeks gestation presents with severe nausea and vomiting, inability to keep any fluids down for 3 days, weight loss of 5 kg from pre-pregnancy weight, and ketonuria 2+ on dipstick. Per NICE CG69 and RCOG guidelines, what is the diagnosis and management?

options.A: Morning sickness — reassure and discharge
options.B: Hyperemesis gravidarum (HG) — persistent severe nausea and vomiting in pregnancy causing dehydration, weight loss >5% and ketonuria; requires hospital admission; IV fluid resuscitation (Hartmann's or 0.9% saline with potassium supplementation — NOT dextrose alone, risk of Wernicke's encephalopathy); antiemetics (IV/IM cyclizine, promethazine, ondansetron); thiamine (vitamin B1) 100 mg IV/IM TDS (Wernicke's encephalopathy prophylaxis — mandatory); correct electrolyte imbalance; thromboprophylaxis with LMWH (VTE risk from immobility/dehydration)
options.C: Oral metoclopramide only — no admission needed for any level of nausea in pregnancy
options.D: Stop all antiemetics — all are teratogenic in the first trimester
options.E: Ginger supplements — evidence-based treatment for hyperemesis

explanation.correct: Hyperemesis gravidarum (HG): severe end of the nausea and vomiting of pregnancy spectrum; defined by: weight loss >5% of pre-pregnancy body weight (this patient: 5 kg loss = significant); ketonuria; inability to keep fluids down; electrolyte imbalance; dehydration. Per NICE CG69 and RCOG Green-top (Nausea and vomiting in pregnancy): IV fluids: Hartmann's solution or 0.9% saline with KCl supplementation; AVOID dextrose (5%) without thiamine — risk of precipitating Wernicke's encephalopathy; IV/IM antiemetics: cyclizine 50 mg TDS; promethazine 12.5-25 mg TDS; ondansetron 4-8 mg TDS (second-line — limited data pre-12 weeks but used in severe refractory HG); thiamine (Vitamin B1) 100 mg IV or oral 25-50 mg TDS (mandatory for all women admitted with HG — Wernicke's risk from carbohydrate refeeding without B1); LMWH prophylaxis; nutritional support if prolonged; in extreme cases: enteral/TPN. All standard antiemetics are relatively safe in pregnancy — withholding them is NOT appropriate.
explanation.A: Incorrect — This is not morning sickness; 5 kg weight loss + ketonuria + inability to maintain hydration = hyperemesis gravidarum requiring hospital admission.
explanation.B: CORRECT — HG: IV fluids (not dextrose alone), antiemetics, thiamine IV (Wernicke's prophylaxis), LMWH per NICE CG69/RCOG.
explanation.C: Incorrect — Oral metoclopramide may be appropriate for mild-moderate nausea but is insufficient for HG with 5 kg weight loss and ketonuria requiring IV management.
explanation.D: Incorrect — Withholding antiemetics in HG is inappropriate; first-line antiemetics (cyclizine, promethazine) are safe in pregnancy and evidence-based for HG treatment.
explanation.E: Incorrect — Ginger has some evidence for mild nausea of pregnancy but is not an evidence-based treatment for severe hyperemesis gravidarum requiring IV management.

reference: NICE CG69 — Nausea/vomiting in pregnancy. RCOG — Hyperemesis gravidarum. https://www.nice.org.uk/guidance/cg69

question: A 30-year-old woman at 24 weeks presents to the GP with a lower left calf which is red, warm, swollen and tender. She had a previous DVT during the contraceptive pill 4 years ago. Per NICE NG158 (VTE in pregnancy), what is the management?

options.A: D-dimer test — if normal, DVT excluded
options.B: Clinical assessment + compression duplex USS of the leg urgently — per NICE NG158: DVT in pregnancy requires clinical probability assessment + leg compression USS; if DVT confirmed on USS: low molecular weight heparin (LMWH: enoxaparin, tinzaparin or dalteparin) — therapeutic dose weight-adjusted; continue for the remainder of pregnancy + 6 weeks postnatal (minimum 3 months total); LMWH preferred over warfarin and DOACs in pregnancy (warfarin teratogenic in first trimester; DOACs not licensed in pregnancy); D-dimer is unreliable in pregnancy (elevated by normal pregnancy)
options.C: Warfarin immediately — most effective anticoagulant
options.D: Reassure — leg swelling is normal in pregnancy
options.E: Aspirin 75 mg — antiplatelet therapy is first-line for DVT in pregnancy

explanation.correct: Per NICE NG158 (Venous thromboembolism in pregnancy): DVT in pregnancy is a medical emergency — pregnancy is a hypercoagulable state; risk ×4-5 compared to non-pregnant women. D-dimer: NOT useful in pregnancy — physiologically elevated in normal pregnancy (rising from first trimester); a negative D-dimer does not exclude DVT in pregnancy. Investigation: compression duplex USS of both legs (standard diagnostic test); if USS negative but clinical suspicion high: repeat USS in 1 week or consider bilateral iliac vein imaging. Treatment if DVT confirmed: therapeutic LMWH (enoxaparin 1 mg/kg BD or 1.5 mg/kg OD depending on renal function; tinzaparin 175 units/kg OD; dalteparin 100 units/kg BD); weight-adjusted dosing in pregnancy; anti-Xa monitoring if: extremes of weight, renal impairment, recurrent VTE. Duration: throughout pregnancy + 6 weeks postnatal minimum (or 3 months total treatment). Warfarin: avoid in first trimester (warfarin embryopathy — chondrodysplasia punctata); safe in 2nd/3rd trimester for maternal anticoagulation but crosses placenta → fetal bleeding risk; DOACs: all avoid in pregnancy (rivaroxaban, apixaban, edoxaban — not licensed; potential teratogenicity).
explanation.A: Incorrect — D-dimer is NOT a reliable test for DVT in pregnancy due to physiological elevation; a negative result cannot be used to exclude DVT.
explanation.B: CORRECT — Compression USS urgently; if DVT confirmed: therapeutic LMWH weight-adjusted for remainder of pregnancy + 6 weeks postnatal per NICE NG158.
explanation.C: Incorrect — Warfarin is avoided in the first trimester (teratogenic) and carries fetal bleeding risks in later trimesters; LMWH is the drug of choice for VTE in pregnancy.
explanation.D: Incorrect — Leg swelling in pregnancy is common but unilateral calf erythema, warmth and tenderness in a patient with a prior DVT requires urgent DVT exclusion.
explanation.E: Incorrect — Aspirin is an antiplatelet agent — it does not treat DVT and is not anticoagulant therapy.

reference: NICE NG158 — VTE in pregnancy. https://www.nice.org.uk/guidance/ng158

question: A 32-year-old woman with antiphospholipid syndrome (APS — aPL triple positive, prior history of miscarriage and DVT) is planning pregnancy. Per RCOG and BSH guidance on APS in pregnancy, what is the recommended management?

options.A: No specific treatment needed in pregnancy — APS only affects non-pregnant patients
options.B: Low-dose aspirin 75-150 mg daily from pre-conception (or as early in pregnancy as possible) PLUS prophylactic LMWH throughout pregnancy and 6 weeks postnatal — APS with prior thrombosis (thrombotic APS) requires therapeutic anticoagulation during pregnancy (not just prophylactic); warfarin is stopped pre-conception and switched to LMWH; close obstetric and haematology monitoring; surveillance for pre-eclampsia and fetal growth restriction
options.C: Warfarin throughout pregnancy at therapeutic doses
options.D: Aspirin alone is sufficient for all APS in pregnancy
options.E: DOAC (rivaroxaban) is the preferred anticoagulant for APS in pregnancy

explanation.correct: Per RCOG Green-top No.68 and BSH guidelines on APS in pregnancy: APS classification: Obstetric APS: pregnancy morbidity (recurrent miscarriage ≥3, or late fetal loss ≥10 weeks, or severe pre-eclampsia/IUGR <34 weeks) without thrombosis → aspirin + prophylactic LMWH. Thrombotic APS (this patient): prior thrombosis (DVT) + aPL → requires long-term anticoagulation; switch warfarin to LMWH pre-conception or as soon as pregnancy confirmed (warfarin teratogenic in first trimester); LMWH at THERAPEUTIC doses throughout pregnancy (reflects pre-pregnancy warfarin requirement); aspirin 75 mg from pre-conception; postnatal: resume warfarin + continue for 6 weeks (or lifelong anticoagulation as needed). Key complication monitoring: pre-eclampsia, fetal growth restriction, stillbirth — serial growth scans + uterine artery Doppler. DOACs (rivaroxaban, apixaban): AVOID in APS in pregnancy (not licensed; also in non-pregnant APS: rivaroxaban is inferior to warfarin for arterial/triple positive APS per TRAPS trial).
explanation.A: Incorrect — APS in pregnancy carries significant risks of thrombosis, recurrent miscarriage, severe pre-eclampsia and IUGR — specific anticoagulation management is mandatory.
explanation.B: CORRECT — Thrombotic APS in pregnancy: aspirin + therapeutic LMWH (replace warfarin pre-conception); 6 weeks postnatal; serial surveillance per RCOG/BSH.
explanation.C: Incorrect — Warfarin is teratogenic in the first trimester (risk of warfarin embryopathy) and must be switched to LMWH before conception or immediately upon positive pregnancy test.
explanation.D: Incorrect — Aspirin alone is insufficient for thrombotic APS — therapeutic LMWH is additionally required throughout pregnancy.
explanation.E: Incorrect — DOACs are not licensed in pregnancy and are inferior to warfarin for thrombotic APS (including triple-positive APS) per the TRAPS trial; LMWH is the correct choice in pregnancy.

reference: RCOG Green-top No.68 — APS in pregnancy. BSH guidelines. https://www.rcog.org.uk/guidance

question: A forest plot from a systematic review on statin therapy shows 8 randomised controlled trials. The overall pooled effect estimate (diamond) shows a relative risk of 0.78 (95% CI 0.65-0.91). The I² statistic is 72%. Per EBM principles, how should this result be interpreted?

options.A: The result is definitive — RR 0.78 is highly statistically significant so clinical heterogeneity is irrelevant
options.B: The pooled RR of 0.78 (95% CI 0.65-0.91) suggests statins reduce the relative risk by 22% (CI does not cross 1.0 = statistically significant); however I² = 72% indicates HIGH heterogeneity between studies (I² >50% is considered high); this means the studies are not all measuring the same thing — differences in populations, doses, follow-up, or outcomes may explain the variability; a pooled estimate should be interpreted with caution when I² is high; investigate sources of heterogeneity
options.C: I² of 72% means 72% of studies showed benefit — this is a positive finding
options.D: The 95% CI of 0.65-0.91 means the drug is harmful in 9% of patients
options.E: A result is only significant if the 95% CI is entirely below 0.5

explanation.correct: Forest plot and meta-analysis interpretation: RR 0.78 (95% CI 0.65-0.91): statins reduce the risk of the outcome by 22% relative to control; CI does not include 1.0 = statistically significant (p<0.05). I² statistic: measures the proportion of total variation between studies due to heterogeneity (rather than sampling error/chance). Interpretation: I² 0-25%: low heterogeneity; 25-50%: moderate; 50-75%: high; >75%: very high. I² = 72% = HIGH heterogeneity — the studies differ substantially in their results. This does not invalidate the meta-analysis but means: the pooled estimate should be treated cautiously; sources of heterogeneity (populations, doses, outcomes, follow-up duration) should be explored via subgroup analysis; the meta-analysis should ideally use a random-effects model (not fixed-effects) when I² is high.
explanation.A: Incorrect — Statistical significance (CI not crossing 1.0) and clinical heterogeneity (I²) are independent concerns; high I² raises important questions about whether pooling was appropriate.
explanation.B: CORRECT — RR 0.78 is significant (CI 0.65-0.91 does not cross 1.0); but I² 72% = high heterogeneity; interpret pooled estimate cautiously and investigate heterogeneity sources.
explanation.C: Incorrect — I² measures percentage of variability due to heterogeneity between studies — not the proportion of studies showing benefit.
explanation.D: Incorrect — The 95% CI means if the study were repeated 100 times, 95% of the CIs would contain the true RR. It does not mean the drug harms a proportion of patients.
explanation.E: Incorrect — Statistical significance requires the 95% CI to not cross the null value (RR=1.0 for relative risk; RR <1.0 = benefit). The threshold is 1.0, not 0.5.

reference: BMJ Statistics Notes — Forest plots and meta-analysis. Cochrane Handbook for Systematic Reviews.

question: A GP reads a study showing that a new diabetes drug reduces HbA1c by 8 mmol/mol (SD 4) compared to placebo. The p-value is p=0.04 and the 95% CI is 0.2-15.8 mmol/mol. The study included 45 patients. Per EBM principles, what is the correct interpretation?

options.A: The result is clinically and statistically significant — this drug should immediately be adopted
options.B: The result is statistically significant (p=0.04; CI does not cross zero) but the wide 95% CI (0.2-15.8) reflects a small sample size and large uncertainty; the minimum clinically important difference (MCID) for HbA1c reduction is approximately 5-6 mmol/mol; the lower confidence bound (0.2) may be below the MCID — meaning a real-world effect could be minimal; the result is preliminary and needs replication in a larger, adequately powered trial before practice change
options.C: p=0.04 is borderline and means there is a 4% chance the treatment works
options.D: The standard deviation of 4 means the result is not significant
options.E: A 95% CI of 0.2-15.8 means the drug works in 95% of patients

explanation.correct: Statistical versus clinical significance: this study is statistically significant (p=0.04; 95% CI does not include zero — positive values only). However: (1) Small sample (n=45) — underpowered studies produce wide CIs; (2) Wide CI (0.2-15.8): the true effect could be anywhere from barely detectable (0.2 mmol/mol) to very large (15.8 mmol/mol); (3) MCID for HbA1c: approximately 5-6 mmol/mol is considered the minimum clinically meaningful change — the lower CI limit of 0.2 is well below this, meaning a real-world effect of marginal benefit is possible; (4) Interpretation of p-value: p=0.04 means 'if the null hypothesis (no difference) were true, there is a 4% probability of obtaining a result this extreme or more extreme by chance' — it does NOT mean there is a 4% chance the drug works or a 96% chance it works. Practice change should await adequately powered trials with consistent results.
explanation.A: Incorrect — Statistical significance alone (especially in a small study with wide CI) is insufficient to justify immediate adoption into practice.
explanation.B: CORRECT — Statistically significant but wide CI from small sample; lower bound may be below MCID; needs larger replication trial before practice change.
explanation.C: Incorrect — p=0.04 means 4% probability of the observed result under the null hypothesis — NOT that the drug has a 4% probability of working.
explanation.D: Incorrect — Standard deviation describes within-group variability around the mean — it does not by itself determine statistical significance.
explanation.E: Incorrect — 95% CI means 95% probability that the interval contains the true population mean difference — NOT that the drug works in 95% of patients.

reference: BMJ Statistics Notes — Confidence intervals. https://www.bmj.com/about-bmj/resources-readers/publications/statistics-square-one

question: A GP is calculating statistics from a screening test for coeliac disease. In a population of 1,000: 100 truly have coeliac disease, 900 do not. The test correctly identifies 90 of the 100 with coeliac disease. The test incorrectly identifies 45 of the 900 without coeliac disease as positive. Per EBM, calculate the positive predictive value (PPV) and negative predictive value (NPV).

options.A: PPV = 90%, NPV = 95% — sensitivity and PPV are the same statistic
options.B: PPV = 67% (90 true positives ÷ 135 total positives × 100); NPV = 98.8% (855 true negatives ÷ 865 total negatives × 100) — PPV and NPV depend on disease prevalence in the tested population, unlike sensitivity and specificity
options.C: PPV = 90%, NPV = 90% — both equal sensitivity
options.D: PPV cannot be calculated without knowing the specificity
options.E: PPV = 45%, NPV = 45% — based on the false positive rate

explanation.correct: From the data: TP=90 (true positives), FN=10 (missed cases), FP=45 (false positives), TN=855 (true negatives). Totals: Test positive = TP+FP = 90+45 = 135; Test negative = TN+FN = 855+10 = 865. PPV = TP/(TP+FP) = 90/135 = 66.7% ≈ 67%. This means: of all positive tests, 67% are true positives (33% are false positives). NPV = TN/(TN+FN) = 855/865 = 98.8%. This means: of all negative tests, 98.8% are true negatives (1.2% are false negatives — missed cases). Sensitivity = TP/(TP+FN) = 90/100 = 90% (ability to detect true cases). Specificity = TN/(TN+FP) = 855/900 = 95% (ability to correctly exclude non-cases). KEY POINT: PPV and NPV depend on disease prevalence — the same test will have lower PPV in a low-prevalence population and higher PPV in a high-prevalence population. Sensitivity and specificity are inherent test characteristics that do not change with prevalence.
explanation.A: Incorrect — Sensitivity (90%) and PPV (67%) are different statistics. Sensitivity measures the test's ability to detect disease; PPV measures the probability that a positive test result is truly positive.
explanation.B: CORRECT — PPV = 90/135 = 67%; NPV = 855/865 = 98.8%. PPV and NPV are prevalence-dependent.
explanation.C: Incorrect — PPV and NPV are calculated from different 2×2 table denominators and will not equal each other or sensitivity unless under very specific mathematical conditions.
explanation.D: Incorrect — PPV can be calculated directly from the 2×2 table data given without needing to calculate specificity separately.
explanation.E: Incorrect — False positive rate (1-specificity) = 45/900 = 5% — not used to calculate PPV or NPV.

reference: BMJ Statistics Notes — Sensitivity, specificity, PPV, NPV. https://www.bmj.com/about-bmj/resources-readers/publications/statistics-square-one

question: A GP reads a cohort study: among 500 smokers, 50 developed lung cancer over 10 years. Among 1,000 non-smokers, 10 developed lung cancer. Per EBM, calculate the relative risk (RR) and absolute risk increase (ARI) for smokers versus non-smokers.

options.A: RR = 5, ARI = 5% — smoking increases relative risk fivefold and absolute risk by 5%
options.B: RR = 10, ARI = 9% — smokers have 10x the relative risk; the absolute risk increases from 1% (non-smokers) to 10% (smokers), an absolute difference of 9%; NNH = 100/9 = 11 (11 smokers would need to smoke for one additional case of lung cancer compared to non-smokers)
options.C: RR = 2, ARI = 2% — relative risk is doubled
options.D: RR = 0.5, ARI = -5% — non-smokers have lower risk so RR <1
options.E: ARI and RR cannot be calculated from cohort data — only from RCTs

explanation.correct: Calculations: Risk in smokers (exposed) = 50/500 = 0.10 = 10%. Risk in non-smokers (unexposed) = 10/1000 = 0.01 = 1%. Relative Risk (RR) = Risk(exposed) ÷ Risk(unexposed) = 10% ÷ 1% = 10. Interpretation: Smokers have 10 times the risk of lung cancer compared to non-smokers. Absolute Risk Increase (ARI) = Risk(exposed) - Risk(unexposed) = 10% - 1% = 9%. Interpretation: smoking causes 9 additional cases per 100 smokers over 10 years compared to non-smokers. Number Needed to Harm (NNH) = 1/ARI = 1/0.09 = 11. Key teaching point: RR gives the relative scale of risk (impressive-sounding: 10x) while ARI gives the absolute scale (practical: 9% absolute difference); both are essential to present for informed patient decision-making. RR alone without ARI can mislead — a RR of 10 is very different from a baseline risk of 0.0001% vs 0.001% compared to 1% vs 10%.
explanation.A: Incorrect — RR = 10% ÷ 1% = 10, not 5. ARI = 10% - 1% = 9%, not 5%.
explanation.B: CORRECT — RR = 10 (10-fold increase); ARI = 9% (9 additional cases per 100); NNH = 11 per EBM calculation.
explanation.C: Incorrect — RR = 2 would mean risk doubles (e.g. 2% vs 1%). Here risk is 10x higher (10% vs 1%).
explanation.D: Incorrect — RR is calculated as exposed ÷ unexposed. Smokers have higher risk → RR >1.
explanation.E: Incorrect — Relative risk and absolute risk increase can be calculated from cohort studies (and RCTs). Odds ratios are used in case-control studies.

reference: BMJ Statistics Notes — Risk ratios and absolute risk. https://www.bmj.com/about-bmj/resources-readers/publications/statistics-square-one

question: A 28-year-old woman is investigated for iron deficiency anaemia with no obvious cause. Anti-tissue transglutaminase IgA antibodies (anti-tTG IgA) are strongly positive (×10 upper limit of normal). Her total IgA is normal. Per NICE NG20, what is the next step to confirm the diagnosis?

options.A: Start a gluten-free diet immediately — anti-tTG positivity confirms coeliac disease
options.B: Refer for gastroscopy with duodenal biopsy — duodenal biopsy (minimum 4 samples including 1 from the duodenal bulb) is the gold standard for confirming coeliac disease; biopsy shows villous atrophy, crypt hyperplasia and intraepithelial lymphocytosis (Marsh classification); the patient must continue a GLUTEN-CONTAINING diet until after biopsy
options.C: Repeat anti-tTG in 3 months — one positive result is insufficient
options.D: HLA-DQ2/DQ8 genetic testing is needed before biopsy
options.E: Capsule endoscopy is the investigation of choice for coeliac disease confirmation

explanation.correct: Per NICE NG20 (Coeliac disease): serology (anti-tTG IgA or anti-endomysial antibodies IgA) is the first-line screening test. A strongly positive anti-tTG (>10× ULN) has a high positive predictive value for coeliac disease but a BIOPSY is still required to confirm the diagnosis in adults (exceptions: adults with strongly positive anti-tTG >10×ULN may be eligible for a non-biopsy diagnosis pathway in some centres if supported by positive HLA-DQ2/DQ8 and symptoms — per updated BSG guidelines). Gastroscopy with duodenal biopsy: minimum 4 biopsies (2 from D1-D2, 1 from duodenal bulb) while on a GLUTEN-CONTAINING diet — if patient has already started GFD, the biopsy will be falsely normal; Marsh grading: Marsh 1 (lymphocytosis only), Marsh 2 (crypt hyperplasia), Marsh 3 (villous atrophy — graded A/B/C). Diagnosis confirmed: histology + serology + clinical response to GFD.
explanation.A: Incorrect — Starting a GFD before biopsy will cause villous healing and false-negative biopsy. Never start GFD until biopsy is complete per NICE NG20.
explanation.B: CORRECT — Gastroscopy + duodenal biopsy on gluten-containing diet is the gold standard to confirm coeliac disease per NICE NG20.
explanation.C: Incorrect — A strongly positive anti-tTG (×10 ULN) is a clear positive result; repeating serology delays diagnosis. Biopsy is the next step.
explanation.D: Incorrect — HLA-DQ2/DQ8 testing is used to exclude coeliac disease in ambiguous cases (>99% of coeliac patients are HLA-DQ2 or DQ8 positive); it is not routinely required before biopsy.
explanation.E: Incorrect — Capsule endoscopy is used for refractory coeliac disease or suspected complications — not routine first-line confirmation.

reference: NICE NG20 — Coeliac disease. https://www.nice.org.uk/guidance/ng20

question: A 45-year-old woman with confirmed coeliac disease on strict GFD continues to have persistent diarrhoea and weight loss despite 18 months of treatment. A follow-up duodenal biopsy shows persistent villous atrophy (Marsh 3b). She has been adherent to GFD on dietitian assessment. Per BSG guidelines, what is the next step?

options.A: Continue GFD for another 12 months before investigating
options.B: Refer to gastroenterology specialist — persistent villous atrophy despite strict GFD warrants investigation for: refractory coeliac disease (Type I or Type II — clonal T-cell population; type II has 30-50% risk of enteropathy-associated T-cell lymphoma/EATL); collagenous coeliac disease; other causes of villous atrophy (common variable immunodeficiency — CVID, tropical sprue); inadvertent gluten exposure (dietary review); investigation: repeated duodenal biopsy, immunohistochemistry for aberrant T-cell phenotype (CD3+CD8-), CT abdomen for lymphoma
options.C: Start prednisolone immediately — all persistent villous atrophy is autoimmune and responds to steroids
options.D: Colonoscopy only — colon is the affected organ
options.E: Discharge — Marsh 3b is a normal finding in adults on GFD

explanation.correct: Refractory coeliac disease (RCD): persistent or recurrent villous atrophy (Marsh 3) with symptoms despite strict adherence to GFD for ≥12 months, after exclusion of other causes. Type I RCD: normal T-cell phenotype; treated with elemental diet, budesonide, azathioprine. Type II RCD: clonal/aberrant intraepithelial T-lymphocytes (CD3+/CD8-/cytoplasmic CD3+); carries 30-50% risk of EATL (enteropathy-associated T-cell lymphoma); requires oncology involvement; chemotherapy (CHOP regimen) or autologous stem cell transplant. Differential diagnosis for persistent villous atrophy on GFD: inadvertent gluten exposure (most common — check labels, cross-contamination); refractory coeliac disease; collagenous coeliac disease; CVID (common variable immunodeficiency — causes enteropathy); autoimmune enteropathy; tropical sprue; HIV enteropathy. Investigation: flow cytometry on biopsy for T-cell phenotype; CT scan (lymphadenopathy for lymphoma); capsule endoscopy (assess extent); immunoglobulin levels (CVID).
explanation.A: Incorrect — 18 months of strict GFD with persistent Marsh 3b is beyond the expected healing time; further investigation for refractory coeliac disease or alternative diagnoses is required.
explanation.B: CORRECT — Persistent villous atrophy >12 months despite strict GFD: refer to gastroenterology; investigate for RCD types I/II and lymphoma (EATL) per BSG guidelines.
explanation.C: Incorrect — Steroids are used for some forms of RCD (budesonide for Type I) but starting prednisolone without confirming the diagnosis and excluding EATL first is inappropriate.
explanation.D: Incorrect — The pathology is in the small bowel (duodenum/jejunum); colonoscopy alone would miss the relevant pathology.
explanation.E: Incorrect — Marsh 3b (moderate villous atrophy) should have resolved on strict GFD; persistent Marsh 3b is not a normal finding and requires investigation.

reference: BSG Coeliac disease guidelines. https://www.bsg.org.uk/clinical-resources/guidelines/

question: A 34-year-old woman with confirmed coeliac disease has been on a strict gluten-free diet for 18 months. Her anti-tTG antibodies have normalised. She asks her GP when she should have a repeat duodenal biopsy to confirm mucosal healing. Per NICE NG20 and BSG guidelines, what is the recommendation?

options.A: No follow-up biopsy is ever needed once anti-tTG normalises
options.B: A follow-up duodenal biopsy after 12-24 months of strict gluten-free diet is recommended to confirm mucosal healing (villous architecture restored); persistent villous atrophy despite dietary compliance may indicate refractory coeliac disease or inadvertent gluten exposure; anti-tTG normalisation alone does not reliably confirm complete mucosal healing in all patients
options.C: Biopsy should be repeated every 5 years indefinitely
options.D: Biopsy should be performed immediately after starting the GFD (at 3 months)
options.E: Follow-up biopsy is only needed if anti-tTG remains positive at 12 months

explanation.correct: Per NICE NG20 and BSG coeliac guidelines: a follow-up duodenal biopsy after 12-24 months of strict gluten-free diet is recommended in most adults to confirm mucosal healing. Why: anti-tTG antibody normalisation is a good marker of dietary compliance and improving disease but does not perfectly correlate with mucosal healing — studies show up to 30-40% of adults with normalised serology still have persistent villous atrophy on biopsy. Identifying persistent atrophy is important: it may indicate refractory coeliac disease (rare but associated with enteropathy-associated T-cell lymphoma risk), ongoing inadvertent gluten exposure, or alternative diagnoses (microscopic colitis, CVID). Response biopsy: same minimum 4 samples from duodenum. However: BSG 2023 update acknowledges that in patients who are asymptomatic with strongly normalised serology, the follow-up biopsy pathway is evolving and not universally mandatory — discuss with individual patients and gastroenterology.
explanation.A: Incorrect — Anti-tTG normalisation does not guarantee complete mucosal healing; follow-up biopsy is recommended per NICE NG20.
explanation.B: CORRECT — Follow-up biopsy at 12-24 months of GFD confirms mucosal healing; normalised anti-tTG does not reliably confirm complete villous healing per NICE NG20/BSG.
explanation.C: Incorrect — 5-yearly biopsy is not the recommended routine follow-up schedule; biopsy at 12-24 months to confirm healing is the key checkpoint.
explanation.D: Incorrect — Mucosal healing takes 12-24 months on a strict GFD; a biopsy at 3 months would show incomplete healing and be unhelpful.
explanation.E: Incorrect — Follow-up biopsy is recommended even when anti-tTG has normalised, as mucosal healing cannot be assumed from serology alone.

reference: NICE NG20 — Coeliac disease. BSG coeliac guidelines. https://www.nice.org.uk/guidance/ng20

question: A 14-year-old girl is investigated for iron deficiency anaemia. Anti-tTG IgA is positive at ×4 ULN. Her total IgA is low (IgA deficiency — 0.05 g/L). Per NICE NG20, how does IgA deficiency affect the interpretation and what alternative test should be used?

options.A: IgA deficiency does not affect coeliac serology — proceed to biopsy
options.B: IgA deficiency (IgA <0.07 g/L) causes false-negative anti-tTG IgA and anti-EMA IgA results — IgA-based coeliac tests are unreliable; per NICE NG20: use IgG-based tests instead: anti-tTG IgG and/or anti-deamidated gliadin peptide IgG (DGP IgG); if IgG serology is positive — refer for duodenal biopsy as per standard pathway
options.C: IgA deficiency means coeliac disease can be excluded — IgA is needed for intestinal immunity
options.D: Repeat anti-tTG IgA in 3 months — IgA levels normalise with time
options.E: HLA typing only — serology is unreliable in all children

explanation.correct: IgA deficiency: selective IgA deficiency (sIgAD) is the most common primary immunodeficiency (~1 in 600 of the general population); defined as IgA <0.07 g/L with normal IgG and IgM. Crucially: sIgAD is 10-15 times more common in coeliac disease than in the general population. IgA-based coeliac tests: anti-tTG IgA, anti-endomysial antibody IgA — ALL are IgA-based and will be falsely negative or unreliable in IgA deficiency. Per NICE NG20: total IgA MUST be measured at the time of coeliac serological screening; if IgA deficiency confirmed: use IgG-based tests: anti-tTG IgG (most widely used) and anti-deamidated gliadin peptide IgG (DGP IgG); if IgG-based tests are positive → proceed to duodenal biopsy for confirmation. Note: In this case, the anti-tTG IgA was positive despite IgA deficiency — this may mean the result is valid (partial IgA), but the low total IgA level means the result must be interpreted with caution and IgG-based tests should be added.
explanation.A: Incorrect — IgA deficiency directly affects IgA-based coeliac serology — false negatives are common; IgG-based testing is required.
explanation.B: CORRECT — IgA deficiency invalidates IgA-based tests; use anti-tTG IgG and DGP IgG per NICE NG20.
explanation.C: Incorrect — IgA deficiency is associated with INCREASED prevalence of coeliac disease — it does not exclude it.
explanation.D: Incorrect — IgA deficiency is a permanent primary immunodeficiency (in most cases); it does not normalise over time.
explanation.E: Incorrect — HLA-DQ2/DQ8 typing is used to exclude coeliac disease (high negative predictive value if both negative) — but IgG-based serology is the appropriate next step, not HLA typing.

reference: NICE NG20 — Coeliac disease. https://www.nice.org.uk/guidance/ng20

question: A GP is shown a box and whisker plot of blood pressure measurements from a clinical trial. The box contains a horizontal line in the middle. The box extends from the 25th to 75th percentile. Per EBM and statistical principles, what does the horizontal line in the middle of the box represent?

options.A: The mean blood pressure
options.B: The median (50th percentile) — the middle horizontal line in a box and whisker plot always represents the median; the box spans the interquartile range (IQR = 25th to 75th percentile); the whiskers extend to the minimum and maximum values (excluding outliers which are shown as individual dots beyond the whiskers)
options.C: The mode — the most frequently occurring value
options.D: The 95th percentile — the upper confidence interval
options.E: The standard deviation of the distribution

explanation.correct: Box and whisker plot anatomy: the horizontal line inside the box = the MEDIAN (50th percentile) — this is the middle value when all observations are ranked from lowest to highest. The box boundaries: lower edge = 25th percentile (Q1); upper edge = 75th percentile (Q3). Box height = IQR (interquartile range = Q3-Q1) — measures the spread of the middle 50% of data. Whiskers: extend to the lowest and highest values within 1.5×IQR from the box edges; data points beyond whiskers = outliers (plotted individually). Mean vs Median in box plots: box plots show the MEDIAN, not the mean; in skewed distributions the mean and median differ; box plots are preferred over histograms for showing distribution skewness and comparing multiple groups. AKT application: the examiner will show a box plot and ask you to identify the median, IQR, or identify an outlier — always remember the middle line = median, NOT mean.
explanation.A: Incorrect — The mean is not shown directly on a standard box and whisker plot. The middle horizontal line is the MEDIAN.
explanation.B: CORRECT — Middle line = median (50th percentile). Box = IQR (25th-75th percentile). Whiskers = range excluding outliers.
explanation.C: Incorrect — Mode (most common value) is not represented on a standard box and whisker plot.
explanation.D: Incorrect — The 95th percentile is not shown by the middle line of the box. The whisker endpoint may approximate the 5th-95th percentile range but is technically based on 1.5×IQR rule.
explanation.E: Incorrect — Standard deviation is not depicted in a box and whisker plot; it is used in normally distributed data. Box plots are preferred for non-normally distributed data.

reference: BMJ Statistics Notes — Box and whisker plots. https://www.bmj.com/about-bmj/resources-readers/publications/statistics-square-one

question: A clinical trial reports: mean SBP reduction with drug A = 12 mmHg (SD 8, n=100); mean SBP reduction with drug B = 9 mmHg (SD 7, n=100). The difference is 3 mmHg. Per EBM statistical principles, which statistical test is most appropriate to compare these two means?

options.A: Chi-squared test — compares proportions in two groups
options.B: Independent samples t-test — comparing two means from independent groups with continuous, approximately normally distributed data; appropriate here as: two independent groups (drug A vs drug B), continuous outcome (SBP in mmHg), sample size ≥30 (n=100 each — central limit theorem applies), similar standard deviations; result gives a t-statistic and p-value indicating whether the 3 mmHg difference is statistically significant
options.C: Mann-Whitney U test — always preferred over t-test for any clinical data
options.D: Paired t-test — used when the same patients are measured twice
options.E: ANOVA — required whenever comparing more than two data points

explanation.correct: Statistical test selection: (1) Type of outcome variable: continuous (SBP in mmHg) → parametric tests if normally distributed. (2) Number of groups: two groups (A vs B). (3) Independence: separate patients in each group → unpaired/independent test. (4) Distribution: n=100 → central limit theorem ensures approximate normality → parametric test appropriate. Independent samples t-test (Student's t-test): compares two independent group means; appropriate for continuous, approximately normally distributed data with independent groups. Produces: t-statistic, degrees of freedom, p-value, 95% CI for the mean difference. Alternative if non-normally distributed or small samples: Mann-Whitney U test (non-parametric equivalent). Chi-squared: for comparing proportions/categorical data (e.g. % of patients reaching target BP <130/80). Paired t-test: same patients measured before and after. ANOVA: 3 or more independent groups.
explanation.A: Incorrect — Chi-squared compares proportions/categorical outcomes (e.g. % patients reaching a threshold). SBP reduction is continuous — chi-squared is not appropriate.
explanation.B: CORRECT — Independent samples t-test: two independent groups, continuous outcome, large samples (n=100 — normal distribution assumed). Appropriate test for comparing two means.
explanation.C: Incorrect — Mann-Whitney U (non-parametric) is used when data is not normally distributed or samples are small. With n=100, the independent t-test is appropriate and more powerful.
explanation.D: Incorrect — Paired t-test is for paired/dependent data (e.g. same patient measured before and after treatment). These are two different patient groups — unpaired.
explanation.E: Incorrect — ANOVA is used when comparing means across 3 or more groups. Only two groups here.

reference: BMJ Statistics Notes — Statistical tests for comparing means. https://www.bmj.com/about-bmj/resources-readers/publications/statistics-square-one

question: A GP is reviewing a newly prescribed drug for a patient. The Patient Information Leaflet (PIL) shows a black inverted triangle symbol (▼) next to the drug name. Per MHRA guidance, what does this symbol indicate?

options.A: The drug is a controlled drug — special prescription requirements apply
options.B: The black triangle (▼) indicates that the medicine is subject to ADDITIONAL MONITORING by the MHRA; this usually applies to new medicines or those approved under exceptional circumstances where the evidence base is still being established; healthcare professionals and patients are strongly encouraged to report ALL suspected adverse reactions via the Yellow Card scheme (not just serious ones as for established drugs); the symbol appears in PILs and SPCs
options.C: The drug should not be used in patients under 18 — paediatric contraindication
options.D: The drug requires specialist initiation only — GPs cannot prescribe it
options.E: The drug has been withdrawn from the market but stocks are still being used

explanation.correct: Per MHRA (Medicines and Healthcare products Regulatory Agency): the black inverted triangle symbol (▼) on a medicine's PIL/SMP indicates it is subject to additional monitoring. Applies to: newly authorised medicines (less post-market safety data); medicines approved under exceptional circumstances; biosimilar medicines (to detect any differences from the reference biologic). Purpose: to facilitate rapid identification of new safety signals. Reporting: healthcare professionals and patients should report ALL suspected adverse reactions (not just serious ones) via the MHRA Yellow Card scheme (yellowcard.mhra.gov.uk or via the Yellow Card app). The symbol is used across the EU/UK since 2013. Medicines retain the ▼ symbol until sufficient post-market safety data has accumulated (typically 5 years). This is distinct from: CD (controlled drug) scheduling, which has different legal requirements; specialist-only prescribing restrictions (NICE/NHS England criteria).
explanation.A: Incorrect — Controlled drug status is indicated by 'CD' on the prescription and has specific legal requirements (schedule) — not the black triangle symbol.
explanation.B: CORRECT — Black triangle (▼) = additional monitoring; report ALL suspected ADRs via Yellow Card scheme per MHRA guidance.
explanation.C: Incorrect — Paediatric contraindications are stated in the prescribing information and PIL text, not indicated by the black triangle symbol.
explanation.D: Incorrect — Specialist-only prescribing is indicated in NHS England/NICE guidance or SLS endorsements — not the black triangle.
explanation.E: Incorrect — Withdrawn medicines are not in circulation; the black triangle applies to newly licensed medicines requiring additional surveillance.

reference: MHRA — Black triangle scheme. https://www.gov.uk/guidance/the-black-triangle-scheme
