question: A GP identifies that a patient developed a serious adverse drug reaction (sudden onset hearing loss) from gentamicin prescribed in hospital. Per MHRA Yellow Card guidance, who can report this and what constitutes a reportable reaction?

options.A: Only hospital doctors can report reactions to drugs first prescribed in hospital
options.B: Any healthcare professional (GP, nurse, pharmacist) AND patients/carers can report suspected adverse drug reactions via the Yellow Card scheme; for established medicines: report serious, unexpected or unlisted reactions; for black triangle medicines: report ALL suspected reactions regardless of severity; for vaccines: report all suspected adverse reactions
options.C: Only serious reactions (ICU admission or death) qualify for Yellow Card reporting
options.D: The Yellow Card scheme is voluntary and rarely checked by the MHRA
options.E: Yellow Cards can only be submitted by the prescribing doctor

explanation.correct: Per MHRA Yellow Card scheme guidance: Who can report: any healthcare professional (doctor, dentist, nurse, pharmacist, coroner, etc.) AND patients, carers and members of the public. What to report: established medicines: suspected serious reactions (fatal, life-threatening, requiring hospitalisation, causing disability, congenital abnormality, or medically significant); any reaction considered unexpected or unlisted in the product information; black triangle medicines (▼): ALL suspected adverse reactions regardless of severity (even mild reactions); vaccines: ALL suspected adverse reactions; herbal and complementary products: ALL suspected reactions. Purpose: pharmacovigilance — detecting new safety signals, revising prescribing information, withdrawal of harmful medicines when necessary (e.g. withdrawal of vioxx, thalidomide history). Yellow Cards are taken seriously — they have directly contributed to regulatory action. GP's role: reporting from primary care is particularly valuable as it captures long-term and community adverse effects not seen in clinical trials.
explanation.A: Incorrect — Any healthcare professional or patient can report reactions via Yellow Card regardless of where the drug was originally prescribed.
explanation.B: CORRECT — Any HCP or patient can report; for established drugs: serious/unexpected reactions; for black triangle drugs: ALL reactions per MHRA Yellow Card guidance.
explanation.C: Incorrect — Serious reactions (ICU/death) are always reportable, but the threshold for reporting is broader and includes unexpected reactions and all reactions to black triangle drugs.
explanation.D: Incorrect — The Yellow Card scheme is actively monitored by the MHRA — it is a key pharmacovigilance tool that has led to regulatory action on multiple medicines.
explanation.E: Incorrect — The Yellow Card scheme is open to all healthcare professionals and patients, not restricted to the prescriber.

reference: MHRA — Yellow Card scheme. https://yellowcard.mhra.gov.uk/

question: A patient with confirmed cranial diabetes insipidus is prescribed desmopressin. The GP is deciding between oral desmopressin and intranasal desmopressin. During the water deprivation test, the endocrinologist administered desmopressin 2 mcg IM at t=8 hours. Per BNF and clinical pharmacology, what is the key difference in bioavailability between routes and why does it matter for dosing?

options.A: All routes are bioequivalent — dose is the same regardless of route
options.B: There is a large difference in bioavailability between routes: intranasal ~3-4% (higher than oral but lower than parenteral); oral tablets ~0.1-0.2%; parenteral/IM/IV ~100%; the oral dose is therefore much higher than the intranasal or parenteral dose for equivalent effect; for example: oral 120-240 mcg BD is roughly equivalent to intranasal 10-20 mcg BD; patients must never switch routes without dose adjustment as underdosing (DI recurrence) or overdosing (hyponatraemia) can result
options.C: Intranasal desmopressin has the same bioavailability as oral
options.D: Parenteral desmopressin cannot be used for DI — only for haemophilia
options.E: Dose adjustment between routes is not clinically significant for desmopressin

explanation.correct: Desmopressin bioavailability by route (per BNF and pharmacology): IV/IM (parenteral): ~100% bioavailability — used for acute testing (water deprivation test) and haemophilia/vWD (2-4 mcg IV/IM). Intranasal spray/drops: approximately 3-4% bioavailability — used for DI maintenance; dose: 10-40 mcg/day in 1-2 doses. Oral tablets: approximately 0.1-0.2% bioavailability — used for DI, nocturia, primary nocturnal enuresis; dose: 100-400 mcg 2-3 times daily. Sublingual (melt): slightly higher than oral tablets (~0.2-0.3%). The markedly lower oral bioavailability means the oral dose must be 50-100× higher than the intranasal dose for equivalent effect. Clinical significance: switching between routes without dose adjustment is DANGEROUS — can cause: under-treatment (recurrence of DI, hypernatraemia) or over-treatment (dilutional hyponatraemia from over-replacement). Always consult BNF/endocrinologist when switching routes.
explanation.A: Incorrect — Routes are NOT bioequivalent; there are large differences requiring substantial dose adjustments.
explanation.B: CORRECT — Oral bioavailability ~0.1-0.2% vs intranasal ~3-4% vs parenteral ~100%. Route switching requires dose adjustment; failure risks DI recurrence or hyponatraemia per BNF.
explanation.C: Incorrect — Intranasal desmopressin has approximately 20-40× higher bioavailability than oral tablets.
explanation.D: Incorrect — Parenteral desmopressin IS used for acute DI testing (water deprivation test) and for haemophilia A/vWD; both are licensed indications.
explanation.E: Incorrect — The difference in bioavailability is clinically critical — failure to adjust doses between routes has caused serious patient harm (hyponatraemia, seizures).

reference: BNF — Desmopressin. https://bnf.nice.org.uk/drug/desmopressin.html

question: A 19-year-old student presents with secondary enuresis (bed-wetting) for the past 3 months having previously been dry for years. He has no daytime symptoms. He is drinking 4-5 litres of water per day. Per NICE CKS, what differential diagnoses should be considered and what initial investigations should be requested?

options.A: This is normal behaviour in a stressed student — reassure without investigation
options.B: Secondary enuresis in a previously dry adult is a red flag — differentials include: cranial diabetes insipidus (polyuria from ADH deficiency), nephrogenic DI, diabetes mellitus (osmotic diuresis), psychogenic polydipsia, UTI; initial investigations: urine dipstick (glucose, protein, blood), fasting glucose/HbA1c, U&E, serum osmolality, urine osmolality (morning sample), TFTs
options.C: UTI only — urine culture and oral trimethoprim
options.D: Bladder overactivity — refer for urodynamics
options.E: Anxiety disorder — CBT referral

explanation.correct: Secondary enuresis (onset after a period of dryness) in an adult is always a red flag for an underlying pathology — unlike primary enuresis (never been dry). The history of polydipsia (4-5 litres/day) suggests a polyuric disorder. Per NICE CKS: differential diagnoses for adult secondary enuresis + polydipsia: Diabetes mellitus: osmotic diuresis from hyperglycaemia — most common cause; Cranial DI: ADH deficiency causing inability to concentrate urine; Nephrogenic DI: renal resistance to ADH; Psychogenic polydipsia: primary polydipsia without organic cause (psychiatric patients); UTI/LUTS: less likely with daytime dryness. First-line investigations: urine dipstick (glycosuria suggests DM; haematuria/proteinuria); random glucose or HbA1c; U&E (hypokalaemia in Conn's, hypernatraemia in DI); serum and urine osmolality (paired samples for DI assessment); TFTs (hyperthyroidism can cause polyuria). If DM excluded and DI suspected: water deprivation test.
explanation.A: Incorrect — Secondary enuresis in an adult with polydipsia requires investigation for underlying pathology including diabetes mellitus and DI — this cannot be dismissed.
explanation.B: CORRECT — Secondary enuresis + polydipsia: red flag; investigate DM (most common), DI, electrolytes, urine/serum osmolality per NICE CKS.
explanation.C: Incorrect — UTI would cause dysuria and daytime frequency — this patient has secondary enuresis with polydipsia suggesting a systemic polyuric disorder.
explanation.D: Incorrect — Bladder overactivity causes frequency, urgency and nocturia with normal fluid intake — not 4-5 litres/day polydipsia.
explanation.E: Incorrect — Anxiety may cause increased fluid intake but the degree of polydipsia (4-5 litres/day) and secondary enuresis requires organic exclusion before attributing to anxiety.

reference: NICE CKS — Enuresis in adults. Diabetes insipidus. https://cks.nice.org.uk/topics/diabetes-insipidus/

question: A GP practice wants to use patient data from the clinical system for a quality improvement audit examining antibiotic prescribing rates. The data will be anonymised. Per the Data Protection Act 2018, UK GDPR and NHS guidance, does this require individual patient consent?

options.A: Yes — written consent from every patient is always required for any use of their data
options.B: No — clinical audit for quality improvement purposes is classified as a legitimate use of patient data within the health and social care exemption under UK GDPR; provided data is appropriately anonymised (not pseudonymised — true anonymisation removes all identifiers irreversibly) and used for improving care, individual patient consent is not required; the practice should have a data protection policy and register the processing with the Data Protection Officer
options.C: Patient data can never be used for any purpose without explicit consent
options.D: Only a research ethics committee can approve data use for audit
options.E: Consent is only needed if patients are identifiable in the final report

explanation.correct: Per UK GDPR (Data Protection Act 2018), NHS Digital guidance and GMC Confidentiality guidance: clinical audit: formal activity to improve patient care; DOES NOT require individual patient consent when: data is anonymised (true anonymisation — all identifiers removed irreversibly so patients cannot be re-identified) OR pseudonymised data used under legitimate interest/health and social care provisions; purpose is quality improvement, clinical governance, or directly benefiting patient care; processing is proportionate and follows data minimisation principles. Clinical audit vs research: audit = comparing practice against a standard; research = generating new knowledge. UK GDPR lawful bases for health data (Article 9 special category): Article 9(2)(h) — 'processing is necessary for the purposes of preventive or occupational medicine, medical diagnosis, the provision of health or social care or treatment'; this covers audit. Data Protection Officer: practices must inform their DPO of data processing activities. Important distinction: fully anonymised data falls outside GDPR scope entirely (no identifiers); pseudonymised data (using codes) still falls under GDPR and requires a lawful basis.
explanation.A: Incorrect — Individual consent is not required for properly anonymised clinical audit data used for quality improvement within the health and social care exemption under UK GDPR.
explanation.B: CORRECT — Clinical audit with anonymised data does not require individual patient consent per UK GDPR/DPA 2018/NHS guidance; data minimisation and DPO notification required.
explanation.C: Incorrect — UK GDPR provides multiple lawful bases for processing patient data beyond consent, particularly for health and social care purposes including audit.
explanation.D: Incorrect — Research Ethics Committee (REC) review is required for research projects — not for internal clinical quality improvement audit.
explanation.E: Incorrect — The consent threshold is not simply about identifiability in the final report; it relates to the lawful basis for processing during the data handling stage.

reference: UK GDPR — Data Protection Act 2018. GMC Confidentiality guidance. NHS Digital data governance. https://www.gmc-uk.org/ethical-guidance

question: A practice manager informs the GP that a patient has sent a letter requesting erasure of their medical records ('right to be forgotten') under UK GDPR. The patient is angry about their care. Per the Data Protection Act 2018 and ICO guidance, must the practice comply?

options.A: Yes — the right to erasure is absolute and must always be complied with
options.B: No — the right to erasure (Article 17 UK GDPR) is not absolute; in health settings, retention of medical records is required for legal and statutory purposes; the right to erasure can be refused when: processing is necessary for the performance of a task in the public interest or exercise of official authority; processing is necessary for the establishment, exercise or defence of legal claims (medicolegal purposes); processing is necessary for public health purposes; NHS/BMA guidance recommends retaining GP records for 10 years post-death — legal obligations override the erasure request; the patient should be informed of the refusal and reasons
options.C: Delete the records immediately — GDPR takes precedence over everything
options.D: Refer the matter to NHS England before responding
options.E: Erase only the parts of the record the patient specifically objects to

explanation.correct: Per UK GDPR Article 17 and the Data Protection Act 2018: the right to erasure ('right to be forgotten') is NOT absolute. Exemptions that allow organisations to refuse erasure requests include: (1) Processing necessary for a public interest task or in exercise of official authority; (2) Processing necessary for archiving purposes in the public interest, scientific/historical research, or statistical purposes; (3) Processing necessary for the establishment, exercise or defence of legal claims — this is CRITICAL for medical records (medicolegal litigation, complaints, GMC investigations); (4) Processing for public health purposes in the public interest. Medical records retention: NHS records management code of practice requires GP records to be retained for at least 10 years after last entry (or longer in specific circumstances); these obligations override an erasure request from an individual patient. Process: acknowledge the request within 1 month; explain which exemption applies and why; inform the patient of their right to complain to the ICO if they disagree; document the decision and reasoning.
explanation.A: Incorrect — The right to erasure is NOT absolute; the health/social care and medicolegal exemptions override it for medical records.
explanation.B: CORRECT — Medical record erasure can be refused based on medicolegal, public health and statutory retention obligations; inform patient of refusal and right to complain to ICO per UK GDPR/DPA 2018.
explanation.C: Incorrect — Deleting medical records could destroy evidence for medicolegal defence and violate NHS records management obligations — this would be wrong.
explanation.D: Incorrect — GP practices can and should handle erasure requests themselves per ICO guidance; referral to NHS England is not the standard process.
explanation.E: Incorrect — Selective erasure based on what the patient objects to is not the appropriate response; the legal basis for retention applies to the whole record.

reference: UK GDPR Article 17. Data Protection Act 2018. ICO — Right to erasure. https://ico.org.uk/for-organisations/guide-to-data-protection/

question: A GP trainee raises a concern that their educational supervisor (a consultant) appears to be consistently preventing them from attending their mandatory study days by scheduling clinics at the same time. Per GMC and BMA guidance on workplace bullying and educational supervision, what is the appropriate escalation pathway?

options.A: Accept it — consultants have full authority over trainee schedules
options.B: Raise the concern first informally with the educational supervisor; if unresolved, escalate to the Training Programme Director (TPD)/Head of School; if still unresolved, contact the Foundation Programme Director, responsible officer, or the GMC (if patient safety is affected); document all instances; the BMA is available for support and advice; this constitutes potential bullying and undermining — both GMC-prohibited behaviours
options.C: Report directly to the GMC without speaking to anyone at the practice first
options.D: Submit an FOI request about the consultant's rota decisions
options.E: Take annual leave on the affected days to attend study days

explanation.correct: Per GMC guidance (Raising and Acting on Concerns, Good Medical Practice) and BMA guidance on workplace bullying: deliberately preventing a trainee from attending mandatory educational events constitutes potential undermining behaviour. Escalation pathway: (1) Informal resolution: raise directly with the supervisor (non-confrontational, document the conversation); (2) If unresolved: Training Programme Director (TPD) or Head of School for that specialty; (3) Foundation/Core/Higher Training Programme lead; (4) Responsible Officer at the NHS trust/organisation; (5) GMC if patient safety or training integrity is seriously compromised; (6) BMA for employment/contractual support and advice. Documentation is essential: dates, times, evidence that study days were mandatory. The GMC Good Medical Practice (2024) specifically states doctors must support colleagues' professional development and not undermine them. This AKT question tests knowledge of: (a) the concept of workplace undermining as a GMC concern, (b) the correct escalation hierarchy without bypassing steps unnecessarily.
explanation.A: Incorrect — Systematic prevention of mandatory training is potentially bullying and an educational supervision failure — consultants do not have unchecked authority to prevent mandatory training.
explanation.B: CORRECT — Informal → TPD/Head of School → responsible officer → GMC if needed. Document all instances. BMA for support per GMC/BMA guidance.
explanation.C: Incorrect — Going directly to the GMC without attempting local resolution first is disproportionate for this issue and bypasses the recommended escalation pathway.
explanation.D: Incorrect — FOI requests are not the appropriate tool for individual workplace disputes.
explanation.E: Incorrect — Annual leave should not be used to cover mandatory educational events that the employer/training programme has an obligation to facilitate.

reference: GMC — Good Medical Practice 2024. BMA — Bullying and undermining guidance. https://www.gmc-uk.org/ethical-guidance

question: A 6-month-old infant is brought by her parents. The GP is reviewing for red flag signs warranting immediate paediatric referral. Which combination of features would prompt a same-day emergency referral to paediatrics?

options.A: Normal weight gain, smiling and responsive, mild rash, no fever
options.B: Fever >38°C with bulging fontanelle, high-pitched cry, purpuric rash non-blanching on glass test, reduced conscious level — these are meningococcal septicaemia/meningitis red flags requiring immediate 999 call and IM benzylpenicillin if not allergic before transfer
options.C: Single episode of vomiting after feed, no fever, normal examination
options.D: Mild eczema on the face and scalp, no secondary infection signs
options.E: Reduced appetite for one day in a well infant with no other symptoms

explanation.correct: Per NICE NG51 (Meningitis — bacterial) and NICE NG143 (Sepsis): red flags in a febrile infant requiring immediate emergency response: Non-blanching purpuric rash (does not fade with glass tumbler test) — meningococcal septicaemia until proven otherwise; bulging fontanelle (meningism — raised ICP); high-pitched cry (neurological irritation); reduced conscious level/pallor/mottling; cold extremities with fever (septic shock); poor feeding + drowsiness + no eye contact. Management per NICE NG51: immediate call 999; IM/IV benzylpenicillin 300 mg (1-11 months) if meningococcal disease suspected and no penicillin allergy (do not delay transfer for this — if transfer imminent, give in ambulance); immediate hospital transfer. Per NICE NG51 traffic light system for feverish illness: the non-blanching rash alone mandates urgent admission regardless of how well the child appears.
explanation.A: Incorrect — Normal development, mild rash and no fever with a well infant are reassuring features requiring standard management.
explanation.B: CORRECT — Non-blanching purpuric rash + fever + bulging fontanelle + altered consciousness = meningococcal emergency. 999 + benzylpenicillin per NICE NG51.
explanation.C: Incorrect — A single post-feed vomit in a well infant is very common and does not require emergency referral.
explanation.D: Incorrect — Mild facial/scalp eczema without secondary infection is a routine management issue.
explanation.E: Incorrect — Reduced appetite for one day in a well infant with no concerning features does not require same-day emergency referral.

reference: NICE NG51 — Meningitis (bacterial) and meningococcal septicaemia. https://www.nice.org.uk/guidance/ng51

question: A 6-month-old infant presents with fever of 38.8°C for 12 hours. Using the NICE NG143 traffic light system for feverish illness in children, which feature would place the infant in the RED (high risk) category requiring immediate assessment?

options.A: Temperature 38.8°C in a 6-month-old with normal activity and pink colour
options.B: Pallor, reduced activity, not responding normally to social cues, not smiling, and inconsolable high-pitched cry — these are RED category features indicating HIGH risk of serious illness; the infant should be seen and assessed immediately
options.C: Mild nasal congestion with normal activity and wet nappies
options.D: Temperature 38.2°C with runny nose in a 9-month-old who is smiling
options.E: Reduced appetite but alert, pink and interactive

explanation.correct: Per NICE NG143 traffic light system for feverish illness in children under 5: RED (high risk) features: Colour — pallor, mottled, ashen or blue skin. Activity — no response to social cues, appears ill to the clinician, does not wake when roused OR if awake does not stay awake; weak/high-pitched/continuous cry. Respiratory — grunting, RR >60 (all ages), moderate/severe chest indrawing. Hydration — reduced skin turgor. Other — non-blanching rash, bulging fontanelle, neck stiffness, status epilepticus. AMBER (intermediate risk): 6-month-old with fever >39°C; temperature ≥38°C in 3-6 month old (fever alone in this age); rigors; swollen limb/joint. GREEN (low risk): Normal colour, normal activity, moist mucous membranes, no amber/red features. This infant (6 months, pallor, no response to social cues, high-pitched cry) has multiple RED features.
explanation.A: Incorrect — An isolated fever of 38.8°C with normal colour and activity in a 6-month-old would typically be AMBER (age 3-6 months with fever ≥38°C) — not immediately RED without further concerning features.
explanation.B: CORRECT — Pallor + no social response + high-pitched inconsolable cry = multiple RED features per NICE NG143 traffic light system. Immediate assessment required.
explanation.C: Incorrect — Mild nasal congestion with normal activity, pink colour and wet nappies is GREEN (low risk).
explanation.D: Incorrect — Low-grade fever with coryza and normal activity in a 9-month-old who is smiling is GREEN/low risk.
explanation.E: Incorrect — Reduced appetite alone in an otherwise alert, pink and interactive infant is GREEN (low risk) — watchful waiting appropriate.

reference: NICE NG143 — Fever in under 5s. https://www.nice.org.uk/guidance/ng143

question: A 24-year-old man presents with a 3-month history of progressive dyspnoea, digital clubbing and a productive cough with thick mucous sputum since childhood. Spirometry shows an obstructive pattern with FEV1 45% predicted. A sweat chloride test confirms chloride >60 mmol/L on two occasions. Per NICE NG78, what is the diagnosis and what is the key management principle?

options.A: COPD — start LABA/LAMA and pulmonary rehabilitation
options.B: Cystic fibrosis — autosomal recessive mutation in CFTR gene (most commonly ΔF508 deletion); impaired chloride channel function → thick viscous secretions → recurrent pulmonary infections, bronchiectasis, pancreatic exocrine insufficiency, infertility; management: specialist CF centre, airway clearance physiotherapy, DNase (dornase alfa), CFTR modulators (ivacaftor/lumacaftor/tezacaftor/elexacaftor — NICE approved based on genotype), antibiotics for infections, nutritional support, annual surveillance
options.C: Bronchiectasis from recurrent infections — refer to respiratory for long-term azithromycin
options.D: Primary ciliary dyskinesia — nasal NO measurement and electron microscopy
options.E: Alpha-1 antitrypsin deficiency — check serum A1AT and phenotype

explanation.correct: Cystic fibrosis (CF): autosomal recessive disorder caused by mutations in the CFTR (cystic fibrosis transmembrane conductance regulator) gene on chromosome 7. Most common mutation: ΔF508 (deletion of phenylalanine at position 508). Sweat chloride >60 mmol/L on two occasions = gold standard diagnostic test. Per NICE NG78 (Cystic fibrosis): management principles: CF specialist centre; airway clearance techniques (twice daily physiotherapy); recombinant human DNase (dornase alfa) — reduces sputum viscosity; antibiotic treatment and prophylaxis for pulmonary infections (Pseudomonas aeruginosa, Staphylococcus aureus); CFTR modulators (approved by NICE based on genotype): ivacaftor alone (for G551D and other gating mutations), lumacaftor/ivacaftor (for ΔF508 homozygous), tezacaftor/ivacaftor, elexacaftor/tezacaftor/ivacaftor (Kaftrio — for ΔF508 — transformative triple therapy); pancreatic enzyme replacement (PERT); fat-soluble vitamin supplementation; annual surveillance: PFTs, sputum cultures, CF-related diabetes screening, bone density, fertility counselling.
explanation.A: Incorrect — COPD occurs in older smokers with typical history. Childhood cough, clubbing, sweat chloride >60 and obstructive pattern at age 24 is CF.
explanation.B: CORRECT — CF: sweat chloride >60 mmol/L (×2), obstructive spirometry, childhood symptoms, clubbing. CFTR modulators + specialist centre per NICE NG78.
explanation.C: Incorrect — Bronchiectasis can occur from CF but CF is the primary diagnosis here; long-term azithromycin alone does not address the underlying CFTR defect.
explanation.D: Incorrect — Primary ciliary dyskinesia also causes bronchiectasis and clubbing, but the confirmatory test is nasal NO measurement + ciliary biopsy; sweat chloride >60 confirms CF.
explanation.E: Incorrect — Alpha-1 antitrypsin deficiency causes emphysema (panacinar, lower lobe) in young non-smokers but does not cause thick mucus from childhood or sweat chloride elevation.

reference: NICE NG78 — Cystic fibrosis. https://www.nice.org.uk/guidance/ng78

question: A 19-year-old woman with cystic fibrosis attends for a routine review. Her FEV1 has declined from 75% to 62% predicted over the past year. She is homozygous for the ΔF508 CFTR mutation. Per NICE TA766, what CFTR modulator therapy should be considered?

options.A: Ivacaftor alone — effective for ΔF508 homozygous patients
options.B: Elexacaftor/tezacaftor/ivacaftor (Kaftrio plus ivacaftor — brand name Kaftrio/Kalydeco combination) — the triple modulator therapy approved by NICE TA766 for patients aged ≥6 years with at least one ΔF508 mutation; dramatically improves FEV1, reduces exacerbations and hospitalisations, improves BMI and quality of life; has transformed CF outcomes
options.C: CFTR modulators are only for children — no benefit in adults
options.D: Lumacaftor/ivacaftor (Orkambi) is equally effective as Kaftrio for homozygous ΔF508
options.E: CFTR modulators require gene testing — treat empirically without genotype

explanation.correct: Per NICE TA766 (elexacaftor/tezacaftor/ivacaftor for cystic fibrosis): Kaftrio (elexacaftor/tezacaftor) combined with ivacaftor (Kalydeco) is approved for: patients aged ≥6 years with at least ONE ΔF508 mutation (the most common CF mutation). Mechanism: triple combination targets multiple steps in CFTR processing — elexacaftor + tezacaftor stabilise and facilitate CFTR protein folding and trafficking to the cell surface; ivacaftor potentiates the CFTR channel opening (gating corrector + potentiator). Clinical outcomes from AURORA trial: ~14% absolute improvement in FEV1; ~63% reduction in exacerbations; significant improvement in BMI, CFQ-R respiratory domain and sweat chloride levels. Ivacaftor alone is only effective for GATING mutations (G551D etc.) — NOT for ΔF508 (which is a processing/trafficking mutation, not a gating mutation). Lumacaftor/ivacaftor (Orkambi) is less efficacious than Kaftrio for ΔF508 and has been largely superseded.
explanation.A: Incorrect — Ivacaftor alone is a gating corrector effective ONLY for gating mutations (e.g. G551D). It is NOT effective for ΔF508 (processing mutation) when used alone.
explanation.B: CORRECT — Kaftrio (elexacaftor/tezacaftor/ivacaftor): approved for ≥1 ΔF508 mutation from age 6; ~14% FEV1 improvement per NICE TA766.
explanation.C: Incorrect — CFTR modulators are approved and highly effective in adults with CF — age is not a restriction above age 6.
explanation.D: Incorrect — Lumacaftor/ivacaftor (Orkambi) has modest efficacy for ΔF508 homozygous (~2-4% FEV1 improvement) and has largely been superseded by Kaftrio's superior outcomes.
explanation.E: Incorrect — CFTR modulator prescribing requires confirmation of CFTR genotype to select the correct therapy — empirical use is inappropriate.

reference: NICE TA766 — Elexacaftor/tezacaftor/ivacaftor for cystic fibrosis. https://www.nice.org.uk/guidance/ta766

question: A 32-year-old woman with relapsing-remitting MS attends for review following her second relapse in 12 months. Her previous relapse caused optic neuritis, which fully recovered. This relapse caused cerebellar ataxia that has partially resolved. Per NICE NG220, what disease-modifying therapy (DMT) should be discussed?

options.A: Start oral prednisolone long-term to prevent further relapses
options.B: Discuss disease-modifying therapies with her specialist MS team — first-line DMTs include: beta-interferon (Avonex, Rebif, Betaferon), glatiramer acetate, dimethyl fumarate (Tecfidera), teriflunomide; higher efficacy DMTs: natalizumab (for rapidly evolving severe RRMS), alemtuzumab, ocrelizumab, cladribine; NICE NG220 recommends early DMT initiation to reduce relapse rate and delay disability progression
options.C: DMTs are not recommended for RRMS — only for primary progressive MS
options.D: Wait for a third relapse before starting DMT — two relapses are insufficient
options.E: Vitamin D supplementation is the only evidence-based intervention for RRMS

explanation.correct: Per NICE NG220 (Multiple sclerosis in adults): DMTs are recommended for active relapsing-remitting MS (RRMS) to reduce relapse frequency and slow disability accumulation. Two relapses in 12 months with new/enlarging MRI lesions = active disease warranting DMT. DMT decision factors: relapse frequency, severity of relapses, MRI disease activity, disability progression, lifestyle, pregnancy plans, side effect profiles. Efficacy tiers: lower-efficacy first-line: beta-interferon 1a/1b, glatiramer acetate (~30% reduction in relapses); moderate efficacy: dimethyl fumarate (~50%), teriflunomide (~31%); high efficacy: natalizumab (~68%), alemtuzumab (~49%), ocrelizumab, cladribine. NICE recommends high-efficacy therapy early for patients with rapidly evolving severe RRMS (2+ relapses in 12 months with significant disability or active MRI) rather than a 'treat-to-target' escalation approach. Relapses are treated with IV/oral methylprednisolone (high-dose, short-course) for functional impairment — not long-term steroids.
explanation.A: Incorrect — Long-term oral steroids are NOT used as DMT for MS — they cause serious side effects without modifying disease course. Short-course high-dose steroids are for acute relapses only.
explanation.B: CORRECT — Two relapses in 12 months = active RRMS requiring DMT discussion. Early initiation per NICE NG220. High-efficacy DMT consideration for active disease.
explanation.C: Incorrect — DMTs are specifically approved and recommended for RRMS. Ocrelizumab is the only DMT with evidence for primary progressive MS.
explanation.D: Incorrect — NICE NG220 recommends offering DMT after two relapses — waiting for a third is not recommended as it allows continued disease activity and disability accumulation.
explanation.E: Incorrect — Vitamin D supplementation has insufficient evidence to be classified as the only evidence-based intervention; it is discussed as an adjunct but DMTs are the evidence-based standard of care.

reference: NICE NG220 — Multiple sclerosis in adults. https://www.nice.org.uk/guidance/ng220

question: A 28-year-old man with multiple sclerosis is seen for his annual review. He asks which investigation is most useful to monitor his MS disease activity and guide treatment decisions. Per NICE NG220, what is the most important monitoring investigation?

options.A: Annual lumbar puncture for oligoclonal bands
options.B: MRI brain and spine with gadolinium — enhancing lesions indicate active inflammation (new/enlarging); T2 lesion load tracks disease burden; used to detect subclinical disease activity, monitor treatment response, and guide decisions on DMT escalation; VEPs (visual evoked potentials) and neuropsychological testing are additional tools
options.C: Annual PET scan of the brain
options.D: Serum neurofilament light chain (NfL) only — MRI is no longer required
options.E: Annual CSF examination is the gold standard for monitoring MS activity

explanation.correct: Per NICE NG220 (Multiple sclerosis in adults): MRI brain (and spine where clinically relevant) with and without gadolinium is the key imaging modality for monitoring MS. MRI findings: T2 hyperintense lesions: established demyelinating plaques; T1 enhancing lesions (after gadolinium): active inflammation/blood-brain barrier breakdown — indicates current disease activity; T1 black holes: areas of irreversible axonal loss. MRI monitoring: used to: detect subclinical disease activity (new lesions despite clinical stability); assess treatment response (if no new T2 lesions + no relapses = 'no evidence of disease activity' — NEDA); guide escalation from lower to higher-efficacy DMT; detect serious DMT complications (e.g. PML — progressive multifocal leukoencephalopathy — on natalizumab). Serum NfL: emerging biomarker for neuroaxonal damage — increasing evidence for monitoring but not yet NICE standard for routine monitoring. Lumbar puncture: diagnostic (oligoclonal bands) — not routine monitoring.
explanation.A: Incorrect — Lumbar puncture with CSF oligoclonal bands is a diagnostic tool for MS but is not used for routine disease monitoring.
explanation.B: CORRECT — MRI with gadolinium is the principal investigation for monitoring MS activity and treatment response per NICE NG220.
explanation.C: Incorrect — PET scanning is a research tool for MS — not part of routine clinical monitoring.
explanation.D: Incorrect — Serum NfL is an emerging biomarker but MRI remains the gold standard for monitoring; NfL does not replace MRI.
explanation.E: Incorrect — Annual lumbar puncture is not the monitoring standard — MRI is the key monitoring investigation.

reference: NICE NG220 — Multiple sclerosis. https://www.nice.org.uk/guidance/ng220

question: A 72-year-old man presents with a 3-month history of progressive painless obstructive jaundice, weight loss of 6 kg, and a palpable non-tender gallbladder (Courvoisier's sign). Per NICE NG12, what is the most likely diagnosis and immediate management?

options.A: Gallstones causing common bile duct obstruction — ERCP and sphincterotomy
options.B: Carcinoma of the head of the pancreas — Courvoisier's law states that in the presence of jaundice, a palpable non-tender gallbladder is unlikely to be due to gallstones (because gallstones cause a fibrotic, shrunken gallbladder); a distended gallbladder with painless obstructive jaundice + weight loss suggests malignant common bile duct obstruction from pancreatic head carcinoma; urgent 2WW CT chest/abdomen/pelvis; refer to HPB surgery; CA 19-9
options.C: Hepatitis — arrange LFTs and viral hepatitis serology
options.D: Primary sclerosing cholangitis — MRCP and colonoscopy
options.E: Cholangiocarcinoma — always the first differential for obstructive jaundice

explanation.correct: Courvoisier's law: 'In the presence of jaundice, a palpable non-tender gallbladder is unlikely to be due to gallstones' — because chronic gallstone disease causes inflammation and fibrosis, making the gallbladder shrunken and non-distensible. A DILATED, palpable, non-tender gallbladder with obstructive jaundice suggests malignant obstruction below the cystic duct insertion (most commonly pancreatic head carcinoma). Pancreatic head carcinoma (ductal adenocarcinoma): painless progressive jaundice (bile duct compression), weight loss, anorexia, dark urine, pale stools, new-onset diabetes. Per NICE NG12: urgent suspected cancer pathway (2WW); investigate with: CT chest/abdomen/pelvis (triple phase — pancreatic protocol); CA 19-9 (marker — elevated in 70-80%); ERCP/EUS for biliary drainage and biopsy if needed. Surgery (Whipple's pancreaticoduodenectomy): only 15-20% are resectable at presentation — 5-year survival <10% for resected cases. Palliative biliary stenting for inoperable disease.
explanation.A: Incorrect — Courvoisier's law specifically argues AGAINST gallstones as the cause when a palpable non-tender gallbladder is present with jaundice.
explanation.B: CORRECT — Courvoisier's sign + painless progressive jaundice + weight loss = pancreatic head carcinoma until proven otherwise. Urgent 2WW CT per NICE NG12.
explanation.C: Incorrect — Hepatitis causes hepatocellular jaundice (not obstructive) and would not produce a palpable distended gallbladder.
explanation.D: Incorrect — PSC causes cholestatic jaundice in younger patients with IBD; associated with multiple strictures — not typically a palpable gallbladder.
explanation.E: Incorrect — Cholangiocarcinoma (cancer of the bile duct) is also an important differential but Courvoisier's sign in this clinical context points more specifically to pancreatic head carcinoma.

reference: NICE NG12 — Suspected cancer: recognition and referral. https://www.nice.org.uk/guidance/ng12

question: A 68-year-old woman presents with a 2-month history of epigastric pain radiating to the back, new-onset type 2 diabetes, pale stools, and 8 kg weight loss. Her serum amylase is normal. Per NICE NG12, which investigation is most appropriate?

options.A: Repeat serum amylase — normal result excludes pancreatic pathology
options.B: Urgent CT chest/abdomen/pelvis with pancreatic protocol (triple phase) — new-onset diabetes in an older adult with weight loss, back pain and pale stools (steatorrhoea from exocrine insufficiency) is a red flag combination for pancreatic carcinoma; normal amylase does not exclude it (pancreatic cancer rarely causes acute pancreatitis); 2WW cancer referral is appropriate
options.C: Upper GI endoscopy — to exclude peptic ulcer disease
options.D: Abdominal USS only — sufficient to visualise the pancreas
options.E: Stool elastase — diagnoses pancreatic exocrine insufficiency and confirms cancer

explanation.correct: Per NICE NG12: red flag features for pancreatic cancer: unexplained weight loss + upper abdominal or back pain; new-onset diabetes in a person over 60 (diabetes can be the presenting symptom of pancreatic adenocarcinoma — cancer destroys islet cells); obstructive jaundice; pale/fatty stools (steatorrhoea from pancreatic exocrine insufficiency). Investigation: CT abdomen/pelvis with pancreatic protocol (triple phase arterial/portal/delayed) — most sensitive for detecting pancreatic tumour and local/vascular involvement. Why normal amylase does not exclude cancer: pancreatic adenocarcinoma does not typically cause duct obstruction producing acute pancreatitis (elevated amylase) — it grows silently causing weight loss and diabetes. USS abdomen: less sensitive for pancreatic tail lesions and can miss small tumours (>20% pancreatic cancers missed on USS). EUS + FNA: biopsy for tissue diagnosis once CT confirms a mass. CA 19-9: raised in 70-80% but non-specific.
explanation.A: Incorrect — Normal serum amylase DOES NOT exclude pancreatic carcinoma. Amylase is elevated in acute pancreatitis — not in pancreatic cancer.
explanation.B: CORRECT — Red flag combination (new diabetes + weight loss + back pain + steatorrhoea) = urgent CT pancreatic protocol + 2WW cancer referral per NICE NG12.
explanation.C: Incorrect — Upper GI endoscopy assesses oesophageal, gastric and duodenal pathology but cannot adequately visualise the pancreas.
explanation.D: Incorrect — USS has limited sensitivity for pancreatic pathology, particularly the body/tail, and is not adequate as the only investigation for suspected pancreatic cancer.
explanation.E: Incorrect — Stool elastase diagnoses exocrine insufficiency but cannot diagnose pancreatic cancer or exclude malignancy.

reference: NICE NG12 — Suspected cancer. https://www.nice.org.uk/guidance/ng12

question: A 58-year-old man has a follow-up appointment after his first flexible sigmoidoscopy screening. A single 8 mm tubular adenoma was found and removed. Per the NHS Bowel Cancer Screening Programme (BCSP) and BSG guidelines, what is the appropriate surveillance interval?

options.A: Annual colonoscopy — all adenomas require yearly surveillance
options.B: Repeat colonoscopy in 3 years — per BSG 2020 post-polypectomy surveillance guidelines: a single adenoma <10 mm is LOW risk; low-risk adenoma (1-2 small adenomas <10 mm with no high-grade dysplasia) requires no routine colonoscopy surveillance; recall with NHS bowel screening at 55-74 years FIT screening as per the general population; if 3+ adenomas or any adenoma ≥10 mm or any adenoma with high-grade dysplasia = intermediate/high risk requiring 3-year surveillance
options.C: Discharge with no follow-up — one polyp has no cancer risk
options.D: Colonoscopy in 1 year — all adenomas are high risk
options.E: CT colonography in 5 years as alternative to colonoscopy

explanation.correct: Per BSG 2020 Post-Polypectomy Surveillance Guidelines and NHS BCSP: post-polypectomy risk stratification: Low risk: 1-2 adenomas, ALL <10 mm, NO high-grade dysplasia/villous features. Previously: 3-year colonoscopy; Updated BSG 2020: no routine surveillance colonoscopy needed for low-risk patients — return to NHS bowel screening programme (biennial FIT screening age 50-74 in England). Intermediate risk: 3-4 small adenomas (<10 mm) OR any single adenoma ≥10 mm OR adenoma with villous features/high-grade dysplasia → colonoscopy at 3 years. High risk: ≥5 small adenomas OR ≥3 adenomas with at least one ≥10 mm → colonoscopy at 3 years + 3 years again if stable. This patient: single 8 mm tubular adenoma = LOW risk → no surveillance colonoscopy; return to population screening (FIT screening). The question tests knowledge of the 2020 BSG guideline change (less surveillance for low-risk patients than previously recommended).
explanation.A: Incorrect — Annual colonoscopy is not required for low-risk adenomas; this would be over-investigation causing unnecessary risk and resource use.
explanation.B: CORRECT — Single adenoma <10 mm = low risk; per BSG 2020: no routine surveillance colonoscopy; return to FIT screening programme.
explanation.C: Incorrect — While the surveillance interval changes, adenomas do confer a slightly increased risk compared to the population; return to FIT screening is appropriate (not complete discharge with nothing).
explanation.D: Incorrect — 1-year colonoscopy is used for specific high-risk situations (e.g. incomplete resection, unclear resection margins, synchronous cancer) — not for a single small low-risk adenoma.
explanation.E: Incorrect — CT colonography is not the recommended surveillance modality for post-polypectomy follow-up; colonoscopy is the standard if surveillance is needed.

reference: BSG — Post-polypectomy surveillance guidelines 2020. NHS BCSP. https://www.bsg.org.uk/clinical-resources/guidelines/

question: A 58-year-old man presents with a 6-week history of epigastric pain, reflux symptoms and is found to have a platelet count of 680 × 10⁹/L (thrombocytosis) with a normal FBC otherwise. Per NICE NG12 and NG2, what investigation must be done next to exclude serious pathology?

options.A: Start PPI and review in 8 weeks — thrombocytosis is a reactive finding
options.B: Urgent upper GI endoscopy — new dyspeptic symptoms in a patient over 55 (alarm feature) combined with thrombocytosis (which can be reactive to occult malignancy or iron deficiency from GI bleeding) requires urgent 2WW endoscopy referral to exclude gastric cancer or oesophageal cancer per NICE NG12 and NG2 (dyspepsia guidelines)
options.C: Bone marrow biopsy — thrombocytosis always indicates haematological malignancy
options.D: Anti-Helicobacter pylori antibody test and treat — standard first-line for dyspepsia
options.E: Abdominal ultrasound to exclude splenomegaly

explanation.correct: Per NICE NG12 (Suspected cancer) and NICE NG2 (Dyspepsia and GORD): Alarm features in dyspepsia requiring urgent (2WW) upper GI endoscopy: age ≥55 with unexplained weight loss AND one of: upper abdominal pain, reflux, or dyspepsia; dysphagia; upper abdominal mass; treatment-resistant dyspepsia; iron deficiency anaemia; progressive difficulty swallowing; unexplained weight loss. Additionally: per NICE NG12, thrombocytosis combined with dyspeptic symptoms (especially in patients over 55) is a red flag combination — thrombocytosis can be reactive to occult GI malignancy (from chronic blood loss causing iron deficiency, or direct tumour-stimulated thrombopoiesis via IL-6). Therefore: urgent 2WW upper GI endoscopy is required. H. pylori test and treat is first-line for UNCOMPLICATED dyspepsia in under 55s without alarm features — NOT for this alarm feature presentation.
explanation.A: Incorrect — Starting PPI without investigating alarm features (age + thrombocytosis) delays diagnosis of potentially resectable upper GI cancer.
explanation.B: CORRECT — Dyspepsia + age ≥55 + thrombocytosis = alarm features requiring urgent 2WW upper GI endoscopy to exclude gastric/oesophageal cancer per NICE NG12.
explanation.C: Incorrect — Reactive thrombocytosis is more common than primary haematological causes; bone marrow biopsy is not first-line. Investigate GI malignancy (a common cause of reactive thrombocytosis) first.
explanation.D: Incorrect — H. pylori test and treat is appropriate for UNCOMPLICATED dyspepsia in patients under 55 without alarm features. Alarm features mandate urgent endoscopy first.
explanation.E: Incorrect — Abdominal USS can be useful but does not visualise the gastric/oesophageal mucosa and cannot exclude upper GI cancer — endoscopy is required.

reference: NICE NG12 — Suspected cancer. NICE NG2 — Dyspepsia and GORD. https://www.nice.org.uk/guidance/ng12

question: A 42-year-old woman presents with epigastric pain and nausea for 3 months. She is an otherwise well non-smoker with no alarm features. She is not on NSAIDs. Per NICE NG2, what is the recommended first-line management in primary care?

options.A: Urgent upper GI endoscopy — all dyspepsia requires endoscopy
options.B: H. pylori test (urea breath test or stool antigen test — NOT serology) and treat if positive; if H. pylori negative or symptoms persist after successful eradication: full-dose PPI for 4-8 weeks; review and step down to lowest effective maintenance dose if required
options.C: Empirical PPI trial only — H. pylori testing is not recommended in primary care
options.D: Ranitidine (H2 blocker) — first-line per NICE NG2
options.E: Immediate referral to gastroenterology for all dyspepsia lasting more than 4 weeks

explanation.correct: Per NICE NG2 (Dyspepsia and GORD): for uncomplicated dyspepsia in adults <55 without alarm features: H. pylori test and treat is the recommended first-line strategy. Why: H. pylori causes peptic ulcer disease and can cause dyspepsia — eradication achieves long-term symptom resolution in H. pylori-positive patients (superior to just treating with a PPI). Testing method: urea breath test (UBT) or stool antigen test — NOT serology (serology detects past exposure, not current active infection and cannot confirm eradication). Before testing: stop PPIs for 2 weeks, antibiotics for 4 weeks (to avoid false negatives). Eradication therapy: 7-day triple therapy: PPI + amoxicillin + clarithromycin (first-line); PPI + metronidazole + clarithromycin if penicillin allergic; confirm eradication: repeat UBT or stool antigen ≥4 weeks after completing treatment. If H. pylori negative or refractory: PPI 4-8 weeks.
explanation.A: Incorrect — Endoscopy is NOT required for uncomplicated dyspepsia without alarm features in patients under 55 per NICE NG2.
explanation.B: CORRECT — H. pylori UBT or stool antigen test first (not serology); treat if positive; PPI if negative or refractory per NICE NG2.
explanation.C: Incorrect — H. pylori testing IS recommended in primary care for uncomplicated dyspepsia — empirical PPI alone is a second-line approach after H. pylori strategy.
explanation.D: Incorrect — Ranitidine (H2 blocker) was withdrawn from the UK market in 2020 due to NDMA contamination concerns. PPIs are the recommended acid suppression therapy per NICE NG2.
explanation.E: Incorrect — Uncomplicated dyspepsia without alarm features is managed in primary care per NICE NG2; gastroenterology referral is for alarm features or refractory cases.

reference: NICE NG2 — Dyspepsia and GORD. https://www.nice.org.uk/guidance/ng2

question: A 48-year-old woman presents with a 6-month history of an irregular pigmented lesion on her right upper back. She noticed it has changed colour (now dark brown with areas of black) and grown to approximately 12 mm diameter. It has an irregular border. Per NICE NG12 and the ABCDE criteria, what is the most important management step?

options.A: Reassure — benign seborrhoeic keratosis; review in 12 months
options.B: Urgent 2-week wait (2WW) referral to dermatology for excision biopsy — this lesion meets multiple ABCDE melanoma criteria: A (asymmetry), B (irregular border), C (colour variation — dark brown/black), D (diameter >6 mm — 12 mm), E (evolving — growing, changing colour); per NICE NG12: refer any suspicious pigmented lesion on a 2WW basis; do NOT perform excision biopsy in primary care; excision biopsy with 2 mm margin in secondary care for histological diagnosis; if melanoma confirmed: wide local excision with 1-2 cm margins depending on Breslow thickness
options.C: Topical imiquimod — first-line for all pigmented lesions
options.D: Punch biopsy of the darkest area in the GP surgery to save time
options.E: Full-body skin check only — no referral needed without ulceration

explanation.correct: Per NICE NG12 and British Association of Dermatology (BAD) melanoma guidelines: ABCDE criteria for suspicious pigmented lesions: A — Asymmetry; B — Border irregularity; C — Colour variation (multiple shades); D — Diameter >6 mm; E — Evolution/change over time. This lesion: irregular (A), irregular border (B), dark brown + black (C = colour variation), 12 mm (D = >6mm), growing and changing colour (E = evolving) → high suspicion for melanoma. Per NICE NG12: urgent 2WW referral to dermatology for any lesion suspicious for melanoma; do NOT attempt excision biopsy or punch biopsy in primary care — incomplete excision or inadequate margin information can compromise pathological staging (Breslow thickness) and surgical planning. If melanoma confirmed histologically: Stage-dependent management: Breslow <1 mm: 1 cm margin WLE; Breslow 1-2 mm: 1-2 cm margin; Breslow >2 mm: 2 cm margin; sentinel lymph node biopsy for Breslow ≥0.8 mm in selected cases; advanced melanoma: immunotherapy (pembrolizumab, nivolumab + ipilimumab) or BRAF/MEK inhibitors (vemurafenib + cobimetinib).
explanation.A: Incorrect — Seborrhoeic keratoses are typically stuck-on, warty, uniform colour; this lesion with ABCDE features is suspicious for melanoma requiring urgent referral.
explanation.B: CORRECT — Urgent 2WW referral; do NOT biopsy in primary care; excision biopsy (2 mm margin) in secondary care for histological staging per NICE NG12/BAD.
explanation.C: Incorrect — Imiquimod is used for superficial BCC and some superficial skin lesions — never for suspected melanoma without histological confirmation.
explanation.D: Incorrect — Punch biopsy in primary care is strongly discouraged for suspected melanoma — it disrupts the lesion, prevents full Breslow thickness measurement, and may compromise staging.
explanation.E: Incorrect — Ulceration is not required for 2WW referral; multiple ABCDE features are sufficient and compelling criteria for urgent referral per NICE NG12.

reference: NICE NG12 — Suspected cancer. BAD melanoma guidelines. https://www.nice.org.uk/guidance/ng12

question: A 65-year-old man is referred by his GP with a suspicious pigmented lesion on his forearm. Excision biopsy in the dermatology clinic shows: nodular melanoma, Breslow thickness 2.8 mm, Clark level IV, no ulceration, no mitoses. Per BAD melanoma guidelines, what is the recommended surgical margin for wide local excision (WLE)?

options.A: 0.5 cm margin — sufficient for thin melanomas
options.B: 2 cm margin — per BAD and ESMO guidelines: Breslow thickness >2 mm requires 2 cm excision margin for wide local excision; also consider sentinel lymph node biopsy (SLNB) for Breslow ≥0.8 mm (this patient at 2.8 mm: SLNB strongly recommended to assess regional nodal involvement and guide staging)
options.C: 5 cm margin — to ensure clear margins
options.D: 1 cm margin — appropriate for all melanomas
options.E: No WLE needed — excision biopsy with 2 mm margin is sufficient treatment

explanation.correct: Per BAD (British Association of Dermatology) and ESMO melanoma guidelines: WLE margin based on Breslow thickness: In situ melanoma: 0.5-1 cm margin; Breslow ≤1.0 mm: 1 cm margin; Breslow 1.01-2.0 mm: 1-2 cm margin (1 cm is accepted if 2 cm anatomically difficult); Breslow >2.0 mm: 2 cm margin (evidence from WHO Melanoma Trial and Intergroup Melanoma Surgical Trial). This patient: Breslow 2.8 mm → 2 cm margin WLE. Sentinel lymph node biopsy (SLNB): indicated for Breslow ≥0.8 mm (MSLT-I trial); provides important staging information; positive SLNB: stage III disease → consider completion lymph node dissection and/or adjuvant systemic therapy (pembrolizumab, nivolumab adjuvant — KEYNOTE-716, CheckMate-238 trials). Breslow 2.8 mm, no ulceration, no mitoses: pT3a (stage IIA/IIB); SLNB strongly recommended for this thickness.
explanation.A: Incorrect — 0.5 cm margin is used for melanoma in situ — insufficient for a Breslow 2.8 mm invasive melanoma.
explanation.B: CORRECT — Breslow >2 mm: 2 cm margin WLE; SLNB recommended for Breslow ≥0.8 mm per BAD/ESMO guidelines.
explanation.C: Incorrect — 5 cm margins are not recommended in any melanoma guideline; 2 cm is the maximum recommended margin.
explanation.D: Incorrect — 1 cm margin is appropriate for Breslow ≤1 mm; for Breslow 2.8 mm, a 2 cm margin is required.
explanation.E: Incorrect — The initial excision biopsy with 2 mm margin is diagnostic only; WLE with appropriate margins is required for definitive surgical treatment of invasive melanoma.

reference: BAD — Melanoma guidelines. ESMO Melanoma Clinical Practice Guidelines. https://www.bad.org.uk/clinical-services/clinical-guidelines/

question: A 55-year-old man is diagnosed with stage IV metastatic melanoma (liver and lung metastases). His tumour is BRAF V600E mutation positive. Per NICE and BAD guidelines, what systemic treatment options are available?

options.A: Cytotoxic chemotherapy (dacarbazine) — the only treatment for stage IV melanoma
options.B: Two main options: (1) BRAF/MEK inhibitor combination (vemurafenib + cobimetinib, or dabrafenib + trametinib) — targeted therapy for BRAF V600E-mutant melanoma; rapid response rates (~60-70%) but resistance typically develops within 6-12 months; (2) Anti-PD-1 immunotherapy (pembrolizumab or nivolumab ± ipilimumab) — immune checkpoint inhibitors; lower initial response rate but more durable long-term responses; BRAF-positive patients may receive targeted or immunotherapy depending on clinical urgency; combination ipilimumab + nivolumab has highest response rate but also highest toxicity
options.C: Radiotherapy only — systemic treatment has no role in stage IV melanoma
options.D: Watch and wait — stage IV melanoma is not treatable
options.E: Interferon-alpha — gold standard for all advanced melanoma

explanation.correct: Per NICE TA321, TA366, TA394 and BAD advanced melanoma guidelines: stage IV metastatic melanoma — treatment landscape transformed since 2010. BRAF status is now mandatory testing for all metastatic melanoma (detected in ~50% of cutaneous melanomas). BRAF V600E-mutant melanoma treatment options: (1) BRAF + MEK inhibitor combinations (all NICE approved): vemurafenib (BRAF) + cobimetinib (MEK) — COBRIM trial; dabrafenib (BRAF) + trametinib (MEK) — COMBI-d/v trials; encorafenib + binimetinib — COLUMBUS trial; response rates 60-70%; median PFS ~12 months; (2) Immune checkpoint inhibitors: pembrolizumab (anti-PD-1) — KEYNOTE-006 trial (NICE TA366); nivolumab (anti-PD-1) — CheckMate-066; ipilimumab (anti-CTLA-4) + nivolumab — CheckMate-067 — highest response rate (~58%) with durable responses; toxicity profile. Choice: clinical urgency (rapid progression → BRAF targeted for fast response), CNS metastases, patient preference. Dacarbazine: old-generation chemotherapy with <15% response rate; largely superseded by above agents.
explanation.A: Incorrect — Dacarbazine has <15% response rate and has been largely superseded by BRAF/MEK inhibitors and immunotherapy in BRAF-mutant stage IV melanoma.
explanation.B: CORRECT — BRAF V600E-positive stage IV melanoma: BRAF/MEK inhibitors (vemurafenib/cobimetinib, dabrafenib/trametinib) OR anti-PD-1 immunotherapy (pembrolizumab, nivolumab ± ipilimumab) per NICE/BAD.
explanation.C: Incorrect — Radiotherapy has a role in palliative symptom control (bone/brain metastases) but systemic therapy is the primary treatment for stage IV melanoma.
explanation.D: Incorrect — Stage IV melanoma is now treatable with meaningful response rates and prolonged survival — watch and wait is not appropriate.
explanation.E: Incorrect — Interferon-alpha was previously used in adjuvant melanoma but has been superseded by anti-PD-1 adjuvant therapy; it is not used for stage IV disease.

reference: NICE TA321, TA366 — Advanced melanoma. BAD melanoma guidelines. https://www.nice.org.uk/guidance/ta321

question: A 45-year-old man presents with a 3-week history of fever, night sweats, malaise and a new pansystolic murmur at the apex. He is an IV drug user. Blood cultures are pending. Per NICE CG64 and BSC guidelines, what is the most likely diagnosis and priority investigation?

options.A: Rheumatic fever — arrange anti-streptolysin O titre (ASOT)
options.B: Infective endocarditis — the combination of fever, new murmur and IV drug use meets Duke criteria (major criterion: new murmur; minor: fever, IV drug use); priority investigation is transthoracic echocardiogram (TTE) and minimum 3 sets of blood cultures from different sites before starting antibiotics
options.C: Viral myocarditis — arrange ECG and troponin only
options.D: Pulmonary embolism — request D-dimer and CTPA
options.E: Septic arthritis — blood cultures and joint aspiration

explanation.correct: Infective endocarditis (IE) — the modified Duke criteria combine major criteria (positive blood cultures for typical organisms, echocardiographic evidence of endocardial involvement, new regurgitant murmur) and minor criteria (predisposing heart condition or IV drug use, fever >38°C, vascular/immunological phenomena). This patient meets 1 major (new murmur) and 2 minor criteria (fever, IVDU) — 'possible IE' by Duke. Per NICE CG64 and BSC guidance: minimum 3 sets of blood cultures from separate sites before antibiotics; transthoracic echocardiogram urgently; if TTE negative but clinical suspicion remains high, transoesophageal echocardiogram (TOE) is more sensitive. IV antibiotics (benzylpenicillin + gentamicin empirically per local protocol). Cardiology and cardiac surgery referral for consideration of surgical intervention.
explanation.A: Incorrect — Rheumatic fever typically follows streptococcal pharyngitis in younger patients; IVDU and new murmur points to IE.
explanation.B: CORRECT — Infective endocarditis: fever + new murmur + IVDU. Minimum 3 blood cultures + TTE urgently per NICE CG64.
explanation.C: Incorrect — Viral myocarditis rarely causes a pansystolic murmur and does not explain the 3-week fever in an IV drug user.
explanation.D: Incorrect — PE does not cause a pansystolic murmur; fever + murmur + IVDU is IE until proven otherwise.
explanation.E: Incorrect — Septic arthritis does not explain a new cardiac murmur, though it can be a complication of IE (septic emboli).

reference: NICE CG64 — Prophylaxis against infective endocarditis. BSC — IE guidelines. https://www.nice.org.uk/guidance/cg64

question: A 70-year-old woman has a routine ECG showing: P waves present at 80/min, QRS complexes at 38/min wide and bizarre, no consistent relationship between P waves and QRS complexes. She is asymptomatic. Per ESC guidelines and NICE TA324, what does this ECG show and what is the correct management?

options.A: First-degree heart block — reassure and repeat ECG annually
options.B: Complete (third-degree) heart block with ventricular escape rhythm — permanent pacemaker implantation is indicated even in asymptomatic patients when a slow wide-complex escape rhythm is present due to the risk of sudden asystolic death
options.C: Mobitz Type I (Wenckebach) — observe and avoid AV-nodal blocking drugs
options.D: Atrial fibrillation with aberrant conduction — rate control with bisoprolol
options.E: Bundle branch block — no treatment required

explanation.correct: Complete (third-degree) heart block: P waves and QRS complexes are completely independent (AV dissociation); P rate faster than QRS rate; QRS is wide (ventricular escape, not junctional) at 38 bpm. A slow wide-complex ventricular escape rhythm is inherently unreliable and carries a high risk of asystole — even if currently asymptomatic, the patient may experience sudden loss of consciousness or cardiac arrest without warning. Per ESC Cardiac Pacing Guidelines and NICE TA324: permanent pacemaker implantation is indicated for complete AV block regardless of symptoms when the escape rate is slow or the escape rhythm is ventricular (wide complex). Urgent cardiology referral and consideration of temporary pacing bridge pending permanent pacemaker.
explanation.A: Incorrect — First-degree heart block has a prolonged PR interval with ALL P waves conducted. This ECG shows complete AV dissociation.
explanation.B: CORRECT — Complete heart block with slow ventricular escape: permanent pacemaker indicated even if asymptomatic per ESC/NICE TA324.
explanation.C: Incorrect — Wenckebach (Mobitz I) shows progressive PR prolongation then a dropped beat, with eventual reset — not complete AV dissociation.
explanation.D: Incorrect — AF shows absence of P waves with irregular narrow QRS. This ECG has identifiable P waves at 80/min independent of QRS.
explanation.E: Incorrect — Bundle branch block has a normal P-QRS relationship with wide QRS but normal PR; this ECG shows AV dissociation.

reference: ESC Guidelines on Cardiac Pacing 2021. NICE TA324. https://www.nice.org.uk/guidance/ta324

question: A 58-year-old man presents to the GP with 2 hours of central crushing chest pain radiating to the left arm. His ECG shows ST elevation ≥2mm in leads V1-V4 with reciprocal ST depression in II, III and aVF. He has no prior cardiac history. Per NICE NG185, what is the immediate management?

options.A: Start oral aspirin and arrange urgent outpatient cardiology review within 48 hours
options.B: Call 999 immediately for primary percutaneous coronary intervention (PPCI) — this is an anterior STEMI (ST elevation in V1-V4 indicates LAD territory); aspirin 300mg stat; transfer without delay to PPCI centre; door-to-balloon time target <90 minutes from first medical contact
options.C: Give sublingual GTN and repeat ECG in 30 minutes before deciding on treatment
options.D: Administer IV thrombolysis in the GP surgery if PPCI centre is more than 30 minutes away
options.E: Admit to local hospital for cardiac monitoring and reassess in the morning

explanation.correct: This is an anterior STEMI (ST elevation in V1-V4 = LAD territory). Per NICE NG185 (Acute coronary syndromes) and national STEMI guidelines: call 999 immediately for emergency transfer to a PPCI-capable centre; aspirin 300mg immediately (chewed); GTN if not hypotensive; morphine for pain relief; oxygen only if SpO2 <94%. PPCI is the preferred reperfusion strategy — target door-to-balloon time <90 minutes from first medical contact. In the UK, ambulance services have direct transfer protocols to PPCI centres, bypassing local hospitals. Fibrinolysis is now rarely used in the UK outside remote areas where PPCI cannot be achieved within 120 minutes of diagnosis.
explanation.A: Incorrect — STEMI is a time-critical medical emergency requiring immediate 999 activation — outpatient review is completely inappropriate.
explanation.B: CORRECT — Anterior STEMI: 999 immediately for PPCI, aspirin 300mg stat, target door-to-balloon <90 minutes per NICE NG185.
explanation.C: Incorrect — Delaying for 30 minutes in an evolving STEMI costs myocardium — 'time is muscle'. GTN has no role in decision-making.
explanation.D: Incorrect — In-surgery thrombolysis is not recommended in UK practice — PPCI is overwhelmingly preferred and accessible.
explanation.E: Incorrect — Local admission without immediate PPCI pathway activation is inferior to direct transfer and is not recommended.

reference: NICE NG185 — Acute coronary syndromes. https://www.nice.org.uk/guidance/ng185

question: A 58-year-old man presents with central chest pain and an ECG showing anterior ST elevation. He is given aspirin 300mg. Per NICE NG185, which additional medications should be prescribed before transfer for primary PCI?

options.A: Ticagrelor 180mg loading dose, omeprazole 40mg (gastric protection with dual antiplatelet), and diamorphine 5mg IV titrated for pain with metoclopramide 10mg antiemetic
options.B: Furosemide, atorvastatin, and bisoprolol immediately
options.C: Warfarin loading dose and low molecular weight heparin
options.D: Clopidogrel 75mg, GTN spray, and oral codeine for pain
options.E: Thrombolysis with alteplase and IV nitrates immediately

explanation.correct: Per NICE NG185 (Acute coronary syndromes): in confirmed STEMI before PPCI, give: P2Y12 inhibitor loading — ticagrelor 180mg preferred over clopidogrel; diamorphine IV for pain (titrate to effect) with antiemetic (metoclopramide or cyclizine) to counteract opioid-induced nausea; omeprazole (PPI) gastroprotection is given with dual antiplatelet therapy to prevent GI bleeding. Aspirin 300mg already given. GTN if not hypotensive (SBP >90). Oxygen only if SpO2 <94%.
explanation.A: CORRECT — Ticagrelor 180mg + diamorphine + omeprazole + antiemetic are the key pre-PPCI additions per NICE NG185.
explanation.B: Incorrect — Furosemide, atorvastatin and bisoprolol are post-MI medications, not pre-PPCI emergency treatment.
explanation.C: Incorrect — Warfarin loading is not used in STEMI management. Anticoagulation (unfractionated heparin) is given during PPCI by the interventional cardiologist.
explanation.D: Incorrect — Clopidogrel is inferior to ticagrelor for STEMI per NICE NG185; codeine is insufficient for STEMI pain.
explanation.E: Incorrect — Thrombolysis is only used if PPCI cannot be achieved within 120 minutes; it is not first-line in UK practice.

reference: NICE NG185 — Acute coronary syndromes. https://www.nice.org.uk/guidance/ng185

question: A 64-year-old woman with anterior STEMI is given diamorphine 5mg IV for pain relief. Twenty minutes later she becomes confused and drowsy with a respiratory rate of 8 breaths/minute and pin-point pupils. Per BNF, what is the antidote and dose?

options.A: Flumazenil 200mcg IV — benzodiazepine antagonist
options.B: Activated charcoal — absorbs oral opioids only
options.C: Naloxone 400mcg IV (or IM) — opioid receptor antagonist; repeat every 2-3 minutes up to 10mg if no response; titrate to maintain adequate respiration without fully reversing analgesia
options.D: Glucose 50ml of 50% IV — reverses hypoglycaemia
options.E: Atropine 600mcg IV — reverses bradycardia only

explanation.correct: Opioid toxicity triad: reduced conscious level, respiratory depression (RR <12), pin-point miosis. Antidote: naloxone (Narcan) — competitive opioid receptor antagonist. Per BNF: 400mcg IV/IM stat; repeat every 2-3 minutes; titrate carefully — over-reversal causes acute pain and agitation in a STEMI patient (harmful). Infusion may be needed for longer-acting opioids. In prehospital/community: naloxone 2mg intranasal (Nyxoid) is available. Half-life of naloxone (~60-90 min) is shorter than most opioids — re-sedation can occur; monitor closely.
explanation.A: Incorrect — Flumazenil reverses benzodiazepine toxicity, not opioid toxicity.
explanation.B: Incorrect — Activated charcoal is for oral ingestion within 1 hour; diamorphine was given IV.
explanation.C: CORRECT — Naloxone 400mcg IV for opioid toxicity; repeat every 2-3 minutes per BNF.
explanation.D: Incorrect — Glucose reverses hypoglycaemia; pin-point pupils and respiratory depression indicate opioid toxicity.
explanation.E: Incorrect — Atropine treats bradycardia and organophosphate toxicity, not opioid respiratory depression.

reference: BNF — Naloxone hydrochloride. https://bnf.nice.org.uk/drug/naloxone-hydrochloride.html

question: A 71-year-old man with confirmed peptic ulcer disease is prescribed dual antiplatelet therapy (aspirin + ticagrelor) following a STEMI. Per NICE NG185 and BNF, what gastroprotection should be co-prescribed?

options.A: Antacids as required — taken when symptomatic
options.B: Misoprostol — first-line gastroprotection with antiplatelets
options.C: H2 antagonist (ranitidine) — equivalent to PPI for this indication
options.D: A proton pump inhibitor (PPI) such as omeprazole 20mg or lansoprazole 30mg daily — gastroprotection is routinely recommended with dual antiplatelet therapy; it significantly reduces upper GI bleeding risk without clinically significant interaction with ticagrelor
options.E: No gastroprotection needed — the benefits of antiplatelet therapy outweigh any GI risk

explanation.correct: Per NICE NG185 and BNF: PPI co-prescription is strongly recommended with dual antiplatelet therapy (DAPT), particularly in patients with prior peptic ulcer disease, GI bleeding history, or multiple GI risk factors. Omeprazole or lansoprazole are preferred. Historical concerns about omeprazole-clopidogrel CYP2C19 interaction are less relevant with ticagrelor (different metabolic pathway). Duration of DAPT post-STEMI: typically 12 months. PPI reduces GI bleeding risk by approximately 50% in patients on DAPT without reducing cardiovascular efficacy.
explanation.A: Incorrect — As-required antacids provide symptomatic relief only; they do not prevent NSAID/antiplatelet-induced ulceration.
explanation.B: Incorrect — Misoprostol is used for NSAID-associated ulcer prevention but is not first-line with antiplatelets.
explanation.C: Incorrect — H2 antagonists are inferior to PPIs for prevention of antiplatelet-associated gastropathy.
explanation.D: CORRECT — PPI (omeprazole/lansoprazole) daily with DAPT reduces GI bleeding risk significantly per NICE NG185.
explanation.E: Incorrect — With prior peptic ulcer disease, GI protection is essential — unprotected DAPT carries high bleeding risk.

reference: NICE NG185 — Acute coronary syndromes. https://www.nice.org.uk/guidance/ng185

question: A 52-year-old woman reports two episodes per week of palpitations lasting 10-15 minutes, which start and stop abruptly. She is otherwise well with a normal examination and a normal 12-lead ECG in clinic. Per NICE NG196, what is the most appropriate investigation to capture the rhythm during symptoms?

options.A: Standard 12-lead ECG only — repeat the resting ECG
options.B: 24-hour Holter monitor — suitable for daily symptoms only
options.C: 7-day ambulatory ECG monitor — the most appropriate investigation for palpitations occurring several times per week; longer duration than 24-hour Holter maximises the chance of recording the arrhythmia during a symptomatic episode
options.D: Echocardiogram — structural heart disease screening first
options.E: Electrophysiology study — invasive investigation for first-line diagnosis

explanation.correct: Per NICE NG196 (Atrial fibrillation: diagnosis and management) and NICE guidance on palpitations: the investigation of choice is guided by symptom frequency. 24-hour Holter: appropriate for daily or very frequent symptoms. 7-day (or up to 2-week) ambulatory ECG: appropriate for symptoms occurring several times per week — twice weekly symptoms have a high probability of being captured over 7 days. Event recorder (patient-activated): appropriate for infrequent symptoms (monthly or less). Implantable loop recorder: for very infrequent unexplained symptoms over months. This patient has twice-weekly symptoms — a 7-day ambulatory ECG is the most cost-effective investigation to capture the arrhythmia.
explanation.A: Incorrect — A resting 12-lead ECG will almost certainly be normal between episodes; it provides no diagnostic information for intermittent arrhythmia.
explanation.B: Incorrect — 24-hour Holter has only a 50% yield for daily symptoms; with twice-weekly symptoms, the yield over 24 hours is very low.
explanation.C: CORRECT — 7-day ambulatory ECG is the most appropriate for palpitations occurring several times per week per NICE NG196.
explanation.D: Incorrect — Echocardiogram assesses structural heart disease but cannot capture rhythm during palpitations; it is a secondary investigation.
explanation.E: Incorrect — Electrophysiology study is invasive and used for treatment (e.g. ablation) after the arrhythmia has been identified non-invasively.

reference: NICE NG196 — Atrial fibrillation: diagnosis and management. https://www.nice.org.uk/guidance/ng196

question: A 22-year-old man with Marfan syndrome attends his annual cardiology review. His echocardiogram shows an aortic root diameter of 42mm (upper limit of normal ~40mm for his BSA). He is currently on no medication. Per cardiology guidelines, which medication class is most evidence-based for reducing the rate of aortic root dilatation in Marfan syndrome?

options.A: Beta-blockers (e.g. atenolol or bisoprolol) — reduce aortic wall stress by lowering heart rate and dp/dt (rate of pressure rise); they are the established first-line medical therapy for aortic root dilatation in Marfan syndrome; losartan (ARB) is also used as an alternative or adjunct in some centres
options.B: Amlodipine (calcium channel blocker) — reduces aortic wall stress
options.C: ACE inhibitors — reduce afterload and aortic root size
options.D: Statins — reduce connective tissue inflammation in Marfan syndrome
options.E: Aspirin — antiplatelet therapy prevents dissection

explanation.correct: Marfan syndrome: autosomal dominant connective tissue disorder caused by FBN1 mutations affecting fibrillin-1; leads to progressive aortic root dilatation, aortic regurgitation, and risk of aortic dissection/rupture. Medical management to slow aortic root dilatation: beta-blockers (atenolol, propranolol, bisoprolol) — most established evidence; reduce aortic wall stress by lowering dP/dt; recommended when aortic root >40mm or dilatation rate >3mm/year. Losartan (ARB — TGF-β pathway inhibitor) has emerged as an alternative/adjunct based on animal and some clinical trial data. Surgical threshold: aortic root >50mm (or >45-48mm with rapid growth, family history of dissection, or planned pregnancy) — prophylactic aortic root replacement. Annual echo surveillance is essential. Lifestyle: avoid high-impact contact sports and heavy isometric exercise.
explanation.A: CORRECT — Beta-blockers (atenolol/bisoprolol) are established first-line therapy for aortic root dilatation in Marfan syndrome; losartan is an alternative.
explanation.B: Incorrect — Amlodipine is not the standard medical therapy for aortic root dilatation in Marfan syndrome; it has no specific evidence in this indication.
explanation.C: Incorrect — ACE inhibitors are not specifically recommended over beta-blockers or ARBs for Marfan aortic dilatation.
explanation.D: Incorrect — Statins have no established role in reducing aortic root dilatation in Marfan syndrome.
explanation.E: Incorrect — Aspirin has no role in preventing aortic dilatation or dissection in Marfan syndrome.

reference: ESC Guidelines — Management of aortic diseases. https://www.escardio.org/Guidelines

question: A 28-year-old woman with Marfan syndrome and an aortic root of 48mm is planning a pregnancy. Per ESC guidelines on pregnancy and cardiac disease, what is the key advice?

options.A: Pregnancy is absolutely contraindicated in all women with Marfan syndrome
options.B: Pregnancy is safe in Marfan syndrome — no special monitoring is needed
options.C: She should be counselled that pregnancy increases the risk of aortic dissection due to cardiovascular changes; surgical aortic root replacement is advisable before pregnancy if the root is >45mm; if proceeding, she needs joint cardiology and obstetric care, serial echo every 4-8 weeks in pregnancy, and delivery planning at a tertiary centre
options.D: Beta-blockers must be stopped in pregnancy as they cause fetal growth restriction
options.E: The aortic root diameter must reach 55mm before surgical intervention is considered

explanation.correct: Per ESC Guidelines on Cardiovascular Disease in Pregnancy: Marfan syndrome with aortic root >45mm carries high risk of aortic dissection during pregnancy (Type A dissection carries ~25% maternal mortality). The cardiovascular changes of pregnancy — increased blood volume, heart rate, cardiac output, and connective tissue laxity — significantly increase aortic wall stress. Recommendations: aortic root replacement is advised before pregnancy if root >45mm; if 40-45mm: individual risk assessment; if <40mm: lower risk but still requires monitoring. During pregnancy: serial echocardiography every 4-8 weeks; continue beta-blockers (benefits outweigh risk of mild fetal growth restriction); delivery at specialist centre; avoid prolonged Valsalva (epidural recommended); caesarean section considered if root >45mm at delivery. Genetic counselling: 50% inheritance risk.
explanation.A: Incorrect — Pregnancy is not absolutely contraindicated in all Marfan patients; it depends on aortic root dimensions and individual risk assessment.
explanation.B: Incorrect — Pregnancy is not safe without specialist monitoring in Marfan syndrome — significant risk of aortic dissection.
