explanation.C: CORRECT — Root 48mm: counselling about dissection risk; consider surgical repair before pregnancy; serial echo; tertiary centre delivery per ESC guidelines.
explanation.D: Incorrect — Beta-blockers are continued during pregnancy in Marfan syndrome; the benefit of reducing aortic wall stress outweighs the modest risk of fetal growth restriction.
explanation.E: Incorrect — The surgical threshold in Marfan syndrome before pregnancy is >45mm, not 55mm.

reference: ESC Guidelines — Cardiovascular Diseases during Pregnancy 2018. https://www.escardio.org/Guidelines

question: A 35-year-old man with bicuspid aortic valve and a mildly dilated aortic root of 41mm has been started on bisoprolol. Per current guidelines, what is the rationale and monitoring plan?

options.A: Bisoprolol is prescribed to prevent AF — annual ECG monitoring
options.B: The medication prevents infective endocarditis — no monitoring needed
options.C: Bisoprolol treats the aortic stenosis — titrate dose based on gradient
options.D: Beta-blockers reduce the rate of aortic dilatation by reducing arterial wall stress — annual echocardiogram surveillance to monitor aortic root size; surgical referral if root reaches 55mm (or 50mm with rapid progression or bicuspid AV-specific risk factors)
options.E: Annual CT angiography is required — echocardiography is insufficient

explanation.correct: Bicuspid aortic valve (BAV) is associated with aortopathy — progressive dilatation of the aortic root and/or ascending aorta due to abnormal smooth muscle biology. Beta-blockers reduce aortic wall stress (dP/dt) and may slow dilatation progression. Surveillance: annual echocardiogram to monitor aortic root dimensions. Surgical thresholds for bicuspid AV aortopathy (slightly higher than Marfan): intervention considered at ≥55mm ascending aorta (or ≥50mm with risk factors: rapid growth >3mm/year, family history of dissection, planned pregnancy, severe valve disease). Lifestyle: avoid competitive sports with risk of trauma or extreme exertion. Echo is the first-line surveillance tool; CT/MRI for surgical planning or incomplete echo windows.
explanation.A: Incorrect — Beta-blockers in BAV aortopathy target aortic wall stress reduction, not AF prevention.
explanation.B: Incorrect — Beta-blockers do not prevent infective endocarditis; IE prophylaxis is separate (no longer routinely recommended per NICE CG64).
explanation.C: Incorrect — Beta-blockers do not treat aortic stenosis; they may be used for symptom relief in some cases but are not valve-specific therapy.
explanation.D: CORRECT — Beta-blockers reduce aortic wall stress; annual echo surveillance; surgical referral at 55mm (or 50mm with risk factors).
explanation.E: Incorrect — Echocardiography is first-line surveillance; CT/MRI is reserved for surgical planning or poor echo windows.

reference: ESC Guidelines — Valvular Heart Disease. https://www.escardio.org/Guidelines

question: A 38-year-old woman presents with a 3-month history of a persistent dry cough and erythema nodosum on both shins. She has no significant past medical history. A CXR shows bilateral hilar lymphadenopathy. Per NICE CKS, what is the most likely diagnosis?

options.A: Tuberculosis — sputum AFB culture and treatment
options.B: Sarcoidosis — the combination of erythema nodosum, bilateral hilar lymphadenopathy (BHL) and dry cough is Löfgren's syndrome (a classical acute presentation of sarcoidosis); this carries a good prognosis with spontaneous remission in most cases
options.C: Lymphoma — urgent 2WW haematology referral
options.D: Community-acquired pneumonia — oral amoxicillin for 5 days
options.E: Systemic lupus erythematosus — ANA and anti-dsDNA

explanation.correct: Löfgren's syndrome is a classic acute presentation of sarcoidosis comprising: bilateral hilar lymphadenopathy (BHL), erythema nodosum, arthralgia/arthritis, and fever. It predominantly affects young women. Per NICE CKS (Sarcoidosis): Löfgren's syndrome has an excellent prognosis — approximately 80-90% achieve spontaneous remission within 2 years. Management: NSAIDs for erythema nodosum and arthralgia; systemic corticosteroids for severe systemic involvement; refer to respiratory/rheumatology for confirmation and monitoring. Investigations: ACE level (elevated in 60-80% of active sarcoidosis), CXR (BHL), CT chest, serum calcium (hypercalcaemia in active disease), LFTs, FBC. Tissue biopsy (lymph node, skin, BAL) for definitive diagnosis if non-Löfgren's presentation.
explanation.A: Incorrect — TB can cause BHL, but the combination with erythema nodosum and dry cough in a young woman is classic Löfgren's/sarcoidosis.
explanation.B: CORRECT — Löfgren's syndrome (sarcoidosis): erythema nodosum + BHL + cough. Good prognosis; NSAIDs + monitoring per NICE CKS.
explanation.C: Incorrect — Lymphoma causes lymphadenopathy but not typically erythema nodosum; it would have a different CXR pattern.
explanation.D: Incorrect — CAP would show consolidation on CXR, not bilateral hilar lymphadenopathy.
explanation.E: Incorrect — SLE can cause a malar rash and multi-organ involvement but does not typically present with BHL and erythema nodosum.

reference: NICE CKS — Sarcoidosis. https://cks.nice.org.uk/topics/sarcoidosis/

question: A 68-year-old woman presents with a 3-month history of bilateral ankle and leg swelling extending to the knees, associated with a non-pitting quality. She has no cardiac, hepatic or renal disease. Review of her medications shows she was started on ramipril for hypertension 4 months ago. Per NICE and BNF guidance, what is the most likely cause?

options.A: Deep vein thrombosis — Doppler ultrasound urgently
options.B: ACE inhibitor-induced angioedema — ACE inhibitors cause bradykinin accumulation by inhibiting its degradation; this results in angioedema which can affect the limbs (non-pitting oedema), face, tongue, throat and gut; stop ramipril immediately and switch to an alternative antihypertensive (ARB with caution — 10-15% cross-reactivity; calcium channel blocker preferred)
options.C: Lymphoedema — refer to lymphoedema clinic for compression bandaging
options.D: Amlodipine side effect — peripheral oedema is more likely with calcium channel blockers
options.E: Heart failure — arrange BNP, ECG and echocardiogram

explanation.correct: ACE inhibitor-induced angioedema: occurs in up to 0.7% of ACE inhibitor users. Mechanism: ACE normally degrades bradykinin; ACE inhibition allows bradykinin accumulation → increased vascular permeability → angioedema. Key features: non-pitting oedema (bradykinin-mediated, unlike aldosterone-mediated pitting oedema); can affect the face, lips, tongue, larynx (life-threatening), limbs, intestines (abdominal angioedema — cramping pain); can occur at any point during treatment (months to years after initiation). Management: stop ACE inhibitor immediately; in facial/laryngeal angioedema — emergency (adrenaline, antihistamines, steroids); in limb angioedema: stop drug, oedema resolves over weeks. Switch to CCB (amlodipine) or ARB (with caution). Note: amlodipine causes PITTING ankle oedema from arteriolar vasodilation — distinct from the non-pitting bilateral angioedema here.
explanation.A: Incorrect — DVT causes unilateral oedema with tenderness; bilateral non-pitting oedema temporal to ACE inhibitor use is angioedema.
explanation.B: CORRECT — ACE inhibitor (ramipril) causing limb angioedema (non-pitting bilateral oedema): stop ramipril, switch to CCB per BNF/NICE.
explanation.C: Incorrect — Lymphoedema develops chronically and is not temporally related to a new medication.
explanation.D: Incorrect — Amlodipine causes PITTING ankle oedema. The patient is not on amlodipine, and the oedema is non-pitting.
explanation.E: Incorrect — Heart failure causes pitting oedema with additional cardiac symptoms; no cardiac disease is mentioned and the temporal relationship to ramipril initiation points to drug cause.

reference: BNF — ACE inhibitor side effects. NICE CKS — Angioedema. https://bnf.nice.org.uk/drug/ramipril.html

question: A 72-year-old man has had a persistent, well-demarcated, erythematous plaque on his right lower leg for 3 years. It has never changed shape or size. The surface is slightly scaly. He is a farmer and has had significant sun exposure throughout his life. Biopsy shows full-thickness epidermal dysplasia without dermal invasion. Per NICE CKS, what is the diagnosis?

options.A: Psoriasis — topical calcipotriol and betamethasone
options.B: Bowen's disease (squamous cell carcinoma in situ) — characterised by a persistent, well-demarcated, slowly enlarging erythematous scaly plaque; full-thickness epidermal dysplasia without dermal invasion = SCC in situ; risk of progression to invasive SCC is approximately 3-5%; treatment: cryotherapy, topical 5-fluorouracil, or photodynamic therapy
options.C: Discoid eczema — emollients and topical steroids
options.D: Tinea corporis — oral terbinafine
options.E: Kaposi's sarcoma — HIV test and antiretroviral therapy

explanation.correct: Bowen's disease (SCC in situ): an intraepidermal squamous cell carcinoma where dysplasia involves the full thickness of the epidermis but has not breached the basement membrane (i.e., not invasive). Risk factors: UV exposure (outdoor/occupational), immunosuppression, HPV infection, arsenic exposure. Clinical features: slowly enlarging, well-demarcated, erythematous/scaly plaque, usually solitary, on sun-exposed sites; does not heal spontaneously; static or slowly growing over years (distinguishes from inflammatory conditions). Biopsy: full-thickness epidermal dysplasia without dermal invasion. Risk of progression to invasive SCC: approximately 3-5%. Per NICE CKS: treatment options include cryotherapy, topical 5-fluorouracil 5% cream, imiquimod, photodynamic therapy (PDT — most effective for large lesions), or excision. Follow-up recommended.
explanation.A: Incorrect — Psoriasis causes well-demarcated silvery-scaled plaques with nail involvement and symmetrical distribution, not a single non-healing lesion with full-thickness epidermal dysplasia on biopsy.
explanation.B: CORRECT — Bowen's disease: SCC in situ; full-thickness epidermal dysplasia without invasion; treatment: cryotherapy/5-FU/PDT per NICE CKS.
explanation.C: Incorrect — Discoid eczema causes itchy coin-shaped lesions often with vesicles; biopsy shows inflammatory changes, not full-thickness dysplasia.
explanation.D: Incorrect — Tinea corporis causes a scaly ring-shaped lesion with central clearing; Wood's lamp/KOH preparation would show fungal hyphae.
explanation.E: Incorrect — Kaposi's sarcoma presents as violaceous lesions in immunocompromised patients; histology shows vascular proliferation — not epidermal dysplasia.

reference: NICE CKS — Bowen's disease. https://cks.nice.org.uk/topics/bowens-disease/

question: A 55-year-old woman presents with a 3-month history of a heliotrope (violaceous) rash around her eyelids bilaterally, Gottron's papules over her knuckles, and progressive proximal muscle weakness (difficulty rising from a chair). Per NICE CKS, what is the diagnosis and what malignancy screening is required?

options.A: Systemic lupus erythematosus — check ANA and anti-dsDNA; no malignancy screening
options.B: Dermatomyositis — an inflammatory myopathy with characteristic skin manifestations (heliotrope rash, Gottron's papules, V-sign, shawl sign); associated with an increased risk of underlying malignancy (approximately 15-25% of adult dermatomyositis); comprehensive malignancy screening is mandatory at diagnosis
options.C: Eczema with muscle pain — topical steroids and physiotherapy
options.D: Psoriatic arthritis — topical treatment and DMARD
options.E: Hypothyroid myopathy — check TSH and start levothyroxine

explanation.correct: Dermatomyositis (DM): an idiopathic inflammatory myopathy with characteristic skin features. Key cutaneous signs: heliotrope rash (violaceous periorbital oedema/rash — pathognomonic), Gottron's papules (erythematous papules over MCP/PIP joints — pathognomonic), V-sign (chest/neck), shawl sign (upper back/shoulders), mechanic's hands (cracked palms). Muscle involvement: symmetric proximal weakness (hips, shoulders), raised CK and LDH. Investigations: CK, LDH, aldolase, myositis-specific antibodies (anti-Jo-1, anti-Mi-2, anti-MDA5), EMG, MRI muscles, muscle biopsy. Critical association: 15-25% of adult DM is paraneoplastic — malignancy screen is mandatory at diagnosis. Screen includes: CT chest/abdomen/pelvis, mammogram (women), PSA (men), colonoscopy, pelvic USS. Treatment: high-dose oral prednisolone + steroid-sparing agents (azathioprine, methotrexate).
explanation.A: Incorrect — SLE causes a malar (butterfly) rash and systemic features but NOT heliotrope rash or Gottron's papules. No malignancy screen is routinely needed for SLE.
explanation.B: CORRECT — Dermatomyositis: heliotrope rash + Gottron's papules + proximal weakness. Mandatory malignancy screen in adults (15-25% paraneoplastic) per NICE CKS.
explanation.C: Incorrect — Eczema does not cause heliotrope rash or Gottron's papules, and does not cause proximal muscle weakness.
explanation.D: Incorrect — Psoriatic arthritis causes psoriatic skin changes and inflammatory arthritis — not the specific DM skin signs or proximal muscle weakness.
explanation.E: Incorrect — Hypothyroid myopathy can cause proximal weakness and is important to exclude, but does not cause heliotrope rash or Gottron's papules.

reference: NICE CKS — Dermatomyositis and polymyositis. https://cks.nice.org.uk/topics/dermatomyositis-and-polymyositis/

question: A 65-year-old man presents with a rapidly growing nodule on his right cheek. It appeared 6 weeks ago as a small papule, grew quickly to 2cm with a central keratin-filled crater, and appears to be spontaneously involuting. He has significant sun damage to his face. Per NICE CKS, what is the diagnosis and appropriate management?

options.A: Molluscum contagiosum — self-limiting viral infection, reassure
options.B: Pyoderma gangrenosum — systemic immunosuppression
options.C: Sebaceous cyst — simple excision in primary care
options.D: Basal cell carcinoma — refer to dermatology for standard excision
options.E: Keratoacanthoma — a rapidly growing squamous epithelial tumour that may represent a well-differentiated SCC; due to inability to reliably distinguish from invasive SCC clinically or histologically, excision biopsy is recommended in all cases

explanation.correct: Keratoacanthoma (KA): a rapidly growing squamous epithelial tumour with a classic central keratin-filled crater; typically on sun-exposed skin in older adults; characteristically grows rapidly over 6-8 weeks then may involute spontaneously. Critical issue: KA is histologically and clinically indistinguishable from well-differentiated squamous cell carcinoma (SCC) in many cases — even expert pathologists may disagree. Per NICE CKS: excision biopsy is mandatory for all KA because: (1) cannot reliably distinguish from SCC; (2) spontaneous regression is unpredictable; (3) if it is SCC, delay allows invasion and metastasis risk. Awaiting spontaneous regression is not appropriate. Referred to dermatology or plastics for excision with clear margins. Histology is definitive.
explanation.A: Incorrect — Molluscum contagiosum causes small pearly umbilicated papules in children/immunocompromised; not a rapidly growing 2cm crater nodule in an elderly man.
explanation.B: Incorrect — Pyoderma gangrenosum is an ulcerating wound with purple undermined edges; not a keratin-filled nodule.
explanation.C: Incorrect — Sebaceous cysts are slow-growing, non-keratin-filled, usually have a punctum; not appropriate diagnosis here.
explanation.D: Incorrect — BCC is a slow-growing pearly rolled-edge lesion; not a rapidly growing keratin-filled crater nodule.
explanation.E: CORRECT — Keratoacanthoma: excision biopsy mandatory — cannot reliably exclude SCC per NICE CKS.

reference: NICE CKS — Keratoacanthoma. https://cks.nice.org.uk/topics/squamous-cell-carcinoma-cutaneous/

question: A 58-year-old man has a growing keratoacanthoma-like lesion on his right temple confirmed as a well-differentiated SCC on biopsy. The lesion is 1.8cm. Per NICE NG12 and BAD guidelines, what is the appropriate management?

options.A: Surgical excision with adequate clear margins (typically 4-6mm for well-differentiated SCC <2cm) — primary treatment for cutaneous SCC; refer to dermatology or plastics; high-risk features warranting wider margins or additional treatment: >2cm, poorly differentiated, depth >4mm, perineural invasion, immunosuppressed patient, ear/lip location
options.B: Topical 5-fluorouracil cream — effective for all facial SCC
options.C: Cryotherapy alone is sufficient for all facial SCC
options.D: Mohs micrographic surgery is required for all SCCs regardless of size or location
options.E: Radiotherapy only — surgery is contraindicated for facial lesions

explanation.correct: Cutaneous SCC: second most common skin cancer; UV radiation is the main risk factor. Per NICE NG12 and British Association of Dermatologists (BAD) guidelines: surgical excision with histologically confirmed clear margins is the primary treatment. Recommended margins: 4-6mm for well-differentiated SCC <2cm with clearly defined margins. High-risk features requiring wider margins (6-10mm) or Mohs surgery: >2cm, poorly differentiated grade, depth >4mm (Clark level IV-V), perineural/lymphovascular invasion, immunosuppressed host, ears/lips/temples/scalp (functional/cosmetic challenge), recurrent tumour. Metastatic risk for cutaneous SCC: approximately 4% overall; higher with high-risk features. Sentinel lymph node biopsy: for high-risk; staging CT if lymph nodes clinically suspicious.
explanation.A: CORRECT — Surgical excision with 4-6mm margins for well-differentiated SCC <2cm. Refer to dermatology/plastics per NICE NG12/BAD.
explanation.B: Incorrect — Topical 5-FU is used for Bowen's disease (SCC in situ) and actinic keratoses; it is insufficient for invasive SCC.
explanation.C: Incorrect — Cryotherapy is appropriate for actinic keratoses and Bowen's disease; it is not adequate for invasive SCC.
explanation.D: Incorrect — Mohs micrographic surgery is reserved for high-risk or anatomically challenging SCCs; not required for all SCC.
explanation.E: Incorrect — Surgery is the primary treatment; radiotherapy is an alternative for inoperable lesions or adjuvant in high-risk cases.

reference: NICE NG12 — Suspected cancer referral. BAD — SCC guidelines. https://www.nice.org.uk/guidance/ng12

question: A 72-year-old woman on long-term immunosuppression (azathioprine for renal transplant) is found to have multiple cutaneous squamous cell carcinomas at her annual skin check. Per NICE and transplant dermatology guidance, what additional risk does immunosuppression confer and what monitoring is recommended?

options.A: Immunosuppression has no effect on skin cancer risk or behaviour
options.B: Increased risk only applies to basal cell carcinomas, not SCC
options.C: Solid organ transplant recipients on immunosuppression have a 65-100 times higher risk of SCC compared to the general population; SCCs in this group are more aggressive (higher metastatic rate approximately 8% vs 4%); annual full skin examination by a dermatologist is recommended; sun avoidance and SPF50 sunscreen are essential
options.D: The risk normalises after 5 years of immunosuppression
options.E: Only HIV-positive patients have significantly elevated skin cancer risk

explanation.correct: Immunosuppression (organ transplant, haematological malignancy, HIV, iatrogenic) markedly increases risk of cutaneous SCC via: (1) impaired immune surveillance of UV-damaged cells; (2) direct oncogenic effect of some immunosuppressants (azathioprine generates oxidative DNA damage under UV). Solid organ transplant recipients: SCC risk 65-100x baseline; BCC risk 10x. Characteristics: multiple, often more aggressive, higher recurrence and metastatic rates. BRITISH TRANSPLANTATION SOCIETY and BAD guidance: annual full skin examination by dermatologist; consistent high-factor sunscreen (SPF50); sun-protective clothing; consider switching from azathioprine to mTOR inhibitor (sirolimus/everolimus) which has anti-tumour activity; acitretin (oral retinoid) reduces new SCC formation in high-risk cases.
explanation.A: Incorrect — Immunosuppression dramatically increases SCC risk; this is a major clinical concern in transplant medicine.
explanation.B: Incorrect — Both SCC and BCC risks are elevated, but SCC risk is disproportionately elevated (65-100x vs 10x for BCC).
explanation.C: CORRECT — 65-100x SCC risk in transplant recipients; more aggressive behaviour; annual dermatology surveillance and sun protection per BAD/BTS guidance.
explanation.D: Incorrect — The risk accumulates with cumulative immunosuppression duration and UV exposure — it does not normalise.
explanation.E: Incorrect — All forms of significant immunosuppression (transplant, HIV, haematological) elevate skin cancer risk.

reference: BAD — Guidelines for dermatological surveillance in organ transplant recipients. https://www.bad.org.uk/

question: A 48-year-old woman presents with persistent facial redness, flushing, papules and pustules on her cheeks, nose and forehead for 8 months. She has no comedones. She reports flushing with hot drinks and alcohol. Per NICE CKS, what is the diagnosis and first-line topical treatment?

options.A: Acne vulgaris — topical benzoyl peroxide
options.B: Systemic lupus erythematosus — check ANA and anti-dsDNA
options.C: Seborrhoeic dermatitis — topical ketoconazole shampoo
options.D: Rosacea — topical metronidazole 0.75% gel or cream applied twice daily; brimonidine gel for erythema; oral tetracycline (doxycycline 40mg modified release) for papulopustular rosacea unresponsive to topicals; avoid triggers (sun, alcohol, hot drinks, spicy food)
options.E: Perioral dermatitis — stop topical steroids and give oral metronidazole

explanation.correct: Rosacea: a chronic inflammatory facial skin condition characterised by: erythema and flushing (centrofacial), papules and pustules (no comedones — this distinguishes from acne), telangiectasia, and in severe cases rhinophyma (nose enlargement) or ocular involvement. Per NICE CKS: First-line topical: metronidazole 0.75% gel/cream (BD) or azelaic acid 15-20% gel. Brimonidine 0.33% gel: for persistent erythema (alpha-2 agonist — causes vasoconstriction). Oral antibiotics for moderate-severe papulopustular rosacea: doxycycline 40mg modified-release OD (anti-inflammatory dose) — preferred over standard-dose tetracyclines. Trigger avoidance: UV (SPF50), alcohol, hot drinks, spicy food, extreme temperatures. Ocular rosacea: lid hygiene + topical/oral antibiotics. No comedones distinguishes rosacea from acne.
explanation.A: Incorrect — Acne vulgaris has comedones (blackheads/whiteheads); rosacea does not. Benzoyl peroxide can irritate rosacea.
explanation.B: Incorrect — SLE butterfly rash spares the nasolabial folds; rosacea involves the nose and central cheeks with papulopustules — systemic lupus features would be additional.
explanation.C: Incorrect — Seborrhoeic dermatitis mainly affects the scalp, eyebrows, nasolabial folds with greasy scales; not papules/pustules on cheeks.
explanation.D: CORRECT — Rosacea: topical metronidazole 0.75% gel first-line; brimonidine for erythema; doxycycline 40mg MR for moderate disease per NICE CKS.
explanation.E: Incorrect — Perioral dermatitis is specifically around the mouth; rosacea is centrofacial. Also, perioral dermatitis is caused by topical steroid overuse — no mention of this here.

reference: NICE CKS — Rosacea. https://cks.nice.org.uk/topics/rosacea/

question: A 55-year-old man with rosacea has developed thickening, nodularity and enlargement of his nose over several years. His skin is oily with visible dilated follicles. Per NICE CKS, what is this complication and how is it managed?

options.A: Sebaceous hyperplasia — topical retinoids
options.B: Lymphoedema of the nose — compression and referral to lymphoedema clinic
options.C: Basal cell carcinoma — urgent 2WW referral
options.D: Acromegaly — check IGF-1 and growth hormone
options.E: Rhinophyma — a severe complication of rosacea affecting predominantly men; caused by hypertrophy of sebaceous glands and fibrotic thickening of nasal skin; medical treatment has limited effect once established; laser therapy (CO2 laser), electrosurgery or surgical debulking are the main treatments; refer to dermatology or plastics

explanation.correct: Rhinophyma: the most severe subtype of rosacea, predominantly in men; involves hyperplasia and fibrosis of sebaceous glands of the nose producing characteristic bulbous, irregular, thickened appearance with visible dilated follicles. Contrary to popular myth, rhinophyma is NOT caused by alcohol consumption. Once established, medical treatment (topical metronidazole, oral antibiotics) has limited effect on the structural changes. Management per NICE CKS and BAD: laser surgery (CO2 laser ablation — most evidence), electrosurgery, dermabrasion, or surgical debulking — all performed by dermatology or plastic surgery. Prevention: early aggressive treatment of rosacea before rhinophyma develops.
explanation.A: Incorrect — Sebaceous hyperplasia causes small yellowish facial papules, not the gross nodular enlargement of rhinophyma.
explanation.B: Incorrect — Nasal lymphoedema does not produce the sebaceous follicular changes characteristic of rhinophyma.
explanation.C: Incorrect — BCC causes a pearly rolled-edge nodule with telangiectasia — not generalised nasal enlargement with follicular dilation.
explanation.D: Incorrect — Acromegaly causes bony enlargement of the jaw, hands, feet, and coarsening of features — not isolated sebaceous nasal hypertrophy.
explanation.E: CORRECT — Rhinophyma: severe rosacea complication; laser/surgical treatment; medical therapy limited once established per NICE CKS.

reference: NICE CKS — Rosacea. BAD — Rosacea guidelines. https://cks.nice.org.uk/topics/rosacea/

question: A 40-year-old woman with rosacea has developed painful red eyes, gritty sensation, light sensitivity and blurred vision. Slit-lamp examination shows anterior uveitis and blepharitis. Per NICE CKS, what is the diagnosis and management?

options.A: Ocular rosacea — affects up to 50% of rosacea patients; manage with lid hygiene (warm compresses, lid massage, hypochlorous acid cleaning); lubricating eye drops for dryness; oral doxycycline 40mg MR for both skin and ocular inflammation; same-day ophthalmology referral for anterior uveitis (can cause permanent visual damage if untreated)
options.B: Allergic conjunctivitis — topical antihistamine eye drops
options.C: Dry eye syndrome only — artificial tears and discharge
options.D: Viral conjunctivitis — self-limiting, reassure
options.E: Herpes simplex keratitis — topical aciclovir eye ointment only

explanation.correct: Ocular rosacea occurs in approximately 50% of rosacea patients and can precede or follow skin manifestations. Features: blepharitis (lid margin inflammation), meibomian gland dysfunction, recurrent styes, conjunctivitis, and in severe cases: keratitis, episcleritis, anterior uveitis (iritis). Anterior uveitis requires SAME-DAY urgent ophthalmology referral — untreated uveitis causes synechiae (iris adhesions), glaucoma, cataracts, and permanent vision loss. Per NICE CKS: lid hygiene is the cornerstone of ocular rosacea management; oral doxycycline (anti-inflammatory effect on meibomian gland secretions) helps both skin and ocular disease; topical ciclosporin eye drops for severe cases. Ophthalmology co-management for ocular involvement beyond blepharitis.
explanation.A: CORRECT — Ocular rosacea with anterior uveitis: same-day ophthalmology referral + lid hygiene + oral doxycycline per NICE CKS.
explanation.B: Incorrect — Allergic conjunctivitis causes itching and watering, not the gritty/painful anterior uveitis pattern seen here.
explanation.C: Incorrect — Dry eye alone does not explain anterior uveitis; this requires urgent ophthalmology assessment.
explanation.D: Incorrect — Viral conjunctivitis is self-limiting but does not cause anterior uveitis with photophobia and visual blurring.
explanation.E: Incorrect — HSV keratitis causes dendritic corneal ulceration visible on fluorescein staining; the rosacea context points to ocular rosacea.

reference: NICE CKS — Rosacea. https://cks.nice.org.uk/topics/rosacea/

question: A 72-year-old woman has multiple rough, scaly, erythematous papules on her forehead and temples. They feel like sandpaper. She has had significant cumulative sun exposure. Per NICE CKS, what is the diagnosis and appropriate treatment?

options.A: Seborrhoeic keratoses — reassure, benign lesions
options.B: Tinea versicolor — topical antifungal
options.C: Actinic keratoses (solar keratoses) — premalignant lesions caused by cumulative UV damage; risk of progression to SCC approximately 0.1-0.5%/year per lesion; treatments include: diclofenac sodium 3% gel BD for 60-90 days (preferred for widespread field-change treatment), cryotherapy (single lesions), topical 5-fluorouracil, imiquimod, or photodynamic therapy (PDT); field treatment preferred when multiple lesions
options.D: Granuloma annulare — topical steroids
options.E: Discoid eczema — emollients and topical steroids

explanation.correct: Actinic keratoses (AK/solar keratoses): UV-induced dysplastic keratinocyte lesions; considered part of a continuum with SCC in situ and invasive SCC. Features: rough, scaly, erythematous or flesh-coloured papules/patches on sun-damaged skin; sandpaper texture on palpation; face, scalp, hands, arms most affected. Per NICE CKS: Risk of individual AK → SCC: 0.1-0.5%/year; but in a field of multiple AKs, the field is at risk. Treatment options: diclofenac sodium 3% gel (Solaraze) BD for 60-90 days — good tolerability, suitable for field treatment; cryotherapy — for isolated lesions; topical 5-FU (Efudix) — highly effective but significant local skin reaction; imiquimod 5% — immune modulation, 3x/week for 4 weeks; PDT — particularly good for face/scalp, cosmetically superior. All patients should use SPF50 sunscreen and reduce further UV exposure.
explanation.A: Incorrect — Seborrhoeic keratoses are benign 'stuck-on' warty plaques with a waxy surface; they are not rough sandpaper-like papules on sun-exposed areas.
explanation.B: Incorrect — Tinea versicolor causes hypo/hyperpigmented patches on the trunk; not rough scaly papules on the face.
explanation.C: CORRECT — Actinic keratoses: premalignant, UV-related; diclofenac 3% gel, cryotherapy, 5-FU, or PDT per NICE CKS.
explanation.D: Incorrect — Granuloma annulare causes smooth annular papules typically on the hands/feet in younger patients.
explanation.E: Incorrect — Discoid eczema causes coin-shaped itchy lesions with vesicles; not sun-exposed distribution rough keratotic papules.

reference: NICE CKS — Actinic keratosis. https://cks.nice.org.uk/topics/actinic-keratosis/

question: A 68-year-old man has been using diclofenac 3% gel for actinic keratoses for 60 days. He asks how much longer he needs to use it. Per NICE CKS product guidance, what is the recommended treatment duration for diclofenac sodium 3% gel (Solaraze)?

options.A: 28 days only — longer courses cause systemic absorption
options.B: Lifelong continuous treatment is required
options.C: 7 days only — the same as topical NSAID treatment for musculoskeletal pain
options.D: 60-90 days of twice-daily application — the recommended treatment duration for diclofenac 3% gel for actinic keratoses; full response may take 30 days post-treatment to assess; skin should be re-examined 3 months after treatment completion
options.E: Until lesions are no longer visible — no defined treatment duration

explanation.correct: Per NICE CKS and Summary of Product Characteristics for Solaraze (diclofenac sodium 3% gel): the recommended treatment is twice-daily application for 60-90 days. Mechanism: diclofenac inhibits COX enzymes, reducing prostaglandin-mediated proliferation of UV-damaged keratinocytes. Efficacy: approximately 50% complete clearance of AKs with full course. Review 3 months post-treatment to assess response. If incomplete clearance, further treatment (cryotherapy, 5-FU, PDT) may be needed for residual lesions. Advantages of diclofenac gel: well tolerated; no significant skin reaction (unlike 5-FU); suitable for field treatment on large areas. Caution: avoid in aspirin/NSAID allergy; may worsen renal function in susceptible patients.
explanation.A: Incorrect — 28 days is insufficient for actinic keratosis treatment with diclofenac gel; systemic absorption is minimal with topical application.
explanation.B: Incorrect — Diclofenac 3% gel is used as a finite treatment course; long-term continuous treatment is not the standard.
explanation.C: Incorrect — 7 days is the duration for musculoskeletal pain indication; actinic keratosis requires 60-90 days.
explanation.D: CORRECT — 60-90 days BD application is the recommended course for diclofenac 3% gel for AKs per NICE CKS/SPC.
explanation.E: Incorrect — A defined 60-90 day treatment duration is specified; the absence of visible lesions before the course ends does not mean treatment should stop early.

reference: NICE CKS — Actinic keratosis. https://cks.nice.org.uk/topics/actinic-keratosis/

question: A 75-year-old woman has a single 8mm actinic keratosis on her right forearm. A GP applies cryotherapy using liquid nitrogen. Per NICE CKS, what is the expected outcome and follow-up?

options.A: Single freeze-thaw cycle always achieves complete clearance — no follow-up needed
options.B: Cryotherapy is only effective for pigmented AKs
options.C: Cryotherapy is contraindicated for facial lesions — causes scarring
options.D: Two treatments are always required 1 week apart for all AKs
options.E: Cryotherapy with a single freeze-thaw cycle clears approximately 70-80% of individual AKs; review at 3 months post-treatment; if the lesion persists, thickens, ulcerates or fails to clear, consider biopsy to exclude SCC, and alternative treatment (PDT, 5-FU, excision)

explanation.correct: Cryotherapy with liquid nitrogen for actinic keratoses: simple, quick office procedure; most effective for single or few discrete, well-defined AKs. A single freeze-thaw cycle: clearance rate approximately 70-80% per lesion. Two freeze-thaw cycles: higher clearance (~85%) but more scarring risk. Per NICE CKS: review at 3 months post-treatment. Red flags requiring biopsy: persistent/recurrent lesion after adequate treatment; increase in thickness, induration, size; ulceration or bleeding (suggesting transformation to invasive SCC). Biopsy any lesion with concerning features — do not simply retreat without histological exclusion of SCC. Cryotherapy is suitable for facial AKs when carefully applied (avoid periorbital area); pigmentation changes (hypopigmentation) are a common side effect.
explanation.A: Incorrect — Complete clearance with single freeze is not guaranteed (~70-80%); follow-up at 3 months is essential.
explanation.B: Incorrect — Cryotherapy is effective for typical AKs regardless of pigmentation; it is not restricted to pigmented variants.
explanation.C: Incorrect — Cryotherapy is routinely used for facial AKs; temporary hypopigmentation is common but significant scarring is uncommon if technique is appropriate.
explanation.D: Incorrect — Two freeze-thaw cycles within a single session can improve efficacy; two separate treatment visits are not always required.
explanation.E: CORRECT — ~70-80% clearance with cryotherapy; review at 3 months; biopsy if persistent/thickened per NICE CKS.

reference: NICE CKS — Actinic keratosis. https://cks.nice.org.uk/topics/actinic-keratosis/

question: A 55-year-old woman with a known small cell lung cancer (SCLC) presents with hypokalaemia (K+ 2.9 mmol/L), hypertension, hyperglycaemia, and rapidly progressive proximal myopathy. Her urinary cortisol is markedly elevated and her ACTH is 450 pg/mL (very high). Per endocrine guidelines, what is the diagnosis?

options.A: Addison's disease — high ACTH with low cortisol
options.B: Pseudo-Cushing's syndrome from alcohol — no alcohol history mentioned
options.C: Pituitary Cushing's disease — MRI pituitary will show adenoma
options.D: Primary adrenal adenoma — low ACTH expected
options.E: Ectopic ACTH syndrome — SCLC (and other neuroendocrine tumours: bronchial carcinoid, pancreatic neuroendocrine) can secrete ACTH autonomously, causing very high ACTH and cortisol; features include hypokalaemia (cortisol acting on mineralocorticoid receptors), rapid onset, severe symptoms; ACTH-dependent Cushing's with very high ACTH not suppressed on high-dose dexamethasone and no pituitary lesion on MRI

explanation.correct: Ectopic ACTH syndrome: autonomous ACTH secretion by a non-pituitary tumour (most commonly: SCLC 50%, bronchial carcinoid, pancreatic NET, medullary thyroid carcinoma, phaeochromocytoma). Results in bilateral adrenal hyperplasia with massive cortisol overproduction. Features distinguishing ectopic from pituitary Cushing's: very high ACTH (>200 pg/mL); rapid onset/severe; marked hypokalaemia (cortisol saturates 11β-HSD2 → acts as mineralocorticoid); NOT suppressed by high-dose dexamethasone suppression test (vs pituitary Cushing's which does suppress); no pituitary adenoma on MRI; IPSS (inferior petrosal sinus sampling) shows no central:peripheral gradient. Treatment: treat the underlying tumour; cortisol-lowering agents (metyrapone, ketoconazole) to control Cushing's; bilateral adrenalectomy for refractory cases.
explanation.A: Incorrect — Addison's disease has high ACTH (compensatory) but LOW cortisol. This patient has ELEVATED cortisol causing Cushing's features.
explanation.B: Incorrect — Pseudo-Cushing's from alcohol: failed ONDST with otherwise mild features; no ectopic tumour context; ACTH is not this elevated.
explanation.C: Incorrect — Pituitary Cushing's disease: moderately elevated ACTH; suppresses on high-dose dexamethasone; pituitary adenoma on MRI. ACTH of 450 pg/mL is much higher than typical pituitary disease.
explanation.D: Incorrect — Primary adrenal adenoma causes ACTH-INDEPENDENT Cushing's — ACTH would be suppressed (LOW), not 450 pg/mL.
explanation.E: CORRECT — Ectopic ACTH from SCLC: very high ACTH + Cushing's features + hypokalaemia; not suppressed on high-dose dexamethasone.

reference: Endocrine Society — Cushing's guidelines. NICE CKS — Cushing's syndrome. https://cks.nice.org.uk/topics/cushings-syndrome/

question: A 38-year-old woman presents with fatigue, weight loss, postural dizziness and skin hyperpigmentation, including the buccal mucosa. Her GP suspects Addison's disease. Per NICE CKS, which is the most appropriate first-line test to confirm adrenal insufficiency?

options.A: Random serum cortisol — morning cortisol >400 nmol/L excludes Addison's
options.B: Short Synacthen test (SST) — 250 mcg tetracosactide IM; measure serum cortisol at 0 and 30 minutes; a peak cortisol <450 nmol/L (some labs 500 nmol/L) confirms adrenal insufficiency
options.C: 24-hour urinary cortisol collection
options.D: Dexamethasone suppression test — 1mg overnight dexamethasone
options.E: ACTH stimulation test using 1 mcg low-dose tetracosactide only

explanation.correct: Per NICE CKS (Addison's disease) and Society for Endocrinology guidance: the short Synacthen test (SST) is the gold standard investigation for suspected primary adrenal insufficiency (Addison's disease). Protocol: 250 mcg tetracosactide (synthetic ACTH) given IM or IV; serum cortisol measured at 0 minutes and 30 minutes. Normal response: peak cortisol ≥450 nmol/L (some centres use ≥500 nmol/L). Interpretation: peak cortisol <450 nmol/L = inadequate adrenal response = adrenal insufficiency confirmed. In acute adrenal crisis: do not delay treatment for SST — take blood for cortisol and ACTH, then give IV hydrocortisone immediately. Random cortisol: only useful if very low (<100 nmol/L in a sick patient) or very high (>550 nmol/L excludes Addison's); intermediate values require SST. Dexamethasone suppression test diagnoses Cushing's — the opposite condition.
explanation.A: Incorrect — Random serum cortisol is unreliable for diagnosis due to diurnal variation; a specific threshold cannot be applied without the Synacthen stimulation context.
explanation.B: CORRECT — Short Synacthen test is the gold standard for Addison's diagnosis: peak cortisol <450 nmol/L at 30 minutes = adrenal insufficiency per NICE CKS.
explanation.C: Incorrect — 24-hour urinary cortisol is used in the investigation of Cushing's syndrome (excess cortisol), not Addison's disease (deficient cortisol).
explanation.D: Incorrect — Dexamethasone suppression test is used to screen for Cushing's syndrome, not adrenal insufficiency.
explanation.E: Incorrect — Low-dose (1 mcg) SST may be marginally more sensitive for secondary adrenal insufficiency but is NOT the recommended standard first-line test per NICE CKS; the standard 250 mcg SST is used.

reference: NICE CKS — Addison's disease. https://cks.nice.org.uk/topics/addisons-disease/

question: A 48-year-old man presents with weight gain, hypertension, proximal myopathy, easy bruising and purple striae. His GP performs an overnight dexamethasone suppression test (ONDST) — 1mg dexamethasone at 11pm; 9am cortisol = 210 nmol/L. Per NICE CKS and endocrine society guidelines, what does this result indicate?

options.A: Normal — cortisol 210 nmol/L confirms suppression and excludes Cushing's
options.B: Failed suppression — cortisol >50 nmol/L after ONDST is a positive screen for Cushing's syndrome; this patient requires further confirmatory testing (repeat ONDST, 24-hour urinary free cortisol, late-night salivary cortisol) and endocrinology referral
options.C: The test is borderline — only retest if symptoms worsen
options.D: Adrenal insufficiency — cortisol 210 nmol/L is too low
options.E: This result confirms iatrogenic Cushing's — dexamethasone itself caused this result

explanation.correct: Overnight dexamethasone suppression test (ONDST): in normal individuals, 1mg dexamethasone at 11pm suppresses the hypothalamic-pituitary-adrenal axis and 9am cortisol should be <50 nmol/L. A 9am cortisol >50 nmol/L = FAILED SUPPRESSION = positive screen for Cushing's syndrome. This patient's cortisol of 210 nmol/L is well above the 50 nmol/L cutoff — a strongly positive screen. However, a single positive ONDST is not sufficient for diagnosis (false-positive rate ~15-20% from: depression, alcoholism, obesity, exogenous steroids, CBG-elevating drugs). Per NICE CKS and Endocrine Society: confirmatory tests required: low-dose dexamethasone suppression test (LDDST), 24-hour urinary free cortisol (×2 samples), late-night salivary cortisol; endocrinology referral. Then: ACTH measurement to determine cause (ACTH-dependent vs independent).
explanation.A: Incorrect — Cortisol 210 nmol/L AFTER ONDST is NOT suppressed (threshold is <50 nmol/L). This is a positive screen result.
explanation.B: CORRECT — Failed ONDST (cortisol >50 nmol/L): positive screen for Cushing's. Confirmatory testing + endocrinology referral per NICE CKS.
explanation.C: Incorrect — Cortisol 210 nmol/L is well above the 50 nmol/L cutoff — this is a clearly positive result, not borderline.
explanation.D: Incorrect — A cortisol of 210 nmol/L is not indicative of adrenal insufficiency (which would show a low cortisol without suppression stimulus).
explanation.E: Incorrect — The dexamethasone itself does not cause elevated cortisol — failed suppression means endogenous cortisol production is inappropriately high despite dexamethasone.

reference: NICE CKS — Cushing's syndrome. Endocrine Society guidelines. https://cks.nice.org.uk/topics/cushings-syndrome/

question: A 28-year-old man presents with polyuria (8 litres/day), polydipsia and a urine osmolality of 95 mOsm/kg (very dilute) with a serum osmolality of 302 mOsm/kg (elevated). Following a water deprivation test, urine osmolality remains <300 mOsm/kg after 8 hours of fasting. After administration of desmopressin, urine osmolality rises to 680 mOsm/kg. Per NICE CKS, what is the interpretation?

options.A: Primary polydipsia — normal response after desmopressin
options.B: Cranial (central) diabetes insipidus — urine fails to concentrate on water deprivation (= ADH-dependent mechanism is needed); responds dramatically to desmopressin (urine osmolality rises >50% from baseline), confirming the kidneys can respond to ADH but the pituitary is not producing adequate ADH; MRI pituitary urgently
options.C: Nephrogenic diabetes insipidus — kidneys cannot respond to desmopressin
options.D: Type 1 diabetes — check blood glucose urgently
options.E: Psychogenic polydipsia — reassure and reduce fluid intake

explanation.correct: Water deprivation test interpretation: (1) Normal: urine concentrates >600 mOsm/kg during deprivation; minimal desmopressin response (already maximally concentrating). (2) Cranial (central) DI: urine does NOT concentrate during deprivation (pituitary produces insufficient ADH); after desmopressin: urine concentrates >50% rise (kidneys respond normally — proving ADH deficiency not nephrogenic). (3) Nephrogenic DI: urine does NOT concentrate during deprivation AND does NOT respond to desmopressin (kidneys resistant to ADH). (4) Primary polydipsia: urine concentrates partially or fully during prolonged deprivation; minimal desmopressin response. This patient: no concentration on deprivation + dramatic response to desmopressin (95 → 680 mOsm/kg = >600% rise) = CRANIAL DI. Per NICE CKS: MRI pituitary/hypothalamus is mandatory (tumour, infiltrative disease, trauma, post-surgical); treatment: desmopressin nasal spray or oral.
explanation.A: Incorrect — Primary polydipsia shows urine concentration during water deprivation (osmoreceptors are intact but chronically suppressed). This patient did not concentrate at all during deprivation.
explanation.B: CORRECT — Cranial DI: no concentration on deprivation + responds to desmopressin. MRI pituitary urgently per NICE CKS.
explanation.C: Incorrect — Nephrogenic DI would show NO response to desmopressin (kidneys resistant to ADH). This patient had a dramatic response.
explanation.D: Incorrect — Type 1 diabetes causes hyperglycaemic osmotic diuresis with glucose in urine — different mechanism and different water deprivation test results.
explanation.E: Incorrect — Psychogenic polydipsia would show urine concentration during prolonged deprivation; this patient showed no concentration.

reference: NICE CKS — Diabetes insipidus. https://cks.nice.org.uk/topics/diabetes-insipidus/

question: A 32-year-old man undergoes a water deprivation test for suspected diabetes insipidus. After 8 hours of fasting, his urine osmolality is 180 mOsm/kg and serum osmolality is 310 mOsm/kg. Desmopressin is given. After 2 hours, his urine osmolality rises to 600 mOsm/kg. Per NICE CKS, what does this response confirm and what is the next investigation?

options.A: Primary polydipsia — the kidney responded to desmopressin
options.B: Cranial diabetes insipidus confirmed — the kidney CAN respond to exogenous ADH (desmopressin) but is not receiving sufficient endogenous ADH; MRI pituitary and hypothalamus urgently to identify the underlying cause (tumour, trauma, infiltrative disease, post-surgical, autoimmune, idiopathic)
options.C: Nephrogenic diabetes insipidus — no response to desmopressin expected
options.D: SIADH — characterised by concentrated urine and low serum osmolality
options.E: Type 2 diabetes mellitus — glucose-driven osmotic diuresis

explanation.correct: Water deprivation test recap: failure to concentrate urine during deprivation (urine osm 180, serum osm 310 = hyperosmolar serum + dilute urine) = DI confirmed. Post-desmopressin: urine osm rises from 180 → 600 mOsm/kg = >50% rise = CRANIAL DI (kidneys respond to exogenous ADH = kidneys are normal, problem is insufficient endogenous ADH production from posterior pituitary/hypothalamus). Per NICE CKS: MRI pituitary and hypothalamus is the key next investigation — identifies: craniopharyngioma, germ cell tumour, metastases, sarcoidosis, Langerhans cell histiocytosis, lymphocytic infundibulo-neurohypophysitis (autoimmune), post-surgical/traumatic damage. If MRI normal: repeat MRI in 6 months (small occult lesions may not be immediately apparent). Treatment: intranasal or oral desmopressin (synthetic ADH analogue).
explanation.A: Incorrect — Primary polydipsia: urine would concentrate DURING water deprivation (as endogenous ADH is present but chronically suppressed). This patient failed to concentrate during deprivation.
explanation.B: CORRECT — Cranial DI: failed water deprivation + responds to desmopressin. MRI pituitary/hypothalamus urgently per NICE CKS.
explanation.C: Incorrect — Nephrogenic DI: kidneys RESISTANT to ADH — desmopressin would have NO effect. This patient's urine concentrated markedly after desmopressin.
explanation.D: Incorrect — SIADH causes inappropriately concentrated urine with low serum osmolality — the opposite pattern to this patient.
explanation.E: Incorrect — Diabetic osmotic diuresis causes glycosuria-driven polyuria with hyperglycaemia; this is a different mechanism tested by different investigations.

reference: NICE CKS — Diabetes insipidus. https://cks.nice.org.uk/topics/diabetes-insipidus/

question: A 45-year-old man woke up this morning with complete loss of hearing in his right ear with no pain, vertigo or preceding illness. Audiometry confirms unilateral right-sided sensorineural hearing loss (SNHL). The Rinne test is positive bilaterally (AC>BC), and the Weber lateralises to the LEFT (better) ear. Per NICE CKS, what is the diagnosis and urgency of management?

options.A: Right conductive hearing loss from wax impaction — ear syringing
options.B: Idiopathic sudden sensorineural hearing loss (ISSNHL) — a medical emergency; audiometry confirms unilateral SNHL (Rinne positive on right, Weber to better/left ear); requires SAME-DAY urgent ENT referral for high-dose oral corticosteroids (prednisolone 1mg/kg/day) initiated within 72 hours of onset to maximise chance of recovery
options.C: Presbyacusis — gradual bilateral hearing loss in elderly patients; no urgent treatment needed
options.D: Noise-induced hearing loss — hearing protection advice and annual monitoring
options.E: Ménière's disease — betahistine and low-sodium diet

explanation.correct: Idiopathic sudden sensorineural hearing loss (ISSNHL): defined as ≥30 dB SNHL in 3 consecutive frequencies occurring within 72 hours. Cause unknown in ~90% (hence 'idiopathic' — viral, vascular and autoimmune hypotheses exist). Weber lateralises to the BETTER (left) ear in unilateral SNHL — because the healthy cochlea perceives sound better than the damaged right cochlea. This distinguishes SNHL from conductive loss (where Weber lateralises to the AFFECTED ear). Per NICE CKS and British Society of Audiology guidelines: ISSNHL is a medical EMERGENCY requiring SAME-DAY urgent ENT referral. Spontaneous recovery: approximately 32-65% without treatment. High-dose oral prednisolone (1mg/kg/day up to 60mg, for 10-14 days): significantly improves recovery rates if started within 72 hours of onset. Intratympanic corticosteroid injection: second-line option.
explanation.A: Incorrect — Wax impaction causes CONDUCTIVE hearing loss (Rinne negative — BC>AC; Weber lateralises to the AFFECTED ear). This patient has sensorineural loss.
explanation.B: CORRECT — ISSNHL: same-day urgent ENT referral, oral prednisolone 1mg/kg within 72 hours to maximise recovery per NICE CKS.
explanation.C: Incorrect — Presbyacusis is a bilateral gradual high-frequency hearing loss in elderly patients — not sudden unilateral SNHL.
explanation.D: Incorrect — Noise-induced hearing loss is gradual and bilateral (high-frequency initially) — not acute onset.
explanation.E: Incorrect — Ménière's disease causes episodic vertigo + fluctuating hearing loss + tinnitus + aural fullness — not sudden complete unilateral SNHL without vertigo.

reference: NICE CKS — Sudden sensorineural hearing loss. https://cks.nice.org.uk/topics/hearing-loss-in-adults/

question: A receptionist at a GP practice asks a doctor who qualifies for Statutory Sick Pay (SSP). A patient attends wanting to know if they qualify. Per current UK employment legislation, which statement about SSP eligibility is correct?

options.A: All employees qualify for SSP from day 1 of sickness absence
options.B: SSP is paid from day 4 of sickness absence (days 1-3 are 'waiting days' and are not paid); employees must have average weekly earnings above the lower earnings limit (£123/week as of 2024); it is paid at a fixed rate (£116.75/week as of 2024) for up to 28 weeks; it is paid by the employer, not the government; a fit note is required after 7 days of absence
options.C: SSP is paid by HMRC directly to the employee
options.D: GPs provide SSP certification — the fit note is the SSP certificate
options.E: SSP begins from day 1 if hospitalised, day 4 for all other absences

explanation.correct: Statutory Sick Pay (SSP) per UK government SSP rules (current 2024): qualifying criteria: employee earning ≥£123/week (lower earnings limit); must have been sick for at least 4 consecutive days (including non-working days). Waiting days: first 3 days are 'waiting days' — SSP is not paid. SSP rate: £116.75/week (2024-25). Duration: up to 28 weeks. Paid by: the EMPLOYER (not HMRC). After 28 weeks: employer may issue an SSP1 form directing employee to claim Universal Credit or Employment and Support Allowance. GP fit note: required after 7 days of sickness absence (first 7 days: employee can self-certify). Self-employed individuals, agency workers below earnings limit, and those who have already received 28 weeks SSP in the previous 3 years do not qualify.
explanation.A: Incorrect — SSP begins from day 4 of absence; days 1-3 are unpaid waiting days.
explanation.B: CORRECT — SSP from day 4, paid by employer at £116.75/week for up to 28 weeks; fit note after 7 days per DWP guidance.
explanation.C: Incorrect — SSP is paid by the employer, not directly by HMRC.
explanation.D: Incorrect — A GP fit note supports sickness absence and enables SSP after 7 days, but GPs do not issue SSP certificates — SSP administration is the employer's responsibility.
explanation.E: Incorrect — There is no different rule for hospital admissions; the 3 waiting days apply in all cases.

reference: DWP — Statutory Sick Pay guidance. https://www.gov.uk/statutory-sick-pay

question: A GP is asked to complete a DS1500 form for a patient with advanced metastatic lung cancer. Per DWP guidance and the FAST TRACK benefits system, what is the purpose and eligibility criteria for the DS1500?

options.A: DS1500 is a form for elderly patients over 80 to access heating allowance
options.B: The DS1500 (now the SR1 form from 2023) is a medical report supporting a 'Special Rules for Terminal Illness' (SRTI) claim allowing terminally ill patients to access certain DWP benefits (PIP, Universal Credit, ESA, DLA, AA) quickly without waiting periods or face-to-face assessments; eligible if the person has a progressive disease and death can reasonably be expected within 12 months
options.C: DS1500 provides evidence for housing benefit claims only
options.D: It is completed by the hospital consultant only — GPs cannot complete it
options.E: The patient must consent to the DS1500 — it cannot be completed without a direct patient request

explanation.correct: The DS1500 was replaced by the SR1 form from July 2023, but many practitioners still refer to it as DS1500. Purpose: a medical report supporting a Special Rules for Terminal Illness (SRTI) claim — formerly the '6-month rule', now updated to a '12-month rule' (progressive disease and death reasonably expected within 12 months). Benefits supported: Personal Independence Payment (PIP), Universal Credit, Employment and Support Allowance (ESA), Disability Living Allowance (DLA), Attendance Allowance (AA). Key features: expedited processing (fast-track without waiting periods); no face-to-face assessment for the claimant; can be completed by GP or hospital clinician; the patient does NOT have to know about the form (the doctor can complete it without telling the patient — to protect them from distress, if appropriate). Claim can be made by a third party (family, carer). Free to complete — no charge to patients.
explanation.A: Incorrect — DS1500/SR1 is for terminally ill patients of any age accessing fast-track benefits, not specifically for elderly patients or heating allowances.
explanation.B: CORRECT — SR1/DS1500: terminally ill patients (death within 12 months); fast-track DWP benefits access; GP or hospital clinician can complete; patient consent not required per DWP guidance.
explanation.C: Incorrect — DS1500/SR1 supports PIP, ESA, Universal Credit, DLA, AA — not housing benefit.
explanation.D: Incorrect — GPs can and regularly do complete DS1500/SR1 forms — it is not restricted to hospital consultants.
explanation.E: Incorrect — The patient does not need to be aware of or consent to the form — it can be completed to enable a family member to claim on their behalf.

reference: DWP — SR1 form (formerly DS1500). https://www.gov.uk/government/publications/sr1-supporting-information-for-terminal-illness

question: A junior doctor reports to a GP trainer that the lead consultant has repeatedly refused to grant her annual leave on multiple occasions without justification, creating significant personal and family difficulties for the junior doctor. Per GMC and NHS workplace guidance, what best describes this behaviour and what should the junior doctor do?

options.A: This is normal consultant behaviour — there is no issue to raise
options.B: This is workplace bullying — defined as behaviour that harasses, offends, or socially excludes a person or negatively affects their work; the junior doctor should document each incident, raise concerns informally with the consultant first if safe to do so, then use the formal trust grievance procedure; the GP trainer or educational supervisor should offer support; if safety concerns arise, the BMA can provide advice
options.C: The junior doctor should accept it — consultants have authority over junior leave
options.D: Only physical aggression constitutes workplace bullying
options.E: Raise concerns directly with the GMC as a first step

explanation.correct: Per GMC (Good Medical Practice), NHS Employers, and ACAS guidance: workplace bullying includes: harassment, exclusion, unreasonable allocation of workload, repeatedly refusing reasonable requests without justification. Refusing to grant annual leave repeatedly without good reason is a form of workplace bullying. It affects the doctor's wellbeing and potentially patient safety (fatigued doctors). Steps: (1) Document every incident with dates, witness details; (2) Attempt informal resolution (speak to consultant directly if safe); (3) Formal grievance through Trust HR/people management; (4) Educational supervisor / TPD involvement; (5) BMA legal and pastoral support; (6) NHS Speak Up Guardian (Freedom to Speak Up). GMC referral is for concerns about patient safety or fitness to practise — not the first step for workplace conduct issues. The GMC document 'Raising and acting on concerns about patient safety' and NHS England 'Freedom to Speak Up' policy are relevant frameworks.
explanation.A: Incorrect — Repeated unjustified refusal of annual leave constitutes workplace bullying per GMC and NHS guidance; it should not be accepted.
explanation.B: CORRECT — Workplace bullying: document, try informal resolution, use formal grievance, BMA support; educational supervisor involvement per GMC/NHS guidance.
explanation.C: Incorrect — Consultants do not have unchecked authority to repeatedly deny annual leave; doctors have employment rights and the right to raise concerns.
explanation.D: Incorrect — Workplace bullying encompasses psychological and behavioural mistreatment — not only physical aggression.
explanation.E: Incorrect — GMC referral is for patient safety/fitness to practise concerns; workplace bullying grievances should go through Trust HR/Freedom to Speak Up processes first.

reference: GMC — Good Medical Practice. NHS — Freedom to Speak Up. https://www.gmc-uk.org/ethical-guidance/ethical-guidance-for-doctors/good-medical-practice

question: A 22-year-old man presents with recurrent mild jaundice, particularly after a viral illness or prolonged fasting. His bilirubin is 38 umol/L (unconjugated), all other LFTs are completely normal. He is otherwise well and has had similar episodes since his late teens. Per NICE CKS, what is the most likely diagnosis and appropriate management?

options.A: Haemolytic anaemia — check reticulocyte count and Coombs test
options.B: Gilbert's syndrome — a benign autosomal recessive condition caused by reduced UGT1A1 enzyme activity leading to unconjugated hyperbilirubinaemia; exacerbated by fasting, illness, exercise and stress; completely benign with no treatment required; reassure the patient
options.C: Primary sclerosing cholangitis — urgent ERCP
options.D: Hepatitis B infection — serology and consider antiviral therapy
options.E: Crigler-Najjar syndrome — urgent liver transplant assessment

explanation.correct: Gilbert's syndrome: the most common hereditary cause of unconjugated hyperbilirubinaemia, affecting approximately 5-10% of the population. Caused by a promoter polymorphism in the UGT1A1 gene causing reduced glucuronyl transferase activity → impaired conjugation of bilirubin → mild unconjugated hyperbilirubinaemia. Triggers: fasting, infection, exercise, stress, menstruation, dehydration — all increase bilirubin release or reduce conjugation capacity. Clinical features: mild intermittent jaundice; all other liver function tests normal; normal FBC (no haemolysis); no liver pathology. Diagnosis: clinical — normal LFTs except mildly elevated unconjugated bilirubin; confirmed by genetic testing if needed. Management: completely benign; reassure patient; no treatment needed; advise regarding triggers. Crigler-Najjar is a severe form causing very high unconjugated bilirubin (kernicterus in infants) — not this mild presentation.
explanation.A: Incorrect — Haemolytic anaemia causes unconjugated hyperbilirubinaemia but also low Hb, raised reticulocytes, raised LDH — not normal LFTs and a well patient.
explanation.B: CORRECT — Gilbert's syndrome: benign unconjugated hyperbilirubinaemia precipitated by fasting/illness; reassure, no treatment per NICE CKS.
explanation.C: Incorrect — PSC causes conjugated hyperbilirubinaemia with cholestatic LFTs; typically associated with IBD.
explanation.D: Incorrect — Hepatitis B causes hepatocellular damage with elevated transaminases; all other LFTs are normal here.
explanation.E: Incorrect — Crigler-Najjar is a severe, rare condition presenting in infancy with very high bilirubin (>200 umol/L) requiring phototherapy and transplantation.

reference: NICE CKS — Gilbert's syndrome. https://cks.nice.org.uk/topics/gilberts-syndrome/

question: A 58-year-old man has been on PPI (omeprazole 20mg) for 12 months for reflux. He was very well controlled but now has recurrence of heartburn when he recently trialled stopping the PPI. An upper GI endoscopy shows specialised intestinal metaplasia in the distal oesophagus. Per NICE CG106, what is the diagnosis and surveillance requirement?

options.A: Oesophageal candidiasis — oral fluconazole and continue PPI
options.B: Barrett's oesophagus — replacement of normal squamous epithelium of the distal oesophagus with specialised columnar intestinal metaplasia due to chronic acid reflux; risk of progression to oesophageal adenocarcinoma (~0.1-0.3%/year); long-term PPI; endoscopic surveillance per NICE CG106 guidelines based on segment length
options.C: Oesophageal squamous cell carcinoma — urgent 2WW upper GI cancer referral
options.D: Helicobacter pylori infection — test and treat; no surveillance needed
options.E: Oesophageal motility disorder — oesophageal manometry

explanation.correct: Barrett's oesophagus (BO): replacement of the normal stratified squamous epithelium of the distal oesophagus with specialised intestinal metaplasia (columnar epithelium with goblet cells) as a result of chronic gastro-oesophageal reflux. Risk of progression to oesophageal adenocarcinoma: approximately 0.1-0.3%/year overall (higher with dysplasia). Per NICE CG106 (Barrett's oesophagus and gastro-oesophageal reflux disease): ongoing PPI for symptom control and mucosal protection; endoscopic surveillance: <3cm non-dysplastic BO: every 3-5 years; ≥3cm non-dysplastic: every 2-3 years; low-grade dysplasia: 6-monthly then annual; high-grade dysplasia: endoscopic mucosal resection (EMR) or radiofrequency ablation (RFA). Continued PPI is standard management.
explanation.A: Incorrect — Oesophageal candidiasis causes white plaques in immunocompromised patients; intestinal metaplasia is not candidiasis.
explanation.B: CORRECT — Barrett's oesophagus: intestinal metaplasia from chronic reflux; PPI + surveillance endoscopy per NICE CG106.
explanation.C: Incorrect — Barrett's without dysplasia is not oesophageal carcinoma; surveillance is the appropriate management.
explanation.D: Incorrect — H. pylori eradication is for peptic ulcer/gastritis; intestinal metaplasia in the distal oesophagus indicates Barrett's, not H. pylori.
explanation.E: Incorrect — Oesophageal manometry assesses motility disorders (achalasia, diffuse oesophageal spasm) — not indicated for Barrett's.

reference: NICE CG106 — Barrett's oesophagus. https://www.nice.org.uk/guidance/cg106

question: A patient with confirmed coeliac disease asks when they can stop their gluten-free diet. They feel completely well and their symptoms have resolved. Per NICE NG20, what is the correct advice?

options.A: They can reintroduce gluten after 2 years if they feel well
options.B: A gluten-free diet must be maintained lifelong — coeliac disease is a permanent autoimmune condition; even after mucosal healing and symptom resolution, gluten ingestion causes villous atrophy to recur; the gluten-free diet can only be stopped after repeat duodenal biopsy confirms mucosal healing (not before), but lifelong adherence is recommended as stopping increases risk of complications
options.C: The diet can be stopped once anti-tTG antibodies normalise
options.D: Children can stop the diet at puberty if the diagnosis was uncertain
options.E: The diet is optional once symptoms resolve — it is only needed for symptom control

explanation.correct: Per NICE NG20 (Coeliac disease: recognition, assessment and management): coeliac disease is a lifelong autoimmune condition triggered by gluten (in wheat, rye, barley). There is NO established 'cure' — a strict lifelong gluten-free diet is the only treatment. Even asymptomatic patients who reintroduce gluten develop villous atrophy and face increased long-term risks: refractory coeliac disease, enteropathy-associated T-cell lymphoma (EATL), small bowel adenocarcinoma, osteoporosis, and other autoimmune conditions. Anti-tTG antibody normalisation indicates dietary adherence and mucosal healing but does NOT mean the condition has resolved. A biopsy AFTER 12-24 months of strict gluten-free diet confirms mucosal healing (the clinical endpoint) — but this healing is dependent on continued diet adherence, not a sign that gluten can be reintroduced.
explanation.A: Incorrect — There is no timeframe after which gluten can be safely reintroduced in coeliac disease.
explanation.B: CORRECT — Lifelong gluten-free diet is mandatory in coeliac disease regardless of symptom resolution per NICE NG20.
explanation.C: Incorrect — Normalised anti-tTG confirms good dietary adherence; it does NOT mean the diet can be stopped.
explanation.D: Incorrect — Coeliac disease does not remit at puberty. If the diagnosis is genuinely uncertain, re-evaluation with a gluten challenge + biopsy is needed — not simply stopping the diet.
explanation.E: Incorrect — The gluten-free diet prevents long-term complications (lymphoma, adenocarcinoma, osteoporosis) — it is not merely for symptom control.

reference: NICE NG20 — Coeliac disease. https://www.nice.org.uk/guidance/ng20

question: A 62-year-old man presents with 3 months of progressive central abdominal pain, 8 kg weight loss, new-onset diabetes and a palpable epigastric mass. CT scan shows a hypoechoic mass in the head of the pancreas with biliary duct dilatation. Per NICE NG85, what is the most likely diagnosis and immediate management?

options.A: Chronic pancreatitis — oral pancreatic enzyme replacement
options.B: Lymphoma — CT-guided biopsy and haematology referral
options.C: Pancreatic cyst — surveillance USS in 12 months
options.D: Gastric cancer — urgent 2WW upper GI endoscopy
options.E: Carcinoma of the head of the pancreas — the triad of painless jaundice, weight loss and new-onset diabetes in an older patient with a pancreatic head mass; urgent CT (already done), Ca 19-9 tumour marker, biopsy planning; urgent HPB (hepatopancreatobiliary) surgical referral; assess resectability; Whipple's procedure (pancreaticoduodenectomy) if resectable

explanation.correct: Pancreatic ductal adenocarcinoma (PDAC), specifically pancreatic head carcinoma: the combination of progressive abdominal pain, significant weight loss, new-onset diabetes (exocrine/endocrine destruction), and a pancreatic head mass with biliary duct dilatation is highly suggestive. Classic 'painless jaundice' (Courvoisier's sign) occurs when the tumour obstructs the common bile duct. Per NICE NG85 (Pancreatic cancer in adults): urgent CT pancreatic protocol for staging; Ca 19-9 and CEA tumour markers (limited sensitivity); urgent HPB surgical referral; staging assessment: resectable (±Whipple's), borderline resectable (neoadjuvant chemotherapy), or metastatic (palliative chemotherapy — FOLFIRINOX or gemcitabine). Only approximately 20% of pancreatic head cancers are resectable at diagnosis. 5-year survival: <10% overall; approximately 25-30% post-Whipple in node-negative disease.
explanation.A: Incorrect — Chronic pancreatitis causes recurrent pain, steatorrhoea, gradual weight loss; the acute progressive presentation with a mass points to malignancy.
explanation.B: Incorrect — Pancreatic lymphoma is rare; the clinical picture, location and biliary dilatation are much more consistent with adenocarcinoma.
explanation.C: Incorrect — Pancreatic cysts on imaging are a different finding; a solid hypoechoic mass in the pancreatic head with biliary dilatation needs urgent cancer workup.
explanation.D: Incorrect — Gastric cancer causes upper GI symptoms (dysphagia, haematemesis); CT has already shown the pancreatic primary.
explanation.E: CORRECT — Pancreatic head carcinoma: abdominal pain + weight loss + new DM + mass + biliary dilatation. Urgent HPB referral; assess resectability per NICE NG85.

reference: NICE NG85 — Pancreatic cancer in adults. https://www.nice.org.uk/guidance/ng85

question: A 55-year-old man has a 3-month history of epigastric pain, reflux symptoms and unexpected thrombocytosis (platelets 620 × 10⁹/L). Helicobacter pylori breath test is negative. Per NICE NG12, what is the most appropriate next investigation?

options.A: Treat empirically with PPI and review in 4 weeks
options.B: Urgent upper GI endoscopy — unexplained thrombocytosis (reactive thrombocytosis is commonly associated with GI malignancy as a paraneoplastic phenomenon) combined with new upper GI symptoms in a 55-year-old warrants urgent endoscopy to exclude gastric or oesophageal carcinoma; thrombocytosis is a recognised red flag in upper GI cancer presentations
options.C: Haematology referral for suspected essential thrombocythaemia
options.D: Colonoscopy — thrombocytosis indicates lower GI pathology
options.E: Repeat FBC in 3 months to confirm persistent thrombocytosis

explanation.correct: Thrombocytosis (platelets >400 × 10⁹/L) in the context of GI symptoms: reactive thrombocytosis (secondary thrombocytosis) is common and has many causes including infection, inflammation, iron deficiency, and malignancy. Malignancy-associated thrombocytosis: tumours release cytokines (IL-6, IL-11, thrombopoietin) that stimulate platelet production; this is a well-recognised paraneoplastic phenomenon in GI, lung, ovarian, and other cancers. Per NICE NG12 (Suspected cancer): upper GI symptoms + thrombocytosis in patients ≥55 years is a reason for urgent 2WW upper GI endoscopy. Other 2WW criteria for upper GI cancer: dysphagia, unexplained weight loss + upper abdominal pain, persistent vomiting, iron deficiency anaemia, H. pylori positive with persistent symptoms after eradication. Do not simply attribute thrombocytosis to reactive cause without excluding malignancy in this age group with concurrent symptoms.
explanation.A: Incorrect — A 55-year-old with thrombocytosis and GI symptoms should not be empirically treated without endoscopic exclusion of malignancy per NICE NG12.
explanation.B: CORRECT — Thrombocytosis + upper GI symptoms age 55+: urgent 2WW upper GI endoscopy to exclude gastric/oesophageal cancer per NICE NG12.
explanation.C: Incorrect — Essential thrombocythaemia (myeloproliferative neoplasm) is possible but should only be considered after reactive causes (including malignancy) have been excluded.
explanation.D: Incorrect — The presenting symptoms are upper GI (epigastric pain, reflux); upper GI endoscopy is the appropriate first investigation.
explanation.E: Incorrect — Waiting 3 months to recheck FBC while a potential cancer progresses is dangerous and not compliant with NICE NG12.

reference: NICE NG12 — Suspected cancer: recognition and referral. https://www.nice.org.uk/guidance/ng12

question: A 50-year-old woman has unexplained thrombocytosis with platelets of 580 × 10⁹/L discovered on a routine blood test. She has no GI symptoms and a recent colonoscopy and upper GI endoscopy were both normal. Her inflammatory markers are also elevated. Per NICE NG12 and haematology guidelines, what is the next appropriate step?

options.A: Start aspirin 75mg — all thrombocytosis requires antiplatelet therapy
options.B: Investigate for reactive causes — thrombocytosis in this context may be reactive (infection, inflammation, iron deficiency, connective tissue disease, occult malignancy); check iron studies, CRP, CT chest/abdomen/pelvis, LFTs, TFTs; JAK2 mutation testing if reactive causes excluded (to assess for essential thrombocythaemia)
options.C: Bone marrow biopsy immediately — this is essential thrombocythaemia
options.D: Reassure — thrombocytosis is always benign in women
options.E: Start hydroxycarbamide — cytoreductive therapy for high platelet count

explanation.correct: Thrombocytosis work-up: reactive (secondary) thrombocytosis is far more common than primary (essential thrombocythaemia — ET). Common reactive causes: iron deficiency (most common), infection, inflammation, post-splenectomy, tissue damage, occult malignancy. Per NICE NG12 and haematology guidelines: with GI endoscopies normal, investigate for other reactive causes: iron studies (IDA is the most common cause of thrombocytosis); CT chest/abdomen/pelvis (occult malignancy, lymphoma); CRP/ESR (chronic inflammation); connective tissue screen; TFTs (hyperthyroidism). If ALL reactive causes excluded and thrombocytosis persists: JAK2 V617F mutation testing (positive in approximately 50-60% of ET); if JAK2 negative — consider CALR/MPL testing; bone marrow biopsy for definitive ET diagnosis. Do NOT start cytoreductive therapy without haematology-confirmed ET diagnosis.
explanation.A: Incorrect — Aspirin is used in ET for thrombosis prevention but is not automatically started for unexplained thrombocytosis before a diagnosis is confirmed.
explanation.B: CORRECT — Investigate reactive causes first (iron deficiency, inflammation, occult malignancy, CT staging); JAK2 testing if reactive causes excluded per haematology guidelines.
explanation.C: Incorrect — Bone marrow biopsy is required to confirm ET but is not the immediate next step; reactive causes must first be excluded.
explanation.D: Incorrect — Thrombocytosis is not always benign; occult malignancy, ET, and reactive causes all require investigation.
explanation.E: Incorrect — Hydroxycarbamide is cytoreductive therapy for confirmed high-risk ET; it must not be started without a confirmed diagnosis.

reference: NICE NG12. BSH — Guidelines for essential thrombocythaemia. https://www.nice.org.uk/guidance/ng12

question: A 45-year-old man is found to have a platelet count of 520 × 10⁹/L on a routine FBC. He also has a ferritin of 4 mcg/L (very low), MCV of 72 fl, and has complained of fatigue. Per NICE CKS, what is the most likely cause of his thrombocytosis?

options.A: Essential thrombocythaemia — JAK2 testing and haematology referral urgently
options.B: Iron deficiency anaemia causing reactive thrombocytosis — iron deficiency is the most common cause of a mildly elevated platelet count; the microcytic anaemia, very low ferritin, and thrombocytosis form a classic triad; treat with oral iron (ferrous sulphate 200mg TDS); recheck FBC after 4 weeks to confirm improvement and platelet normalisation
options.C: Polycythaemia vera — elevated red cell mass drives platelet overproduction
options.D: Myelofibrosis — splenomegaly with extramedullary haematopoiesis
options.E: B12 deficiency — macrocytic anaemia and thrombocytosis

explanation.correct: Iron deficiency anaemia (IDA) is the single most common cause of reactive thrombocytosis. Mechanism: iron deficiency stimulates thrombopoietin production and platelet generation; also, thrombocytes (platelets) share common progenitors with erythrocytes — iron-deficient erythropoiesis diverts progenitors toward platelet production. Classic triad: microcytic anaemia (low MCV, low Hb) + low ferritin + thrombocytosis. Per NICE CKS: treat IDA with oral ferrous sulphate 200mg TDS (or ferrous fumarate, ferrous gluconate); check Hb and MCV after 4 weeks (Hb should rise by 10 g/L per 2 weeks); platelet count typically normalises as IDA is corrected. Important: always investigate the CAUSE of IDA in adults (>50 years or with GI symptoms: colonoscopy/endoscopy to exclude GI blood loss/malignancy).
explanation.A: Incorrect — ET should only be considered after reactive causes (including IDA — the most common) have been excluded; this presentation with clear IDA is reactive.
explanation.B: CORRECT — IDA: most common cause of reactive thrombocytosis. Very low ferritin + microcytic anaemia + raised platelets = IDA. Treat with oral iron per NICE CKS.
explanation.C: Incorrect — Polycythaemia vera causes raised red cell mass (high Hb, low MCV not typical), not microcytic anaemia.
explanation.D: Incorrect — Myelofibrosis causes pancytopaenia, splenomegaly, and tear-drop red cells on film; not isolated thrombocytosis with IDA.
explanation.E: Incorrect — B12 deficiency causes macrocytic anaemia (high MCV) and typically thrombocytopaenia (low platelets), not thrombocytosis.

reference: NICE CKS — Iron deficiency anaemia. https://cks.nice.org.uk/topics/anaemia-iron-deficiency/

question: A GP partner is reviewing the practice complaints policy. A patient submits a formal complaint about a missed diagnosis. Per NHS England Complaints Handling guidance and the NHS Constitution, within what timeframe should the practice acknowledge the complaint?

options.A: Within 28 working days
options.B: Within 7 working days
