options.B: Parvovirus B19 (erythema infectiosum / fifth disease) — the child is now non-infectious (infectivity is highest during the prodromal phase before the rash appears); a pregnant contact who is seronegative is at risk of hydrops fetalis and fetal loss, particularly in the first 20 weeks
options.C: Roseola infantum (HHV-6) — high fever followed by diffuse macular rash
options.D: Scarlet fever — sandpaper rash with strawberry tongue requiring antibiotics
options.E: Kawasaki disease — requires urgent echocardiogram and aspirin

explanation.correct: Erythema infectiosum (fifth disease) is caused by Parvovirus B19. The classic presentation is slapped cheeks followed by a lacy/reticular rash on limbs/trunk. Crucially, by the time the rash appears, the child is NO LONGER infectious — the infectious period is during the prodromal phase (fever, rhinorrhoea). Implications for pregnant contacts: Parvovirus B19 can cross the placenta and infect the fetus — risk of fetal anaemia, hydrops fetalis, and miscarriage, especially before 20 weeks. Susceptible pregnant women exposed during the prodromal phase should be urgently referred for maternal-fetal medicine review, serology, and serial fetal USS monitoring.
explanation.A: Incorrect — Rubella causes a fine maculopapular rash with lymphadenopathy, not slapped cheeks with reticular rash.
explanation.B: CORRECT — Parvovirus B19: slapped cheeks + lacy rash; non-infectious once rash appears; risk of hydrops fetalis for seronegative pregnant contacts per NICE CKS.
explanation.C: Incorrect — Roseola causes high fever for 3-5 days followed by a macular rash as the fever breaks — no slapped cheeks.
explanation.D: Incorrect — Scarlet fever has a rough sandpaper rash on the trunk, strawberry tongue, and responds to penicillin.
explanation.E: Incorrect — Kawasaki disease requires prolonged fever ≥5 days plus other features; different from this presentation.

reference: NICE CKS — Parvovirus B19 infection. https://cks.nice.org.uk/topics/parvovirus-b19-infection/

question: A 28-year-old primary school teacher, 12 weeks pregnant, reports that several children in her class have been off school with 'slapped cheek disease'. She has no prior serology for parvovirus B19. Per RCOG and PHE guidance, what is the correct management?

options.A: Reassure — parvovirus B19 is harmless in pregnancy at 12 weeks
options.B: Arrange urgent serology (parvovirus B19 IgM and IgG): if IgG positive (prior immunity) — reassure, no further action; if IgG negative and IgM positive (recent/acute infection) — urgent referral to maternal-fetal medicine for serial fetal USS to monitor for hydrops fetalis and fetal anaemia
options.C: Advise her to leave work immediately and remain off until the outbreak resolves
options.D: Prescribe prophylactic aciclovir — effective against parvovirus B19 in pregnancy
options.E: Amniocentesis is the first-line investigation for parvovirus exposure in pregnancy

explanation.correct: Per RCOG Green-Top Guideline 33 (Management of Viral Rash Illness in Pregnancy) and PHE guidance: parvovirus B19 in pregnancy (especially first 20 weeks) carries a risk of fetal hydrops (approximately 9% if infection occurs before 20 weeks). By the time the rash appears in affected children, they are no longer infectious — but the teacher may have already been exposed during the prodromal phase. Serology is the key first step: IgG positive = immune (reassure). IgG negative + IgM positive = acute infection, urgent referral for serial USS (2-4 weekly) to detect fetal anaemia/hydrops. Treatment of fetal hydrops: intrauterine blood transfusion. There is no prophylactic treatment or vaccine.
explanation.A: Incorrect — Parvovirus B19 in the first 20 weeks carries a significant risk of fetal hydrops and miscarriage — this cannot be dismissed.
explanation.B: CORRECT — Serology first. If susceptible with recent exposure, urgent maternal-fetal medicine referral + serial fetal USS per RCOG GTG 33.
explanation.C: Incorrect — Exclusion from work is not routinely recommended as by the time the rash appears, children are no longer infectious.
explanation.D: Incorrect — Aciclovir is not effective against parvovirus B19; there is no antiviral treatment available.
explanation.E: Incorrect — Amniocentesis is not first-line for parvovirus exposure; serology and USS monitoring are the investigation pathway.

reference: RCOG GTG 33 — Viral Rash in Pregnancy. https://www.rcog.org.uk/guidance/browse-all-guidance/green-top-guidelines/viral-rashes-in-pregnancy-green-top-guideline-no-33/

question: A 32-year-old woman at 16 weeks gestation is confirmed to have acute parvovirus B19 infection (IgM positive, IgG negative). A fetal USS at 18 weeks shows moderate fetal ascites and scalp oedema consistent with early hydrops fetalis. Per RCOG guidelines, what is the definitive treatment for affected fetuses?

options.A: Maternal IV immunoglobulin — crosses the placenta and treats fetal anaemia
options.B: Intrauterine blood transfusion (IUT) — the fetal anaemia driving hydrops is treated by direct fetal blood transfusion via cordocentesis; this is performed at a tertiary fetal medicine centre; survival rates are significantly improved with early IUT
options.C: Emergency caesarean section at 24 weeks — delivery is the only treatment
options.D: Maternal IV aciclovir — antiviral treatment resolves fetal hydrops
options.E: Conservative management only — most cases of fetal hydrops from parvovirus resolve spontaneously without intervention

explanation.correct: Parvovirus B19 causes fetal anaemia by infecting erythroid precursors in the fetal bone marrow, leading to aplastic crisis. If severe, this results in fetal hydrops from high-output cardiac failure. Per RCOG GTG 33: the definitive treatment for fetal hydrops secondary to parvovirus B19 is intrauterine blood transfusion (IUT) via cordocentesis at a specialist fetal medicine centre. Procedure: needle inserted through the maternal abdomen into the umbilical vein under USS guidance; packed red cells transfused directly into the fetal circulation; may need to be repeated. Survival with IUT: approximately 80-85%. Without treatment, hydrops is associated with a high fetal mortality rate. Many cases in the second trimester do resolve spontaneously before intervention is needed, but established moderate-severe hydrops requires IUT.
explanation.A: Incorrect — There is no evidence that maternal IV immunoglobulin is effective for fetal parvovirus B19 hydrops.
explanation.B: CORRECT — Intrauterine blood transfusion via cordocentesis is the definitive treatment for fetal hydrops from parvovirus B19 per RCOG GTG 33.
explanation.C: Incorrect — Delivery at 24 weeks in a previable/extremely preterm fetus carries higher risk than IUT.
explanation.D: Incorrect — Aciclovir is not effective against parvovirus B19.
explanation.E: Incorrect — While mild cases may resolve, established moderate-severe hydrops has high fetal mortality without IUT and should not be managed conservatively.

reference: RCOG GTG 33 — Viral Rash in Pregnancy. https://www.rcog.org.uk/guidance/browse-all-guidance/green-top-guidelines/viral-rashes-in-pregnancy-green-top-guideline-no-33/

question: A 30-week pregnant woman attends her GP after spending time with a child subsequently confirmed to have chickenpox. She has no recollection of having had chickenpox or the varicella vaccine. The contact occurred 18 hours ago. Per RCOG and PHE guidance, what is the first step?

options.A: Administer varicella vaccine immediately — safe in any trimester
options.B: Check varicella IgG serology urgently — if immune (IgG positive), no further action needed; if susceptible (IgG negative), administer varicella zoster immunoglobulin (VZIG) as soon as possible within 96 hours of exposure
options.C: Start oral aciclovir prophylactically for 10 days
options.D: Admit to hospital immediately for monitoring — all chickenpox exposures in pregnancy require admission
options.E: Reassure — chickenpox in pregnancy at 30 weeks carries no significant fetal risk

explanation.correct: Per RCOG GTG 13 (Chickenpox in Pregnancy) and PHE guidance: first step is urgent varicella IgG serology — approximately 90% of UK adults are immune even without a recalled history of chickenpox. If IgG positive: immune, no action needed. If IgG negative (susceptible): administer VZIG (varicella-zoster immunoglobulin) as soon as possible, within 96 hours of contact. VZIG does not prevent infection but reduces severity. If she develops varicella despite VZIG: oral aciclovir if ≥20 weeks (before 20 weeks: risk of fetal varicella syndrome; after 20 weeks: maternal varicella pneumonia is the main risk). Varicella vaccine is a live attenuated vaccine — absolutely contraindicated in pregnancy.
explanation.A: Incorrect — Varicella vaccine is a live attenuated vaccine and is absolutely contraindicated throughout pregnancy.
explanation.B: CORRECT — Urgent varicella IgG serology first. If susceptible: VZIG within 96 hours per RCOG GTG 13.
explanation.C: Incorrect — Prophylactic aciclovir is not first-line for exposure without confirmed susceptibility; serology and VZIG are the priority.
explanation.D: Incorrect — Admission is not required for exposure alone — only if the woman develops varicella with complications.
explanation.E: Incorrect — Chickenpox at 30 weeks carries risk of maternal varicella pneumonia (serious) and neonatal varicella if near delivery.

reference: RCOG GTG 13 — Chickenpox in pregnancy. https://www.rcog.org.uk/guidance/browse-all-guidance/green-top-guidelines/chickenpox-in-pregnancy-green-top-guideline-no-13/

question: A 30-week pregnant woman with confirmed susceptibility to varicella develops a vesicular rash 3 days after her last VZIG dose. She is now febrile and short of breath. Per RCOG GTG 13, what is the immediate concern and management?

options.A: This is normal — chickenpox always causes a short-lived fever and does not require any specific treatment in the third trimester
options.B: Varicella pneumonia — a serious and potentially fatal complication of chickenpox in pregnancy; requires immediate hospital admission for IV aciclovir, oxygen, chest X-ray, and respiratory monitoring; neonatal team must be alerted given gestation
options.C: Start oral amoxicillin — this is secondary bacterial pneumonia requiring antibiotics
options.D: The breathlessness is from the pregnancy itself — no specific action needed beyond reassurance
options.E: Prescribe oral aciclovir 200mg five times daily and manage at home

explanation.correct: Varicella pneumonia is the most serious complication of chickenpox in pregnancy, occurring in up to 10% of pregnant women with varicella — significantly higher than in non-pregnant adults. It carries a maternal mortality rate of approximately 3-14% if untreated. Per RCOG GTG 13: any pregnant woman with chickenpox who develops respiratory symptoms (breathlessness, cough, hypoxia) must be admitted urgently for: IV aciclovir (10mg/kg TDS for minimum 5-7 days), oxygen therapy (target SpO2 ≥95%), chest X-ray (bilateral infiltrates), close monitoring. ICU involvement if deteriorating. Neonatal team must be alerted regarding timing relative to delivery (neonatal varicella risk if delivery within 7 days of rash onset).
explanation.A: Incorrect — Breathlessness in a pregnant woman with active varicella is a red flag for varicella pneumonia — not a benign finding.
explanation.B: CORRECT — Varicella pneumonia: immediately life-threatening in pregnancy; IV aciclovir + hospital admission per RCOG GTG 13.
explanation.C: Incorrect — Amoxicillin does not cover VZV; this is viral pneumonia requiring IV aciclovir.
explanation.D: Incorrect — Breathlessness in this context should always prompt assessment for varicella pneumonia — it must not be dismissed as pregnancy-related.
explanation.E: Incorrect — Oral aciclovir at the lower dose (200mg) and community management is insufficient for suspected varicella pneumonia — IV aciclovir and hospital admission are required.

reference: RCOG GTG 13 — Chickenpox in pregnancy. https://www.rcog.org.uk/guidance/browse-all-guidance/green-top-guidelines/chickenpox-in-pregnancy-green-top-guideline-no-13/

question: A 30-week pregnant woman with varicella (confirmed by a vesicular rash) delivers an emergency preterm infant 5 days after her rash appeared. The neonate appears well initially. Per RCOG GTG 13 and NICE CKS, what is the risk to the neonate and what prophylaxis should be given?

options.A: The baby is fully protected by maternal IgG — no action needed
options.B: Neonatal varicella: if the mother develops rash 5 days before to 2 days after delivery, insufficient time for protective maternal antibodies to develop and transfer; the neonate should receive VZIG immediately after birth and be monitored for disseminated neonatal varicella; IV aciclovir if rash develops
options.C: The baby only needs monitoring — VZIG is not indicated for term or preterm neonates
options.D: Vaccinate the baby with varicella vaccine at birth
options.E: Isolate mother only — the baby is not at risk as it did not have direct contact with lesions

explanation.correct: Per RCOG GTG 13: the highest risk period for neonatal varicella is when the mother develops the rash 5 days BEFORE to 2 days AFTER delivery — there is insufficient time for protective IgG antibodies to cross the placenta. Neonatal varicella from perinatal infection can cause disseminated infection with up to 30% mortality if untreated. Management: VZIG to the neonate immediately after birth; if neonatal varicella develops: IV aciclovir immediately. The neonate should be closely monitored in a neonatal unit. If the mother's rash appeared more than 7 days before delivery, adequate maternal antibodies have usually transferred and the risk to the neonate is much lower.
explanation.A: Incorrect — If the rash appeared only 5 days before delivery, there is insufficient time for adequate protective antibody transfer to the neonate.
explanation.B: CORRECT — Neonatal VZIG immediately if maternal rash 5 days before to 2 days after delivery; IV aciclovir if neonatal varicella develops per RCOG GTG 13.
explanation.C: Incorrect — VZIG IS indicated for neonates born in this time window per RCOG and PHE guidance.
explanation.D: Incorrect — Varicella vaccine is a live vaccine — not given to neonates.
explanation.E: Incorrect — Neonatal varicella can be transmitted via the airborne route as well as direct contact; the neonate is at risk.

reference: RCOG GTG 13 — Chickenpox in pregnancy. https://www.rcog.org.uk/guidance/browse-all-guidance/green-top-guidelines/chickenpox-in-pregnancy-green-top-guideline-no-13/

question: A 3-year-old boy presents with a 3-day history of profuse watery diarrhoea that has now become bloodstained. He has colicky abdominal pain and is irritable. His temperature is 38.1°C. He attended a birthday party 5 days ago. Per NICE NG184, what is the most likely causative organism?

options.A: Rotavirus — most common cause of viral gastroenteritis in young children
options.B: Enterohaemorrhagic Escherichia coli (EHEC/STEC — particularly E. coli O157:H7) — produces Shiga toxin causing bloody diarrhoea; associated with contaminated food at gatherings; risk of haemolytic uraemic syndrome (HUS) in children
options.C: Clostridium difficile — associated with prior antibiotic use
options.D: Giardia lamblia — causes chronic watery diarrhoea without blood
options.E: Campylobacter jejuni — the most common bacterial cause of gastroenteritis in the UK

explanation.correct: Enterohaemorrhagic E. coli (STEC/EHEC — especially O157:H7) is a key cause of bloody diarrhoea in children, particularly following food-borne outbreaks at parties or through contaminated meat. It produces Shiga toxin causing haemorrhagic colitis. Critical complication: haemolytic uraemic syndrome (HUS) — thrombocytopaenia, microangiopathic haemolytic anaemia, acute kidney injury — occurring in approximately 10-15% of paediatric STEC cases. Per NICE NG184: send stool cultures; check FBC, renal function, urine dipstick for haematuria/proteinuria; avoid antibiotics (may increase HUS risk by triggering Shiga toxin release); avoid anti-motility agents (loperamide). Notify PHE for food-borne outbreak investigation.
explanation.A: Incorrect — Rotavirus causes watery (not bloody) diarrhoea; blood in stool points to a bacterial or STEC cause.
explanation.B: CORRECT — STEC (E. coli O157): bloody diarrhoea after food gathering + risk of HUS; avoid antibiotics per NICE NG184.
explanation.C: Incorrect — C. difficile is associated with antibiotic use and healthcare settings — no mention of either here.
explanation.D: Incorrect — Giardia causes watery, offensive stool without blood; associated with contaminated water.
explanation.E: Incorrect — Campylobacter can cause bloody diarrhoea and is the most common bacterial cause overall, but the party outbreak context and HUS risk makes STEC the priority concern here.

reference: NICE NG184 — Diarrhoea and vomiting caused by gastroenteritis in under 5s. https://www.nice.org.uk/guidance/ng184

question: A 4-year-old girl has bloody diarrhoea following an E. coli O157 infection. On day 7 she becomes pale and oliguric. Her blood results show: Hb 72 g/L, platelets 38 × 10⁹/L, creatinine 185 umol/L, blood film showing schistocytes. Per NICE CKS, what is the diagnosis and management?

options.A: Severe dehydration — IV fluid resuscitation only
options.B: Haemolytic uraemic syndrome (HUS) — the triad of microangiopathic haemolytic anaemia, thrombocytopaenia and acute kidney injury; requires immediate PICU/renal admission, supportive care (dialysis if oliguric renal failure), platelet transfusions only if active bleeding, NOT for low platelet count alone; plasma exchange may be used; notify PHE
options.C: Immune thrombocytopaenic purpura — IV immunoglobulin and observation
options.D: Disseminated intravascular coagulation — fresh frozen plasma and cryoprecipitate
options.E: Leukaemia — bone marrow biopsy urgently

explanation.correct: Haemolytic uraemic syndrome (HUS): the classic triad of microangiopathic haemolytic anaemia (low Hb + schistocytes on film), thrombocytopaenia, and acute kidney injury, occurring typically 5-10 days after STEC diarrhoea in children. It is the most common cause of acute renal failure in children under 5 in the UK. Management per NICE CKS and paediatric nephrology guidelines: immediate hospital/PICU admission; supportive care — IV fluid management, antihypertensives; dialysis (peritoneal or haemodialysis) for oligoanuria/renal failure; do NOT transfuse platelets unless active life-threatening bleeding (transfusion can worsen microvascular thrombosis); do NOT use antibiotics or anti-motility drugs. Eculizumab (anti-C5 antibody) is used for atypical HUS.
explanation.A: Incorrect — This is not simple dehydration; the clinical picture is HUS requiring specialist paediatric nephrology management.
explanation.B: CORRECT — HUS: microangiopathic anaemia + thrombocytopaenia + AKI post-STEC. Supportive care, dialysis if needed, avoid platelet transfusion unless bleeding per NICE CKS.
explanation.C: Incorrect — ITP causes isolated thrombocytopaenia without haemolysis or renal failure.
explanation.D: Incorrect — DIC causes consumption of clotting factors (prolonged PT/APTT) — not the typical STEC-HUS picture.
explanation.E: Incorrect — Leukaemia would present differently without a preceding diarrhoeal illness and STEC exposure.

reference: NICE CKS — Haemolytic uraemic syndrome. https://cks.nice.org.uk/topics/haemolytic-uraemic-syndrome/

question: A 2-year-old girl presents with 48 hours of watery diarrhoea and vomiting. She is mildly dehydrated but alert. Her nappy shows no blood. Her mother asks if she should be given oral rehydration solution (ORS). Per NICE NG184, what is the first-line management for mild-moderate dehydration in this age group?

options.A: Intravenous Hartmann's solution — all young children with diarrhoea need IV fluids
options.B: Rice-based gruel or flat carbonated drinks — traditional home remedies
options.C: Oral rehydration solution (ORS — e.g. Dioralyte) given frequently in small amounts — 50 ml/kg over 4 hours for mild dehydration plus replacement of ongoing losses; continue normal feeding alongside; avoid fruit juices and carbonated drinks
options.D: Loperamide — reduces bowel motility and stops diarrhoea quickly
options.E: Antbiiotics empirically to prevent progression to bloody diarrhoea

explanation.correct: Per NICE NG184 (Diarrhoea and vomiting caused by gastroenteritis in under 5s): oral rehydration solution (ORS) is the first-line treatment for mild to moderate dehydration in children with gastroenteritis. Give 50 ml/kg ORS over 3-4 hours for mild dehydration. Continue normal diet/breastfeeding alongside ORS. Do NOT give: carbonated drinks, fruit juice, or rice water (hyperosmolar, worsen diarrhoea); loperamide (not licensed in under 12s, can cause ileus); antibiotics empirically. Red flags requiring hospital admission: clinical signs of severe dehydration, bilious vomiting, bloody diarrhoea, altered consciousness, high fever in young infant.
explanation.A: Incorrect — IV fluids are reserved for severe dehydration or failure of oral rehydration; not first-line for mild dehydration per NICE NG184.
explanation.B: Incorrect — Carbonated drinks and rice gruel are not recommended — they are hyperosmolar and worsen dehydration.
explanation.C: CORRECT — ORS (Dioralyte) 50 ml/kg over 4 hours for mild dehydration is first-line per NICE NG184.
explanation.D: Incorrect — Loperamide is not licensed in under 12s and is contraindicated in acute gastroenteritis in young children.
explanation.E: Incorrect — Empirical antibiotics are not recommended for acute gastroenteritis and may worsen STEC/HUS outcomes.

reference: NICE NG184 — Diarrhoea and vomiting in under 5s. https://www.nice.org.uk/guidance/ng184

question: A worried mother brings her 8-year-old boy to the GP with a 3-hour history of central abdominal pain. He has had one episode of nausea and reduced appetite. He is afebrile, his abdomen is soft and non-tender, and he is running around the waiting room without distress. His urine dipstick is normal. Per NICE CKS, what is the appropriate management?

options.A: Urgent referral to paediatric surgery — all abdominal pain in children must be investigated for appendicitis
options.B: Reassure and observe — non-specific abdominal pain in children is common and usually self-limiting; advise parents on red flags to watch for (persistent vomiting, worsening pain, fever, inability to walk/stand upright) and to return if concerned; no investigation or treatment needed at this stage
options.C: Prescribe oral amoxicillin — most childhood abdominal pain is due to mesenteric adenitis
options.D: Arrange urgent FBC and CRP — inflammatory markers are always needed for childhood abdominal pain
options.E: Arrange an urgent USS abdomen same-day

explanation.correct: Non-specific abdominal pain (NSAP) is the most common cause of acute abdominal pain in children — responsible for up to 35% of paediatric emergency abdominal presentations. Key features reassuring against a surgical emergency: short duration (3 hours), mild severity, no fever, soft non-tender abdomen, child is mobile and not distressed. Per NICE CKS and paediatric guidance: watchful waiting with clear safety-netting advice is appropriate. Red flags requiring same-day assessment/admission: severe constant pain, right iliac fossa tenderness with guarding, fever, bilious vomiting, inability to stand upright (suggesting peritonism), blood in stool. Antibiotics for mesenteric adenitis are not routinely indicated.
explanation.A: Incorrect — Not all childhood abdominal pain needs surgical referral; this presentation has no red flags.
explanation.B: CORRECT — NSAP in a well child: reassure, safety-net for red flags, no investigation needed per NICE CKS.
explanation.C: Incorrect — Antibiotics are not routinely indicated for non-specific abdominal pain or mesenteric adenitis.
explanation.D: Incorrect — Blood tests are not required for mild self-limiting abdominal pain without red flags.
explanation.E: Incorrect — USS is indicated if there is suspicion of appendicitis, intussusception, or other surgical pathology — not for mild NSAP.

reference: NICE CKS — Abdominal pain (acute) in children. https://cks.nice.org.uk/topics/abdominal-pain-acute-in-children/

question: A 3-year-old boy is brought with a 10-day history of increasing pallor, fatigue and multiple petechiae. On examination he is pale, has scattered petechiae on his trunk and legs, and has cervical lymphadenopathy. His FBC shows: Hb 68 g/L, WBC 42 × 10⁹/L, platelets 18 × 10⁹/L, blast cells on film. Per NICE NG12, what is the most likely diagnosis and next step?

options.A: Immune thrombocytopaenic purpura — reassure and repeat FBC in 2 weeks
options.B: Acute lymphoblastic leukaemia (ALL) — most common childhood malignancy; pancytopaenia + lymphadenopathy + blast cells on film; same-day urgent paediatric haematology referral is mandatory; do not delay for outpatient investigation
options.C: Aplastic anaemia — refer to haematology for bone marrow biopsy in 2 weeks
options.D: Iron deficiency anaemia — prescribe oral ferrous sulphate and review in 4 weeks
options.E: Viral infection — reassure mother and review in 1 week

explanation.correct: Acute lymphoblastic leukaemia (ALL) is the most common childhood malignancy, accounting for approximately 25% of all childhood cancers and 75% of childhood leukaemias. The classic presentation is pancytopaenia (anaemia, thrombocytopaenia, neutropaenia) from bone marrow infiltration, with blast cells on blood film. Associated features: lymphadenopathy, hepatosplenomegaly, bone pain, pallor, fatigue, petechiae/bruising. Per NICE NG12 (Suspected cancer) and NICE NG147 (Haematological cancers): same-day referral to paediatric haematology/oncology is required. Treatment: multi-agent chemotherapy (induction, consolidation, maintenance — total 2-3 years); 5-year survival >90% in children with standard-risk ALL.
explanation.A: Incorrect — ITP causes isolated thrombocytopaenia without anaemia or blast cells; WBC 42 × 10⁹/L with blasts cannot be attributed to ITP.
explanation.B: CORRECT — ALL: pancytopaenia + blasts + lymphadenopathy in a 3-year-old. Same-day urgent paediatric haematology referral per NICE NG12.
explanation.C: Incorrect — Aplastic anaemia causes hypocellular marrow and pancytopaenia without blast cells or WBC elevation to 42.
explanation.D: Incorrect — Iron deficiency causes microcytic anaemia but does not cause blast cells, elevated WBC or thrombocytopaenia.
explanation.E: Incorrect — Viral infections can cause mild transient pancytopaenia but not blast cells and WBC of 42 × 10⁹/L.

reference: NICE NG12 — Suspected cancer: recognition and referral. https://www.nice.org.uk/guidance/ng12

question: A 12-year-old boy attends for his routine immunisations. His parents ask which vaccine he should receive at this age. Per the UK immunisation schedule (NHS/PHE), which vaccine is offered to 12-13-year-old boys and girls in the UK?

options.A: Human papillomavirus (HPV) vaccine — offered to all boys and girls aged 12-13 (Year 8 in school) as part of the school immunisation programme; protects against HPV types 6, 11, 16, 18 (and additional types in the Gardasil-9 vaccine); prevents cervical, anal, penile, oropharyngeal cancers and genital warts
options.B: Meningococcal ACWY only
options.C: MMR booster — given at 12-13 years as a third dose
options.D: Hepatitis B booster — required at 12 years
options.E: BCG vaccine — routine schedule at 12-13 years

explanation.correct: UK childhood immunisation schedule (NHS England 2024): HPV vaccine (Gardasil-9) is offered at age 12-13 (Year 8) to all boys and girls as part of the school immunisation programme. Gardasil-9 protects against 9 HPV types: 6, 11, 16, 18, 31, 33, 45, 52, 58 — preventing approximately 90% of cervical cancers, genital warts, and other HPV-related cancers. Schedule: 2 doses given 6-12 months apart if started under 15; 3 doses if started 15 or over. Boys were added to the programme in 2019. Catch-up: available up to age 25 for missed doses. Td/IPV (diphtheria/tetanus/polio) booster is given at 14 years, NOT 12-13.
explanation.A: CORRECT — HPV vaccine (Gardasil-9) is given to all 12-13-year-olds (Year 8) in the UK school programme per NHS/PHE schedule.
explanation.B: Incorrect — MenACWY is given at 14 years (with Td/IPV), not 12-13 years.
explanation.C: Incorrect — MMR is given at 1 year and 3-4 years; there is no routine third dose at 12 years.
explanation.D: Incorrect — Hepatitis B booster is not a routine 12-year immunisation in the UK general schedule (it is in the newborn schedule for at-risk infants).
explanation.E: Incorrect — BCG is given at birth to at-risk neonates or to tuberculin test-negative children in high-risk groups; it is not a routine age-12 immunisation.

reference: NHS/PHE — UK childhood immunisation schedule. https://www.nhs.uk/conditions/vaccinations/nhs-vaccinations-and-when-to-have-them/

question: A 6-month-old infant is brought by her parents with fever 38.8°C for 24 hours, reduced feeding, and lethargy. Per NICE NG143, which feature would be a red flag warranting immediate emergency admission?

options.A: Temperature of 38.8°C in a 6-month-old with no other features
options.B: Temperature >37.5°C at this age alone
options.C: Reduced feeding with a normal capillary refill time
options.D: Mild tachycardia up to 150 bpm without other features
options.E: Non-blanching purpuric rash — a red flag for meningococcal septicaemia requiring immediate 999 call and IV/IM benzylpenicillin before transfer; other red flags include: bulging fontanelle, neck stiffness, altered consciousness, high-pitched cry, focal neurological signs, or signs of shock (capillary refill >2 seconds, mottled cold skin)

explanation.correct: Per NICE NG143 (Fever in under 5s: assessment and initial management) — traffic light system: Red features (immediate emergency assessment): non-blanching rash; bulging fontanelle; neck stiffness; altered consciousness; focal neurological signs; high-pitched unusual cry; HR >160 (0-12 months); SpO2 <95%; capillary refill >2 seconds; moderate-severe dehydration. Non-blanching purpuric rash: most critical red flag — indicates possible meningococcal disease until proven otherwise. Action: call 999 immediately; if suspected meningococcal disease, give benzylpenicillin 300mg IM/IV before transfer (do not delay transfer to set up IV). Amber features: parental concern; high fever duration >5 days; not responding to fever medications. Age <3 months with any fever: automatic high-risk.
explanation.A: Incorrect — Fever of 38.8°C alone in a 6-month-old without red flags is amber, not immediately red; it warrants assessment but not emergency admission automatically.
explanation.B: Incorrect — Any fever >38°C in a child aged 0-3 months is red; in a 6-month-old, the temperature alone without red/amber features is not a standalone admission criterion.
explanation.C: Incorrect — Reduced feeding with normal CRT is an amber feature; it warrants GP review but not automatic emergency admission.
explanation.D: Incorrect — HR 150 in a 6-month-old with fever is expected (fever raises HR); the red flag threshold is >160 bpm persistently without fever explanation.
explanation.E: CORRECT — Non-blanching purpuric rash = red flag; 999 + benzylpenicillin before transfer per NICE NG143.

reference: NICE NG143 — Fever in under 5s. https://www.nice.org.uk/guidance/ng143

question: A patient on methotrexate 15mg weekly attends with a sore throat. Their GP reviews the medication list and notices they were recently prescribed trimethoprim by an on-call doctor. Per BNF, what is the significance of this drug combination?

options.A: No significant interaction — trimethoprim is safe with methotrexate
options.B: Dangerous drug interaction — both trimethoprim and methotrexate are dihydrofolate reductase (DHFR) inhibitors; concurrent use causes severe folate deficiency leading to pancytopaenia (potentially fatal bone marrow suppression) and severe mucositis; trimethoprim must be stopped immediately and FBC checked urgently
options.C: Trimethoprim reduces methotrexate renal clearance only — monitor serum creatinine
options.D: The interaction is only significant with high-dose methotrexate used in oncology
options.E: Separate the doses by 4 hours — this eliminates the interaction

explanation.correct: Per BNF drug interactions (Appendix 1): trimethoprim-methotrexate interaction is a category A (major/contraindicated) interaction. Both drugs inhibit dihydrofolate reductase (DHFR): methotrexate inhibits DHFR as its primary therapeutic mechanism; trimethoprim also inhibits DHFR (its antibacterial mechanism in bacteria — with some human DHFR inhibition). Combined DHFR inhibition causes severe folate deficiency even in patients taking supplemental folic acid. Consequences: bone marrow suppression (pancytopenia — potentially fatal), severe mucositis, megaloblastic changes. This interaction applies to LOW-DOSE weekly methotrexate (for RA, psoriasis, IBD) — not only oncology doses. Management: stop trimethoprim immediately; check FBC urgently; consider folinic acid (leucovorin) if significant toxicity. Safe UTI alternatives: nitrofurantoin (if eGFR >45 and lower UTI), cefalexin.
explanation.A: Incorrect — This is a major, potentially fatal drug interaction listed in the BNF. Trimethoprim is NOT safe with methotrexate.
explanation.B: CORRECT — Dual DHFR inhibition: stop trimethoprim immediately, urgent FBC per BNF. This is a contraindicated combination.
explanation.C: Incorrect — While trimethoprim can reduce renal methotrexate clearance (secondary mechanism), the primary danger is dual DHFR inhibition causing bone marrow suppression.
explanation.D: Incorrect — The DHFR interaction applies to low-dose weekly methotrexate as well as high-dose oncology regimens.
explanation.E: Incorrect — Time-separation does not eliminate a pharmacodynamic interaction. Both drugs are systemically active for extended periods.

reference: BNF — Methotrexate drug interactions. https://bnf.nice.org.uk/interaction/methotrexate.html

question: A 15-year-old boy having an ingrowing toenail removed under local anaesthesia begins to experience perioral tingling, tinnitus, agitation and then a tonic-clonic seizure. His blood pressure drops and his heart rate slows. Per AAGBI guidelines on local anaesthetic systemic toxicity (LAST), what is the specific antidote?

options.A: IV naloxone — reverses opioid-induced seizures
options.B: IV diazepam — first-line treatment for all seizures
options.C: 20% Intralipid (lipid emulsion) 1.5 ml/kg IV bolus — the specific antidote for LAST; sequesters lipophilic local anaesthetic molecules in the bloodstream away from cardiac and neural tissue ('lipid sink' effect); follow AAGBI LAST guidelines
options.D: IV atropine 600 mcg — for the bradycardia
options.E: IV adrenaline 1mg — standard cardiac arrest protocol

explanation.correct: Local anaesthetic systemic toxicity (LAST): occurs from inadvertent intravascular injection or overdose of local anaesthetic. Neurological features (first): perioral tingling, tinnitus, agitation, metallic taste, followed by seizures and CNS depression. Cardiovascular features (later/more severe): bradycardia, hypotension, ventricular arrhythmias, cardiac arrest. Per AAGBI LAST guidelines: the SPECIFIC antidote is 20% Intralipid (intravenous lipid emulsion): immediate IV bolus of 1.5 ml/kg followed by infusion of 15 ml/kg/hour; can repeat bolus (up to 3 times); mechanism — 'lipid sink': lipid emulsion sequesters the highly lipophilic local anaesthetic (bupivacaine > lignocaine) away from cardiac and neural membranes. Standard resuscitation alongside: 100% oxygen, benzodiazepines for seizure control, CPR if arrest. Note: adrenaline doses should be reduced in LAST (small doses only — large doses worsen outcome). AAGBI Intralipid protocol should be available wherever local anaesthetic is used.
explanation.A: Incorrect — Naloxone reverses opioid toxicity — it has no effect on local anaesthetic toxicity.
explanation.B: Incorrect — Benzodiazepines control seizures symptomatically but Intralipid is the specific antidote that treats the underlying LA toxicity.
explanation.C: CORRECT — 20% Intralipid 1.5 ml/kg IV bolus is the specific antidote for LAST per AAGBI guidelines.
explanation.D: Incorrect — Atropine may transiently help bradycardia but does not address the underlying LA toxicity requiring Intralipid.
explanation.E: Incorrect — Standard cardiac arrest adrenaline 1mg doses can be harmful in LAST; Intralipid is the priority treatment.

reference: AAGBI — Management of Severe Local Anaesthetic Toxicity. https://www.aagbi.org/

question: A GP sees a newly licensed drug on a prescription with an inverted black equilateral triangle symbol (▼) next to its name. Per MHRA guidance, what does this symbol signify?

options.A: The drug is a controlled drug requiring a triplicate prescription
options.B: The drug has been recalled and should not be dispensed
options.C: The drug is not licensed in the UK and is experimental
options.D: The drug is a biosimilar and must be prescribed by brand name only
options.E: The drug is subject to additional monitoring — it is a newly licensed medicine or has a new indication; healthcare professionals are required to report ALL suspected adverse drug reactions via the Yellow Card scheme (MHRA); this includes adverse reactions that would normally be reportable only if serious for established drugs

explanation.correct: The black inverted triangle (▼) symbol: introduced by the EMA/MHRA to identify medicines subject to additional monitoring. It appears on the Summary of Product Characteristics (SmPC) and patient information leaflet. Medicines with ▼: newly approved medicines, biologicals (particularly biosimilars), medicines approved under exceptional circumstances, or medicines with conditional marketing authorisation. Reporting obligations: for medicines with ▼, ALL suspected adverse reactions should be reported via the MHRA Yellow Card scheme (not just serious ones — unlike established drugs where only serious/unlisted reactions need reporting). This accelerated pharmacovigilance helps identify new safety signals faster. The ▼ status is reviewed every 5 years and can be removed when sufficient post-marketing safety data is accumulated.
explanation.A: Incorrect — Controlled drugs use the schedule system (Schedule 1-5); they do not use the inverted triangle symbol.
explanation.B: Incorrect — A drug recall would be communicated by a separate MHRA Drug Alert — the ▼ symbol does not indicate recall.
explanation.C: Incorrect — The ▼ symbol is applied to licensed medicines only — it does not indicate unlicensed or experimental status.
explanation.D: Incorrect — Biosimilars require brand-name prescribing per MHRA guidance, but the ▼ symbol applies to any additional monitoring medicine, not biosimilars exclusively.
explanation.E: CORRECT — ▼ = additional monitoring; report ALL ADRs via Yellow Card (not just serious) per MHRA guidance.

reference: MHRA — Black triangle medicines. https://www.gov.uk/guidance/black-triangle-medicines

question: A 42-year-old woman with a 6-month history of nocturnal cough and breathlessness attends for review. Her peak flow diary shows readings consistently above 600 L/min throughout the day and night, with no diurnal variation. Her symptoms are worse after spicy meals and when she lies flat. Per NICE NG80, what is the most likely diagnosis?

options.A: Asthma — add a LABA to her existing ICS
options.B: Gastro-oesophageal reflux disease (GORD) — reflux-induced chronic cough and nocturnal breathlessness; peak flow consistently >600 with no diurnal variation effectively excludes variable airflow obstruction; trial of PPI (omeprazole/lansoprazole) and lifestyle advice is appropriate
options.C: Cardiac asthma from left ventricular failure — arrange echocardiogram urgently
options.D: COPD — arrange spirometry
options.E: Vocal cord dysfunction — refer to ENT

explanation.correct: Per NICE NG80 (Asthma: diagnosis, monitoring and chronic asthma management), the diagnosis of asthma requires objective evidence of variable airflow obstruction: peak flow diurnal variability >20% or bronchodilator reversibility on spirometry. A consistently high peak flow (>600 L/min) with NO diurnal variation effectively excludes asthma as the cause of these symptoms. GORD is a classic cause of nocturnal cough and breathlessness — acid reflux stimulates the oesophago-bronchial reflex (via vagal nerve) causing cough and bronchoconstriction; postural worsening (lying flat) and food triggers (spicy food) are classic GORD features. Management: lifestyle modification (head of bed elevation, avoid triggers, weight loss if overweight), trial of PPI for 4-8 weeks. If symptoms persist: 24-hour pH-impedance monitoring.
explanation.A: Incorrect — Adding LABA to ICS is the wrong approach when peak flow is consistently normal/high and shows no variability — this is not asthma.
explanation.B: CORRECT — No peak flow variability excludes asthma. Nocturnal cough + postural worsening + food triggers = GORD. PPI trial per NICE NG80.
explanation.C: Incorrect — Cardiac asthma (LVF) should be considered, but would not explain food-related and postural triggers without other LVF features.
explanation.D: Incorrect — COPD would show irreversible airflow obstruction on spirometry and typically in smokers with exertional symptoms.
explanation.E: Incorrect — Vocal cord dysfunction causes inspiratory stridor/wheeze — not primarily nocturnal cough with food triggers.

reference: NICE NG80 — Asthma: diagnosis, monitoring and chronic asthma management. https://www.nice.org.uk/guidance/ng80

question: A 58-year-old farmer presents with progressive dyspnoea on exertion and dry cough over 18 months. He has never smoked. Spirometry shows FEV1 84% predicted, FVC 72% predicted, FEV1/FVC ratio 1.17 (>0.70). Chest CT shows bilateral upper lobe ground-glass opacities. Per BTS guidelines, what does the spirometry pattern indicate and what is the most likely diagnosis?

options.A: Obstructive pattern — COPD from occupational dust exposure
options.B: Restrictive pattern (reduced FVC with preserved or raised FEV1/FVC ratio >0.70) — consistent with extrinsic allergic alveolitis (hypersensitivity pneumonitis) in a farmer with upper lobe ground-glass changes; likely caused by thermophilic actinomycetes in mouldy hay ('Farmer's lung'); further investigation: specific serum precipitins (IgG antibodies to relevant antigens), BAL, high-resolution CT
options.C: Normal spirometry — no respiratory disease
options.D: Mixed obstructive and restrictive — sarcoidosis
options.E: Restrictive pattern — idiopathic pulmonary fibrosis causing lower lobe honeycombing

explanation.correct: Restrictive spirometry pattern: reduced FVC (72% predicted) with preserved/elevated FEV1/FVC ratio (>0.70 = no obstruction). This distinguishes restriction from obstruction. Extrinsic allergic alveolitis (EAA/hypersensitivity pneumonitis): an immune-mediated granulomatous lung disease from repeated inhalation of organic antigens. Farmer's lung: caused by thermophilic actinomycetes in mouldy hay — classic occupational EAA. Features: progressive exertional dyspnoea, dry cough, systemic symptoms (malaise, fever in acute episodes), upper lobe predominant CT changes. Per BTS EAA guidelines: specific IgG serum precipitins to causative antigens; HRCT; bronchoalveolar lavage; spirometry (restrictive). Treatment: antigen avoidance (most important), oral prednisolone for severe disease. Note: IPF typically causes LOWER lobe honeycombing — not upper lobe changes.
explanation.A: Incorrect — COPD causes an OBSTRUCTIVE pattern (FEV1/FVC <0.70). This spirometry is restrictive. Non-smoker also makes COPD unlikely.
explanation.B: CORRECT — Restrictive spirometry + farmer + upper lobe ground-glass = extrinsic allergic alveolitis (Farmer's lung). Serum precipitins + HRCT per BTS.
explanation.C: Incorrect — Reduced FVC at 72% with elevated FEV1/FVC ratio is not normal — it is a restrictive pattern.
explanation.D: Incorrect — Sarcoidosis can cause a restrictive pattern, but the occupational history (farmer) and upper lobe ground-glass changes in this clinical context points to EAA.
explanation.E: Incorrect — IPF (UIP pattern) causes lower lobe subpleural honeycombing with traction bronchiectasis — not upper lobe ground-glass opacities in a farmer.

reference: BTS — Hypersensitivity pneumonitis guidelines. https://www.brit-thoracic.org.uk/quality-improvement/guidelines/hypersensitivity-pneumonitis/

question: A 34-year-old woman with known asthma presents with wheeze and breathlessness. Her peak flow is measured at 330 L/min. Her personal best is 500 L/min. Per BTS/SIGN asthma guidelines, how is this attack classified and what does this mean for management?

options.A: Moderate acute asthma — peak flow 50-75% of personal best; 330/500 = 66%; manage with salbutamol nebulisers, oral prednisolone 40-50mg, reassess in 15-30 minutes; admit if no improvement
options.B: Mild attack — salbutamol inhaler and discharge home
options.C: Severe acute asthma — peak flow <33% best; requires ICU
options.D: Life-threatening asthma — silent chest and SpO2 <92%
options.E: Near-fatal asthma — requires immediate intubation

explanation.correct: BTS/SIGN asthma classification by peak flow: Mild: PEFR >75% best/predicted; Moderate: PEFR 50-75% (330/500 = 66% = MODERATE); Severe: PEFR 33-50%; Life-threatening: PEFR <33% with any of: silent chest, cyanosis, feeble respiratory effort, bradycardia, hypotension, exhaustion, SpO2 <92%, PaO2 <8kPa, PaCO2 normal/high (indicating fatigue). Management of moderate attack: salbutamol 5mg nebuliser (or 4-10 puffs via spacer) every 20-30 minutes; ipratropium 500mcg nebuliser; oral prednisolone 40-50mg; 15-minute reassessment; discharge if PEFR recovers to >75% and sustained; written asthma action plan on discharge.
explanation.A: CORRECT — PEFR 330/500 = 66% = moderate asthma. Nebulised bronchodilators + oral prednisolone per BTS/SIGN.
explanation.B: Incorrect — PEFR 66% of best indicates a moderate attack, not mild. Mild would be >75% best.
explanation.C: Incorrect — Severe asthma is PEFR 33-50%; this patient is at 66% = moderate.
explanation.D: Incorrect — Life-threatening asthma criteria include PEFR <33% plus clinical features of exhaustion/cyanosis — not present here.
explanation.E: Incorrect — Near-fatal asthma requires hypercapnia/mechanical ventilation — this patient has moderate asthma by PEFR.

reference: BTS/SIGN — British Guideline on the Management of Asthma 2019. https://www.sign.ac.uk/our-guidelines/british-guideline-on-the-management-of-asthma/

question: A 29-year-old man is brought to A&E with severe acute asthma. His PEFR is 38% best, SpO2 94% on air, RR 28. He is given salbutamol nebs and ipratropium. Per BTS/SIGN, what is the next medication to add?

options.A: IV theophylline — first-line bronchodilator in severe asthma
options.B: Antibiotics — all severe asthma is caused by bacterial infection
options.C: IV/oral corticosteroids (prednisolone 40-50mg orally or IV hydrocortisone 100mg) — systemic corticosteroids are essential in all moderate-to-severe asthma attacks to reduce airway inflammation; IV magnesium sulphate 1.2-2g over 20 minutes is added in severe attacks not responding to initial bronchodilators
options.D: IV adrenaline — first-line for all severe asthma
options.E: Heliox (helium-oxygen mixture) — first-line in all severe attacks

explanation.correct: Per BTS/SIGN asthma guidelines: severe attack (PEFR 33-50% + RR >25 + HR >110 or inability to complete sentences). Step-wise management: (1) High-flow oxygen to target SpO2 94-98%; (2) Salbutamol 5mg nebulised with oxygen (repeat every 15-30 min); (3) Ipratropium 500mcg nebulised; (4) Systemic corticosteroids: prednisolone 40-50mg oral (or IV hydrocortisone 100mg if cannot swallow) — continue for 5 days; (5) IV magnesium sulphate 1.2-2g over 20 min — for severe/life-threatening attacks not responding to bronchodilators, or if SpO2 <92%. IV aminophylline: second-line, specialist use. ICU referral if deteriorating, PaCO2 rising, or PEFR <33% persisting.
explanation.A: Incorrect — IV theophylline is second-line/specialist use; systemic corticosteroids and IV magnesium are prioritised over aminophylline.
explanation.B: Incorrect — Antibiotics are not routinely given in acute asthma; viral triggers are most common. Only give if clinical evidence of bacterial infection.
explanation.C: CORRECT — Systemic steroids (prednisolone/hydrocortisone) + consider IV magnesium 1.2-2g for severe asthma per BTS/SIGN.
explanation.D: Incorrect — IV adrenaline is used for anaphylaxis, not routine severe asthma management.
explanation.E: Incorrect — Heliox is not standard first-line treatment in acute asthma per BTS/SIGN.

reference: BTS/SIGN — British Guideline on the Management of Asthma. https://www.sign.ac.uk/our-guidelines/british-guideline-on-the-management-of-asthma/

question: A GP practice nurse is giving asthma education to a newly diagnosed patient. He asks how to know when his asthma is out of control and he needs to act. Per NICE NG80, which peak flow reading should trigger him to call his GP urgently?

options.A: Any reading below 500 L/min
options.B: Any variation between morning and evening readings
options.C: Only if he cannot breathe at all — PEFR is not a useful guide
options.D: A peak flow reading below 75% of his personal best — this represents at least a moderate exacerbation; he should follow his written asthma action plan which should specify the threshold to call for help or start oral steroids
options.E: Below 200 L/min only — readings above this are always safe

explanation.correct: Per NICE NG80 and BTS/SIGN asthma self-management: a written personalised asthma action plan (PAAP) should be given to all patients with asthma. It defines action zones based on PEFR percentage of personal best: Green zone (>75-80% best): asthma well controlled, continue usual treatment. Yellow/amber zone (50-75% best): worsening asthma, start rescue medication and consider oral steroids, contact GP. Red zone (<50% best): severe attack — start oral prednisolone, call GP urgently or go to A&E. Patients with life-threatening features (<33% or SpO2 <92%) should call 999. The personal best is established over 2-4 weeks of optimal treatment.
explanation.A: Incorrect — The threshold depends on percentage of personal best, not an absolute number; 500 L/min may be normal for some patients.
explanation.B: Incorrect — Some morning dipping is expected in asthma; the action threshold is based on percentage of personal best, not any variation.
explanation.C: Incorrect — PEFR is a validated, practical tool for asthma self-monitoring and should be central to the self-management plan.
explanation.D: CORRECT — PEFR <75% personal best indicates at least moderate exacerbation; written action plan specifies threshold per NICE NG80.
explanation.E: Incorrect — 200 L/min is an absolute number and not appropriate as a universal threshold; percentage of personal best is the correct metric.

reference: NICE NG80 — Asthma: diagnosis, monitoring and chronic asthma management. https://www.nice.org.uk/guidance/ng80

question: A 26-year-old woman at 18 weeks gestation has poorly controlled asthma with daily symptoms and night waking. She is worried about taking prednisolone. Per NICE NG80 and RCOG guidance, what is the correct advice regarding oral prednisolone use in pregnancy for asthma?

options.A: All oral steroids are absolutely contraindicated in pregnancy and must be avoided
options.B: Oral prednisolone should be used when clinically indicated — poorly controlled asthma poses a greater risk to mother and fetus than the small risks associated with corticosteroid use; the benefits of treating acute severe asthma or preventing exacerbations in pregnancy clearly outweigh the risks
options.C: Use oral prednisolone only in the third trimester — it is safe after 28 weeks
options.D: Switch to intramuscular corticosteroids instead — the oral route is contraindicated in pregnancy
options.E: Reduce ICS dose first before considering oral prednisolone

explanation.correct: Per NICE NG80 and RCOG guidance on asthma in pregnancy: uncontrolled asthma in pregnancy carries significant risks — preterm birth, low birth weight, pre-eclampsia, perinatal mortality. These risks are greater than the risks associated with appropriate asthma medications. Oral prednisolone: safe in all trimesters when clinically indicated; there is a theoretical risk of oral cleft with first-trimester high-dose corticosteroids (very small, mainly with systemic steroids), but this does not outweigh the risk of severe uncontrolled asthma. Women should NOT be denied appropriate asthma therapy because of pregnancy. Inhaled corticosteroids and beta-agonists are considered safe throughout pregnancy. Oral prednisolone for acute severe asthma or as maintenance for severe disease: appropriate and recommended when necessary.
explanation.A: Incorrect — This is dangerous advice. Poorly controlled asthma in pregnancy is associated with serious maternal and fetal risks — corticosteroids are not absolutely contraindicated.
explanation.B: CORRECT — Oral prednisolone should be used when indicated in pregnancy — benefits outweigh risks of undertreating asthma per NICE NG80/RCOG.
explanation.C: Incorrect — There is no trimester-specific restriction; prednisolone can be used at any trimester when clinically indicated.
explanation.D: Incorrect — There is no evidence to support IM over oral route; this is not a recommended approach.
explanation.E: Incorrect — Poorly controlled asthma requires appropriate step-up, not step-down of ICS. If oral prednisolone is clinically indicated, it should be given.

reference: NICE NG80 — Asthma. RCOG — Asthma in pregnancy. https://www.nice.org.uk/guidance/ng80

question: A 9-year-old boy with asthma remains poorly controlled on a low-dose ICS (beclometasone 100mcg/day). He has daytime symptoms 3-4 times per week and wakes once weekly at night. Per NICE NG80 Step 2→3, what is the recommended next treatment step?

options.A: Add a long-acting beta-2 agonist (LABA) — salmeterol or formoterol — as an add-on to ICS; in children aged 5-12, LABA addition is the preferred step 3 intervention per NICE NG80; if no benefit from LABA within 6-8 weeks, consider stopping LABA and increasing ICS to medium dose
options.B: Start oral theophylline — first addition to ICS in children
options.C: Add montelukast (leukotriene receptor antagonist) only — no evidence for LABA in children
options.D: Start oral prednisolone daily — systemic steroids are step 3
options.E: Switch to a combined MART regimen immediately

explanation.correct: Per NICE NG80 (Asthma — paediatric pathway, age 5-16): Step 1: SABA as needed. Step 2: low-dose ICS (beclometasone 100-200mcg/day). Step 3: add LABA (salmeterol or formoterol) to ICS — this is the preferred addition for children aged 5 and over (similar to adults). If LABA response inadequate at 6-8 weeks: stop LABA, increase ICS to medium dose (400mcg/day), or add leukotriene receptor antagonist (LTRA — montelukast). Step 4: medium-dose ICS + LABA ± other add-ons (LTRA, slow-release theophylline). Step 5: refer to specialist; consider high-dose ICS, oral theophylline, or biologics. The MART regimen (maintenance and reliever therapy with combined ICS/LABA) is used in adults from step 3; its use in children under 12 is more limited.
explanation.A: CORRECT — Add LABA (salmeterol/formoterol) as step 3 addition to ICS in children 5-16 per NICE NG80; reassess at 6-8 weeks.
explanation.B: Incorrect — Oral theophylline is a step 4-5 option, not step 3 first addition in paediatric asthma per NICE NG80.
explanation.C: Incorrect — Montelukast (LTRA) can be used but LABA is the preferred first addition at step 3 for children ≥5 years per NICE NG80.
explanation.D: Incorrect — Daily oral prednisolone is a last resort step 5 option and should never be step 3.
explanation.E: Incorrect — MART regimen is used in adults from step 3; not routinely applied in children under 12 years.

reference: NICE NG80 — Asthma: diagnosis, monitoring and chronic asthma management. https://www.nice.org.uk/guidance/ng80

question: An 8-year-old girl with asthma is being reviewed at step 3. She is on ICS + salmeterol. Her asthma remains uncontrolled. The GP considers increasing to step 4. Per NICE NG80, before stepping up, what should be confirmed?

options.A: Step up immediately without further assessment
options.B: Order spirometry and CT chest before any step change
options.C: Confirm adherence to current treatment, correct inhaler technique, and that allergen/trigger avoidance has been optimised before stepping up — poor adherence or incorrect technique accounts for many cases of apparent treatment failure
options.D: Refer immediately to secondary care before any step 4 change
options.E: Swap to a different ICS molecule before stepping up the dose

explanation.correct: Per NICE NG80: before stepping up asthma treatment at any step, always check: (1) Adherence — poor adherence is very common (up to 50% of patients); (2) Inhaler technique — incorrect technique renders treatment ineffective; demonstrate and observe technique at every review; (3) Trigger/allergen avoidance — exposure to relevant triggers (pets, moulds, smoke) can prevent effective control regardless of medication; (4) Diagnosis — is this really asthma? (other causes of wheeze/cough). Only after these are confirmed should treatment be stepped up. Stepping down: when asthma is well controlled for ≥3 months, consider step-down every 3-6 months to find the minimum effective dose.
explanation.A: Incorrect — Stepping up without checking adherence and technique wastes opportunity to correct a common, easily fixable cause of poor control.
explanation.B: Incorrect — Spirometry is useful for diagnosis/monitoring but CT chest is not required before a step-up decision.
explanation.C: CORRECT — Check adherence, inhaler technique, and trigger avoidance before stepping up per NICE NG80.
explanation.D: Incorrect — Step 4 does not automatically require secondary care referral; step 5 (high-dose ICS + multiple add-ons failing) warrants specialist referral.
explanation.E: Incorrect — Switching ICS molecule is not a standard action before stepping up; dose and add-on therapy adjustments per the step protocol are correct.

reference: NICE NG80 — Asthma: diagnosis, monitoring and chronic asthma management. https://www.nice.org.uk/guidance/ng80

question: A 6-year-old boy is newly diagnosed with asthma and started on his first preventer inhaler. Per NICE NG80, what is the first-line preventer therapy and appropriate device for this age group?

options.A: Dry powder inhaler (DPI) with salmeterol — LABAs are first-line preventers
options.B: High-dose ICS immediately — higher doses are more effective from the start
options.C: Oral montelukast alone — swallowed tablets are easier for children than inhalers
options.D: Low-dose inhaled corticosteroid (ICS) via pressurised metered dose inhaler (pMDI) with spacer — beclometasone or budesonide 100-200mcg/day; spacer is essential for children to ensure adequate lung deposition; face mask attachment needed for children under 3 years
options.E: Oral prednisolone — systemic steroids are preferred in young children

explanation.correct: Per NICE NG80 and BTS/SIGN paediatric asthma: Step 2 (first preventer): low-dose ICS (beclometasone 100-200mcg/day or budesonide equivalent). Device: for children aged 5 and under — pMDI + spacer (± face mask for under 3s); for children 6-12 — pMDI + spacer preferred; DPIs can be used if the child can generate adequate inspiratory flow. Spacers dramatically improve drug delivery to the lungs: without a spacer, most of the drug deposits in the oropharynx; with a spacer, approximately 15-20% reaches the lungs vs 10% without. Instruct parents to clean spacers monthly (not after every use — electrostatic charge impairs drug delivery).
explanation.A: Incorrect — LABAs are never used as monotherapy in asthma; they are always added to ICS (step 3 add-on). ICS is the first-line preventer.
explanation.B: Incorrect — Always start with the lowest effective dose (step 2) and step up if needed — high-dose ICS carries greater systemic side-effect risk.
explanation.C: Incorrect — Montelukast is a second-line add-on or alternative preventer for mild disease; it is not recommended as sole first-line therapy per NICE NG80.
explanation.D: CORRECT — Low-dose ICS via pMDI + spacer is the correct first preventer at step 2 for a 6-year-old per NICE NG80.
explanation.E: Incorrect — Oral prednisolone as regular preventer is a step 5 last resort and causes significant systemic side effects; it is absolutely not first-line.

reference: NICE NG80 — Asthma: diagnosis, monitoring and chronic asthma management. https://www.nice.org.uk/guidance/ng80

question: A 22-year-old man with cystic fibrosis (CF) has bilateral finger clubbing, chronic productive cough, bronchiectasis on CT, and recurrent Pseudomonas aeruginosa chest infections. Per NICE NG78, what is the pathophysiology of finger clubbing in CF and what does its presence indicate?

options.A: Clubbing indicates liver disease from CF-related cirrhosis only
options.B: Clubbing in CF develops secondary to chronic hypoxia and inflammation from suppurative lung disease (bronchiectasis and recurrent infections); its presence correlates with severity and chronicity of pulmonary disease; other CF causes of clubbing: liver disease (biliary cirrhosis); clubbing per se does not change management but signals established chronic lung damage
options.C: Finger clubbing is a normal variant in CF patients
options.D: Clubbing indicates acute respiratory failure requiring immediate ventilation
options.E: Clubbing only occurs in CF patients with pancreatic insufficiency

explanation.correct: Finger clubbing: painless enlargement of the terminal phalanges with loss of the nail-bed angle and increased nail curvature. In CF, it develops from chronic suppurative pulmonary disease — bronchiectasis, recurrent Pseudomonas/Staphylococcus infections, and chronic hypoxia. Pathophysiology of clubbing: not fully understood; proposed mechanisms include platelet-derived growth factor (PDGF) bypassing the pulmonary microcirculation in hypoxic/inflamed lungs, megakaryocyte fragments, and systemic cytokines. CF-specific causes of clubbing: (1) Chronic suppurative lung disease (most common); (2) CF-related liver disease (biliary cirrhosis with portal hypertension). Per NICE NG78 (CF management): Pseudomonas eradication therapy at first isolation; long-term nebulised antibiotics (tobramycin/colistin) for chronic Pseudomonas; physiotherapy; CFTR modulators (e.g. ivacaftor/tezacaftor/elexacaftor combination) now transform prognosis for eligible genotypes.
explanation.A: Incorrect — Clubbing in CF is primarily from lung disease; liver disease is a secondary cause. 'Only' liver disease is incorrect.
explanation.B: CORRECT — Clubbing in CF: chronic suppurative lung disease + hypoxia; correlates with pulmonary disease severity per NICE NG78.
explanation.C: Incorrect — Clubbing is pathological in CF; it indicates significant chronic pulmonary or hepatic disease.
explanation.D: Incorrect — Established clubbing from chronic disease does not indicate acute respiratory failure; it reflects chronic, not acute, pathology.
explanation.E: Incorrect — Pancreatic insufficiency is a common CF complication causing malabsorption but is not the cause of finger clubbing.

reference: NICE NG78 — Cystic fibrosis: diagnosis and management. https://www.nice.org.uk/guidance/ng78

question: A 75-year-old woman with a long-term urethral catheter develops fever, rigors, confusion and loin pain. Her eGFR is 58 ml/min. Per NICE NG111 and NG195, which antibiotic should NOT be used for this upper UTI?

options.A: Co-amoxiclav — broad spectrum, covers catheter-associated pathogens
options.B: Nitrofurantoin — it achieves inadequate tissue concentrations in the renal parenchyma and is therefore contraindicated for upper UTI (pyelonephritis); it is only appropriate for uncomplicated lower UTI and is also contraindicated when eGFR <45 ml/min
options.C: Ciprofloxacin — appropriate if penicillin allergic
options.D: Trimethoprim — if susceptibility confirmed
options.E: Ceftriaxone IV — for severe urosepsis

explanation.correct: Per NICE NG111 and NICE NG195 (Urinary tract infection in adults — antimicrobial prescribing): nitrofurantoin is specifically contraindicated for upper UTI (pyelonephritis) because it does not achieve adequate tissue concentrations in the renal parenchyma (it is concentrated in urine but not in renal tissue/bloodstream). It is also contraindicated when eGFR <45 ml/min as it does not achieve adequate urinary concentrations and may cause peripheral neuropathy. For catheter-associated upper UTI (with fever, rigors, loin pain): co-amoxiclav (orally if well enough) or ceftriaxone IV (for urosepsis) are appropriate. Duration for upper UTI/catheter-associated UTI: 7-14 days (not 3 days as for uncomplicated lower UTI).
explanation.A: Incorrect — Co-amoxiclav IS appropriate for catheter-associated upper UTI per NICE NG111.
explanation.B: CORRECT — Nitrofurantoin: contraindicated for upper UTI (no renal tissue penetration) and contraindicated with eGFR <45 per NICE NG111/NG195.
explanation.C: Incorrect — Ciprofloxacin is an appropriate alternative for upper UTI in penicillin-allergic patients (though NICE advises caution regarding quinolone resistance).
explanation.D: Incorrect — Trimethoprim can be used for upper UTI if susceptibility is confirmed on culture, though it is less commonly first-line.
explanation.E: Incorrect — Ceftriaxone IV is appropriate for severe urosepsis requiring parenteral treatment.

reference: NICE NG111 — Urinary tract infection in adults. NICE NG195. https://www.nice.org.uk/guidance/ng111

question: A GP is reviewing a 78-year-old man's medication list. He is on rivaroxaban 20mg for AF and his recent eGFR is 32 ml/min. Per the BNF and NICE NG196, what monitoring is required before prescribing rivaroxaban and why is eGFR critical?

options.A: eGFR monitoring is not required for rivaroxaban — DOACs have fixed dosing
options.B: Creatinine clearance (CrCl) must be calculated before prescribing rivaroxaban and during treatment — rivaroxaban is 33% renally excreted; as CrCl declines, drug accumulation increases bleeding risk; rivaroxaban is contraindicated when CrCl <15 ml/min; dose reduction to 15mg daily is required when CrCl 15-49 ml/min in AF; at CrCl 32 ml/min this patient likely requires the 15mg daily dose, not 20mg
options.C: Warfarin must replace rivaroxaban at any eGFR below 50
options.D: Creatinine clearance only matters for dabigatran — other DOACs are unaffected by renal function
options.E: Stop rivaroxaban at eGFR <30 and switch to aspirin 75mg

explanation.correct: Per BNF and NICE NG196, rivaroxaban dosing in AF is governed by creatinine clearance (CrCl — calculated by Cockcroft-Gault equation, not eGFR): standard dose: 20mg daily with evening meal (CrCl >50 ml/min); REDUCED DOSE: 15mg daily with evening meal (CrCl 15-49 ml/min) — this patient with CrCl ~32 ml/min should be on 15mg, not 20mg; CONTRAINDICATED: CrCl <15 ml/min. The Cockcroft-Gault CrCl calculation is preferred over eGFR (which is standardised to body surface area) for DOAC dosing — particularly important in elderly, underweight patients where the difference can be significant. All DOACs require renal monitoring: rivaroxaban, apixaban, dabigatran, and edoxaban are all renally excreted to varying degrees. Annual CrCl monitoring (or more frequently if CrCl <60 ml/min) is recommended.
explanation.A: Incorrect — Renal function monitoring is specifically required for all DOACs, including rivaroxaban, as dosing depends on creatinine clearance.
explanation.B: CORRECT — CrCl 32 ml/min: rivaroxaban dose should be reduced to 15mg daily (CrCl 15-49 range) per BNF/NICE NG196. Regular CrCl monitoring required.
explanation.C: Incorrect — NICE NG196 does not recommend switching to warfarin for moderate CKD; dose adjustment of the DOAC is the appropriate response.
explanation.D: Incorrect — All DOACs require renal monitoring; dabigatran is the most renally excreted (~80%) but all DOACs are affected.
explanation.E: Incorrect — Aspirin is not an anticoagulant and is not appropriate for stroke prevention in AF; DOAC dose adjustment (not cessation) is correct.

reference: BNF — Rivaroxaban renal dosing. NICE NG196 — Atrial fibrillation. https://bnf.nice.org.uk/drug/rivaroxaban.html

question: A GP is reviewing a linear graph from a study showing that as BMI increases, systolic blood pressure also increases in a consistent upward linear trend. The correlation coefficient (r) is 0.78. Per EBM principles, what does this graph and r value represent?

options.A: This shows causation — higher BMI directly causes higher blood pressure
options.B: This shows a strong positive correlation (r = 0.78) between BMI and systolic blood pressure — as BMI increases, SBP tends to increase; r ranges from -1 to +1 (1 = perfect positive correlation, 0 = no correlation, -1 = perfect negative correlation); correlation does not imply causation; r² = 0.61 means 61% of the variation in SBP is explained by BMI
options.C: r = 0.78 represents a weak correlation — it is below 0.9 (the threshold for a strong correlation)
options.D: A linear graph proves that the relationship is causal and that treating obesity will directly lower blood pressure
options.E: The p-value is needed to interpret the graph — r = 0.78 is meaningless without it

explanation.correct: Correlation coefficient (r — Pearson's for linear relationships): measures the strength and direction of the linear relationship between two continuous variables. Values: +1 = perfect positive linear correlation; 0 = no linear correlation; -1 = perfect negative linear correlation. Strength interpretation: |r| < 0.3 = weak; |r| 0.3-0.7 = moderate; |r| >0.7 = strong. r = 0.78 is a STRONG POSITIVE correlation — as BMI increases, SBP increases. r² (coefficient of determination) = 0.78² = 0.61 = 61% of the variance in SBP is explained by BMI; 39% is explained by other factors. Critical limitation: CORRELATION DOES NOT IMPLY CAUSATION — there may be confounders (age, sodium intake, alcohol). A p-value tells you whether the correlation is statistically significant (unlikely to be due to chance) but does not affect the interpretation of the strength of the correlation (r = 0.78 remains a strong correlation regardless of p-value).
explanation.A: Incorrect — Correlation does not prove causation. A strong positive correlation demonstrates association, not a direct causal mechanism.
explanation.B: CORRECT — r = 0.78: strong positive correlation; r² = 0.61 (61% variance explained); correlation ≠ causation per EBM principles.
explanation.C: Incorrect — r = 0.78 is a STRONG correlation (>0.7). There is no universal threshold of 0.9 for 'strong' in clinical EBM.
explanation.D: Incorrect — A linear graph and correlation coefficient cannot prove causation; a randomised controlled trial would be needed to establish causal inference.
explanation.E: Incorrect — r = 0.78 has a clear interpretation (strong positive correlation) independently of the p-value. The p-value adds information about statistical significance but does not change the interpretation of r.

reference: BMJ Statistics Notes — Correlation. https://www.bmj.com/about-bmj/resources-readers/publications/statistics-square-one

question: A GP is reading a meta-analysis of 8 trials comparing a new antihypertensive to placebo. The forest plot shows most studies to the left of the line of no effect, with a diamond that does not cross the vertical line. The I² statistic is 78%. Per EBM principles, how should this result be interpreted?

options.A: The diamond to the left of no effect suggests the treatment reduces BP (benefit); however, I² of 78% indicates substantial heterogeneity (variability between studies); the pooled result should be interpreted cautiously — heterogeneity must be explored (different populations, doses, follow-up periods) before applying results to clinical practice
options.B: The treatment is effective and the results are consistent across all trials
options.C: I² of 78% means the study is invalid and should be ignored
options.D: The p-value determines the result — I² is irrelevant to interpretation
options.E: A diamond that does not cross the line means the treatment is harmful

explanation.correct: Forest plot interpretation: each horizontal line = one study (length = 95% CI; central point = effect estimate); line of no effect at 1.0 (RR/OR) or 0 (MD/SMD); diamond = pooled effect (width = 95% CI of pooled estimate; position = direction of effect). Diamond to the LEFT of no effect with narrow CI not crossing the line = statistically significant benefit. I² statistic (Higgins): measures % of variation between studies attributable to heterogeneity rather than chance. I² interpretation: 0-25% = low; 25-50% = moderate; 50-75% = substantial; >75% = considerable heterogeneity. I² = 78% = considerable heterogeneity. Clinical implication: the pooled estimate may not accurately represent a single consistent treatment effect; results may not be broadly generalisable; subgroup analyses and sensitivity analyses are needed to understand sources of heterogeneity.
explanation.A: CORRECT — Diamond left of no effect = benefit; I² 78% = considerable heterogeneity; interpret pooled result with caution per EBM principles.
explanation.B: Incorrect — I² of 78% indicates CONSIDERABLE heterogeneity — results are NOT consistent across all trials; this is a critical limitation.
explanation.C: Incorrect — High heterogeneity is a limitation, not invalidation; the study requires cautious interpretation, not dismissal.
explanation.D: Incorrect — I² is essential for interpreting meta-analysis validity; ignoring it gives a misleading picture of evidence quality.
explanation.E: Incorrect — Diamond to the LEFT of no effect (for outcomes like BP reduction where lower is better) indicates benefit, not harm.

reference: BMJ Statistics Notes — Forest plots and meta-analysis. https://www.bmj.com/about-bmj/resources-readers/publications/statistics-square-one

question: A dataset contains the following 7 values: 3, 5, 7, 9, 12, 15, 18. Per basic statistics, what is the mean?

options.A: 9 — the middle value
options.B: 12 — the most common value
options.C: 9.86 — the mean is calculated as the sum of all values (3+5+7+9+12+15+18=69) divided by the number of values (7); 69÷7 = 9.86
options.D: 7.5 — the average of the two middle values
options.E: 15 — the range midpoint

explanation.correct: Mean (arithmetic mean): sum of all values ÷ number of values. Calculation: 3+5+7+9+12+15+18 = 69. 69 ÷ 7 = 9.857 ≈ 9.86. Key statistical measures for this dataset: Mean = 9.86 (affected by all values including outliers); Median = 9 (middle value in ranked dataset — 4th of 7 values); Mode = none (all values occur once). Clinical relevance: mean is most appropriate for normally distributed data; median is preferred for skewed data (e.g. waiting times, income distributions, length of hospital stay) as it is not affected by extreme outliers.
explanation.A: Incorrect — 9 is the MEDIAN (middle value) not the mean. Mean and median only coincide in perfectly symmetric distributions.
explanation.B: Incorrect — 12 would be the mode if it were the most frequently occurring value; all values appear once so there is no mode.
explanation.C: CORRECT — Mean = sum (69) ÷ n (7) = 9.86.
explanation.D: Incorrect — Averaging two middle values is used to calculate the median in a dataset with an even number of values; this dataset has 7 values (odd), so the median is simply the 4th value.
explanation.E: Incorrect — Range midpoint = (max + min)/2 = (18+3)/2 = 10.5; this is the midrange, not the mean.

reference: BMJ Statistics Notes — Mean, median and mode. https://www.bmj.com/about-bmj/resources-readers/publications/statistics-square-one

question: A box-and-whisker plot shows the following features: lower whisker at 20, lower box edge at 35, central line at 50, upper box edge at 65, upper whisker at 80. Per EBM statistics, what value does the central line represent?

options.A: The mean of all data points
options.B: The range midpoint
options.C: The mode of the data
options.D: The median (50th percentile) — the value that divides the dataset into two equal halves; in a box plot the box spans the interquartile range (IQR = Q3 minus Q1 = 65-35 = 30); the central line is always the median
options.E: The standard deviation

explanation.correct: Box-and-whisker plot anatomy: Lower whisker: minimum value (excluding outliers) = 20; Lower box edge (Q1 = 25th percentile) = 35; Central line = MEDIAN (Q2 = 50th percentile) = 50; Upper box edge (Q3 = 75th percentile) = 65; Upper whisker: maximum value (excluding outliers) = 80. IQR = Q3 − Q1 = 65 − 35 = 30 (middle 50% of data). Outliers: plotted as individual points beyond the whiskers. Key: the central line is ALWAYS the MEDIAN, NOT the mean. In skewed data, the median line will not be in the centre of the box — it will be closer to Q1 (positive skew) or Q3 (negative skew). Box plots are particularly useful for visualising skewed distributions and comparing medians across groups.
explanation.A: Incorrect — The mean is not represented directly in a box plot; only the median, quartiles and range are shown.
explanation.B: Incorrect — Range midpoint = (max + min)/2 = (80+20)/2 = 50 in this case (coincidental equality with median here); the central line represents the MEDIAN, not the range midpoint.
explanation.C: Incorrect — The mode is not shown in a box plot.
explanation.D: CORRECT — Central line of a box-and-whisker plot = median (50th percentile).
explanation.E: Incorrect — Standard deviation is not shown in a box plot; it is represented in error bar graphs.

reference: BMJ Statistics Notes — Box-and-whisker plots. https://www.bmj.com/about-bmj/resources-readers/publications/statistics-square-one

question: A GP is reviewing data about colon cancer in a district. In 2018, 450 people in a population of 100,000 were living with a confirmed diagnosis of colon cancer. Per epidemiological definitions, what does this figure represent?

options.A: Incidence — the number of NEW cases diagnosed in 2018
options.B: Point prevalence — the number of people WITH the disease (existing + new) at a specific point in time expressed as a proportion of the population (450/100,000 = 4.5 per 1,000 at that point in time)
options.C: Period prevalence — the number of cases over a defined time period
options.D: Cumulative incidence — the risk of developing the disease over time
options.E: Mortality rate — the proportion who died from the disease

explanation.correct: Epidemiological measures: Point prevalence = total number of cases (existing + new) with the disease at a SPECIFIC POINT IN TIME ÷ total population at that time. Formula: Point prevalence = 450/100,000 = 0.0045 = 4.5 per 1,000 (or 0.45%). This is point prevalence because it is measured at a specific year (2018) and includes all living people WITH the disease at that time — not just new cases. Incidence = number of NEW cases diagnosed in a defined period. Period prevalence = number of cases at any point DURING a time period. Prevalence is affected by: incidence (new cases), duration of disease (longer survival → higher prevalence), immigration/emigration of cases. Conditions with high prevalence include chronic conditions; conditions with high incidence but short duration (death or cure) have lower prevalence.
explanation.A: Incorrect — Incidence counts only NEW cases diagnosed in the period. This figure includes all living people WITH the disease at the given time point.
explanation.B: CORRECT — Point prevalence: total existing cases at a specific time point ÷ population = 450/100,000 = 4.5 per 1,000.
explanation.C: Incorrect — Period prevalence counts cases at any point during a time interval, not at a single year snapshot.
explanation.D: Incorrect — Cumulative incidence = risk of developing the disease over a specified period (includes only new cases developing the disease).
explanation.E: Incorrect — Mortality rate = deaths from the disease ÷ population; this figure includes all living patients, not deaths.

reference: BMJ Statistics Notes — Measures of disease frequency. https://www.bmj.com/about-bmj/resources-readers/publications/statistics-square-one
